description: Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati, and to victory.
Sauti comes to the sages at Saunaka's twelve-year sacrifice and is asked where he has been.
The question to Sauti is answered in measured, fitting words.
Sauti says he heard Vyasa's epic recited, visited holy places, and came from Kurukshetra to offer them a story.
The sages ask for the history Vaishampayana recited at Janamejaya's sacrifice.
Sauti praises the supreme being and says the epic is told in many forms.
The cosmic egg, Brahma, the Prajapatis, gods and sages arise at the world's beginning.
The world is destroyed and renewed in cycles of ages.
Genealogy of gods leading to the Kurus, Yadus and Bharatas, and the scope of Vyasa's work.
The epic is read in different ways, long or short, by different scholars.
Brahma visits Vyasa, who lists the many subjects of his poem and complains that no scribe exists.
Brahma praises the poem and tells Vyasa to call on Ganesha.
Vyasa calls Ganesha and asks him to write the Bharata.
Ganesha agrees if his pen never stops; Vyasa answers that he must understand before writing, and he ties hard knots of verse.
Sauti says he knows 8,800 hard verses and that Ganesha too paused over them.
The epic is compared to an instrument that opens the blind eye and a lamp lighting a house.
The epic is described as a tree whose parts are the books, ending with the fruit and sap.
Vyasa had three sons by Vichitravirya's wives and then withdrew to his hermitage.
After they were grown and gone, Vyasa taught Vaishampayana, who recited it at the sacrifice.
The epic shows the Kuru house, Gandhari, Vidura, Kunti, Vasudeva and the Pandavas.
The epic's length in verses and who recited which version in which world.
The Pandavas are compared to a tree with Yudhishthira as the trunk of virtue.
Pandu's hunt, the curse that followed, the five sons born from gods, and their arrival with the sages.
The people of Hastinapura argue about the boys, then welcome them with joy.
The Pandavas study the Vedas and live safely in the city.
The people love the Pandavas for their virtues.
Arjuna wins Draupadi at the swayamvara and gains fame; the brothers prepare the Rajasuya.
Yudhishthira performs the Rajasuya after Jarasandha and Shishupala are slain; Duryodhana is envious and humiliated in Maya's hall.
Dhritarashtra allows the dice game; Krishna lets the quarrel run and the war follows.
Dhritarashtra ponders and begins to address Sanjaya.
Dhritarashtra says he never wanted war and starts listing the signs of his side's loss.
A long list of early events, from Draupadi's winning to her disgrace, each ending with no hope of success.
The list continues through the exile, Virata, Krishna's embassy, the war, the deaths of Bhishma, Drona, Karna and Duryodhana, and Aswatthaman's night attack.
He mourns Gandhari, left without children, kindred or family.
Only ten survive the war and he feels his mind failing.
Dhritarashtra faints from grief, then speaks again.
He wishes to end his life.
Sanjaya answers him, sighing, with weighty words.
Sanjaya lists great kings of the past who all died, and tells him that Time creates and ends all things.
Sanjaya's comfort calms Dhritarashtra, and Vyasa composes an Upanishad on the matter.
Sauti lists the many beings and subjects the epic describes, including the supreme spirit.
Reading the introduction frees one of sin and keeps one from trouble; the epic is like butter in curd.
Reciting even one foot at a funeral rite makes the offering inexhaustible.
The Veda is understood through history and the Puranas; hearing the epic gives long life and heaven.
The gods weighed the epic against the four Vedas, and it was heavier, hence the name Mahabharata.
Closing line: harmless practices become harmful when misused.
The sages ask Sauti to explain Samanta-panchaka.
Parashurama destroys the warrior class, makes five blood lakes there, and his ancestors appear and offer him a boon.
Parashurama asks to be cleansed of his sin and for the lakes to be holy; later the Kuru-Pandava armies gather and die on that same ground.
The sages ask what an Akshauhini is.
Sauti defines the army unit, gives the numbers of chariots, elephants, foot and horse, and lists how long each commander led the war.
Sauti praises the Bharata as the first of all texts and says it was recited at Janamejaya's sacrifice.
He says he will list the parts of the epic.
A long list of the sub-books in order, from the first to the last, with a line on the content of each.
Vyasa's hundred sub-books are grouped into eighteen books.
A detailed contents of the first book, Adi Parva, from the stories of Utanka and Bhrigu through the Pandavas' marriage, exile and the burning of the Khandava forest.
Contents of Sabha Parva: the hall, Rajasuya, dice game and exile.
Contents of Vana Parva: the forest years, Arjuna's weapons, Nala, pilgrimages, Savitri and the Rama story.
Contents of Virata Parva: the year in disguise, Kichaka's death, the cattle raids, Uttara's marriage.
Contents of Udyoga Parva: war preparations, Sanjaya's embassy, Krishna's peace mission and its failure.
Contents of Bhishma Parva: the Gita and Bhishma's fall.
Contents of Drona Parva: Drona as commander, Abhimanyu's death, Jayadratha's death, Ghatotkacha's death.
Contents of Karna Parva: Karna as commander and his death at Arjuna's hands.
Contents of Shalya Parva: Shalya's fall, Shakuni's death, and the club fight between Duryodhana and Bhima.
Contents of Sauptika Parva: Ashwatthaman's night raid on the sleeping Pandava camp.
Contents of Stri Parva: Dhritarashtra's rage and grief, the women on the battlefield, the cremations.
Contents of Shanti Parva: Yudhishthira's despair and Bhishma's teaching on duty.
Contents of Anushasana Parva: further teachings and Bhishma's death.
Contents of Aswamedhika Parva: the horse sacrifice, Parikshit's revival, and the golden treasure.
Contents of Asramavasika Parva: Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti retire to the forest.
The same book ends with Vidura's and Sanjaya's passing and news of the Vrishnis' fate.
Contents of Mausala Parva: the Vrishnis kill each other and Krishna and Balarama depart.
Introduces the seventeenth book.
Mahaprasthanika Parva: the Pandavas' last journey, in which the brothers fall one by one.
Svargarohana Parva: Yudhishthira refuses heaven without his dog, then sees hell and then heaven.
The Harivamsa is added as a supplement to the eighteen books.
Sauti praises the epic as the root of all later poetry and learning.
He tells the sages to turn to virtue and says hearing the epic removes sin.
Closing line that ends the contents section.
Chapter title card: the Paushya section begins.

At Janamejaya's long sacrifice at Kurukshetra, his three brothers beat the pup of Sarama. The pup runs crying to its mother, who storms in, asks why her innocent son was hit, gets no answer, and curses the brothers with sudden misfortune.
Alarmed by the curse, Janamejaya returns to Hastinapura after the sacrifice and starts searching for a priest who can undo it.

On a hunt the king finds the hermitage of the sage Srutasrava. He asks for the sage's son Somasrava as his priest and accepts the one condition, that the son gives any Brahmana whatever he asks. He orders his brothers to obey the new priest and conquers Takshashila.

New tale: the teacher Ayoda-Dhaumya has three pupils, Upamanyu, Aruni and Veda. Aruni is told to repair a broken water channel in a field, finds he cannot, and lies down in the gap to hold the water back.
Dhaumya asks where Aruni is, remembers sending him to the field, and takes the other pupils to find him.
Dhaumya calls out and Aruni rises from the channel, explaining what he did and letting the water escape as he came out.
Dhaumya names him Uddalaka for opening the channel, promises him success in all the Vedas and law books, and Aruni goes home.

Upamanyu is sent to herd the cows and comes back plump. Dhaumya forbids him in turn from keeping begged food, begging twice, drinking the cows' milk and sipping the calves' froth, until he has nothing left to eat.
Starving, Upamanyu eats the leaves of the arka plant, goes blind and falls into a pit. At sunset he has not returned, and the pupils report he went out with the cows.
Dhaumya guesses Upamanyu is weak from his restrictions and goes out with the pupils to look for him. Upamanyu answers from the bottom of a well and is told to praise the Aswins to get his sight back.
First part of Upamanyu's hymn to the Aswins, praising them as eternal, pure, and present in all things.
The hymn continues: the Aswins weave the year from night and day, and the 360 days are cows with a single calf, the year.
The hymn compares the year to a wheel with 720 spokes (days and nights) and twelve months, which the Aswins set in motion.
The hymn asks the Aswins to free him from the wheel of time, to make him independent of the five elements, and describes them as the Supreme appearing in forms.
The hymn recalls that the Aswins created the ten directions, the Sun and the sky, and that all sacrifices follow the Sun's course.
They mixed the three colours that make everything visible, and from these the world and its beings arose.
Upamanyu declares his worship of the Aswins and the sky they made, who give the results of all deeds yet are free of them.
He calls them parents of all and begs them for his sight.

The Aswins appear and offer him a cake. He refuses to eat it before offering it to his teacher, even after they say Dhaumya once ate theirs without offering it. Pleased, they promise him golden teeth, sight and good fortune.
Sight restored, Upamanyu tells Dhaumya everything and is blessed with knowledge of all the Vedas. This ends his trial.
The third pupil Veda is told to stay and serve. He endures heat, cold, hunger and thirst like a burden-ox and is rewarded with learning. This is his trial.
Veda leaves, marries and takes three pupils of his own, but treats them gently because he remembers his own hardships.
Kings Janamejaya and Paushya make Veda their priest. When he has to go away for a sacrifice, he leaves his pupil Utanka in charge of the house.
The women of the household tell Utanka his teacher's wife is fertile this month and that he should take the absent teacher's place. Utanka refuses, saying his teacher gave no such order.
Veda returns, hears what happened, praises Utanka and gives him leave to depart.
Utanka asks to bring a teacher's fee. Veda sends him to ask his wife, who asks for Queen Paushya's earrings, which she wants to wear on the fourth day to a feast for Brahmanas.
On the road Utanka meets a huge bull with a tall rider who makes him eat its dung and drink its urine, saying his teacher did the same. Utanka obeys, washes and goes on to King Paushya.
At the palace Utanka greets King Paushya and asks for the queen's earrings as a gift for his teacher.
Paushya sends him to the women's rooms. Utanka cannot find the queen and objects. The king says she cannot be seen by anyone who is ritually unclean from a meal and asks him to think.
Utanka remembers he washed while standing, which Paushya says is improper. He washes correctly, finds the queen, who gives him the earrings but warns him that Takshaka wants them.

Utanka brags that Takshaka cannot catch him. Paushya serves him a meal that is cold and has hair in it. Utanka curses the king to go blind, Paushya curses him to be childless, and Utanka tells him to look at the food himself.

Paushya sees the food really was unclean and begs forgiveness. Utanka says his curse stands but will lift soon; Paushya says he cannot undo his own. Utanka points out that curse cannot hold on unclean food and leaves with the earrings.

On the road a naked beggar keeps appearing and vanishing. While Utanka puts down the earrings to wash, the beggar grabs them and runs. Utanka catches him but the beggar becomes Takshaka and escapes into a hole to the serpent world.

Utanka tries to dig after him with a stick. Indra, seeing him struggle, sends the thunderbolt into the stick and widens the hole. Utanka goes in and sees the huge serpent city, and starts to praise the serpents.
First part of Utanka's praise of the serpents, naming Airavata, Dhritarashtra and their followers.
He praises Takshaka and his brother Srutasena and other serpents of Kurukshetra.
The earrings do not appear, so Utanka thinks and looks around. He sees two women weaving black and white thread on a loom, a twelve-spoked wheel turned by six boys, and a man with a horse.
Utanka recites verses about the wheel of time and the weaving of the world, praising Indra, god of thunder.

The man with the horse offers help. Utanka asks for control over the serpents. He is told to blow into the horse; fire and smoke pour out and threaten the serpent land. Terrified, Takshaka brings the earrings out and gives them back.
Utanka realises it is the day for the earrings and he is far away. The man tells him to ride the horse, which carries him to his teacher's house at once.
The teacher's wife is about to curse Utanka for being late when he arrives and presents the earrings. She blesses him instead.
Utanka tells his teacher about the delay caused by Takshaka, and asks what the weaving women, the wheel, the man with the horse and the man on the bull mean.

His teacher explains: the women are Dhata and Vidhata and the threads are night and day; the wheel is the year; the man is the rain god Parjanya and the horse is fire; the bull is Airavata, the rider Indra, and the dung was nectar, which saved Utanka's life.
Given leave to go, Utanka goes to Hastinapura, angry at Takshaka, and finds Janamejaya freshly back from Takshashila. He asks why the king acts like a child when something urgent needs him.
Janamejaya answers that he is doing his royal duty and asks what Utanka wants.

Utanka tells the king that Takshaka killed his father Parikshit and also turned back the healer Kasyapa. He urges Janamejaya to burn Takshaka in a snake sacrifice, which would also repay Utanka's own grievance.
The king flares up in anger at Takshaka, asks his ministers for the story of his father's death, and is overcome with sorrow when he hears it.
Closing line: the Paushya section of the Adi Parva ends.
Remainder of the closing line (title of the epic).
Heading: the Pauloma sub-section begins.

Sauti, standing before the sages at Saunaka's twelve-year sacrifice, says he has told Utanka's story and asks what to tell next. The sages say they will wait for Saunaka, whom they describe as learned, truthful and respected.
Sauti agrees. Saunaka finishes his prayers and offerings, returns to the sacrifice hall, sits among the priests, and begins to speak.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Saunaka asks whether Sauti has studied the old Puranas and the Bharata like his father, and requests the history of the Bhrigu family.
Sauti says he learned everything his father and Vaisampayana did and promises the Bhrigu story.
He lists Bhrigu's descendants: Chyavana, Pramati, Ruru, and Sunaka, an ancestor of Saunaka.
Saunaka starts a question about why Bhrigu's son was named Chyavana (the sentence continues in the next shot).
The question finishes: why was he named Chyavana?
Bhrigu's pregnant wife Puloma is alone while he bathes. A Rakshasa also named Puloma arrives, is welcomed with forest fruit, becomes lustful, and plans to carry her off.
He seizes her. It was for this woman that her father had first promised him before marrying her to Bhrigu, so he sees his chance.
He sees the sacred fire burning and asks Agni, the mouth of the gods, to say truthfully whose wife she is.
He presses Agni again. Agni fears speaking; the Rakshasa insists that, since Agni lives in every creature as witness, he must answer, then he will take her.
Agni answers slowly: she was chosen by the Rakshasa but not married to him with rites. Her father gave her to Bhrigu and the marriage was done before Agni, so she is Bhrigu's wife.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.

As the boar-demon runs with Puloma, the child falls from her womb, which is why he is called Chyavana. The demon is burnt to ashes. Brahma comforts the weeping mother and her tears become the river Vadhusara, which flows past Chyavana's hermitage.
Bhrigu angrily asks how the Rakshasa knew his wife. Puloma says Agni told him and that the child's brilliance saved her.
Bhrigu curses Agni: "Thou shalt eat of all things."
Closing line: the sixth section, the curse on Agni.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Agni replies that a truthful witness cannot be blamed, explains that he is the mouth through which gods and ancestors receive offerings, and asks how he can be an eater of unclean things.

Agni withdraws from all sacrificial fires; rites stop and creatures suffer. The gods and sages go to Brahma, who calls Agni and says the curse will only apply to his lower flame, and that everything burnt by Agni is purified.
Agni accepts, the gods and sages leave happy, and rituals resume.
Sauti sums up: this is how Agni was cursed and how the Rakshasa Puloma died and Chyavana was born.
Closing line: the seventh section of the Pauloma Parva ends.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Sauti repeats the line (Chyavana, Pramati, Ruru, Sunaka) and promises the full story of Ruru.

The Apsara Menaka bears a girl by the Gandharva king Viswavasu and abandons her by Sthulakesa's hermitage. The sage raises her and names her Pramadvara. Ruru sees her, falls in love, and Pramati asks for her hand; the wedding is fixed for an auspicious star.

Days before the wedding, while playing, Pramadvara steps on a hidden snake and is bitten. She dies, yet looks more beautiful than before. Sages and friends gather and weep, and Ruru, overwhelmed, withdraws.
Closing line: the eighth section ends.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Ruru runs into the forest and cries out, offering all his good deeds and vows if Pramadvara can live again.
A messenger from heaven tells him the dead cannot normally return, but the gods have made one provision to restore her.
Ruru asks what it is. The messenger says he must give half of his own life to her. Ruru agrees gladly.
The messenger and the Gandharva king ask Dharma, judge of the dead, to let Pramadvara rise with half of Ruru's life. Dharma agrees.
Pramadvara wakes as if from sleep. Because Ruru gave half his lifespan, his own life is cut short.
Their fathers marry them. Ruru, now vowing to destroy snakes, kills every serpent he sees.
In a forest Ruru finds an old Dundubha snake and lifts a staff to kill it. The snake asks what harm it ever did him.
Closing line: the ninth section ends.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Ruru says a snake killed his wife, so he has vowed to kill every snake and intends to kill this one.
The Dundubha says the snakes that bite men are different from Dundubhas, who are snakes in name only and share the sufferings but not the fortunes of other serpents.
Ruru sees the snake is terrified and does not kill it. He asks who it really is, and the snake says it was once a sage named Sahasrapat, cursed by a Brahmana. Ruru asks why and for how long.
Closing line: the tenth section ends.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Sahasrapat tells how he frightened his friend Khagama at his fire rite with a grass snake. Khagama cursed him to be a snake until Ruru appeared, and the sage said sight of Ruru would end the curse.

Restored to human form, Sahasrapat tells Ruru that the highest duty is to spare life, Brahmanas should be gentle, and ruling and punishing are for kings. He promises to tell of the snake-sacrifice of Janamejaya and how Astika saved the serpents.
Closing line: the eleventh section ends.
Heading: the Pauloma section continues.
Ruru asks why Janamejaya tried to destroy the serpents and how Astika saved them.
The sage replies that Brahmanas will tell him the story and disappears.
Ruru searches the woods, collapses, then goes home and asks his father, who tells him the story.
Closing line: the twelfth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section begins.
Saunaka asks why Janamejaya wanted to kill the snakes, why Astika saved them, and whose sons they were.
Sauti says the story is long and promises to tell it fully.
Saunaka asks to hear it at length.
Sauti says Vyasa first told this Purana, his father Lomaharshana repeated it, and he will tell it as he heard it.
Jaratkaru is a strict celibate ascetic who travels the world. One day he sees his ancestors hanging head down in a hole.
He asks who they are, noting that the rope holding them is being gnawed by a rat.
They say they are sages hanging for lack of descendants, because their son Jaratkaru does only austerities and will not marry.
Jaratkaru says he is that son.
He asks how to help them.
They tell him to marry and have a son, because becoming a father is worth more than penance.
Jaratkaru promises to marry only for their sake, with a bride who shares his name, offered freely, and to have a child with her so they can reach heaven.
Closing line: the thirteenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
After wandering without success, Jaratkaru asks aloud in the forest for a bride. Vasuki appears with his sister. The sage asks her name because he will wed only one with his own name.
Vasuki says her name is Jaratkaru and gives her to him. They marry with proper rites.
Closing line (numbered thirteenth in the source, though it is the fourteenth section).
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The mother of the snakes had cursed them to burn in Janamejaya's sacrifice. Vasuki married his sister to the sage to counter it, and their son Astika was born, a wise Vedic scholar.
Later, at the snake sacrifice, Astika saved his brothers and uncles. By his austerities, sacrifices and offspring he paid his debts to the sages, gods and ancestors.
Jaratkaru's ancestors rose to heaven, and he too went there after many years. Sauti ends his summary and asks what to tell next.
Closing line: the fifteenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka praises Sauti's speech and asks him to tell Astika's story in full as his father did.

Sauti tells how Prajapati's daughters Kadru and Vinata marry Kasyapa. Kasyapa offers each a boon: Kadru asks for a thousand equal snakes, Vinata asks for two sons stronger than all of them. Both are granted.

Kadru lays a thousand eggs and Vinata two. After five hundred years Kadru's hatch but Vinata's do not. Vinata breaks one egg early and finds a half-formed son, who curses her to become a slave unless she waits for the second egg. He rises to the sky as Aruna, charioteer of the sun.
After five hundred years the second egg hatches and out comes Garuda, who leaves his mother at once and flies off to find food.
Closing line: the sixteenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Kadru and Vinata see the beautiful horse Uchchaihsravas, who rose from the churning of the ocean.
Saunaka asks why the gods churned the ocean and how the horse arose.
Sauti describes shining Mount Meru, where the gods meet. Wanting nectar, they hear Narayana tell Brahma to churn the ocean with the gods and Asuras, to win nectar, herbs and jewels.
Closing line: the seventeenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Mount Mandara is described. The gods cannot lift it as a churning rod and ask Vishnu and Brahma for a plan.
Vishnu has Ananta tear up the mountain. The ocean agrees to be churned if it gets a share, and the king of tortoises agrees to carry the mountain on his back.
With Mandara as staff and Vasuki as rope (Asuras at the head, gods at the tail), they churn. Vasuki's smoke becomes rain clouds that refresh the gods.
The ocean roars, creatures are crushed, trees burst into fire, and the mountain burns until Indra puts the fire out with rain.
Plant juices turn the water into butter, but no nectar appears. The gods tell Brahma they are spent.
Brahma asks Narayana to give the gods strength.
Narayana gives them strength and tells them to resume.
Churning resumes. The moon, Lakshmi, Soma, the white horse, the jewel Kaustubha and Dhanwantari with the nectar jar rise. The Asuras shout that the nectar is theirs.

The elephant Airavata rises and Indra takes him. Then the poison Kalakuta spreads, and Siva swallows it at Brahma's request and becomes blue-throated. The Asuras prepare to fight, and Narayana charms them as a beautiful woman and takes the nectar.
Closing line: the eighteenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The Asuras attack the gods, but Vishnu, in female form with Nara, tricks them and takes the nectar.

The gods drink. Rahu drinks in disguise, the sun and moon warn the gods, and Narayana cuts off his head with a discus. Head and body fall, and the head's grudge against the sun and moon explains eclipses.
Narayana drops the disguise and the gods and Asuras battle on the shore. The field fills with blood, cries and fallen warriors.
Nara and Narayana join the fight. Narayana calls his discus Sudarsana, which arrives blazing and destroys Asuras by thousands.
The Asuras hurl mountains from the sky. Nara shatters them with golden arrows. Seeing the discus, the Asuras flee into the earth and the sea.
The gods return Mandara to its place, shout in victory, go home, and give the nectar to Narayana to guard.
Closing line: the nineteenth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Sauti ends the churning story. Kadru and Vinata argue about the colour of the horse Uchchaihsravas and wager slavery: Vinata says it is all white, Kadru says the tail is black.

Kadru tells her snake sons to become black hairs on the tail. They refuse, so she curses them to burn at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Brahma and the gods approve, reasoning that deadly snakes deserve it, and Brahma comforts Kasyapa and teaches him how to cure poison.
Closing line: the twentieth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
On their way the sisters see the ocean, described at length as vast, roaring, full of monsters, gems, Nagas and Asuras, and as the bed of Vishnu in his cosmic sleep.
They see rivers flowing into it, its waves dancing and its limitless expanse.
Closing line: the twenty-first section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The snakes reason it is safer to please their mother, hope she may lift the curse, and turn into black hairs in the horse's tail.
The two sisters fly across the sky and the ocean, described again in detail.
Closing line: the twenty-second section ends.
Heading of the next section (XXIII) printed here in the source.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The sisters reach the horse and see the black hairs in its tail. Kadru makes Vinata her slave, and Vinata is deeply sorry.

Meanwhile Garuda is born, shining like the fire at the end of the age. Frightened, the gods go to Agni, who says this is not fire but Garuda, Kasyapa's son, born to please Vinata and an enemy of the snakes.
The gods approach Garuda and praise him with a long hymn, calling him the creator, the lord of all, and asking him to be merciful and lessen his brightness.
Pleased by the praise, Garuda reduces his energy and splendour.
Closing line: the twenty-third section ends (the sentence continues in the next shot).
Rest of the closing line.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Garuda hears the praise, sees his own huge form, and shrinks it.
He tells all creatures not to be afraid, as he will lessen his fire.
Carrying his brother Aruna, Garuda goes to his mother across the ocean and sets Aruna in the east just as the sun was about to scorch the worlds.
Saunaka asks why Surya wanted to burn the worlds and what the gods did to anger him.
Surya had exposed Rahu to the gods. Rahu now wanted to devour him, and Surya, feeling abandoned by the gods, decided to destroy the worlds and went to the western mountains.
A great heat spreads at midnight and the gods and sages go to Brahma in alarm. Brahma says Surya will burn everything, but Aruna will stand before him as charioteer and take his heat away.
Aruna does so and the sun rises veiled by him. Sauti has answered the question and will now continue.
Closing line: the twenty-fourth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

Vinata, enslaved, carries Kadru on her shoulders and Garuda carries the snakes. As he flies up toward the sun the heat makes the snakes faint, so Kadru prays to Indra at length, praising him as the source of rain, the creator and destroyer, and everything else, and asks him to protect her sons.
Closing line: the twenty-fifth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Indra covers the sky with dark clouds and orders them to pour. The downpour is so heavy that the sky seems to dance and the sun and moon vanish.
The snakes rejoice. Water covers the earth and reaches the underworld. They arrive at the island Ramaniyaka.
Closing line: the twenty-sixth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Garuda carries the snakes to an island by the salt ocean, described as a lovely forest with flowers, lakes, bees and birds, which delights them.

The snakes then tell Garuda to take them to another island. Garuda asks his mother why he must serve them. Vinata tells him how she lost the wager by the snakes' deceit. Garuda asks the snakes what he can do to free them both.
The snakes answer: bring amrita by force and you will be free.
Closing line of the twenty-seventh section begins (it ends in the next shot).
Rest of the closing line.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

Garuda asks his mother for food before he goes. She sends him to the Nishadas but warns him never to kill a Brahmana, who is dangerous when angry. Garuda asks how to recognise one. She says he will burn his throat like a fish-hook and not be digested. She blesses him with protection by the wind, sun, moon, fire and Vasus.
Garuda flies off and raids the Nishada town. He stirs up dust, blocks the roads with his open mouth, and the blinded people rush into it. He shuts his mouth, killing countless fishermen.
Closing line: the twenty-eighth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
A Brahmana with a Nishada wife burns Garuda's throat. Garuda tells him to come out. The Brahmana asks to bring his wife too, and Garuda agrees.
The couple leave and Garuda flies on. Kasyapa greets him and asks if he finds enough food.
Garuda says his mother is well but he is still hungry. He has eaten thousands of Nishadas and wants more food, enough to be strong to take the nectar.
Kasyapa points to a lake where an elephant keeps dragging a tortoise, and begins to tell why.

Two brothers, Vibhavasu and Supritika, quarrelled over dividing their inheritance. Vibhavasu warned against partition, and when Supritika insisted he cursed him to become an elephant. Supritika cursed him in turn to become a tortoise.
They now fight in the lake, the elephant six yojanas tall and the tortoise three. Kasyapa tells Garuda to eat both and then fetch the nectar.
Kasyapa blesses Garuda for the coming fight with the gods.
Garuda picks up the elephant and the tortoise, flies to a grove of gold and gem-bearing trees, and a huge banyan offers its branch. As he lands the branch breaks.
Closing line: the twenty-ninth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

The branch breaks and Garuda sees the Valakhilya sages hanging from it head down. To save them he holds the branch in his beak and rises. The astonished sages name him Garuda, the bearer of heavy weight.
He cannot find a place to put the branch and goes to Mount Gandhamadana, where his father Kasyapa is meditating. Kasyapa sees his huge form.
Kasyapa warns him not to act rashly, because the sages could burn him with their anger.
Kasyapa asks the Valakhilyas to let Garuda do his task, which is for the good of all.
The sages leave the branch and go to the Himalayas. Kasyapa directs Garuda to a mountain without people. He flies there and drops the giant branch, shaking the mountain.
Garuda sits on the peak, eats the elephant and tortoise, and flies up again.

Omens strike heaven: Indra's thunderbolt flares, meteors fall, weapons clash and blood rains. Indra asks Vrihaspati why. Vrihaspati says Garuda is coming to take the nectar, because of Indra's carelessness and the Valakhilyas' penance.
Indra warns the nectar's guards, and the gods put on armour and take up weapons and surround the nectar.
Closing line: the thirtieth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka asks what Indra's fault was, how the Valakhilyas' penance made Garuda, and why Garuda has such powers.
Sauti says the Purana tells it and promises a short account.

At Kasyapa's sacrifice Indra fetches fuel. He passes the thumb-sized Valakhilyas, weak and carrying one leaf-stalk, laughs and steps over them. They begin a rite to create another Indra. Frightened, Indra runs to Kasyapa, who asks the sages not to break Brahma's order that Indra rules.
The Valakhilyas begin to reply to Kasyapa (the speech continues in the next shot).
They say the rite was meant for an Indra and also for a son of Kasyapa's.
They leave the matter to Kasyapa to settle as he thinks right.
End of their words.
Vinata, after her penance, approaches Kasyapa. He says the sacrifice has borne fruit and she will have two mighty sons who will rule all winged creatures.

Kasyapa tells Indra that the two sons will be his helpers, not rivals, and warns him never to insult Brahmanas again. Vinata gives birth to Aruna, who is the forerunner of the sun, and Garuda, lord of birds.
Closing line: the thirty-first section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Garuda reaches the gods, who tremble. He crushes the guard Viswakarma in an instant and blinds the rest with the dust from his wings.
Indra orders the wind to clear the dust. The gods attack with swords, maces, lances and discuses. Garuda fights on, and the gods flee in all four directions.
Garuda fights ten named Yaksha guards and leaves them bleeding.
He finds the nectar ringed by flames. He takes ninety times ninety mouths, drinks many rivers, puts out the fire, and shrinks himself to enter.
Closing line: the thirty-second section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

Garuda enters in a golden form, shrinks to slip between the spokes of the cutting wheel, blinds the two fire-breathing guard snakes with dust and tears them apart, shatters the machine and flies off with the nectar without drinking it.

Vishnu, pleased by Garuda's self-denial, offers a boon. Garuda asks to stay above him and to be immortal without the nectar. Vishnu agrees and asks Garuda to be his carrier, placing him on his chariot flag.

Indra hurls his thunderbolt at Garuda, who laughs and says he respects the thunderbolt, Indra and the sage Dadhichi whose bone made it, drops one feather as a sign of this, and is named Suparna for it.
Indra asks to know Garuda's strength and to be his friend.
Closing line: the thirty-third section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Garuda accepts the friendship and says he can carry the earth, mountains and oceans on one feather.
Indra agrees and asks for the nectar back, since those who drink it will oppose the gods. Garuda says he'll not give it to anyone but will set it down for Indra to take. Indra offers him a boon.
Garuda asks that snakes become his food. Indra agrees and Vishnu approves. Garuda returns to his mother.
Garuda puts the nectar on kusa grass and tells the snakes to wash first. While they bathe, Indra takes it. The snakes lick the grass and their tongues are split in two. The grass becomes sacred.
Garuda lives happily in the woods with his mother, eating snakes.
Sauti says whoever hears or recites this story goes to heaven.
Closing line: the thirty-fourth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka asks for the names of the principal snakes.
Sauti agrees to give only the chief ones, to avoid length.
The list begins: Sesha first, then Vasuki, then Airavata.
Names continued: Takshaka, Karkotaka, Dhananjaya and others.
Names continued: Pinjaraka, Elapatra and others.
Names continued: Ugra, Kalasapotaka and others.
Names continued: Samkha, Valisikha, Nahusha and others.
Names continued: Hastipada, Kaliyaka and others.
Names continued: Padma, Mahapadma and others.
Names continued: Vilwaka and others.
Names continued: Purnabhadra, Kauravya and others.
Names continued: Dhritarashtra, Sankhapinda and others.
Names continued: Kunjara, Kumuda and others.
Names continued: Kumudaksha, Karkara and others.
Last names: Kundodara and Mahodara.
Sauti says the sons and grandsons of these snakes are countless, so he will not name them.
Closing line: the thirty-fifth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka asks what the snakes did after hearing the curse.
Sesha leaves his mother and brothers and does hard penances in holy places. Brahma finds him thin and asks what he wants.
Sesha says his brothers are wicked and envy Garuda, so he wants to give up his body to escape them.
Brahma says he already provided a remedy for the snakes' danger and offers a boon.
Sesha asks that his heart always delight in virtue and penance.
Brahma praises him and tells him to hold the unsteady earth steady.
Sesha agrees and asks that the earth be placed on his head.
Brahma says the earth will open a passage for him under it.
Sesha enters the opening, goes under the earth, and holds it up with his head.
Brahma calls Sesha the god Dharma for supporting the earth alone.
Sesha, also called Ananta, stays under the earth supporting it. Brahma gives him Garuda to help.
Closing line: the thirty-sixth section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Vasuki, hearing the curse, calls his brothers to a council.
He says no remedy exists for a mother's curse, and even the Lord did not stop it, so they must plan quickly to stop Janamejaya's sacrifice.

The snakes propose plans: pose as Brahmanas to beg the king to stop, become his advisers, kill the priests, send storm clouds, steal the soma vessels, foul the food, demand fees, carry off the king, or simply bite him. The kinder ones object to killing Brahmanas. Vasuki rejects them all and says only Kasyapa's grace can help.
Closing line: the thirty-seventh section ends.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

Elapatra says fate cannot be prevented. From his mother's lap he once heard the gods ask Brahma why he let Kadru curse her sons. Brahma replied that only the wicked snakes will die, and a sage Jaratkaru will have a son, Astika, with a wife of the same name, Vasuki's sister, and Astika will stop the sacrifice.
Elapatra urges Vasuki to give his sister as alms to the sage when he comes wandering for a bride.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The snakes approve Elapatra's counsel and Vasuki starts raising his sister Jaratkaru with great care.
Later, after the ocean churning in which he was the rope, Vasuki goes to Brahma with the gods, who ask Brahma to ease his sorrow.
Brahma says Elapatra's plan stands: only the wicked will die, Jaratkaru is performing penance, and Vasuki should give him his sister at the right time.
Vasuki orders the snakes to watch the sage Jaratkaru and tell him as soon as he asks for a wife.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka asks why the sage was called Jaratkaru.
Sauti says Jara means waste and karu means huge: the sage had a huge body that he wore down with penance. Vasuki's sister had the same name.
Saunaka smiles and agrees.
Saunaka asks how Astika was born.
Sauti begins to answer according to the scriptures.
Vasuki waits, but the sage Jaratkaru wanders the earth without asking for a wife.

King Parikshit of the Kuru line, a great archer who loves hunting, loses a wounded deer in the forest. Tired and thirsty, he finds a sage in a cow-pen, silent and drinking the froth from calves. The sage does not answer, so the king puts a dead snake on his shoulder with his bow. The sage lets him and does not curse him, and the king goes home regretful.
The sage has a fierce young son, Sringin, who is studying with a teacher.
On his way home, Sringin's companion Krisa teases him about his father, and Sringin flares up.
Krisa mocks Sringin's pride: how can he boast when his own father carries a dead snake on his shoulders?
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Sringin asks why his father carries a dead snake. Krisa says the king put it there.
Sringin asks what wrong his father did the king.
Krisa tells what happened: the king chased a stag, found Samika silent in his vow, and put the snake on his shoulder.
Furious, Sringin touches water to make a curse.
He curses the king: within seven nights Takshaka will take him to the realm of death.
Sringin goes to his father and tells him. Samika says he is displeased: sages should forgive kings, who protect dharma, sacrifices and rain, and the king acted from hunger and fatigue, not malice.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Sringin says his words are never false, whether his father likes it or not.
Samika agrees the curse will hold, but advises him to keep calm and forgiving, since anger drains an ascetic's merit, and says he will warn the king.
Samika sends his pupil Gaurmukha to the king with instructions to ask after his welfare and then give the message. Gaurmukha is announced at the palace.
The king honours him, and Gaurmukha repeats Samika's words to the king and ministers.
Gaurmukha says the sage forgave the king but his son cursed him: Takshaka will kill him in seven nights, and nobody can undo his son's curse. He was sent for the king's good.
The king is more distressed by his own act against the sage than by the curse of death.
He sends Gaurmukha away and, with his ministers, builds a mansion on a single pillar, guarded day and night by physicians, medicines and mantra-knowing Brahmanas, and rules from there.
On the seventh day, the Brahmana Kasyapa travels to cure the king after the bite, hoping for wealth and merit. Takshaka, disguised as an old Brahmana, meets him and asks where he is going.
Kasyapa says he is going to cure the king after Takshaka's bite. Takshaka reveals he is Takshaka and says Kasyapa cannot cure him. Kasyapa says he can.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Takshaka challenges Kasyapa to revive a banyan he will burn with a bite.
Kasyapa accepts.
Takshaka bites the tree, which blazes up, and asks Kasyapa to revive it.

Kasyapa takes the ashes and, by his lore, brings back the sprout, leaves, stem, branches and full tree. Takshaka says reviving a tree is no surprise, offers him whatever he wants from the king, and warns that he may fail on a king whose life has ended.
Kasyapa says he goes for wealth. Takshaka offers more and tells him not to go.
Kasyapa meditates, sees the king's life has run out, takes the wealth from Takshaka and goes back.
Takshaka enters Hastinapura and hears the king is protected by mantras and medicines.
Takshaka sends snakes disguised as ascetics with fruit, kusa grass and water as gifts to get past the guards.
The king accepts the gifts and eats a fruit with his ministers. A small worm is in it. The king jokes it can be Takshaka and puts it on his neck. It becomes Takshaka, coils around him and bites.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
The councillors see the king in Takshaka's coils and flee in grief. They see Takshaka flying across the sky like a streak.
The mansion burns with Takshaka's poison and the king falls dead.

The ministers and royal priest perform the last rites and make the boy prince king as Janamejaya. They arrange his marriage to Vapushtama, daughter of Suvarnavarman of Kasi, and he spends his time happily with her.
Heading: the Astika section continues.

Jaratkaru wanders the earth living on air and bathing in holy places. He finds his ancestors hanging head down by a single root thread that a rat is gnawing. He offers any part of his merit to save them.

The ancestors say his penance cannot help them, only a son can. They are Yayavara sages, and the only thread left is their son Jaratkaru, who lives alone in penance. The rope is their line, the eaten threads are lost descendants, the half-eaten root is Jaratkaru and the rat is Time. They ask the stranger to tell Jaratkaru to marry, and ask who he is.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Jaratkaru is stricken by their words.
Speaking through tears, he says the pitris are his own forefathers.
He asks how to help them and calls himself the sinful son.
He begs to be punished (the sentence continues in the next shot).
End of his plea.
The ancestors ask why he has not married.

He says he had planned to remain celibate, but seeing them has changed his mind. He will marry a bride of his own name who is offered freely and whom he won't need to maintain, and her son will save them.

Now old, he cannot find a bride and weeps in the forest, then calls three times for one. The watching snakes tell Vasuki, who brings his sister. Jaratkaru does not accept right away. He asks her name and says he won't maintain her.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Vasuki says the bride has the same name, is his sister and he will maintain her. Jaratkaru agrees to marry, on the condition that she never does anything he dislikes.
They marry with proper rites and he lives in a chamber provided by Vasuki, repeating his condition: if she does anything against his wishes, he will leave.
She accepts, serves him with great care, and soon conceives a child as bright as fire.
One evening the sage sleeps with his head on her lap and the sun is about to set. She worries: if she wakes him he will be angry; if she lets the twilight pass he will lose his religious merit.
She decides to wake him gently and tells him it is time for the evening prayer.
He is angry and says she has insulted him, and that he will leave. She explains she woke him only to protect his merit.
He says he never lies, so he must go, and tells her to inform her brother and not to grieve.
She pleads with joined hands: the offspring her relatives need has not yet come, and she has done nothing wrong.
He says the child in her womb is a great Vedic sage like fire.
With that, Jaratkaru leaves to take up severe penance again.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
She goes to her brother and tells him everything. Vasuki, even more distressed, asks her about the child.
Vasuki says the whole purpose of the marriage was a son who would save the snakes, and asks whether she conceived.
She says her husband told her, 'There is,' that a son would be born, and he never lies. She asks Vasuki to cast off his sorrow.
Vasuki accepts and honours her with gifts. The child begins to grow, bright as the waxing moon.
A son is born and raised in Vasuki's house. He studies with Chyavana and is known as Astika, from his father's word 'there is' when he was still in the womb. He grows up a delight to the snakes.
Heading: the Astika section continues.
Saunaka asks Sauti to tell again what Janamejaya asked his ministers.
Sauti agrees.
Janamejaya asks his ministers to tell all that happened to his father and says he will act if it benefits the world.

The minister describes Parikshit as a virtuous king: son of Abhimanyu, born when the Kuru line was nearly extinct, a pupil of Saradwat, protector of the poor and the widows and of all four orders, who ruled sixty years before dying, after which Janamejaya was crowned as a child.
Janamejaya says no king of his line was disliked and asks how his father died.
The ministers agree to tell exactly what happened.

The ministers say Parikshit, an old man fond of hunting, pursued a wounded deer, grew tired and hungry, found a Rishi silent in a vow, and angrily put a dead snake on his shoulders. The Rishi did not respond.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
The ministers resume: the king returns to his capital after placing a dead snake on the sage's shoulders, and the sage's son Sringin hears of the insult to his father.
Sringin curses the king's father, saying Takshaka will burn him with poison within seven nights, and the sage sends his disciple Gaurmukha to warn the king.
Takshaka bites a banyan tree and burns it to ashes, then offers Kasyapa wealth to turn back, and Kasyapa accepts and goes home.
Takshaka, in disguise, burns the king in his mansion, and the ministers ask Janamejaya to decide what follows, since the sage Utanka was insulted.
Janamejaya asks when the ministers learned these events and says he wants to know what passed in the forest.
The ministers describe a man who climbed a dry tree, was burned with it, and was revived by a Brahmana's power, and who then reported the exchange between Takshaka and Kasyapa.
Janamejaya, having heard all this, is overcome with grief, weeps, and breathes heavily.
Janamejaya declares his resolve to avenge his father on Takshaka, whom he blames for the death and for the insult to the sage.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
The ministers approve, and Janamejaya resolves on a snake-sacrifice, asking his priests how to burn Takshaka and his kin.
The chief priest says the gods devised a snake-sacrifice, known from the Puranas, that only the king can perform.
The king prepares for the rite, the priests measure the platform, and a Suta builder warns that a Brahmana will obstruct the sacrifice, so the king orders the gatekeepers to admit no one.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
The priests pour butter into the fire while naming the snakes, and snakes of all colours and sizes fall into the flames in great numbers.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Saunaka asks which great sages served as priests and assembly members at the snake-sacrifice.
Sauti names the priests and sages, including Chandabhargava as Hotri, Kautsa as Udgatri, and Vyasa with his disciples as members.
Snakes continue to fall into the fire, their fat flows like rivers, and the air fills with stench and cries.
Takshaka goes to Indra's palace, confesses his fault, and Indra promises that Takshaka has nothing to fear from the sacrifice.
Vasuki, seeing his family reduced to a few, laments his fate and asks his sister to send her son Astika to end the sacrifice.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Jaratkaru calls her son and, on Vasuki's instruction, tells him that the time has come for the purpose for which she was given to his father.
Astika asks why his mother was given to his father by his uncle, and asks her to explain it truly.
Jaratkaru explains that Kadru cursed her sons to burn in Janamejaya's sacrifice, after they refused to lie about the horse Uchchaihsravas in a wager.
The gods, led by Vasuki, ask Brahman how the curse can be made ineffective.
Brahman replies that Jaratkaru will marry a wife also named Jaratkaru, and the Brahmana born of her will relieve the snakes.
Jaratkaru reminds her son that Vasuki gave her to his father for this purpose, and asks what he thinks.
Astika agrees and promises Vasuki that he will free him from the curse.
Vasuki says his head swims and his heart breaks under the curse.
Astika tells Vasuki to stop grieving, promising to extinguish the punishment of the sacrifice.
Astika goes to the sacrifice, is refused by the doorkeepers, wins them over, enters, and honours the king, the priests, and the fire.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Astika praises the king's sacrifice by comparing it with the rites of gods, sages and kings, and praises the priests and Vyasa with many comparisons.
Sauti says Astika has pleased the king, the priests and the sacred fire, and that the king, seeing the omens, speaks to them.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Janamejaya says the boy speaks like a wise old man and offers him a boon.
The Sadasyas say a Brahmana deserves respect and may have his wish, but only after Takshaka comes.
The king tells Astika to ask for a boon, but the Hotri objects that Takshaka has not yet come into the sacrifice.
Janamejaya urges the priests to complete the sacrifice and bring Takshaka, whom he calls his enemy.
The Ritwiks say the scriptures and the fire show that Takshaka is staying in Indra's abode, afraid.
The Suta Lohitaksha, learned in the Puranas, had said this before.
Asked again, Lohitaksha explains that Indra granted Takshaka a boon: hiding with Indra means Agni cannot burn him.
Indra arrives in his car with the gods, and Takshaka hides in his garment, so the king orders that Takshaka be cast into the fire with Indra.
The Hotri names Takshaka in his libations, Indra releases him and leaves, and the mantras draw Takshaka near the flames.
The Ritwiks tell the king the sacrifice is going well and that he should grant a boon to the Brahmana.
Janamejaya promises to grant any boon Astika asks for, even one that seems impossible.
The Ritwiks report that Takshaka, disabled by the mantras, is falling from the sky toward the fire.
As Takshaka falls, Astika asks that the sacrifice end and that no more snakes burn in the fire.
Janamejaya, sorry, offers gold, silver, cattle and other wealth, but not an end to the sacrifice.
Astika refuses wealth and asks that the sacrifice end so his maternal relatives can be saved.
The king repeatedly offers Astika another boon, Astika holds to his request, and the Sadasyas tell the king to grant it.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Saunaka asks for the names of all the snakes that fell into the sacrificial fire.
Sauti says the snakes are too many to count, and names the chief snakes of Vasuki's race, who fell into the fire like libations of butter.
Sauti names more chief snakes of the lines of Takshaka, Airavata, Kauravya and Dhritarashtra, all of whom fell into the fire.
Sauti says the sons and grandsons of these snakes were burned too, by the thousands.
Many other huge, swift snakes, able to take any shape and strength, were burned in the great sacrifice.
Heading: the Astika Parva continues.
Sauti tells how Takshaka hung in mid-air just as the king was about to grant Astika's boon, and how this puzzled Janamejaya.
Saunaka asks whether the priests' mantras failed, since Takshaka did not fall into the fire.
Sauti explains that Astika had three times told the falling Takshaka to stay, and the snake remained in the sky.
The king ends the sacrifice, rewards the priests and Lohitaksha, and sends Astika home, where he tells his uncle and mother what happened.
The pleased snakes, now saved, offer Astika a boon.
Astika asks that anyone who reads the account of his deed be free from fear of snakes, and the snakes agree and add their own protective words.
Gratified, the great Brahmana Astika prepares to leave.
Astika ascends to heaven when his time comes, leaving sons and grandsons behind.
Sauti says that this is the account of Astika exactly as it happened.
A closing line says that reciting this history removes all fear of snakes.
Sauti says he has recited the whole history of Astika as Pramati once told it to his son Ruru, and asks Saunaka to be satisfied.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva.
Saunaka thanks Sauti and asks him to recite the history composed by Vyasa, along with the stories told at the sacrifice.
Sauti says the Brahmanas spoke on many Vedic topics, but Vyasa recited the great Bharata.
Saunaka asks to hear the Mahabharata, which Vyasa recited at Janamejaya's request after the sacrifice, and says he is not satisfied yet.
Sauti agrees to recite the Mahabharata from its beginning and says he enjoys doing so.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva continues.
Vyasa, born of Kali to Parasara, is praised for his learning, his division of the Vedas, and his begetting of Pandu, Dhritarashtra and Vidura.
Vyasa enters the sacrificial pavilion, where Janamejaya greets him, offers him a golden seat and worship, and asks after his welfare.
Janamejaya asks Vyasa to tell him the history of the Kurus and Pandavas, and why the disunion and great battle happened.
Vyasa tells his disciple Vaisampayana to recount to the king the discord between the Kurus and Pandavas as he heard it.
Vaisampayana recites the whole history to the king, the Sadasyas and the chieftains, covering the hostility and destruction of the two houses.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva continues.
Vaisampayana bows to his preceptor and says he will recite what he heard from Vyasa.
Vaisampayana says he will explain why the disunion between the Kurus and Pandavas came about, and why the dice game led to exile.
After their father's death the Pandavas return home and grow skilled in archery, which makes Duryodhana and his allies jealous; they try poison and drowning against Bhima, and Vidura protects them.
Duryodhana and his council have a house of lac built, and Dhritarashtra sends the Pandavas to Varanavata, where Vidura warns them of the danger.
The Pandavas escape the lac house, slay Purochana, meet Hidimba and Ghatotkacha, kill the Rakshasa Vaka, win Draupadi, and receive Khandavaprastha, where they extend their power over the lands.

Arjuna is exiled to the forest, marries Subhadra, helps burn the Khandava forest, and receives Gandiva and a chariot; Duryodhana then wins the kingdom by dice and sends the Pandavas into exile for thirteen years.
When the Pandavas return and are refused their kingdom, war breaks out, the Kshatriyas are destroyed, Duryodhana is slain, and the Pandavas regain their ruined kingdom.
Closing line: this is the history of the Pandavas and the disunion that cost the Kurus their kingdom.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks for the full story, not a short version, and wants to know why the Pandavas bore their persecution and why Bhima and Draupadi held back.
Vaisampayana agrees to recite the whole work, calls it a vast composition of about a hundred thousand verses, and lists the benefits of reading or hearing it.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa composed the work to honour the Pandavas and other Kshatriyas, and describes the merit gained by having it recited to Brahmanas.
Vaisampayana lists the subjects the work covers, including gods, sages, Krishna, Shiva and Kartikeya, and claims it is a mine of virtue and a complete guide to every topic of life.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva continues.
Vaisampayana introduces King Uparichara Vasu, a devoted and hunting-loving king of the Paurava line, who conquers Chedi and then takes up severe austerities.
The gods, led by Indra, come to Vasu and ask him to protect virtue, and Indra gives him a crystal car and a garland of lotuses that protects him in battle.
Indra gives Vasu a bamboo pole, and after a year Vasu plants it to worship Indra, starting a custom that other kings follow.
Indra blesses Vasu for his festival, and Vasu rules Chedi virtuously for a long time.
Vasu installs his five sons as governors of various provinces.
The text names the sons, including Vrihadratha in Magadha, who is also called Maharatha.
The five sons found kingdoms and towns named after themselves, which last for ages.
Riding his crystal car, Vasu is called Uparichara, and a river is freed from the mountain Kolahala, producing twin children who are given to Vasu.
Vasu's wife Girika is ready after her monthly course, but the Pitris ask Vasu to hunt deer for their rite, so he goes into a spring forest thinking of her, and a hawk is sent with his seed for her.
The hawk is attacked by another hawk, the seed falls into the Yamuna, and an Apsara turned into a fish swallows it, and the fish later yields a boy and a girl.
The Apsara is freed from her curse after giving birth, and rises back to her celestial form.
The king gives the girl to the fishermen, and she is named Satyavati, living with the fishermen and ferrying a boat on the Yamuna.
The sage Parasara sees Satyavati and asks her to accept his embraces, but she points out that the Rishis on both banks are watching.
Parasara creates a fog to hide them, Satyavati asks that her virginity be kept, and he grants her a boon that her body will smell sweet.
After the boon, Satyavati's season comes, she accepts Parasara, and she is known as Gandhavati and Yojanagandha for her scent.
Satyavati gives birth on an island in the Yamuna to a son, who sets out for asceticism and promises to appear when she calls.
The son is named Dwaipayana for being island-born, and then Vyasa for arranging the Vedas, and he teaches the Vedas, with the Mahabharata as the fifth, to his disciples.

Bhishma is born of Ganga and Santanu, and a sage cursed by Dharma as a thief is reborn as Vidura, while Kunti's son by Surya is born with armour and earrings, and Vishnu is born to Devaki and Vasudeva.
The births of Satyaki, Kritavarma, Drona, Kripa, Dhrishtadyumna, Draupadi, Sakuni, Duryodhana, the Pandavas, and Abhimanyu are listed, along with the sons of Draupadi and Ghatotkacha.
The text says that hundreds of thousands of kings fought in the great battle, too many to name, so only the principal ones are listed.
Heading: the Adivansavatarana Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks for a detailed account of the named and unnamed kings, and of the purpose for which these great warriors were born.

Vaisampayana says Parasurama cleared the Kshatriyas twenty-one times, and Kshatriya women then had children by Brahmanas, so the Kshatriyas were restored and the four orders and the world thrived in a golden age.
The Asuras, driven out of heaven by the gods, are reborn on earth as proud kings and creatures, and they oppress Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and sages.
The earth, weighed down by the Asuras, goes to Brahman for protection, and Brahman says he will appoint the dwellers of heaven to help her.
Brahman bids the earth farewell and tells the gods to be born on earth to ease her burden and fight the Asuras there.
Indra goes to Narayana in Vaikuntha and asks him to be incarnated, and Narayana agrees.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva.
Indra consults Narayana, returns to heaven, and the gods are reborn among Brahmarshis and royal sages to destroy the Danavas, Rakshasas, Gandharvas and Snakes.
Heading: Section LXVI.
Janamejaya asks for the births of the gods, Danavas, Gandharvas, Apsaras, men, Yakshas and Rakshasas, from the beginning.

Vaisampayana starts the genealogy: Brahman's sons, Kasyapa, Daksha's thirteen daughters, the twelve Adityas, Hiranyakasipu and Prahlada of the Daityas, the forty sons of Danu, and the children of Sinhika, Krodha, Kala and Sukra.
Vaisampayana says the descendants of these beings are too many to count, and he has recited only what is known from the Purana.
He names the sons of Vinata, including Garuda and Aruna, the sons of Kadru, including Vasuki and Takshaka, and the lines of Muni, Pradha, and Kapila, which include Gandharvas, Apsaras and kine.
He closes the list of creatures, saying that this account is sacred and that it should be heard and recited in a proper frame of mind.
He promises that anyone who reads this account before gods and Brahmanas gains progeny, good fortune, fame and excellent worlds.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Vaisampayana names Brahman's six great Rishis, the eleven Rudras, and the lines of Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu, then describes how Daksha's daughters were given to Dharma, Soma and Kasyapa.
He names the eight Vasus and their sons and descendants, including Kartikeya, and Viswakarman, the craftsman and maker of the gods' cars.
Dharma comes out of Brahman's breast in human form, and his three sons, Sama, Kama and Harsha, support the worlds.
Kasyapa, son of Marichi, is the father of gods and Asuras, and the twelve Adityas are led by Indra, with Vishnu the youngest.
He lists the thirty-three gods and the groups they form, including the Rudras, Maruts, Vasus and Adityas.
He says that reciting this list of the gods' groups washes men of all sins.
He traces Bhrigu's line: Sukra, Chyavana, Aurva, Richika, Jamadagni, and Parasurama, the slayer of Kshatriyas, and Aurva's hundred sons.

He lists the offspring of Brahman's other children, of Lakshmi, Divi, Adharma, Tamra's daughters, Krodha's daughters, Surabhi, Surasa, Kadru, and Vinata, covering birds, deer, elephants, cattle, horses and Nagas.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks for the births among men of gods, Danavas, Gandharvas, Rakshasas, animals, snakes and birds, and for their deeds after they took human form.
Vaisampayana names Asuras reborn as kings, such as Viprachitti as Jarasandha and Hiranyakasipu as Sisupala, along with the Kaleya brothers and the Krodhavasa line.
He names the rebirths of Kansa, Devaka, Drona, Ashwatthama, Bhishma, Kripa, Sakuni, Satyaki, Drupada, Virata, Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura and Duryodhana, along with their portions of divine beings.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to name Dhritarashtra's sons in the order of their birth.
Vaisampayana lists the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra, Duhsala the daughter, and Yuyutsu born of a Vaisya wife, and says all were skilled warriors and learned men.
The Pandavas are portions of Dharma, Vayu, Indra and the Aswins, and Abhimanyu is the son of Soma, who had asked the gods to let his son go to earth for a limited time.
Dhrishtadyumna is a portion of Agni, Sikhandin was a Rakshasa, and Draupadi's five sons are portions of the Viswas.

Pritha, after receiving a mantra from Durvasa, has Surya's son Karna, who is adopted by Radha's husband and later gives his armour to Indra, and the account then gives the divine births of Krishna and Balarama, Rukmini and Draupadi.
Closing: the account of these incarnations brings wealth, fame and long life to those who hear it, and gives wisdom about creation and destruction.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks to hear the dynasty of the Kurus from the very beginning, in front of the Rishis.
Vaisampayana says Dushmanta founded the Paurava line and ruled the earth bounded by the four seas, and even the lands of the Mlechchhas.
Under Dushmanta there were no mixed castes or sinful men, no fear of theft, famine or disease, and the rains came on time, and the king was strong, skilled in arms, and loved by his people.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks to hear about Bharata's birth, Sakuntala's origin, and how Dushmanta won her.
Dushmanta sets out with a four-fold army, the women of the city praise and bless him, and the citizens follow him to the edge of the forest.
Dushmanta hunts in the forest, killing and wounding tigers and other beasts with bow, sword and mace.
The lions and herds flee in panic, many animals and elephants die, and the forest is stripped of its wild beasts.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Dushmanta, with a single follower and exhausted, crosses a barren plain and comes to another forest full of hermitages.
The forest is described in detail, with flowering trees, bees, birds, cool breezes, and spots of grass, and the king is charmed.
In the forest the king finds a retreat with a sacred fire, flowing by the Malini river, and worships it.
The king goes to the bank of the river, then decides to visit Kanwa of the race of Kasyapa, halting his army at the forest entrance.
He enters the hermitage with only his minister and priest, hears the Vedas chanted and the learning of its Brahmanas, and wishes to stay longer.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Dushmanta enters the hermitage alone, finds it empty, and calls out, and a maiden as lovely as Sri comes out and welcomes him.
Sakuntala says her father has gone to fetch fruit and asks the king to wait.
Dushmanta admires her beauty and asks who she is, whose daughter she is, and why she is in the woods.
Dushmanta points out that a sage who has kept his vows could not have fathered a child, and asks her to explain how she came to be his daughter.
Sakuntala says she will tell what she learned about her birth, including the question a visiting Rishi once asked her father.
Kanwa's account begins: Indra, fearing Viswamitra's penances, sends Menaka to tempt him, and Menaka lists his feats and voices her fear of him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Marut strips Menaka, Viswamitra desires her, and their daughter is left on a river bank, where vultures guard her until Kanwa adopts her and names her Sakuntala.
Sakuntala closes by saying Kanwa is her father, though she does not know her real one.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Dushmanta asks Sakuntala to be his wife and offers her gold, robes, pearls and his whole kingdom, and asks her to marry him in the Gandharva form.
Sakuntala says her father has gone to fetch fruit and will give her in marriage when he returns.
Dushmanta argues that a marriage in the Gandharva form is lawful for a Kshatriya, and he lists the eight forms of marriage and which are proper for each class.
Sakuntala agrees to the marriage on one condition: the son born of it must become the heir-apparent.
Dushmanta agrees, marries Sakuntala, and promises to send his troops to escort her to his capital, then leaves.
On his way home Dushmanta wonders what the ascetic will say once he knows all.
Kanwa returns, knows what has happened through his spiritual sight, and approves the Gandharva union, saying the son will be mighty and rule the sea.
Sakuntala washes her father's feet and asks him to bless Dushmanta and his ministers.
Kanwa agrees to bless the king for Sakuntala's sake and offers her a boon.
Sakuntala asks for the boon that the Paurava monarchs may always be virtuous and never lose their thrones.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The boy grows up strong and is named Sarvadamana, and Kanwa sends Sakuntala and her son to Hastinapura, where she presents the boy and reminds Dushmanta of his promise.
Dushmanta says he remembers nothing, and Sakuntala, angry, answers with a long speech on the gods who witness every deed and on a wife's and a son's place in the family.
Dushmanta replies that women speak untruths, that Menaka and Viswamitra are unworthy parents, and he calls Sakuntala a lewd woman and refuses the child.
Sakuntala answers that she is of higher birth than the king, that the wicked slander the good, and that truth outweighs a hundred horse-sacrifices, and she offers to leave.
After Sakuntala leaves, a voice from heaven tells Dushmanta to acknowledge his son, and says the boy shall be called Bharata; the king says he already knew the boy was his.
Dushmanta welcomes Sakuntala back with honour, installs Bharata as heir, and Bharata's conquests, sacrifices and gifts to Kanwa are described.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Vaisampayana says he will recite the sacred genealogy of Daksha, Manu, Bharata, Ruru, Puru and Ajamidha, and of the Yadavas, Kurus and Bharatas.
He recounts Prachetas's sons, Daksha's daughters married to Dharma, Kasyapa and Chandra, Manu's sons, and Pururavas, who robbed Brahmanas and was destroyed by their curse.
Pururavas brings the sacred fires and Urvasi from the Gandharvas, Nahusha rules well but humbles the Rishis, and Yayati, grown old, asks his sons to take his old age, and only Puru agrees.
Yayati enjoys Puru's youth for a thousand years, finds his desires unsatisfied, returns the youth to Puru, and names him his true heir.
Yayati crowns Puru, goes to the mount of Bhrigu for asceticism, and after long years dies and ascends to heaven with his wives.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks how Yayati obtained Sukra's daughter and asks for the founders of the dynasties in order.
Vaisampayana says Sukra and Vrishaparvan gave their daughters in marriage to Yayati, and that Yayati's union with Devayani is the subject.
In the war between gods and Asuras, Sukra revives the slain Asuras, Vrihaspati cannot, so the gods send his son Kacha to learn the science from Sukra.
Kacha asks Sukra to accept him as a disciple, and Sukra welcomes him, saying it honours Vrihaspati.
Kacha takes his vow, wins Devayani's affection by serving her, and after five hundred years the Danavas kill him while he herds the kine.
Devayani tells her father that Kacha is lost and that she will not live without him.
Sukra revives Kacha, who explains that the Danavas killed him under a banyan tree when they learned his purpose.
The Danavas kill Kacha a second time, grind his body into the ocean, then kill him a third time and mix his ashes into Sukra's wine.
Sukra says he can revive Kacha but he will keep being killed, and Devayani says she will starve if Kacha is lost.
Sukra realises the Danavas have killed his disciple, and Kacha calls from inside Sukra's stomach, asking for mercy.
Sukra asks how Kacha got inside him, and Kacha says he was given to Sukra in the wine and has kept his memory.
Devayani says she cannot live without Kacha, and Sukra teaches Kacha the science, since Kacha can only come out by Sukra's death.
Kacha tears open Sukra's stomach, comes out, and revives Sukra with the science, and thanks him as a father and mother.
Sukra, ashamed after drinking wine with Kacha inside him, curses any Brahmana who drinks wine, and tells the Danavas that Kacha will live with him.
The Danavas go home, and after a thousand years of study Kacha takes his leave to return to the gods.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Devayani, now that his vow is over, praises Kacha and asks him to take her hand with the proper mantras.
Kacha says she is dearer than life to his preceptor and is to be honoured as his daughter, and Devayani answers that he is the son of her father's preceptor's son.
Kacha refuses her, calls her his sister, asks her blessing for his journey, and Devayani says his knowledge will then not bear fruit.
Kacha says he refused only because she is his preceptor's daughter, and curses her that no son of a Rishi will ever marry her, and that his knowledge will bear fruit only in those he teaches.
Kacha goes to heaven, and the gods, led by Indra, praise him and promise him a share in sacrificial offerings.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The gods celebrate Kacha's science, and Indra, as wind, mixes up the clothes of bathing maidens, so Sarmishtha takes Devayani's garment and insults her.
Devayani tries to pull her clothes back, and Sarmishtha throws her into a well and goes home, thinking she is dead.
Yayati, out hunting with thirsty horses, finds the well dry and sees a maiden shining inside it, and asks who she is.
Devayani says she is Sukra's daughter and asks Yayati to take her by the hand and lift her out.
Yayati takes her by the right hand, lifts her from the well, and returns to his capital.
Devayani sends her maid Ghurnika to tell her father what happened, and refuses to enter the city of Vrishaparvan.
Ghurnika tells Sukra, who finds Devayani in the woods, and she repeats Sarmishtha's insult that Sukra is only a hired chanter of praise.
Sukra says his daughter is the child of one who is adored by all, and that he is the lord who sends rain and makes the crops grow.
Sukra soothes his grieving, angry daughter with these words.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Sukra urges Devayani to forgive and hold her anger, and Devayani replies that she will not live where bad conduct is tolerated and that she would rather die than be insulted.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Sukra, angered, goes to Vrishaparvan and says that sinful acts bear fruit in time, and that he will leave the Asuras because of the slaying of Kacha and the mistreatment of his daughter.
Vrishaparvan says Sukra has never been false and begs him not to go, saying the Asuras would then go into the ocean.
Sukra says he cannot bear his daughter's grief and asks the Asuras to please her, as Vrihaspati works for Indra.
Vrishaparvan says Sukra is lord of all the wealth of the Asura chiefs, including their herds and horses and himself.
Sukra tells Vrishaparvan that if he is lord of Asura wealth, he should go and gratify Devayani.
Devayani says the king must come himself and promise, and then asks for Sarmishtha with a thousand maids to wait on her and follow her wherever she is given away.
Vrishaparvan orders a maid to bring Sarmishtha quickly.
The order continues: Sarmishtha is to be brought, and she is to do what Devayani wishes.
The order closes with the same instruction, so that Devayani's wish is carried out.
The maid tells Sarmishtha that Sukra is about to leave the Asuras because of Devayani, and Sarmishtha says she will do what Devayani wishes.
Sarmishtha comes with a thousand maids in a palanquin and offers to be Devayani's attendant, but Devayani reminds her that she is the daughter of a beggar.
Sarmishtha replies that one must help afflicted relatives, and says she will follow Devayani wherever she is given away.
Devayani, now satisfied, tells her father that she will enter the Asura capital, since his power has not been in vain.
Sukra enters the Asura capital in gladness, and the Danavas worship him with great reverence.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Devayani and Sarmishtha, with a thousand maids, drink flower-honey in the woods, when Yayati arrives, thirsty and tired from hunting, and sees them.
Yayati asks their names and parentage, and Devayani says she is Sukra's daughter and Sarmishtha her attendant.
Yayati asks why Sarmishtha, a daughter of the Asuras, serves Devayani, and Devayani says it is fate and asks his name.
Yayati names himself, a king's son, and says he came in search of water after hunting.
Devayani says she waits on his commands and wishes him well as her lord.
Yayati says he is unworthy of her, Devayani insists on marrying him, and Yayati says a Brahmana is to be feared more than a snake, so he needs her father's consent.
Sukra comes to meet Yayati, who worships him and waits for his commands.
Devayani asks her father to give her to Yayati, and Sukra agrees.
Yayati asks to be absolved from the sin of begetting mixed offspring, and Sukra grants absolution and tells him not to summon Sarmishtha to his bed.
Yayati marries Devayani with the rites, receives her with Sarmishtha and two thousand maids, and returns to his capital.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Yayati puts Devayani in his inner rooms and Sarmishtha in a separate mansion with a thousand maids; Devayani has a son, and Sarmishtha, reaching puberty, worries that she has no husband and wants a child.
Sarmishtha approaches the king in the Asoka grove, when no one can see them, and asks him to give her a child.
Yayati refuses, saying he knows she is of noble birth but Usanas forbade him to summon her to his bed.
Sarmishtha argues that a lie is excusable on certain occasions, and that as Devayani's husband he is her husband too; Yayati, bound by his vow to grant requests, yields.
Yayati honours Sarmishtha by keeping her virtue, and after a time they part.
Sarmishtha conceives from the king and bears a lotus-eyed son who shines like a celestial child.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Devayani, jealous of Sarmishtha's child, asks what sin she has committed, and Sarmishtha says a Rishi is the father, which Devayani accepts if it is true.
Devayani has two sons by Yayati and Sarmishtha has three, and they part on friendly terms.
Devayani finds three boys of celestial beauty playing with perfect trust in the king's park, and asks whose children they are.
The boys point at Yayati and name Sarmishtha as their mother.
The boys run to their mother, Yayati, abashed, does not caress them, and Devayani accuses Sarmishtha of wronging her.
Sarmishtha says she chose the king as her friend's husband, and holds him in higher esteem than Devayani's father.
Devayani says Yayati has wronged her and leaves, weeping and angry, and goes to her father Usanas, ignoring the king's pleas.
Devayani tells Sukra that Yayati has deviated from virtue and that Sarmishtha has three sons by him.
Sukra curses Yayati with decrepitude, Yayati defends his action as a duty, and Sukra calls it theft.
Yayati begs for relief, and Sukra says he can pass the decrepitude to a son who will give him his youth, and that son will become king.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Yayati, aged by the curse, asks his eldest son Yadu to take his decrepitude for a thousand years in exchange for his youth.
