Yadu refuses, listing the miseries of old age, and asks his father to ask another son.
Yayati curses Yadu's line and asks Turvasu to take the decrepitude.
Turvasu refuses, and Yayati curses him to rule over impure peoples.
Drahyu and Anu each refuse, and Yayati curses them with the loss of their desires and of their progeny.
Yayati asks his youngest son Puru to take his decrepitude.
Puru agrees humbly, and Yayati promises that his people will have their desires fulfilled.
Yayati transfers his decrepitude to Puru.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Yayati enjoys Puru's youth, honours gods, ancestors and Brahmanas, and after a thousand years concludes that desire is never satisfied and resolves to renounce it.
Yayati takes back his decrepitude and offers the kingdom to Puru, but the four orders object to passing over the elder sons.
Yayati explains that his elder sons disobeyed him, that Puru alone obeyed, and that Sukra said the obedient son would rule.
The people agree that Puru deserves the crown, since he did his father good.
Yayati has Puru crowned, performs the rites for retiring to the woods, and leaves his capital with Brahmanas and ascetics.
The peoples descended from his sons are named: the Yadavas, Yavanas, Bhojas, Mlechchhas, and the Pauravas, to which Janamejaya belongs.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Yayati lives in the forest with Brahmanas, then ascends to heaven, is hurled down by Indra, stays in the sky, and later returns to the celestials with several other kings.
Janamejaya asks why Yayati was hurled from heaven, how he regained admission, and for the full story of his life on earth and in heaven.
Vaisampayana agrees to recite Yayati's adventures on earth and in heaven, which destroy the sins of those who hear them.
Yayati lives the forest life, feeding guests, gratifying gods and ancestors, keeping vows, and performing austerities, before ascending to heaven.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Yayati lives in heaven, honoured by the gods, and sometimes goes to the region of Brahman.
One day Yayati talks with Indra, who asks him a question.
Indra asks what Yayati said when Puru took his decrepitude and he gave up the kingdom.
The question continues, asking what Yayati said when he handed over the earth to Puru.
Yayati says he told Puru the land between the Ganga and Yamuna was his, that the forgiving and the wise are superior, and that he should speak kindly and follow the virtuous.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Indra asks Yayati to whom he is equal in austerities, Yayati says he knows no equal, and Indra says his virtue has diminished from disregarding others, so he must fall, and Yayati asks to fall among the virtuous.
Yayati falls from heaven, and the royal sage Ashtaka sees him, asks who he is, and tells him he is safe among the virtuous and the wise.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Yayati introduces himself as Puru's father, says he is falling for having disregarded others, and explains that he did not greet Ashtaka first because he is older.
Ashtaka replies that a man deserves honour for learning and ascetic merit rather than for age.
Yayati says vanity destroys merit, destiny rules all, and all created things return to the Supreme Soul when freed from their acts.
Ashtaka asks about the regions Yayati has visited, and Yayati describes his long stay in the heavens, the messenger's cry of ruin, and the fall that brought him here.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Ashtaka asks why Yayati left Nandana and how one loses virtue in the other world, and Yayati says the celestials forsake one who has lost righteousness.
Yayati says that those who boast of their merits go to the earth-hell called Bhauma, where they are consumed by their own descendants.
Ashtaka asks where man goes after death, and says he has never heard of the earth-hell.
Yayati describes rebirth through the mother's womb, and says the fallen are tormented by Rakshasas in the form of sons and kin.
Ashtaka asks why the fallen are attacked and how they enter the womb again.
Yayati explains that the fallen being becomes a subtle substance in water, then seed, then embryo, and finally takes visible form.
Ashtaka asks how the body and senses form, and Yayati says the subtle being is drawn to the seed according to its merits and gains its senses at birth.
Ashtaka asks how one is revived after death, and Yayati says the dead keep their memory and enter new forms, with the virtuous rising and the vicious sinking.
Ashtaka asks whether the regions of no return are reached by asceticism or by knowledge.
Yayati lists seven gates to heaven, which vanity destroys, and says learning without humility does not lead to Brahma.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Ashtaka says the learned differ on how the four stages of life should be followed for religious merit.
Yayati describes the duties of the student, the householder, the mendicant and the forest-dweller.
Ashtaka asks how many kinds of Munis there are.
Yayati says a Muni may live in the woods with a village near, or in a village with the woods near.
Ashtaka asks what a Muni is, and Yayati says he is one who has withdrawn from worldly objects and remains content, whether he lives in woods or in a hamlet.
Yayati praises the silent, pure and detached ascetic who takes only what comes to him, and says he attains salvation.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Ashtaka asks whether the ascetic or the man of knowledge reaches communion with Brahma first.
Yayati says the wise attain it through knowledge, while yogis take longer, and that sacrifices done for reward bear no fruit.
Ashtaka notes that Yayati looks young and asks where he is going.
Yayati says he is falling into the earth-hell, but Indra granted that he would fall among the wise.
Ashtaka asks whether there are regions in heaven for him to enjoy, so that Yayati need not fall.
Yayati says there are as many regions for Ashtaka as there are cows and horses on earth.
Ashtaka offers Yayati all the regions his merits have earned, so that Yayati will not fall.
Yayati refuses, saying only a Brahmana who knows Brahma may take gifts, and that he has never accepted one.
Pratardana asks whether there are regions in heaven for him to enjoy as the fruit of his merit.
Yayati says numberless blissful worlds await Pratardana, enough to last seven days in each.
Pratardana offers Yayati all the worlds he has earned, so that Yayati will not fall.
Yayati refuses, saying a king should not take another king's merit, and that he will not accept what others do not.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Vasumat, son of Oshadaswa, asks whether there are worlds for him to enjoy as fruit of his merit.
Yayati says there are as many regions for Vasumat as there are places in the sky, the earth and the ten directions.
Vasumat offers his regions to Yayati, and if a gift is improper, suggests Yayati buy them for a straw.
Yayati says he has never bought or sold anything unfairly, and that other kings have not done so either.
Vasumat says that if buying is improper, Yayati should take the regions as a gift, since he will never go to them.
Sivi, son of Usinara, asks whether there are worlds in heaven for him to enjoy.
Yayati says Sivi has never disregarded the virtuous and that infinite worlds await him; Sivi offers to give Yayati all of them.
Yayati declines, saying he does not want regions given by others.
Ashtaka says each of them has offered Yayati their worlds, and that if he refuses they will descend to the earth-hell.
Yayati says he will receive only what he deserves, and that he cannot do what he has never done.
Ashtaka asks whose five golden cars these are, and whether men ride them to the regions of bliss.
Yayati says the five golden cars would carry them to the regions of bliss.
Ashtaka asks Yayati to ride ahead in one of the cars.
Ashtaka says they can wait and will follow him later.
Yayati says they can all go together, since they have conquered heaven, and the path is now visible.
Vaisampayana says the monarchs ride toward heaven, lighting the sky with the glory of their virtues.
Ashtaka asks why Sivi, son of Usinara, has gone ahead of him, since he thought Indra was his friend.
Yayati answers that Sivi gave all he had for the region of Brahma, and that his generosity and virtues are unmatched.
Ashtaka asks who Yayati is, and Yayati identifies himself as Nahusha's son and Puru's father, recounts his gifts of land and cattle, and says truth sustains the world.
Vaisampayana says Yayati ascends to heaven, rescued by his collateral descendants, and covers the three worlds with his fame.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks for the histories of the kings of Puru's line, none of whom lacked virtue, prowess or sons.
Vaisampayana promises to tell of the heroic kings of Puru's line, all equal to Indra in prowess.

The line runs from Puru's sons through Manasyu, Kaudraswa's ten sons, Matinara, Tansu, Ilina, Dushmanta, Bharata and Suhotra to Ajamidha, and the Panchalas defeat Samvarana until Vasishtha restores him.
Samvarana's son Kuru, after whom Kurukshetra is named, is followed by Janamejaya, Parikshit, Dhritarashtra, Pratipa and Santanu.
Many more excellent monarchs were born in the lines of Bharata and Manu, and the Aila dynasty grew great.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya says the earlier account was too short and asks for the full genealogy from Manu, the lord of creation.
Vaisampayana says he will recite the genealogy of Janamejaya's own race as he heard it from Dwaipayana.
The line runs from Daksha and Aditi through Vivaswat, Manu, Pururavas, Nahusha, Yayati and Puru, then through Janamejaya, Prachinwat, Sanyati, Ahayanti, Sarvabhauma and Ayutanayi, down to Tansu.
A verse says Tansu was born of Saraswati by Matinara, and that Tansu begot Ilina on Kalingi.
Ilina begets five sons with Rathantari, and Dushmanta is the eldest.
Dushmanta takes Sakuntala, the daughter of Viswamitra, as his wife.
They have a son, Bharata, and the text introduces two verses about Dushmanta's descendants.
The text completes the introduction of the verses on Dushmanta's descendants.
A verse says the father is reborn as the son, and urges Dushmanta to support his son and not insult Sakuntala.
Bharata is so called because he was supported, and the line runs through Bhumanyu, Suhotra, Hasti, who founded Hastinapura, Ajamidha, Samvarana, Kuru, Parikshit and Santanu.
An opening verse says the old men touched by Santanu regained their youth, which is why he was named Santanu.

The text traces the line from Santanu and Ganga's son Bhishma through Satyavati's sons Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura, Pandu's curse, the five Pandavas, their rivalry with Duryodhana, their marriages and children, and the rebirth of Parikshit.
The narrator says this history should be heard by all four orders with reverence, that it brings heaven to those who hear it, and quotes a verse in its praise.
Heading: Section XCVI.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
King Mahabhisha of Ikshvaku's line wins heaven through a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rajasuyas.
When Ganga's garment is blown aside before the gods, Mahabhisha stares at her, and Brahman curses him to be reborn and to face Ganga again.
Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of Pratipa, and Ganga, meeting the Vasus, learns they were cursed by Vasishtha to be born among men and asks them how they will be her children.
The Vasus ask Ganga to drown their children at birth so they can return quickly, and Ganga agrees on condition that one son lives.
The Vasus make their arrangement with Ganga and go their way.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Ganga comes to the ascetic-king Pratipa as a beautiful maiden and sits on his right thigh, asking him to take her, but he refuses on grounds of his vow and offers to accept her as his son's wife.
Ganga agrees to become a wife of Bharata's race, and asks that Santanu never judge the propriety of her acts.
Ganga disappears, and Pratipa waits for the birth of the son to fulfil his promise.

Santanu is born after Pratipa's penance, Pratipa tells him to accept the damsel as his wife, and Pratipa then retires to the woods; later Santanu sees Ganga on the riverbank and asks her to marry him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Ganga marries Santanu on the conditions that he never interfere with her, and she drowns the first seven sons; when the eighth is threatened, Santanu protests and she reveals she is the Ganga, bore the Vasus, and will leave, giving the child to him to rear as Gangadatta.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Santanu asks Ganga why the Vasus were cursed to be born among men, who Apava was, and what his son Gangadatta has done.
Ganga says the sage Vasishtha, also called Apava, lived in a sacred asylum on Mount Meru, where he performed his austerities.
Ganga describes Nandini, the cow of plenty, born to Surabhi and Kasyapa, who was given to the sage for his sacrifices.
The Vasus come to the sage's woods, and Dyu's wife, seeing Nandini, asks her husband to steal the cow for her friend, and he does so.
When the sage returns and finds the cow gone, he sees by his power that the Vasus took her and curses them to be born on earth.
The Vasus beg for mercy; the sage says they will be freed within a year of birth, but Dyu must live on earth for a time, childless.
Ganga says the Vasus asked her to drown them at birth, which she agreed to do, and that only Dyu must remain on earth for a time.
Ganga disappears with the child, who is named Gangeya and Devavrata, and excels his father in all skills.
Santanu returns to his capital sorrowful, and the narrator says he will now recount Santanu's virtues.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Santanu is praised for his wisdom, virtue and truthfulness, his peaceful reign, and his kindness to all creatures, and he retires to the woods after thirty-six years.
Santanu's son Devavrata, born to Ganga, grows into a skilled and mighty warrior like his father.
Santanu, chasing a deer, finds the Ganges run shallow and sees a youth stop its flow with a celestial weapon.
Ganga presents the grown youth to Santanu as his eighth son, and Santanu takes him home and makes him heir.
Santanu meets a fragrant fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna and asks her father for her hand.
The fisherman says the match depends on a pledge that the son of his daughter will be the next king.
Santanu, unwilling to make the pledge, grows melancholy, and when Devavrata asks why, he explains his fear of having no heir.
Devavrata learns of the pledge from the old minister and goes with elder chiefs to ask for the maiden, and the fisherman says the only objection is the rivalry his own sons might pose to her son.
Devavrata vows that the son of the maiden shall be king, and the fisherman, though satisfied, still has doubts about the children Devavrata may have.
Devavrata renounces his right to the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, and says that if he dies sonless he will attain heaven.
The fisherman gives his daughter, flowers fall from the sky, the gods name Devavrata Bhishma, and he helps the maiden into his chariot.
Bhishma takes the maiden to Hastinapura, the kings praise him, and Santanu grants him the boon of dying only when he chooses.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

After Santanu's marriage to Satyavati, their sons Chitrangada and Vichitravirya are born; Santanu dies, Bhishma places Chitrangada on the throne, a Gandharva of the same name kills him in battle, and Bhishma crowns the young Vichitravirya, who obeys him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
After Chitrangada's death, Bhishma rules under Satyavati, and goes to Kasi, where he carries off three princesses for his brother, saying that taking a bride by force is a lawful form of marriage.
The challenged kings give chase, and Bhishma defeats them all, cutting down bows, armour and heads, and takes the princesses on to Hastinapura.
King Salya challenges Bhishma, who destroys Salya's charioteer and horses and defeats him, but lets him live.

Bhishma brings the princesses to Hastinapura, allows Amba to go to the king she loved, and marries Ambika and Ambalika to Vichitravirya, who dies of consumption after seven years, and Bhishma performs his funeral rites.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Satyavati, grieving, asks Bhishma to raise children on Ambika and Ambalika, to keep the line alive, and to take the throne and marry.
Bhishma refuses, reminding her of his vow of truth, saying he would give up the three worlds before he would give up truth, and promising to suggest a Kshatriya remedy.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma says Parashurama slew the Kshatriya king of the Haihayas and then destroyed the Kshatriyas twenty-one times.
When the earth was emptied of Kshatriyas, Kshatriya women had children by Brahmanas, and the children belonged to the husband, so the Kshatriya race was revived.
Utathya's wife Mamata was with child when Brihaspati approached her, and the unborn child protested; Brihaspati cursed the child, who was born blind and named Dirghatamas.
Dirghatamas marries and has children, but his wife complains that he does not support her, and he tells her that a woman must keep one husband only.

Dirghatamas's sons, at their mother's command, cast him into the Ganges; King Vali rescues him and asks him to father children on his queen, and he fathers eleven sons through the queen's nurse and five through the queen, after whom five countries are named.
Bhishma says that the line of Vali was perpetuated by a great Rishi, that many warriors were born of Brahmanas' seed, and tells Satyavati to do as she likes.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma proposes that an accomplished Brahmana be paid to raise children on Vichitravirya's wives.
Satyavati, smiling and shy, says she will name the means, calling Bhishma the embodiment of virtue and truth.
Satyavati recalls that as a young ferrywoman she carried Parashara across the Yamuna and bore Vyasa, who divided the Vedas, and offers to summon him.
Bhishma approves, Vyasa comes to his mother, and Satyavati asks him to beget children on the widows.
Vyasa agrees to beget children for his brother, provided the women first keep a vow for one year.
Satyavati urges that the women conceive at once, since a kingdom without a king falls into ruin.
Vyasa says his looks and odour are grim, and asks that the princess accept him anyway.
Vyasa asks that the princess of Kosala wait for him, and Satyavati persuades her daughter-in-law to accept.
Satyavati feeds Brahmanas, Rishis and guests for the occasion.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Satyavati prepares the princess of Kosala, who shuts her eyes in fear when Vyasa enters, and Vyasa says her son will be blind because of her fault.
Ambalika turns pale at Vyasa's sight, so he says her son will be pale and named Pandu, and Pandu is born.
The third widow sends a maidservant to Vyasa, who promises that her son will be wise and fortunate, and this son is Vidura.
Thus Vyasa's sons, the splendid heirs of the Kuru line, are born in Vichitravirya's field.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks what the god of justice did to be cursed, and which Brahmana cursed him to be born a Sudra.

The learned sage Mandavya sits silent under a tree while thieves hide their loot in his hermitage, and the officers impale him as a thief, and other sages come as birds to ask what sin he has committed.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Mandavya, still living on the stake, forgives the king, who cuts the stake off so that a part remains in him, and he becomes known as Ani-Mandavya, and goes to ask the god of justice why he was punished.
The god of justice says Mandavya pricked a little insect as a child, and Mandavya rules that a child's offence is not sin and curses the god to be born a Sudra.
Dharma is born as Vidura in the Sudra order, learned in morality and politics, free from greed and anger, and devoted to the Kurus.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

The text describes the prosperity of the Kuru land, with good harvests, a splendid capital, honest people, and the upbringing of Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura by Bhishma, who excel in archery, strength and virtue, and the reasons Pandu rules, and then Bhishma speaks to Vidura.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma says the Kuru line must be expanded, names three maidens of pure blood from the Yadava, Suvala and Madra families, and asks Vidura for his view, which Vidura defers to him.

Bhishma hears that Gandhari, daughter of Suvala, has a boon of a hundred sons from Siva; Suvala gives her to the blind Dhritarashtra, Gandhari blindfolds herself, and Sakuni brings her to Hastinapura, where she serves her husband and family faithfully.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Sura's daughter Pritha is given to Kuntibhoja, and when she serves the sage Durvasa, he gives her a mantra to summon any god, so she summons the Sun.
Pritha asks the Sun's pardon for testing the mantra, and the Sun insists that his approach must bear fruit.

Pritha consents, and bears Karna with armour and earrings, then casts him into the water, and Radha and her husband raise him as Vasusena; Karna later gives his armour to Indra in disguise and receives a dart.
Karna, having cut off his natural armour, is called Karna.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

Kunti, though beautiful and virtuous, has no suitors, so her father invites kings to an assembly; she places the garland on Pandu, and the rites are performed before he returns to Hastinapura with his bride.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma goes to Madra for Madri, Salya says his family custom must be kept, Bhishma accepts it and gives him gold, gems and carriages, and Salya gives his sister, whom Bhishma brings to Hastinapura.

Pandu marries Madri, then sets out to conquer, subduing the robber tribes, Magadha, Videha, Kasi and others, and receives tribute before returning to Hastinapura, where Bhishma welcomes him with tears of joy.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.

At Dhritarashtra's command, Pandu gives his conquest wealth to Bhishma, Satyavati, the mothers and relatives, and Ambalika embraces her son with joy; Dhritarashtra then performs five great sacrifices with the wealth.
Pandu retires with Kunti and Madri to a hilly region of the Himalaya, where he hunts deer and roams freely.
At Dhritarashtra's command, people supply Pandu in his retreat with all pleasures.
Bhishma marries Devaka's daughter, born of a Sudra wife, to Vidura, and they have many sons like him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Vaisampayana says Dhritarashtra had a hundred sons and a son by a Vaisya woman, while Pandu had five sons by Kunti and Madri, begotten by the gods.
Janamejaya asks how Gandhari bore her hundred sons, how long each lived, how Yuyutsu was born, and how Pandu's sons were begotten despite his curse.
Vyasa grants Gandhari a boon of a hundred sons; after two years she strikes her womb in grief and produces a hard lump of flesh, which Vyasa then tells her to sprinkle with water and keep in pots.
The lump is divided into a hundred and one parts, put in pots of butter, and kept under watch, and Vyasa goes off to the Himalaya for asceticism.
Duryodhana is born from one of the pots, and Yudhishthira is named the oldest, and the news goes to Bhishma and Vidura.

Duryodhana brays like an ass and omens of disaster follow, Dhritarashtra asks whether his son or Yudhishthira should be king, Vidura advises casting off the first son, and Dhritarashtra refuses; a hundred sons, a daughter, and Yuyutsu by a Vaisya maid are born.
The text closes its account of the sons: a hundred heroic sons, a daughter, and Yuyutsu of a Vaisya woman.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks how Gandhari had a daughter in addition to the hundred sons, when the lump was divided into only a hundred parts.
Vaisampayana explains that Gandhari secretly longed for a daughter, and Vyasa counted out the hundred parts and set an extra part aside, which was put in its own pot to become Duhsala.
Vaisampayana says he has now told the whole story of Duhsala's birth.
Vaisampayana asks Janamejaya what more he should tell.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks for the names of Dhritarashtra's sons in the order they were born.
Vaisampayana recites the long list, says the sons were warriors and scholars, and reports that Duhsala was wed to Jayadratha.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks to hear everything about the Pandavas from the moment of their birth.
Pandu, hunting on the slopes of the Himavat, shoots with five arrows a deer that is serving its mate, and the wounded animal turns out to be a sage in deer form who cries out like a man.
The deer rebukes Pandu for a cruel act against dharma, and Pandu replies that kings hunt deer as they hunt enemies, citing an old precedent from the sage Agastya.
The deer answers that striking an unprepared foe is wrong, though killing after war has been declared openly is not.
Pandu says deer are killed in many ways whether they are careful or not, so the deer has no reason to reproach him.
The deer says its real grievance is that it was shot mid-act, reveals that it is the sage Kindama, and curses Pandu to die at the moment desire rises in him, with his wife dying alongside him.
The deer dies, and Pandu is overcome with grief.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Pandu, grieving over the deer's curse, blames his own lust and fate and vows to live as a celibate ascetic, listing the restraints he will keep.
Pandu asks that his family and court be told he has gone to the forest, and his wives Kunti and Madri insist on following him in austerity.
Pandu agrees to take up the forest life of severe penances, offerings to the gods and ancestors, and the Vanaprastha rules with his wives.
Pandu gives his jewels and robes to Brahmanas, his attendants leave for Hastinapura, and Dhritarashtra mourns his brother and loses his taste for comfort.
Pandu and his wives travel through named mountains and lakes of the Himalayas, guarded by Siddhas and sages, and reach the Hundred-Peak mountain where he keeps up his austerities.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Pandu's austerities win him the favour of the Siddhas and Charanas, and sages treat him as a brother, friend or son, so that he becomes almost a Brahmarshi.
On a new-moon day the great sages set out to see Brahman, and Pandu asks where they are going.
Pandu prepares to follow the sages with his wives, but they warn him that the northern heights are too dangerous for ordinary beings and for the princesses.
Pandu replies that a sonless man cannot reach heaven, that his debt to his ancestors is unpaid, and asks whether his wives may bear children.
The sages say a sinless, godlike son is destined for Pandu, and tell him to act on that destiny.
Pandu, remembering that the deer's curse took his power to father children, asks Kunti to bear sons by another man of high standing, citing Saradandayana's daughter as a precedent.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Kunti tells Pandu she will accept no other man and asks him to father children on her, then announces she will tell an old story.
She tells of King Vyushitaswa, a great sacrificer of the Puru line, whose early death left his widow Bhadra sonless, and of her grief as she asks to follow him.
Kunti continues: a voice promises Bhadra children, and the dead king's body fathers seven of them; she asks Pandu to act with his ascetic power the same way.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Pandu agrees that Vyushitaswa's example is true, then says women in older times were free and not bound to one husband, without that being sinful.
He explains that Swetaketu set the present rule of wifely fidelity in anger after a Brahmana led off his mother, and says that breaking the rule is a sin for women and men alike.
Pandu cites Madayanti, who had a son by Vasishtha at her husband's bidding, and says a wife must obey a husband's order to bear children, so Kunti should bear sons through a Brahmana.
Kunti recalls that as a girl she served the sage Durvasa, who gave her a mantra to summon any god as a child's father, and asks Pandu which god to call.
Pandu names Dharma, the god of justice, as the one who would never bring sin on them and whose son would be the most virtuous of the Kurus.
Kunti agrees, bows to Pandu, and walks around him before resolving to do as he asks.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Kunti calls on Dharma, who fathers Yudhishthira, and a voice from the sky foretells that he will be the best of men and a famed king.
Pandu asks for a child of greater strength, and Kunti calls on Vayu, who fathers Bhima; the infant's fall breaks a rock without harm, and Duryodhana is born the same day.
Pandu resolves to win Indra's favour through severe austerity, so that he can have a son of great strength.
Pandu has Kunti keep a yearlong vow, while he stands on one leg through the days and practises austerities.
Indra comes to Pandu and promises a famous son who will be a slayer of foes, and Pandu tells Kunti her vow has succeeded and to call on Indra.
Kunti calls on Indra, who fathers Arjuna, and a loud voice foretells his great deeds and his fame.
Gods, sages, Gandharvas and Apsaras gather in celebration, shower flowers, and dance, and a long list of divine beings honours the son of Pritha.
Pandu wishes to call on another god for more children, but Kunti refuses, saying the wise do not sanction a fourth union.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Madri, princess of the Madras, tells Pandu she is childless while Kunti has sons, and asks him to help her have children.
Pandu says he has thought about it and will ask Kunti, whom he believes will not refuse.
Pandu asks Kunti privately to give Madri children, pointing to the benefit of offerings and of fame.
Kunti tells Madri to think of a celestial, and Madri summons the Ashvins, who father the twins Nakula and Sahadeva; a voice says they will outshine the Ashvins.
The sages on the mountain name the five sons, Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, and the boys become favourites of the sages.
Pandu asks Kunti again on Madri's behalf, but Kunti refuses, complaining that Madri gained two sons from one mantra and that she was misled.
The five Pandavas, begotten by gods, grow up strong and learned, alongside the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
In a blossoming spring forest, Pandu, feeling his strength return, is overcome by desire, seizes Madri against her will, and dies in the act, as the curse foretold.
Madri calls Kunti, who comes grieving and blames Madri for taking Pandu into solitude.
Madri replies that she resisted, but Pandu could not control himself, as if he were making the sage's curse come true.
Kunti claims the right to follow Pandu as the senior wife, but Madri asks for Kunti's leave to go with him instead, saying Kunti is better able to raise her sons.
Madri ascends her husband's funeral pyre.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The sages on the mountain agree that Pandu left his sons in their trust, and resolve to take them to Hastinapura.
The sages set out with the children, Kunti and the two bodies; Kunti, unused to hardship, finds the journey short, and at Kurujangala the city comes out in crowds.
Bhishma, Dhritarashtra, Vidura and the court welcome the sages, and the eldest sage tells how Pandu retired, how each son was divinely born, and how Madri died, asking that the rites be performed.
The sages vanish before the eyes of the people, and the citizens return home in wonder.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Dhritarashtra tells Vidura to give Pandu and Madri a royal funeral with gifts to those who ask, and to wrap Madri's body so the sun and wind cannot see it.
Vidura and Bhishma choose a sacred site, and the bodies are carried in procession with priests, music and gifts to a wood on the Ganga, where they are washed, anointed and dressed.
The Kauravas light the pyre with lotuses, sandal paste and other fragrant offerings.
Kausalya falls senseless at the sight of the burning bodies, and the citizens, the birds and the beasts join in the lament, while Bhishma and Vidura are left disconsolate.
The Kurus perform the water rite, the Pandavas and their friends sleep on the ground, and the city mourns for twelve days with them.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma and Kunti perform Pandu's rites and feed the Kauravas and many Brahmanas, and the citizens return to Hastinapura in mourning.
Vyasa tells his mother Satyavati that sin is rising, the Kuru empire will not last, and she should retire to the forest.
Satyavati asks her daughter-in-law Ambika and Bhishma for leave, goes to the forest with two daughters-in-law, and leaves her body to ascend to heaven.
The Pandava boys are purified and grow up, and Bhima outplays the hundred Kaurava boys by pulling them by the hair and tormenting them in rough play, though not out of malice.
Duryodhana, jealous of Bhima's strength, plans to drown him in the Ganga and builds a water-sport house at Pramanakoti for an outing.

At the feast Duryodhana poisons Bhima's food; after bathing, Bhima collapses, is bound with creepers and thrown into the river, and sinks into the Naga realm, where the serpents' bites neutralise the poison.
Bhima wakes, breaks his bonds and presses the serpents underground, and the survivors report to their king Vasuki.
Vasuki goes to see Bhima, finds that Aryaka is a relative of Kunti's family, and offers Bhima wealth and gems.
Aryaka suggests that Bhima be allowed to drink from the nectar vessels, which hold the strength of a thousand elephants each.
The serpents perform rites, Bhima purifies himself, drinks eight jars of nectar, and lies down on a bed they prepare for him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The Kauravas ride home without Bhima, assuming he has gone ahead, and Duryodhana is glad to be rid of him.
Yudhishthira, trusting others to be as honest as himself, asks Kunti whether Bhima has come home, and fears he is dead.
Kunti, alarmed, says Bhima has not come to her and urges the brothers to search for him.
Kunti calls Vidura and says she fears Duryodhana, who covets the throne, has killed Bhima.
Vidura tells Kunti not to say such things and to protect her other sons.
He warns that accusing Duryodhana openly could lead him to harm her remaining sons.
He says a great sage has foretold that all her sons will live long.
So Bhima will surely return and gladden her heart.
Vidura goes home, and Kunti remains anxious with her children.
On the eighth day Bhima wakes, his strength increased by the nectar, and the Nagas encourage him and urge him to go home.
Bhima bathes, dresses in white with garlands, eats a rice pudding offered by the Nagas, and is carried back to the garden where he had been playing.
Bhima embraces his mother and brothers, who all rejoice at his return.
Bhima tells his brothers of Duryodhana's treachery and of his time in the Naga realm; Yudhishthira asks them to keep silent and guard one another, and Vidura keeps advising them.
Duryodhana poisons Bhima's food again, but Yuyutsu warns the Pandavas, and Bhima swallows it without harm.
Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni devise more schemes against the Pandavas, who keep their anger in check on Vidura's advice.
Dhritarashtra appoints Gautama, also called Kripa, who was born in a clump of heath, to teach the princes the use of arms.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Janamejaya asks how Kripa was born from a clump of heath and where he got his weapons.
Vaisampayana tells how Saradwat, son of Gautama, was born with arms and had a gift for them, and how Indra sent the nymph Janapadi to tempt him, so that his seed fell on heath and became twins.

A soldier of King Santanu finds the twins by their bow and deer-skin, and the king adopts them as Kripa and Kripi; Saradwat then learns where his children are, explains their lineage, and trains Kripa, who later teaches many princes.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma, wanting his grandsons well taught, chooses Drona, son of Bharadwaja, as their teacher, and the Kurus and Pandavas soon master the weapons.
Janamejaya asks how Drona was born, where he got his weapons, and how his son Aswatthaman came to be.
Vaisampayana tells how Bharadwaja caught his seed in a vessel after seeing the nymph Ghritachi, which produced Drona, who learned the Vedas and received the Agneya weapon from Agnivesa.
Drupada, son of Prishata, becomes Drona's playmate; after Bharadwaja's death Drona marries Kripi, whose son Aswatthaman is named for his horse-like cry at birth.
Drona hears that Rama, Jamadagni's son, is giving away his wealth and travels to Mahendra to ask for his weapons and wisdom.
Rama says he has given away his gold and lands and offers his body or his weapons, and Drona asks for the weapons.
Drona asks for the weapons along with the secrets of hurling and recalling them.
Rama gives Drona all his weapons and the whole science of arms, and Drona sets out for the city of his friend Drupada, well rewarded.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Drona presents himself to Drupada as his friend, but Drupada, proud of his wealth, scorns him and says old friendships fade and cannot join unequals.
Drona, filled with anger, resolves to check Drupada's arrogance and leaves the Panchala capital for Hastinapura.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Drona lives privately in Kripa's house, and his son Aswatthaman gives the Kuru princes a few lessons, though his skill is still unknown.
A section marker announces Section CXXXIV.
The princes lose their ball in a dry well, and a lean Brahmana, Drona in disguise, offers to bring it up with grass blades for a meal, then drops his ring in as well.
Drona does as he promised, lifting the ball by a chain of grass blades, and the amazed princes ask him to bring up the ring too.
Drona shoots an arrow through the ring and lifts it from the well, and the princes greet him as a master of arms and ask who he is.
The princes tell Bhishma, who recognises Drona, welcomes him to the palace, and asks why he has come.
Drona recounts his marriage to Kripi and the birth of his son Aswatthaman.
Drona tells how, in poverty, his crying son was fooled into thinking rice water was milk, how Drupada, now a king, scorned their old friendship, and why he has come to the Kurus.
Bhishma asks Drona to teach the Kuru princes and promises him the wealth and kingdom of the Kurus.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Bhishma honours Drona with a house and gifts and hands the Kaurava and Pandava princes over to him as pupils.
Drona asks the princes to promise a future service; they stay silent, but Arjuna vows to fulfil it, and Drona embraces him in tears. Karna, backed by Duryodhana, begins to defy Arjuna.
Drona gives his son a wide water jar and the other pupils narrow ones, but Arjuna fills his jar with a water weapon and keeps pace with Aswatthaman, and Drona praises his practice in the dark.

Drona trains Arjuna in fighting from horse, elephant, chariot and ground, and with many weapons; Ekalavya, son of the Nishada king, is refused as a pupil, so he makes a clay image of Drona and practises before it.
On a hunt, a servant's dog wanders into the woods, where it sees the dark, matted Ekalavya and barks at him.
Ekalavya shoots seven arrows into the dog's open mouth; the Pandavas, amazed, search the woods, find him, and learn he is a pupil of Drona.
The Pandavas report to Drona, and Arjuna complains that Drona had promised no pupil would match him.
Drona goes to Ekalavya, who bows and offers anything as a gift to his teacher; Drona asks for the thumb of his right hand as fee.
Ekalavya cheerfully cuts off his thumb and gives it, and when he shoots again he has lost his skill, so Arjuna is relieved.

The princes are rated in turn: Duryodhana and Bhima with the mace, the twins with the sword, Yudhishthira as a chariot warrior, and Arjuna as the best of all, able to fight sixty thousand foes; the Kauravas grow jealous.
Drona sets an artificial bird atop a tree and orders his pupils to shoot off its head when he gives the signal.
Drona asks Yudhishthira what he sees, and Yudhishthira says he sees the tree, himself, his brothers and the bird, so he is sent aside; the other pupils give the same answer and are sent aside too.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Drona tests the princes again; only Arjuna, who sees just the vulture's head, is able to shoot it off, and Drona clasps him in delight.
While Drona bathes in the Ganga, a crocodile seizes his thigh; Arjuna kills it with arrows, and Drona gives him the Brahmasira weapon with a warning never to use it on a human foe.
Drona tells Arjuna that no one will surpass him as a bowman and that he will never be defeated.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Drona asks Dhritarashtra for leave to show the princes' skill, the king agrees, and Drona consecrates a cleared field where the stages and galleries are built.
On the day, the king, Bhishma, Kripa, the women of the household and the citizens gather in such numbers that the arena looks like a churning ocean.

Drona, dressed all in white, enters with Aswatthaman; the princes, led by Yudhishthira, show archery and horsemanship, then swordsmanship, and finally Bhima and Duryodhana enter with maces like two warring elephants.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The crowd splits into partisans of Duryodhana and of Bhima, and Drona has Aswatthaman restrain the two maces before the uproar grows.
Drona calls for silence and presents Arjuna, Partha, as the dearest of his pupils, and Arjuna enters the lists in golden mail.
The crowd cheers Arjuna, Kunti weeps with joy, and Dhritarashtra, told by Vidura that Phalguna has entered, rejoices in his sons.
Arjuna conjures fire, water, wind, clouds and mountains with his weapons, makes them vanish, and hits moving targets with great skill, and the crowd calms down.
As the show winds down, a sound like thunder comes from the gate, and the crowd turns to look; Duryodhana rises with his hundred brothers and Aswatthaman.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
The narrator says Karna was born to Kunti in her maidenhood, a son of the Sun; he enters the lists, performs Arjuna's feats, and Duryodhana embraces him and welcomes him.
Arjuna, feeling disgraced, tells Karna he will die by his hand; Karna replies that the arena is open to all and offers to answer with arrows.

The two prepare to fight while the sky seems to favour one side or the other, and Kunti swoons and is revived by Vidura; Kripa asks Karna to name his lineage before a prince of royal birth fights him.
Karna is shamed, and Duryodhana proposes making Karna king of Anga, since only kings fight kings.
Karna is crowned king of Anga on a golden seat, promises to do whatever Duryodhana asks, and the two embrace in friendship.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Adhiratha enters the lists, perspiring and trembling, leaning on a staff with his sheet hanging loose.

Karna bows to the charioteer, who embraces him as his son in tears; Bhima mocks Karna as a charioteer's son unworthy of Anga, and Duryodhana rises to defend him, citing the unknown origins of heroes like Drona and Kripa.
The sun sets and the crowd, divided in its praise, disperses; Duryodhana leads Karna out, Kunti recognises her son and is pleased, and Duryodhana, freed from fear of Arjuna's skill, relies on Karna.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Drona asks the princes to seize Drupada as their fee, and Duryodhana, Karna, Yuyutsu and the other princes race to attack Drupada's capital.
Drupada comes out with his brothers, and the Kauravas rain arrows on him, but he fires back with force from his white chariot.
Arjuna waits outside the town with his brothers, and Drupada routs the Kauravas, who flee wailing toward the Pandavas.
The Pandavas advance, Bhima strikes down Drupada's elephants with his mace, and the Pandavas drive the Panchala army before them like a herdsman driving cattle.
Arjuna fells Drupada from his elephant and fights fiercely against the Panchalas and Srinjayas.
Arjuna defeats Satyajit by cutting his bows and horses to pieces, then cuts Drupada's bow and flag, leaps onto his chariot, and seizes him, and the Panchala troops flee.
Arjuna asks Bhima to spare the soldiers, since Drupada is a Kuru kinsman, and says they should only deliver the fee to Drona.
Bhima holds back, and the princes bring the captive Drupada to Drona, who humbles him and reminds him of their old friendship.
Drupada says he is moved by Drona's nobility and wants a lasting friendship with him.
Drona frees Drupada, gives him half the kingdom, and Drupada, sorrowful at Kampilya, concludes that Kshatriya might cannot beat Brahmanical power and goes searching for a son to defeat Drona.
Drona settles at Ahicchatra, a territory Arjuna had won and given to him.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
After a year, Dhritarashtra makes Yudhishthira heir apparent for his honesty and patience; Bhima trains under Balarama, and Arjuna masters every weapon, so that Drona says no one equals him.

Drona recalls the Brahmasira weapon he received from Agnivesa, reminds Arjuna of the fee he owes, and Arjuna pledges to pay it; the Pandavas then defeat the Sauviras, the Yavanas and the kings of the east and south.
Dhritarashtra grows uneasy at the great prowess of the Pandavas, and from that day he can hardly sleep.
Heading: the Sambhava Parva continues.
Dhritarashtra, troubled by the Pandavas' growing power, asks his minister Kanika whether he should make peace or war with them.
Kanika, a learned Brahmana skilled in politics, prepares to answer frankly.
Kanika says a king should always be ready to strike, hide his own weaknesses, exploit his foes' weaknesses, destroy enemies root and branch, and win their trust before he attacks.
Dhritarashtra asks how a foe can be destroyed by conciliation, money, division or force.
Kanika tells the fable of a clever jackal who lives with a tiger, mouse, wolf and mongoose, and who, after they kill a deer, turns the tiger against the mouse by reporting a false insult.
The jackal sends the mouse, wolf and mongoose away in turn with half-truths and threats, until only he is left with the carcass.
The jackal eats the deer alone, and Kanika says the timid should be frightened, the courageous won by conciliation, the greedy bought, and equals and inferiors subdued by show of force.
Kanika gives more advice: crush foes by any means, hide anger behind smiles, keep spies in every place, never trust the faithless, and guard the Kuru throne against the Pandavas.
Kanika leaves, and Dhritarashtra is left pensive and melancholy.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva begins.
Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni, with Dhritarashtra's sanction, plot to burn Kunti and her sons; Vidura reads their intent from their faces, arranges a boat, and urges Kunti to flee.

Kunti and her sons cross the Ganga and enter the forest, while the house of lac burns, killing a Nishada woman, her children and Purochana; the people tell Dhritarashtra he has won, and he puts on a show of mourning.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to recite in full the story of the house of lac and the escape, which he sees as a cruel act by the Kurus.

Vaisampayana says Duryodhana grew gloomy at the skill of Bhima and Arjuna, and that the citizens, noting that the blind Dhritarashtra could not rule and Bhishma would not, wanted Yudhishthira crowned.
Duryodhana, jealous and distressed, goes to Dhritarashtra and warns that if Pandu's son inherits the throne, the line of Pandu will keep it, and that the king should act now.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
Dhritarashtra wavers after Kanika's counsel, and Duryodhana urges him to send the Pandavas to Varanavata, but Dhritarashtra recalls Pandu's virtue and the people's loyalty to Yudhishthira.
Duryodhana argues that buying the people with wealth and honours will secure their support, and that the Pandavas can be sent away gently and recalled later.
Dhritarashtra admits the exile is in his mind but calls it sinful, since Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and Kripa would never sanction it and the world would condemn them.
Duryodhana replies that Bhishma will stay neutral, Aswatthaman and Kripa are with him, Vidura depends on them, and he urges the exile to happen that very day.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
Duryodhana wins the people with wealth and honours, and Dhritarashtra's councillors praise a festival of Shiva at Varanavata, until the Pandavas wish to go and the king tells them to enjoy it.
Yudhishthira, knowing he is weak and friendless, agrees, and asks Bhishma, Vidura, Drona, Kripa, Gandhari and the others for their blessings, which they give.
The Pandavas complete their preparations and set out for Varanavata.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
Duryodhana takes Purochana aside, orders him to build a richly furnished house of flammable materials by the arsenal, and to set it alight once the Pandavas sleep, so the fire looks accidental.
Purochana obeys, travels to Varanavata in a swift car, and carries out Duryodhana's orders.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
The Pandavas take leave of Bhishma, Dhritarashtra, Drona, Kripa, Vidura and the elders, and set out for Varanavata while Vidura and the citizens follow.
Citizens lament the injustice of the exile and offer to follow the Pandavas, but Yudhishthira asks them to go home, obey the king, and bless him.
Vidura speaks to Yudhishthira in a foreign tongue that only he understands, warning him to beware of flammable traps and to keep many exits and his senses under control.
Yudhishthira replies that he understands, Vidura goes home, and Kunti asks Yudhishthira what the two of them said.
Yudhishthira tells Kunti that Vidura warned the house was built of flammable material, that they should know the path of escape, and that those who control their senses can win the world.
The Pandavas set out on the eighth day of Phalguna under the star Rohini and arrive at Varanavata, where they see the town and its people.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
The citizens welcome the Pandavas with rituals, and they are installed in Purochana's palace with fine food, beds and robes.
After ten nights Purochana shows them the Blessed Home, and Yudhishthira, smelling fat and lac, recognises that the house is made of flammable material and recalls Vidura's warning.
Bhima suggests they go back to their old quarters, but Yudhishthira says they should seem unsuspicious, dig a secret passage, and live in disguise until they can escape.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.

A miner sent by Vidura reveals himself and warns of a fire on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight; Yudhishthira trusts him, and the miner digs a secret passage, covered with planks, while the Pandavas sleep armed and hunt in the forest by day.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
Seeing Purochana deceived for a full year, Yudhishthira judges the time to escape has come and proposes burning the arsenal and Purochana and leaving unseen.

At Kunti's almsgiving a Nishada woman and her five sons, drunk, fall asleep in the house; Bhima sets fire to it, and the citizens watching the blaze lament Purochana's wickedness and Dhritarashtra's partiality.
The Pandavas and Kunti enter the tunnel and flee unseen while the citizens wait outside, and Bhima carries his mother and brothers through the dark, breaking trees and treading the earth deep.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.

Vidura's trusted agent finds the Pandavas and their mother measuring the depth of a river, shows them a sturdy boat, and proves who sent him with Vidura's coded words and his promise that Yudhishthira will defeat Karna and Duryodhana.
The agent takes them into the boat and reminds them, in Vidura's name, not to be careless on their journey.
He ferries them across the Ganga, sees them safe on the far bank, wishes them victory, and returns to his own place.
The Pandavas send a message to Vidura through the agent and hurry on in secret after crossing the river.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.
At dawn a crowd comes to the burnt house, finds the lac-built ruins and Purochana dead, and blames Duryodhana, with Dhritarashtra's knowledge, for the murder of the Pandavas.
Searching the ashes, the people find the Nishada woman and her five sons burnt, while Vidura's miner covers his tunnel with ash so that it goes unnoticed.
The citizens report to Dhritarashtra that the Pandavas are dead, and he weeps and orders funeral rites for them and their mother, to be paid for with wealth.
The Kauravas offer water in mourning, calling the Pandavas' names, and the citizens weep, but Vidura does not weep much because he knows the truth.
The six fugitives cross the Ganga with the boatmen's help, then head south by starlight into a dense forest, exhausted and thirsty.
Yudhishthira tells Bhima that they cannot find their way and asks him to carry them, and Bhima takes his mother and brothers on his body and goes swiftly on.
Heading: the Jatugriha (house of lac) Parva continues.

Bhima forces a path through the forest like a rutting elephant with his mother and brothers on his back, reaches a wild place at evening, fetches water for Kunti from a lake, and laments their fall while threatening Dhritarashtra's sons, held back only by Yudhishthira.
Angry and sorrowful, Bhima sits awake to guard his sleeping mother and brothers, thinking a town must be nearby.
Heading: the Hidimva-vadha (slaying of Hidimva) Parva begins.
Hidimva, a grim red-haired man-eater in a sal tree, smells the sleeping Pandavas and orders his sister to bring them to him as food.
The sister finds Bhima awake, falls in love with him, decides to disobey her brother, and offers herself as his wife.
Bhima refuses to leave his sleeping mother and brothers to the Rakshasa or to his own desire.
The Rakshasa woman says she will wake the family and save them from her brother.
Bhima refuses to wake his family while the Rakshasa is near, tells her she may go or send her brother, and says no Rakshasa can match his arms.
Heading: the Hidimva-vadha (slaying of Hidimva) Parva continues.
The Rakshasa Hidimva comes down from the tree, and his sister, alarmed, asks Bhima to let her carry the family away through the sky.
Bhima tells her not to fear, promises to slay the cannibal before her eyes, and boasts of his arms and chest.
The sister replies that she does not scorn Bhima, but she knows what Rakshasas do to men.
Hidimva sees his sister disguised and smitten, is enraged at her disobedience, and rushes at her to kill her, but Bhima cries out to stop him.
Bhima mocks Hidimva's threat, says his sister is not to blame for desire, and challenges him to single combat.
Hidimva answers that Bhima should prove his strength first, and vows to kill Bhima, then the brothers, then his sister.
Hidimva charges; Bhima seizes his arms and drags him away from the sleepers, and the two fight like rutting elephants, waking the Pandavas, who see Hidimva before them.
Heading: the Hidimva-vadha (slaying of Hidimva) Parva continues.
Kunti is charmed by the Rakshasa woman and asks who she is, and Hidimva explains that her brother was sent to kill them, that she loves Bhima, and that Bhima is now fighting her brother.
The brothers wake to see Bhima and the Rakshasa grappling in the dust; Arjuna offers to help, then urges Bhima to finish before the Rakshasa grows stronger at dawn.
Bhima whirls the Rakshasa in the air a hundred times, rebukes him, and vows to end his man-eating; Arjuna offers help again.
Bhima dashes Hidimva to the ground and kills him, then breaks the body in two, and his brothers praise him and urge that they leave before Duryodhana finds them.
The Pandavas and their mother set out, and Hidimva's sister follows them.
Heading: the Hidimva-vadha (slaying of Hidimva) Parva continues.
Bhima warns the Rakshasa woman to follow her brother, but Yudhishthira stops him from harming a woman, since her brother is already dead.
Hidimva humbly asks Kunti and Yudhishthira to let her have Bhima as her husband, pleading that she will serve them and carry them through dangers.
Yudhishthira agrees, on condition that Bhima attend to her during the day and that she bring him back to the family each nightfall.
Bhima agrees to stay with her until she has a son; Hidimva carries him through many regions until she bears Ghatotkacha, a bald, fierce child who grows up quickly and becomes devoted to the Pandavas.
Hidimva takes leave, Ghatotkacha promises his father to come when needed and goes north, and the narrator says Indra made Ghatotkacha as a match for Karna's dart.
Heading: the Hidimva-vadha (slaying of Hidimva) Parva continues.
The Pandavas travel in disguise through the lands of the Matsyas, Trigartas, Panchalas and Kichakas, sometimes carrying their mother, studying the Vedas, and then meet their grandfather Vyasa.
Vyasa says he foresaw their exile, that it is meant for their happiness, and tells them to wait in disguise in a nearby town until he returns.
Vyasa leads them to Ekachakra and comforts Kunti by predicting that Yudhishthira will rule the earth and that the brothers will perform great sacrifices.
Vyasa places the Pandavas in the house of a Brahmana and tells Yudhishthira to wait for him, adding that they will be happy if they adapt to the country.
The Pandavas agree, and Vyasa returns to the place he came from.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva begins.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after arriving at Ekachakra.
The Pandavas live by alms and win the townspeople's favour, and Kunti divides the food they bring into two shares, one for herself and her sons and one for Bhima.
One day, while the brothers are out begging, Kunti hears a heart-rending wail from the Brahmana's house and feels compelled to help, since they are living under his roof.
Bhima tells his mother to learn the cause of the Brahmana's distress, and promises to relieve it however hard the task may be.
Kunti enters and finds the Brahmana with his wife, son and daughter in despair; he laments the emptiness of life and his inability to give up any of them, so he thinks of dying with them.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
The Brahmana's wife tells him not to mourn, says death is inevitable, and offers herself to the Rakshasa, arguing that her husband and their children must be saved.
The Brahmana embraces his wife, and the two weep together in silence.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
The daughter asks her parents to stop weeping and offers herself, likening herself to a raft that can carry them across their troubles.
The little son, lisping sweetly, tells his parents and sister not to weep and says he will slay the man-eating Rakshasa with a blade of grass; their faces brighten, and Kunti steps in.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
Kunti asks the Brahmana to tell her the cause of his grief, promising to remove it if she can.

The Brahmana explains that the man-eater Vaka is fed in turn by each household with rice, buffaloes and a man, that his family's turn has come, and that with no money for a substitute he will take his whole family to be devoured.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
Kunti tells the Brahmana not to grieve, since she has five sons and will send one of them with the tribute, because his children are too young.
The Brahmana refuses, saying he will never sacrifice a Brahmana or a guest to save himself, and that he would rather die himself.
Kunti replies that she values Brahmanas, and that her son Bhima, endowed with great might and mantras, will deliver the food and save himself, and asks the Brahmana to keep this secret.
The Brahmana, relieved, accepts, and Kunti takes the matter to Bhima, who says so be it.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
Bhima pledges to do the task, and the brothers return with the day's alms; Yudhishthira, reading the matter from Bhima's face, asks his mother privately what task Bhima has taken on.
Yudhishthira calls the plan rash and almost suicidal, condemns sacrificing one's child against custom and the Vedas, and reminds Kunti that the family's hopes rest on Bhima's arms.

Kunti replies that her judgement is sound, that she is repaying the Brahmana's kindness, that Bhima's might was proved at the house of lac and against Hidimva, and that Kshatriyas must protect Brahmanas, as Vyasa taught.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
Yudhishthira says Kunti's compassion is admirable and that Bhima will surely return alive, but asks that the Brahmana keep the arrangement secret from the townspeople.
At night Bhima carries the food into the forest, begins to eat it, and calls the Rakshasa by name, and Vaka comes out in rage.
Vaka, huge and red-haired, rushes at Bhima, who keeps eating unperturbed; the two hurl trees at each other, Bhima wrestles him down, bends him double over his knee, and Vaka begins to vomit blood.
Heading: the Vaka-vadha (slaying of Vaka) Parva continues.
Bhima comforts Vaka's terrified kin and makes them promise never to kill human beings again, then drags the corpse to a town gate and leaves unseen.
Bhima tells Yudhishthira everything; the next morning the people find the mangled Rakshasa, and their Brahmana host says a Brahmana skilled in mantras took the food to the forest and did the deed.
The Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras hold a festival in which the worship of Brahmanas is the main ceremony.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva begins.
The citizens go home, and the Pandavas stay at Ekachakra as before.
Janamejaya asks the Brahmana what the tigers among men did after slaying Vaka.
The question ends by naming the Pandavas and Vaka's death.

Vaisampayana says a visiting Brahmana of rigid vows lodges with their host, and at the Pandavas' request he tells of lands and shrines, and of Draupadi and Dhrishtadyumna's births at Drupada's sacrifice.
The Pandavas ask how Dhrishtadyumna and Krishna were born, how Drupada's son learned all weapons from Drona, and why the friendship between Drona and Drupada broke off.
Vaisampayana says the Brahmana then began to tell all the particulars of Draupadi's birth.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
The Brahmana recounts Drona's birth from Bharadwaja's seed caught in a pot, his boyhood friendship with Drupada, and his journey to Rama to ask for weapons.
Rama gives Drona all his weapons; Drona then goes to Drupada, asks to be his friend, and is scorned by him as unworthy.
Humiliated, Drona takes up the Kuru princes as pupils, sets them to capture Drupada as his fee, and divides Drupada's kingdom between them.
The defeated Drupada accepts a bond of friendship and returns home, but the humiliation stays with him and he begins to waste away.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.

Drupada, despondent that his children lack accomplishment and bent on revenge, courts the sages Yaja and Upayaja; Upayaja at first refuses the sacrifice and then points him to his greedy brother Yaja, who agrees for a great fee.
Yaja pours the oblation, and when the queen asks to wait, he refuses, since the offering is already prepared and consecrated.

From the fire rises an armoured, crowned son destined to slay Drona, followed by a dark-complexioned, beautiful daughter; an unseen voice says the girl will cause many Kshatriyas to die, and the Brahmanas name them Dhrishtadyumna and Krishna.
Drona takes the prince as a pupil and teaches him all weapons, in return for the half of Drupada's kingdom he took earlier, and the narrator notes that Drona accepts destiny.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
The Pandavas are unsettled by the Brahmana's tale, and Kunti suggests they leave for Panchala, where alms are plentiful and the king is devoted to Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira agrees that his mother's command is for their good, but wonders whether his younger brothers will be willing.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Kunti tells her sons of the plan, they agree, and the family takes leave of their host and sets out for Drupada's city.

Vyasa visits the Pandavas, asks whether they keep the law and honour Brahmanas, and tells of a maiden who was promised five husbands by Shiva, so Draupadi of Drupada's line is to be the wife of all five; he urges them to go to Panchala.
Vyasa blesses the Pandavas and departs for his own place.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
The Pandavas walk north toward Panchala, Arjuna leading with a torch, and reach the Ganga, where the Gandharva Angaraparna, bathing with his wives, boasts of his strength and orders them away.
Arjuna retorts that no one can bar people from the sacred Ganga, which flows to the sea and purifies all who bathe in it.
The Gandharva shoots arrows at the Pandavas, Arjuna shields himself and answers that he will fight with a celestial weapon, the fiery weapon passed down from Vrihaspati to Drona.

Arjuna hurls the fire weapon, burning the Gandharva's chariot, then drags him by the hair; his wife Kumbhinasi begs for mercy, and Yudhishthira, seeing a defeated foe under a woman's protection, orders Arjuna to spare him.

The Gandharva acknowledges defeat, gives up his old name, and offers Arjuna his science of illusion, called Chakshushi, and a hundred Gandharva horses, explaining the thunderbolt's fragments that make a warrior's strength.
A section marker begins Section CLXXIII.
Arjuna says he will not accept the gifts for free, and the Gandharva asks in exchange for Arjuna's fiery weapon.
Arjuna accepts the horses in exchange for his weapon, asks why the Gandharva rebuked them at night, and wants a lasting friendship.
The Gandharva says the Pandavas travelled without wives or a priest, that he knows their ancestors, and that a king with a priest prevails and the realm lasts where Brahmanas hold power.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Arjuna asks what the name Tapatya means, since his family is called Kaunteya and not after Tapati.
The Gandharva agrees to tell the story, which is well known throughout the three worlds.
The Gandharva says Tapati, daughter of the Sun and younger sister of Savitri, has no equal in beauty, and the Sun chooses King Samvarana, a devoted worshipper of him, as her husband.
While hunting in the mountains, Samvarana's horse dies of exhaustion, and on foot he comes upon Tapati, who shines like gold, and is struck with desire.
Burning with desire, the king asks the maiden who she is and whose she is, praises her beauty, and says Kama is tormenting him.
Tapati says nothing and vanishes like lightning, and the king searches the forest in a daze, lamenting and standing motionless in grief.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Tapati reappears and gently tells the fallen king to rise, and the king begs her in passionate words to accept him and to wed him in the Gandharva form.

Tapati replies that she is under her father's control, so the king should ask the Sun for her hand with worship and penance, and she names herself as Tapati, Savitri's younger sister and the Sun's daughter.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.

Samvarana, revived by his minister, worships the Sun; Vasishtha goes to the Sun, asks for Tapati on the king's behalf, and after the marriage on the mountain the couple live together twelve years, until a long drought is ended when Vasishtha brings the king home and the rains return.
The Gandharva says this is the history of Tapati, and that Arjuna is called Tapatya because Samvarana's son Kuru was born of her.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.

Arjuna asks about Vasishtha, and the Gandharva describes him as Brahma's mind-born son and the family priest of the Pandavas' forebears, whose austerity overcame Desire and Wrath, and urges them to choose a learned Brahmana as their priest.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Arjuna asks what caused the hostility between Viswamitra and Vasishtha, who both dwelt in a celestial hermitage.
The Gandharva tells how Viswamitra, son of King Gadhi, came weary from hunting to Vasishtha's hermitage, where he was fed with food and drink from Nandini, the wish-granting cow.
Viswamitra asks Vasishtha to give him Nandini in exchange for ten thousand cows or his kingdom.
Vasishtha refuses, since the cow is kept for the gods, guests, the ancestors and sacrifices, and Viswamitra says he will take her by force.
Vasishtha tells the king to act at once without concern for propriety, since he is a powerful Kshatriya.
Viswamitra seizes Nandini and beats her, and she lows piteously and goes back to Vasishtha's hermitage, refusing to leave it.
Vasishtha, seeing her plight, speaks to the cow.
He says he hears her cries, but that Viswamitra is carrying her off by force.
He says he can do nothing about it, as a forgiving Brahmana.
He asks what he can do, since he is a forgiving Brahmana.
Nandini protests that he is casting her off, and Vasishtha replies that she may stay if she can, pointing to her calf tied with a stout cord nearby.

Nandini rages, sending out armies of Palhavas, Dravidas, Sakas, Yavanas and many other tribes from her body, and routs Viswamitra's army; Viswamitra says the Brahmana's power is true strength, renounces his kingdom, and becomes a Brahmana who drinks Soma with Indra.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
King Kalmashapada of the Ikshvaku line hunts in the forest, killing deer, boars and rhinoceroses, and tires, and gives up the chase to rest.

On a forest path he meets Shakti, Vasishtha's eldest son; neither will yield, the king strikes him with a whip, Shakti curses him to become a man-eating Rakshasa, and Viswamitra, who had wanted the king as his disciple, sends a Rakshasa named Kinkara to possess him.
The possessed king, having forgotten his promise to a hungry Brahmana, sends his cook to feed him with meat.
The cook, finding no meat, serves human flesh, and the Brahmana, seeing it is unholy, curses the king to become fond of such food and wander the earth as a man-eater.

The possessed king kills and devours Shakti, the Rakshasa, urged on by Viswamitra, devours Vasishtha's other sons, and Vasishtha, grieving, throws himself from Meru, into fire and into the sea, but cannot die, and returns to his hermitage.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.

Grieving over his lost sons, Vasishtha ties himself with cords and throws himself into flooded rivers, but the currents break the cords and cast him ashore; the rivers are named for his failure, and he cannot die.

Hearing the Vedas recited behind him, Vasishtha learns from his daughter-in-law Adrisyanti that she is carrying Shakti's child, and he refrains from self-destruction; then he meets the Rakshasa-possessed King Kalmashapada, who is about to devour him.
Vasishtha restrains the king with a sacred sound and sanctified water, freeing him from the curse, and the king asks for a son to carry on the Ikshvaku line.
Vasishtha agrees, goes to the king's capital Ayodhya, and beds the queen; after twelve years of pregnancy the queen tears open her womb and Asmaka is born, the founder of Paudanya.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Adrisyanti bears Parasara, a second Shakti, whom Vasishtha raises; when the boy calls Vasishtha father, his mother corrects him, and in grief and anger he resolves to destroy the world.

Vasishtha tells how the descendants of King Kritavirya begged from the Bhrigus, found the treasure the Bhrigus had hidden, and then slaughtered the Bhrigus, even their unborn children, until a Bhrigu woman's son burst from her thigh and blinded the Kshatriyas.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.

The Bhrigu woman tells the Kshatriyas she did not blind them, but her unborn son, held in her thigh for a hundred years, was angered by their slaughter of his race and has blinded them, so they must propitiate him.

The Kshatriyas propitiate the child, who is named Aurva for being born from the thigh and restores their sight; Aurva then sets out to destroy the whole world through severe austerity to avenge his ancestors.
The Pitris come to Aurva and beg him to restrain his wrath, explaining that the Bhrigus had let themselves be slain by choice and that he should not destroy the Kshatriyas or the worlds.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
The Gandharva says Vasishtha goes on with the story, telling how Aurva replied to the Pitris.

Aurva answers that his vow cannot be undone, that wrath is useful to restrain the wicked, and that kings failed to protect the Bhrigus, so his fire must consume the worlds unless he finds a way to quench it.
The Pitris advise him to throw his wrath into the waters, since the worlds depend on water and his fire can be contained in the great ocean.
Aurva casts the fire into the ocean, where it becomes the horse-headed fire Vadavamukha that consumes the sea, and Vasishtha tells Parasara not to destroy the worlds.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Parasara, restrained from destroying the worlds, performs a grand Rakshasa sacrifice to avenge Shakti, while Vasishtha does not stop him, and he sits like a fourth fire among three blazing ones.

Sages Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu come to save the Rakshasas, and Pulastya tells Parasara that Shakti brought on his own death, that the Rakshasas are innocent, and that he should end the sacrifice.
Persuaded by Pulastya and Vasishtha, Parasara ends the sacrifice and casts its fire into the deep woods north of the Himalayas, where it still burns Rakshasas and trees.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Arjuna asks why King Kalmashapada sent his queen to Vasishtha, and whether Vasishtha committed a sin in knowing her.

The Gandharva explains that the cursed king devoured a Brahmana while his wife wept, that she cursed him to die when he went to his queen and to have a son by Vasishtha, and that the king, remembering the curse after his queen sent him away, repented and asked Vasishtha for an heir.
Heading: the Chaitraratha Parva continues.
Arjuna asks the Gandharva which Brahmana learned in the Vedas would make a worthy priest for them.
The Gandharva names Dhaumya, younger brother of Devala, who performs austerities at the shrine of Utkochaka.

Arjuna gives the Gandharva his fire weapon, leaves the horses with him for later, and the Pandavas install Dhaumya as their priest; they then set out for the Swayamvara, regarding their kingdom and Draupadi as already as good as theirs.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva begins.

The Pandavas set out for Panchala, and on the road they meet Brahmanas bound for Drupada's Swayamvara, who describe the lovely Draupadi, sister of Dhrishtadyumna, and the princes who will compete for her, and invite the brothers to come.
Yudhishthira agrees to go with the Brahmanas to witness the Swayamvara.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.
On the road the Pandavas meet Vyasa, then enter Panchala and take lodging as Brahmanas in a potter's house, where no one recognises them.
Drupada, who secretly wants Arjuna for his daughter, has a very stiff bow made that only Arjuna could bend, and sets up a mark to be shot through a machine in the sky.
Drupada proclaims the Swayamvara, and kings, sages, Duryodhana, Karna and the Kurus arrive, and the splendid amphitheatre with its white mansions is described in detail.
The Pandavas sit among the Brahmanas, and on the sixteenth day Draupadi enters with a golden dish and garland, the sacrificial fire is lit, and Dhrishtadyumna proclaims the contest.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.

Dhrishtadyumna names Duryodhana and his brothers with Karna, Shakuni, Aswatthaman, a huge roll of kings from Kalinga to Madra, the Vrishnis, Jarasandha and Shishupala, and says that the one who shoots the mark is the one Draupadi should choose.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.
The princes, jealous and lovesick, rise to win Draupadi while the gods, sages and Yadavas watch; Krishna points out the Pandavas to Balarama, and the princes try the bow but cannot string it.
Several kings are thrown down and gasp, their hopes cooled; Karna picks up the bow and strings it, but Draupadi declares she will not choose a Suta, and Karna throws the bow down in vexation.
Shishupala, Jarasandha and Shalya each fall to their knees trying the bow, and when the others have given up, Arjuna rises to string it.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.

Arjuna, a Brahmana to all appearances, rises as Brahmanas murmur about the stripling's boldness, bows to Shiva, strings the bow effortlessly, and shoots the mark through the machine; the gods shower flowers, bards sing, Krishna greets him with a garland, and Arjuna leaves the hall with Draupadi as his bride.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.
The rejected kings, angry that Drupada has given his daughter to a Brahmana, resolve to kill him, arguing that the Swayamvara is for Kshatriyas only.

The kings rush at Drupada, who seeks protection from the Brahmanas; Bhima uproots a tree to use as a weapon and stands with Arjuna, and Krishna tells Balarama that the warriors are the Pandavas who escaped the fire of the house of lac, and Balarama is glad that Pritha survived.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.

Arjuna tells the Brahmanas to stand aside and watch as he and Bhima charge the kings, and he duels Karna until Karna guesses who he might be, and Arjuna answers that he is a Brahmana skilled in weapons who will defeat him.
Bhima wrestles Shalya and tosses him to the ground without hurting him; the kings, alarmed, ask who these Brahmanas are and call for a halt to the fight.
Krishna tells the kings that the maiden was justly won, and they withdraw, while the Pandavas, wounded and surrounded by Brahmanas, leave the crowd with Krishna.

Kunti, anxious at her sons' delay, imagines that the Kauravas or Rakshasas have killed them, and wonders whether Vyasa has misled them, until Arjuna enters the potter's house with a group of Brahmanas.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.
The brothers return to their mother and present Draupadi as the alms they got; Kunti, not yet seeing what they have brought, tells them to share it, but when she sees Krishna she cries out in alarm.
Kunti asks Yudhishthira how to keep her word without sin, and Yudhishthira tells Arjuna, who won the maiden, to take her hand in marriage.
Arjuna refuses to be party to sin and says the eldest should marry first, then Bhima, then himself, the twins, and that they all obey Yudhishthira's command.
The brothers look at Draupadi and at one another, all overcome with desire for her; Yudhishthira, fearing division among the brothers, declares that she shall be the common wife of all five.
Krishna and Balarama come to the potter's house, find the five brothers, greet Yudhishthira, praise their escape from the fire, and urge them to return to the tents; then they leave.
Heading: the Swayamvara Parva continues.

Dhrishtadyumna secretly follows the Pandavas and hides in the potter's house; Kunti divides the food, the brothers eat and sleep on kusha grass with Draupadi at their feet, and Dhrishtadyumna listens to their talk.
At dawn Dhrishtadyumna hurries to report everything to Drupada, who is anxious and asks who has taken his daughter, and hopes it was Arjuna who shot the mark.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section.
