Dhrishtadyumna reports the contest: the archer hits the mark, the rival kings are beaten, and the winners take Krishna to a potter's house where their mother waits.
Drupada, delighted, sends his priest to ask who the strangers are, adding that he had long hoped Arjuna would wed his daughter.
Yudhishthira has the priest honoured with water and offerings, then argues that the bride was won fairly and Drupada should not grieve.
A messenger hurries in to say the wedding feast is ready.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
A messenger invites the group to the wedding feast and says the chariots are ready.

The party rides to the palace, Kunti goes inside, and the guests are seated and fed; while Drupada gathers goods to test their rank, the guests' interest in the weapons persuades Drupada and his son that they are royal.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
Drupada asks cheerfully whether they are Kshatriyas, Brahmanas or gods in disguise, and asks for the plain truth.
Yudhishthira declares that they are Kshatriyas and sons of Pandu, names his brothers, and says Kunti and the twins are waiting nearby.
Drupada, overjoyed, asks how they escaped Varanavata, hears the account, blames Dhritarashtra, and vows to restore Yudhishthira's throne.
Drupada gives the group a home and asks Arjuna to take his daughter's hand in marriage that day.
Drupada offers to give Krishna to Yudhishthira or any brother, and Yudhishthira replies that she must be the common wife of all five, as their mother ordered.
Drupada objects that a man may have many wives but no woman has had many husbands, and Yudhishthira answers that morality is subtle and his mother's command settles it.
Drupada asks Yudhishthira, Kunti and Dhrishtadyumna to settle the matter among themselves and tell him by morning.
Yudhishthira, Kunti and Dhrishtadyumna begin to discuss it, and then Vyasa arrives on his wanderings.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
Everyone rises to greet Vyasa, and after Drupada asks how one woman can wed many men without sin, Vyasa calls the practice obsolete and asks each man's view.
Drupada says the custom is sinful, contrary to usage and the Vedas, and that he cannot agree to it.
Dhrishtadyumna objects that an elder brother should not approach a younger brother's wife, and he refuses to say Draupadi should be shared.
Yudhishthira cites old precedents, a woman who married seven sages and a tree-born maiden who married ten brothers, and argues that his mother's command makes the match virtuous.
Kunti agrees with Yudhishthira but fears her own words may prove untrue.
Vyasa says the matter is an old and eternal virtue, that Yudhishthira's view is sound, and that he will explain it only to Drupada in private.
Vyasa takes Drupada into a private room while the others wait, and begins to explain why the custom is not sinful.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
Vyasa says that when Yama paused killing during a sacrifice, humans multiplied, and the gods went to Prajapati, who said Yama would resume his work later.
Indra sees golden lotuses floating down the Bhagirathi, follows the stream to its source, and finds a weeping woman washing there.
The woman leads Indra to a peak where Mahadeva is playing dice; Indra's pride is punished, and he and four other Indras are cursed to be born as men.

Indra makes a fifth Indra, the five are named, Sri is given as their common wife, and Narayana sends two hairs that become Valadeva and Krishna, while the brothers are the Indras and Arjuna is part of Sakra.
Vyasa explains that the Pandavas are those Indras and Draupadi is Sri, who must be born in an extraordinary way, and grants Drupada spiritual sight.
With this sight Drupada sees the brothers in celestial form, is amazed, and hears Vyasa tell of a maiden who asked Mahadeva for five husbands.
Vyasa applies the story to Drupada's daughter, who was pre-ordained to be the common wife of five husbands, and tells the king to do as he wishes.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
Drupada says he now accepts what the gods have ordained, since fate, not his own acts, has settled the marriage, and gives his consent.

The wedding is held on Vyasa's auspicious day, with Dhaumya lighting the fire, the brothers taking Krishna's hand in turn, and Drupada giving rich gifts; the text also notes a marvel that Krishna regained her maidenhood each day.
Heading: the Vaivahika Parva section continues.
Drupada's household women greet Kunti, and Kunti blesses Krishna, comparing her to famous wives and asking for sons and a royal future.
Hari (Krishna) sends the brothers ornaments, robes, servants, elephants, horses and gold, and Yudhishthira accepts them gladly to please Govinda.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section.
Spies report that Draupadi has married the Pandavas, and the kings, who had thought the brothers dead in the lac house, blame Bhishma and Dhritarashtra.
Duryodhana and his company return dejected, and Duhsasana says Arjuna only won by disguising himself as a Brahmana and that fate rules.
Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that the Pandavas are alive and allied with Drupada, but the blind king first thinks his own son has won Draupadi and orders ornaments made for her.
Dhritarashtra says the Pandavas are as dear to him as they were to Pandu, and that an alliance with Drupada is a fine thing.

Vidura tells the king to keep his good sense for a hundred years and goes home; then Duryodhana and Karna come to Dhritarashtra alone, accuse him of favouring his enemies, and urge him to weaken the Pandavas before they swallow the Kauravas.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Dhritarashtra says he will keep his plans from Vidura and asks his son and Karna to speak now that Vidura has left.

Duryodhana lists his schemes, including sowing discord, bribing Drupada, luring the brothers to Panchala or Hastinapura, turning Krishna against them, and having Bhima killed, then asks Karna for his view.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Karna rejects the subtle plans, argues that the brothers cannot be divided or turned against Krishna, and urges an open attack on Drupada before Krishna's forces gather.
Dhritarashtra praises Karna's courage but asks Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the others to advise on a course that benefits all.
Dhritarashtra calls his chief ministers together to take counsel.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Bhishma opposes any quarrel, urges Dhritarashtra to give the Pandavas half the kingdom, and appeals to the king's good name and the brothers' rightful share.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Drona agrees with Bhishma, proposes a messenger with gifts to Drupada and the Pandavas, and then the brothers' return and their installation on the throne.
Karna accuses Bhishma and Drona of bias and tells the tale of the Magadha king Amvuvicha, whose minister seized power, to argue that kingship depends on fate.
Drona calls Karna wicked for trying to harm the Pandavas and warns that the Kurus will be ruined if his advice is followed.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.

Vidura trusts Bhishma and Drona, argues that the Pandavas cannot be beaten given their allies, urges the king to make peace with them and win Drupada as an ally, and warns against Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Dhritarashtra accepts the counsel, calls the Pandavas his children by ordinance, and orders them brought back with Kunti and Krishna.
Vidura travels to Drupada with gifts, embraces the brothers, greets Vasudeva, and hands over the jewels and wealth the Kauravas sent.
Vidura delivers Dhritarashtra's message to Drupada: the Kurus are glad of the alliance and ask that the Pandavas be allowed to return home with Krishna.
Heading: the Viduragamana Parva section continues.
Drupada says he is glad of the alliance, but the brothers should go only if they and Rama and Krishna agree.
Yudhishthira replies that he and his brothers depend on Drupada and will do as he commands.
Vasudeva says the Pandavas should go, but that the decision should rest with Drupada.
Drupada agrees with Vasudeva and says he regards the brothers as dear as Vasudeva does.
The Pandavas travel toward Hastinapura, where Vikarna, Chitrasena, Drona and Kripa are sent out to meet them, and the citizens cheer their return.
The brothers pay their respects to Dhritarashtra and Bhishma and to the others present, then go to their rooms.
Dhritarashtra tells Yudhishthira to take up residence at Khandavaprastha, under Arjuna's protection, and rule half the kingdom.
The brothers leave for Khandavaprastha, choose a site with Dwaipayana's help, and build a walled city with a trench and war machines, which they name Indraprastha.
Brahmanas, merchants and craftsmen come to the new city, which is surrounded by gardens, lakes and pleasure-houses, and the brothers' joy grows.
Because Bhishma and Dhritarashtra treated them well, the Pandavas settle at Khandavaprastha, and Krishna goes back to Dwaravati with Rama.
Heading: the Rajya-labha Parva section.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after gaining Indraprastha and how no quarrel arose among brothers sharing one wife.
Narada visits the Pandavas, is honoured, and warns them to make a rule about Draupadi so that no quarrel arises, citing the brothers Sunda and Upasunda who killed each other.
Yudhishthira asks Narada who Sunda and Upasunda were, where the quarrel came from, and who Tilottama was, and asks for the full story.
Heading: the Rajya-labha Parva section continues.
The brothers, sons of Nikumbha, perform harsh penance on the Vindhya mountains, resist the gods' temptations and illusions, and win Brahma's favour, though he refuses them immortality.
Brahma grants them invulnerability to all beings except each other, and the brothers return home, where they and their people give themselves to feasting and merriment.
Heading: the Rajya-labha Parva section continues.
The brothers set out with a great army, conquer heaven and the lower worlds, order the killing of sacrificers and Brahmanas, and finally settle at Kurukshetra as the earth falls into ruin.
Heading: the Rajya-labha Parva section continues.
The grieved gods and Rishis approach Brahma, who has Viswakarman create the maiden Tilottama and send her to make the brothers quarrel over her.
Tilottama walks round the assembly, Mahadeva grows four faces and a thousand eyes to watch her, and after she leaves for the Asuras, the great god First Cause dismisses the gathering.
Heading: the Rajya-labha Parva section continues.
Having conquered all rivals, the brothers grow idle and indulge in pleasure on a Vindhya plateau, where women dance and sing in their praise.
Tilottama appears, both brothers lust after her and claim her, they fight with their maces and kill each other, and Brahma grants her a boon.
Narada tells the Pandavas that the Asuras destroyed each other over a woman, and asks them to arrange matters so they do not quarrel over Draupadi.
The Pandavas agree on a rule that a brother who sees another with Draupadi must live as a celibate forest-dweller for twelve years, and Narada departs.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva section.
The Pandavas rule well, bring many kings under their sway, and Draupadi delights in her five husbands, so the Kuru race prospers.
Robbers steal a Brahmana's cattle, and the weeping Brahmana appeals to the Pandavas to protect his wealth.
Arjuna resolves to act, enters the chamber where Yudhishthira is with Draupadi, recovers the cattle, then asks leave for exile; Yudhishthira says a younger brother's entry is no fault.
Arjuna answers that he cannot waver from truth, which is his weapon.
With the king's permission, Arjuna prepares for forest life and sets out for twelve years.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva section continues.
Brahmanas and ascetics follow Arjuna for a distance, he journeys like Indra with the Maruts, and at the source of the Ganga he decides to stay.
At the Ganga's source, Ulupi, daughter of the Naga king Kauravya, pulls Arjuna into the water and into her palace, and he asks who she is.
Ulupi says she is Kauravya's daughter, overcome by desire for him, and asks him to yield to her.
Arjuna replies that his twelve-year vow binds him and asks how he can please her without breaking truth or duty.
Ulupi argues that the rule only concerns the brothers' shared wife, that helping the distressed is virtuous, and that she will destroy herself if refused.
Arjuna yields, spends the night in her palace, returns in the morning, and Ulupi grants him invincibility in water.
Heading: section CCXVII.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva continues.

Arjuna tells the Brahmanas what happened, visits holy peaks and waters, and at Manipura is given Chitrangada by King Chitravahana on terms that her son continue the line; after she bears a son, Arjuna goes on his way.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva section continues.
Arjuna visits five sacred waters on the southern ocean, finds them shunned, and asks the ascetics why, and they say crocodiles seize bathers there.
Arjuna plunges into the Saubhadra water, drags a seizing crocodile ashore, and it becomes the Apsara Varga, who begins to explain how she and her companions were cursed after tempting a Brahmana.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva section continues.
Varga and her companions beg the Brahmana to pardon them, arguing that women should not be slain and that a Brahmana should protect those who seek shelter.
The Brahmana relents, but says they will be crocodiles for a hundred years until a worthy man frees them, and that the waters will be called Nari-tirthas.
Varga says Narada sent them to the five southern waters, where Arjuna would free them, and she asks him to help her companions as well.
Arjuna frees all the Apsaras, who regain their own forms, then visits Chitrangada and his son Vabhruvahana at Manipura and goes on to Gokarna.
Heading: the Arjuna-vanavasa Parva section continues.
Arjuna tours the western holy places, meets Krishna at Prabhasa and on Raivataka, and is welcomed into Dwaraka, where the two friends stay together for many days.
Heading: the Subhadra-harana Parva section.
A grand festival of the Vrishnis and Andhakas begins on Raivataka, with gifts to Brahmanas, music, dancing, and the presence of many heroes including Haladhara (Valarama).
Arjuna sees Bhadra, Krishna's sister, is struck with desire, and Krishna offers to speak to their father if Arjuna is serious.
Arjuna asks for her hand; the reply, attributed to Vasudeva, says a self-choice is doubtful, so abduction is praised for brave warriors, and messengers carry the plan to Yudhishthira, who consents.
Heading: the Subhadra-harana Parva section continues.
Arjuna, with Krishna's assent, seizes Subhadra on her way back from Raivataka and drives toward Indraprastha, while her attendants flee to Dwaraka and the court sounds the alarm and the warriors arm.
Valadeva, wine-flushed, first tells the warriors to wait for Krishna's word, then rages at Arjuna's insult and vows to make the earth empty of Kauravas, and the assembly roars its approval.
Heading: the Haranaharana Parva section.
Persuaded by Vasudeva, the Vrishnis bring Arjuna back to Dwaraka for a lawful marriage, and later Draupadi's jealousy fades when the new bride Subhadra humbly greets her.
Krishna comes to Indraprastha with a great Vrishni host, Yudhishthira honours them, and Krishna and Rama load the Pandavas with gifts before the visitors return home; Subhadra then bears Abhimanyu.
Abhimanyu grows into a skilled warrior, and Draupadi bears five sons, Prativindhya, Sutasoma, Srutakarman, Satanika and Srutasena, who are educated by Dhaumya.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section.
Yudhishthira rules Indraprastha so justly that his subjects, brothers and other kings prosper, and the people love him for his fairness and affection.
After some days, Arjuna proposes a summer outing on the banks of the Yamuna, and Vasudeva agrees.
With Yudhishthira's leave, Arjuna and Krishna go with friends to a pleasant grove, where the women and company drink, dance, sing and play.
Arjuna and Krishna sit apart and talk of past deeds, and when a radiant Brahmana approaches they rise and wait for his commands.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Agni, in the guise of a Brahmana, asks Arjuna and Krishna to help him burn Khandava, which Indra protects for his friend Takshaka, by holding back the rain and stopping any escape.
Janamejaya asks why Agni wants to burn the forest full of creatures and asks for the full story.
Vaisampayana tells how King Swetaki, abandoned by his weary priests, won Rudra's help after a long penance and twelve years of offerings, and Rudra sent Durvasa to officiate.
A closing line: King Swetaki's story ends with his ascent to heaven, accompanied by the priests who served him.
Agni, sick from the butter of Swetaki's sacrifice, is told by the Creator to eat the forest's creatures, but the dwellers of the forest put his fire out seven times.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Brahma tells Agni that Arjuna and Vasudeva are Nara and Narayana, so Agni goes to them for help, and Arjuna asks for a bow, quivers and a car, plus the means to thwart Indra's rain.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Varuna gives Arjuna the bow Gandiva, two quivers and a car, Agni gives Krishna a discus, Varuna adds a mace, and the two heroes promise to help Agni.
Agni surrounds the forest with his seven flames and burns it with a roar that makes every creature tremble.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Arjuna and Krishna take up opposite sides of the forest and cut down fleeing creatures while the others perish in the flames, and the gods go to Indra to ask whether the world is ending.
Indra covers the sky with clouds to protect Khandava, but the heat dries his showers, so he gathers heavier clouds and the forest fills with smoke and lightning.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.

Arjuna blocks Indra's rain and beheads the Naga mother who tries to swallow her son Aswasena, but Indra's wind stuns Arjuna and Aswasena escapes; then the gods, including Yama, Kuvera, Skanda and Varuna, join the battle and are beaten back, and Arjuna shatters the mountain-peak Indra hurls at him.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.

The creatures of Khandava flee in terror, Krishna's discus and Arjuna's arrows cut them down, and an unseen voice tells Indra that the two heroes are Nara and Narayana and that Khandava's destruction is fated, so the gods withdraw.
Krishna sees the Asura Maya escaping, Agni pursues him, and Maya begs Arjuna for protection, which Arjuna grants.
Protected from Indra by Krishna and Arjuna, Agni sets about burning the forest in earnest.
Agni burns the forest for five and ten days, gorging on the fat and flesh of its creatures.
Agni spares only six of the forest's dwellers.
The six survivors are named as Aswasena, Maya and four birds called Sarngakas.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Janamejaya asks why Agni did not burn the Sarngaka birds and asks for the reason.
Vaisampayana tells of the learned and austere ascetic Mandapala, who on reaching the realm of the Pitris finds that he is refused the expected reward.
The celestials tell him that men are born in debt, that children discharge it, and that his lack of offspring is why heaven is closed to him, so he should beget children.

Mandapala takes the form of a Sarngaka, fathers four Vedic sons with the bird Jarita, then leaves them in the forest and goes to another wife, and when he sees Agni coming to burn Khandava he praises the god at length.
Pleased by the praise, Agni asks what boon he can grant, and Mandapala asks him to spare his children while burning the forest, which Agni agrees to do.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
As the fire approaches, the helpless mother Jarita weeps, unable to save all her chicks, and asks herself what she should do.
The chicks tell their mother to save herself, since she can bear more children while their deaths would end the line.
Jarita suggests the chicks hide in a mouse's hole and that she will cover its mouth with dust until the fire has passed.
The chicks refuse, arguing that without feathers they would be eaten by the mouse, and that death by fire is more honourable than being devoured.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Jarita says a hawk has seized the mouse, so the hole is safe, but the chicks reply that other mice may remain and urge their mother to save herself.
Jarita insists she saw the hawk carry the mouse off and urges them to enter, but the chicks still refuse and tell her to go and find another husband.
Jarita leaves her sons in the forest and goes to a place without fire, and Agni rushes toward the chicks, and the eldest, Jaritari, begins to speak to the god.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Jaritari says the wise remain awake facing death and feel no pangs, while the confused suffer and gain no salvation.
Sarisrikka praises his eldest brother's patience and wisdom, noting that only one among many is wise and brave.
Stamvamitra says the eldest is the protector, and if he cannot save them the younger brothers can do nothing.
Drona warns that the seven-tongued fire of the god is quickly approaching their home.
Vaisampayana introduces the four hymns that each son addresses to Agni.
Jaritari's hymn calls Agni the soul of air and the body of vegetation, with flames stretching in every direction.
Sarisrikka's hymn describes the brothers' orphaned state and feathers not yet grown, and begs Agni for protection by another route.
Stamvamitra's hymn calls Agni the all-in-one, the sustainer of creatures, and the one who both creates and destroys the universe.
Drona's hymn praises Agni as the digester of food and the sun that draws up water as rain, and asks him to spare them by going another way.
Pleased, and recalling his promise to Mandapala, Agni calls Drona a Rishi and says he will do as they ask.
Drona asks Agni to consume the cats that trouble them every day, along with their friends and relatives.
Agni agrees, tells the Sarngakas his intentions, and begins to burn the forest of Khandava with greater strength.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Mandapala worries aloud to his second wife Lapita about his sons' safety and the danger from the fire and wind.
Lapita answers jealously that Agni has promised to save them, and accuses Mandapala of caring more for his rival Jarita.
Mandapala replies that he sought children for their sake, that abandoning what he has is wicked, and that Lapita may do as she chooses.
Jarita finds her children safe and embraces them, but when Mandapala arrives his sons greet him coldly and neither they nor Jarita speak kindly to him.
Mandapala asks which child is the eldest and why no one answers him, saying he left them but was unhappy elsewhere.
Jarita tells him to return to Lapita, and Mandapala argues that co-wives and lovers ruin women's happiness, citing Arundhati's jealousy of Vasishtha.
The sons come forward to worship their father, and he gives them every assurance.
Heading: the Khandava-daha Parva section continues.
Mandapala tells his sons that he had Agni's promise and delayed out of trust, and asks them to bear no resentment, since they are all learned Rishis.
Mandapala takes his wife and sons and leaves the region for another country.
Agni, having consumed the forest with Krishna and Arjuna's help, shows himself to Arjuna, and Indra, surrounded by the Maruts, descends to offer each of them a boon.
Arjuna asks for Indra's weapons, Krishna asks for an eternal friendship, and Agni lets the heroes go wherever they choose, after which Arjuna, Krishna and Maya sit down by a river.
Heading: the end of the Adi Parva.
Boilerplate from the Project Gutenberg licence, not part of the epic text.
Heading naming the Sabhakriya Parva.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and the goddess Saraswati.
Vaisampayana says Maya, in Vasudeva's presence, thanks Arjuna for saving him from fire and flood and offers his services.
Arjuna says everything is already done, wishes Maya well and tells him to go freely.
Maya insists he is a great craftsman among the Danavas and wants to do something for Arjuna.
Arjuna tells Maya that he cannot make him do anything, and asks him to do something for Krishna instead.
Krishna reflects, then asks Maya to build a grand assembly hall for Yudhishthira, with designs that mix divine, demonic and human styles.
Maya is delighted, is introduced to Yudhishthira, tells the story of the Danava Vrishaparva, and marks out a five-thousand-cubit plot after a foundation rite and gifts to Brahmins.

Krishna leaves Khandavaprastha after bidding farewell to the Pandavas, his aunt Kunti, his sister Subhadra and Draupadi, then drives off in his golden chariot and sends the Pandavas back after half a yojana.
Yudhishthira reaches his capital and sends his relatives away, while Krishna is honoured at Dwaraka by his parents, Balarama and the Yadava princes and enters Rukmini's apartments.
Maya leaves Arjuna, collects the treasures near Mount Kailasa, describes the holy sites there, builds the palace and its grounds, and reports it finished to Yudhishthira in fourteen months.
Yudhishthira feeds and rewards the Brahmins, enters the hall to music and entertainments, and a long list of sages, kings, Yadava princes and Gandharvas take their places and attend him.
Heading naming the Lokapala Sabhakhayana Parva.
Narada arrives at the assembly of the Pandavas, is described as a learned sage, is welcomed with a seat and gifts, and blesses Yudhishthira.
Narada questions Yudhishthira closely on how he rules: his spending, justice, officials, spies, army pay, farming, taxes, punishments and freedom from the kings' common vices.
Yudhishthira asks Narada how learning, wealth, a wife and knowledge of the sacred texts bear fruit.
Narada says these bear fruit through sacrifice, through use and charity, through a wife's usefulness and children, and through humility and good conduct.
Narada asks whether officials collect only fair dues from distant traders and whether merchants can trade safely in the king's lands.
Narada asks whether the king heeds wise counsel, pays artisans on time, guards against fire, snakes, disease and demons, cares for the disabled and homeless, and has cast off six faults.
Yudhishthira bows to Narada and vows to follow his advice, and gains the whole earth in time. Narada says such a king is protected and reaches heaven.
Yudhishthira worships Narada and begins to answer his questions briefly.
Yudhishthira says he tries to follow the rules of duty and wants to walk the path of virtuous rulers before him.
Yudhishthira asks Narada, who travels freely among the worlds, whether he has ever seen a hall like his own or a better one.
Narada says he has never seen a hall of gems on earth, and offers to describe the halls of Yama, Varuna, Indra, Kuvera and Brahma.
Yudhishthira and his brothers ask Narada to describe each hall in detail, including its materials, size and attendants, and Narada agrees to do so.
Narada describes Indra's hall at length: its splendour and dimensions, Indra seated with Sachi, and the gods, Maruts, sages and celestial musicians who serve him.
Narada describes Yama's hall as a comfortable place of plenty, lists the many dead kings and sages who attend Yama there, and then announces the next description, Varuna's hall.
Narada describes Varuna's white hall within the waters, with Varuna and his queen, and the snakes, demons, rivers and seas who serve him, then announces the hall of Kuvera.
Narada describes Kuvera's hall in detail: its size, its floating gold chambers, Kuvera and his wives, the Apsaras, Gandharvas and Yakshas who attend him, and Shiva's friendship with Kuvera.
Narada's speech continues, describing the hall as attached to the sky and able to move through it.
The sentence ends, confirming that the hall is such as Narada has described.
Narada turns to the next assembly, the hall of Brahma the Grandsire.
A closing line of Narada's speech, introducing Brahma's hall.

Narada tells how the sun god guided him to Brahma's hall after a thousand-year vow, describes the beings who attend Brahma there, and concludes that Yudhishthira's hall is unrivalled among human halls.
Yudhishthira notes which beings Narada placed in each hall and asks what deeds made Harishchandra worthy of Indra's hall and how Narada met his father Pandu.

Narada tells of Harishchandra, an emperor whose Rajasuya sacrifice was famous for generous gifts, and relays Pandu's message urging Yudhishthira to hold the same sacrifice, while warning of obstacles such as Brahma Rakshasas and war.
Narada departs, and Yudhishthira and his brothers begin to think about the Rajasuya.
Yudhishthira broods over Narada's words, and the narrator describes his peaceful, prosperous rule under his brothers and why he is called Ajatasatru.
His ministers urge him to perform the Rajasuya, and he consults his brothers, priests and counsellors again.
Yudhishthira asks how his wish for the sacrifice can bear fruit through faith and speech alone.
The priests and sages say he is worthy, but Yudhishthira weighs his own means and sends for Krishna, who arrives at Indraprastha and is warmly received.
Yudhishthira explains the plan to Krishna and asks for honest counsel, since flatterers and self-interested advisers cannot be trusted.
Heading naming the Rajasuyarambha Parva.

Krishna calls Yudhishthira worthy of the sacrifice, lists the kings who serve Jarasandha, tells how the Yadavas fled from him and how he has imprisoned rival kings, and says the Rajasuya cannot proceed while Jarasandha lives.
Yudhishthira praises Krishna's wisdom, reflects on the difficulty of gaining imperial rule, and says he fears Jarasandha's power and whether the sacrifice is worth attempting.
Bhima answers that weak kings who provoke strong ones are destroyed, but that policy, strength and Arjuna's skill can defeat Jarasandha.
Krishna says the impatient seek reward without foresight, names earlier emperors who ruled by virtue, and argues that Jarasandha, though cruel, must be stopped before he takes his hundredth king.
Yudhishthira says he regards Bhima and Arjuna as his eyes and Krishna as his mind, fears Jarasandha's vast army, and asks that the plan be dropped.
Arjuna answers that valour outweighs birth and that they are capable, and insists that they should fight Jarasandha and win the imperial dignity.
Krishna, called Vasudeva here, argues that a warrior must fight and that a secret attack on the too-powerful Jarasandha is justified, foreseeing his downfall.
Yudhishthira asks who Jarasandha is and why he survived close contact with Krishna without harm.
Krishna begins Jarasandha's story with King Vrihadratha of Magadha, who is powerful and rich but has no son, along with his two wives.
The sage Chanda-kausika gives the king a mango. The queens each bear a half-body, which the midwives discard, and the Rakshasa woman Jara joins them into one strong child.
The queens nurse the child and the delighted king asks the Rakshasa woman who she is.
Jara says she is a Rakshasa woman and household goddess whom families worship, and that she gave the joined child to the king because she was pleased with his devotion.
Jara vanishes, the king performs the infant rites and holds a festival, names the boy Jarasandha, and the boy grows strong like a fire fed with butter.

The sage Chanda-kausika returns to Magadha, is welcomed by King Vrihadratha, and foretells Jarasandha's future power, invulnerability and vision of Shiva, after which Vrihadratha retires to the forest and Jarasandha takes the throne.

Vaisampayana says Vrihadratha dies in the forest, Jarasandha is granted boons and rules well, and after Kansa's death he hurls a mace toward Mathura, while his allies Hansa and Dimvaka make the Yadavas hesitate to fight.
Heading naming the Jarasandha-badha Parva.
Krishna says Jarasandha's allies are dead and that he should be defeated in a bare-armed contest, with Bhima as the fighter, and asks Yudhishthira to pledge Bhima and Arjuna to him.
Yudhishthira refuses to give up his brothers, praises Krishna's leadership, and the three set out disguised as Brahmanas, crossing many rivers and reaching the city of Magadha.
Krishna points out the fortified capital Girivraja, its hills and sacred sites, and says Jarasandha will be humbled by being slain.
The three break the sacred Chaityaka peak, enter the city in Brahmin disguise and take their seats before Jarasandha, who questions them.
Krishna explains that Snataka Brahmanas may wear flowers, that Kshatriyas act through strength, and that they enter an enemy's house by the wrong gate and refuse worship there.
Jarasandha protests that he has done no wrong to these Brahmanas and asks why they treat him as an enemy.
Krishna accuses Jarasandha of holding kings captive for sacrifice, reveals who he and the Pandavas are, and challenges him to free the kings or die.
Jarasandha replies that he takes kings only after defeating them, and accepts the challenge to fight.
Jarasandha installs his son Sahadeva as king, and Krishna, mindful of destiny, leaves the fight to Bhima, who is destined to slay him.

Krishna asks Jarasandha which man he will fight, Jarasandha chooses Bhima, and the two wrestle with bare arms through many moves and holds, watched by the whole city, until Jarasandha tires and Krishna urges Bhima to finish him.

Bhima whirls Jarasandha in the air and breaks him over his knee, the people of Magadha are terrified, Krishna frees the captive kings and takes Jarasandha's chariot, and the freed kings promise to help Yudhishthira's sacrifice.
Sahadeva, Jarasandha's son, pays respect to Krishna and is installed as king of Magadha, then Krishna returns to Indraprastha with the Pandavas, takes leave of the family, and goes home to Dwarka.
The Pandavas' fame grows, and Yudhishthira rules his people while the brothers keep Draupadi happy.
Heading naming the Digvijaya Parva, the conquest of the quarters.
Arjuna, having the bow, quivers, chariot and assembly hall, asks Yudhishthira's leave to conquer the northern quarter and fill the treasury with tribute.
Yudhishthira blesses Arjuna and urges him to set out with the Brahmanas' blessings.
Arjuna sets out north, Bhima goes east, Sahadeva south and Nakula west, while Yudhishthira stays in Khandavaprastha.
Bhagadatta agrees to do all that Arjuna asks and offers to do more.
Arjuna wins Bhagadatta's promise, then marches north, beats one king after another in mountain and frontier lands, takes horses and tribute, and camps on the White Mountains.
Arjuna crosses the White Mountains, subdues the Limpurushas and the Guhakas, admires the sacred lakes, and at North Harivarsha accepts tribute after its guardians say the land cannot be conquered.
Arjuna returns to the capital with the horses, treasure and animals of the north, offers them all to Yudhishthira, and rests.
Bhima marches east with Yudhishthira's blessing, conquers and wins over many peoples, makes Sudharman his commander, is hosted by Sisupala for thirty nights, and then moves on.
Bhima conquers many kingdoms from Kumara to the coast, takes tribute from Jarasandha's son and the Mlechchha kings, and returns to Indraprastha to present the treasure to Yudhishthira.

Sahadeva marches south, conquers the Surasenas, Matsyas, Adhirajas, Avantis, Kosalas and others, and fights the monkey kings near Kishkindha before reaching Mahishmati, where King Nila's fire blocks his advance.
Janamejaya asks why Agni turned against Sahadeva, who was fighting for a sacrifice that honours the god.
Vaisampayana tells how Agni took the form of a Brahmana to court Nila's daughter, how Nila punished him, and how the god then granted Nila a boon and the city's women freedom.
Sahadeva prays to Agni, naming his many titles and asking for purity, strength and prosperity.
Vaisampayana says that whoever pours butter into the fire while reciting these mantras will gain prosperity and be cleansed of sin.

Sahadeva sits down to face the fire, and Agni relents, assures him that he was only testing him, and promises to grant his wish; Nila then pays tribute, and Sahadeva wins Tripura, Paurava, Saurashtra, Rukmin and the southern and coastal peoples, sending messengers to Vibhishana, who submits.
Sahadeva returns to Yudhishthira with the wealth and considers his campaign a success.

Nakula sets out west from Khandavaprastha, conquers the Rohitakas, desert lands, the Dasarnas, Trigartas, Malavas and many other peoples, receives Vasudeva's submission, and returns with a huge treasure presented to Yudhishthira.
Vaisampayana closes the account by saying that Nakula subdued the western lands that Krishna had once conquered.
Heading naming the Rajasuyika Parva.
Yudhishthira's just rule brings good rain, prosperity and a full treasury, his advisers urge the sacrifice, and Krishna arrives at Indraprastha with a vast treasure.
Yudhishthira thanks Krishna for his help and asks him to take part in the sacrifice, so that he may be cleansed of sin.
Krishna encourages Yudhishthira to hold the sacrifice, and Yudhishthira replies that his resolve is already rewarded by Krishna's presence.
Yudhishthira orders Sahadeva, Indrasena and the others to gather the materials and food the Brahmanas have specified.
The chief priests are chosen, with Dwaipayana as the principal priest, and workers erect halls and messengers invite Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras.
The guests arrive, the Brahmanas are installed and lodged, Yudhishthira is installed at the sacrifice, and the sacrifice begins with gifts of cows, beds, gold and maidens.
Nakula is sent to Hastinapura to bring Bhishma, Drona, Dhritarashtra, Vidura, Kripa and well-disposed cousins.
Nakula invites Bhishma and Dhritarashtra, who come with the preceptors, and a long list of kings and kinsmen arrive with jewels, including the Kauravas, Salya, Bhagadatta, Sisupala and the Vrishnis.
Yudhishthira assigns each guest a mansion with gardens, and the guests see him surrounded by priests, performing a sacrifice with large gifts.
The text notes that the section ends and gives its place in the Rajasuyika Parva of the Sabha Parva.
A short line completing the section heading in the Sabha Parva.
Yudhishthira thanks Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Ashvatthama, Duryodhana and Vivingsati, asks for their help, and gives them the treasure to guide.

Yudhishthira assigns offices: Dussasana to food, Ashvatthama to the Brahmanas, Sanjaya to return honours, Bhishma and Drona to oversee, Kripa to treasure and gifts, Vidura as paymaster, Duryodhana to tribute, and Krishna to washing the Brahmanas' feet.
Kings bring tribute and jewels, the sacrifice goes on with six fires and generous gifts, and gods, Brahmanas and the people are all satisfied.
Heading naming the Arghyaharana Parva, the taking of the first honour.
On the last day, the sacred sages and kings gather in the inner enclosure, speak freely, and debate with one another.
Narada, seeing the gathering, recalls that Narayana, the supreme god, has taken birth as a Yadava and is living among men.
Bhishma explains that six kinds of guest deserve the Arghya, and that the foremost of them should receive it first.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to name the foremost guest.
Bhishma names Krishna, Sahadeva presents the Arghya, and Sisupala protests at the honour given to Krishna.

Sisupala rebukes the Pandavas and Bhishma for honouring Krishna, names many greater men who were passed over, accuses Krishna of unfairly killing Jarasandha, and calls the honour an insult to the kings.
Sisupala rises from his seat and walks out of the assembly with the kings who came with him.
Yudhishthira runs after Sisupala and pleads with him, calling his words improper and cruel, and saying the older kings accept the honour and that he should bear it patiently.

Bhishma says that whoever rejects Krishna's honour deserves no courtesy, lists Krishna's victories and virtues, and calls him the origin of the universe, while dismissing Sisupala as a boy who does not understand.
Heading marking Section XXXVIII.
Sahadeva challenges any king who cannot accept Krishna's honour to answer him, declaring his own foot placed on the heads of the proud.
No king answers, flowers fall on Sahadeva, a voice approves, and Narada declares those who refuse to worship Krishna as dead though moving.
Sisupala, red with anger, calls on the kings to battle against the Vrishnis and Pandavas, and the kings plot to stop the sacrifice while Krishna watches the gathering storm.
Heading naming the Sisupala-badha Parva, the slaying of Sisupala.
Yudhishthira, seeing the sea of angry kings, asks the grandsire Bhishma what he should do to protect the sacrifice and his subjects.
Bhishma replies that the kings are like dogs barking at a sleeping lion, that Sisupala is foolish, and that Krishna is the source of all beings, so Sisupala's folly is part of a divine plan.
Sisupala answers Bhishma in stern and rough words.
Sisupala calls Bhishma a shameless old man who misleads the Kurus, mocks Krishna's childhood deeds, and accuses Bhishma of hypocrisy and past wrongs such as his treatment of Amba.
Sisupala tells the story of an old swan who preached virtue but ate the eggs of trusting birds until they killed him.
Sisupala says Bhishma is like the swan and warns that the kings may slay him as the birds slew the swan.
Sisupala says Jarasandha was worthy of respect, accuses Krishna of entering in disguise and refusing the host's hospitality, and mocks the Pandavas' advisers as womanish and old.
Bhima, furious, is nearly ready to attack, Bhishma holds him back, and Sisupala laughs and tells Bhishma to release him so the kings can see him scorched.

Bhishma tells how Sisupala was born with three eyes and four arms, how a voice foretold his death, how Krishna's lap revealed his fate, and how Krishna promised to pardon his aunt's son for a hundred offences.
Bhishma says Sisupala now dares to challenge Bhima because of the boon Govinda granted him.
Bhishma says Sisupala's challenge is not his own purpose but Krishna's, since Krishna is a portion of Hari who wants to take back his energy.
Vaisampayana says Sisupala cannot bear the rebuke and answers Bhishma in a rage.
Sisupala tells Bhishma to praise the other kings instead of Krishna, names Darada, Karna, Drona, Ashvatthama, Duryodhana, Jayadratha, Kripa and others, and calls Bhishma a foolish bird.
Bhishma says he regards the kings as worth no more than a straw, the angry kings threaten to kill or burn him, and Bhishma invites anyone wishing a quick death to fight Krishna.
Sisupala challenges Krishna and the Pandavas to a fight, calling Krishna a slave and no king, and Krishna answers the kings with a long list of Sisupala's wrongs.
Sisupala laughs at Krishna's claim about Rukmini and asks him to pardon him or not as he wishes.
Krishna calls up his discus, declares that the hundred pardons are used up, and beheads Sisupala, after which Sisupala's energy enters Krishna and the sky and earth shake.
Yudhishthira orders the funeral rites for Sisupala and installs his son as king of Chedi.
The sacrifice is completed under Krishna's protection, and the kings praise Yudhishthira and ask leave to return home.
Yudhishthira sends his brothers to see the kings to their borders, and the Pandava princes escort each of them according to rank.
Krishna takes leave of Yudhishthira, Pritha, Draupadi and Subhadra and drives off to Dwaravati, while Duryodhana and Sakuni stay on in the assembly hall.
Heading naming the Dyuta Parva, the dice-play.
Vyasa comes to the completed sacrifice, is honoured by Yudhishthira, and Yudhishthira asks whether the omens have ended with Sisupala's death.
Vyasa says the omens will bring ruin on the Kshatriyas within thirteen years through Duryodhana's sins, and foretells a dream of Shiva, then departs for Kailasa.
Yudhishthira, troubled, vows to bear hardship for thirteen years without harsh words or war, and his brothers approve; Duryodhana and Sakuni remain in the assembly hall.

Duryodhana wanders the Pandavas' hall, mistakes crystal floors and doors for water and open passages, falls into a crystal pool, and is laughed at by Bhima, Arjuna and the twins until he leaves for Hastinapura.
On the way home Duryodhana broods on the Pandavas' prosperity and ignores Sakuni's questions, until Sakuni asks what is troubling him.
Duryodhana explains that he is consumed with jealousy at Yudhishthira's sway, his sacrifice and the tribute of kings.
Duryodhana says he would rather die than live with the Pandavas' prosperity, that Fate seems supreme, and asks Sakuni to tell Dhritarashtra of his grief.
Sakuni tells Duryodhana not to envy the Pandavas, since their fortune is their own, and that their gains, including Gandiva, Maya's hall and their allies, were earned.
Duryodhana says that with Sakuni and the great warriors he will subdue the Pandavas if the king approves.
Sakuni says the Pandavas cannot be beaten in battle, but that he knows how to defeat Yudhishthira himself.
Duryodhana asks Sakuni to name the way to defeat Yudhishthira without danger to his friends.
Sakuni says Yudhishthira loves dice without being skilled at it, cannot refuse a game, and that Sakuni is unmatched at dice, so Duryodhana should ask his father to permit the match.
Duryodhana asks Sakuni to present the plan to Dhritarashtra, saying he cannot do it himself.
Sakuni, having learnt Duryodhana's mind on the road home, tells the blind king Dhritarashtra that his son is pale, emaciated and anxious, and asks him to find out the cause.
Dhritarashtra asks Duryodhana what troubles him, reminding him of his wealth, servants, food and pleasures.

Duryodhana replies that he is consumed by jealousy of Yudhishthira's wealth, lists the tribute of kings, the Brahmanas kept at the gate, and his humiliations in the crystal hall, and says he cannot find peace.
Sakuni says he is a master of dice, that Yudhishthira is fond of the game though unskilled, and promises to win the Pandavas' wealth for Duryodhana.
Duryodhana urges his father to let Sakuni play for the Pandavas' wealth.
Dhritarashtra says he will follow the counsel of Vidura, and asks that Vidura's judgment be sought before he decides.
Duryodhana says that if his father consults Vidura and forbids the match, he will kill himself, and that Vidura would then inherit the throne.
Dhritarashtra, moved by his son's threat, orders artisans to build a grand hall with a hundred doors and a thousand columns, and sends for Vidura, whose counsel he usually follows.
Vidura comes and warns his brother that the match should not be held, lest quarrels arise among the sons.
Dhritarashtra, accepting fate, tells Vidura to bring Yudhishthira to the match, and Vidura, grieved, goes to Bhishma.
Janamejaya asks how the dice match came about, who attended the assembly, and who approved or opposed it.
The narrator, a disciple of Vyasa, agrees to tell the whole story.
Vaisampayana says he will narrate the events again in detail for the king.
Dhritarashtra asks Duryodhana to drop the dice plan, praising Vidura's wisdom and listing Duryodhana's advantages.
Duryodhana answers that his prosperity brings him no pleasure, lists the tribute and the crystal-floor mockery, and says the laughter of Bhima and Draupadi is a wound.

Duryodhana lists the tribute to Yudhishthira from Kamboja, the coastal lands, Bhagadatta, the one-legged and many-eyed peoples, the Valhikas, the Sakas and the eastern kings, and notes the Brahmanas and tribes kept waiting at the gate.
Duryodhana catalogues the tribute from mountain tribes, Kiratas, eastern and western kingdoms, Virata, Yajnasena and Vasudeva, the gems from the Singhalas, and the kings who were kept at the gate.

Duryodhana describes the crowds of soldiers and servants fed in Yudhishthira's palace, the Brahmanas and ascetics who eat daily, and Draupadi who makes sure everyone is fed, and notes that only the Panchalas and the Andhakas and Vrishnis pay no tribute.

Duryodhana describes the Rajasuya consecration, in which kings served Yudhishthira, Krishna bathed him with a great conch, and the Pandavas' conquests brought treasures from distant seas, leaving Duryodhana despairing that he sees no purpose in life.
Dhritarashtra tells Duryodhana not to be jealous of Yudhishthira, who is honest and equally wealthy, urges him to hold his own sacrifice, and warns that quarrels with kin are sinful.

Duryodhana tells his father that his counsel is confusing, that kings must act for their own advantage, that foes must be crushed while they are weak, and that he will take the Pandavas' prosperity or die in battle.
Sakuni boasts that he can win Yudhishthira's wealth at dice, comparing his betting to an archer's bow and arrows, and asks that Yudhishthira be summoned.
Duryodhana asks his father to allow Sakuni to play.
Dhritarashtra says he will consult his brother Vidura before deciding.
Duryodhana distrusts Vidura, who favours the Pandavas, and urges that his purpose be carried out at once.
Dhritarashtra warns that hostility with the strong brings war, and that Duryodhana is wrong to welcome such a thing.
Duryodhana argues that dice was invented long ago and involves no bloodshed, and asks that the hall be built so that he can gamble with the Pandavas as equals.
Dhritarashtra says he does not like Duryodhana's words, that he will regret them, and that the destruction of the Kshatriyas is fated.
Dhritarashtra, bowing to fate and his son, orders a grand crystal-arched hall with a thousand columns built, and asks Vidura to bring Yudhishthira for a friendly match at dice.
Vidura warns his brother that the match will end in dissension and the ruin of their race, and says he cannot approve.
Dhritarashtra replies that the world moves under fate and tells Vidura to go to Yudhishthira and bring him to Hastinapura.
Vidura, reluctantly obeying Dhritarashtra, rides to the Pandavas' city and goes to Yudhishthira's palace, where Yudhishthira greets him and asks after the family.
Vidura says Dhritarashtra is well and invites the Pandavas to Hastinapura to see the new palace and to play a friendly match at dice, warning that cheats will be there.
Yudhishthira worries that a dice match may lead to quarrels and asks Vidura what he advises.
Vidura says he has opposed gambling but was sent by the king, and asks Yudhishthira to do what is right.
Yudhishthira asks who the dishonest gamblers are that will play against him.
Vidura names Sakuni, the king of Gandhara, and other skilled players, including Vivingati, Chitrasena, Satyavrata, Purumitra and Jaya.
Yudhishthira says fate rules everything, that he will not gamble at the king's command, and that he will play only if Sakuni challenges him in the hall.

Yudhishthira sets out with his brothers, Draupadi and the household, arrives at Hastinapura, is embraced by the elders and the Kaurava princes, sees Gandhari and Dhritarashtra, and spends a night of music and pleasure before the match.
The Pandavas enter the hall, greet the kings and take their seats, and Sakuni calls for the dice to be cast now that the assembly is full.
Yudhishthira says gambling is sinful and not a Kshatriya's virtue, and asks Sakuni to beat him fairly rather than by trickery.
Sakuni says gambling is dangerous only in its stakes, and urges Yudhishthira to begin without delay.
Yudhishthira cites the sage Devala, saying deceitful play is sinful and that he wants no wealth gained by cunning.
Sakuni argues that every contest, whether of birth, learning or skill, is driven by a wish to win, and so dice is no worse.
Yudhishthira says he will not withdraw from a summons, that fate rules all, and asks who in the hall can match his stake.
Duryodhana offers to supply jewels and wealth and says that Sakuni, his uncle, will play for him.
Yudhishthira objects that gambling by proxy goes against the rules, but agrees to begin if Duryodhana insists.
The kings and elders take their seats in the hall, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vidura sit behind, and the friendly match at dice begins.
Yudhishthira offers a precious pearl necklace from the ocean as his first stake and asks what Duryodhana will wager.
Duryodhana says he has much wealth, but asks Yudhishthira to take that stake.
Sakuni, skilled at dice, casts them and says that he has won.
Yudhishthira says Sakuni has won unfairly and stakes his treasury of gold, silver and jars of coins.
Sakuni claims the win.
Yudhishthira stakes his royal chariot, drawn by eight white steeds and decked with bells.
Sakuni claims the chariot.
Yudhishthira stakes a hundred thousand young serving-girls, skilled in the arts and in attendance on kings and Brahmanas.
Sakuni claims the serving-girls.
Yudhishthira stakes thousands of serving-men, trained to wait on guests.
Sakuni claims the serving-men.
Yudhishthira stakes a thousand elephants with golden girdles and their attendants.
Sakuni laughs and claims the elephants.
Yudhishthira stakes as many cars as elephants, with trained horses and warriors paid a monthly wage.
The narrator calls Sakuni a wretch pledged to enmity, and says he continues.
Sakuni claims the cars and warriors.
Yudhishthira stakes the horses that Chitraratha gave Arjuna.
Sakuni claims the horses.
Yudhishthira stakes ten thousand cars and sixty thousand picked warriors.
Sakuni claims them.
Yudhishthira stakes four hundred gem-filled caskets of gold.
Sakuni claims the four hundred caskets.

Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that Duryodhana is a jackal in human form who will destroy the family, quotes Sukra and fables of honey-gatherers and golden birds, and urges him not to pursue the Pandavas for gain or to send his sons to Yama's realm.

Vidura says gambling is the root of quarrels, that Duryodhana's intoxication will ruin the Kauravas, and urges the Kauravas not to enter the fire, asking why Dhritarashtra would take wealth rather than win the Pandavas as allies, and telling Sakuni to return home.
Duryodhana accuses Vidura of favouring the Pandavas, of harsh words and of hostility under a show of loyalty, and tells him to go wherever he likes.
Vidura answers Dhritarashtra that kings who cast off honest counsellors are like fickle children, that Duryodhana is foolish, and that he takes his leave, wishing the family well.
Sakuni asks Yudhishthira whether he has any wealth left unstaked.
Yudhishthira says he has untold wealth and stakes it in huge numbers.
Sakuni claims the win.
Yudhishthira stakes his herds of cattle, horses and sheep across the lands from the Parnasa to the Sindhu.
Sakuni claims these as well.
Yudhishthira stakes his city, the lands, the wealth and the people, except the Brahmanas.
Sakuni claims them.
Yudhishthira stakes the princes, adorned in jewels and earrings.
Sakuni claims the princes.
Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, strong and red-eyed.
Sakuni notes that Nakula is already in his power, and asks what stake Yudhishthira will offer next.
Sakuni casts the dice.
Sakuni declares that Nakula has been won.
Yudhishthira stakes Sahadeva, who administers justice and is learned.
Sakuni claims Sahadeva.
Sakuni says the twins, dear to Yudhishthira, are already won, and asks whether Bhima and Arjuna are dearer still.
Yudhishthira calls Sakuni a wretch for sowing disunion among brothers who share one heart.
Sakuni offers an apology, saying that gamblers rave in play and do not recall it afterwards.
Yudhishthira stakes Arjuna, the great archer and leader.
Sakuni claims Arjuna.
Sakuni says Arjuna is now won and urges Yudhishthira to play with Bhima.
Yudhishthira stakes Bhima, the mace-wielder who is unmatched in strength.
Sakuni claims Bhima.
Sakuni asks whether Yudhishthira still has anything that has not been lost.
Yudhishthira says that only he, the eldest, is still unwon, and that he will accept whatever the winner decides.
Sakuni claims Yudhishthira himself.
Sakuni tells Yudhishthira that staking himself is sinful, since wealth remains to him.
Sakuni urges Yudhishthira to stake Draupadi to win himself back.
Yudhishthira stakes Draupadi, praising her beauty and virtue.

The elders cry out in shame, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa sweat, Vidura sits in grief, Dhritarashtra keeps asking whether it has been won, and Karna and Dussasana laugh, while Sakuni takes up the dice and claims the win.
Duryodhana orders Vidura to bring Draupadi to sweep the rooms and stay with the serving-women.

Vidura warns Duryodhana that he is courting ruin, argues that Draupadi cannot be enslaved since Yudhishthira had already lost himself, and tells the fable of the goat that swallowed a hook to urge him to stop.
Duryodhana, drunk with pride, orders the messenger to bring Draupadi, saying Vidura alone is afraid and the Pandavas have nothing to fear.
The messenger, a Suta, goes into the Pandavas' quarters and tells Draupadi that Duryodhana has won her and that she must come to the palace as a servant.
Draupadi asks how any prince could stake his wife, and says the king must have been mad with dice.
The messenger says Yudhishthira first staked his brothers, then himself, then Draupadi.
Draupadi asks the messenger to find out from the gambler whether he lost himself first or her.
The messenger takes Draupadi's question to the assembly, and Yudhishthira sits silent like one out of his mind.
Duryodhana orders that Draupadi come into the hall to put her question before everyone.
The messenger returns to Draupadi, distressed, and warns her that the Kauravas' end is near.
Draupadi says morality should guide them and asks the elders to say what she must do.
The messenger brings her reply back, but the assembly sits silent with lowered faces.
Yudhishthira sends word that Draupadi should come weeping before her father-in-law, while Duryodhana orders the messenger to fetch her and the messenger hesitates in fear.
Duryodhana sends his brother Dussasana, who goes to Draupadi, calls her a slave, seizes her by her locks and drags her toward the hall.
Draupadi, dragged and half-clothed, cries out that the elders are silent, that virtue has vanished, and that Bhishma, Drona and Vidura have lost their energy.
Draupadi's look enrages the Pandavas, Dussasana calls her a slave, Karna and Sakuni applaud, and Bhishma says the question is too subtle to decide.
Draupadi answers that Yudhishthira was summoned and tricked by cheats and cannot have staked her willingly, and asks the Kurus to judge.
Dussasana insults Draupadi, and Bhima, seeing her in her distress, fixes his anger on Yudhishthira.
Bhima protests that Draupadi, the wife of the Pandavas, does not deserve this, and says he will burn Yudhishthira's hands, asking Sahadeva to bring fire.
Arjuna asks Bhima not to fulfil the enemy's wishes, saying Yudhishthira acted under Kshatriya usage after being summoned.
Bhima says that if he had not known Yudhishthira acted by Kshatriya custom, he would have burned his hands.
Vikarna, a son of Dhritarashtra, urges the kings to answer Draupadi, and then argues that the vices of kings make the staking void, so Draupadi was not won.
Karna rebukes Vikarna as a boy, says Draupadi was won fairly, and orders Dussasana to strip the Pandavas' upper garments and Draupadi's clothing, which he begins.
Draupadi calls on Krishna to save her, and Dharma covers her with robes that keep appearing as each is pulled off.
Bhima swears in the hearing of the kings that he will tear open Dussasana's breast and drink his blood.
The assembly cries shame on Dussasana, Vidura calls for an answer to Draupadi's question, and he argues that silence in the face of injustice shares its guilt.
Vidura tells the tale of Prahlada, who was asked to judge a wager between Virochana and Sudhanwan and was taught by Kasyapa that a lie before an assembly brings sin.
Vidura urges everyone present to think carefully about the answer Draupadi needs.
The kings say nothing, Karna orders Dussasana to take the serving-woman Draupadi into the inner apartments, and Dussasana drags her before the spectators.
Draupadi asks Dussasana to wait, saying she has a duty to perform, that she was overpowered by his strength, and that she bows to the elders present.
Draupadi falls to the ground, dragged with greater force, and weeps before the Kuru assembly.
Draupadi recalls her swayamvara, asks whether she is a servant or a wife, condemns the Kurus for allowing the shame, and asks the kings to say whether she is won.
Bhishma says that dharma is subtle, that the Kurus are ruined by greed, and that Yudhishthira must decide whether she was won.
Duryodhana, seeing the kings silent, tells Draupadi that her husbands should say whether Yudhishthira is their lord, so that she may be freed from slavery.
The assembly applauds Duryodhana, and Bhima speaks, saying that he and his brothers are bound to Yudhishthira's word and would kill the Kauravas if commanded.
Bhishma, Drona and Vidura tell Bhima to hold back, since with his strength everything is possible.
Karna says that the three independent elders, Bhishma, Vidura and Drona, speak against Duryodhana, and that Draupadi, now a slave, should go to the inner apartments and choose another husband.
Bhima, bound by duty to the king, says he cannot be angry at a Suta's son, since they are now in servitude, but he would not bear such words from enemies had the king not staked her.
Duryodhana tells Yudhishthira to answer, then exposes his thigh to Draupadi, and Bhima vows to break it in battle.
Vidura warns the kings that the calamity has come from fate, that the match was improper, and that a stake made by one who has lost himself is like winning a treasure in a dream.
Duryodhana says he will accept whatever Bhima, Arjuna and the twins declare, if they deny that Yudhishthira is their master.
Arjuna says Yudhishthira was their master until he lost himself, and that the Kauravas must judge whose master he can be after that.
A jackal howls in the sacred chamber, asses bray and birds scream, and Bhishma, Drona and Kripa call out a blessing, while Vidura and Gandhari report the omens to Dhritarashtra.
A footnote explains that the blessing used in the text is a word of benediction, like Amen.
Dhritarashtra scolds Duryodhana for insulting the wife of the Kuru princes and offers Draupadi any boon she desires.
Draupadi asks that Yudhishthira be freed from slavery and that her son Prativindhya not be called the son of a slave.
Dhritarashtra agrees and offers her a second boon, saying she deserves more than one.
Draupadi asks that Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, with their chariots and bows, be freed from bondage.
Dhritarashtra grants this and offers a third boon.
Draupadi declines a third boon, citing the rule that a Vaisya may ask one, a Kshatriya woman two and a Brahmana a hundred, and says her husbands will prosper by their own virtue.
Karna says Draupadi has saved the Pandavas, becoming a boat for them in a boatless ocean of distress.
Bhima, angered, says that his inner light is dimmed by this insult and asks how a son born of such an insult can be of use.
Arjuna answers that superior men do not remember the harsh words of inferiors, but only their good deeds.
Bhima offers to slay the whole assembly, Arjuna pacifies him, and Yudhishthira embraces Bhima and calms him, then approaches Dhritarashtra with folded hands.
Yudhishthira tells Dhritarashtra that he is their master and asks for his command.
Dhritarashtra blesses him, tells him to rule his kingdom with his wealth, and advises him to forgive and not remember Duryodhana's harsh words, reminding him of his mother Gandhari and himself.
Yudhishthira takes his leave with courtesy, and he and his brothers ride with Draupadi toward Indraprastha.
Janamejaya asks how the sons of Dhritarashtra reacted when they learned that the Pandavas had been released with their wealth.
Dussasana tells Duryodhana that their father has returned the Pandavas' wealth, and Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni go to Dhritarashtra in private.
Duryodhana argues that the Pandavas will attack and proposes a rematch, with the loser to live twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth in disguise.
Dhritarashtra orders that the Pandavas be brought back to play again.
The list of elders begins with Drona, Somadatta, Bahlika and Kripa.
The list continues with names including Ashvatthama, Bhurisravas and Bhishma.
The list names Vikarna, another son of the king, among those counselling against the match.
All of them urge that the play not begin and that there be peace.
Dhritarashtra, partial to his sons, ignores the counsel of his wise friends and relatives.
Dhritarashtra summons the Pandavas back for another match at dice.
Gandhari reminds Dhritarashtra of Vidura's warning at Duryodhana's birth, begs him not to ruin the race for his sons' sake, and urges him to cast off the wicked youth.
Dhritarashtra says that if the family's ruin is fated, let it come, and that the Pandavas should return so the dice may be cast again.
The royal messenger overtakes Yudhishthira and delivers Dhritarashtra's summons to the dice.
Yudhishthira says fate decides the fruits of action, that he cannot refuse the old king's summons, and that he expects ruin but will go back.
The narrator compares Yudhishthira's fate to Rama's, tempted by a golden deer, and says the brothers return to the hall to play.
Sakuni says the old king has returned their wealth and proposes exile as the stake: twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year in hiding for the loser.
The assembly cries out that Duryodhana's friends have not warned him of his danger, and that the elders should tell the king plainly.
Yudhishthira, from shame and a sense of duty, sits down to play again, knowing that ruin is near for the Kurus.
Yudhishthira says a king of his order cannot refuse a summons to dice, and agrees to play with Sakuni.
Sakuni lists the old stakes of cattle, horses, gold and slaves, and sets the single stake of exile to the woods for the loser.
Yudhishthira accepts this one stake, and Sakuni casts the dice and says that he has won.
The Pandavas take off their royal robes and put on deer-skins, and Dussasana gloats that the Kauravas now rule, mocking the brothers as grains of sesame without kernel.
Dussasana insults the Pandavas and Draupadi, and Bhima answers that he will pierce his heart in battle and slay the Kauravas and their followers.
Dussasana, shameless, dances around the Kurus and calls out to Bhima mocking him as a cow.
Bhima answers that he will drink Dussasana's blood in battle, and that he will pacify his wrath by slaying the sons of Dhritarashtra.
As the Pandavas leave, Duryodhana mimics Bhima's walk, and Bhima vows to slay Duryodhana and his followers and to drink Dussasana's blood.
Arjuna says that the resolutions of superior men are not spoken but shown, and that the Kauravas will see what happens in the fourteenth year.
Bhima says that the earth will drink the blood of Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni and Dussasana.
Arjuna vows to slay Karna and his followers and the kings who fight him, and says the vow will stand unless Duryodhana restores their kingdom in the fourteenth year.
Sahadeva vows to slay Sakuni with his followers, calling him the disgrace of the Gandhara kings.
Nakula vows to send the sons of Dhritarashtra to Yama for insulting Draupadi at the match.
The brothers, bound by their vows, approach Dhritarashtra.
Yudhishthira bids farewell to Bhishma, Somadatta, Vahlika, Drona, Kripa, Ashvatthama, Vidura, Dhritarashtra, his sons, Yuyutsu and Sanjaya, promising to return.
The courtiers, too ashamed to answer, silently pray for his welfare.
Vidura asks that Kunti, a princess, not go to the forest but stay in his own house.
The Pandavas agree to Vidura's wish, call him their father and respected elder, and ask him to say what else must be done.
Vidura advises Yudhishthira not to grieve at a defeat won by foul means, lists his brothers' strengths and virtues, and blesses him with the powers of the gods and his teachers.
Yudhishthira agrees, bows to Bhishma and Drona, and goes on his way.
Draupadi takes leave of Kunti and the household women, who all weep at the loss.
Kunti tells Draupadi not to grieve, praises her chastity and conduct, and asks her to watch over Sahadeva in the woods.
Draupadi leaves weeping in a single blood-stained cloth, Kunti follows, and finds her sons stripped of ornaments, clad in deer-skins and surrounded by rejoicing foes.
Kunti embraces her sons, laments their ruin, calls on Krishna, Pandu, Bhishma and Drona, and begs Sahadeva to stay with her.
A heading marks the start of Section LXXIX.
The Pandavas comfort their mother and set out for the woods, Vidura takes Kunti to his house, and the Kaurava women grieve while Dhritarashtra, anxious for his sons, sends for Vidura.
Vidura comes at once, and Dhritarashtra anxiously asks how the Pandavas left Hastinapura.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura, in a timid voice, how Yudhishthira, Arjuna, the twins, Dhaumya and Draupadi are faring on their journey.

Vidura describes how each brother departs: Yudhishthira covering his face, Bhima admiring his arms, Arjuna scattering sand, the twins smearing their faces and staining themselves with dust, Draupadi weeping with her hair loose, and Dhaumya chanting Yama's mantras.
Dhritarashtra asks why the Pandavas are leaving Hastinapura in such different guises.

Vidura explains that each gesture signals a resolve, that the citizens lament the Kurus' injustice, and that portents of lightning, an eclipse and jackals and vultures foretell the ruin of the Bharatas.

A celestial sage appears before the assembly and foretells that the Kauravas will be destroyed in fourteen years through Duryodhana's fault, and Drona then warns the Kauravas that Dhrishtadyumna, born to slay him, has sided with the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra accepts Drona's words and tells Vidura to bring the Pandavas back with weapons, chariots and every honour, or let them go with respect.
After the Pandavas leave for the forest, Dhritarashtra is overcome with anxiety, and Sanjaya asks why he grieves now that he has won the earth and sent the Pandavas into exile.
Dhritarashtra says that he fears the battle with the Pandavas, who will fight in great chariots with allies.
Sanjaya blames Dhritarashtra's mistaken action and Duryodhana's insult to Draupadi, and says that ruin clouds the judgement of those whom the gods mean to destroy.
Dhritarashtra recounts the omens, admits that he freed the Pandavas after Draupadi asked, and recalls that Vidura urged peace with the sons of Pandu, which he refused out of love for his son.
A heading marks the end of the Sabha Parva.
A Project Gutenberg licence notice follows the text.
Section heading: the Aranyaka Parva, the Book of the Forest.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati, and the word Jaya is to be spoken.
Janamejaya asks how his ancestors, the sons of Pritha, lived in the forest after their defeat at dice, and how Draupadi bore her exile.
Vaisampayana says the Pandavas left Hastinapura by the northern gate with Draupadi, their attendants and servants.
The citizens lament that Duryodhana and his allies will ruin the kingdom, and they resolve to follow the Pandavas.
The citizens go after the Pandavas and address them with joined hands.
The citizens plead to go with the Pandavas, arguing that good company brings virtue and that they do not want to live under the Kuru king.
Yudhishthira thanks them but asks them to go back and look after Bhishma, Dhritarashtra, Vidura, his mother and the others left in the city.
The people wail and, though unwillingly, turn back and take leave of the Pandavas.
The Pandavas reach the great banyan tree called Pramana on the Ganges, bathe, and spend the night fasting on water, with Brahmanas keeping them company.
At dawn the Brahmanas who live on alms stand before the Pandavas, who are about to enter the forest. Yudhishthira warns them of the hardships and tells them to go home.
The Brahmanas refuse to leave, saying the gods favor those who serve them and that the Pandavas' path is theirs too.
Yudhishthira says he honors Brahmanas, but he is ashamed to ask his grieving brothers to do the hard work of gathering food.
The Brahmanas promise to find their own food and to comfort the king with prayers and pleasant talk.
Yudhishthira accepts, but says it shames him that good men must toil for food because of him, and he curses the sons of Dhritarashtra.

Saunaka, a learned Brahmana, tells the weeping king that the wise are not undone by loss. He recites Janaka's teaching that attachment causes suffering, wealth brings fear and desire never ends, and contentment is the highest good.
Yudhishthira replies that he wants wealth only to support Brahmanas and guests, not out of greed, and he describes a householder's duty to share food and to honor guests.
Saunaka says the world is full of contradictions, and describes how the senses lead people through desire and resolve into ignorance and endless rebirth.
Saunaka sets out the path of the wise: act without attachment, follow the eight duties, practise yoga and austerity, and serve the Brahmanas. The section ends with this counsel.
Yudhishthira tells Dhaumya that the Brahmanas following him into the forest are more than he can support, and asks what he should do.
Dhaumya explains that the sun feeds all creatures through rain and crops, and urges Yudhishthira to take refuge in him and practise austerity, as past kings did.
Janamejaya asks how Yudhishthira worshipped the sun for the sake of the Brahmanas.
Vaisampayana introduces a hymn of the sun's 108 names, which Dhaumya recites, and says it brings prosperity, children, learning and freedom from grief.
Yudhishthira bathes, stands in the Ganges facing the sun, and begins his hymn of praise.
Yudhishthira's hymn calls the sun the eye and soul of the universe and lists the gods and beings who honour him, and his power over seasons and the cosmic cycles.
The sun appears and promises Yudhishthira food for years, gives him a copper vessel that keeps the food inexhaustible, and says he will regain his kingdom in the fourteenth year.
Vaisampayana says the hymn grants a devotee what he asks, and traces its passage from Brahma to Indra, then Narada, then Dhaumya, and finally Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira bathes, embraces his brothers, and cooks with Draupadi. The food multiplies, the Brahmanas and brothers are fed, and the food runs out only after Draupadi eats.
After feeding the Brahmanas and performing sacrifices with Dhaumya, the Pandavas set out with the Brahmanas for the Kamyaka woods.
Dhritarashtra, sorrowful after the Pandavas leave, asks Vidura what the Kauravas should do to keep the citizens from turning against them.
Vidura advises him to act with justice, to restore what was taken from the Pandavas, and to set Duryodhana aside, warning that Bhima and Arjuna will destroy the Kurus otherwise.
Dhritarashtra rejects this counsel, saying Duryodhana is his own flesh and blood and he cannot abandon him, and tells Vidura to go wherever he likes.
Dhritarashtra goes into the inner apartments, and Vidura, saying the race is doomed, goes off to the Pandavas.

The Pandavas travel from the Ganges through holy places to Kamyaka forest, where Munis visit them. Vidura arrives in a single chariot, and Yudhishthira, fearing Sakuni has sent him to propose another dice game, wonders what he wants.
Yudhishthira welcomes Vidura, who sits among them and begins to explain Dhritarashtra's conduct.
Vidura reports that Dhritarashtra rejected his advice and repeats it: wait patiently, gather adherents, share your wealth with them, and speak truthfully.
Yudhishthira says he will follow Vidura's counsel and the guidance he gives about time and place.
Dhritarashtra regrets driving Vidura away, collapses senseless at the door of the hall, and orders Sanjaya to bring Vidura back, saying he will die if Sanjaya fails.
Sanjaya reaches Kamyaka and finds Yudhishthira with Vidura among Brahmanas and brothers. He passes on the king's request, and Yudhishthira agrees to let Vidura go.
Vidura returns to Hastinapura. Dhritarashtra embraces him and asks forgiveness for his harsh words, and Vidura forgives him, explaining that he favours the Pandavas because they are in distress.
The two brothers apologise to one another and are greatly happy.
Duryodhana, distressed that Vidura has come back, calls on Sakuni, Karna and Dussasana and vows he will die rather than see the Pandavas prosper again.
Sakuni says the Pandavas will keep their pledge and will not accept recall, and advises the Kauravas to act quietly and watch them.
Dussasana agrees with Sakuni. Karna says the Pandavas will not return before their term ends, and if they do, the Kauravas should defeat them at dice again.
Duryodhana turns away, gloomy. Karna, angry, urges the princes to attack the Pandavas in the forest while they are in distress.
The princes applaud, arm themselves and set out, but Vyasa stops them and then goes to the king.

Vyasa warns Dhritarashtra that the dishonest dice defeat of the Pandavas will bring revenge after thirteen years, and urges him to restrain Duryodhana, since the Kauravas will suffer if he does not. He asks what Bhishma, Drona and Vidura think.
Dhritarashtra says he disliked the dice game but was pushed into it by fate, and admits that out of paternal love he cannot cast off his foolish son Duryodhana.
Vyasa agrees that a son is precious and begins a story: the mother cow Suravi weeps in heaven as a farmer beats one of her calves while it pulls the plough.
Indra asks why she grieves for one calf when thousands of her offspring suffer. She replies that she loves all equally but pities the weakest most.
Indra is moved and sends rain to stop the farmer's work. Vyasa applies the lesson to Dhritarashtra and urges him to favour the weaker Pandavas and to have Duryodhana make peace with them.
Dhritarashtra tells the sage that Vidura, Bhishma and Drona have already counselled him, and asks for help in restraining Duryodhana.
Vyasa says Maitreya is coming to advise Duryodhana, and warns that if his counsel is ignored the sage will curse the prince.
Maitreya arrives and is welcomed with honour. Dhritarashtra asks about the Pandavas and whether the Kurus will keep their brotherly bonds.
Maitreya says he met Yudhishthira at Kamyaka, heard of the disaster caused by the dice game, and came out of affection to warn that the quarrel must stop.
Maitreya urges Duryodhana to make peace, recalling how Bhima killed the Rakshasas Hidimba and Kirmira and the warrior Jarasandha.
Duryodhana stays silent and scornful, scratching the ground and slapping his thigh. Maitreya, angered, curses him that Bhima will break his thigh in the war.
Dhritarashtra tries to calm the sage. Maitreya says the curse will stand unless Duryodhana makes peace with the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra asks how Bhima slew Kirmira.
Maitreya refuses to speak further, says Vidura will tell the story, and leaves. Duryodhana goes out, troubled by the news of Kirmira's death.
Section heading: the Kirmirabadha Parva, the Book of the Slaying of Kirmira.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to describe how Kirmira and Bhima met in combat.
Vidura says the Pandavas, after their defeat at dice, reached Kamyaka after dark, where a Rakshasa blocked their path with illusions that Dhaumya dispelled with mantras.
The Rakshasa demands to know who they are. Yudhishthira names himself, and the Rakshasa, Vaka's brother, boasts that he will eat them.
Kirmira says he has long sought to avenge Vaka and Hidimba on Bhima, and vows to devour Bhima before Yudhishthira's eyes.
