Yudhishthira rebukes the Rakshasa. Bhima fights him with a tree, then wrestles him down, binds and crushes him, and kills him, after which the Pandavas leave for the Dwaita woods.
Vidura says the Pandavas settled peacefully in the cleared forest with Draupadi, and that he himself saw the dead Rakshasa and heard the tale from the Brahmanas.
Dhritarashtra sighs in sorrow and falls into thought at the account of Kirmira's death.
Section heading: the Arjunabhigamana Parva.

Hearing of the exile, the Bhojas, Vrishnis, Andhakas, Panchalas, Dhrishtaketu and the Kaikeyas come to the forest. Krishna vows that Duryodhana, Karna, Dussasana and Sakuni will be slain and Yudhishthira restored.
Krishna's anger grows until Arjuna steps in to calm him by recounting Krishna's deeds.
Arjuna lists Krishna's feats across many ages, including long austerities, sacrifices, the slaying of demons, and his role as creator and sustainer of the world.
Krishna replies that he and Arjuna are the sages Nara and Narayana, born on earth for a purpose, and that no one can tell them apart.
Draupadi appeals to Krishna, recalls her humiliation in the assembly and the Pandavas' failure to defend her, and lists the Kauravas' earlier plots against the brothers.
Draupadi asks why the mighty heroes sit still while weak enemies treat her with contempt, and recalls her own noble birth and marriage.
Draupadi weeps and says she has no husband, son, brother or father to protect her, and asks Krishna for his protection.
Krishna promises Draupadi that he will act for the Pandavas and make her queen again, and Arjuna assures her the same.
Dhrishtadyumna vows that he will kill Drona, Sikhandin will kill Bhishma, Bhima will kill Duryodhana, and Arjuna will kill Karna, with Rama and Krishna as allies.
The assembled heroes turn towards Vasudeva, who begins to speak.

Krishna says that had he been at Dwaraka he would have stopped the dice game, by warning of its evils and by force if necessary. He says he came as soon as he learned of their plight from Yuyudhana, and grieves to see the brothers in distress.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna why he was absent from the Anartta country, where he stayed, and what he did while away.

Krishna explains that he killed Sisupala at the Rajasuya, that Salwa then attacked the empty Dwaraka and killed many young Vrishnis, and that Krishna chased him to an ocean island, fought the Danavas there, and came to the Pandavas on hearing of the dice game.
Yudhishthira asks Vasudeva to describe in full the death of the lord of Saubha, since he is not satisfied with the earlier account.

Vasudeva says Salwa came to avenge Sisupala and besieged the city, and describes the Vrishnis' preparations: fortified walls, weapons, guards, pay for the warriors, bans on drinking, and traps outside the walls.

Vasudeva describes Salwa's great army, the princes Samva, Charudeshna and Pradyumna sallying out, Samva's defeat of Kshemavriddhi and Vegavat, Charudeshna's killing of Vivindhya, and Pradyumna's call to the Yadavas as Salwa returns.
Pradyumna charges Salwa on his golden chariot, Salwa is felled by an arrow to the heart and recovers, and then wounds Pradyumna until he falls senseless on the battlefield.
The Vrishnis despair when Pradyumna falls and the enemy rejoices. Daruka's son drives him off the field, and when he wakes he asks the charioteer why he is retreating.
Pradyumna orders the charioteer to turn back, insisting that a Vrishni never flees and that he would be shamed before his kinsmen if he ran.
The charioteer explains that he retreated to protect the wounded warrior, and offers to show his skill by driving back into the enemy array.

The charioteer drives with great skill and Pradyumna again wounds Salwa, who falls. Narada and the wind god stop Pradyumna from loosing his deadly arrow, because Salwa is fated to die at Krishna's hand, and Salwa flees across the sky.
Krishna returns to a mourning Dwaraka, learns from Kritavarman of Salwa's raid, vows to slay him, and chases him to the ocean, where a long battle of arrows, illusions and counter-illusions follows.
Salwa's weapons wound Daruka badly, and the charioteer says he can no longer hold on. Krishna looks him over and cheers him up.

A messenger from Ahuka arrives with the false news that Salwa has killed Vasudeva in Dwaraka and urges Krishna to stop fighting and defend the city. Krishna is grief-stricken, sees an illusion of his father falling, swoons, and then resumes the battle with arrows.

Krishna describes fighting illusory Danavas and an illusory car, being buried under a shower of rocks, and breaking free with the thunderbolt. Daruka urges him to kill Salwa, and Krishna hurls the discus, which destroys Saubha and Salwa, and says he could not come to the dice game in time.

Krishna takes leave of the Pandavas, who honour him, and sets out for Dwaraka with Subhadra and Abhimanyu. Dhrishtadyumna, Dhrishtaketu and the Kaikeyas also depart, while the Brahmanas and people stay with Yudhishthira, who orders his chariot readied.

The Pandavas set out into the forest after giving gifts, and the people of Kurujangala lament their exile, blame Duryodhana and his allies, and beg them to return. Arjuna asks the Brahmanas to plead for them with the ascetics, and the people go home sorrowful.
Yudhishthira tells his brothers they must live twelve years in the forest and asks them to find a fitting place. Arjuna suggests the lake of Dwaitavana, and Yudhishthira agrees.

The Pandavas go to the lake with many Brahmanas and ascetics, entering a forest of flowering trees, birds and elephants. The ascetics welcome Yudhishthira, who sits under a great tree with his brothers around him.
Heading for Section XXV, which begins the next part of the book.

The Pandavas settle in the forest, Yudhishthira and Dhaumya serve the sages, and the old sage Markandeya arrives as a guest. When Markandeya smiles at the sight of them, Yudhishthira asks why, and the sage recalls Rama's dutiful exile and argues that no one should act wrongly out of pride, predicting that Yudhishthira will win back his fortune.
Markandeya blesses the company and sets out to the north.

The woods fill with Brahmanas at their rites, and the Vedic chanting mixes with the twang of the Pandavas' bows. Vaka of the Dalvya line tells Yudhishthira that Kshatriya might needs Brahmanical wisdom, cites Vali's fall after he wronged the Brahmanas, and urges him to keep a learned Brahmana as counsellor.
Many named sages, including Dwaipayana and Narada, praise Yudhishthira and honour him, as Rishis honour Indra in heaven.

Draupadi laments the Pandavas' fall from luxury, accuses Duryodhana and his allies of cruelty, and asks why Yudhishthira shows no anger at his brothers' hardship. She urges him to act, saying a Kshatriya who does not strike back at the right time is disregarded by all.
Draupadi tells of Prahlada's advice to Vali: a man who always forgives is despised, robbed by servants and disrespected by all.
Prahlada warns that the constantly angry man loses friends, wealth and respect, so one should use might and forgiveness each at the proper time.
Prahlada lists the occasions for forgiveness, such as a past service, an offence from ignorance, or an offence done by accident, and says might should be used against others.
Draupadi concludes that the time has come for Yudhishthira to show his might against the covetous Kauravas, since forgiveness is not right towards them.

Yudhishthira argues at length that anger ruins those who feel it and that the wise forgive even when strong, citing Kasyapa's verses in praise of forgiveness. He expects the elders to urge peace and the king to return the kingdom, judges Duryodhana unworthy, and resolves to keep to forgiveness.

Draupadi laments that virtue has not protected Yudhishthira, though he honoured Brahmanas, performed great sacrifices, and was undone by the dice game. She argues that God moves all creatures like puppets, and asks how God can let the sinful prosper while the good suffer. If God is responsible for every act, she asks, then human might must be the true cause, and she concludes that she grieves for those without might.

Yudhishthira says Draupadi speaks like an atheist. He argues that he acts out of duty and not for reward, that doubting virtue leads to a worse rebirth, and that sages such as Markandeya, Vyasa and Narada prove the rewards of virtue. He urges her to put aside doubt, have faith, and honour God.

Draupadi says she has never scorned religion or God, and that her grief has made her speak wildly. She argues that every creature must act, that those who rely only on fate or chance are foolish, and that success depends on human effort, intelligence and the fruits of past deeds. She urges action with confidence, and recalls the lessons she heard as a child from her father's Brahmana teacher.
Bhima, sighing in anger, tells Yudhishthira that the forest life is weak and shameful, that the kingdom was lost to unfair dice, and that he should stop hiding behind his promise and fight.

Bhima continues that a man must balance virtue, wealth and pleasure, that a Kshatriya's duty is might and stratagem, and that Yudhishthira should march on Hastinapura with his brothers and allies to win back the kingdom.

Yudhishthira says he cannot blame Bhima's harsh words, but explains that Sakuni cheated him at dice and that the agreed terms bound them to twelve years in the forest and a year in disguise. He refuses to break his oath, says Bhima's anger is misplaced, and asks him to wait for a better time and to remember that he once wanted to burn the king's hands and was stopped by Arjuna.

Bhima argues that life is brief and uncertain, so waiting for thirteen years is pointless, and that the Pandavas will be recognised and betrayed by spies and vanquished kings. He says they have already spent thirteen months in the forest, calls Yudhishthira's forbearance misplaced, and urges him to fight, since that is the Kshatriya's duty.
Yudhishthira sighs and reflects that true virtue is hard to know, and that he cannot force it aside like crushing a mountain. He settles on a course and answers Bhima without further delay.
Yudhishthira tells Bhima that rash deeds fail, and that the Kaurava champions, including Bhishma, Drona, Karna and the allied kings, are too strong to beat by force alone.
Vyasa arrives, is honoured by the brothers, and says he has come to dispel Yudhishthira's fear of the Kaurava champions by means of a sacred rite.
Vyasa teaches Yudhishthira a science called Pratismriti, tells him Arjuna should seek weapons from Indra and the other gods, and advises the brothers to move to another forest.
Vyasa departs, Yudhishthira keeps the knowledge in his mind, and the Pandavas return to Kamyaka with their Brahmanas to live by archery, hunting and sacred rites.
Yudhishthira takes Arjuna aside and explains that the Kaurava side has the best teachers, weapons and allies, and that Arjuna must go north to Indra. He passes on the science Vyasa taught him.
Arjuna sets out fully armed after his brothers and the Brahmanas bless him. Krishna grieves at his departure, recalls Duryodhana's insults, and gives him her blessing.

Draupadi, here also called Krishna, blesses Arjuna as he walks around his brothers and Dhaumya. Arjuna crosses the Himalayas, and at Indrakila an ascetic tells him to lay down his weapons, but he refuses. The ascetic, revealed as Indra, tells him to first behold Shiva before receiving the weapons.
Section heading: the Kairata Parva.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to tell in full how Arjuna gained weapons, how he entered the solitary forest, and how he fought with the god Bhava.
Vaisampayana agrees to tell of Arjuna's meeting with the three-eyed god and his contact with the god's person.

Arjuna sets out for the Himalayas to see Indra and Shiva, enters the forest with heavenly signs, and practises austerities that grow harsher, from fruit to fortnightly meals to air alone, standing on his toes. Alarmed by the heat of his penance, the sages go to Shiva, who says he knows Arjuna's wish and will grant it.
The truthful sages hear Shiva's words and return to their homes.

Shiva comes down to the Himalayas as a Kirata hunter with Uma and attendants. The demon Muka, in boar form, attacks Arjuna, and both Arjuna and the hunter shoot it, each claiming it. Their duel is fierce: Arjuna's arrows, sword and then his bare fists fail, the hunter's blows leave him senseless, and when he revives he makes a clay image of Bhava and finds his garland on the hunter's crown. Shiva, pleased, says he will grant him an irresistible weapon.
Arjuna kneels before the god, praises him as the cause of all things, and begs pardon for the fight he began in ignorance.
Shiva forgives Arjuna and embraces him, and then speaks again.

Shiva tells Arjuna that he was once Nara, friend of Narayana, and that he himself had taken the Gandiva from him by illusion. He now restores the bow and the inexhaustible quivers, saying Arjuna's body will be free of pain and that he may ask a boon.
Arjuna asks for the Brahmasira, a weapon that can destroy the universe, so that he can win the coming battle against Karna, Bhishma, Kripa and Drona.
Shiva agrees to give Arjuna the Pasupata weapon, which no god knows, and warns that it must not be used against a weak foe, since it could destroy the world.

Arjuna asks to be taught, and Shiva teaches him the weapon's mysteries. The weapon attends Arjuna, the earth trembles, and Shiva restores Arjuna's body before giving him the Gandiva and departing with Uma.

Shiva vanishes and Arjuna rejoices that he has seen and touched the god. Varuna, Kubera, Yama and Indra on his elephant come to the mountain, and Yama, reminding Arjuna that he was once Nara, promises he will defeat Bhishma and Karna and offers him his mace.
Arjuna receives Yama's weapon and its mysteries. Varuna then offers his nooses and the Varuna weapons, recalling how they once bound many Daityas.
Kubera gives Arjuna the celestial weapon Antardhana, which can put a foe to sleep, and says Arjuna is worthy to hold it.
Indra tells Arjuna that he has already reached the stature of a god, but must come to heaven to receive the celestial weapons, and says his chariot with Matali will soon come down for him.
Arjuna worships the assembled guardians, who return the worship and depart to their own realms.
Arjuna, having obtained the weapons, is filled with pleasure and regards himself as having achieved his desire.
Section heading: the Indralokagamana Parva, the Book of Going to Indra's World.

Indra's splendid chariot, driven by Matali, comes down through the clouds, bristling with celestial weapons. Matali tells Arjuna that Indra's father has sent for him so the gods can see him and he can receive weapons.
Arjuna asks Matali to mount first, since the chariot cannot be ridden by anyone without ascetic merit.

Arjuna bathes in the Ganges, performs his rites, and bids farewell to Mount Mandara, then rides up past the lights of the virtuous and the heroic dead, the Gandharvas and the elephant Airavata, until he reaches Amaravati.

Arjuna enters Amaravati, a city of celestial gardens and flowers reserved for the virtuous, and is greeted by the gods, Gandharvas and sages. Indra embraces him, seats him on his own throne, and delights in the sight of his son while heavenly dancers perform.
The gods honour Arjuna, who receives Indra's thunderbolt and the other celestial weapons, and recalls his brothers. At Indra's command he lives in heaven for five years, surrounded by comfort.
Indra tells Arjuna to learn celestial music and dance from Chitrasena, who becomes his friend and teaches him. Arjuna finds no peace, remembering the dice game, Dussasana and his brothers and mother.
Indra, seeing Arjuna's glances at Urvasi, sends Chitrasena to ask her to wait upon him and teach him the arts of female company. Chitrasena delivers the message, praising Arjuna's many virtues.
Urvasi replies with a smile that she is already moved by love for Arjuna, and agrees to go to him.
Urvasi bathes, adorns herself and goes at night to Arjuna's palace, her mind fixed on him. Arjuna, bashful, shuts his eyes and offers her the respect due to a superior, asking what she commands.
Urvasi explains that Indra held an assembly at which she and others danced, and that Chitrasena came to her with Indra's request. She says she has long cherished her wish for Arjuna.

Arjuna, embarrassed, covers his ears and says she is to him like a wife of a superior, like his mother Kunti or Indra's queen Sachi, and that he gazed at her only in the thought she was the mother of his race.
Urvasi replies that Apsaras are free in their choice, that the sons of Puru freely enjoy their company, and asks him to accept her.
Arjuna repeats that he sees her as his mother, bows at her feet, and asks her to go back and protect him as a son.
Urvasi, enraged and trembling, curses Arjuna to pass a year among women as a dancer, without manhood and scorned as a eunuch, because he rejected her.

Urvasi returns home. Arjuna tells Chitrasena what happened, and Chitrasena reports it to Indra, who says the curse will serve Arjuna well in the thirteenth year of exile, when the brothers must live unknown.
Relieved of worry about the curse, Arjuna sports in heaven with Chitrasena.
Closing lines: listening to this account of Arjuna's pure conduct frees a man from lust, pride and anger, and carries him to heaven.

Lomasa visits Indra's court and sees Arjuna on Indra's seat, wondering what merit won him that place. Indra explains that Arjuna is his son, that Nara and Narayana were reborn on earth to help the gods against the Nivatakavachas, and sends Lomasa to Yudhishthira with a message that he should visit sacred waters and be guarded from Rakshasas.
Heading for Section XLVIII, the next part of the book.
Arjuna asks Lomasa to protect Yudhishthira, to let him visit holy places, and to give gifts to Brahmanas.
Lomasa agrees, sets out for the earth, and reaches Kamyaka, where he finds Yudhishthira surrounded by ascetics and his brothers.
Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra said when he heard of Arjuna's feats.

Dhritarashtra, having heard of Arjuna's stay in Indra's abode from Vyasa, asks Sanjaya for details. He calls Duryodhana's policy vulgar, names the warriors who might face Arjuna, and says that Arjuna's arrows will consume his sons and that no one can stand before him.

Sanjaya agrees with Dhritarashtra, saying the Pandavas are enraged by Draupadi's shaming and that Arjuna has won the favour of the gods, including Shiva, whom he fought as a hunter. He repeats Bhima's vow to smash Duryodhana's thighs when the thirteen years end.

Dhritarashtra laments that Karna's cruel words have stirred the Pandavas further, says his blind and foolish son listens only to counsellors who indulge his vices, and admits that Arjuna, with Krishna as his ally, cannot be overcome by his sons.
Janamejaya asks why Dhritarashtra let Duryodhana provoke the Pandavas, and what food the exiles ate, whether from the wild or from cultivation.

Vaisampayana says the Pandavas hunted deer and shared the meat, feeding Brahmanas first. Yudhishthira supported ten thousand Snataka Brahmanas, Draupadi fed the others before herself, and the brothers hunted in all directions for five years at Kamyaka, anxious for Arjuna, yet busy with study and sacrifice.

Dhritarashtra, unable to rest, describes the Pandavas' heroism and strength, especially the twins, Bhima and Arjuna, and predicts his army will be wiped out, regretting that he did not heed his friends' advice.

Sanjaya replies that Krishna came to the forest, promised to restore Yudhishthira's kingdom and to slay Duryodhana and his allies in a single day when the term ends, and that Draupadi's allies also vowed revenge. Yudhishthira asked Krishna to keep this promise when the thirteen years are over.
Dhritarashtra recalls Vidura's warning that the dice game would bring a terrible bloodshed that would destroy the Kurus, and says it is about to come true.
Section heading: the Nalopakhyana Parva, the Tale of Nala.
Janamejaya asks what Yudhishthira and his brothers did while Arjuna was in Indra's realm.
Vaisampayana says the brothers and Draupadi grieved for Arjuna. Bhima urges Yudhishthira to leave the forest, fight the Kauravas before the term ends, and count the thirteen years loosely.
Yudhishthira calms Bhima, promising he will defeat Duryodhana when the term ends, but saying he cannot lie or break his word.
The sage Vrihadaswa arrives. Yudhishthira honours him and speaks to him in sorrow.
Yudhishthira laments that he was cheated at dice, that his wife was dragged into the assembly, and that he is exiled in the forest in deerskins. He asks whether any king has ever been more wretched.
Vrihadaswa says he will tell of a king more wretched than Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira asks for the story of that king.

Vrihadaswa names Nala, son of Virasena and king of the Nishadhas, who lost his kingdom at dice to Pushkara and lived in the forest with his wife, without servants, brothers or friends. He tells Yudhishthira that he has the support of his brothers and priests, and so should not grieve.
Yudhishthira asks Vrihadaswa to tell the story of Nala in full.

Vrihadaswa describes Nala's virtues and Bhima's daughter Damayanti, whose beauty is unmatched, and how the two fall in love through the reports of heralds. Nala catches a golden swan that promises to speak well of him to Damayanti, and it flies to Vidarbha and praises him to her.
Damayanti, lovesick, grows pale, sighs and weeps. Her attendants tell her father, who decides his daughter is ready for marriage and summons all the kings to a swayamvara.
The sages Narada and Parvata visit Indra's court. Indra asks for news, and Narada tells him that Damayanti's swayamvara is near and that kings from every quarter are heading there.
Indra and the guardians of the world set out for Vidarbha. On the way they see Nala, struck by his beauty, and ask him to carry their message to Damayanti.

Nala asks who the gods are and what they want. Indra names himself, Agni, Varuna and Yama, and asks Nala to tell Damayanti to choose one of them as husband. Nala protests that he is in love himself, but the gods insist that he keep his promise.

Nala enters the guarded palace by the gods' power and sees Damayanti, whose beauty humbles the moon, surrounded by her attendants, who marvel at him. Damayanti asks who he is and why he has come, and Nala says he is a messenger of the gods, asking her to choose one of them.

Damayanti bows to the gods and tells Nala she chooses him, pleading for his love and threatening to end her life if he refuses. Nala answers that the gods are worthy of her and urges her to choose one of them, but she insists, and he agrees to report back, and the gods ask him what happened, and he tells them she will choose him at the swayamvara in their presence, so that no blame falls on him.

Vrihadaswa describes the kings gathering for Damayanti's swayamvara, her entrance, and her confusion at seeing five men who all look like Nala. She prays to the gods to show their true forms, and by the signs of mortality she chooses Nala, garlanding him, and the gods grant the couple boons. Nala and Damayanti then live happily, rule well, and have a son and a daughter.

On the road home, Indra meets Kali and Dvapara, who are going to the swayamvara. Indra says it is already over, and Kali, angry, says that Damayanti should suffer for choosing a mortal. The gods rebuke Kali for wanting to curse so virtuous a king, and Kali then asks Dvapara to enter the dice so he can take Nala's kingdom.

Kali waits for a chance and enters Nala when he fails to wash his feet before prayers. Possessed, Nala is challenged by Pushkara and loses his wealth, his cars and his robes, and the citizens are unable to persuade him to stop, and his wife's pleas go unheard, so that the play goes on for months with Nala always losing.

Damayanti, seeing Nala lose everything, asks her nurse to summon the councillors, but Nala ignores her. She then asks the charioteer Varshneya to take the children to her kinsfolk, leaving the horses and car, and he goes to Vidarbha and then to Ayodhya, where he serves King Rituparna.

Pushkara wins Nala's remaining kingdom and mocks him by proposing Damayanti as the next stake. Nala, enraged but silent, strips off his ornaments and leaves the city with Damayanti in a single cloth, while Pushkara forbids anyone to help him. Starving, Nala tries to catch golden birds with his cloth, but they are the dice in disguise and fly off with it, and Nala points out the roads, and Damayanti urges him to go with her to Vidarbha.
Nala says that he will not go to her father's kingdom in disgrace, since he once went there in glory and does not want to cause her sorrow.

Nala comforts his wife and they reach a travellers' shelter, where they sleep on the bare earth. Nala, under Kali's influence, takes a sword and cuts her cloth in half, then leaves her sleeping, returns in grief, and finally walks away from her in the forest.

Damayanti wakes alone, cries out for Nala, and wanders in grief and fear, while a serpent seizes her and she laments for her husband. A hunter kills the serpent and frees her, but when he tries to force himself on her she curses him, and he falls dead.

Damayanti wanders through the wild forest, passing trees, beasts and rivers, and sits down to lament. She calls on Nala, pleads with a mountain and a tiger for news, and describes her father, her husband and their royal families.
She goes north to a hermitage of ascetics, who welcome her and ask who she is. She tells them her story and her search for Nala.
The ascetics foretell that she will see Nala again, and then they vanish with their sacred fires and asylum.

Puzzled and grieving, Damayanti addresses an Ashoka tree and then goes on to a merchants' caravan. Its leader, Suchi, says he has not seen Nala, and that the caravan is bound for Suvahu, the city of the Chedi king.

The caravan camps at a fragrant lotus lake. At midnight a herd of wild elephants stampedes through the sleeping merchants and kills many. The survivors blame the strange woman who joined them, and Damayanti, terrified and ashamed, flees into the woods and laments her ill fortune as the fruit of sins.

Next morning the survivors leave, mourning their dead. Damayanti laments again, reaches the Chedi city of Suvahu in a single garment, and is noticed by the queen mother, who sends for her. Damayanti tells her story of the dice game and of Nala's desertion of her.

The queen mother offers to have her men search for Nala, and asks Damayanti to stay. Damayanti sets conditions: she will not serve, be pursued by men, or eat leftovers, and she wants to meet the Brahmanas searching for her husband.
The queen mother agrees and gives Damayanti to her daughter Sunanda as a companion, and Damayanti lives there with her needs met.

Nala rescues the snake Karkotaka from a fire, and the snake explains that he was cursed by Narada. Karkotaka bites Nala, disguising him, promises that the poison will torment the one who deceived him, gives him garments that will restore his form, and tells him to serve King Rituparna at Ayodhya.

On the tenth day Nala reaches Rituparna's city and offers his services as Vahuka, a charioteer, horse-trainer and cook. Rituparna accepts and makes him superintendent of the stables, with Varshneya and Jivala as companions.

Nala, living in the king's city, recites a verse each night lamenting his helpless wife. When Jivala asks whom he mourns, Nala answers with a story about a man who had a wife, was false to her, and lost her in the forest.
Nala lives on in the king's service, unknown, remembering Damayanti.

Bhima sends Brahmanas out in all directions with rich rewards to find Nala and Damayanti. The Brahmana Sudeva finds her in the Chedi palace beside Sunanda, recognises her though she is soiled and frail, and reflects on the beauty of her and the loss of her husband.
Sudeva greets Damayanti as the friend of her brother, and tells her that her parents, brothers and children are well, and that many Brahmanas are searching for her.
Damayanti weeps and asks after her family. Sunanda tells the queen mother, who asks Sudeva who Damayanti is and how she fell into this state, and Sudeva begins to tell the true story.
Sudeva tells the queen-mother who the woman is: Bhima's daughter and Nala's wife, who went off unseen with him after Nala lost his kingdom at dice.
The dust is washed from the mark, the queen-mother recognizes her niece, Damayanti is sent home to Vidarbha, and she asks that Nala be searched for.
The Brahmanas set out through cities, hermitages and cowherd lands, repeating Damayanti's message wherever they go.
Parnada says Rituparna ignored the message, but the charioteer Vahuka answered with sympathetic words about the patience a faithful wife should show.
Damayanti asks her mother to keep the plan from Bhima, sends Sudeva off with the false swayamvara news, and rewards Parnada with wealth and a promise of more.
Nala, disguised as Vahuka, doubts Damayanti's motive yet agrees to go; he yokes the horses, the car rushes off, and Varshneya, judging Vahuka's skill, begins to suspect he is Nala.
After a garment falls and a tree is counted and felled to prove Rituparna's skill, the two trade knowledge, and Kali leaves Nala and hides in the Vibhitaka tree.
The people announce Rituparna's arrival, his car is heard across the city, and Damayanti, believing it may be Nala's, laments and longs for him.
Rituparna greets Bhima, who finds no swayamvara preparations, and Rituparna says he came only to pay his respects, which Bhima suspects is not the real reason.
Vahuka stables the horses while Damayanti, unsure who the charioteer is, decides to send a female messenger to find out.
Damayanti tells Kesini to test the charioteer, and Vahuka gives an account of his master's journey and of Varshneya's departure while claiming no one knows Nala's whereabouts.
Hearing Kesini repeat the old words, Nala answers with a speech about patient, faithful wives, cannot hold back his tears, and Kesini goes back to report.
Heading: the next section, LXXV, begins here.
Damayanti asks Kesini to watch Vahuka closely, and Kesini reports a string of wonders, from widened passages and filling vessels to fire from sun-held grass and flowers made fragrant by pressing.
Damayanti has Kesini bring meat he cooked, recognizes Nala's cooking, and sends her children to him; Nala embraces them in tears and asks Kesini to leave, so that people will not talk.
Damayanti questions Vahuka about his desertion, Nala blames Kali, the Wind-god vouches for Damayanti, Nala resumes his true form, and the couple spend happy days together in Bhima's palace.
Nala and Damayanti pay respects to Bhima, Rituparna asks forgiveness and gets back the horse-lore, and the story closes with Rituparna leaving and Nala soon departing Kundina.

Nala marches into his country and offers Pushkara a rematch of dice or battle with Damayanti and the kingdom at stake; Pushkara mocks him, the game is played, and Nala wins everything back and pardons his brother, blaming Kali for the earlier defeat.
Nala embraces Pushkara and sends him home after a month of hospitality, and Nala rules his kingdom to the delight of his subjects.
Damayanti returns with her children to a restored Nala, and Vrihadaswa presents the story as a comfort against misfortune and offers Yudhishthira the science of dice.
Yudhishthira asks for the dice-lore and receives it, and the sage goes off to bathe in the sacred waters of Hayasirsha.
Yudhishthira hears from visiting Brahmanas that Arjuna is performing harsh penance alone in the forest, and he grieves for his brother while seeking comfort from the Brahmanas there.
Heading: the Tirtha-yatra Parva begins here.
Janamejaya asks how his grandsires passed their time in the forest without Arjuna, whose skill made him their protector.
Vaisampayana says the brothers were cheerless without Arjuna, and Draupadi and Bhima each speak of the emptiness the forest now has without him.
Nakula laments that Arjuna's feats are famous even among the gods, recalls the horses he brought from the north, and says he no longer wants to stay in Kamyaka.
Sahadeva recalls Arjuna's deeds, from his victories and his winning of wives at the Rajasuya to defeating Drupada to pay Drona's fee, and prefers to leave the forest.
Yudhishthira, troubled by his brothers' and Krishna's sorrow, honours the arriving Narada and asks what merit comes from visiting the sacred waters and shrines on earth.
Narada begins the tale of Bhishma, who during his Pitrya vow by the source of the Ganga met the sage Pulastya, worshipped him, and was filled with joy at his sight.
Pulastya is pleased with Bhishma's virtue and offers to grant him whatever he asks.
Bhishma says he is already content to have seen the sage, and asks him to explain the merit of going round the earth visiting tirthas.
Pulastya explains that the merit of tirthas comes from self-control and virtue, that they can be reached by people who lack wealth, and that Pushkara is among the holiest of them.
Pulastya praises Pushkara at length, saying that bathing there, feeding Brahmanas, and living there for a time bring the merit of great sacrifices.
Pulastya names a long route of further tirthas, each with the reward it brings, from Jamvu-marga and Kanwa's asylum to Prabhasa, Dwaravati and beyond.
Pulastya continues the itinerary from Kurukshetra, listing dozens of tirthas and their rewards, including Rama's lakes, and ends by praising Kurukshetra as the sacrificial altar of the Grandsire.
Pulastya's list runs on through many more tirthas, from Dharma's bathing place and the Ganges source to Naimisha, Gaya and the Gandaki, each promising a specific merit and ending with Lalitika.
Pulastya lists more sacred places, from Samvedya and Lauhitya to the Kaveri, the Godavari and Dandaka, with the merit each one gives.

The list runs through Gokarna, Gayatri, Tungaka and Kalanjara, then praises Prayaga as the foremost tirtha of all, where the Ganga meets the Yamuna, and gives the age-by-age holiness of the Ganga and the other tirthas.
Pulastya advises that the account be recited only to worthy people, and promises that reciting or hearing it cleanses sins and brings boons such as sons, wealth and royal power.
Narada reports that Pulastya took his leave and that Bhishma ended his tour at Prayaga, then promises Yudhishthira fame and merit if he visits the tirthas with the sages, guided by Lomasa.
Vaisampayana says Narada departed, and Yudhishthira, reflecting on the matter, begins to recite the merits of the tirthas to the ascetics.
Yudhishthira tells Dhaumya that he sent Arjuna to gain weapons from Indra, names the Kaurava champions including Karna, judges Arjuna alone able to face them, and asks for a new forest to live in.
Dhaumya comforts the Pandavas and introduces the eastern holy places he will describe, from Naimisha and Gaya through Prayaga and Mahendra to sites linked with sages and kings.
Dhaumya describes the southern holy places, from the Godavari and the Payoshni, where King Nriga's tale is set, to Gokarna, Devasabha and Agastya's hermitage.
Dhaumya moves to Surashtra, naming Prabhasa, Pindaraka and Mount Ujjayanta, and closes with Dwaravati, where Hari dwells, praising Krishna as the embodiment of virtue.

Dhaumya lists the western sites, from the Narmada and the Vaidurya peak to Yayati's fall at the Viswamitra river and the Pushkara lake, and ends with a verse on how imagined pilgrimage to Pushkara cleanses sin.
Dhaumya describes the northern sites, from the Saraswati, the Yamuna and Sahadeva's sacrifice to Gangadwara and Badari, and urges Yudhishthira to visit them to be freed from anxiety.
Heading: Section XCI begins here.

Lomasa tells Yudhishthira that he has seen Arjuna in Indra's heaven, lists the weapons and arts Arjuna has gained, and relays Indra's word that Arjuna will return soon, that Karna is no match for him, and that the brothers should practise asceticism meanwhile.
Lomasa relays Arjuna's request that he guide Yudhishthira through the tirthas and guard them from Rakshasas, and says he will go along, as earlier royal sages did.
Yudhishthira is overjoyed, says he had already decided on the pilgrimage, and agrees to set out whenever Lomasa chooses.
Lomasa advises Yudhishthira to travel with a light retinue so that the journey will be easier.
Yudhishthira asks those who cannot bear the hardships of travel, and the cooks and dependants, to turn back, and sends the loyal citizens to Dhritarashtra for their allowances.
The citizens and Brahmanas return to Hastinapura, where Dhritarashtra provides for them, while Yudhishthira stays three nights at Kamyaka with a few Brahmanas and Lomasa.
The Brahmanas beg to join Yudhishthira on the pilgrimage, pointing out that the tirthas are dangerous and need protection from Rakshasas.
Yudhishthira agrees with tears of joy, and Vyasa, Parvata and Narada advise purifying the body by rule and the heart by goodwill toward all before visiting the tirthas.
After worship and rites, the party sets out in bark and hides, armed, with cooks and servants, facing east.
Yudhishthira asks Lomasa why his sinful enemies prosper while he suffers.

Lomasa replies that sinners may prosper briefly but are finally ruined, recounting how the Asuras fell through pride, urging Yudhishthira to bathe at the tirthas like the gods, and predicting the destruction of Dhritarashtra's sons.

The Pandavas bathe and give gifts at the Gomati, Vahuda and Prayaga, then reach Gayasira and the Brahmasara lake, where they keep the Chaturmasya vow among many Brahmanas, and Shamatha recounts King Gaya's vast sacrifices.
Shamatha closes by noting that King Gaya held many such sacrifices beside this same Brahmasara.
Yudhishthira settles at Agastya's hermitage and asks why Agastya slew Vatapi and how strong that demon was.
Lomasa tells how the demon Ilwala, angered at being denied a son like Indra, turned his brother Vatapi into a ram, served him to Brahmanas, and called him back to tear them open.

Agastya finds his ancestors hanging head-down in a pit, who ask for offspring; he creates the woman Lopamudra, who is born to the king of Vidarbha and grows into a beautiful princess whom her father must find a husband for.
Agastya asks for Lopamudra's hand, the king and queen are distressed, Lopamudra urges her father to give her, and the couple take up penance at Gangadwara after she gives up her fine robes.

When Lopamudra, in her season, asks for a palace-style bed and ornaments, Agastya says he lacks such wealth, and she suggests he summon it by his power, which he refuses because it would cost his merit.
Agastya says he will go out to find wealth, and tells Lopamudra to stay and do as she pleases in the meantime.
Agastya goes to King Srutarvan, who is wealthy, and asks for a share of his riches without harming others.
Srutarvan says his spending matches his income, and Agastya refuses to take anything, then goes with Srutarvan to King Vradhnaswa.
Vradhnaswa likewise says his spending equals his income, so Agastya and the two kings go on to Trasadasyu, the wealthy son of Purokutsa.
Trasadasyu says the same, and the kings suggest asking the Danava Ilwala, the richest man on earth, for wealth.
The company agrees that begging from Ilwala is the right course, and they all go to him together.

Ilwala serves Vatapi to Agastya and the kings, Agastya digests him when Ilwala calls, and Agastya then asks for wealth and offers Lopamudra a choice of sons, to which she answers that one powerful son is best.
Lopamudra conceives, Agastya retreats to the forest, and after seven years the son Dridhasyu is born, earning the name Idhmavaha for carrying sacred wood.
Lomasa explains how the asylum got its name, praises the Bhagirathi and Bhrigu's tirtha, and says that bathing there restored Rama's might, which Yudhishthira may likewise recover from Duryodhana.
Yudhishthira bathes with his brothers and Krishna, his body blazes with new brilliance, and he asks why Rama's energy was once taken and how he got it back.
Lomasa begins the story: Vishnu was born as Rama, son of Dasaratha, and Rama of Bhrigu's line came to Ayodhya to test him by having him string his bow.
Dasaratha's son strings the bow, reveals a vision of the cosmos, and Bhrigu's Rama is stripped of his energy until the Pitris send him to a sacred river, where he recovers it.
Yudhishthira asks Lomasa to describe Agastya's exploits in detail.
Lomasa tells how Vritra's Kalakeya Danavas harried the gods, how Brahma advised seeking Dadhicha's bones, and how Dadhicha gave his life and Twashtri forged the Vajra for Indra.
Indra, empowered by Vishnu, the gods and sages, attacks Vritra and slays him with the Vajra, then the Danavas retreat into the sea and plot the destruction of the ascetics.
Lomasa describes how the Kalakeyas, sheltering in the sea, killed sages in their hermitages at night, halting sacrifices, and how the gods appeal to Narayana for protection.
The gods tell Vishnu that the killing of Brahmanas threatens the whole universe and beg him to act.
Vishnu says only Agastya can dry up the sea where the Kalakeyas hide, so the gods go to Agastya and praise him as their protector.
Yudhishthira asks why Vindhya suddenly grew huge in his anger.
Lomasa explains that Vindhya, jealous of Meru, demanded that the sun circle him as well, and then grew to obstruct the sun, so the gods went to Agastya.
The gods ask Agastya to stop Vindhya, and he asks the mountain to make way for his trip south until he returns, a promise that keeps Vindhya low because Agastya never came back.
The gods ask Agastya to drink the ocean so they can destroy the Kalakeyas, he agrees, and he sets out for the sea with sages, gods and other beings following.
Agastya drinks up the sea while the gods praise him and slay the Kalakeyas, and when asked to refill it he says the water is digested, so the gods must find another way.
Brahma tells the gods they must wait, since the ocean will be refilled through the descendants of Bhagiratha's family.
Yudhishthira asks how Bhagiratha's kin refilled the ocean and asks Lomasa to tell of the achievements of King Sagara.
Vaisampayana says Lomasa begins to narrate the achievements of King Sagara.

Lomasa describes Sagara, who was childless and prayed to Shiva on Mount Kailasa, and was promised sixty thousand sons; his queens bore a gourd and a boy, and a voice from the sky told him to keep the gourd's seeds in vessels.

The sixty thousand sons grow fierce and harass gods and men, Brahma foretells their doom, and when Sagara's sacrificial horse vanishes at the sea, the sons search the world and, failing, are ordered by their angry father never to return without it.
The sons dig into the sea toward the netherworld, find the horse beside the sage Kapila, and are burned to ashes; Narada reports this to Sagara, who sends for his grandson Ansuman.
Yudhishthira asks why Sagara abandoned his own valiant son.
Lomasa explains that Asamanjas, Sagara's son by the princess of Sivi, threw townsmen's children into the river, the townspeople begged for relief, and Sagara banished him.

Sagara sends Ansuman to win back the horse, Kapila grants Ansuman's wish for the horse and for his ancestors' purification, the sacrifice is finished, and the line passes to Dilipa and then Bhagiratha, who will try to bring the Ganga down.
Bhagiratha, grieving over his ancestors, hands over his kingdom and performs austerities for a thousand years in the Himalayas, which are described in lush detail.
Ganga appears and asks what he wants, and Bhagiratha asks her to wash the bodies of the sons of Sagara so they can reach heaven.
Ganga agrees but warns that only Shiva can bear her fall, so Bhagiratha goes to Kailasa and wins Shiva's favor to sustain her descent.
Shiva agrees to bear Ganga's fall, Ganga comes down in three streams and follows Bhagiratha to fill the sea, and Lomasa ends by recalling how the sea was drunk, Ganga brought down, and Vatapi slain.
Yudhishthira and his brothers see strange sights on the Hemakuta hill, where speech brings stones and storms, and Yudhishthira asks Lomasa about them.

Lomasa explains that a wrathful sage named Rishava made the hill forbid speech, that the gods hid the place from mortals, and that bathing there cleanses sin, and he sends the party on to the Kausiki.
Lomasa names the hermitages of Viswamitra and of Kasyapa, whose son Rishyasringa made Indra send rain and was given the princess Santa by King Lomapada.
Yudhishthira asks how Rishyasringa was born of a hind, why Indra feared him, and what Santa was like, and he asks Lomasa to tell the whole story.

Lomasa tells how Vibhandaka's seed fell into a hind to produce Rishyasringa, the horn-headed sage raised without any woman, and how Lomapada, facing drought and the Brahmanas' anger, decided to bring the sage to his land.
The courtesan prepares a floating hermitage near Kasyapa's son's hut and sends her daughter, a clever courtesan, who finds Rishyasringa.
The courtesan greets Rishyasringa with courteous questions about his austerities, his father and his studies.
Rishyasringa welcomes her, offers water, fruit and a seat, and asks what vow she is keeping.
She explains that her hermitage lies three yojanas away and that her vow requires him to embrace her.
Rishyasringa offers her ripe fruits instead, such as gallnuts and myrobalans.

She discards the fruit, gives him garlands, drink and playful embraces, then leaves pretending to make offerings, and Rishyasringa, overcome with love, sighs until his father Vibhandaka finds him and asks who has come.
Rishyasringa describes the visitor's beauty, dress and gifts to his father, and says he is pining and wants to follow her and live the same austere life.

Vibhandaka warns that the visitors were demons; Rishyasringa is lured onto the floating hermitage to the king, who gives him Santa and brings rain, and then arranges cattle and fields to appease the angry father.
The angry Vibhandaka, finding cowherds and fields that belong to his son, is appeased, sees Santa and his son, and blesses them, and Lomasa then sends Yudhishthira on to the holy lake.
Yudhishthira bathes where the Ganga meets the sea and walks along the shore toward Kalinga country.
Lomasa describes the Vaitarani river, where Rudra seized a sacrificial beast and was appeased by the gods, who then reserved a best share for him.
Yudhishthira, his brothers and Draupadi bathe in the Vaitarani and make offerings to their ancestors.
Yudhishthira marvels at the power of pious acts and hears the sound of forest dwellers reciting prayers.

Lomasa explains the far-off sound, recounts how the Earth, given to Kasyapa, rose as an altar into the sea after he appeased her, and tells Yudhishthira to recite a formula and mount it to cross the sea.
Yudhishthira completes the rites, goes into the sea, and spends the night at the skirts of Mount Mahendra.
Yudhishthira spends the night among the sages, honouring them, and asks Akritavrana when Parasurama, the descendant of Bhrigu, will appear.
Akritavrana says Rama, who knows of the visit, will appear to the sages on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, dressed in black deerskin with matted hair.
Yudhishthira asks Akritavrana to tell how Rama defeated the warriors and what caused their conflicts.

Akritavrana begins with Arjuna of the Haihayas, the thousand-armed king who oppressed the world until Vishnu was asked to kill him, and introduces Richika's marriage to Gadhi's daughter and Gadhi's demand for a dowry of horses.
Richika obtains a thousand horses from Varuna, marries Satyavati, and Bhrigu, pleased, grants a boon to the two women.
Bhrigu reveals that the pots and trees were swapped, asks that the warrior nature pass to Satyavati's grandson instead of her son, and Jamadagni is born, growing learned and gaining the arts of war.

Akritavrana recounts how Jamadagni married Renuka, how she was stirred by a king in the water and Rama beheaded her at his father's command, how Rama won a boon to restore her, and how Arjuna's sons killed Jamadagni while Rama was away, leaving Rama grieving.

Rama laments his father's death, cremates him, and vows to wipe out the warrior caste, killing Kartavirya's sons and seven times exterminating the Kshatriyas, forming five lakes of blood, then giving the earth to the priests and an altar to Kasyapa before withdrawing to Mahendra.
On the fourteenth day Rama appears to Yudhishthira and his brothers, who honour him and the Brahmanas, and after a night on Mahendra the Pandavas set out southward.

Yudhishthira bathes at sacred places along the coast, visits shrines of many gods, fasts at Prabhasa, and is then met by the Vrishnis, led by Valarama and Krishna, who weep at the sight of the Pandavas' wretched state.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what the Pandavas and the Vrishnis said and did together at Prabhasa.
Valarama, seeing Yudhishthira wretched, denounces the Kuru elders and Duryodhana's prosperity, lists each brother's heroic skills, and asks how they can bear their exile.
Satyaki urges Rama and Krishna not to lament but to march the Vrishni army at once against Dhritarashtra's sons, naming warriors such as Pradyumna, Samva and Abhimanyu, and vowing to slay Duryodhana.
Krishna agrees that the war is just, but says Yudhishthira will take sovereignty only by his own prowess, and that the Pandavas' allies should join their strength.
Heading: Section CXXI begins here.
Yudhishthira says truth comes before power, asks the Vrishnis to go home, and promises to meet them again when the time for battle comes.
The Vrishnis and Pandavas part with greetings and embraces, and Yudhishthira goes on with Lomasa to the Payosini, where Brahmanas greet him.
Lomasa describes sacrifices held by Nriga, Amurtarayasa and Gaya on the Payosini, with rich gifts to the priests, and says that a bath there brings Gaya's reward.
Yudhishthira and his brothers bathe in the Payosini, then visit the sapphire hill and the Narmada, where Lomasa names the holy places and Brahmanas receive gifts.
Lomasa says that bathing on the sapphire hill and in the Narmada brings the regions of gods and kings, and recalls Saryati's sacrifice and Chyavana's feud with Indra.
Yudhishthira asks how Chyavana paralysed Indra and how the celestial physicians came to drink Soma.

Chyavana, sitting motionless, is covered by an anthill; Sukanya pokes his eyes with thorns, the sage blocks the army's calls of nature, and Saryati, seeking the cause, asks forgiveness and is told he must give his daughter to the sage.
Saryati gives his daughter to Chyavana, who accepts her, and Sukanya attends her husband with devoted service.
The Ashvins see Sukanya bathing, ask whose daughter she is, and mock her for serving a decrepit old husband.

Sukanya refuses them, and the Ashvins offer to restore Chyavana to youth if she chooses one of them; she tells her husband, all three enter the water, and she recognizes her own husband among the identical young men.
Chyavana, now young and beautiful, promises the Ashvins that he will make them Soma-drinkers before the lord of gods, and they ascend to heaven while the couple live happily.
Saryati visits and delights in the youthful couple, Chyavana agrees to officiate, and when he prepares Soma for the Ashvins, Indra protests that the twins are mere physicians with no right to it.
Chyavana defies Indra, paralyses his arm when Indra raises the thunderbolt, and conjures a huge demon named Mada to devour the god.

Indra, terrified by Mada, agrees that the Ashvins may drink Soma; Chyavana scatters the demon among drink, women, dice and hunting; and Lomasa directs Yudhishthira to the lake, Archika hill and Yamuna sites where sages and gods worshipped.
Yudhishthira asks Lomasa how Mandhata, Yuvanaswa's son, was born and how he gained his power and name.

Lomasa tells how childless Yuvanaswa, athirst after a fast, drank the consecrated water from Bhrigu's hermitage, how a son came out of his side, how Indra's finger named him Mandhata, and how the boy grew to conquer the three worlds, perform sacrifices and end a drought.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira then asks Lomasa about Somaka.
Yudhishthira asks Lomasa about the power and deeds of King Somaka.
Lomasa tells how Somaka, with a hundred wives, has only one son, Jantu, and how an ant's sting makes the boy scream, bringing the king to the women's quarters.
Somaka laments that one son is a burden, that he is old, and asks whether any rite exists to get a hundred sons.
The family priest says that such a rite exists, if Somaka is able to perform it.
Somaka says he will do whatever the rite requires, and asks the priest to explain it.
The priest proposes that Jantu be the sacrificial victim, so that the mothers, breathing the smoke of his fat, will bear a hundred sons, and Jantu will be reborn with a golden mark.
Somaka agrees to whatever rite the priest orders, so that he may have many sons.
The mothers try to save Jantu, but the priest drags him away and sacrifices him; the mothers faint at the smoke, then all conceive, and a hundred sons are born, with Jantu the eldest.
After death Somaka sees the priest in hell and asks why; the priest explains that it is the result of officiating at the sacrifice, and Somaka asks Dharmaraja to free him.
Dharmaraja replies that no one can suffer for another's deeds, but Somaka insists on sharing the priest's fate, since their deeds are identical.
Dharmaraja agrees that Somaka may share the priest's fruit for the same time, after which both will go to the blessed regions.
Lomasa says the king and the priest worked off their sins, were freed, and shared their rewards, and he recommends six nights of self-control at this hermitage for those who seek heaven.

Lomasa names sacred sites on the Yamuna and in the Kuru field, where great rites and gifts were performed by Amvarisha, Yayati, Bharata and Marutta, and says that bathing there lets one behold all worlds.
Yudhishthira bathes with his brothers and says that through this rite he can see all the worlds, and even Arjuna, the rider of the white steed.
Lomasa confirms that the saints see all regions from here, and points to the holy Saraswati, the altar of the lord of beings and the field of the Kurus.

Lomasa names a long series of sacred places, from the Saraswati's hidden course and Vasistha's release at the Vipasa to Lopamudra's site, and ends by telling how Indra and Agni, as a hawk and a pigeon, came to test King Usinara.
The hawk demands the pigeon as food and argues that a king must not withhold it, while Usinara refuses to surrender a suppliant and offers other food or any gift except the pigeon.
Usinara offers to weigh his own flesh against the pigeon, and the hawk accepts the offer.
Usinara cuts off flesh to balance the pigeon, and when the pigeon outweighs it, he climbs onto the scale himself, having no flesh left.
Indra and Agni reveal themselves, promise Usinara lasting glory, and Usinara ascends to heaven, where holy sages and gods are seen at his old residence.
Lomasa points out the hermitage of Swetaketu, who received speech from Saraswati, and tells of Swetaketu's nephew Ashtavakra, who defeated Vandin in a contest.
Yudhishthira asks Lomasa how Ashtavakra came to be crooked in eight places and how he defeated Vandin.

Lomasa tells how Kahoda, a pupil of Uddalaka and husband of Sujata, was cursed in the womb for faulty recitation, lost a debate to Vandin and was drowned, how the family hid the truth from Ashtavakra until Swetaketu mocked him, and how the two then set out for Janaka's sacrifice.
Ashtavakra claims his right of entry at Janaka's gate, debates the gatekeeper about age and learning, challenges Vandin, and answers the king's riddles with sharp replies.
Janaka, impressed, admits the boy as a learned man rather than a child, and sends him in to meet Vandin.
Ashtavakra enters Janaka's assembly, challenges Vandin in boastful similes, and asks the king to bring Vandin before him.
Vandin and Ashtavakra take turns reciting verses that count from one up to thirteen, each naming things in the world by number.
When Vandin falters at thirteen, Ashtavakra completes the last verse, and the assembly erupts as the Brahmanas honour him.
Ashtavakra orders that Vandin be drowned as he drowned other Brahmanas, and Vandin answers that he is a son of Varuna and that his victims will return.
Ashtavakra declares that Vandin's false arguments have been defeated and calls on the assembly to judge, comparing Janaka's silence to a man stupefied by a fruit.
Janaka praises Ashtavakra and places Vandin at his disposal, but Ashtavakra insists that Vandin be drowned, and Vandin promises that Ashtavakra will see his lost father Kahoda.
Kahoda, now restored, praises his son's achievement, and Vandin praises Janaka's sacrifice as the Brahmanas rise.

Vandin enters the sea, Ashtavakra is honoured and goes home with his uncle, and at his father's word he bathes in the Samanga, where his crooked limbs are straightened; Lomasa then invites Yudhishthira to bathe there too.
Lomasa points out the Samanga, Kardamila, Vinasana and other holy sites, including where Indra was cleansed after slaying Vritra, and urges the brothers to bathe there.
Yudhishthira asks how Yavakri, son of Bharadwaja, attained Vedic learning and how he met his end.
Lomasa explains that Yavakri, grieved that his father was slighted while Raivya and his sons were honoured, undertook severe penance until Indra came and asked why.
Yavakri says he wants Vedic learning quickly through asceticism, and when Indra forbids it, he threatens to offer his own limbs to the fire unless his wish is granted.

Indra disguises himself as a feeble old Brahmana and tries to dam the Ganga with sand; Yavakri laughs at the task, and Indra points out the futility of Yavakri's own penance, so Yavakri asks for boons.
Indra grants Yavakri and his father the revelation of the Vedas and all the other boons Yavakri desires.

Yavakri tells his father of his gifts, and Bharadwaja warns that pride brings ruin, citing Medhavi, whose life was tied to a mountain and who perished when it was shattered; Yavakri promises caution but goes on insulting other sages.
Lomasa tells how Yavakri's advances lead to Raivya's anger, the two beings he makes from his hair, Yavakri's chase and death, and the demon's return to Raivya.
Bharadwaja finds the sacred fires silent, questions the Sudra, learns that Yavakri was killed, laments, curses Raivya, and dies in a blazing fire.
Vrihadyumna's sacrifice draws Raivya's two sons, and Paravasu kills his father by mistake and asks his brother to take on the vow for him.
Paravasu accuses Arvavasu of being a Brahmana-slayer, Arvavasu is driven out, and he turns to deep penance until the Sun appears to him.
The gods reward Arvavasu, make him chief priest, and grant his requests to restore the dead; Yavakri then asks why Raivya could kill him, and the gods explain.
The gods restore all of the dead and return to heaven, and Lomasa says the hermitage is a place where a person is freed from sin.
Lomasa names the mountains passed, describes the holy sites and guardian spirits ahead, and asks the gods and rivers to protect the king.
Lomasa tells Yudhishthira to be careful.
Yudhishthira tells his people to guard Krishna carefully and to keep the place clean, since Lomasa calls it hard to reach.
Yudhishthira asks Bhima to protect Krishna, since she looks to him for safety when Arjuna is away.
Yudhishthira comforts the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, with tears and tells them to proceed carefully.
Yudhishthira warns of unseen spirits and asks Bhima to take the servants back while he goes on with Nakula and Lomasa.
Bhima refuses to leave, saying he will carry Draupadi and the twins over the rough mountains.
Yudhishthira blesses Bhima for his courage and his offer to carry the others.
Draupadi, called Krishna here, says with a smile that she is able to go on.
Lomasa says Gandhamadana can be reached only through asceticism, so all of them must practise austerities to see Arjuna.
The travellers reach Suvahu's lands in the Himalayas, which Suvahu welcomes, and after leaving their servants with him they set out for the mountains.
Yudhishthira laments Arjuna's absence, recalls past losses, and proposes going with Brahmanas to Gandhamadana to seek him.
Lomasa describes the sacred Alakananda river and the holy places around Mandara, and tells the Pandavas to worship the Ganga.
Lomasa explains that a white mass in the distance is the bones of the demon Naraka, whom Vishnu killed, and mentions Vishnu's earlier rescue of the Earth.
Yudhishthira asks how Vishnu raised the sunken Earth and asks Lomasa to tell the full story.
Lomasa begins the tale: in the Krita age no creature died, the population grew, and the overburdened Earth sank and called on Narayana for help.
Vishnu becomes a one-tusked boar and lifts the Earth, the gods go to Brahma, and Brahma sends them to find Vishnu.
Lomasa says the gods, led by Brahma, praise Vishnu and then return to their own realm.
Vaisampayana says that after hearing the story, the Pandavas set out promptly along Lomasa's route.
The Pandavas pass rivers and forests toward Gandhamadana, are struck by a violent storm, shelter separately, and regroup when the rain stops.
Draupadi, unused to walking, falls to the ground exhausted by the hailstorm, and Nakula catches her and asks Yudhishthira to tend her.
Yudhishthira laments that she suffers because of his gambling losses, and blames himself for bringing her into the forest.
Dhaumya and the Brahmins recite mantras, the brothers tend Draupadi until she revives, and Bhima offers to carry the party or send for his son.
Bhima calls on his son Ghatotkacha, who appears, greets the Pandavas and Brahmins, and offers to do whatever his father asks.
Yudhishthira asks Bhima to have his son carry Draupadi, and expects to reach Gandhamadana safely with her.
Bhima tells Ghatotkacha to carry Draupadi, and Ghatotkacha says he and other Rakshasas can carry the whole company.
The party is carried over many lands to the jujube tree and the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, where the sages welcome them and the Pandavas settle in to enjoy the forest and the river.
Draupadi finds a thousand-petalled lotus and asks Bhima to find more; he sets off up the mountain, and his roars startle the animals.
