Animals scatter as Bhima slays elephants and lions, bathes in a lake, and shouts, and Hanuman lies across the path.
Hanuman, lying in a plantain grove, wakes at Bhima's approach and rebukes him for disturbing him and harming animals, urging him to turn back.
Bhima names his lineage and strength and demands passage; Hanuman refuses, and Bhima threatens to send him to Yama.
Hanuman says he is too weak to rise, Bhima fails to lift his tail, and then humbly asks who he is; Hanuman names himself and tells of Rama and Sita.
Hanuman tells how Rama's search for Sita ended in victory and return to Ayodhya, explains his own boon to live on, and says the path is closed to mortals.
Hanuman says his former form cannot be shown in this age, describes the four yugas as virtue declines, and tells Bhima to return home.
Bhima refuses to leave without seeing Hanuman's true form and asks him to show it.
Hanuman grows into a gigantic body that fills the plantain grove, so large that Bhima closes his eyes, and says he can grow larger still.
Bhima, amazed, asks Hanuman to shrink, and recalls how Hanuman alone could have destroyed Lanka.
Hanuman says he spared Ravana to protect Rama's glory, warns Bhima not to take the flowers by force, and gives a long lecture on the duties of each class and of kings.
Hanuman shrinks, embraces Bhima to restore his strength, asks him to keep the meeting secret, and offers to punish the sons of Dhritarashtra.
Bhima asks Hanuman for help in battle, Hanuman promises to roar from Arjuna's flagstaff to weaken the enemy, and then he vanishes.
Bhima walks on through forests, lakes and wild animals, reaches a river full of Saugandhika lotuses, and thinks of Draupadi waiting for them.
Bhima finds Kuvera's lotus lake near Kailasa, drinks its water, and is questioned by the armed Rakshasas who guard it.
Bhima says he is Pandu's son come for lotuses for Draupadi; the Rakshasas say he must ask Kuvera for permission, but Bhima says a Kshatriya does not beg.
Bhima plunges into the lake despite warnings, fights the Krodhavasas with his mace, and kills more than a hundred of them, forcing the rest to flee.
The beaten Rakshasas report to Kuvera, who smiles and tells them to let Bhima take as many lotuses as he likes for Krishna.
Bhima gathers the rare flowers in abundance.
Portents of battle appear; Yudhishthira follows Bhima with the others, finds the slain Yakshas, gently rebukes him, and pacifies the garden warders.
Yudhishthira lists the sacred places they have visited and asks Bhima how to reach Kuvera's abode.
An aerial voice says that place cannot be reached directly and gives a route through several hermitages; Dhaumya agrees, and they return to Nara and Narayana's hermitage.
Jatasura, a Rakshasa disguised as a Brahmana who had been a guest of the Pandavas, carries off Yudhishthira, the twins and Draupadi.
Yudhishthira rebukes the Rakshasa for breaking the order of virtue, and Sahadeva seizes back a sword and challenges him to fight.
Bhima returns, reproaches Jatasura for betraying a guest, and warns that Fate has trapped him.
Bhima and Jatasura wrestle, uprooting trees and hurling rocks, until Bhima strikes him down, breaks his limbs and beheads him, and the Brahmanas praise Bhima.
Yudhishthira reminds his brothers that Arjuna is due at Sweta in the fifth year; the company takes leave of the sages and of Vrishaparva, leaves some of its goods behind, and sets out north.
The Pandavas cross the Gandhamadana, and a long passage describes its trees, birds, lakes and minerals, which Yudhishthira praises to Bhima.
They reach Arshtishena's hermitage and are received by the sage, who is thin from long austerity.
Arshtishena welcomes Yudhishthira and asks whether he keeps to virtue, honours his parents and elders, and avoids sin; Yudhishthira says he tries to do so.
Arshtishena warns that the region beyond belongs to the gods and to Vaisravana, that trespassers are killed by Rakshasas, and asks them to stay until Arjuna comes.
Janamejaya asks how the Pandavas lived on Gandhamadana and whether Bhima fought the Yakshas and met Kuvera.
The Pandavas live on ascetic food and hear stories for years; when Suparna seizes a Naga and the wind scatters flowers, Krishna asks Bhima to drive the Rakshasas from the summit.
Stung by Draupadi's words, Bhima climbs the summit, sounds his conch, and fights the Yakshas and Rakshasas until Maniman, Kuvera's friend, falls to his mace.
Yudhishthira finds Bhima among the fallen Rakshasas and gently but firmly scolds him for an act that may offend the gods.
Yudhishthira falls silent to reflect on what Bhima has done.
The surviving Rakshasas flee to Kuvera's abode and report the slaughter; Kuvera rides out on his car with his Yakshas, and Bhima stands ready, undaunted by his wounds.
Kuvera tells Yudhishthira to stay on the summit and not blame Bhima, since the Rakshasas were already doomed by fate.
Kuvera tells Bhima he is pleased, that the deed freed him from a curse, and that Bhima bears no blame.
Yudhishthira asks why Agastya cursed Kuvera and wonders why the sage's anger did not burn Kuvera's whole host.
Kuvera recounts that at Kusasthali Maniman defiled Agastya, and the sage cursed Maniman and his followers to die at a mortal's hands, freeing Kuvera once he saw that mortal.
Kuvera tells Yudhishthira that patience, ability, timing, place and prowess bring success, praises Arjuna, and asks him to restrain Bhima's rashness.
Kuvera tells the Pandavas to live in his region, promises the Yakshas will not oppose them, and says Arjuna will soon return.
Kuvera vanishes from the mountain with his Yakshas and Rakshasas, and his horses carry him swiftly toward his abode.
Kuvera has the dead Rakshasas removed, since Agastya's curse had set the limit that ends with their death, and the Pandavas stay several nights among them.
Dhaumya points out the regions of Indra, Yama, Varuna, Brahma and Narayana around Mount Meru, and explains how the sun and moon orbit it to bring the seasons.
The Pandavas pass a month on Gandhamadana, grieving for Arjuna, who spent five years in Indra's heaven gaining celestial weapons and now returns to them.
Indra's chariot, driven by Matali, brings Arjuna down; he bows to Dhaumya, Yudhishthira, Bhima and the twins, and Matali is honoured and returns to heaven.
Arjuna gives Draupadi jewels from Indra and tells how he learned weapons from Indra, Vayu and Shiva.
After describing his time in heaven, Arjuna spends the night with the twins.
Indra arrives with heavenly music, Yudhishthira honours him, and Indra says Yudhishthira will rule the earth and should return to Kamyaka.
The narrator promises that a learned man who studies this meeting for a year will live a hundred years free of disturbance.
Yudhishthira asks Arjuna how he gained the weapons, how he served the gods, and whether they were pleased.
Arjuna relates his penances and his duel with a boar and a hunter, who is revealed as Shiva, who grants him the Pasupata weapon.
Arjuna recounts how the gods came to honour him after Shiva's blessing, how Indra invited him to heaven, and how Matali drove him there smoothly.
Arjuna describes the wonders of heaven, the gods who bless him, and his years of learning arms there, with Chitrasena as his friend.
Indra praises Arjuna's skill and asks him to pay his fee by destroying the thirty million Nivata-Kavacha Danavas who live under the ocean.
Indra gives Arjuna a chariot, a diadem, ornaments and armour and the string for the Gandiva, and the gods give him the conch Devadatta and send him off.
Arjuna reaches the ocean and the Danava city, Matali drives in, and the Nivata-Kavachas, taking him for Indra, pour out to fight while sages and gods watch.
The Nivata-Kavachas charge; Arjuna's arrows and Matali's horses cut down many, Arjuna breaks their weapons with Indra's missile, and the demons turn to illusion.
The Danavas send rock showers, floods, fire, wind and darkness; Arjuna counters them with Indra's weapons, and Matali falters until Arjuna steadies him and dispels the illusions.
Arjuna defeats the hidden Nivata-Kavachas with Indra's thunderbolt, enters their city, and hears from Matali that it once belonged to Indra.
After destroying the Danavas and taking their city, Arjuna returns with Matali to Indra's abode.
Arjuna sees the moving aerial city of Hiranyapura, and Matali explains its Danava dwellers' boons and that Brahma foretold their destruction at mortal hands.
Arjuna attacks the flying city, calls on Rudra's weapon to destroy the Danavas, watches their wives mourn, and returns to Indra, who praises him and says Yudhishthira will rule the earth.
Indra tells Arjuna no mortal can match him, names Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna and Sakuni as far weaker, and gives him armour, the conch, a garland and a diadem.
Yudhishthira rejoices at Arjuna's success and Shiva's favour, and asks to see the celestial weapons.
Arjuna promises to show all the celestial weapons the next morning.
Vaisampayana says Arjuna spent that night with his brothers after telling his story.
Arjuna displays his celestial weapons before Yudhishthira, the earth trembles, beings and gods gather, and Narada warns him against using them without cause.
The gods depart, and the Pandavas go on living in the forest with Krishna.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did with Arjuna after his return from Indra's abode.
Vaisampayana says Arjuna roamed Kuvera's gardens with his bow, and that the Pandavas spent four years there as if they were a single night.
Bhima, with Arjuna and the twins, urges Yudhishthira to leave the forest and reclaim the kingdom from Duryodhana, as their years of exile are nearly over.
Yudhishthira bids farewell to Kuvera's realm, and the brothers set out with the Brahmanas; Ghatotkacha carries them over the cascades and the sages send them off.

The brothers travel back through hermitages and Suvahu's realm, spend a year in the Visakhayupa forest where a huge snake seizes Bhima in a cave, and reach the Saraswati and Dvaitavana, where ascetics greet them.
Janamejaya asks how Bhima, who had defeated Kuvera's Yakshas, came to be struck with fear by the snake.
Bhima roams the Himalayan forests hunting, uprooting trees and roaring, until a huge snake in a cave coils around him and, by its boon, drains his strength.
Bhima asks the snake who it is and what boon lets it overpower his great strength.
The snake reveals itself as King Nahusha, Yudhishthira's ancestor, cursed by Agastya, and says it will eat Bhima; Bhima accepts destiny and grieves for his brothers and mother.
Yudhishthira sees ill omens, asks Draupadi where Bhima is, sets out with Dhaumya, and finds Bhima caught in the snake's folds in a barren cave.
Yudhishthira asks the snake to release Bhima in exchange for other food, but the snake says Bhima is the meal it has been waiting for.
The snake sets its terms: it will release Bhima if Yudhishthira answers its question about who a Brahmana is and what should be known.
Yudhishthira answers that a Brahmana has truth, charity, forgiveness and good conduct, and that the thing to know is Brahma, beyond happiness and misery.
The snake replies that these qualities also appear in Sudras, and doubts that any object exists free of happiness and misery.
Yudhishthira answers that birth alone does not make a Brahmana or a Sudra, and that no thing is free of both joy and sorrow.
The snake says that if a man is judged a Brahmana by character, caste distinctions lose their meaning.
Yudhishthira argues that caste is hard to tell in mixed society and that character defines a Brahmana, and the snake accepts that it cannot eat Bhima.
A heading marks the start of Section CLXXX.
Yudhishthira asks the snake what one should do to attain salvation.
The snake says that giving alms, speaking kindly, telling the truth and not harming any creature lead to heaven.
Yudhishthira asks which virtue is higher, and the snake says each is judged by its effects.
The snake explains that people are reborn in higher or lower forms according to their deeds, and that the wise rest in the Supreme Spirit.
Yudhishthira asks how the spirit perceives sounds, touch and taste, and the snake explains that the senses and mind serve the soul as its instruments.
Yudhishthira asks for the distinguishing marks of the mind and the intellect.
The snake says the intellect can be ruled by illusion, while the mind alone produces sensations, and explains the difference between them.
The snake admits prosperity deluded him, recounts Agastya's curse, and says Yudhishthira's wisdom has freed him, and then prepares to return to heaven.
Nahusha returns to heaven, Yudhishthira goes back to the hermitage and tells the Brahmanas, who admonish Bhima for his rashness.
A heading marks the start of the Markandeya-Samasya Parva.
The rains come and go, autumn brings clear skies, and the Pandavas celebrate the holy full moon of Kartika by the Saraswati before entering the Kamyaka forest.
Krishna arrives with Satyabhama, greets everyone, praises Yudhishthira's virtue, and offers to help regain the kingdom once the term is over.
The ageless sage Markandeya arrives and is honoured by the Brahmanas and by Krishna.
Krishna asks Markandeya to tell the old stories and rules of righteous conduct.
Narada arrives and is honoured, and Markandeya asks for a moment to prepare his teaching.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya whether human action or God controls fate, and whether deeds bear fruit in this life or the next.
Markandeya explains that deeds follow each being through rebirth, shaping happiness and misery, and that the wise attain the highest good.
Markandeya tells how a Haihaya prince killed a sage by mistake, how Tarkshya restored him, and why Brahmanas have no fear of death.
Markandeya tells how the sage Atri, wanting wealth before retiring to the forest, is urged by his wife to seek gifts from King Vainya.
Atri praises Vainya at the sacrifice, and Gautama angrily replies that Indra alone is the highest sovereign.
The sages' quarrel draws attention at the sacrifice, and Kasyapa asks the disputants what the matter is.
The Munis take the question to Sanatkumara, who rules that the king is the protector and lord of men's destinies.
Vainya, pleased with the verdict, gives Atri a hundred million gold coins and ten bharas of gold, which Atri shares with his sons before going to the forest.
Markandeya says Saraswati once answered Tarkshya's question about how a man can keep to virtue and what he should offer.
Markandeya notes that Tarkshya was eager to learn, and Saraswati begins to answer.
Saraswati says that Vedic study leads to heaven, then lists the rewards for gifts of cows, bullocks, clothes, gold and daughters, and for steady offerings to the fire.
Tarkshya asks Saraswati for the rules for keeping the sacred fire as set out in the Vedas.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to tell the history of Vaivasvata Manu.
Manu rescues a fish that grows until he takes it to the sea; the fish warns of a flood, guides Manu's boat to the Himalaya, and reveals itself as Brahma, who will recreate the world.
Markandeya says that Manu recreated the world after the flood and that hearing this story brings merit and heaven.
Yudhishthira, honouring Markandeya's long life, asks him to explain the causes of things and praises his knowledge of creation.
Markandeya praises the Lord who creates all things, gives the lengths of the four yugas and a day of Brahma, and describes the decline of the Kali age into disorder, falsehood and corrupt rule.
Markandeya describes the end of the world: drought, seven suns drying up the waters, the fire Samvartaka, and years of rain and flood.
Alone on the waters, Markandeya finds a boy resting on a banyan leaf, enters his body, sees the whole universe inside him, and asks him to explain it.
The god reveals himself as Narayana, the source of all things and the Lord in many forms, and says he showed Markandeya the universe to cure his melancholy.
Markandeya says the god he saw is Janardana, now Krishna of the Vrishni race, and urges the Pandavas to seek his protection.
The Pandavas, with Draupadi and the twins, bow to Janardana, who consoles them with gentle words.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira once more asks Markandeya about the future course of government on earth.
Yudhishthira asks what will happen in the Kali age, how men will live and eat, and when the Krita age will return.
Markandeya describes how virtue shrinks in each age, and how in the Kali age people deceive one another, castes blur, rulers and Brahmanas fail, and portents and disorder spread.
Markandeya says that after these terrible times creation begins anew, and a Brahmana named Kalki will be born to restore order and destroy the Mlecchas.
Markandeya says Kalki will destroy thieves and robbers, give the earth to the Brahmanas after a horse-sacrifice, and restore virtue in the Krita age.
Markandeya sums up the four ages, says he has told all he has seen, and urges Yudhishthira to fix his mind on virtue and never humiliate a Brahmana.
Yudhishthira asks how he should protect his subjects and keep to the duties of his order.
Markandeya advises him to be merciful, truthful, humble and devoted to his people, and to expiate his faults with charity.
Yudhishthira promises to follow the instructions, saying that he has no greed, lust, fear or pride.
The Pandavas, Krishna and the Brahmanas are filled with joy and wonder at Markandeya's teaching.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to tell the greatness of Brahmanas as Markandeya taught it.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira asked Markandeya for the greatness of Brahmanas, and Markandeya begins with King Parikshit.
King Parikshit marries a maiden who vanishes into a tank, the frog-king reveals that she is his daughter, and Parikshit's son Sala later seizes Vamadeva's horses.
Vamadeva sends a disciple to ask for the horses back, the king refuses, and Vamadeva warns that Rakshasas will punish him.
Four Rakshasas sent by Vamadeva kill Sala, Dala is set on the throne, and Vamadeva demands the horses from him.
Dala's poisoned arrow kills his son Senajita, his second arrow fails, and the queen's plea frees him from sin.
Vamadeva accepts the queen's plea, and Dala gives the Vami horses back to him with reverence.
The Rishis and Brahmanas ask Markandeya how Vaka became so long-lived.
Markandeya says Vaka's great asceticism is the reason, and that nothing more need be asked.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to recount the meeting between Vaka and Indra.
Markandeya describes Indra's rule after the war with the Asuras, the prosperity of the world, and Indra's visit on his elephant Airavata to Vaka's hermitage.
Vaka answers Indra's question about the sorrows of the immortal, naming separation from loved ones, dependence on others, and the insult of the poor by the rich.
Indra asks Vaka to describe the joys of the deathless life.
Vaka praises a simple meal eaten at home, the merit of feeding guests and Brahmanas, and the purity of a Brahmana who has been fed.
After speaking with Vaka, Indra returns to heaven.
Markandeya tells how King Suhotra and King Sivi refuse to yield the road, Narada quotes verses on virtue, and Suhotra finally gives way out of honour.
Yayati, son of Nahusha, gives a thousand cows to a Brahmana who asked for them for his teacher, saying he never boasts of or regrets a gift.
Seduka sends a Brahmana to Vrishadarbha, who had vowed to give only gold and silver; when the Brahmana asks for steeds the king whips him, then makes amends with the day's full revenue.
Agni, as a pigeon, flees to King Sivi, and Indra, as a hawk, demands it as his food; Sivi offers his own flesh until the gods reveal themselves and promise him a son.
At Ashtaka's horse-sacrifice, Narada names the king who will fall first and gives reasons for Ashtaka, Pratardana and Vasumanas.
Narada says he will fall himself, since he is not Sivi's equal, and tells how Sivi was willing to cook his son for a Brahmana who was the god Vidhatri in disguise.
Fallen from heaven, Indradyumna is passed from Markandeya to the owl, the crane and the tortoise, and the tortoise recalls his sacrifices and gifts, and a heavenly car takes him back.
Indradyumna returns to heaven with an aerial voice's praise of virtue, and Markandeya says he has witnessed this as one who lives long.
The Pandavas praise Markandeya, who says Krishna once raised King Nriga from hell to heaven.
Yudhishthira asks when and in what stage of life charity wins entry to Indra's heaven.
Markandeya lists the futile kinds of life and of gifts, such as gifts to thieves, false teachers, and those who sell the Vedas.
Yudhishthira asks how Brahmanas who accept gifts can save both others and themselves.
Markandeya says Brahmanas save others through recitation, mantras and sacrifice, names who should and should not be fed, and calls food the greatest gift.
Yudhishthira asks how far Yama's realm lies from the world of men and how one crosses the distance.
Markandeya describes Yama's road, eighty-six thousand yojanas long, where a traveller's past gifts decide his comfort, and says honouring Brahmanas pleases the gods.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to keep speaking on virtue and morality.
Markandeya says that washing a Brahmana's feet, giving a cow at birth, and giving to the virtuous bring great merit, and that a Brahmana's weapon is his anger.
Yudhishthira asks what purification keeps a Brahmana always pure.
Markandeya names three kinds of purity, says penance without a pure heart is useless, and holds that knowledge alone brings final liberation.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya about the rules of meritorious charity.
Markandeya lists the times, seasons and places when gifts earn the greatest merit, and says there is nothing higher than giving.
Vaisampayana reports Yudhishthira's request that Markandeya explain why Kuvalaswa took the name Dhundhumara, praising the sage's wide knowledge.
Vaisampayana says Markandeya then begins the story of Dhundhumara.
Utanka, after long penances, praises Vishnu, who grants his wishes and foretells that a king named Kuvalaswa will slay the demon Dhundhu.
Markandeya lists the kings of Ayodhya in order down to Kuvalaswa, who has twenty-one thousand sons, and says his father then made him king and went into the woods.
Utanka hears of the retirement and urges the king to stay and protect his people, describing the demon Dhundhu buried in a sand desert whose breath shakes the earth each year.
Vrihadaswa tells Utanka that his son Kuvalaswa will carry out the task, and then he goes off into an excellent forest.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya who the demon Dhundhu was and whose son and grandson he was.

Markandeya describes the cosmic flood, Vishnu sleeping on Sesha, and Brahma born from a lotus, until the demons Madhu and Kaitabha trouble Brahma, wake Vishnu, and ask to be slain in an uncovered place.
Vishnu finds no uncovered spot except his own thighs, and there he beheads the two demons.

Dhundhu gets Brahma's boon against being killed by gods or demons, then lies under the sands; when Kuvalaswa and his sons come against him, the demon burns the sons until the king's water douses the fire and he kills him with the Brahma weapon.
Markandeya concludes that the king took the name Dhundhumara from this victory and that the name was truly earned.
Markandeya closes by saying that hearing this story brings virtue, children, long life and freedom from disease.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to explain the virtue of chaste women, the duties of sons to their parents, and the duties of the Kshatriya order.
Markandeya agrees to answer, says a mother's burden is the greater, and explains that parents hope their sons will bring fame and virtue, while a wife finds heaven only by serving her husband.
A heading marking the start of the next section, Section CCV.
Kausika, a learned Brahmana, angrily glares at a crane that has fouled him from a tree, and when she falls dead he laments the deed.
Kausika goes on his alms round and calls at a house he knows, where a housewife tells him to wait while she tends her hungry husband.
The housewife remembers that she told him to wait, brings him alms, and Kausika rebukes her for keeping him waiting.
The wife pleads for forgiveness, says serving her husband is her highest duty, and sends the Brahmana to a truthful fowler in Mithila to learn true virtue.
Kausika, now calm, thanks her for the rebuke and says he will go on to do what is good for him.
Markandeya says that Kausika, dismissed by her, left the house and returned to his own home, reproaching himself.
Kausika, reflecting on the woman's words, travels to Mithila and finds the fowler selling meat in a butcher's yard, who greets him and knows why he has come.
The fowler defends his hereditary trade, describes the duties of each class and King Janaka's just rule, and gives moral teaching on honesty, repentance and the hidden faults of the wicked.
Kausika asks how to recognise virtuous conduct, and the fowler lists its marks, including sacrifice, gift, asceticism, study of the Vedas and truth.
The fowler argues that Destiny makes his trade unavoidable, that meat offered to gods and ancestors is lawful, and that every creature harms other life, so no one is blameless.
The fowler says that right conduct is subtle, that fortune, misfortune and disease follow from past karma, and that the body perishes while the soul goes on.

Kausika asks how the soul is eternal, and the fowler explains rebirth by deeds, the paths of the virtuous and the sinful, and liberation through wisdom and restraint, before Kausika asks what the senses are.

The fowler explains how desire, envy and greed lead a man from learning into sin, contrasts the wise man who resists them, and then begins to list the elements, qualities and principles of the universe.

The fowler lists the qualities that belong to each of the five elements, distinguishes the perceptible from the imperceptible, and compares the self-controlled man to a charioteer who holds his unruly senses in check.
The fowler defines tamas, rajas and sattwa by their marks and concludes that a man of good qualities can rise from the Sudra caste to a higher one.

The fowler explains how the vital airs and inner heat sustain the body, describes the soul as the Supreme Spirit reached by yogins, and then urges self-control, renunciation and non-violence as the way to liberation.
The fowler leads the Brahmana into his fine house to meet his aged parents, and explains that he serves them as gods, bathing and feeding them and speaking only pleasant words.

The fowler says the Brahmana was sent to him by the lady, scolds him for leaving his grieving parents to study without permission, and urges him to go home; the Brahmana thanks him and asks why such a virtuous man is a fowler.
The fowler reveals that he was once a Brahmana who, while hunting deer with a king, accidentally struck a sage, and the sage cursed him to be a fowler in the Sudra class.
The fowler recounts that the sage, sparing him, promised he would stay pious and regain Brahmana status, and the Brahmana replies that a man's character, not his birth, makes him a Brahmana.
The fowler teaches that bodily ills need medicine and grief needs knowledge, and that contentment is the highest happiness, and the Brahmana praises him and takes his leave.
Markandeya says the Brahmana went home to care for his parents, and Yudhishthira declares he is not yet satisfied with the teaching.

Yudhishthira asks why the fire-god hid in water, why Angiras acted as fire, and how Kumara came to be called Agni's son, and Markandeya tells how Angiras persuaded the depressed Agni to resume his place and fathered Vrihaspati.
Markandeya names Angiras's son Vrihaspati and his several daughters, explaining how each got her name from a trait such as beauty, brightness or accepting oblations.
Markandeya names Vrihaspati's sons by Tara, each a fire with its own sacrificial role, and Swaha's three sons, linked to the three qualities.

After Uktha's long penance, a radiant being with five colours arises from the sacred fires and five sages, and goes on to create the fire of the manes, day and night, many beings, and fifteen gods who obstruct sacrifices unless they are appeased.

Markandeya lists more fire-gods, from Bharata and Siva to Bhanu's six sons, and then prescribes the rites that set right the sacred fire when it is disturbed, such as contact with a woman in her monthly course or the presence of death.

Markandeya tells how the fire Swaha hid in the sea to avoid defilement, and how the sage Atharvan, who carried the oblations, gave up his body, which yielded metals and woods, until Atharvan restored the fire.
Markandeya names a long list of rivers as the mothers of the fires, and says that all the fires are one, arising from Brahma's spirit and from the sage Atri.

Markandeya introduces Kartikeya's story and tells how Indra, seeking a leader for the gods, rescues a woman from the Asura Kesin in the Manasa mountains, cutting down his mace and rock with his thunderbolt.
Devasena, daughter of Prajapati, says her sister was carried off by Kesin and asks Indra to find her a husband who is devoted to Brahma and able to conquer every class of being.

Indra reads omens in the conjunction of Sun, Moon and Agni and goes to Brahma, who approves; meanwhile the fire Adbhuta, seeing the Rishis' wives, is struck by desire and resolves to look at them only as his household fire.
Frustrated and lovesick, the Adbhuta fire goes into a forest to die, and Swaha, who loves him, plans to take the form of the seven Rishis' wives to win him.
Swaha, in the disguise of Siva, wife of Angiras, approaches Agni, declares her love, and says she was sent by the wives of the other Rishis.
Agni asks how she knew of his love, and how the Rishis' wives could have known it.
Swaha replies that the wives read his mind by signs and sent her, and urges him to act quickly because her sisters-in-law are waiting.
Agni, delighted, marries Swaha in Siva's guise, and she then decides to take a bird's form so that no one will slander the Brahmana ladies.

Swaha flies to the White Mountain, throws Agni's seed into a golden lake, and a six-faced child, Skanda, is born, grows quickly, and fights and tears a mountain, leaving the gods and creatures to seek his protection.
The birth brings strange omens, Swaha reveals to Skanda that she is his mother, and the seven Rishis divorce six of their wives, keeping only Arundhati.
Viswamitra, who had followed Agni, tells the Rishis their wives are innocent, performs the child's rites, and promotes Skanda's worship, though the Rishis still abandon their spouses.
The gods urge Indra to kill Skanda, but he hesitates, and the Mothers, awed by the child's power, adopt him and nurse him while Agni comes disguised as a trader with toys.
Indra and the gods advance against Skanda, whose fiery breath burns the forces, and when the gods desert Indra he hurls his thunderbolt, from which a new being named Visakha springs.
The wound gives rise to a host of followers, including Bhadrasakha, and the seven Mothers and their son Sisu are named, which is why Skanda is called father of the Kumaras.
Skanda's beauty and good fortune are described, and the Maharshis urge him to become Indra, lord of the three worlds.
Indra offers to anoint Skanda as lord that very day.
Skanda declines the sovereignty and says he would rather serve as Indra's humble servant.
Indra explains that if he stepped aside, the gods would split into factions and war would follow, which Skanda would surely win.
Skanda replies that Indra remains his sovereign and asks what commands he is to obey.
Indra asks Skanda to take up leadership of the celestial forces, if that is truly what he wishes.
Skanda asks to be anointed leader for the destruction of the Danavas, the good of the gods, and the protection of cows and Brahmanas.
Skanda is anointed by Indra and the gods, Rudra gives him a golden wreath, and Markandeya explains why he is called the son of Rudra.
Skanda is dressed in red with a red cock as his emblem, and his inborn virtues, including devotion to Brahmanas, are listed as the gods rejoice.
Indra brings Devasena, whom he had rescued, and she is married to Skanda, and the fifth and sixth days of the lunar month are named after his anointing and victory.
The six Rishis' wives, cast out on a rumour, come to Skanda and ask him to adopt them and clear their name.
Skanda agrees to accept them as his mothers and promises them their desires.
Indra notes that the star Abhijit has left its place and that Krittika must fill it, and Vinata asks Skanda to honour her as a son.
Skanda agrees to honour Vinata as a mother, and says she will live with him.
The great Mothers say they are already mothers of all creatures, but want to be Skanda's mothers too and asks him to honour them.
Skanda tells the Mothers they are all his mothers and asks what he can do to please them.
The Mothers ask to replace the earlier mother goddesses in worship and to recover the offspring taken from them.
Skanda refuses to return what was given away, but offers other offspring instead.
The Mothers ask to live with Skanda and devour the offspring of rival mothers and their guardians.
Skanda grants them progeny, but asks them to protect the children and calls the topic painful.
The Mothers agree to protect the children as Skanda asks, and ask to stay with him always.
Skanda says the Mothers shall afflict children until their sixteenth year, and that they will be worshipped with a fierce spirit.
Markandeya lists the evil spirits that trouble children and the unborn until age sixteen, including the Skandapasmara and the Mothers Putana, Revati and Sarama, and says they are appeased by worship.

Markandeya lists the spirits that drive men mad after sixteen, including the celestial, ancestral, Siddha, Rakshasa, Gandharva, Pisacha and Yaksha spirits, and says that self-controlled men are free from them.
Swaha, having been given these powers, appears before Skanda, calls him her natural son, and asks him to grant her happiness.
Skanda asks what kind of happiness she wishes.
Swaha says she has loved the Fire-god since her youth and asks to live forever with him as his wife.
Skanda decrees that offerings made through Agni will carry Swaha's name, so she will always be joined with him.
Pleased, Swaha honours Skanda in return, along with her husband Agni.
Brahma tells Skanda to visit his father Mahadeva, explaining that Rudra and Agni, Uma and Swaha made him invincible and that his fierce followers came from Rudra's seed.

Markandeya describes how the five classes of spirits should be worshipped, gives the origin of Skanda's two bells and red banners, and pictures the White Mountain full of gods and celestial creatures.
Mahadeva and Parvati set out in a lion-drawn chariot, with the gods, spirits and celestial powers marching in a great procession, and Pingala leads as standard-bearer.
Skanda, leader of the army, follows Mahadeva, who asks him to command the seventh corps.
Skanda accepts the command and asks whether anything else needs doing.
Rudra tells Skanda that he will always find him on the field of action, and that devotion to him brings welfare.
Maheswara embraces Skanda and sends him off, and then prodigies disturb the gods.
Terrible omens appear, a vast Asura host attacks the celestial army with weapons and rocks, and Indra rallies the wavering gods.
Encouraged by Indra, the gods charge the Danavas and inflict heavy losses, but the Danavas soon regain the upper hand.
The Danava Mahisha crushes ten thousand gods with a rock and seizes Rudra's chariot, and Skanda rushes in and cuts off Mahisha's head with his spear.
Skanda's spear returns to his hand after killing thousands, his followers devour the Danavas, Indra praises him, and the reader of this story is promised prosperity.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya for the different names by which Skanda is known across the three worlds.
Markandeya lists more than fifty names of Kartikeya, each with a meaning, and says that reciting them brings fame, wealth and salvation.
Markandeya prays to Guha, calling him devoted to Brahma, the six-flamed fire, the seasons and the universe, and many other names and forms.
Markandeya promises that whoever reads, tells or hears this story of Skanda's birth gains wealth, long life, children, victory and Skanda's companionship.
A heading naming the section as the dialogue between Draupadi and Satyabhama.
Vaisampayana describes Draupadi and Satyabhama meeting after a long time, and Satyabhama asks how Draupadi keeps the Pandavas so obedient, listing possible charms, drugs or vows.

Draupadi calls such charms the practice of wicked women, describes her humble service to her husbands and to Kunti, and lists how she manages the palace servants, the feeding of Brahmanas and the treasury.
Satyabhama asks Draupadi's forgiveness for her jest, saying such talk arises naturally among friends.

Draupadi advises Satyabhama to win Krishna through devoted, humble service and discretion, such as rising promptly to greet him, keeping his secrets, avoiding his enemies, and adorning herself for him.

Krishna takes leave of the Pandavas and the Brahmanas, and Satyabhama comforts Draupadi, foreseeing the Pandavas' return to power and the ruin of the Kuru sons, and reporting that the Pandava sons are well in Dwaraka.
Satyabhama circles Draupadi, mounts Krishna's car, and Krishna, comforting Draupadi with a smile, returns with her to his own city.
A heading naming the section as the Ghosha-yatra Parva.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after reaching the Dwaita lake and enduring the heat and cold of the forest.
The Pandavas settle in the Dwaita forest, a talkative Brahmana carries news of their misery to Dhritarashtra, and the king laments their hardships at length, blaming fate and his own role.
Sakuni, son of Suvala, tells Duryodhana in private what the king said, and Duryodhana, though foolish, is grieved.
Sakuni, with Karna's support, urges Duryodhana to rule without rival and go to see the Pandavas at Dwaitavana, displaying his prosperity to their suffering.
Vaisampayana says that Karna and Sakuni fell silent after their speech was over.
Duryodhana is pleased by Karna's words, but doubts his father will allow him to visit the Pandavas, and says he longs to see them humbled in the woods.
Karna proposes that they go to Dwaitavana under the pretext of supervising the royal cattle stations, and Sakuni agrees that this will work.
The three laugh together, shake hands, and go to see the king.
The three greet Dhritarashtra, a cowherd named Samanga speaks of the cattle, and Karna and Sakuni ask leave for Duryodhana to inspect the herds and go hunting.
Dhritarashtra warns that the Pandavas are near the cattle stations and that their anger and Draupadi's power could injure the Kauravas, so he advises that Duryodhana should not go himself.
Sakuni reassures the king that Yudhishthira will not be angry and that the Kauravas have no wish to meet the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra reluctantly permits the trip, and Duryodhana sets out with a large host and camps four miles from the lake.
Duryodhana inspects and marks his cattle at the stations, and then enjoys songs, dances and generous gifts with his attendants and ladies.

He hunts widely and reaches the lake where Yudhishthira is performing a daily rite with Draupadi, but when his men try to enter, Gandharvas under Chitrasena block the way and mock the Kuru messengers, who turn back.
A heading marking the start of Section CCXXXIX.

Duryodhana orders an attack, the Kuru army charges into the forest, Chitrasena's Gandharvas rush at them, and the Kuru army flees, leaving only Karna to slaughter many before the Gandharvas overwhelm the field.
Chitrasena uses illusions to overpower the Kauravas, only Karna, Duryodhana and Sakuni keep fighting, and the Gandharvas break Karna's chariot until he escapes on Vikarna's car.
After the rout Duryodhana is captured by Chitrasena, Dussasana and others are seized, the royal ladies are taken, and the fleeing soldiers appeal to the Pandavas to rescue the captives.
Bhima, speaking sarcastically, says the Kauravas are now paying the price of their deceit, and insists the Pandavas are not wicked.
Yudhishthira reproves Bhima, saying this is not the time for cruel words.
Yudhishthira rebukes Bhima and urges his brothers to rescue Duryodhana and defend the honour of the family, first by conciliation and then by force if necessary.
Arjuna pledges to free the Kauravas or make the earth drink the Gandharva king's blood, and the Kauravas regain their spirit.
The Pandavas arm in gold-trimmed mail and march to the Gandharvas, and when Arjuna asks them to free Duryodhana, they refuse, saying they obey only Indra, and battle begins.

The Pandavas battle the Gandharvas, Arjuna's weapons slaughter thousands and trap those carrying the Kauravas, and when Chitrasena hides by illusion Arjuna reveals him, and Chitrasena announces himself as Arjuna's friend, ending the battle.
Arjuna asks Chitrasena why he has punished the Kauravas, and why Duryodhana and his wives were seized.
Chitrasena explains that Duryodhana and Karna came to mock the exiles, and that Indra ordered him to bring Duryodhana back in chains.
Arjuna asks Chitrasena to free Duryodhana, since he is their brother.
Chitrasena refuses, calling Duryodhana a vain and deceitful wretch, and says Yudhishthira must hear the whole matter first.
The Gandharvas and Pandavas go to Yudhishthira, who frees the Kauravas, praises the Gandharvas, and asks what he can do in return.
The Gandharvas leave with the Apsaras, Indra revives the slain Gandharvas, and Yudhishthira warns Duryodhana never to act rashly again and sends him home.
Duryodhana sets off for his capital in shame and despair, and Yudhishthira stays in the Dwaita woods, honoured by the Brahmanas.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to describe how the proud and shamed Duryodhana entered his capital after his defeat and rescue.
Duryodhana sets out in shame, camps, and at night Karna congratulates him on his survival and the brothers' victory, while admitting he himself fled the battle.
Vaisampayana says Duryodhana replied to Karna in a voice choked with tears.

Duryodhana tells Karna that the Gandharvas, using illusions, captured the Kauravas, that the soldiers appealed to the Pandavas, and that Yudhishthira ordered his brothers to free them, after which Chitrasena and Arjuna embraced and the Gandharvas laid down their arms.
Duryodhana recalls how Chitrasena revealed their plan to mock the Pandavas, how they were handed over in chains, and, in shame, resolves to fast to death rather than return to his city.
Duryodhana offers the kingship to Dussasana, who refuses in tears and begs him to relent, and Dussasana vows he will never rule without his brother.
Karna scolds the brothers for weeping, says the Pandavas were only doing their duty, and urges Duryodhana to return to the city and console his brothers.
Karna calls Duryodhana's grief childish, says the Pandavas were bound to rescue him as subjects of the king, urges him to rise, and warns that self-starvation would make him a laughing-stock.
Vaisampayana says Duryodhana, firmly resolved to leave the world, would not rise from where he sat.
Sakuni tells Duryodhana that Karna's words are wise, that his grief is foolish, and urges him to return the kingdom to the Pandavas and make peace.
Duryodhana, seeing Dussasana lying prostrate in grief, refuses all counsel and resolves to die by fasting.
His friends reply that they will not enter the city without him.
Duryodhana spreads kusa grass, sits down in rags, and begins his fast in silent prayer.
The Danavas, fearing that Duryodhana's death would weaken them, hold a fire rite, and a goddess carries the king to the nether world, where the Danavas flatter him.

The Danavas urge Duryodhana to give up his fast, saying he is of celestial origin, that demon-possessed warriors will side with him, and that Karna, possessed by the soul of Naraka, and the Samsaptakas will slay Arjuna.
The Danavas embrace Duryodhana and send him back, where he takes it all for a dream, and the Danavas' influence makes Bhishma, Drona and Kripa less friendly to the Pandavas.
Karna urges Duryodhana to rise and vows to defeat Arjuna within thirteen years, and Duryodhana rises and marches with his army back to the city.
Janamejaya asks what the sons of Dhritarashtra, Karna, Sakuni, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa did while the Pandavas lived in the forest.
Bhishma rebukes Duryodhana for his journey to the forest and his capture, notes that Karna fled from the Gandharvas, and urges peace with the Pandavas.
Duryodhana laughs and walks off, Bhishma goes home ashamed, and Karna vows to conquer the earth alone and show Bhishma his might.
Duryodhana is delighted by Karna's vow, and Karna sets out on an auspicious day with a rattling chariot that fills the three worlds with noise.

Karna besieges Drupada's city, forces him to pay tribute, and then conquers the north, the east, the south and the west, including the Yavanas, before returning to Hastinapura, where Duryodhana honours him.

The city erupts in comment, some praising Karna and some censuring him, and after Karna bows to Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, who embrace him, Duryodhana and Sakuni begin to think the Pandavas already beaten.
Karna tells Duryodhana that the earth is rid of enemies, and urges him to rule it like Indra.
Duryodhana says he wishes to hold the Rajasuya sacrifice that the Pandavas performed, and Karna urges him to summon the Brahmanas and gather the materials.
The priest refuses the Rajasuya, since Yudhishthira and Dhritarashtra are alive, and proposes the Vaishnava sacrifice, to be ploughed with gold from the tribute.
Duryodhana and his brothers agree, and the king orders craftsmen to build the sacrificial plough.
The sacrifice begins with its rites, and Dussasana sends a messenger to the Pandavas in the Dwaita forest to invite them to witness it.
Yudhishthira says he cannot attend until his vow of exile ends, Bhima answers with a threat against Duryodhana, and Vidura looks after the many guests who arrive.
The citizens praise Duryodhana's sacrifice, some compare it unfavourably with Yudhishthira's, and Karna vows he will not wash his feet or eat meat until he has slain Arjuna.
Spies report Karna's vow to kill Arjuna, the Pandavas grow anxious, and Yudhishthira resolves to leave the Dwaita woods.
Duryodhana rules with his brothers and his elders, giving generously to Brahmanas, because he believes that giving and enjoying are the only uses of wealth.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did in the forest after Duryodhana was rescued.
Yudhishthira dreams that the surviving deer ask him to leave the forest, he is moved by pity, and the Pandavas set out for the Kamyaka forest near Lake Trinavindu.
The Pandavas spend eleven years in misery, and Yudhishthira, blaming himself for their suffering, cannot sleep, while the brothers are changed by rage and hope.
The sage Vyasa visits, and seeing his grandsons thin and wasted in the forest, teaches that happiness and sorrow alternate and that asceticism and virtue bring merit.
Yudhishthira asks which practice is more fruitful in the next world, charity or asceticism.
Vyasa says charity is the hardest discipline, that even a small gift given purely is greatly rewarded, and begins the story of Mudgala's gift of a drona of corn.
Yudhishthira asks why and to whom Mudgala gave a drona of corn, and what makes a life bear fruit.
Vyasa describes Mudgala, a sage in Kurukshetra who lives by gleaning and feeds his guests, whose grain multiplies with each pure gift.
The fierce sage Durvasa visits Mudgala repeatedly, eating his food and smearing himself with the leftovers, but Mudgala stays calm, generous and steady.
A celestial messenger arrives with a swan-drawn chariot and tells Mudgala that he has earned his place in heaven.
Mudgala asks the messenger about the austerities, purposes and pleasures of heaven and what drawbacks it has before he ascends.
The messenger describes the bliss of heaven, its regions and gardens, and the higher worlds of Brahma and the Ribhus, where desire and grief are absent.
The messenger describes the drawbacks of heaven, where one must exhaust one's merit and then fall, with regret and fear.

Mudgala rejects heaven, the messenger describes Vishnu's supreme seat, and Mudgala attains liberation; Vyasa then tells Yudhishthira that happiness and misery alternate and that his kingdom will return after thirteen years.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa went back to his hermitage to perform austerities.
Janamejaya asks how Duryodhana and his counsellors treated the Pandavas in the forest.
Duryodhana plots against the Pandavas with Karna and Dussasana, and Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples and tests the prince, who serves him patiently.
Duryodhana asks Durvasa to visit Yudhishthira after Draupadi has eaten, and the sage agrees, while Karna and the prince rejoice that the Pandavas will suffer.
Duryodhana and his companions return home, pleased with their scheme.
A heading naming the section as the Draupadi-harana Parva.
Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples at a time when Draupadi has eaten, and Yudhishthira welcomes him and asks him to return after his bath.
Draupadi, worried that no food is left, prays to Krishna, who comes, eats the last grain stuck to the sun-given vessel, and sends Bhima to invite the sages.
The sages, feeling full after bathing, fear the Pandavas' wrath and flee, and Krishna appears to tell the Pandavas they need not fear Durvasa.
The Pandavas, relieved, thank Krishna, who departs for his capital, while they continue their wanderings with Draupadi, and the Kauravas' plot is defeated.
The Pandavas hunt in the Kamyaka forest, leaving Draupadi alone at the hermitage, when Jayadratha sees her, is struck with desire, and sends Kotika to ask who she is.
Kotika asks Draupadi who she is, guesses at divine origins, and names his companions, including Kshemankara of Trigarta and Jayadratha of Sauvira, with his chariots and standard-bearers.

Draupadi answers Kotika, introduces herself as Drupada's daughter and the wife of the five Pandavas, who have gone hunting in the four directions, and invites the visitors to dismount and wait to be welcomed.
Kotika tells Jayadratha that the lady is Drupada's daughter and the wife of the five Pandavas, and Jayadratha, captivated, tells him to take her to Sauvira.
Jayadratha enters the hermitage, and after Draupadi offers him food and a seat, he urges her to abandon the ruined Pandavas and share his kingdoms of Sindhu and Sauvira.
Draupadi withdraws with contempt, warns him sharply to be careful, and waits for her husbands to return.
Draupadi, furious, rebukes Jayadratha for insulting the Pandavas and compares his folly to provoking lions and venomous snakes.
Jayadratha replies that he is not frightened, that his clan is noble, and orders Draupadi onto his chariot or to beg mercy of the Sauvira king.
Draupadi replies that Arjuna, Bhima and the Vrishni and Andhaka warriors will come after her, and that Jayadratha will have cause to regret his deed.
Jayadratha seizes Draupadi, who pushes him down and calls for Dhaumya, and the ravisher drags her to his chariot, while Dhaumya warns that he will pay for this deed.
Dhaumya follows the ravisher's infantry as Draupadi is carried off.

The Pandavas return from hunting, Yudhishthira reads omens of an invasion, and at the hermitage Draupadi's maid Dhatreyika tells Indrasena that Jayadratha has carried Draupadi away, urging them to pursue.
Yudhishthira tells the maid to be silent, warning that princes and kings who are drunk with power come to grief.
The brothers follow the tracks, see the dust of Jayadratha's army and Dhaumya among the infantry, and rush at the enemy in fury, causing them to lose their bearings.

Jayadratha asks Draupadi to name her husbands, and she describes each Pandava, from Yudhishthira's virtue to Bhima's vengeance, Arjuna's skill and the twins' gifts, and warns that his men will not survive.
The five brothers, enraged, leave the panic-stricken infantry and attack the charioteers, darkening the air with a thick shower of arrows.

The Pandavas attack the Sindhu army and cut down its warriors, Yudhishthira is wounded and his horses slain, Jayadratha flees leaving Draupadi behind, and Arjuna urges Bhima to seek Jayadratha instead of slaughtering the rest.
Bhima vows he will not let Jayadratha live, and Yudhishthira asks him to spare the king for the sake of their sister Dussala and Gandhari.
Draupadi, incensed, urges Bhima and Arjuna to slay the mean wretch, and the brothers go in search of him, while Yudhishthira returns to the hermitage with Draupadi.
Arjuna kills Jayadratha's horses and overtakes the fleeing king, rebuking him for his cowardice, and Bhima catches up with him, though Arjuna asks that he not be killed.

Bhima seizes Jayadratha, humiliates him, and forces him to declare himself a slave of the Pandavas, and Yudhishthira frees him with a rebuke, after which Jayadratha obtains a limited boon from Shiva, who explains Arjuna's divine power and recounts Vishnu's incarnations.
Shiva vanishes with Uma from the place, and the wicked Jayadratha returns home, while the Pandavas continue to dwell in the forest of Kamyaka.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after Draupadi's abduction.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya whether anyone has suffered as he has, noting that Draupadi was innocent, that Jayadratha was punished, and that their life in the forest is full of hardship.
Markandeya says that Rama also suffered when Ravana carried off Sita, and that Rama recovered her with Sugriva's help, bridging the sea and burning Lanka.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya about Rama's family and might, and about Ravana's ancestry and quarrel with Rama.
Markandeya begins the tale, naming Rama's royal line and his brothers, and then tells of the birth of Sita and of Ravana's ancestors, Pulastya and Visrava.
Visrava's Rakshasa wives bear him sons, including Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Vibhishana, Khara and Surpanakha, and Ravana's penance wins Brahma's promise that only men may harm him.
Brahma grants Kumbhakarna long sleep and Vibhishana immortality, because Vibhishana's soul is inclined to righteousness even though he was born a Rakshasa.
Ravana defeats Kubera, takes Lanka and the Pushpaka chariot, and Kubera curses him that the chariot will bear the man who slays him.

Vibhishana follows Kubera and is given command of the Yakshas and Rakshasas, while Ravana, granted supremacy by the Rakshasas, attacks the gods and Daityas and earns the name Ravana for terrifying all creatures.
The sages and gods, led by Agni, beg Brahma to protect them from the Ten-headed Ravana, who cannot be slain by gods or demons because of his boon.
Brahma replies that Ravana's death is near, that he has arranged it, and that Vishnu will achieve it.
Brahma orders the gods to beget monkey and bear sons as Vishnu's allies, and sends a Gandharva woman to be born as the hunchback Manthara to stir up quarrels.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya why Rama, Lakshmana and Sita went to the forest in exile.
Markandeya describes Rama's skill and virtues, and Dasaratha, pleased with his son, plans to install him as regent at an auspicious hour.
Kaikeyi's maid Manthara tells her mistress that Rama's coronation is a disaster for Bharata and that Kausalya will be the happy one.

Kaikeyi holds Dasaratha to his promise and demands that Bharata be made king and Rama exiled for fourteen years, Rama leaves with Lakshmana and Sita, Dasaratha dies, Bharata refuses the throne and rules with Rama's sandals, and Rama destroys the Rakshasas Khara and Dushana in Dandaka.
Surpanakha, her face mutilated, goes to Ravana, who vows revenge, and after making arrangements for his capital he flies to Gokarna to meet his old friend Maricha.
Ravana visits Maricha, who warns him against Rama, but Ravana threatens him with death and orders him to lure Sita in the form of a golden deer.
Ravana disguises himself as an ascetic and Maricha as a deer; Sita sends Rama after it, Rama kills the Rakshasa, who cries out in Rama's voice, and Sita angrily sends Lakshmana to help.
Ravana, disguised as a hermit, approaches Sita, who refuses him, and he seizes her and flies off with her, while the vulture Jatayu watches.
The vulture Jatayu, a friend of Dasaratha, attacks Ravana to free Sita, is cut down when Ravana severs his wings, and Sita drops her ornaments and a cloth among five monkeys as Ravana flies to Lanka.

Rama returns, reproaches Lakshmana for leaving Sita, learns of her abduction, and finds the dying Jatayu, who points south; Rama and Lakshmana then slay a headless Rakshasa, who turns out to be a Gandharva cursed by a Brahmana and directs them to Sugriva at Pampa.

Rama grieves at Pampa, Lakshmana rouses him, and the brothers reach Rishyamuka and make an alliance with Sugriva; Rama shoots Vali, Sugriva regains his kingdom and Tara, and Rama stays four months on the Malyavat hill.

Ravana keeps Sita in an Asoka grove guarded by Rakshasa women; she says she would rather die than live without Rama, and Trijata reassures her with a message that Rama is allied with Sugriva and will come, and with a dream of Ravana's downfall.
Heading marking the start of the next section, CCLXXIX.

Ravana approaches Sita in the grove, lists his wealth, servants and descent and offers her the place of queen; Sita rejects him, cries, and reproaches him for disgracing his brother; Ravana vanishes, and Sita stays grieving with Trijata.
Rama, awake on the hill and troubled by thoughts of Sita, sends Lakshmana to Kishkindhya to hold Sugriva to his word, and Sugriva replies that his monkeys are searching every land.
Lakshmana brings Sugriva back to Rama, the searchers from the north, east and west return empty-handed, and Rama keeps his hope on the southern party.

Hanuman tells how the southern party crossed a cave, met an ascetic woman, learned of Jatayu from his brother Sampati, and how Hanuman crossed the sea, found Sita in Lanka, gave her Rama's message, took a jewel from her as proof, and set fire to the city.

Monkey and bear chiefs gather from many regions, the army marches to the southern sea, and after Rama prays to the Ocean, the Ocean lets Nala build a bridge of floating materials that is still called Nala's bridge.

Vibhishana comes to Rama and is made king of the Rakshasas, the army crosses on the bridge and damages Lanka's gardens, two of Ravana's spies are seized and sent back, and Rama sends Angada to Ravana as envoy.
Rama's army settles in the groves, Ravana builds layered defenses around Lanka, and Angada enters, delivers Rama's defiant message, is seized by four Rakshasas, leaps free, and returns to Rama.
Rama's army breaks down the ramparts, Lakshmana breaches the southern gate, and the monkeys and bears swarm over the walls until the city's guards flee.
Ravana sends out Rakshasas in great numbers, the battle becomes fierce on the walls, Rama and Lakshmana shoot down many enemies, and the monkeys withdraw after damaging the city's defenses.

Ravana's lesser demons sneak into the monkey camp invisibly, Vibhishana breaks their spell, they are killed, and Ravana forms his army for a general battle in which Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva and others each take on a chosen opponent.
Prahasta is killed by Vibhishana, Hanuman defeats and kills Dhumraksha after the monkeys rally, and Ravana wakes Kumbhakarna and sends him, with Vajravega and Promathin, into battle.

Kumbhakarna eats several monkey leaders and grabs Sugriva, until Lakshmana's arrows, the growing arms and a Brahma weapon bring him down, and then Hanuman and Nala kill his brothers Vajravega and Promathin.

Ravana urges Indrajit to kill Rama, Sugriva and Lakshmana, Indrajit duels Lakshmana and Angada until Angada wrecks his chariot, and Indrajit vanishes by illusion and shoots Rama and Lakshmana until they fall.

Indrajit binds the brothers in a net of arrows, Vibhishana revives them with a weapon, Sugriva pulls out the arrows with healing medicine, and Vibhishana gives them and the monkeys water from Kuvera that lets them see invisible creatures.

Indrajit returns and Lakshmana, guided by Vibhishana, kills him with three arrows and then kills his charioteer; Ravana, grieving, rushes at Sita with a sword, Avindhya argues him out of it, and Ravana sets out to fight.
Ravana's illusions fail, Matali brings Indra's chariot, and Rama fires a Brahma weapon that burns Ravana to nothing.
The gods and sages honor Rama and celebrate after Ravana is slain.

Rama gives Lanka to Vibhishana, then harshly doubts Sita's chastity; Sita calls on the elements to witness her innocence, and the gods, including Brahma and Dasaratha, declare her pure and urge Rama to take her back.
Dasaratha tells Rama the fourteen years of exile are over, Rama rewards Avindhya and Trijata, asks Brahma to restore the slain monkeys to life, and Sita blesses Hanuman with long life.

The gods leave, Rama flies home on the Pushpaka with Sita and his allies, installs Angada as prince-regent, is reunited with Bharata, is crowned at Ayodhya, sends his allies home, returns the chariot, and performs ten horse-sacrifices.

Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Rama also suffered, that a warrior must act rather than mourn, and that his brothers and allies such as Dhananjaya, Bhima and the twins make victory likely, so he should not grieve.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira was comforted and then spoke again to Markandeya.
Heading marking the Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, a section on the glory of devoted wives.
Yudhishthira says he grieves most for Draupadi, who saved them at the dice game and was carried off by Jayadratha, and asks whether Markandeya has known a more faithful lady.
Markandeya tells how King Aswapati of the Madras, without children, prayed for eighteen years, and the goddess Savitri promised him a daughter.
The daughter is born to the king's eldest queen, is named Savitri, and grows so beautiful that no suitor dares ask for her hand.
Aswapati tells his grown daughter to find her own husband, warning that a father who does not give his daughter in marriage falls into disgrace.
Savitri, with her father's old counsellors, travels to the forest hermitages, serves the elders and gives gifts at holy places in her search for a husband.
Savitri returns from her travels and finds her father with Narada, who asks where she has been and whom she has chosen.
Savitri names Satyavan, son of the blind, exiled Dyumatsena; Narada praises him but warns he will die within a year, and Savitri refuses to choose another, so Narada gives his approval and leaves.
Narada rises into the sky and departs, and Aswapati begins to prepare his daughter's wedding.
Aswapati visits Dyumatsena's hermitage, asks that Savitri be accepted as Satyavan's wife, and Dyumatsena, after noting their hardship, agrees.
The wedding is performed with rites, Savitri serves her husband and in-laws devotedly and pleases them all, but Narada's words stay in her mind day and night.
Savitri, who has counted the days to the death Narada foretold, keeps a three-night fast, and after her morning rites, the hermitage ascetics bless her that she will never be widowed.
Her in-laws tell her to eat, but she answers that she will eat only after sunset, as her vow requires.
Satyavan takes his axe and sets out for the forest, and Savitri insists on going with him despite her fast, while he warns her of the hard paths.
Savitri asks her in-laws for leave to go into the forest with her husband, and Dyumatsena grants it.
Savitri walks with Satyavan through the woods, smiling outwardly while grieving, and, remembering Narada's words, watches him closely, expecting his death at that moment.
Satyavan, with head pain from chopping wood, lays his head in Savitri's lap, and she sees Yama in red standing beside him with a noose and learns that Yama has come to take her husband.

Yama draws Satyavan's life out of his body and Savitri follows him; her replies on righteousness win her boons for Dyumatsena's sight and kingdom, sons for her father, and a century of sons, before she asks for Satyavan's life.
Yama frees Satyavan, promises him a long life and many sons, and departs, and Satyavan wakes in Savitri's lap.
Satyavan, recovered, recalls his vision and worries about his blind father and aged mother, and Savitri urges him to rest and wait for morning, though he insists on going home.
Savitri takes the axe and wallet and supports Satyavan, and he guides them along the path to the north toward the hermitage, eager to see his parents.
Dyumatsena, now able to see, searches the hermitages with his wife Saivya, and each sage assures him that Satyavan must still be alive, giving his reasons.
Satyavan and Savitri come back at night; Satyavan describes his sleep, the sages ask what happened, and Savitri explains Yama's boons, which the sages hail as rescuing the family.
The sages praise Savitri and bid farewell to the king and his son, and they go home.

Messengers from Salwa report the usurper's death and invite Dyumatsena back, he is installed on the throne with Satyavan as prince-regent, Savitri bears a hundred sons, and Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Draupadi, like Savitri, will rescue them.
Vaisampayana says that encouraged by the story, Yudhishthira kept living in the Kamyaka forest, and that anyone who hears the tale of Savitri with reverence gains happiness.
Janamejaya asks why Yudhishthira feared Karna and kept the fear hidden, even though Indra had promised through Lomasa to remove it.
Vaisampayana explains that in the thirteenth year of exile Indra resolved to beg Karna's earrings, and Surya came to Karna in a dream disguised as a Brahmana to warn him.
Karna asks who the Brahmana is, and when Surya reveals himself, Karna refuses to break his vow of giving, prefers lasting fame to life, and resolves to give Indra his earrings and armor.
Surya warns Karna that fame is worthless to the dead, urges him to refuse Indra's request for the earrings, and says that with them Karna cannot be beaten by Arjuna.
Karna tells Surya he would sooner die than lie, will give his earrings and armor to Brahmanas, and promises to defeat Arjuna in battle anyway.
Surya advises Karna to demand from Indra an infallible dart that never fails to slay enemies as the price for the earrings.
Surya vanishes, Karna tells him of the dream the next morning, Surya confirms it, and Karna waits for Indra to come for the dart.
Janamejaya asks what secret Surya kept from Karna and where Karna's earrings and armor came from.
Vaisampayana says a Brahmana of fierce energy asked King Kuntibhoja to host him as a guest, and the king tells his adopted daughter Pritha to wait on the Brahmana with care.
Kunti promises to serve the Brahmana faithfully, her father asks forgiveness for any fault in her, and she attends the guest as if he were a god.
Kunti serves the Brahmana at all hours through a year without complaint, and when he offers a boon, she declines, and he gives her a mantra to summon any god she wishes.
Fearing his curse, Kunti accepts the mantras, the Brahmana vanishes after saying he is leaving, and Kuntibhoja is amazed.
Kunti tests the mantra by summoning the sun, who appears and tells her that she must yield to him or face his curse, and that the gods are watching.
Kunti begs Surya to leave and says a maiden's body belongs to her father or mother; Surya replies that she is still a girl, that her virginity is hers, and that he will not go away empty-handed.
Kunti fails to dissuade Surya and, weighing the danger to her father and the Brahmana, reflects at length on her dilemma.
Kunti pleads that a son born of an unmarried union would bring disgrace, Surya argues that a maiden is free by nature, and he promises her a son with Amrita armor and earrings, and she consents.
Surya enters Kunti by yoga and touches her navel, leaving her stupefied, and says she will bear a son who will be the best of warriors while remaining a virgin.
Kunti, half-fainting, accepts; Surya places the child in her womb without harming her maidenhood, and she regains consciousness after he has gone.
Pritha secretly gives birth to a son born with armor and earrings, and, weeping and fearing disgrace, places him in a wicker box and prays for his protection as she sets him on the Aswa.
Pritha casts the box into the river at night and returns to the palace, and the box floats on through the Charmanwati, the Yamuna and the Ganga to Champa, where his armor and earrings keep him alive.

The charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha find the box in the Ganga, adopt the golden-armored boy, and raise him as their son, and the boy is later called Vasusena and Vrisha; he is trained by Drona, befriends Duryodhana and challenges Arjuna, while Yudhishthira is troubled by his armor and his rivalry.
Indra in the guise of a Brahmana asks Karna for his armor and earrings, and Karna offers gold, damsels and cattle, but the Brahmana asks for nothing else.
Karna explains that the armor and earrings make him unslayable and offers the whole kingdom instead, but the Brahmana still asks only for the armor and earrings.
Karna says he knew Indra's identity, and Indra admits that Surya had warned Karna and offers him any boon except the thunderbolt.
Karna asks for an infallible dart, and Indra sets its terms: it kills one powerful enemy and then returns to him, while Karna asks that his body not be disfigured and Indra agrees.
Karna cuts off his armor and earrings and gives them to Indra, earning the name Karna; Indra goes to heaven, the Kauravas are dismayed, and the Pandavas rejoice.
Janamejaya asks where the Pandavas were when they heard the news, and what they did when their twelfth year of exile ended.
Vaisampayana says the Pandavas, having defeated Jayadratha, rescued Draupadi, finished their exile, and heard Markandeya's tales, returned from Kamyaka to Dwaitavana with their people.
Heading marking the Aranya Parva, the book of the forest.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after their grief over Draupadi's abduction and her rescue.

Vaisampayana says the Pandavas lived at Dwaitavana, and after a deer ran off with a Brahmana's fire-sticks and churning staff, they chased it in vain and sat down exhausted under a banyan, where Nakula asked why disaster had come to them.
Yudhishthira says calamity has no clear cause, and Bhima, Arjuna and Sahadeva each blame a past lapse for their misfortune.

Yudhishthira sends Nakula, then Sahadeva and Arjuna, to fetch water, and each drinks from the lake without answering a voice's questions and dies; Bhima also goes, is warned by the same voice, and is about to drink.
Bhima drinks without answering and dies, and Yudhishthira, uneasy at the long delay, searches the forest and comes upon a beautiful lake.

Yudhishthira mourns his four dead brothers, recalls the promises made at their births, wonders who could have killed them, and, going to bathe in the lake, hears a Yaksha say from the sky that he is the one who slew them.

Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's questions one by one on duty, learning, the sun, wealth, friendship and conduct, and when offered one brother's life he chooses Nakula out of fairness to both of his father's wives, so the Yaksha restores all the brothers.
Heading marking Section CCCXII.

The brothers rise refreshed, and the Yaksha reveals himself as Yudhishthira's father, the Lord of justice, who had carried off the fire-sticks as a deer to test him; Yudhishthira asks that the Brahmana's worship of Agni not be interrupted.
The Yaksha grants that boon and offers another, and Yudhishthira asks that no one recognize the brothers during the thirteenth year.

The Yaksha grants that the brothers may spend the year unrecognized in Virata's kingdom and take any form they wish, and when Yudhishthira asks for steadiness against greed, anger and folly, the god says he already has those virtues.
The Lord of justice vanishes, the brothers wake and return to the hermitage to give the Brahmana his fire-sticks, and the text promises rewards to anyone who hears the tale.

Yudhishthira asks the ascetics for leave to spend the thirteenth year in disguise, faints in grief, and is encouraged by Dhaumya's examples of gods who hid and won, and by Bhima's readiness to act; the Brahmanas bless them and leave, and the brothers set out with Krishna to take counsel.
Heading marking the end of the Vana Parva.
