Footnote 77 explains the five as tranquillity, self-restraint, abstention from sensual pleasures, resignation and yoga meditation.
Footnote 78 explains the six as hunger, thirst, sorrow, the loss of mortal feeling, decrepitude and death.
Heading of the Project Gutenberg license that follows the text; it is publisher boilerplate and not part of the epic.
Heading that names the Pandava-Pravesa section.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati, and a call to utter the word Jaya.
Janamejaya asks how his ancestors lived unrecognized in Virata's city while fearing Duryodhana, and how Draupadi passed her days.

Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira returned from the asylum after gaining a boon from Dharma, returned a lost ritual item to a Brahmana, and told his brothers that the thirteenth year must now be spent hidden.
Arjuna says Dharma's boon lets them roam unseen, then lists the fertile neighboring kingdoms and asks which one Yudhishthira prefers.
Yudhishthira picks Virata's Matsya, calling its aged king virtuous and fond of the Pandavas, and says they will serve him in disguise.
Arjuna asks Yudhishthira what service he will take in Virata's court and how a king will bear such hardship.
Yudhishthira says he will appear as the Brahmana Kanka, a dice player and courtier who entertains the king with ivory pieces and dice. He asks Bhima what office he will fill.
Bhima says he will present himself as the cook Vallava, boast of his skill with curries and loads of wood, and take on wrestlers and beasts without killing them.
Yudhishthira asks what role Arjuna will take, and lists his deeds and his powers in a long run of comparisons that praise him as the finest of warriors.
Arjuna says he will pass as a eunuch named Vrihannala, cover his scarred arms with bangles, and teach singing and dance to the women, claiming to be Draupadi's former attendant.
Vaisampayana says Arjuna fell silent and the king turned to another brother.
Yudhishthira asks Nakula what work he will take up in the king's realm.
Nakula says he will be keeper of Virata's horses under the name Granthika, and cites his skill in training horses and his old service to Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira asks Sahadeva how he will carry himself and what disguise he will use.
Sahadeva says he will tend the king's cows under the name Tantripala, citing his skill with cattle, bulls and their markings.
Yudhishthira grieves over Draupadi, who is young, delicate and used only to garlands and fine robes, and asks what work she will do.
Draupadi offers to pass as a Sairindhri, a hairdresser who serves in other households, and to attend Queen Sudeshna under a cover story.
Yudhishthira agrees with her plan but warns her, given her noble birth and chastity, to behave so that wicked men are not drawn to look at her.
Yudhishthira states the plan: priests and cooks go to Drupada's realm, Indrasena's group goes to Dwaravati, and Draupadi's maids say they do not know where the Pandavas went.
The brothers seek Dhaumya's advice, and he gives a long list of rules for serving a king, covering courtesy, speech, seating, dress, and loyalty.
Yudhishthira thanks Dhaumya for the counsel and asks him to make the arrangements for their departure and their safety.
Dhaumya performs the departure rites and offers prayers at the fires. The brothers leave with Draupadi, Dhaumya takes the sacred fires to the Panchalas, and Indrasena's group goes to the Yadavas.
The brothers leave the forest with swords and finger guards, cross the Yamuna and enter Matsya, and Draupadi notes they are still a distance from the city and asks for rest.
Yudhishthira tells Arjuna to carry Draupadi, since the city is just beyond the forest.
Arjuna lifts Draupadi and sets her down near the city. Yudhishthira asks where to leave the weapons, since bringing the famous bow inside could expose them and end the disguise.
Arjuna suggests a huge Sami tree near a cemetery in a remote forest, where no one is likely to see them hide their arms.

The brothers unstring their bows and hide them and their weapons in the tree, hang a corpse nearby to keep people away, and claim it is their mother. They take the names Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Jayatsena and Jayadvala, and enter the city to pass the thirteenth year.
Yudhishthira, travelling toward Virata's city, prays to Durga, listing her many names and her powers over danger, and asks her for protection in his exile.

Durga appears and tells him he will defeat the Kauravas and recover his kingdom. She adds that those who recite her praises will be blessed, and that the Kurus' spies and the Matsyas will not recognize the brothers in Virata's city.
Yudhishthira appears in Virata's court with golden dice, looking like a king veiled in cloud. Virata asks his courtiers who this stranger is, noting he seems like a lord but has no retinue.
Yudhishthira asks to live near the king as a Brahmana who has lost his wealth. Virata welcomes him and asks his name, family and skills.
Yudhishthira gives his name as Kanka, a Brahmana of the Vaiyaghra family who is skilled at dice and once a friend of Yudhishthira.
Virata offers Kanka a share in ruling the Matsyas and says he likes skilled gamblers.
Yudhishthira asks for two boons: no quarrels with low people over dice, and no keeping of winnings by a loser.
Virata promises to punish anyone who displeases Kanka and makes him an equal friend, with access to clothes, food, the king's affairs and open doors.
Kanka lives happily and is well regarded in the court, and no one recognizes him.
Bhima comes into court holding cooking tools and a dark sword. Virata asks his people who this strong, handsome man is, then Bhima says he is Vallava, a cook who wants work in the kitchen.
Virata doubts that cooking is Bhima's true trade, and says he looks like a king.
Bhima says he is a cook who once served Yudhishthira, and also a wrestler who fights lions and elephants to amuse the king.
Virata grants his request and makes him superintendent of the kitchen, though he thinks the post is beneath him.
Bhima becomes the king's favourite in the kitchen and stays unrecognized by the other servants and the public.

Draupadi binds her hair in a braid, puts on a dirty single cloth, and wanders the city as a hairdresser. People find her too striking to be a common maid, and Queen Sudeshna notices her from a terrace.
Draupadi says she is a hairdresser who can also prepare perfumes and garlands, and says she served Satyabhama and Draupadi earlier under the name Malini.
Sudeshna praises Draupadi's beauty at length, guesses she may be a goddess or a celestial, and says she fears the king will be drawn to her.
Draupadi says her five Gandharva husbands protect her, and any man who tries to have her will die that very night.
Sudeshna agrees to take her into the household, on the condition that she never has to eat another's leftovers or wash another's feet.
Krishna (Draupadi), devoted to her husbands, begins to live in the city, and nobody learns who she really is.
Sahadeva arrives at the cowpens in a cowherd's dress and speech. Virata is amazed by his splendour and asks who he is and what work he wants.
Sahadeva says he is a Vaisya named Arishtanemi, who once tended the Kuru bulls, the sons of Pandu, and will serve no one else.
Virata doubts he is only a herdsman and asks him to name his true origin, skills and the pay he wants.
Sahadeva describes Yudhishthira's large herds, his old name Tantripala, his knowledge of cattle, their health and breeding, and the bulls whose markings are prized.
Virata gives him a hundred thousand cows with their herdsmen, placing all of them under his care.
Sahadeva lives happily under Virata's protection, and no one apart from his brothers recognizes him.

Arjuna enters the court, huge and graceful, wearing women's ornaments and a braid. Virata asks where he came from and offers him a son's place or a share in ruling the Matsyas, saying he cannot be a eunuch.
Arjuna says he is skilled in dance, song and instruments, asks to be made dance teacher to princess Uttara, and gives his name as Vrihannala, without father or mother.
Virata agrees to assign him to his daughter and her companions, though he feels the post is beneath Arjuna.

Virata tests Vrihannala in dance and music and has women examine him. Finding the condition permanent, the king sends him to the women's apartments, where Arjuna teaches singing and music and lives unknown to anyone.
Nakula comes toward Virata, shining like the sun. Virata notices him studying the royal horses and, judging him a skilled horseman, orders him brought in.
Nakula presents himself as a horse trainer, names Yudhishthira as his former master, and lists his skill with breaking, correcting and healing horses. He says his name is Granthika.

Virata gives Nakula charge of all his horses, keepers and charioteers, and says his bearing makes him look like a king. He wonders how Yudhishthira is getting on in the forest, now that he has no servants.
The brothers live in Matsya as Virata's servants, well regarded, and no one recognizes them. The narrator notes they keep their pledge to pass the year in hiding.
Heading that names the Samayapalana section.
Janamejaya asks what the mighty Kuru princes did while living disguised in Matsya.

Vaisampayana describes their hidden lives: Yudhishthira's dice winnings shared with his brothers, Bhima's meat sales, Arjuna's earnings from the women, Draupadi's care for the others, and a festival where Bhima kills the athlete Jimuta. The king rewards each of the brothers for their service.
Heading that names the Kichaka-badha section.

Vaisampayana says the brothers have passed ten months in disguise, and Draupadi serves Sudeshna in misery. Kichaka sees her, asks his sister Sudeshna about her, and then makes a lavish, lust-filled proposal to Draupadi with praise of her beauty. Draupadi refuses him, citing her position and her marriage, and asks him to respect moral law.

Kichaka, driven by desire, ignores her refusal and claims to be the true lord of the kingdom, offering her power and luxury. Draupadi warns him that her husbands are Gandharvas who will punish him, and that his attempt is hopeless and fatal.
Kichaka, rejected by Draupadi, begs Sudeshna to make the maid yield to him.
Sudeshna pities him and suggests he prepare food and wine for a festival, after which she will send the maid to bring wine and he can win her over in private.

Kichaka arranges fine food and drink. Sudeshna asks Draupadi to fetch wine from his house, and Draupadi objects, pointing to Kichaka's shameless nature and the vow she made on entering the palace. Sudeshna insists she will be safe and hands over a covered golden vessel, and Draupadi sets out after praying for protection.

Draupadi prays to the Sun god, who sends a Rakshasa to protect her unseen. When Kichaka sees her approaching like a frightened doe, he rises from his seat with a joy like that of a man reaching a boat to cross a river.
Kichaka greets Draupadi, offers her jewels and wine, and when she says she has only come to fetch wine for the queen, he seizes her arm. Draupadi swears that he will end up dragged on the ground.
Kichaka grabs her garment and hair and kicks her before King Virata. A Rakshasa knocks him down, Bhima's rage is checked by Yudhishthira, and Draupadi cries out against the court.
Virata says he did not know what the quarrel was about. The courtiers, having learned the facts, condemn Kichaka and praise Draupadi's beauty.
Yudhishthira, sweating with anger, tells Draupadi to go to Sudeshna's apartments, and remarks that her Gandharva husbands are not coming to her aid.
Draupadi goes to Sudeshna in distress. The queen offers to have Kichaka killed, and Draupadi replies that those he has wronged will do it first.

Draupadi bathes and, unable to find a remedy for her grief, thinks of Bhima as the only one who can carry out her revenge. She goes to his quarters at night and rouses him, asking how he can sleep while Kichaka is alive.
She finds Bhima in the kitchen, embraces and wakes him. He sits up, asks why she has come in such haste, and promises to help her if she tells him everything.

Draupadi tells Bhima of her many humiliations, including her dragging into the assembly, the insults of the forest, and Kichaka's assault. She blames Yudhishthira's gambling for their fall and laments how the once-honoured king now serves as the courtier Kanka.

Draupadi laments, at length, that Bhima serves as a cook and fights beasts before the court, that Arjuna teaches dance as a disguised eunuch, that Sahadeva tends cattle and Nakula trains horses, and that Sudeshna's women laugh at her and suspect her of favouring Bhima.

Draupadi describes her servitude under Sudeshna and her wait for the end of the exile, reasoning that fortune turns like a wheel. She lists her humiliations, including grinding sandal for others and showing Bhima her corn-marked hands.
Draupadi weeps and says the gods must be angry with her, since she is still alive when she should be dead.
Bhima weeps, holding her hands to his face and tears streaming down, as he begins to answer her.

Bhima regrets his restraint and recalls the enemies he has not yet slain, urging Draupadi to hold her anger for her husbands' sake. Draupadi answers that she does not blame Yudhishthira, recounts Kichaka's pursuit, Sudeshna's jealousy and the kick, and says she will take poison if Kichaka is still alive when tomorrow's sun rises.
Draupadi hides her tear-streaked face against Bhima's chest, and he comforts her and wipes her face. He then licks his lips in anger at the thought of Kichaka and speaks to her.
Bhima tells Draupadi he will kill Kichaka, and describes the dance hall where the girls dance by day and go home at night. He asks her to arrange the meeting so no one sees her.

Kichaka comes to Draupadi, boasts that he is the real power in Matsya, and offers her wealth and servants if she yields to him. Draupadi sets the condition that the meeting stay secret, and sends him to the dance hall at night.
Kichaka, delighted, dresses and adorns himself while Draupadi goes to Bhima in the kitchen and reports the plan, urging him to kill Kichaka in the hall.
Bhima welcomes the news and swears on truth and his brothers that he will kill Kichaka and anyone who defends him. He tells Draupadi he will do it that same night, unseen by others.
Bhima waits in the dark hall like a lion for its prey. Kichaka enters, boasts of the gifts he has given the woman, and Bhima answers with mocking flattery of Kichaka's skills.

Bhima seizes Kichaka by the hair and they wrestle at length, with Bhima overpowering him and finally crushing him to death. Bhima then shows the body to Draupadi, and she has the dance-hall guards told that Gandharvas slew him.
Heading that marks a new section.
Kichaka's kinsmen wail over his body and, with Virata's consent, seize Draupadi and carry her toward the cemetery to be burned with him. She calls on her husbands by their names for help.
Bhima hears her cries, tells her she need no longer fear the Sutas, and rises from his bed.

Bhima leaves the palace by a back way, climbs a wall, and uproots a huge tree to carry against the Sutas. He drives them off and kills a hundred and five of them, then frees Draupadi and comforts her before returning to the kitchen by another route.
The dead lie scattered like fallen trees after a storm. With Kichaka himself, the number slain comes to a hundred and six, and onlookers are left astonished.

Citizens tell Virata that the Sutas were slain by Gandharvas and warn that Draupadi endangers his realm. Virata orders the Kichakas burned with rich honours and asks Sudeshna to tell Draupadi she may go wherever she pleases, since he dares not speak to her directly.

Freed from her captors, Draupadi washes and walks back to the city, where people flee in fear of the Gandharvas. At the kitchen gate she sees Bhima and thanks the Gandharva who rescued her, and Bhima replies in riddles that those who once answered to Kichaka are now free.

Draupadi finds Arjuna instructing Virata's daughters in dance. The girls congratulate her on her escape, and Vrihannala asks how it happened, while Draupadi answers with bitter mockery and Arjuna answers that he has sorrows of his own.

Draupadi goes to Sudeshna, who passes on the king's word that she may go wherever she likes. Draupadi asks to remain in the king's service for thirteen more days, since then the Gandharvas will take her away.
People across the provinces talk of Kichaka's slaying by the Gandharvas and of his reputation as a wicked oppressor, while Vallava is praised for courage.

The spies return to Duryodhana's court and report that they found no trace of the Pandavas, that the charioteers returned to Dwaravati without them, and that Kichaka and his brothers are dead, which they call good news for the Kauravas.
Heading that names the Go-harana section.

Duryodhana notes most of the thirteenth year has passed and asks his men to find the brothers before the year ends. Karna urges more and better spies in many places, and Duhsasana doubts they will be found and urges Duryodhana to put his mind at rest.
Drona says the Pandavas will never perish, praises their loyalty to Yudhishthira and his virtue, and urges that the search be renewed with Brahmanas, Charanas and ascetics.

Bhishma approves Drona's words, praises the Pandavas' virtue and discipline, and advises against using spies to expose them now. He describes the prosperity of any land where Yudhishthira lives, and urges Duryodhana to act wisely and honestly.
Kripa agrees with Bhishma but advises Duryodhana to keep tracking the brothers through spies, weigh his own strength and allies, and expand his army and treasury before the Pandavas return.

Susarman, humiliated by Kichaka, urges an invasion of Virata's kingdom to seize his gems, wealth and cattle. Karna approves, saying the sons of Pandu are either dead or gone and that the raid will be profitable.
Duryodhana orders his brother Duhsasana to muster the forces. The Trigartas are to go first and seize the cowherds' cattle, and the Kauravas will follow in two divisions.
The Trigartas march south-east, and Susarman sets out on the seventh day of the dark fortnight. The next day the Kauravas begin seizing cattle by thousands.

With the exile complete, a herdsman tells Virata the Trigartas are seizing his cattle. The king arms his brothers and sons in splendid armour, orders chariots and mail for the disguised Pandavas by their assumed names, and the brothers ride out with the army of Matsya.

The Matsya army marches out and meets the Trigartas in a battle that rages from afternoon into dusk. Heads, limbs and bodies cover the field, and by nightfall neither side has routed the other, while the king duels Susarman and both are wounded.
The fighting resumes under the moon, and Susarman and his brother capture Virata and drive him away. Yudhishthira tells Bhima that the brothers owe the king a debt and must rescue him.
Bhima prepares to uproot a huge tree as a weapon, but Yudhishthira forbids such superhuman feats, warning that people would recognize him, and tells him to use an ordinary weapon.

Bhima routs the Trigarta cars and soldiers, while the brothers slay many hundreds and thousands of enemies. Bhima seizes and kicks Susarman, binds him and brings him to Yudhishthira, who orders him freed after Bhima sets the humbling condition that Susarman call himself a slave.
Susarman, humiliated, bows his head, is released, and departs. Virata rewards the Pandavas with gems, damsels and wealth, and tells them they may live happily and become lords of the Matsyas.

Yudhishthira thanks Virata, and Virata offers him the sovereignty of the Matsyas, gems, kine and gold. Yudhishthira asks him to send messengers to proclaim the victory, and Virata has them announce it at the city gates at sunrise.

Duryodhana, Karna, Drona, Bhishma and other warriors invade Matsya, drive off the cowherds and seize sixty thousand cows. The chief cowherd reaches the city, tells Bhuminjaya what has happened, and urges him to rescue the herds, comparing the bow to a lute.
Hearing this in front of the women, the prince boasts of his own courage and skill.

Uttara declares he would ride after the cattle at once if he had a skilled charioteer, since his own was slain in the battle. He boasts that he would drive into the Kuru army and defeat even its mightiest warriors.
Arjuna speaks privately to Draupadi and asks her to tell Uttara that Vrihannala was once Arjuna's own charioteer.
Draupadi shyly tells Uttara that Vrihannala was Arjuna's disciple and a peerless driver, who once held the reins at Khandava and in the conquest of Khandavaprastha.
Uttara says Draupadi knows this youth and what he is, but he cannot himself ask Vrihannala to drive his horses.
Draupadi says Vrihannala will obey Uttara's younger sister, and if he agrees to drive, Uttara will win back the cattle.
Uttara sends his sister to the dance hall, where Arjuna is staying in disguise, to bring Vrihannala.
Virata's daughter, richly adorned, hurries to the dance hall and greets Arjuna, asking why he is there and why she finds him in such a state of hurry.

She explains that her brother must fight the Kurus who have driven off the cattle and has no charioteer. She says the Sairindhri praised Vrihannala's skill, and she begs him to drive, saying she will die if he refuses.
Uttara orders Vrihannala to hold the reins and mount the chariot.
Arjuna pretends not to know how to put on the armour and the maidens burst out laughing. Uttara arms him himself, and Vrihannala promises the maidens cloth for their dolls if the Kurus are defeated.
The elderly women and Brahmanas walk around the chariot to bless the prince and his charioteer as they set out, wishing Vrihannala the kind of victory Arjuna won at Khandava.
Uttara orders Vrihannala to drive straight at the Kuru army, which he says has come to take the cattle. Arjuna drives on and the two see the enormous host, with its flags and great warriors.
Uttara, terrified, bewails his fate, saying his father has taken the army away and that he is only a boy with little training, and begs Vrihannala to stop the chariot.
Vrihannala mocks Uttara's fear, reminds him that he boasted before the women, and says he cannot return without the cattle.
Uttara replies that the Kurus may take the cattle and that people may laugh at him, but there is no need to fight.

Uttara throws down his bow and flees. Vrihannala rebukes him for running, and Arjuna leaps from the chariot and runs after him, his braid and red garments streaming, while some soldiers laugh. The Kurus argue over the identity of the figure and guess it may be Arjuna himself.
Arjuna overtakes Uttara and seizes him by the hair. Uttara begs him to turn back, promising a hundred gold coins and a chariot with ten elephants in return for his freedom.
Arjuna laughs, pulls the prince back to the chariot, and tells him to hold the reins while he fights. He reassures Uttara that he is a Kshatriya and a prince, then lifts him onto the car.
Heading that marks the next section.

The Kuru warriors, Bhishma and Drona at their head, see the disguised charioteer carrying Uttara toward the Sami tree and suspect it is Arjuna. Drona reads omens of storms, dry clouds, restless weapons and frightened animals, and names Arjuna by his many epithets. Karna belittles Arjuna, and Duryodhana says the Pandavas would be sent back to the forest if it is him, or he will strike down a disguised eunuch.
Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Drona's son applaud Duryodhana's manliness.

Arjuna, seeing Uttara is unpracticed in battle, tells him to climb the tree and take down the bows of the Pandavas, which are tied there along with their arrows, banners and armour. He names the Gandiva and explains that Uttara's own bows could not bear his strength.
Uttara says he has heard a corpse hangs in the tree, and that as a prince of the Kshatriya order he must not touch it.
Vrihannala assures him he will stay clean, since only bows hang in the tree and no corpse, and asks why he would make a prince do something shameful.

Uttara climbs the tree reluctantly, cuts away the wrappings and ropes, and finds the Gandiva with four other bows. Their brilliance and their snake-like shape frighten him, and he speaks to Arjuna as he holds them.
Uttara asks, one item after another, whose the golden-decorated bow, the arrows, the quivers and the various swords and scimitars are, and asks Vrihannala to tell him truly, since he marvels at them.

Arjuna identifies the Gandiva as his own and traces its history through gods before it came to him from Varuna, then assigns the other bows, arrows, quivers and swords to Bhima, Yudhishthira, Nakula and Sahadeva, and gives the owner of each of the weapons described.
Uttara admires the golden weapons and asks where the Pandavas have gone, since they lost their kingdom at dice and have not been heard of, and where Draupadi is.

Arjuna says he is Arjuna, and that Yudhishthira is the courtier, Bhima the cook, Nakula the horse-keeper and Sahadeva the cowherd. He adds that the Sairindhri is Draupadi, for whose sake the Kichakas were killed.
Uttara says he will believe it only if Arjuna can recite the ten names he has heard for him.
Arjuna lists his ten names: Arjuna, Phalguna, Jishnu, Kiritin, Svetavahana, Vibhatsu, Vijaya, Krishna, Savyasachin and Dhananjaya.
Uttara asks Arjuna to explain why he has each name, so he can check the answer against what he has heard.

Arjuna explains that Dhananjaya comes from his winning of wealth, Vijaya from his victories, Svetavahana from his white horses, Phalguna from his birth under a particular constellation, and Kiritin from the diadem Indra gave him. He also explains Vibhatsu, Savyasachin, Arjuna, Jishnu and Krishna, the last being a name his father gave him.
Uttara comes closer, greets Partha and begs pardon for his earlier ignorance, saying his fear is gone and his affection is great.
Uttara offers to drive Arjuna wherever he wants to go in the enemy army.
Arjuna says he is pleased with the prince, promises to rout the foes, and asks him to tie the quivers to the chariot and take a golden sword.
Uttara climbs down and brings Arjuna's weapons. Arjuna says the chariot will be a fortress, with its pole and quiver as defenses, its banner a grand gate, and the bowstring as a catapult.
Uttara says he is no longer afraid, but wonders how a man so handsome and well marked could have lost his manhood, and asks if he is a god in disguise.
Arjuna explains that he is keeping a year-long eunuch vow because his elder brother asked him to, and that he is not truly a eunuch.
Uttara calls Arjuna the best of men, says he now has an ally, and praises the chariot and the four horses, naming each one and comparing them to famous steeds.

Arjuna removes his bracelets, puts on gloves, binds his hair, and summons his weapons, which greet him as their master. He sounds the Gandiva so loudly that the earth and sky shake, and when Uttara fears the Kuru numbers, Arjuna laughs and recalls his past battles against gods, demons and kings.

Arjuna circles the Sami tree, takes down the lion banner, and raises his ape banner, a gift from Agni. He sounds his conch, the horses kneel, and Uttara sits down in fear, and Arjuna urges him not to be afraid.
Uttara says he has never heard such a conch, bow or banner, and that the noise and the sight have confused his senses and deafened him.
Arjuna tells Uttara to brace himself on the car and hold the reins firmly, because he will sound the conch again.
Arjuna sounds the conch again, and the sound shakes hills and mountains. Uttara clings to the chariot once more, and Arjuna comforts him again.

Drona says the thunder of the chariot and the darkened sky mean the driver is Savyasachin, and he lists bad omens among the Kuru ranks. He advises sending the cattle ahead and standing ready with the army in order.

Duryodhana argues that the thirteenth year is not yet done, so if this is Arjuna the Pandavas must return to the forest for twelve years, and that the army must fight whoever it is. Karna then mocks Drona for praising Arjuna, says the preceptor is partial to the Pandavas, and urges the Kauravas to arrange their army and hold their ground.

Karna, seeing his comrades anxious, boasts that he will meet Arjuna with arrows that cover him like locusts, will break his chariot and strike down his ape banner, and that the Kauravas may take the cattle or stay and watch.
Kripa warns Karna that his rashness will lead to disaster, lists Arjuna's great deeds, and urges the six car-warriors to stand together in ranks instead of facing Arjuna alone.

Ashvatthaman tells Karna that the cattle are not yet won, that real heroes do not boast, and that Duryodhana won his kingdom by dishonest dice, while the Pandavas acted honourably. He warns that Arjuna will destroy the Kurus, and declares that he himself will fight the Matsya king and not Arjuna.

Bhishma says Kripa and Drona's son are right, that Karna only spoke to raise courage, and that the leaders must forgive each other because disunity is the worst of calamities. Ashvatthaman answers that Bhishma's counsel was proper, but Drona had praised Arjuna in his anger, and an enemy's merits and a teacher's faults may both be spoken of.
Duryodhana asks the preceptor to forgive, so that peace can be restored.
Duryodhana, with Karna, Kripa and Bhishma, pacifies Drona.

Drona says he is now calmed by Bhishma's words, and asks that the army be placed so that Arjuna cannot reach Duryodhana or harm the troops. He says Arjuna has not revealed himself before the term ended, and that he will not pardon the raid on the cattle.

Bhishma works out that the thirteen years are complete with time to spare, so the Pandavas kept their promise and Arjuna's appearance is lawful. He warns that the Pandavas will not give up their kingdom and that the Kurus must prepare for battle.
Duryodhana refuses to return the kingdom and orders every preparation for battle without delay.

Bhishma advises Duryodhana to return to the capital with a fourth of the army, have another fourth escort the cattle, and fight with the rest, while Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Ashvatthaman and Kripa face Arjuna.
Bhishma arranges the army: Drona in the centre, Ashvatthaman on the left, Kripa on the right, Karna in the van, and Bhishma himself guarding the rear.
Arjuna's chariot rushes at the Kurus with its roaring ape banner, and Drona recognizes Partha by his banner, the twang of his bow and his bearing, comparing him to a sacrificial fire.
Arjuna asks Uttara to hold the horses where his arrows can reach the enemy, then says he will strike at Duryodhana, who must be retreating with the kine by the south.

Kripa, seeing Arjuna head for Duryodhana, urges his men to strike Arjuna's flank, since the cattle would be worthless if Duryodhana were lost. Arjuna shoots down the Kuru troops, blows his conch, and the cattle turn back along the southern road.

Arjuna, having recovered the cattle, turns back and drives Uttara into the Kuru army. He routs several Kuru warriors, kills Satruntapa, and drives off Vikarna, then meets Karna in a long archery duel in which he wounds him on the arms, head and body until Karna retreats.

Arjuna's arrows cover the field, and the Kuru ranks are shattered by his arrows, his dazzling bow and the roar of his conch. He refrains from killing the defenceless, strikes the army from behind, and keeps shooting until the sky turns red at evening, wounding Drona, Duryodhana, Bhishma, Karna and others.

Arjuna asks Uttara to drive to Kripa first, then to Drona, Ashvatthaman, Duryodhana and Karna by their banners, warning him to be careful near Karna, and to approach Bhishma last. Uttara obeys and turns the chariot toward Kripa.

The Kuru ranks stand ready, and the gods arrive on celestial cars with Indra at their head to watch the battle between Arjuna and the Kurus. Divine perfumes spread over the field, the dust settles, and Indra cannot take his eyes off his son.
Arjuna orders Uttara to head toward Kripa's chariot, then sounds his conch Devadatta. Kripa answers with his own conch, and the two warriors begin shooting at each other.

Arjuna cuts down each new bow Kripa takes up, cuts off his armour, kills his horses and driver, and wounds him. When Kripa hurls a mace, Arjuna sends it back. Kripa's warriors surround Arjuna, but Uttara wheels the chariot in circles and holds them off while Kripa is led away.
Arjuna tells Uttara to drive toward Drona's car with the golden altar banner, and praises Drona as the master of the Vedas, the celestial weapons and every virtue. He says he wishes to fight Drona.

Arjuna approaches with respect and promises not to strike unless struck first. The two shoot at each other with celestial weapons in a duel the spectators admire. When Ashvatthaman charges Arjuna, Arjuna turns toward him, leaving Drona to escape, wounded and with his armour and banner gone.

Ashvatthaman rushes at Arjuna and shoots in a fierce duel that darkens the sky. He cuts the Gandiva's string, but Arjuna restrings it and gains the advantage as Ashvatthaman's arrows run low, and then Karna twangs his bow and Arjuna turns toward him, enraged.

Arjuna challenges Karna to make good his boast before the Kurus, reproaching him for the insult to Draupadi and for the twelve years of suffering. Karna replies that Arjuna's words outrun his deeds and that Arjuna's forbearance was the result of his vow. Arjuna retorts that Karna ran from battle when his brother was slain, and calls him shameful.

The two duel with volleys of arrows. Arjuna cuts Karna's quiver strings, bow and steeds, pierces his breast, and Karna, who briefly loses consciousness from the wound, regains himself and flees northward while Arjuna and Uttara taunt him.

Uttara says he is overwhelmed by the horror of the battlefield, the stench of blood, the noise of conches and the twang of the Gandiva, and that he can no longer hold the reins. Arjuna tells him not to lose heart, as a prince of the Matsya line, and to stay on the car and steady the horses.
Arjuna orders Uttara to drive to Bhishma's division, boasting that he will cut Bhishma's bowstring and send the Kuru army fleeing, and he names the celestial gods who taught him his weapons.

Arjuna cuts off Bhishma's banner at the root. Duhsasana, Vikarna, Dussaha and Vivingsati then attack him. Arjuna wounds Duhsasana and Vikarna, who falls from his car, kills the horses of Dussaha and Vivingsati, and the brothers are carried away from the field.

The Kuru warriors close in on Arjuna, but he covers them in clouds of arrows, breaks their armour and cuts down heaps of men, elephants and horses, while his bow seems to dance. The Kurus lose heart in front of Duryodhana and flee, and the field becomes a vast river of blood, heaped with corpses.

Bhishma comes at Arjuna with a golden bow and a shower of arrows, and blows his conch to challenge him. Arjuna cuts off Bhishma's umbrella and banner, and then his horses and drivers, and the two exchange celestial weapons while the Kauravas praise them both.
Arjuna cuts Bhishma's golden bow, and Bhishma takes up another and shoots back. The two trade volleys until no one can tell them apart, and the Gandharva Chitrasena praises both warriors to Indra.
Indra honours both with a shower of flowers. Arjuna cuts Bhishma's bow again and wounds him in the breast with ten arrows, and Bhishma leans on his car, senseless, until his driver takes him away.

Duryodhana attacks Arjuna, wounds him on the forehead, and the two exchange wounds. Arjuna kills Vikarna's huge elephant with an iron arrow, wounds Duryodhana in the breast, and the Kuru warriors flee. Duryodhana turns his chariot to run, and Arjuna shames him, saying a king should not run, and tells him to turn back and show his face.

Duryodhana turns back, and Karna, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Vivingsati, Duhsasana and others advance to surround Arjuna. Arjuna releases a celestial weapon called Sanmohana and blows his conch, which stuns the whole army so that the warriors drop their bows. Arjuna has Uttara take the garments of the fallen, and Bhishma, who is not stunned, attacks and fights him until his steeds are killed.

Bhishma tells Duryodhana that his lapse was shameful and that he should go home to Hastinapura, since Arjuna will not kill for the sake of cowardice. Arjuna then salutes the elders and breaks Duryodhana's jewelled crown with an arrow, and sounds his conch as the Kurus depart, while the gods leave pleased with his feats.
Arjuna drives the recovered cattle home, and a band of frightened Kuru soldiers comes out of the forest, hands joined and hair dishevelled, and calls itself his slave.
Arjuna tells them to go in peace, that he will not kill the afflicted, and gives them his protection.

The soldiers bless Arjuna, and the Kurus cannot match him as he goes back toward Virata's city. Arjuna tells Uttara not to reveal the Pandavas, and to claim the victory himself, since the king might hide in fear if he heard their praise.
Uttara says he could never perform such a feat, and promises not to reveal Arjuna's identity unless asked.

Arjuna returns to the Sami tree, the ape banner dissolves, and Uttara's lion banner is raised again. The weapons are restored to the car, and Arjuna takes up the reins once more, binds his hair in a braid, and enters the city as Vrihannala, Uttara's driver.
On the way, Arjuna asks Uttara to send cowherds ahead with the good news, so that the city can prepare to receive them.

Uttara sends messengers to proclaim the king's victory. The Matsya and Bharata princes return to the Sami tree, dress in the garments they left there, and ride back to the city with Vrihannala as driver.

Virata enters his city in triumph with the four Pandavas, sits on his throne, and receives his subjects. He asks where Uttara has gone, and the women reply that the prince went out alone with Vrihannala to face the six great Kuru warriors.
Virata grieves and sends horses, elephants, chariots and foot-soldiers after his son, saying that a prince with a eunuch as driver is surely dead.
Yudhishthira smiles and says that if Vrihannala is the driver, the Kurus will never take the cattle and Uttara will prevail against all the lords of the earth.
The messengers arrive and report the Kuru defeat, the recovered cattle and Uttara's safe return. Yudhishthira says he is not surprised, since Vrihannala is the driver.
Virata is overjoyed and orders the highways decorated and the gods honoured, and sends out musicians and courtesans to meet his son, with proclamations at the crossroads.

The citizens, with music and hymns, go out to welcome Uttara. Virata calls for the dice, and Kanka says a man whose heart is full of joy should not gamble with a cunning player, but agrees to play if the king wishes.
Virata offers to wager his cows, women and gold, and Kanka warns that gambling brings many evils and recalls how Yudhishthira lost his kingdom at dice.
Virata says his son has defeated the Kurus. Yudhishthira answers that a warrior with Vrihannala as driver will surely conquer.
Virata grows angry, calling Kanka a Brahmana who compares a eunuch with his son, and warns him not to say it again.
Yudhishthira insists that no one in the world can match Vrihannala, and Virata replies that without punishment no one would practise virtue.

Virata strikes Yudhishthira's face with a die and his nose bleeds. Draupadi catches the blood in a golden vessel. Uttara arrives at the gate, and Yudhishthira warns the porter that Uttara must enter alone, since Vrihannala would avenge any bloodshed of Yudhishthira's.
Uttara bows to his father and sees Kanka covered in blood, seated at the edge of the court and attended by the Sairindhri. He asks in alarm who struck him.
Virata says he struck the crooked Brahmana, who deserved more, for praising a person of the third sex while Virata was praising his son.
Uttara warns his father that he must appease Kanka before a Brahmana's curse consumes him.

Kanka says he has long forgiven the blow. Had his blood fallen to the ground, the king and his kingdom would have been destroyed, but he does not blame him, since the powerful often act without reason.

When the bleeding stops, Vrihannala enters and salutes the king and Kanka. Virata praises Uttara as a true son, asks how he could have faced Karna, Bhishma, Drona, Ashvatthaman and Duryodhana, and says he has routed the foe and taken back the kine like prey snatched from a tiger.
Uttara says the cattle were not recovered by him, but by a celestial youth who stopped him from fleeing, took the reins, and challenged Duryodhana to fight for sovereignty or death.
Uttara describes how the youth routed Kripa, Drona, Ashvatthaman, Karna and Bhishma, stripped the Kuru warriors of their garments, and defeated six great car-warriors alone.
Virata asks to see the celestial youth who saved his wealth, so that he may honour him.
Uttara says the youth disappeared after the battle and will probably show himself in a day or two.
Virata does not recognize that the youth is living in his palace in disguise. Arjuna presents the costly garments he has brought to Virata's daughter, and Uttara and his sister are delighted.

On the third day, the five Pandavas enter the palace dressed in white and jewels, and sit on royal thrones in the council hall, shining like sacrificial fires. Virata, filled with anger, rebukes Kanka for sitting in royal seat and dress as though he were a courtier who was once a dice-player.

Arjuna answers with a jesting speech, saying that Kanka deserves the seat of Indra. He praises Yudhishthira's learning, austerity, generosity, wealth, followers and command over the kings, and asks whether such a king does not deserve a royal seat.
Virata asks which of the men is Yudhishthira, which Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, and where the famous Draupadi is, since no one has heard of them since their defeat at dice.

Arjuna names Vallava as Bhima, and recounts his feats such as slaying Rakshasas and killing the Kichakas. He names Nakula as the horse-keeper and Sahadeva as the cowherd, identifies Draupadi as the Sairindhri, and says they lived secretly in the king's house like infants in a womb.
Uttara points out Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins and Krishna by their looks and bearing, describing each in turn.

Uttara describes Arjuna's feats: he slew warriors in the chariot-throng, killed a huge elephant with a single arrow, recovered the kine, deafened him with his conch, and vanquished Bhishma, Drona and Duryodhana.
Virata, feeling he has wronged Yudhishthira, says it is time to propitiate the Pandavas, and offers to give his daughter Uttara to Arjuna.
Uttara says the time has come to worship the illustrious sons of Pandu.
Virata credits Bhima with rescuing him and Arjuna with recovering the cattle, asks the Pandavas to forgive any offence, and says Yudhishthira is virtuous.

Virata makes an alliance, offers his kingdom, treasury and capital to Yudhishthira, embraces the brothers and asks Arjuna to take Uttara's hand. Arjuna, with Yudhishthira's approval, accepts her as a daughter-in-law.
Virata asks why Arjuna will not take his daughter as a wife.

Arjuna says he saw the princess daily in the palace and lived with her for a year, so to remove any suspicion he accepts her as a daughter-in-law for his son Abhimanyu, the favoured nephew of Krishna.
Virata praises Arjuna's words and leaves the next steps to him, saying that whoever has Arjuna as a son-in-law has all his desires fulfilled.

Yudhishthira agrees, and invitations go out to Krishna and the allies, who gather at Upaplavya with their troops. The wedding of Uttara and Abhimanyu is celebrated with dowry of horses, elephants and wealth, Virata offers his kingdom, Yudhishthira gives gifts to the Brahmanas, and the city holds a great festival.
A closing line marks the end of the Virata Parva.

Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati, before the story begins.

Vaisampayana describes the assembled kings in Virata's court, then Krishna's speech on the Pandavas' treatment and his call for an envoy to seek a peaceful settlement; the paragraph ends with Balarama praising Krishna's words.
Balarama's speech: he backs a peaceful settlement, names the elders and princes the envoy should greet, and recalls the dice game as a reason for humility rather than war.
Vaisampayana notes that Satyaki stands up in indignation while Balarama is still speaking.
Satyaki's speech: he calls Balarama's counsel a reflection of his nature, condemns the dice game as an unfair win, and promises to force the Kauravas to yield through war.

Drupada's speech: he doubts Duryodhana will yield, sees a gentle approach as weakness, and lists the kings, by name, whom messengers should summon, along with a priest to carry the message to Dhritarashtra.
Krishna's speech: he sees the Pandavas' cause as just, asks that a peaceful message be sent to the Kauravas first, and warns that Arjuna will act if Duryodhana refuses.
Vaisampayana reports that Virata sends Krishna away with honor, that both sides gather forces across the land, and that Drupada sends his priest to the Kauravas.

Drupada's speech: he ranks living beings, names the priest among the wisest, explains how Dhritarashtra was complicit in the dice cheating, and tells the envoy how to win over the elders and the army before setting out at a lucky hour.
Vaisampayana says that the priest, following Drupada's instructions, sets out for Hastinapura with his disciples to serve the Pandavas.
The Pandava and Kaurava messengers are sent out, Arjuna sets off for Dwaraka, and Duryodhana arrives there first with a few troops and waits while Krishna sleeps; Arjuna comes in after him.

Duryodhana asks Krishna for help, and Krishna replies that both came to him and offers his army or himself unarmed, letting Arjuna choose first. Arjuna chooses Krishna, and Duryodhana takes the army. Balarama then declines to fight for either side.
Duryodhana, though he has lost Krishna, is pleased with the army and gains a further army from Kritavarman. Krishna asks Arjuna why he picked a man who will not fight.
Arjuna explains that Krishna is strong enough to win alone, that he wants the fame of having Krishna on his side, and that he has long wished for Krishna to drive his chariot.
Krishna agrees to be Arjuna's charioteer and says the wish will be granted.
Arjuna and Krishna, along with other leaders of the Dasarha clan, return happily to Yudhishthira.

Salya's huge army marches toward the Pandavas, shaking the earth. Duryodhana, hearing of his approach, arranges lavish entertainment along the route, and Salya is so pleased that he asks to reward the men who built it.
Duryodhana, revealed as the host, asks Salya for a boon: that he lead the entire army.
Salya agrees, and the two men part. Salya goes to meet the Pandavas, greets them warmly, and praises Yudhishthira's virtue and the hardships he endured.

Yudhishthira tells Salya about the boon Duryodhana has won. He asks Salya to be Karna's charioteer in the coming duel with Arjuna and to undermine Karna's confidence. Salya agrees to do so, saying that Destiny rules and that even the gods have suffered.
Yudhishthira asks Salya to explain how Indra and his queen came to endure such great misery.

Salya begins the tale: Twashtri, out of hatred for Indra, makes a three-headed son who practices austerities and eyes Indra's throne. Indra, afraid, sends nymphs to tempt him away from his austerities.
The nymphs agree to try to seduce the three-headed son and so ease Indra's fear.

The nymphs fail, since the son's senses are fully under control. Indra then strikes him down with his thunderbolt, and when the body still looks alive, Indra orders a passing carpenter to cut off the heads. The carpenter objects, Indra insists, and promises the carpenter a share of sacrificial offerings.

The carpenter severs the heads, and birds fly out of each mouth. Twashtri, furious, creates Vritra to kill Indra, and a long battle follows in which Vritra swallows Indra. Indra escapes through a yawn, the gods are defeated, and they finally turn to Vishnu for help.
Indra tells the gods that Vritra has pervaded the universe and that he himself is no longer able to oppose him, so they must seek Vishnu's help.
The gods and sages praise Vishnu and ask for his help. Vishnu advises them to seek peace with Vritra and says he will enter Indra's thunderbolt to secure victory.

The sages approach Vritra and urge him to make friends with Indra. Vritra replies that friendship between enemies is impossible, and the sages argue that friendship with the righteous is always worth seeking.

Vritra agrees to peace on the condition that he not be killed by any material, weapon, or time of day. Indra later finds him at dusk by the sea and kills him with a mass of froth fused with the thunderbolt, with Vishnu inside it. Indra is then overcome by guilt for killing the holy man's son and hides, and the world is left in disorder and without a king.

The gods and sages crown Nahusha as king of heaven despite his protests. His power grows, but he turns to indulgence and demands that Sachi come to him. Sachi asks Vrihaspati for protection, and he promises she will be reunited with Indra, which angers Nahusha.
The gods plead with Nahusha to restrain his anger and give up his designs on another man's wife, but he is blinded by lust and refuses, citing Indra's own past misdeeds.
The gods promise to bring Indra's queen to Nahusha and urge him to calm down.
The gods go to Vrihaspati and ask him to hand Sachi over, and Sachi begs him for protection and deliverance from Nahusha.
Vrihaspati refuses to betray someone who has sought his protection, and he cites a saying of Brahma that anyone who gives up a suppliant will lose protection and be ruined.
The gods ask Vrihaspati for a practical solution, and he advises that Sachi ask Nahusha for time to decide, which will help both her and the gods.
The gods accept this advice, and led by Agni they urge Sachi to go to Nahusha, saying he will soon fall and Indra will regain his rule. Sachi goes to Nahusha, who is pleased by her beauty.
Heading: Section XIII begins.

Sachi asks Nahusha for time to search for Indra and promises to return. The gods consult Vishnu, who tells Indra to perform a horse sacrifice to cleanse himself. Indra does so, shares out his guilt among the natural world, and still fears Nahusha, so he vanishes again. Sachi grieves and invokes Night and the goddess of Divination.

Divination appears to Sachi and offers to lead her to Indra. They journey over mountains and across the sea to a lake, where Sachi finds Indra hidden in a lotus stalk. She describes Nahusha's acts and begs Indra to destroy him and reclaim his throne.
Indra tells Sachi that force will not work against Nahusha and asks her to secretly tell Nahusha that he will yield if carried in a vehicle borne by sages.
Sachi goes to Nahusha, who welcomes her warmly and swears to do as she asks. She then makes her request for a vehicle carried by sages, which Indra has never had before.
Nahusha is flattered, agrees, and boasts of his power, saying the seven sages and other holy men will carry him.
Nahusha harnesses sages to his car, treats them with contempt, and drives them. Sachi goes to Vrihaspati, saying her time is nearly up, and asks him to find Indra quickly.

Vrihaspati reassures Sachi that Nahusha will soon fall. He makes a fire offering and asks Agni to search for Indra. Agni searches everywhere on land and sky, returns, and says the waters are the only place left, which he does not want to enter.
Agni protests that entering water would mean his extinction, and he leaves himself in Vrihaspati's hands. He notes that the sources of the things that conquer others are not overcome by them.
Vrihaspati praises Agni as the mouth of the gods and carrier of offerings, and Agni agrees to enter the waters to find Indra.
Agni finds Indra inside a lotus stalk and reports back. Vrihaspati and the gods go to Indra and praise his past victories, urging him to rise and act once more.
Vrihaspati tells Indra that the human king Nahusha, given the throne by the sages, is causing great trouble.
Indra asks how Nahusha got the throne and what austerities earned him such power.

Vrihaspati explains that the gods, frightened after Indra left, made Nahusha king by giving him their power. Now Nahusha is terrifying, uses the sages to carry him, and his gaze can drain others' strength, so the gods hide from him.

The guardian gods, Kuvera, Yama, Soma and Varuna, arrive and congratulate Indra. They say they fear Nahusha and agree to help if Indra defeats him and they keep their shares of sacrifice. Agni asks for a share too, and Indra agrees.
Indra rewards the guardians, giving Kuvera rule over the Yakshas and wealth, Yama rule over the ancestors, and Varuna rule over the waters.
The sage Agastya arrives while Indra is planning against Nahusha and congratulates Indra on surviving the death of Vritra and the son of Twashtri, and on Nahusha's fall.
Indra welcomes Agastya and offers him the customary water, seat and cow.
Indra asks Agastya to tell how Nahusha was thrown from heaven.

Agastya tells how the sages carrying Nahusha asked whether certain Vedic hymns were valid. Nahusha, blinded by pride, declared them false and kicked Agastya on the head, and Agastya cursed him to become a huge snake for ten thousand years.
The gods, sages, spirits and even the rivers and seas rejoice at Nahusha's downfall and at Indra's survival.

Indra returns to the three worlds on his elephant, with the gods, Agni, Yama and the others, and is reunited with Sachi. He honors the sage Angiras, rules well, and Salya tells Yudhishthira that he too will regain his kingdom, while Karna and Duryodhana will fall, and that the tale brings victory to its listeners.
Yudhishthira thanks Salya and asks him to serve as Karna's charioteer and damp his spirit by praising Arjuna.
Salya agrees to do as Yudhishthira asks and to help in any other way he can.
Salya takes leave of the Pandavas and marches with his army to Duryodhana.

The armies gather: Yuyudhana, Dhrishtaketu, Jayatsena, Drupada, Virata, and many other kings join the Pandavas. Bhagadatta, Salya, Bhurishravas, Kritavarman, Jayadratha, and many others join Duryodhana, and the Kaurava force grows to eleven akshauhinis, too large for Hastinapura, so it spreads across the surrounding regions, where the Pandava priest sees it.

The priest greets Dhritarashtra, Bhishma and Vidura, and asks after the Kauravas before stating the Pandavas' case. He recounts their plunder at dice, their exile and humiliation, and says they desire peace and would rather not destroy the world. He notes their army of seven akshauhinis and the allies that match the Kauravas, and asks the Kauravas to give back what is due.

Bhishma welcomes the priest's words, grants the Pandavas their claim, and praises Arjuna's skill. Karna interrupts with insults, recalls the dice match and the exile, and says the Pandavas must accept their place or face war.
Bhishma tells Karna that his talk is idle and reminds him how Arjuna once beat six warriors alone, and that the Kauravas will be destroyed if they do not follow the priest's advice.
Dhritarashtra calms Bhishma, rebukes Karna, and says he will send Sanjaya to the Pandavas. He honors the priest and sends him back, and then calls Sanjaya to the council.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to go to Upaplavya and greet the Pandavas, praising their virtue, blaming Duryodhana and Karna for the hatred, and listing the Pandava champions, including Arjuna, Bhima, the twins, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Pandya, and the Kekaya princes, whose strength he fears. He admits he fears Yudhishthira's wrath, and asks Sanjaya to visit Krishna and say that Dhritarashtra wants peace, without saying anything that might provoke war.
Sanjaya greets Yudhishthira and asks after his health, the health of his brothers, and Draupadi and her sons, and says that Dhritarashtra has inquired after them.

Yudhishthira returns the greetings and asks after Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, and the women and servants of the household, and whether Brahmins still receive their gifts. He then asks whether the Kauravas remember Arjuna's archery, Bhima's strength, the twins' bravery, and their rescue at Dwaitavana, and concludes that peace cannot be reached while Duryodhana stands in the way.

Sanjaya tells Yudhishthira that the Kauravas are well and that Dhritarashtra regrets the injustice, since he knows that causing internal strife is a great sin. He praises the Pandava heroes, notes that the future is hidden, and asks Yudhishthira to seek a peace that satisfies everyone. He then says he will pass on Dhritarashtra's counsel.
Yudhishthira asks Sanjaya to gather the allied leaders and tell them what Dhritarashtra has sent him to say.

Sanjaya greets the Pandava leaders and their allies, says that Dhritarashtra welcomes peace, and praises the Pandavas' virtue while warning that a war would destroy their family and cannot be justified by its outcome. He notes the strength of the Kaurava side and asks the Pandavas to yield to peace, a wish that Bhishma and Dhritarashtra also share.

Yudhishthira says that peace is better than war and that the Pandavas seek only the happiness that comes from righteousness. He describes the comforts that Dhritarashtra enjoys and says the king has followed his wicked son against the advice of Vidura. He names Duryodhana's counselors and argues that the Kauravas are wrong to think they can keep the kingdom while the Pandava warriors are alive, though he would forgive them and asks for Indraprastha as his share.

Sanjaya urges Yudhishthira to avoid war, arguing that a good name matters more than a kingdom and that living on alms would be better than winning by war. He argues that desire and greed bind people and that virtue is what counts, and he reminds Yudhishthira of his past holy life, of the rites and gifts he has made, and of the cost of war to the elders. He says the Pandavas could have struck earlier, questions why they now choose war, calls wrath a poison, and tells Yudhishthira to yield, saying that giving everything up is better than the path to war.

Yudhishthira agrees that virtue is the highest course but argues that right and wrong can be hard to tell apart, and that duties shift in times of distress. He says he will not gain even heaven by unrighteous means. He asks Krishna, who is wise and well informed, to say whether the Pandavas would be blameworthy for refusing peace and fighting instead, and he notes that his allies follow Krishna's counsel and that he always defers to Krishna.

Krishna's long reply: he wants peace for both families, defends the Pandavas' conduct as lawful, argues that work brings rewards as seen in the gods, sages and the rest of the world, and sets out the duties of each caste. He says the king must punish wrongdoers, that Dhritarashtra has unlawfully seized the Pandava share, and recalls how Draupadi was humiliated and how the Kauravas and Karna stood by. He concludes that he will go to the Kauravas to seek peace, warning that they will be destroyed by the Pandavas if they refuse.
Sanjaya takes leave of Yudhishthira and of Krishna, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Satyaki and Chekitana, asking that all the kings look on him kindly.

Yudhishthira praises Sanjaya as an honest and trusted envoy and sends him off with greetings for the Brahmins, Drona, Ashvatthama, Kripa, Bhishma, Dhritarashtra, Duryodhana, Dussasana, the kings who have joined the Kauravas, the women, servants and others. He ends by telling Sanjaya to tell Duryodhana to return Indraprastha or fight.

Yudhishthira's long message: he tells Sanjaya to speak to the Kaurava elders, asks Dhritarashtra to keep the family together, requests a share of the kingdom from Duryodhana, offers peace for five villages, and says that he is ready for either peace or war.
Sanjaya reaches Hastinapura and asks the gatekeeper to tell Dhritarashtra that he has arrived from the Pandavas, and the gatekeeper goes to inform the king.
Dhritarashtra tells the gatekeeper to admit Sanjaya at once.
Sanjaya enters the chamber, bows to Dhritarashtra, and passes on Yudhishthira's greetings and his enquiry after the king's sons and counselors.
Dhritarashtra blesses Yudhishthira and asks whether he is well with his brothers and counselors.

Sanjaya replies that Yudhishthira is well and virtuous, and that he cares for justice above wealth. He tells Dhritarashtra that his own unjust conduct is shameful and will bring misery on the family, notes that the counselors are determined not to restore the Pandava share, and warns that Arjuna will burn the Kurus. He ends by asking leave to rest, since the council will hear Yudhishthira's message the next morning.
Dhritarashtra sends for Vidura, and the attendant brings Vidura in to the inner chamber, where the king says he is always ready to see him.
Vidura enters with joined hands and offers to do whatever the king needs.
Dhritarashtra admits that Sanjaya has returned and rebuked him, that he does not know Yudhishthira's message, and that his worry has left him burning and unable to sleep.
Vidura says that sleeplessness afflicts thieves, the lustful, the ruined and the weak, and asks whether the king is himself grieving over the wealth of others.

Vidura gives a long discourse on the marks of wise and foolish people, the power of forgiveness, the dangers of pride, greed and anger, and proper conduct for kings. He points out the wrongs done to Yudhishthira and urges the king to return the Pandavas' share of the kingdom, which would bring him credit with gods and men.
Dhritarashtra admits he is sleepless and anxious and asks Vidura to advise him on what would be good for Yudhishthira and for the Kurus.

Vidura says he will speak truthfully, warns against unjust aims, and sets out the marks of a wise king: he must know his own strength, control his senses, and avoid evil counsel. He says the tongue can wound more deeply than any weapon, that the blindness of his sons has clouded their minds, and that Yudhishthira deserves to rule the earth.
Heading: section XXXV begins.
Dhritarashtra asks for more of Vidura's teaching, saying he has not had enough.
Vidura begins a tale in which the maiden Kesini must choose between the Asura Virochana and the Brahmin Sudhanwan, and Virochana boasts that the Asuras are the best of creatures.
Sudhanwan refuses to sit as Virochana's equal, and the two agree to wager their lives on the question of which is superior, taking the matter to Prahlada.

Prahlada declares that Sudhanwan is the superior and that Virochana has lost. He explains that a lie told for gain, whether for cattle, horses or land, brings ruin on one's ancestors and family, and he refuses to lie even to save his son. Sudhanwan spares Virochana's life on condition that he wash the feet of Kesini.

Vidura concludes that a king should never lie for land, that the gods help those who value righteousness, and that the Vedas abandon the deceitful. He lists the sinful acts to avoid, the kinds of people who cannot testify, and the ways character is tested by hardship, and says that a king who favors a person can help that person shine with the eight marks of good character.

Vidura lists the paths of righteousness, the marks of the wise and the foolish, and the ways to act across each day and season of life. He warns that wrongful wealth leaves gaps, that a sinful person is punished for sin, and he ends by urging Dhritarashtra to trust the Pandavas, who depend on him as their father, and not to rely on Duryodhana, Sakuni, Dussasana and Karna.

Vidura tells the tale of the sage son of Atri, who teaches the Sadhyas that patience, restraint and avoiding harsh speech and bad company lead to virtue, and that the slanderer carries the sin of his words.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura what makes a family high.

Vidura says that noble families are marked by asceticism, self-control, study of the Vedas, sacrifice, proper marriage and generosity, and that they decline through quarrels, disrespect to Brahmins and dishonesty. He notes that good conduct matters more than wealth, that true friends are tested by need, and that grief and restless passions weaken a person.
Dhritarashtra admits that he has deceived Yudhishthira and fears that the Pandavas will destroy his sons, and he asks Vidura for words to calm his anxiety.

Vidura urges the king to seek knowledge and self-control and to give up greed, notes that kinsmen are strong when they stay together, and asks him to make peace with the Pandavas and restrain Duryodhana, since strength combined with gentleness brings lasting prosperity.
Vidura lists the seventeen kinds of foolish people, such as those who try to control the uncontrollable or ask for gifts they should not ask for, and notes that Yama's messengers drag them to hell.
Dhritarashtra asks why, if the Vedas give a hundred years of life, people often do not reach that span.
Vidura says that excess pride, talk, eating, anger, pleasure and quarrels are the six swords that cut life short.
Vidura lists the sins equal to killing a Brahmin and the qualities that lead to heaven, such as gratitude, truthfulness and generosity.

Vidura gives long advice: frank counsel is rare and valuable, wealth and family are to be used for protection, gambling leads to quarrels, the king has preferred jackals to lions, and a king should treat his servants and counselors fairly and choose his men with care.

Vidura warns that a break with the Pandavas would bring enmity among the sons, endless anxiety, shame on the Kurus, and joy to their enemies. He again uses the image of the forest and the tigers to plead that the family must be kept together.
Vidura lists five kinds of strength, placing the strength of intellect above arms, counselors, wealth and birth, and warns against trusting the untrustworthy.

Vidura gives long rules on receiving guests, on who should not be welcomed, on guarding wives and the household, on keeping state secrets, choosing ministers, managing enemies, and avoiding pointless quarrels, and he ends by warning that Dhritarashtra's prosperity will fall as Bali's did after he cast off the Pandavas and gave power to Duryodhana.
Dhritarashtra says that man does not control his fortune and is like a wooden doll moved by strings, since the Creator placed him under destiny, and he asks Vidura to continue.
Vidura gives maxims on pleasing others and on sound judgment, then says that Duryodhana should have been abandoned at birth, since the loss of one son would have secured the hundred.
Dhritarashtra says that Vidura's advice is wise but that he cannot abandon his son, and he adds that where there is righteousness there is victory.

Vidura urges the king to help poor relatives, to give the Pandavas a few villages, to undo the wrongs Duryodhana has done, and to keep his family together. He adds long maxims on friendship, forgiveness, perseverance, and the dangers of envy and pride.

Vidura gives a long discourse on pride and modesty, the faults of students and rulers, the dangers of envy and greed, the lasting value of virtue, the soul as a river, the duties of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras, and finally urges that Yudhishthira be restored to the duties of a king.
Dhritarashtra says he agrees with Vidura and inclines toward the Pandavas, but that his mind turns away when he meets Duryodhana, and he concludes that destiny cannot be averted.
Heading: the Sanat-sujata section begins.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to say whatever remains unsaid, since he finds the discourse charming.
Vidura names the ancient sage Sanatsujata, who has taught that there is no death, and says he can resolve all of the king's doubts.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to give the teaching himself, if he has the wisdom.
Vidura declines, saying he was born a Sudra and so should not go further, but he praises the sage's wisdom.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura how he might meet the ancient sage in his present body.
Vaisampayana reports that Vidura calls the sage, who appears. Vidura asks him to explain Dhritarashtra's doubts so that the king can bear loss, gain, sorrow, age and death.
Dhritarashtra, having praised Vidura's words, asks Sanatsujata in private whether there is death, since he has heard that the gods and Asuras practise austerities to avoid it.

Sanatsujata says both views are true: death comes from ignorance, and knowledge brings immortality. He shows how desire, lust and anger lead men to death, while self-control and knowledge free them from it.
Dhritarashtra asks why a learned person should not still practise rituals, since the Vedas promise liberation to those who perform them.

Sanatsujata replies that those who do not know the truth may reach heaven by ritual, but a person who gives up desire and knows the Self attains liberation at once, while ritual alone requires a path that must be kept free of return.
Dhritarashtra asks who the unborn and ancient one is, and how such a being, which pervades all things, can act or feel happiness.
Sanatsujata says the Supreme Soul is the one reality, that the universe springs from it through transformations, and that the Vedas affirm this power of self-transformation.
Dhritarashtra asks whether virtue can overcome vice, or whether virtue can itself be destroyed by vice.
Sanatsujata says both virtue and inaction lead to liberation, but the wise person succeeds through knowledge while the person of action gains merit and must work to remove sin.
Dhritarashtra asks for the ranks of the eternal worlds reached by virtuous Brahmins, and for descriptions of other worlds too, saying he does not want to hear about sinful acts.

Sanatsujata describes the regions reached by different kinds of Brahmins: those who take pride in yoga go to Brahman, those devoted to sacrifice go to the gods, and the learned man who hides his superiority is praised. Those who display their learning to earn food are condemned, and only the one who knows the Supreme and is humble is truly honored.
Dhritarashtra asks what silence means, which kind of silence Sanatsujata prefers, and whether a learned man can reach liberation through it.
Sanatsujata says the Supreme Soul cannot be grasped by the Vedas or by the mind, and so it is called silent, and that it is the source of the sacred syllable Om and of ordinary speech.
Dhritarashtra asks whether a man who knows the Vedas remains tainted when he commits sin.
Sanatsujata says that a person who has not restrained his senses is not saved by any Veda, and that the Vedas abandon the deceitful as young birds leave their nest.
Dhritarashtra asks why Brahmins still claim that the Vedas destroy sin if they cannot save a person without virtue.

Sanatsujata says the universe springs from the Supreme Soul through conditions, that asceticism and sacrifice lead toward it, and that those who only seek worldly fruits must return to the cycle of action.
Dhritarashtra asks why asceticism sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.
Sanatsujata says that asceticism free from faults leads to liberation, while asceticism spoiled by vanity and lack of true devotion fails.
Dhritarashtra asks for an account of the faults that spoil asceticism.

Sanatsujata lists the faults of human beings, including anger, lust, greed, cruelty, envy and slander, along with other wicked acts, and the twelve practices that belong to Brahmins, such as truth, self-control and learning.

Sanatsujata describes the six kinds of renunciation, from not rejoicing in prosperity and giving up rites, to giving up desire, not grieving at failure, not clinging to loved ones, and giving to the deserving.
Sanatsujata says the faults of pride are to be avoided, that self-knowledge has eight virtues, and that truth is the foundation of self-control, renunciation and self-knowledge.
Dhritarashtra asks which view of the Supreme is correct, since some teach one god, some three or four, and some only Brahman.

Sanatsujata says there is only one Brahman, which is truth, and that people split it into many gods out of ignorance. The person who seeks Brahman through truth finds what he needs at home, and those who have knowledge of the Self hold truth as the highest aim.

Sanatsujata says that knowledge bears fruit at once and asceticism later, that reading the Vedas alone does not make a Brahmin, and that the Self cannot be found by looking in any direction. Only one who knows the Self, is established in truth and can settle others' doubts is truly learned, and a Kshatriya who lives by these virtues can also see Brahman.
Dhritarashtra praises the discourse on Brahman and the origin of the universe and asks Sanatsujata to go on with teaching free of worldly desire.

Sanatsujata says that Brahman cannot be reached quickly, and that after the senses are restrained and the will is absorbed into pure intellect, a state free of worldly thought follows, which is attained only through brahmacharya.
Dhritarashtra asks how immortality follows from Brahman, if its knowledge already dwells in the mind and needs no effort to show itself.
Sanatsujata explains that the knowledge is hidden in the mind and is revealed by pure intellect and brahmacharya, and that eminent teachers hold it. He offers to teach it.
Dhritarashtra asks what brahmacharya should be like so that knowledge of Brahman can be reached without great difficulty.

Sanatsujata describes the disciple who lives with his teacher and serves him in body, word and deed, honoring the teacher's family and giving back what he earns. He lists stages of this discipline and says the disciple who goes this way is rewarded with wealth, fame and liberation, while knowledge alone leads to Brahman.
Dhritarashtra asks what colour and shape Brahman has.

Sanatsujata says that Brahman cannot be seen in earth, sky, water, stars, Vedic texts or sacrifices, and that it is the basis of all things, one without duality, and the root from which creatures spring and to which they return.

Sanatsujata lists the twelve grave faults, the six kinds of wicked men, the seven kinds of sinful men, the twelve virtues of a Brahmin, and the eighteen faults of arrogance, and gives six signs of true friendship, including sharing a friend's joy and sorrow and giving even the dearest things when needed. He says that restraint of the senses is asceticism, that sacrifice without knowledge cannot reach immortality, and that the self should be sought in quiet restraint, with the mind kept free of pride and praise. He calls this the only true philosophy.

Sanatsujata describes the primal Seed as pure knowledge that shines in the sun and the luminous bodies, that is seen by yogins with the mental eye, and that gives rise to the elements, the gods, the rivers and the living beings. He describes the body as a chariot, the four states of the Self, and the illusory stream of the world, and he says that the Self, though one, dwells in all, that the enlightened are free of good and bad deeds, and that the Universal Father is in every heart.

Vaisampayana reports that the king spends the night listening to Sanatsujata and Vidura, and that in the morning the kings and Kaurava leaders gather in the splendid hall. Sanjaya arrives in his chariot, greets the assembly, passes on the Pandavas' greetings, and says he will now report the message he was sent to deliver.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya, in front of his son and the kings, what Arjuna said.

Sanjaya relays Arjuna's long reply in the presence of Krishna: he demands the kingdom for Yudhishthira, names each Pandava hero and predicts Duryodhana's repentance in battle, recounts Krishna's past victories, claims divine favor and his own foresight, and warns that if the Kauravas fight they will all perish, though the Pandavas would be content if the Kauravas chose peace.
Heading: section XLIX begins.

Bhishma tells Duryodhana how the gods gathered before Brahma, and how two ancient sages, Nara and Narayana, left the assembly without honoring him. Brahma explains that they are mighty beings who exist to destroy the Asuras.

Bhishma recounts how Nara and Narayana helped Indra in battle, how Arjuna has defeated many foes, and how Krishna and Arjuna are the same two beings born again to fight. He warns that Duryodhana will remember this when he sees them together, and says that only Karna, Shakuni and Dussasana support him.
Karna replies that Bhishma should not speak to him this way, since he has kept his duties as a Kshatriya and will slay the Pandavas.

Bhishma says that Karna is not a sixteenth the equal of the Pandavas, and recalls that Karna was absent when Arjuna stripped the Kauravas of their robes at Virata and when the Gandharvas took Duryodhana captive, and that it was the Pandavas who rescued him.
Drona urges the king to accept peace before the war begins. Dhritarashtra pays no heed and again asks Sanjaya about the Pandavas, and the Kauravas give up hope.
Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira bears the coming strife, goaded by the deceptions of the Kaurava sons, and whether his brothers and sons await his orders.
Sanjaya says the Pandavas and their allies look to Yudhishthira and gather in joy, with cars, herdsmen, and many women coming to see Arjuna in armor.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to list the forces of Dhrishtadyumna, the Somakas and the others arrayed against the Kauravas.
Sanjaya pauses, sighs deeply, and suddenly faints. Vidura tells the assembly that Sanjaya has fallen senseless.
Dhritarashtra suggests that Sanjaya is overcome by the sight of the mighty Pandavas.

Sanjaya recovers and names the Pandava warriors one by one: Dhrishtadyumna, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Shikhandin, Abhimanyu, Yuyudhana, Virata, the sons of Draupadi, Krishna, Drupada and many kings, each set against a specific Kaurava leader.

Dhritarashtra admits he is terrified of Bhima, describes his strength and mace, recalls his childhood rivalry with Duryodhana and the other sons, and mourns the destruction he foresees. He blames the dice match and fate and asks Sanjaya where he can turn, concluding that his sons will be slain and that Bhima and Arjuna will destroy them.

Dhritarashtra says that no warrior can stand against Arjuna with Krishna as his charioteer, that Drona and Karna would not prevail, and that Arjuna's arrows will consume his troops. He recalls Arjuna's victory at Khandava and sees the omens of destruction, which he takes to mean that the Kurus will fall.

Dhritarashtra describes the Pandava allies as eager to die for their cause, names Krishna, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna as formidable, and admits that he fears the wrath of Yudhishthira, Arjuna and the twins. He says he has acted deceitfully toward Yudhishthira, and urges the Kauravas to consider peace, since Yudhishthira would not be indifferent to their distress.

Sanjaya agrees that the Kshatriyas will be destroyed by Arjuna's bow, asks why the king follows his sons' counsel, and says that a father who harms his children is not a father. He recalls how the king laughed at the Pandavas' defeat, how Arjuna rescued the Kauravas from the Gandharvas, how Krishna and Arjuna are unmatched, and how the kings have turned to the Pandavas. He says the king should check Duryodhana and stop his lament.

Duryodhana says there is no need to fear, recalls how Krishna and the allied kings urged Yudhishthira to reclaim the kingdom during the exile, and how he asked Bhishma, Drona and Kripa for counsel and was told to stand firm.
