He notes that the elders promised to defeat any enemy and vowed that Bhishma's strength was unmatched.

Duryodhana boasts that he is unmatched with the mace and expects to kill Bhima with a single blow, lists the Kaurava warriors and the strength of Karna and Bhishma, and says that his eleven akshauhinis are more than the seven the Pandavas command. He says Yudhishthira seeks only five villages and that the Kauravas need not fear.
Duryodhana asks Sanjaya again about the doings of the Pandavas.
Duryodhana asks what Yudhishthira and his allies are doing now that they have an army of seven akshauhinis.
Sanjaya reports that Yudhishthira and his brothers are cheerful, that the twins are fearless, and that Arjuna, testing his new mantras, declared that victory is certain.
Duryodhana, sneering at the Pandavas' defeat at dice, asks what horses are yoked to Arjuna's car and what banners fly on it.

Sanjaya describes the celestial car made by divine artisans, its banner that covers a yojana and bears Hanuman's image, and the heavenly horses given by Chitrasena and Indra to each of the Pandava brothers and the sons of Subhadra and Draupadi.
Dhritarashtra asks who has come to the Pandavas' side and who will fight his son's forces.

Sanjaya lists the allies: Krishna, Satyaki, Chekitana, Drupada with his sons, Virata with his sons, the kings of Magadha and Chedi, and the Kekaya princes. He then lists the assignments, such as Bhishma to Shikhandin, Duryodhana to Bhima, Karna and Jayadratha to Arjuna, and the Kaurava princes to Subhadra's son, and the Pandava army is arranged.
Dhritarashtra despairs, saying the Pandavas with Krishna, Arjuna, Bhima, Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki, Drupada and many others are invincible, and that his foolish sons insist on fighting them.

Duryodhana tells his father that both sides share the same earth, that the Kaurava champions are invincible, and that the Pandavas cannot even look at his troops, so the kings will capture the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra calls his son mad, says that Yudhishthira cannot be beaten, that Bhishma does not want to fight the Pandavas, and asks Sanjaya for news of their movements.

Sanjaya reports Dhrishtadyumna's vow to fight the Kaurava host alone, and Yudhishthira's request that he lead. Dhrishtadyumna sends Sanjaya to tell the Kauravas to yield the kingdom before Arjuna, protected by the gods, destroys them.

Dhritarashtra says Yudhishthira has the strength of a Kshatriya and has lived the life of a brahmachari, urges Duryodhana to give back the Pandavas' share, and says that the Kauravas deem peace just. He blames Karna, Dussasana and Shakuni for pushing his son toward war, and says that none of the elders wants war.

Duryodhana refuses to rely on his elders and declares that he and Karna and Dussasana will fight the Pandavas. He compares the war to a sacrifice with its own altar, weapons and offerings, with Yudhishthira as the victim, and vows that he will not yield even a needle's point of land.

Dhritarashtra disowns Duryodhana, grieves for the kings who follow him, and foresees Bhima and Satyaki breaking the Kaurava ranks, with the elephants and chariots scattered and the army crushed, and urges his son to remember his warning.
Vaisampayana reports that after speaking to the kings, Dhritarashtra turns and asks Sanjaya another question.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him in full what Krishna and Arjuna said.
Sanjaya describes the two heroes in the inner chambers, relays Krishna's warning to the Kuru elders, and quotes Krishna saying no one can match Arjuna, citing the Virata episode; Arjuna then agrees.
Dhritarashtra weighs the two sides, judges the Pandavas stronger, and tells Duryodhana he fears divine help for Arjuna and prefers peace.
Duryodhana argues the gods, free of desire, will not help the Pandavas, then boasts of his power over nature and foes and predicts their defeat at his hands.
Duryodhana asks Sanjaya again to learn what Yudhishthira is planning for war.
Karna vows to slay the Pandavas despite Rama's curse, and Bhishma warns him that Krishna protects Arjuna and that Karna's weapons would fail against him.
Karna admits Krishna's greatness, lays down his weapons, and says he will appear only in the court and not on the battlefield.
Karna leaves, Bhishma laughs at his broken promises and says he lost his virtue by deceiving Rama, and Duryodhana then turns to Bhishma.
Duryodhana says the Pandavas are only men and that he, Karna and Dussasana will kill them, and Vidura replies with a long teaching on self-restraint and its marks.
A hermit asks a fowler why he chases two birds that flew off with his net, and the fowler answers that they will quarrel and fall to him.

The birds quarrel and are caught, which Vidura applies to kinsmen who fight over wealth; he then tells of hunters who died seeking a honey jar guarded by snakes, likens Duryodhana to them, and urges the king to make peace with Yudhishthira.
Dhritarashtra warns Duryodhana that he has misjudged the Pandavas, lists their champions, and urges him to follow the elders and share the kingdom with his cousins.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to report what Arjuna said after Krishna's speech, since he is eager to hear it.
Sanjaya relays Arjuna's message that the assembled kings are doomed and must return Yudhishthira's share or face his arrows, then says he has come back with that message.
Duryodhana pays little heed to Sanjaya and the kings leave, so Dhritarashtra privately asks Sanjaya which side will be destroyed and how strong each is.
Sanjaya refuses to answer in secret for fear of the king's anger, and asks that Vyasa and Gandhari be brought in to hear him.
Vyasa and Gandhari enter the court, and Vyasa tells Sanjaya to tell the king everything he knows about Vasudeva and Arjuna.
Sanjaya describes Arjuna and Krishna as godlike equals, praises Krishna's discus and his past victories, and says Krishna, the Lord of time, will use the Pandavas to destroy Duryodhana's wicked sons.
Dhritarashtra asks how Sanjaya has come to know Madhava as the Supreme Lord when he himself cannot.
Sanjaya answers that the king lacks knowledge while his own is intact, and says he knows Krishna as the source and end of all things.
Dhritarashtra asks what faith lets Sanjaya know Janardana in this way.
Sanjaya says he has no regard for worldly illusion or empty rites, and that his faith has purified him so that he knows Janardana from the scriptures.
Dhritarashtra tells Duryodhana to seek Krishna's protection, calling Sanjaya a trusted friend who can guide him.
Duryodhana says he will not submit to Krishna even if Krishna, allied with Arjuna, destroyed all mankind.
Dhritarashtra calls his son envious, wicked and vain, and says he is set on his own ruin.
Gandhari rebukes Duryodhana for his greed and defiance, and warns that he will be struck down by Bhimasena.
Vyasa tells the king that Sanjaya can lead him to safety, and that people lacking contentment fall into death like blind men led by the blind.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to name the path that would let him attain Hrishikesa and find salvation.
Sanjaya says Krishna cannot be known by one with an uncontrolled mind, that sacrifice without self-control is useless, and that subduing the senses through true wisdom is the path.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him again about Krishna's names, hoping their meaning will help him know the Supreme Being.
Sanjaya lists many of Krishna's names with the meanings given to them, and closes by saying the slayer of Madhu will come to prevent the Kurus' slaughter.
Dhritarashtra envies those who will see Krishna in person, praises him in many epithets, and places himself in his hands.
Heading: names the Bhagwat Yana Parva section.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after Sanjaya went back to the Kurus.
Yudhishthira turns to Krishna, asking him to protect the Pandavas now that Duryodhana has refused their share of the kingdom.
Krishna replies that he is ready to do whatever Yudhishthira asks.

Yudhishthira says Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana have broken faith, recalls the Pandavas' loyal exile, and then dwells at length on the miseries of poverty, the value of wealth, and the role of shame and wisdom in virtue.
Yudhishthira argues that war is sinful and costly to both sides, prefers humiliation to bloodshed, and asks Krishna what would preserve their interests and their virtue.
Vaisampayana says Krishna agrees to go to the Kuru court, hoping to make peace without harming the Pandavas' interests.
Yudhishthira objects that Duryodhana will not heed Krishna and that Krishna should not walk into a hall full of hostile kings.
Krishna replies that going will spare them blame whatever the outcome, and that no kings can stand against him in battle when he is enraged.
Yudhishthira consents, hopes Krishna returns successful, and asks him to speak whatever will benefit the Pandavas.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira that a Kshatriya should not beg, recalls the dice game and Draupadi's humiliation, calls Duryodhana deserving of death, promises to try for peace, and predicts war from the omens.
Bhima urges Krishna to address Duryodhana gently, calls him wicked and hard to teach, warns that war will destroy the Bharatas, and asks the elders to mediate.
Heading: Section LXXV begins.
Krishna laughs at Bhima's plea for peace, recalls his nightly rage and his oath to kill Duryodhana with his mace, and calls his change of heart a sign of fear.
Bhima, stung by Krishna's rebuke, boasts of his unmatched strength, says he could crush the Kshatriyas, and claims he restrains himself only out of compassion for the Bharatas.

Krishna says his words were meant to test Bhima's resolve, explains that human action and fate combine unpredictably, promises to seek peace at court, and says he will drive Arjuna's chariot if war comes.
Arjuna says peace may be possible if properly proposed and urges Krishna to try, then recalls Duryodhana's dice fraud and Draupadi's insult and doubts he will ever act justly.
Krishna says he will try for peace though fate may defeat human effort, calls Duryodhana wicked and expects him to refuse, and rebukes Arjuna for doubting his commitment to the Pandavas.
Nakula says the situation has changed since the exile, the Pandavas now have a great army, and Krishna should begin with mild words and then turn to threats to make Duryodhana afraid.
Sahadeva says war must come and urges Krishna to provoke it, since his anger over Draupadi's insult can only be appeased by Duryodhana's death.
Satyaki agrees that Duryodhana must die, recalls the Pandavas in rags in the forest, and says the warriors assembled all back Sahadeva.
The warriors roar, cry out in praise of Satyaki, and show their eagerness to fight.
Draupadi says Duryodhana cheated the Pandavas, notes that they asked only for five villages, argues that peace is hopeless, and recalls her humiliation in the assembly.
Draupadi grips her braid, recalls Dussasana's hands, and says she will rest only when he is dead; Krishna comforts her and vows the Kauravas will fall.
Arjuna urges Krishna to bring about peace and to tell Duryodhana that refusing good counsel will bring his own ruin.
Krishna agrees to go to Dhritarashtra, aiming for what is righteous and good for all.
At dawn Krishna sets out in his chariot amid auspicious signs, sages and birds blessing him, and the Pandavas and kings following, until Yudhishthira embraces him and begins his instructions.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna to greet and comfort their mother, the elders, Bhishma, Drona and Vidura, and then Arjuna repeats that the kingdom must be returned or the Kshatriyas will be destroyed.
Bhima roars in approval, Krishna drives on, and sages on the road ask him to speak wisely at the assembly they wish to attend.
Ten car-warriors, a thousand foot-soldiers and a thousand horsemen, with attendants and provisions, follow Krishna on his journey to Hastinapura.
Janamejaya asks how Krishna travelled and what omens appeared as he left.
Vaisampayana lists the unsettling omens at Krishna's departure, then describes the welcome he receives along the road and his night's rest at Vrikasthala among honouring Brahmanas.
Dhritarashtra, hearing from spies that Krishna is coming, asks the elders to prepare a grand welcome, and Duryodhana builds pavilions and sends gifts, but Krishna ignores them all.
Dhritarashtra tells Vidura that Krishna will arrive tomorrow and lists the gifts, processions and cleaning of Dussasana's mansion he has ordered in his honour.
Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that his lavish gifts are a deception meant to lure Krishna away from the Pandavas, which cannot work, and urges him to make peace and treat the Pandavas as sons.
Duryodhana says Krishna is devoted to the Pandavas and should not be honoured, since that would look like fear and war is already decided.
Bhishma tells Duryodhana that Krishna cannot be disrespected and urges him to seek peace through Krishna's good offices.
Duryodhana declares his plan to imprison Krishna when he arrives the next morning, so that the Pandavas and Vrishnis will submit, and asks how to do it unnoticed.
Dhritarashtra, pained, forbids the plan, noting that Krishna came as an envoy and has done no wrong.
Bhishma calls Duryodhana wicked, says his hour has come, and refuses to listen to such a sinful man any longer.
Bhishma rises in anger and leaves the place.

Krishna leaves Vrikasthala at dawn, is welcomed by the Kauravas except Duryodhana and the crowds, is honoured in Dhritarashtra's palace, then visits Vidura's house and begins to tell him of the Pandavas.
Krishna visits his aunt Pritha, who embraces him and asks after each of her sons and Draupadi, speaking with tears of their suffering in exile.
Pritha laments the dice game, the exile and the insult to Draupadi, blames her own father for giving her away, and recalls a prophecy that Arjuna would conquer the world.
Pritha sends messages to Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna urging them to act as Kshatriyas and not to live on others' charity, and to avenge Draupadi's insult.
Krishna comforts her, calling her a lady of great virtue and telling her that her sons, though suffering now, will soon prosper and prevail.
Pritha, comforted, tells Krishna to act without guile, praises his truth and lineage, and says his words must be true.
Krishna takes leave of Pritha, walks round her, and departs for Duryodhana's mansion.
Krishna enters Duryodhana's palace, is honoured by the court, and declines the feast Duryodhana offers, asking Krishna why he refuses.
Krishna replies that envoys eat only after their mission succeeds, and Duryodhana complains that his courtesy deserves better and insists he has no quarrel with Krishna.
Krishna says he would never abandon virtue, condemns Duryodhana's hatred of the Pandavas as unreasonable and sinful, and declares he will eat only Vidura's food.
Krishna leaves the palace for Vidura's house, where Drona, Kripa, Bhishma and other Kauravas offer him their homes and wealth.
Krishna thanks them but declines, and after Vidura hosts him, Kunti serves him food, which he shares first with Brahmanas and then with his attendants.
Vidura warns Krishna at night that his visit is ill-judged, since Duryodhana is wicked, overconfident and backed by the kings, and that his counsel will be ignored.
Krishna answers Vidura that although he knows Duryodhana's wickedness, he goes to make peace, since a sincere attempt earns merit and a friend should be pulled back from ruin.
Vaisampayana says Krishna lies down on his soft bed to sleep.
At dawn Krishna bathes, worships the sun, gives gifts to Brahmanas, and receives Duryodhana and Sakuni, who tell him the court is waiting.

Krishna rides in a grand procession through the decorated streets to the Kuru court, where the kings rise to honour him, he greets Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, asks that the Rishis led by Narada be seated, and the assembly falls silent.
Krishna urges Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons, warns that war means wholesale slaughter, and says the Pandavas ask only for their lawful share of the kingdom.
Vaisampayana says the kings silently applaud Krishna's words but none dares speak in front of Duryodhana.
Rama tells the parable of King Dambhodbhava, who, proud of his power, sought battle with the ascetics Nara and Narayana and was turned away by them.
Nara defeats the king with blades of grass and teaches him humility, and Rama tells Duryodhana that Nara and Narayana are now Arjuna and Krishna, urging him to make peace.
Vaisampayana says the sage Kanwa speaks to Duryodhana after the words of Jamadagni's son.
Kanwa says only Vishnu is eternal while all else perishes, urges Duryodhana to make peace and not trust mere strength, and begins the tale of Matali searching for a husband for his daughter Gunakesi.
Matali finds no suitable husband among gods or men, consults his wife, and sets off for the world of the Nagas.
Kanwa says Narada meets Matali on the way, learns his errand, and takes him to Varuna's realm to look for a groom.
Narada describes Varuna's realm, including his son Pushkara, the weapons of defeated Daityas, Vishnu's discus, and a bow said to be the source of Arjuna's Gandiva, and then suggests moving on.

Narada shows Matali the city of Patala and its marvels, including a fire fed by water, the moon's rays, Airavata's rain and an egg of unknown origin, but Matali finds no suitable groom and asks to leave.
Heading: Section C begins.
Narada shows the Danavas' city of Hiranyapura, with its illusions and mighty demons, and Matali refuses to seek a groom among enemies of the gods.
Narada presents the realm of the birds, the sons of Garuda, who feed on snakes and revere Vishnu, names their chiefs, and offers to move on if none suits.
Narada describes Rasatala, the home of Surabhi, mother of cows, whose milk formed the Milky Ocean and whose offspring support the quarters, and quotes an old verse praising the place.
Narada describes Bhogavati, ruled by Vasuki, where Shesha holds up the earth and countless Nagas dwell, and names many of them, inviting Matali to look for a groom.
Matali, looking at a youth who stands beside Aryaka, asks about his parentage and says he would make the best husband for Gunakesi.
Narada tells Matali the youth is Sumukha, grandson of Aryaka, whose father Chikura was killed by Garuda, and Matali says he is pleased to offer his daughter to him.
Narada praises Matali and asks Aryaka to give his grandson Sumukha in marriage to Gunakesi.
Aryaka is torn between joy and sorrow, fearing Garuda, who killed his son and has threatened to devour Sumukha within a month.
Matali proposes taking Sumukha to Indra's court, and the group goes to heaven, where Vishnu is also present and Narada tells the story.
Vishnu asks Indra to grant Sumukha immortality, but Indra gives him only a long life, and Sumukha marries Gunakesi and returns home, pleasing the others.
Garuda, furious that Indra has spared Sumukha, complains of being disgraced and boasts that he is as strong as the king of the gods.
Vishnu presses one arm on Garuda, who collapses under the weight and begs forgiveness; Vishnu pardons him and sets Sumukha on his breast, and the two become friends.
Kanwa warns Duryodhana that he will survive only so long as he avoids battle with the Pandavas, and says Krishna is Vishnu himself, the bearer of the discus.
Duryodhana laughs, slaps his thigh, and says he is what fate made him, dismissing the sage's words.
Janamejaya asks why Duryodhana's friends and elders did not restrain him.
Vaisampayana says that Krishna, Bhishma and Narada all counselled Duryodhana, and that he will now report what they said.
Narada warns against obstinacy and tells the tale of Galava, who kept pressing his teacher Viswamitra for a fee until Viswamitra demanded eight hundred special horses.
Galava, unable to find the eight hundred horses, laments his ingratitude and resolves to seek Vishnu's protection, when his friend Garuda appears and offers to carry him across the sea to help.
Garuda offers to show Galava the eastern quarter, praising it as the source of the sun, the Vedas and the gods' prosperity, and asks whether another direction would suit him better.

Garuda describes the southern quarter, home of the ancestors and of Yama's realm, with its tales of ancient kings and sages, its river of the dead and the city of Bhogavati, and asks whether Galava wants to go there or hear of the west.
Garuda describes the western quarter, Varuna's realm where the sun sets and the sea begins, and where Vishnu, Kasyapa and other figures dwell, and asks which way Galava would choose.
Garuda describes the northern quarter as the most sacred direction, where Krishna and Arjuna dwell at Vadari, Shiva rests on Himavat, and the Ganges falls from heaven, and lists many marvels there.

Garuda describes the sages who guard the Ganges' source, Vishnu's footprint, King Marutta's sacrifice and the gold mines of Himavat, then says the north is superior to every other quarter and offers to show Galava all of them.
Galava asks Garuda to carry him to the eastern quarter, where the gods and virtue are said to dwell.
Galava, riding on Garuda's back, praises his speed, describes the storm and the sea creatures, begs him to slow down, and says he has no wealth to pay his pledge and sees only death ahead.
Garuda laughs, says death is ordained by God and cannot be brought on by effort, and proposes they rest on Mount Rishabha.

Garuda and Galava rest on Rishabha and eat Sandili's food, then wake to find Garuda's wings gone; after he admits he wanted to carry her off, Sandili forgives him and restores his wings, and when the steeds cannot be found, Viswamitra demands his fee again.
Garuda explains that wealth must be sought from a king, proposes King Yayati of Pratisthana, and when they reach his court, Yayati welcomes them and hears Galava's story of his debt to Viswamitra.

Yayati, though poorer than Garuda supposes, gives his daughter Madhavi to Galava to pay the debt; Garuda departs, and Galava takes her to King Haryyaswa of Ayodhya, asking him to accept her with a dower.
Narada describes Haryyaswa's admiration of Madhavi's beauty and his question about her dower, and Galava's demand for eight hundred steeds.
Haryyaswa says he has only two hundred of the steeds; Madhavi proposes four kings give steeds for four sons, and Galava agrees to a fourth of the dower for one son, who is born as Vasumanas.
When Galava returns for the balance, Haryyaswa cannot make up the six hundred steeds, returns Madhavi, and Galava takes her on to King Divodasa.
Galava introduces Madhavi to Divodasa, king of Kasi, and asks him to beget a child by her.

Divodasa agrees to father one son, says his wealth cannot cover the steeds, and Narada lists many divine and royal couples; Madhavi bears Pratardana, and when Galava returns, Divodasa gives her back as promised.
Galava takes Madhavi to King Usinara of the Bhojas, who agrees to father one son, Sivi, in return for part of the steeds, after which Galava takes her back and goes to see Garuda.

Garuda tells Galava the missing steeds cannot be found, so he should offer Madhavi to Viswamitra, who accepts her, fathers Ashtaka and takes the six hundred steeds, after which Galava returns her to her father and goes into the woods.
Yayati brings Madhavi to a swayamvara at a sacred hermitage, where she passes over all suitors and chooses the forest as her lord, living as an ascetic like a deer.
After many thousands of years, Yayati grows proud in heaven, disregards the gods and sages, and when questioned, none recognises him, and he loses his splendour.
Yayati is hurled from heaven, wishes to fall among the righteous, and lands among four kings holding a sacrifice in Naimisha, who ask who he is.
Madhavi arrives, is greeted as mother by the four kings, tells Yayati her sons will save him, and Galava offers an eighth of his austerities to help him back to heaven.
Yayati rises back to heaven as each of his grandsons, Vasumanas, Pratardana, Sivi and Ashtaka, gives him the merit of his good deeds, and they declare themselves his daughter's sons.
Yayati returns to heaven with honours and asks why his merit was exhausted, and Brahma replies that vanity alone caused his fall and warns against pride and contempt for others.
Narada tells Duryodhana that Yayati's vanity and Galava's obstinacy both led to ruin, and urges him to abandon pride and wrath and make peace with the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra tells Narada he agrees with the counsel but cannot make his son follow it.

Dhritarashtra asks Krishna to persuade Duryodhana, and Krishna warns him at length to make peace with the Pandavas, obey his father, drop his reliance on weak allies, and recognise that no one can beat Arjuna.
Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to accept Krishna's counsel and make peace, warning that Arjuna is greater than any man and that the Pandavas cannot be defeated.
Vidura grieves for the aged parents, who would be left to beg if Duryodhana persists, and Dhritarashtra begs his son to be reconciled with Yudhishthira through Krishna.
Bhishma and Drona plead again, listing the disasters of war that have not yet begun, and urge Duryodhana to make peace while there is still time, embracing the Pandavas as brothers.

Duryodhana angrily answers Krishna that the Pandavas accepted the dice game, that he will not bow to them or give back even a needle's point of land while his father lives, and that a Kshatriya should die on the battlefield rather than yield.
Krishna rebukes Duryodhana for the dice game, the insult to Draupadi, and the plots to burn and poison the Pandavas, and urges him to give them their share.
Dussasana tells Duryodhana that if he will not make peace, the Kauravas will bind him and hand him over to the Pandavas.

Duryodhana storms out with his brothers and counsellors, Bhishma says his enemies will rejoice, and Krishna urges the elders to bind him, citing the defeat of the Daityas and Kansa, and to make peace.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to fetch Gandhari, hoping she can persuade their son to make peace.
Gandhari blames Dhritarashtra for indulging their son and asks that Duryodhana be brought before her without delay.
Vidura brings Duryodhana back into the court, angry and breathing hard, and Gandhari rebukes him for treading the wrong path.
Gandhari urges Duryodhana at length to obey his father and elders, master his lust and wrath, make peace with the Pandavas, and accept Krishna's protection.
Heading: Section CXXX begins.
Duryodhana and his allies plot to seize Krishna, Satyaki learns of it and warns Krishna and the elders, and Krishna says he will not stoop to violence even if they try.
Dhritarashtra orders Vidura to bring Duryodhana back into the court to make one more attempt at persuading him.
Dhritarashtra rebukes Duryodhana, calling his plan an infamous folly that no one, not even the gods, could carry out against Krishna.
Vidura recalls Krishna's past feats, from the attack at Saubha to the defeat of Naraka and Kansa, to show that no one can seize him by force.
Krishna mocks Duryodhana, reveals a dazzling universal form filled with gods and heroes that terrifies the kings, and then Dhritarashtra protests his good faith.
Krishna takes leave of Dhritarashtra and the elders, mounts his chariot, and drives to the house of his aunt Kunti in view of the Kurus.
Krishna reports to Kunti that the court has refused peace and asks what message she would like him to take to the Pandavas.
Kunti tells Krishna to urge Yudhishthira to fight as a Kshatriya, citing Muchukunda and the king's power over the age, and warns him against living on alms.
Kunti introduces an old tale of Vidula and her son and says Yudhishthira should learn from it.
Vidula, a proud and learned woman, scolds her son for lying defeated after losing to the king of the Sindhus, calls him a coward, and urges him to rise and fight.
The son says the earth and life mean nothing to him without his mother's favour, and Vidula replies that a true man supports his friends by his own prowess and lives by his own strength.

Vidula continues to scold her son, telling him that a Kshatriya who avoids battle is like a thief, recalling a Brahmana's prophecy of his future greatness, and urging him to fight bravely, since sovereignty is the door to heaven.
The son replies to his mother, calling her harsh and asking what use the earth and his life would be to her without him.
The mother replies that the wise act for virtue and profit, that a Kshatriya is made for battle, and that a son who shirks action brings shame.
The son asks his mother to show him kindness and to stop speaking so harshly.
The mother says she is pleased to hear it and will keep urging him until he wins.
The son says he has no wealth or allies and asks his mother to tell him the means of success.

The mother urges him that failure is no reason to despair, that he must rally the angry, weakened and humbled to his side with gifts and kind words, since a king who joins his foe can never regain his kingdom.
Vidula tells her son that a king in distress must not give up, that his friends remain loyal, and that she will give him hidden treasure and faithful allies.
Kunti says her son's despair lifts, and he vows to rescue his kingdom or die in the attempt, while keeping his mother's words in mind.
Kunti says a minister should read this tale of Jaya to any king in distress, as it breeds courage and a brave son for any mother who listens.

Kunti asks Krishna to deliver her message: a celestial voice foretold Arjuna's victory, Bhima and the Pandavas should act as warriors, Draupadi's insult must be remembered, and Krishna should protect her sons.
Krishna takes leave of Kunti, dismisses the Kuru chiefs, takes Karna on his chariot, and the Kurus marvel at what they have seen and blame Duryodhana's folly.
Krishna talks with Karna on the road, sends him back, and his fast steeds carry him to Upaplavya.

Bhishma and Drona warn Duryodhana that the Pandavas will not give up without their share, list Arjuna's past feats and the omens of ruin, and beg him to make peace and embrace Yudhishthira and his brothers.
Duryodhana says nothing and looks cheerless, and Bhishma and Drona exchange glances before speaking again.
Bhishma says it grieves him to fight Yudhishthira, who serves his elders, is free of envy, and speaks the truth.
Drona says he loves Arjuna more than his own son, laments that his duty forces him to fight him, and urges Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, whose allies are formidable.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Krishna said to Karna as he took him out of the city.
Sanjaya agrees to repeat Krishna's words exactly, both the stern and the gentle parts.
Krishna tells Karna he is by birth the son of Kunti and Pandu's eldest, so he should join the Pandavas and be crowned king, with Yudhishthira as his heir, and the Pandavas and Vrishnis serving him.

Karna thanks Krishna, explains that he was raised by Adhiratha and is tied to Duryodhana, and asks Krishna to keep their talk secret, since Yudhishthira would refuse a kingdom if he knew. He then describes the coming battle as a great sacrifice, with Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira, the twins and others as its priests, and the slaughter and final bath as its rites.
Karna prays that the Kshatriyas perish at Kurukshetra and asks Krishna to bring Arjuna before him for battle, keeping their discussion a secret.

Krishna answers Karna that victory is certain for the Pandavas, describes Arjuna's banner and the signs of their triumph, and sends word to Drona, Bhishma and Kripa that the battle should begin on the new moon.
Karna tells Krishna that a great slaughter is coming, and lists omens of defeat for the Kauravas, from the planets and the animals to the birds, drums and the sky.
Karna describes a vision in which the Pandavas rule the earth and Bhima devours it with his mace, Arjuna sits on a white elephant, and the Kurus are consumed in the fire of Gandiva.
Krishna replies that when a man's heart cannot accept right counsel, the destruction of all creatures is near.
Karna answers that they will meet again if they survive the battle, or else in heaven.
Sanjaya reports that Karna embraced Krishna, descended from his car when dismissed, and rode back in deep dejection.
Vidura tells Kunti that Duryodhana refuses peace, that the Pandavas are waiting at Upaplavya, and that war now looms over the Kurus.

Kunti laments the coming war, recalls the mantra Durvasa gave her and how she summoned Surya in girlhood, then goes to the Ganga and stands in the shade of Karna's garment while he finishes his prayers to the sun.
Karna introduces himself as the son of Radha and Adhiratha and asks what Kunti wants him to do.
Kunti tells Karna he is her son by Surya, not Radha's, born with his natural armour in her father's palace, and urges him to join the Pandavas as a true Partha and take his place among his brothers.
A voice from the sun, which the text says is Surya's, tells Karna to follow his mother's words.
Karna refuses, listing his grievances against Kunti and his duty to the Kauravas, and promises to fight Arjuna while sparing the other Pandavas for now.
Kunti embraces him, says the Kauravas will fall by fate anyway, and asks him to keep his pledge in mind in battle; they part with blessings.
Krishna returns to Upaplavya and reports to the Pandavas, who meet after sunset and ask him to repeat what he said to Duryodhana.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna to recall exactly what Bhishma, Drona, Dhritarashtra, Vidura, and the other kings said in the assembly.
Krishna repeats Bhishma's speech, which tells how Duryodhana laughed at his words, recounts the royal family's history, and urges Duryodhana to give half the kingdom to the Pandavas.
Drona speaks after Bhishma, citing the righteous rule of Pandu and Bhishma, and tells Duryodhana to give the Pandavas half the kingdom.
Vidura turns to Bhishma, blames him for tolerating Duryodhana's greed, and warns that the Kuru line and many kings face destruction.
Vidura falls silent in sorrow, and Suvala's daughter speaks in anger, telling Duryodhana that the kingdom passes by right to Pandu's sons.
Dhritarashtra addresses Duryodhana with a long genealogy of passed-over heirs, then argues that Yudhishthira rightly holds the kingdom and urges Duryodhana to share half of it.

Krishna reports Duryodhana's angry exit, his order to march to Kurukshetra, Bhishma's command of eleven akshauhinis, and his own failed attempts at conciliation, division, and a five-village offer, ending with the view that war is inevitable.
Yudhishthira reports the assembly's outcome, lists seven possible leaders for his seven akshauhinis, and asks Sahadeva to name the best commander.
Sahadeva proposes Virata, the Matsya king, as a strong ally who can withstand Bhishma.
Nakula proposes Drupada, the father-in-law of the Pandavas, for his experience, learning, and skill with celestial weapons.
Arjuna proposes Dhrishtadyumna, born to destroy Drona, as the only warrior able to stand against Bhishma's arrows.
Bhima proposes Sikhandin, whom he sees as the one warrior who can slay Bhishma in single combat.
Yudhishthira says Krishna knows everyone's strengths and weaknesses, so the leader should be whomever Krishna names, and that the army will march at dawn after worship.
Krishna approves all the proposed warriors and names Dhrishtadyumna as the commander, adding that Duryodhana will not hold out against the Pandavas.

The army marches out in order, with Bhima and the twins at the front, Yudhishthira in the centre with his baggage and attendants, and Draupadi left behind at Upaplavya; they blow conches on reaching the field, and the noise fills the sky.

Yudhishthira chooses a clean site for the camp and Krishna and Arjuna scout the ground, and Krishna has a moat dug by the Hiranwati, with tents and stores for the allied kings, and mechanics and physicians set up; allied kings arrive to support the Pandavas.
Heading: the next section, Section CLIV, begins.
Janamejaya asks what measures Duryodhana took after learning that the Pandavas had camped on Kurukshetra with their many allies, and asks to hear every detail.

Duryodhana tells Karna, Dussasana, and Sakuni to prepare camps and a road, the kings arm and dress for battle, and the capital takes on a war-time air, which the narrator likens to the ocean under the rising moon.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna how to act, given what Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni, Vidura, Bhishma, and Kunti have said.
Krishna answers that Duryodhana is wicked and ignores all counsel, and that the Pandavas will not give up their property, so war must take place.
The kings look to Yudhishthira, who orders the army drawn up, and then laments that he must fight elders and teachers whom he cannot slay in good conscience.
Arjuna repeats Krishna's words to Yudhishthira, says he trusts Vidura and Kunti, and insists they cannot withdraw without fighting.
Krishna agrees, and the Pandavas resolve on war and spend the night with their soldiers in good spirits.

Duryodhana sorts his troops into three grades and equips his cars, elephants, horses, and foot soldiers with a long list of weapons and supplies, and the narrator defines the military units from a sena up to a vahini.

The narrator gives the total of eighteen akshauhinis, defines the smaller units, and says Duryodhana appoints Kripa, Drona, Salya, Karna, and others to lead the eleven divisions and honors them daily.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma to lead, arguing that an army needs one commander and recalling a story of Brahmanas who won against Kshatriyas once they chose a single leader.
Bhishma agrees to lead but says he loves the Pandavas, that Arjuna will never fight him openly, and that he will kill ten thousand warriors a day, and he asks that either Karna or he fight first.
Karna vows he will not fight while Bhishma lives, and will fight Arjuna only after Bhishma falls.
Duryodhana installs Bhishma with gifts, and the narrator lists the omens that follow, then describes the Kuru camp on the plain of Kurukshetra.
Janamejaya asks what Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, and Krishna said on learning that Bhishma had been installed as commander.
Yudhishthira summons his brothers and Krishna, tells them to inspect the troops in armour, says the first clash will be with their grandsire, and orders seven leaders chosen.
Krishna approves Yudhishthira's words and asks him to name seven leaders.
Yudhishthira names seven leaders, puts Dhrishtadyumna over all troops, and makes Arjuna the chief of the leaders, with Krishna as his charioteer.
Balarama arrives with his Vrishni companions, the Pandavas honor him, and he says the slaughter is fated and that he will go on pilgrimage to avoid watching the Kauravas destroyed.
Balarama takes leave of the Pandavas and Krishna, and sets out on his journey to the sacred waters.

Rukmi, Bhishmaka's son and master of the bow Vijaya, arrives with an army, recalls his feud with Krishna over Rukmini, offers to kill Drona, Kripa, Bhishma, and Karna for Arjuna, and Arjuna declines and Duryodhana also refuses him.
Rama and Rukmi have both withdrawn, and the Pandavas sit down again to consult, with Yudhishthira presiding over the assembled kings.
Janamejaya asks what the Kauravas did once their soldiers stood arrayed on the field, urged on by destiny.
The narrator says Dhritarashtra then turns to Sanjaya to ask for the news.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for full details, says he understands war will bring ruin but cannot restrain Duryodhana, and calls a warrior's death in battle a Kshatriya's duty.

Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra not to blame Duryodhana alone, notes the Pandavas patiently bore their wrongs, and sets out three views on whether acts are ordained, freely chosen, or shaped by past lives.
Heading: the section called the Uluka embassy begins.
Duryodhana sends Uluka to Yudhishthira with a message calling him a hypocrite, telling the parable of a cat that won the mice's trust and then ate them, and urging him to act like a warrior.
The message to Krishna mocks his tricks and illusions, reminds him of his boast that Dhritarashtra's sons would be slain, and dares him to fight Arjuna openly.
The message to Bhima taunts him as a cook in Virata's court and challenges him to fulfil his vow to drink Dussasana's blood.
The message to Nakula urges him to fight and to show his hatred for Duryodhana, and to recall the suffering Krishna endured.
The message to Sahadeva tells him to fight with all his strength and remember his woes.
The message to Virata and Drupada says masters never fully understand servants and servants never fully understand masters, and urges the two kings to fight Duryodhana together.
The message to Dhrishtadyumna tells him that his hour has come and that he should face Drona in battle.
The message to Sikhandin says Bhishma will not kill him because he sees him as a woman, and urges him to fight without fear.
Duryodhana laughs and sends a final challenge to Arjuna, mocking his boasts, recalling their exile, and listing the kings and commanders on his side as an army no one can beat.
Uluka presents himself to the Pandavas and asks not to be blamed, since he will repeat only the words Duryodhana gave him.
Yudhishthira tells Uluka to speak freely, and Uluka delivers the message before the Pandavas, Srinjayas, Krishna, Drupada, Virata, and the other kings.
Uluka recites Duryodhana's taunts, recalling the dice loss, the exile, Krishna's humiliation, and Bhima's vow, and boasts that Drona and Bhishma cannot be defeated.
Uluka turns to Arjuna, telling him to stop boasting, reminding him of his past humiliation, and describing the Kaurava army as too great to defeat.
The Pandavas grow enraged, Krishna tells Uluka to leave, and Bhima vows to drink Dussasana's blood and to kill Duryodhana's brothers.
Sahadeva warns Uluka that he will kill him in front of Sakuni, and then kill Sakuni, blaming Dhritarashtra's family for the quarrel.
Arjuna says Uluka should not be harshly treated for carrying messages, and says he will answer Duryodhana with his bow the next day.
The kings praise Arjuna's reply, and Yudhishthira prepares to answer the challenge himself.
Yudhishthira rebukes Duryodhana as crooked and cowardly, calls him a man who relies on others' strength, and challenges him to fight in person.
Krishna says he will serve only as Arjuna's charioteer, and warns Duryodhana that even if he flees to the ends of the earth he will see Arjuna's car.
Arjuna answers Uluka that Duryodhana hides behind Bhishma, and vows to kill Bhishma before the eyes of all the Kurus the next day, and tells Uluka to deliver the answer.
Bhima repeats his vow to drink Dussasana's blood and says he will strike Duryodhana's head with his foot.
Nakula replies briefly that the words have been heard, and that he will do what Duryodhana urged.
Sahadeva says Duryodhana will repent with his children, kinsmen, and counsellors for boasting over the Pandavas' suffering.
Virata and Drupada say they would gladly be the slaves of a virtuous man, and that who is slave or master will be known tomorrow.
Sikhandin vows to kill Bhishma from his car in front of the bowmen, saying he was created for that purpose.
Dhrishtadyumna vows to kill Drona together with his followers and to do a deed no one else will do.
Yudhishthira says he does not want to kill his kinsmen, blames Duryodhana for the war, and asks Uluka to leave.
Uluka returns and reports every reply to Duryodhana, who orders his troops arrayed before sunrise, and messengers spread the order through the camp.
Dhrishtadyumna leads the Pandava army, pairs his warriors against the main Kaurava champions, takes Drona for himself, and waits for battle with a steady heart.
Dhritarashtra laments that he already sees Bhishma, his elder, slain by Arjuna, and asks what his sons and Bhishma did after the vow.
Sanjaya says he will report everything Bhishma said.
Bhishma takes command and tells Duryodhana that he knows the arts of war and will protect his army and dispel his fears.
Duryodhana says he fears nothing with Bhishma and Drona leading, and asks Bhishma to name which warriors on each side are rathas and atirathas.
Bhishma begins with Duryodhana's brothers, the foremost rathas, then names Kritavarman, Salya, Bhurisravas, and Jayadratha as the leading fighters on the Kaurava side.

Bhishma continues the ranking, naming Sudakshina, Nila, Vinda and Anuvinda, the five Trigarta brothers, Lakshmana, Dussasana's son, Dandadhara, Vrihadvala, and Kripa, and says how each will fight the Pandavas.

Bhishma ranks Sakuni, Ashvatthama, Drona, Vrihadvala, Vrishasena, Jalasandha, Vahlika, Satyavan, Alambhusha, and Bhagadatta, noting Ashvatthama's skill and his fondness for life, and Drona's affection for Arjuna, which Bhishma thinks will keep Drona from killing him.
Bhishma calls Karna only half a ratha and predicts he will not survive facing Arjuna; Drona agrees, saying Karna boasts before battle and then retreats.

Karna answers angrily, accusing Bhishma of hostility toward him and of disparaging the kings, and vows not to fight while Bhishma lives, and to fight the rest of the Maharathas only after Bhishma falls.
Bhishma says he will carry the burden of the battle himself, that he will not stir up quarrels now, and that Karna lives only because Bhishma does not want discord.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma and Drona to name the best enemy atirathas and the leaders of the car divisions, with their strengths and weaknesses, since the battle begins at dawn.
Bhishma goes on to rank the Pandava warriors, praising each brother's strength, saying Arjuna cannot be matched on the field, and noting that he and Drona are old.
The narrator says the kings hearing Bhishma's words grow fearful, as their arms hang weak while they recall the Pandavas' past valour.
Bhishma rates Draupadi's five sons as maharathas, Uttara and Abhimanyu as strong fighters, and Satyaki, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu, Virata, and Drupada as warriors who will fight hard for Kunti's sons.
Bhishma gives ratings for Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Kshattradharman, Dhrishtaketu, and many other Pandava allies, from half-rathas to atirathas, ending with Srenimat and Vasudeva.
Bhishma rates Rochamana, Kuntibhoja, and Ghatotkacha, Bhima's rakshasa son, as strong fighters on the Pandava side.
Bhishma says the Pandava leaders are assembled, that he will face them with illusions and a fierce will, and that he will advance against Krishna and Arjuna.
Bhishma states he will spare Sikhandin, recalling that he gave up the throne and vowed never to slay a woman, and noting that Sikhandin was born a daughter who later became male.
Duryodhana asks why Bhishma will not kill Sikhandin when he comes at him with arms raised, reminding him of his old vow to slay the Panchalas.

Bhishma recounts the history of his father Santanu, his vows, the installation of his brothers, and how he took the three princesses of Kasi by force from a gathering of kings, defeating their pursuit, and brought them to Satyavati.
Bhishma tells Satyavati about the abduction, she greets his victory with tears of joy, and at the nuptials Amba explains she had chosen the king of Salwa and begs Bhishma to let her go.
Bhishma consults his mother and counsellors and lets Amba travel to Salwa's city, where Salwa laughs at her and refuses to take her, and Amba pleads that she never wanted Bhishma.
Salwa repeats his refusal, saying he is afraid of Bhishma, and Amba leaves the city sobbing like a bird in grief.
Amba laments her fate, blames Bhishma, her father, Salwa, and herself, vows vengeance on Bhishma, and goes to an ascetics' hermitage, where she tells the sages what happened.
The learned Brahmana Saikhavatya comforts Amba with examples and reasons from the scriptures, and promises, with the other Brahmanas, to do what she asks.
Running head reading The Mahabharata, with no content.
The ascetics debate Amba's fate, with some urging her to go to her father, some urging her to ask Salwa again, and some advising against it, since Salwa has rejected her.
Amba says she cannot go back to Kasi, where her relatives would scorn her, and wants to practise austerities among the ascetics.
King Hotravahana, her maternal grandfather, arrives, pities her, and sends her to Rama, son of Jamadagni, who can end her sorrow and even slay Bhishma if he refuses.
Hotravahana tells Akritavrana, Rama's friend, the whole story of Amba's abduction and rejection, and Amba agrees to go to Rama.
Akritavrana asks whether Amba wants Salwa to marry her or Bhishma to be beaten in battle, and Amba says Bhishma acted without knowing her heart belonged to Salwa.
Akritavrana says Bhishma's seizure is the cause of Salwa's suspicion, so vengeance should fall on Bhishma, and Amba agrees she wants Bhishma slain.
Rama arrives with his disciples, a sage in matted hair and deerskins with bow, sword, and axe, and the ascetics honor him; Hotravahana presents Amba to him.
Amba bows at Rama's feet, weeps, asks for his protection, and begs him to lift her from her sorrow.
Rama is moved by her grief, promises to send word to Bhishma and to fight him if he refuses, and Amba insists that Bhishma be slain as Indra slew Vritra.
Rama tells Amba that he takes up arms only at the command of Brahmanas, but that he will act for her since Bhishma and Salwa both obey him.
Amba asks Rama to slay Bhishma without delay, since Bhishma is the cause of her misery.
Rama offers that Bhishma will, at his word, lay his head at Amba's feet.
Amba insists that Rama slay Bhishma in battle, as he is roaring like an asura, and keep his promise.
Akritavrana reminds Rama of his vow to slay any foe of the Brahmanas and to shield those seeking protection, and urges him to fight Bhishma.
Rama agrees to take Amba to Bhishma, to slay him if Bhishma refuses to obey, and the company travels to Kurukshetra and camps on the banks of the Saraswati.
Bhishma recounts that Rama arrived in his kingdom, and he went out with a cow, Brahmanas, and priests to greet him and offer worship.
Rama asks why Bhishma abducted Amba and then sent her away, says no one will now marry her, and orders Bhishma to take her as his own wife.
Bhishma refuses, saying he cannot give her to his brother and will keep his vow; Rama threatens to slay him, and Bhishma, once Rama's pupil, accepts a duel at Kurukshetra.
Rama laughingly accepts, and Bhishma sets out in a white chariot, but his mother Ganga appears and begs him not to fight his teacher, which he refuses.
Ganga pleads with Rama, who sends her back to Bhishma, and Bhishma still refuses; Rama then appears before him, ready to fight.

Bhishma offers to fight Rama fairly on foot, and Rama answers that the earth is his car and the Vedas his horses, then covers Bhishma with arrows; Bhishma dismounts, bows to his teacher, and asks for his blessing.

Rama wishes him well but says he will defeat him; Rama first wounds Bhishma heavily, then Bhishma cuts Rama's bow and shoots him, sparing his brahminical status, and at sunset Bhishma halts, lamenting that he has harmed his teacher.
The duel resumes at dawn, both trade celestial weapons, Rama wounds Bhishma into a swoon, Bhishma wounds Rama in turn, and the arrows fill the sky until the fight stops at evening.

On the next day the combat grows fiercer, with both men using celestial weapons; Bhishma cuts Rama's lance and darts, Rama breaks Bhishma's chariot, Bhishma wounds his preceptor, and the fight ends when the sun sets.

The next morning the fight resumes; Rama's arrows kill Bhishma's charioteer and knock Bhishma down, eight Brahmanas raise him and his mother Ganga drives his chariot, Bhishma wounds Rama into unconsciousness, omens appear, and the battle lasts twenty-three days.

Unable to defeat Rama, Bhishma prays that the gods show him a sign, and in a dream the eight Brahmanas promise he will win and reveal the Praswapa weapon, which puts a foe to sleep, and the Samvodhana, which wakes him.

Bhishma resumes the fight with new confidence, Rama's dart wounds him on the shoulder, Bhishma's arrow wounds Rama, the two invoke the Brahma weapon until the world burns, and Bhishma resolves to use the Praswapa.

Narada and the gods warn Bhishma not to use the Praswapa, since Rama is his teacher and a Brahmana; Bhishma withdraws it, Rama admits defeat, and his ancestors urge him to stop fighting and to take up ascetic life.
Rama refuses to yield at first, but the sages, the forefathers, and the Pitris urge both men to stop; Rama lays down his weapons, Bhishma worships him, and Rama praises him and summons Amba.

Rama admits he could not defeat Bhishma and tells Amba to seek his protection; Amba vows to kill Bhishma and goes off to penance, Bhishma has spies track her, Narada and Vyasa tell him not to grieve, and Amba performs severe penances for years at many holy places until Ganga tells her she will become a river, with half of her still a maiden.

Amba tells the ascetics she is driven only by her wish to destroy Bhishma; the god promises she will kill him and be reborn as a warrior and then a man; she builds a pyre by the Yamuna and burns herself, crying out for Bhishma's destruction.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma how Sikhandin, born a daughter, later became a man.

Bhishma explains that the childless Drupada prayed to Shiva for a son to avenge himself on Bhishma, and was told the child would be a daughter who later becomes male; the queen gave birth to a daughter, whom Drupada had raised as a son and named Sikhandin, while only a few people knew the truth, and Bhishma learned it through his spies and Narada.

Drupada has his daughter Sikhandin taught the arts and arms under Drona, and the queen and king arrange a marriage with Hiranyavarman's daughter; once the bride learns Sikhandin is a woman, Hiranyavarman is enraged and sends a messenger threatening Drupada with death.
Drupada tries to calm Hiranyavarman with soft messages, but Hiranyavarman marches with an army, and his council plans to bind Drupada, install another king, and kill Drupada and Sikhandin.

Drupada, afraid and in grief, tells his favourite queen, Sikhandin's mother, that Hiranyavarman is coming to attack him, and asks her to say what is true about their child, while pretending innocence before others.

The queen admits the daughter was passed off as a son out of fear of her co-wives and because of the god's words, Drupada informs his counsellors and fortifies the city, and the queen urges prayer and sacrifice; Sikhandini, ashamed, goes into a haunted forest and fasts until the Yaksha Sthuna appears and promises help, and she asks him to make her a true man to spare her father.
The Yaksha Sthuna agrees to lend Sikhandini his manhood, on the condition that Sikhandini return it when the Dasarnaka king leaves, and Sikhandini promises to do so.

The two swap sexes; Sikhandin tells Drupada, who sends word that the child is male; the Dasarnaka king's envoy is sent away after women he sends confirm Sikhandin's manhood; Kubera finds Sthuna in female form and curses him to stay a woman until Sikhandin dies; Sthuna then sends Sikhandin on his way.

Sikhandin returns home and makes offerings, Drupada has him trained by Drona, and Bhishma tells the Kauravas that he will not shoot at a woman or one who was once a woman, so he will not fight Sikhandin.
Sanjaya reports that Duryodhana, reflecting on Bhishma's words, judged his refusal to fight Sikhandin proper.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana asks Bhishma how many days he would need to destroy the Pandava army and lists its formidable leaders.
Bhishma answers that he will slay ten thousand foot soldiers and a thousand car warriors each day, and that with his great weapons he could finish in a month.
Drona says he needs about a month, Kripa two months, Ashvatthama ten nights, and Karna five days, and Bhishma laughs and tells Karna he cannot boast until he meets Arjuna.
Vaisampayana says that after hearing the Kaurava commanders, Yudhishthira summons his brothers and speaks to them in private.

Yudhishthira reports the spies' news and asks Arjuna how long he will need, and Arjuna says he and Krishna could destroy the enemy quickly with Shiva's weapon, but prefers a fair fight, and then names the Pandava allies, including Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Bhima, and Draupadi's five sons.

The Kaurava kings march out in three divisions under Duryodhana, with Drona leading the first, Ashvatthama and Bhishma the second, and Kritavarman, Salya, and Bhurisravas with Duryodhana in the rear, and Duryodhana sets up a camp like a second Hastinapura with supplies for all.

Yudhishthira sends out his commanders in order: Dhrishtadyumna with Abhimanyu and Draupadi's sons in front, Bhima with Nakula and Sahadeva in a leading division, Virata and the Panchala princes with Krishna and Arjuna in the centre, Satyaki leading the cars in the centre, Kshatrahan and Kshatradeva guarding the rear, and Yudhishthira marching slowly with the baggage behind the main divisions.
The narrator sums up the array, which confounds the Kauravas, and notes that allied kings and their followers stream behind, roaring and blowing conches.
Heading: the Udyoga Parva ends here.
Heading: the footnotes begin.
