Footnote 2 notes that divination was done by reading the stars at night.
Footnote 3 explains Dhritarashtra's question about whether knowledge outweighs ritual action, and defines liberation as freedom from rebirth and karma.
Footnote 4 explains the sage's reply: giving up desire leads to the supreme state, while ritual action leads only to temporary rewards that must be earned again.
Footnote 5 explains why Dhritarashtra's next question follows from the sage's answer, asking whether the Supreme Soul could itself become an ordinary soul.
Footnote 6 gives the sage's analogy of the space inside a jar being part of unbounded space, to explain how the soul is linked to the universe without being identical with it.
Footnote 7 lists the kinds of troops: cars, elephants, horses, foot soldiers, other vehicles, and camel-riders.
Footnote 8 gives another name for a fire, the Badava fire.
Footnote 9 explains the allusion to Vishnu's horse-necked incarnation, whose voice the commentator takes to sound out the Vedic chants.
Footnote 10 derives a word for the nether region from a root meaning to flow down, following the commentator's explanation.
Footnote 11 notes the literal sense of an epithet as one with a beautiful or excellent face.
Footnote 12 summarizes the story of Vishwamitra, who, humbled by the Brahmana Vasishtha, gained Brahmanhood through penance, which the notes call the only such case in the scriptures.
Footnote 13 lists clarified butter, milk, and similar items as the libations used in sacrifice.
Footnote 14 says the subdivisions of the sacred syllable, the Pranava, were taken as the origin of the Vedas, Upanishads, and later scriptures.
Footnote 15 gives the meaning of a term as a small division of time.
Footnote 16 lists the bodily marks considered auspicious, such as elevated, slender, deep, and red parts, noting that commentators differ on which ones.
Footnote 17 corrects a variant reading and identifies the river Vitasta as one of the five rivers of the Punjab.
Footnote 18 sorts weapons into four classes: those thrown by hand, those not thrown, those sometimes thrown, and those shot from machines.
Footnote 19 identifies the thousand-armed Arjuna of the Haihaya clan, also called Kartaviryarjuna, as the king Rama slew.
Running head reading The Mahabharata, with no content.
Running head fragment reading of, with no content.
Heading naming the author, Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Section heading for the Jamvu-khanda Nirmana Parva.
An opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati, to be spoken before the telling.
Janamejaya asks how the heroes fought at Kurukshetra.
Vaisampayana begins the account: the Pandavas enter Kurukshetra and camp on the western side, and Yudhishthira provides food, watchwords and badges for the gathered forces from across Jamvudwipa.
Duryodhana arrays his troops, both sides blow their conches amid omens of dust and flesh-and-blood showers, and the warriors agree on rules of fair combat.
Vyasa sees the armies drawn up for battle and speaks privately to the grieving Dhritarashtra about his sons' wrongdoing.
Vyasa tells the king that his sons and the other princes have reached their appointed hour and will kill one another, and offers to give him sight so he can watch.
Dhritarashtra replies that he does not want to see his kinsmen slaughtered, but asks to hear a full account of the fighting.
Vyasa grants Sanjaya celestial sight and hearing, freedom from weapons and fatigue, and says the fame of the Kurus and Pandavas will spread, and that victory lies with righteousness.
Vyasa warns of a great slaughter and lists omens: birds and beasts gathering to feed on the field, strange sights in the sun and moon, eerie cries, and weeping animals.
Vyasa lists monstrous births, odd plant growth, planetary disturbances, eclipses on unusual days, and bloody rivers and winds as portents of a great slaughter.
Dhritarashtra says he thinks all this was ordained long ago, and that kings who die fighting by the duties of their order will win heaven and fame.
Vyasa says Time both destroys and creates the world, urges Dhritarashtra to show his sons the path of righteousness, and asks him to let the Pandavas have their kingdom.
Dhritarashtra replies that he understands life and death as well as Vyasa does, but people lose their judgement where their own interests are concerned, and his sons do not obey him.
Vyasa invites Dhritarashtra to speak freely about what is on his mind so that he can remove his doubts.
Dhritarashtra asks Vyasa to describe the indications that come before victory in battle.

Vyasa lists signs of success, such as a clear fire, pleasant sounds and favourable birds, explains how panic spreads through an army, ranks success by negotiation highest and success by battle lowest, and concludes that victory depends on chance.
Vyasa leaves, Dhritarashtra falls silent and sighs, and then asks Sanjaya to describe the lands and cities from which the assembled kings and their troops came.

Sanjaya sorts living things into mobile and immobile, lists the wild and domestic animals and the kinds of plants, and says the earth is the support of all creatures, which is why kings kill one another for it.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to name and measure the rivers, mountains, provinces and forests on the earth.
Sanjaya explains that all things are built from five elements, each with its own quality, and that some matters are beyond reason to work out.
Sanjaya describes the wheel-shaped island Sudarsana, with its rivers, mountains, cities and trees, ringed by the salt ocean, and its shape as seen in the moon.
Dhritarashtra asks for a fuller account of the island, beginning with the hare-shaped part and then the peepul-shaped part.
Vaisampayana says that the king's request prompted Sanjaya to begin.
Sanjaya names the six mountains that cross the land, the Varshas between them, the golden mountain Meru at the centre, and the sacred places, rivers and peoples on and around it.
Sanjaya sums up the seven Varshas and says the islands Naga-dwipa and Kasyapa-dwipa and the mountains of Maleya form the parts of the hare-shaped region.
Dhritarashtra asks for a detailed account of the regions north and east of Meru and of the mountains of Malyavat.
Sanjaya describes the Northern Kurus, with fruit and flowers that grow to order, milk-giving trees, golden sands, twins born there, long lives, and birds that carry off the dead.
Sanjaya describes Bhadraswa, its Kalamra tree whose juice keeps people youthful, and the Jamvu tree whose name gave this island its name, along with the river and gold that flow from it.
Sanjaya describes Malyavat, where the fire Samvataka burns at the end of an age, and the golden-hued ascetics who enter the sun and later the moon.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to name every Varsha and mountain, and every being that dwells on them.
Sanjaya describes Romanaka, Hiranmaya with its river and the eagle Garuda, the Sringavat mountains, the Airavata Varsha where the sun gives no heat, and the god Hari on his golden car.

Dhritarashtra, absorbed in thought about his sons, says that Time destroys and creates the universe and names Nara and Narayana, also called Vaikuntha and Vishnu, as the power that destroys creatures.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe Bharatavarsha, the land that his son covets, that the sons of Pandu also want, and that troubles his own mind.
Sanjaya says the Pandavas are not greedy for the land, names the kings who are, and then describes the land's ancient royal lovers, its seven Kala mountains, and the many rivers that feed it.
Sanjaya lists the provinces and peoples of the land, a long catalogue of kingdoms and tribes.

Sanjaya lists the kingdoms of the south and the north and compares the earth to a cow that yields virtue, profit and pleasure, and says that kings grasp greedily for it, so the Kurus and Pandavas are fighting over it by negotiation, division, gift and battle.
Dhritarashtra asks for a detailed account of the lifespan, strength and good and bad conditions of people in Bharatavarsha, Himavat and Harivarsha, past, present and future.
Sanjaya explains the four ages, their lifespans, the strength and wisdom of people in each age, the decline in character in the Kali age, and ranks Haimavat and Harivarsha above Bharatavarsha.
Section heading for the Bhumi Parva.
Dhritarashtra asks for the size of Jamvudwipa, the oceans and islands of Sakadwipa, Kusadwipa, Salmalidwipa and Kraunchadwipa, and the planets Rahu, Soma and Surya.
Sanjaya says he will describe seven islands, gives the extent of the Jamvu mountain, and says the salt ocean around it is twice that size and filled with kingdoms and mountains.
Sanjaya describes Sakadwipa, twice the size of Jamvudwipa and surrounded by its own ocean, where people are righteous and never die, and asks what more the king wishes to hear.
Dhritarashtra asks for a full, detailed account of Sakadwipa.

Sanjaya names the island's seven jewelled mountains, starting with Meru, and describes Malaya, Jaladhara, Raivataka and Syama, noting how their clouds, rain and constellation Revati are linked to them.
Dhritarashtra asks why the people of Sakadwipa would be dark-skinned.

Sanjaya answers that people of all complexions live on islands, names the Dark Mountain after its dark people, lists the rest of the mountains, Varshas and rivers, the Saka tree, and the four provinces where people live peacefully by their castes.
Sanjaya describes the oceans of clarified butter, curds, wine and water, the northern islands and their mountains, and the Varshas whose people are almost white and never die.
Sanjaya describes the remaining islands and mountains, the realms where Prajapati rules, and the four great elephants whose breath gives life to creatures.
Dhritarashtra says Sanjaya has described the first subject fully and asks him to go on to what remains.
Sanjaya gives the sizes of the planet Swarbhanu, the moon and the sun, explains that Rahu eclipses them, and urges Dhritarashtra to pacify his son Duryodhana.
Closing passage: a Kshatriya who hears this Bhumi Parva gains prosperity, and hearing it on full-moon or new-moon days brings blessings to the hearer and to ancestors.
Section heading for the Bhagavat-Gita Parva.
Vaisampayana says that Sanjaya, who knows past, present and future, rushes in grief to tell Dhritarashtra, who is lost in thought, that Bhishma has been slain.
Sanjaya announces Bhishma's death, recalls his feats and his long resistance, says he now lies on a bed of arrows struck down by Sikhandin, and blames the king's evil counsel.
Dhritarashtra asks how Bhishma was slain by Sikhandin, who followed and protected him, which heroes opposed the Pandavas, and laments his own wicked counsel and the fall of his protector.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Pandavas overcame Bhishma, what Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni and Dussasana said when he fell, and who won and who was lost, and begs Sanjaya to tell him everything in detail.
Sanjaya says the question is fair but the king should not blame Duryodhana for the consequences of his own misdeeds, and recalls the Pandavas long bore their injuries in the woods.
Sanjaya says the events were predestined, that Vyasa has given him divine sight and hearing, and that he will now describe the battle between the Bharatas.
Duryodhana tells Dussasana to send cars and troops to protect Bhishma, repeats Bhishma's vow not to strike Sikhandin, and names the Pandava guards around Arjuna.
Section heading marking the start of Section XVI.

Sanjaya describes the din and the dawn arrangement of both armies, the glittering weapons and banners, the Kaurava commanders, Bhishma leading the vanguard in white, the Pandava divisions, and the two armies compared to oceans at the end of an age.

Sanjaya describes the ominous signs at the start of battle, the kings assembling as Vyasa foretold, Bhishma's exhortation to the kings to fight for heaven, Karna laying down his arms for Bhishma's sake, the Kaurava divisions and their leaders, and their formation shaped like a body of elephants, kings and horses.

Sanjaya describes the uproar, the glittering standards and armour, the Kaurava warriors who guard Bhishma from behind, the peoples pledged to fight to the death, the huge forces of chariots, elephants and foot soldiers, and the eleven Akshauhinis compared with a river divided.
Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira countered the Kaurava array with fewer men, and how the Pandavas set against Bhishma, who knows every kind of formation.

Yudhishthira cites Vrihaspati's advice that few against many should use a needle-shaped array, and Arjuna answers with the Vajra array, placing Bhima at the front, the other warriors and allies around him, Sikhandin facing Bhishma, and Yudhishthira in the centre.
At dawn, wind, drops of water, dry gusts, dust, falling meteors and a dimmed sun appear, and the Pandava army stands ready with Bhima at its head.
Dhritarashtra asks which army first advanced eagerly, which side the sun, moon and wind favoured, which beasts cried out inauspiciously, and which young men looked cheerful.

Sanjaya says both armies were equally joyful and vast, describes the facing directions, the omens against the Kauravas, the Kaurava leaders and their places, and says the Pandava army seemed invincible because Krishna and Arjuna led it.

Yudhishthira, dismayed at Bhishma's array, asks Arjuna how the Pandavas can win, and Arjuna replies that victory comes from truth, righteousness and energy, and that it is with Krishna, recalling how the gods won through Hari's grace.

Yudhishthira arranges the Pandava army and urges it to fight fairly, places Sikhandin at the centre with Arjuna guarding him, Dhrishtadyumna in the van with Bhima, Yuyudhana on the south, and himself among the elephants with priests blessing him, and Sanjaya describes Arjuna's car and Bhima's terrifying strength.
Krishna, driving Arjuna's car, tells Arjuna that Bhishma stands in the midst of his troops, surrounded by great warriors, and urges him to seek battle with that bull of the Bharatas.
Sanjaya notes that Krishna speaks to Arjuna as the Kaurava army comes forward to fight.
Krishna tells Arjuna to purify himself and recite a hymn to Durga on the eve of battle for victory.
Arjuna dismounts from his car and joins his hands to recite the hymn.
Arjuna's long hymn calls on Durga by many names and epithets, and describes her as the power behind sleep, prosperity, the sun and the moon, and the protector of those who worship her.
Sanjaya says that Durga, pleased by Arjuna's devotion, appears in the sky in Krishna's presence and speaks.
Durga tells Arjuna that he will soon defeat his foes, that Narayana is with him, and that no enemy, not even Indra, can defeat him.
The goddess vanishes, Arjuna mounts his car, and Krishna and Arjuna blow their celestial conches, and the hymn is said to bring protection, safety and success to whoever recites it at dawn.

Sanjaya says he knows this through Vyasa's grace, that Dhritarashtra's sons do not know Nara and Narayana, that the hour of the kingdom has come, and that victory goes where righteousness and Krishna are.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya which side advanced in confidence, which side struck first, and whose troops were praised with fragrance and fierce words.
Sanjaya says both armies were equally cheerful and fragrant, and describes the fierce collision with music, conches, drums, roars and elephant grunts.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter I.
An editor's note by John Bruno Hare says the Gita proper begins here, and that the chapter headings were added for comparison and are not in Ganguli's original.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas did after assembling on the sacred plain of Kurukshetra.
Duryodhana tells Drona that the Pandava army is strong, names the Pandava and Kaurava warriors, says his own army protected by Bhishma is insufficient, and then the conches sound on both sides.
Arjuna asks Krishna to place his car between the two armies so that he can see the warriors who are ready to fight.
Krishna places the car between the armies, and Arjuna sees his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, relatives and friends standing on both sides.
Arjuna, overcome with pity, describes his trembling and dry mouth, says he wants neither victory nor kingdom, and argues that killing his own family destroys its customs and brings sin and disorder.
Sanjaya says Arjuna, troubled with grief, casts aside his bow and arrows and sits down on his car.
A closing editorial note marks the end of the first lesson of the Gita, titled Survey of Forces, within the Bhishma Parva.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter II.
Sanjaya says that Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, speaks to the despairing Arjuna whose eyes are filled with tears.
Krishna asks where this unworthy weakness has come from, tells Arjuna that it shuts out heaven and brings disgrace, and urges him to shake it off and rise to fight.

Arjuna asks how he can fight with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, his worthy teachers, says that begging would be better than killing them, admits he does not know which outcome is better, and asks Krishna to instruct him as a disciple.
Sanjaya reports that Arjuna declares he will not fight and falls silent, and that Krishna then speaks to him between the two armies.

Krishna answers that the wise grieve neither for the living nor the dead, since the soul is eternal, cannot be slain, and simply changes bodies, so Arjuna should fight his just battle as a warrior and act without attachment to results.
Arjuna asks what marks a person of steady mind, and how such a person speaks, sits and moves.

Krishna describes the steady sage as one who is content within, untroubled by calamity, free from desire, fear and anger, who withdraws his senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs, and who attains peace.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter III.
Arjuna asks why Krishna praises devotion yet urges him to dreadful action, and asks for a plain answer about what is good for him.

Krishna explains that there are two paths, knowledge and work, that no one escapes action by refraining from it, and that one should act without attachment as an offering, citing the Lord of creation, Janaka, and his own example of acting to keep the world in order; he adds that one's own duty, however imperfect, is better than another's.
Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin even against his will.
Krishna answers that desire, born of passion and turned to wrath, is the all-devouring enemy that covers knowledge like smoke covers fire, and urges Arjuna to restrain his senses and destroy it.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter IV.

Krishna says he declared this imperishable teaching first to Vivaswat, that it passed through Manu and Ikshaku, that it was lost over time, and that he now gives it to Arjuna as his devotee and friend.
Arjuna points out that Vivaswat was born before Krishna and asks how Krishna could have taught it first.

Krishna says he has taken many births that Arjuna does not remember, appears in each age to protect the righteous, explains action done without craving, the many kinds of sacrifice, and that the sacrifice of knowledge burns away all action; he urges Arjuna to learn from wise teachers and cut his doubt with the sword of knowledge.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter V.
Arjuna asks Krishna which is superior, giving up actions or taking them up with devotion, and asks for a definite answer.

Krishna says both paths lead to freedom but acting with devotion is better, that the wise see the two as one, that acting without attachment and offering it to Brahman leaves a person untouched by sin, and that the sage who is at peace and equal to all beings attains tranquillity, knowing Krishna as the enjoyer of sacrifices.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter VI.

Krishna says that true renunciation means doing required actions without seeking their fruit, then describes meditation: a steady seat in a clean place, a still body, the gaze fixed at the nose tip, moderation in food and sleep, the mind fixed on him, and the devotee who sees himself in all beings is the best.
Arjuna says the restless, strong and stubborn mind seems as hard to restrain as the wind, so he does not see how such steadiness can last.
Krishna agrees the mind is hard to master, but says it can be controlled by practice and by giving up desire.
Arjuna asks what becomes of a faithful person who fails to reach devotion and falls from both paths, and asks Krishna to remove this doubt.
Krishna says the one who falls from devotion is not lost, but is reborn in a good or wise family and continues toward perfection, and that the devotee who worships him with faith is the most devout.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter VII.

Krishna offers to explain knowledge and experience fully, describes his lower eightfold nature and higher living nature, names himself as the essence of many things such as water, light, the sacred syllable Om and the seed of all beings, explains that the three qualities and his illusion hide him, and says few know him, the four kinds of worshippers, and that those who worship other gods gain only what fades while his devotees come to him.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter VIII.
Arjuna asks what Brahman, the self, action and the other terms mean, and how the self-restrained are to be known at the time of death.

Krishna explains that Brahman is supreme and indestructible, that whoever remembers him at death goes to him, that the meditator who holds the breath between the brows and utters Om reaches the highest goal, that the worlds below him are subject to rebirth, that Brahman's day and night are cycles that bring creatures forth and dissolve them, and that the bright and dark paths lead, one to no return and one back to rebirth, and that the knower of these paths is not deluded.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter IX.

Krishna reveals the royal knowledge and mystery, says he pervades the universe while not being bound by it, describes the cycles of creation and dissolution, names himself as the sacrifice, offering, father and mother of the world, says even those who worship other gods without knowing it worship him, and says devotion is open to all, including the sinful, women, Vaisyas and Sudras, urging Arjuna to be devoted.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter X.

Krishna says he will speak his words for Arjuna's good, explains that the gods and sages cannot know his origin because he is their source, that whoever knows him is freed from sin, and that the qualities of creatures and the seven great sages and Manus come from him.
Arjuna praises Krishna as the supreme Brahma and the unborn Lord, and asks him to describe his divine powers, since he never tires of hearing them.

Krishna lists his manifestations among the gods, the Vedas, the mountains, the rivers, the animals, the sacred syllable Om, Death and Time, and says that everything glorious is born from a fragment of his power.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XI.
Arjuna says the teaching has dispelled his delusion and asks Krishna to show him his sovereign and eternal form.
Krishna tells Arjuna to behold his many divine forms, the gods and the whole universe, and says that Arjuna cannot see him with ordinary eyes, so he gives him celestial sight.
Sanjaya describes Krishna's vast form, with many faces, weapons and ornaments, shining like a thousand suns and holding the whole divided universe, before which Arjuna bows in amazement.
Arjuna describes the form, with its endless arms, eyes and mouths, the sun and moon as eyes and fire as its mouth, and says the worlds tremble as warriors rush into its terrible mouths.
Krishna declares that he is Death and the destroyer of the worlds, that the warriors are already slain, and that Arjuna should fight and be only the instrument.
Sanjaya says Arjuna, trembling and with joined hands, bows and speaks again in fear.
Arjuna praises Krishna at length, begs pardon for past familiarity, and asks him to show again his ordinary four-armed form.
Krishna says that this form was shown to Arjuna alone by his own power, that no one else could see it through the Vedas or austerities, and tells him to be free of fear.
Sanjaya says that Krishna shows his gentle form again and comforts the frightened Arjuna.
Arjuna says that seeing Krishna's gentle human form has restored his right mind.
Krishna says that this form is hard to see, that even the gods long for it, and that he can be known and reached only through devotion to him alone, free of attachment and enmity.
Section heading marking the start of Section XXXVI.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XII.
Arjuna asks which worshippers are best acquainted with devotion, those who adore Krishna constantly or those who meditate on the unmanifest and immutable.

Krishna says those who fix their minds on him with supreme faith are the most devoted, that the unmanifest path is harder, that he rescues those who give him their minds and actions, that those unable to do this can practise steady devotion, act for him, or give up the fruits of action for peace, and that the devotees he loves are free from hatred, equal in pleasure and pain, content, steady and detached.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XIII.

Krishna explains that the body is the field and the self is its knower, lists the elements, senses and qualities of the field, names the virtues that make up true knowledge, describes the supreme Brahman as everywhere and beyond the senses, and explains that nature and spirit are both without beginning, that nature produces all qualities while spirit witnesses them, and that one who sees the Lord equal in all beings is freed.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XIV.

Krishna says he will teach the supreme knowledge again, that the great Brahma is his womb and he the seed-giving father of all beings, that goodness, passion and darkness bind the soul, and how each quality shapes the next birth and the fruit of action, ending with the soul that transcends the three qualities and reaches immortality.
Arjuna asks what marks a person who has passed beyond the three qualities, and how such a person conducts himself.

Krishna describes this person as unmoved by light, activity or delusion, equal in pleasure and pain, praise and blame, and friend and foe, who worships him with exclusive devotion and is fit to enter the nature of Brahma.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XV.

Krishna describes the eternal fig tree whose leaves are the Vedas, says it must be cut with detachment to reach the supreme seat, explains that the soul is his eternal part carried between bodies with the senses, that he is the light in the sun, moon and fire and the warmth of digestion, the source of memory and knowledge, and the Supreme Person beyond the perishable and imperishable.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XVI.

Krishna lists divine qualities that lead to liberation and demonic qualities that lead to bondage, describes demonic people who deny truth and moral order and chase endless desires, names lust, anger and greed as the three gates to hell, and says that scripture should guide what one does.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XVII.
Arjuna asks whether the state of those who worship with faith apart from the scriptures is one of goodness, passion or darkness.

Krishna says faith comes in three kinds that follow each person's nature, sorts worship, food, sacrifice, penance of body, speech and mind, and gifts into the three qualities, names Brahma as OM, TAT and SAT, and says that any act done without faith is worthless here and hereafter.
Heading naming the start of Bhagavad Gita Chapter XVIII.
Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the true nature of renunciation and of abandonment.

Krishna explains that renouncing desired acts and their fruit is abandonment, that sacrifice, gifts and penance should still be done without attachment, sorts renunciation, knowledge, action, agent, understanding and happiness into three qualities, sets out the natural duties of each social class and says one's own duty is better even if imperfect, and then urges Arjuna to surrender to him as his devoted friend and promises to free him from sin.
Arjuna says his delusion is destroyed, his memory has returned, his doubts are gone, and he will do as Krishna asks.

Sanjaya says he heard this wonderful dialogue through Vyasa's favour, rejoices in recalling it and the form of Hari, and says that wherever Krishna and Partha are, there is prosperity, victory and justice.
Closing marker, End of the Bhagavad Gita.

After Arjuna takes up his bow again, the armies shout and the gods and sages gather to watch; Yudhishthira puts down his armour and weapons and walks on foot toward the enemy, with his brothers and Krishna behind him.
Arjuna asks Yudhishthira what he means by walking unarmed toward the enemy and leaving his brothers behind.
Bhima asks where his brother is going without his armour and weapons, towards the armoured foe, and leaving his brothers.
Nakula says he is troubled with fear to see his eldest brother going this way and asks where he is headed.
Sahadeva asks why Yudhishthira is heading toward the foe when the terrible enemy divisions are so near.
Krishna says Yudhishthira means to honour his elders before the fight, and the Kaurava warriors mock him as a coward, until Yudhishthira reaches Bhishma and seizes his feet.
Yudhishthira salutes Bhishma and asks for his permission and blessing to fight.
Bhishma says he would have cursed Yudhishthira had he not come, grants his blessing, and says he is bound to the Kauravas by their wealth and must fight for them.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to think of his welfare from day to day, even while he fights for the Kauravas.
Bhishma says he will fight for Yudhishthira's foes and asks what else he wants to say.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how he could be vanquished in battle, and asks for any advice that would help him.
Bhishma says he sees no one who can defeat him in battle while he fights.
Yudhishthira asks how Bhishma's own death could be brought about by his foes.
Bhishma says he sees no one who can vanquish him, and that the time of his death has not yet come.
Sanjaya says Yudhishthira accepts the words, salutes Bhishma again, and goes on through the army to Drona's chariot.
Yudhishthira asks Drona how he may fight without sin and vanquish his foes with Drona's permission.
Drona grants permission and blessing, says he is bound by the Kauravas' wealth, and asks what Yudhishthira wants.
Yudhishthira asks Drona to pray for his victory and advise him for his good, while Drona fights for the Kauravas.
Drona says victory is certain for Yudhishthira because Hari is his counsellor, and that victory goes wherever righteousness and Krishna are.
Yudhishthira asks Drona how he could be vanquished, since he is invincible.
Drona says that victory cannot be Yudhishthira's while he is fighting, and urges him to seek Drona's speedy death.
Yudhishthira asks Drona to name the means of his death, and salutes him.
Drona says no foe can slay him while he fights with wrath and arrows, only when he sets down his weapons and withdraws into meditation, which he will do if he hears something very disagreeable.
Sanjaya says Yudhishthira honours Drona and goes on to Kripa.
Yudhishthira asks for Drona's leave to fight without sin and vanquish his foes.
Kripa says he would have cursed Yudhishthira had he not come, that he is bound to the Kauravas by their wealth, and that he must speak like a eunuch and fight for them.
Yudhishthira begins to speak but, greatly agitated, falls silent.
Sanjaya says Kripa understands what Yudhishthira meant, says he cannot be slain, promises to pray for his victory, and Yudhishthira goes on to Salya.
Yudhishthira asks Salya for leave to fight without sin and vanquish his foes.
Salya grants leave and blessing, says he is bound to the Kauravas by their wealth, and asks what Yudhishthira desires.
Yudhishthira asks Salya to think daily of his welfare and to fight as he pleases for the sake of the foe, and says this is the boon he asks.
Salya says he must fight for the Kauravas, who have bound him with their wealth, and asks what aid he can give.
Yudhishthira asks Salya to weaken the energy of Karna in battle.
Salya agrees to do so and says he will watch over Yudhishthira's victory.
Sanjaya says Yudhishthira and his brothers leave the Kaurava line, and Krishna goes to Karna and asks him to join the Pandavas until Bhishma is slain.

Karna says he will not displease Duryodhana, for whom he has given up his life, so Krishna returns to the Pandavas; Yudhishthira calls for allies, and Yuyutsu, a son of Dhritarashtra, offers to fight for them.
Yudhishthira accepts Yuyutsu's offer, saying the Kaurava line rests on him and the wrathful Duryodhana will not live long.
Yuyutsu leaves the Kauravas for the Pandavas, the armies counter-array, the kings praise the Pandavas' nobility, and onlookers of every kind weep as they witness it.
Dhritarashtra asks who struck the first blow, the Kurus or the Pandavas, once the two armies were arrayed.

Sanjaya describes Dussasana and Bhishma advancing with the Kaurava troops and the Pandavas advancing under Bhima, the deafening uproar, Bhima's roars that frighten the Kaurava sons, the Kaurava princes surrounding him with arrows and the Pandava warriors striking back, and Bhishma shining above the countless host.

Sanjaya describes the uproar at the start of the battle, then the paired duels of Bhishma and Arjuna, Satyaki and Kritavarman, Abhimanyu and Vrihadbala, Bhima and Duryodhana, Nakula and Dussasana, Sahadeva and Durmukha, Yudhishthira and the king of Madra, Dhrishtadyumna and Drona, and many other pairs of warriors, until the melee becomes so confused that nothing can be discerned.

Sanjaya describes the frenzied fighting among foot soldiers, where kin fail to recognise each other, elephants and horses are slaughtered, the wounded call for their kin and for water, and some warriors bear their pain silently, until the Pandava divisions waver before Bhishma, who shines on his silver chariot.

Sanjaya tells how Bhishma, guarded by five Kaurava champions, cuts through the Pandava ranks, how Abhimanyu duels with him and cuts down his palmyra standard, how Bhima's standard also falls to Bhishma, how Salya kills Uttara's elephant, and how Sweta is stopped by seven Kaurava champions until Duryodhana and Bhishma rescue Salya.
Dhritarashtra asks what the Kauravas and Pandavas did when Sweta advanced on Salya's chariot, and what Bhishma did in response.

Sanjaya describes the great slaughter around Sweta, the Kaurava warriors fleeing and leaving Bhishma alone, the duel in which bows and standards fall and Bhishma's chariot is destroyed by Sweta's mace, the celestial voice that marks Bhishma's hour, Sweta's death by Bhishma's shaft, the grief of the Pandavas, the joy of the Kauravas, and the withdrawal of both armies at nightfall.

Dhritarashtra asks how the Pandavas and Panchalas reacted to Sweta's death, reproaches Duryodhana for provoking the war, says Bhishma, Drona and others never wanted it, and fears what Arjuna will do in his wrath.

Sanjaya tells the king to accept his own share of blame, describes Sankha's charge on Salya and Arjuna's stand before Bhishma, then Bhishma's slaughter of the Panchala and Matsya troops and of Drupada's army, and the Pandavas withdrawing for the night as the sun sets.

Yudhishthira goes to Krishna after the first day, lamenting that Bhishma consumes his army like fire, that he would rather go to the forest than see kings slain, that Arjuna seems indifferent while Bhima fights alone, and asks Krishna what can be done.

Krishna comforts Yudhishthira, Yudhishthira makes Dhrishtadyumna commander and compares him to Kartikeya, Dhrishtadyumna vows to slay Bhishma and Drona, and at dawn he forms the Krauncharuma array with Arjuna in the van, Drupada at the head, Virata guarding the rear, and the army's banners shining.
Section heading marking the start of Section LI.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's speech to his commanders, the Kaurava formation with Bhishma at its head, Drona behind him, Duryodhana and his brothers in the centre, allied kings on the flanks and rear, and both sides blowing their conches as the armies advance to battle once again.
Dhritarashtra asks how the foremost warriors began to strike once the two armies were arrayed.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana ordering the attack, Bhishma's arrows driving back the Pandava divisions, Arjuna asking Krishna to drive him at Bhishma and vowing to slay him, Bhishma wounding many warriors including Krishna, Duryodhana urging Bhishma to kill Arjuna because Karna will not fight, and the long duel between Bhishma and Arjuna, which neither wins and which the gods watch in wonder.
Dhritarashtra asks how Drona and Dhrishtadyumna fought, and says fate seems stronger than effort, since even Bhishma could not escape Arjuna.

Sanjaya describes Drona breaking Dhrishtadyumna's bow, charioteer and steeds, cutting down his dart and mace, Dhrishtadyumna charging on foot with shield and sword, Drona holding him off, Bhima rushing to rescue him, and Duryodhana sending the Kalingas against Bhima.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Kalinga king, urged on by his son, fought against Bhima, who wanders the field with his mace like Death himself.

Sanjaya describes the Kalinga attack on Bhima, his slaying of Sakradeva with a mace, the beheading of the king's elephant, his sword rampage among the Kalingas and their allies, the Kalinga flight, Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki joining the fight, and Satyaki felling Bhishma's charioteer so that Bhishma is carried from the field.

Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna killing the horses of Drona's son and attacking Salya, Kripa and Drona's son, Abhimanyu's duel with Lakshmana, Duryodhana's rush to his son's side, Arjuna's rescue of Abhimanyu, the Kaurava kings' charge, the broken weapons strewn across the field, and Bhishma's order to withdraw as the sun sets.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma's Garuda formation with its commanders at each part, Arjuna's half-moon counter-array with Bhima on the right horn and Krishna on the left, the Pandava leaders placed in between, and the armies' clash with its uproar reaching the heavens.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's slaughter of the Kaurava car leaders, the general melee of cars, elephants, cavalry and foot soldiers across a field strewn with broken weapons and bodies, Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha and Sakuni breaking the Pandava ranks, Bhima, Ghatotkacha and the sons of Draupadi grinding the Kaurava host, and Duryodhana, Abhimanyu and Satyaki joining the fight.

Sanjaya describes the kings surrounding Arjuna with a storm of weapons, Sakuni's forces cutting up Satyaki's car until he and Abhimanyu share one car, Drona and Bhishma pressing Yudhishthira, Bhima's arrow wounding Duryodhana so that he swoons and is carried away and his army flees, Arjuna scattering the Kauravas, Duryodhana rallying them and rebuking Bhishma, and Bhishma's vow to check the Pandavas alone, with both sides sounding their conches.
Dhritarashtra asks what Bhishma did against the Pandavas after his dreadful vow in battle, and what the Panchalas did in response.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma's charge through the Pandava army with arrows that cut down warriors and make him seem multiplied, the Pandava rout, Krishna urging Arjuna to strike Bhishma, their arrowy duel in which Krishna's discus is raised and Arjuna holds him back and vows to fight, Arjuna's Indra weapon that fills the field with carnage and a river of blood, and the Kaurava withdrawal at nightfall with praise of Arjuna's feat.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma advancing with the Kaurava princes around him, the glittering banners and elephants, Arjuna's array with Krishna as charioteer, the blare of drums and conches, and the clash in which the sky is covered with dust and warriors, horsemen and elephants fall in heaps.

Bhishma turns to attack Arjuna, Abhimanyu charges into the Kaurava host in the meantime, and Arjuna answers Bhishma's arrows with a shower of his own while both armies watch the single combat between the two champions.

Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's stand against Drona's son, Bhurisravas, Chitrasena and Samyamani's son, the Trigarta, Madra and Kekaya princes surrounding him and his father, Dhrishtadyumna's rescue, the duel in which Dhrishtadyumna's mace kills Samyamani's son, Samyamani's fierce attack on Dhrishtadyumna, and Salya striking Dhrishtadyumna in the chest.
Dhritarashtra complains that Sanjaya always reports his side losing and asks how the Pandavas could be weakened.

Sanjaya blames Duryodhana for the evil and describes Dhrishtadyumna, Salya and Abhimanyu fighting, then Duryodhana's brothers and the Pandava warriors opposing each other in pairs, and finally Bhima's attack on the Magadha elephants.
Sanjaya describes the great army charging Bhima at Duryodhana's order, Bhima's mace shattering the troops, and Satyaki's advance on Bhishma, ending with Bhurisravas rushing to fight Satyaki.

A single long section covering the whole day: Bhurisravas and Satyaki trade arrows, Bhima fights Duryodhana, wounds and swoons, and recovers to kill many of the sons. Bhagadatta blinds Bhima with arrows, Ghatotkacha attacks Bhagadatta's elephant, Bhishma calls for a withdrawal at nightfall, the Pandavas return in triumph, and Duryodhana sits in grief.
Dhritarashtra, fearful and puzzled, asks Sanjaya what gives the Pandavas their power and what his own side did after its retreat.

Sanjaya answers that the Pandavas fight by fair means and keep to righteousness, while the Kauravas acted cruelly and ignored the advice of their elders, and then introduces Duryodhana's question to Bhishma.
Duryodhana, grieved by his brothers' defeats, names his strongest warriors and asks what allows the Pandavas to keep beating them.
Bhishma urges peace with the Pandavas and says that Krishna protects them. He then begins a long tale of Brahma praising Vishnu and asking him to be born among men.
A section heading marking the start of the next section.
Vishnu agrees to Brahma's request and disappears, and Brahma explains to the gods who Vasudeva is and why he must not be despised.
Bhishma says the sages taught him the same, then says Dhritarashtra's sons hate Krishna and Arjuna out of folly and that Krishna sustains the Pandavas.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma about Vasudeva's origin and glory.

Bhishma describes Vasudeva as the supreme god and recounts how he created the elements, the gods, the four classes of people, and the cycles of birth and death, then notes his slaying of Madhu and says Yudhishthira depends on him.
Bhishma gives a hymn that sages say Brahman first spoke, listing the seers who praised Vasudeva under different titles, and ends by urging Duryodhana to turn his heart to Kesava.

Sanjaya says Duryodhana begins to honour Krishna and the Pandavas, and Bhishma again urges peace, telling him that the Pandavas are protected and that disregarding them will bring ruin. Duryodhana then goes back to his tent and lies down for the night.

Sanjaya describes the armies advancing in their formations, the Kaurava Makara array guarded by Bhishma, the Pandava Syena array with its named commanders in each part, Bhima and Arjuna attacking Bhishma, Duryodhana asking Drona for help, and the clashes of Drona with Satyaki and Sikhandin.

A long passage of Sanjaya's report: the uproar of the general battle, the countless fallen heads and bodies, the mixed slaughter of men and animals, and the closing move as Duryodhana leads the Kalingas forward behind Bhishma and the Pandavas charge against Bhishma.

A long passage of Sanjaya's report: Arjuna's attack and his weapons, the Kaurava fear and retreat to Bhishma, the arrival of allied forces, the pairings of Pandava and Kaurava warriors, the dust and omens, and the mass destruction of elephants, chariots and horses.

A long passage of Sanjaya's report: the pairings of warriors, the sun reaching midday, the splendour of the weapons and armour, Bhishma's contest with Bhima and Satyaki, the killing of Satyaki's charioteer, Bhishma's rout of the Pandavas, and the new round of fighting.

Sanjaya describes Virata's arrows against Bhishma, Aswatthaman's wounding of Arjuna and Arjuna's reply, Arjuna's decision to spare Aswatthaman out of respect for Drona, and Bhima's duel with Duryodhana, which ends with both sides bleeding.

Abhimanyu defeats Chitrasena and his fellow princes, fights Lakshmana until Kripa carries him away, and Bhishma then slaughters the Pandava troops until the field is covered with dead elephants and men.
Sanjaya describes Satyaki's archery against Duryodhana's chariots, his duel with Bhurisravas, the killing of Satyaki's sons, the fight on foot, and the rescue of both heroes by Bhima and Duryodhana.
Arjuna destroys twenty-five thousand Kaurava chariot-warriors as the sun goes down, and at twilight Bhishma calls off the battle and both armies go to their camps.
After a night's rest both armies prepare, and Yudhishthira orders Dhrishtadyumna to form the Makara array, with each part given its commander.
Bhishma answers with a crane array, naming the commanders in its beak, eyes, neck, wings and tail.

Sanjaya describes the battle beginning at sunrise, with each kind of fighter matched against another, Drona wounding Bhima and Bhima killing Drona's charioteer, and Drona and Bhishma then forcing the Srinjayas to flee.
Dhritarashtra lists the army's virtues, compares it to an ocean, names its protectors, and then asks whether its slaughter is the work of destiny, recalling Vidura's advice and Duryodhana's refusal.
Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that the calamity is his own fault for the dice match and the war, and that he must bear the consequences, and then promises to recount the battle.
Bhima breaks into the Kaurava line, faces Duryodhana's brothers and their allies, kills many warriors, and is surrounded until he takes up his mace and begins to fight on foot.

Dhrishtadyumna finds Bhima's empty chariot and his charioteer Visoka, and rushes to find Bhima. He rescues Bhima, Duryodhana rallies his brothers to attack Dhrishtadyumna, and a Pramohana weapon leaves the Kauravas unconscious. Drona revives them with a counter-weapon, drives back the Pandavas, and his men cheer.

Duryodhana and Bhima wound each other, the younger brothers attack Bhima and are beaten back, and Yudhishthira sends Abhimanyu and others to support Bhima, so that the sons of Dhritarashtra abandon the fight.

Abhimanyu and Bhima press the Kauravas in the afternoon, Abhimanyu kills Vikarna's horses and wounds him, several duels follow, Bhishma slaughters the Pandava troops, and Arjuna's bowstring is heard on the right of the army.
Sanjaya describes the field as a sea of blood, with elephants as islands and chariots as boats, and notes that no warrior on either side is unwilling to fight.

A long section covering the day's end: Bhima's accusations and attack on Duryodhana, the shooting down of Duryodhana's horses, umbrella and standard, the rescue of Duryodhana by Kripa and Jayadratha, Abhimanyu's duels with the sons and Satanika's killing of Dushkarna, Bhishma's rout of the Pandavas at sunset, and Yudhishthira's embrace of Bhima and Dhrishtadyumna.
Duryodhana, wounded and anxious, asks Bhishma for victory. Bhishma admits the Pandava allies are formidable, pledges to fight to the limit, and the army advances with banners, dust and loud noise.

A long section covering the whole morning: Bhishma names the allies and says the Pandavas are hard to beat, heals Duryodhana, forms the Mandala array, Yudhishthira answers with the Vajra array, the pairings are made, and Arjuna and Krishna fight the kings, using the Aindra weapon until Bhishma rescues the retreating warriors.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana urging the kings to shield Bhishma as he charges toward Arjuna, and the two heroes come face to face.
Drona shoots down Virata's standard, bow, steeds and charioteer, then kills Virata's son Sankha, and Virata flees.

Aswatthaman kills Sikhandin's charioteer and steeds, Sikhandin fights on with a sword and is wounded, Satyaki takes him onto his chariot, and Satyaki uses the Aindra weapon against Alamvusha's illusions, driving him away.
Dhrishtadyumna wounds Duryodhana and kills his horses, and Sakuni rescues him by pulling him onto his own chariot.
Bhima destroys Kritavarman's horses, charioteer and standard, and Kritavarman retreats to another chariot.
Dhritarashtra says that Sanjaya never reports his side as cheerful or unbeaten, and that all of this must be Destiny.
Sanjaya says the valour of the Kaurava troops is wasted against the Pandavas and that the disaster was caused by the king and his sons.
Iravat kills the charioteer and steeds of the Avanti brothers Vinda and Anuvinda, and the Kaurava ranks are thrown into confusion.
Ghatotkacha fights Bhagadatta and his elephant, Bhagadatta destroys Ghatotkacha's horses, and Ghatotkacha flees from a duel he cannot win.
Salya fights the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, Sahadeva wounds Salya with a powerful arrow, and the Kauravas lose heart while the twins rejoice.
Yudhishthira and Srutayush exchange arrows, Yudhishthira kills Srutayush's steeds and charioteer, and Srutayush flees, and Yudhishthira begins slaughtering the Kaurava troops.
Kripa defeats Chekitana's charioteer and steeds, Chekitana fights with a mace and sword, and both he and Gautama are knocked out and carried off by their allies.

Bhurisravas defeats Dhrishtaketu and his charioteer, Abhimanyu fights several Kaurava warriors without killing them, and Arjuna charges Susarman with harsh words and is surrounded and showered with arrows.

Arjuna cuts down the bows of the Trigarta kings and others, clears the way toward Bhishma, and Sikhandin and the Pandava warriors come up to guard his chariot. Yudhishthira then scolds Sikhandin for failing to keep his vow, Sikhandin turns to Bhishma, and Bhishma's attacks on Yudhishthira and Bhima's fight with Chitrasena end the account.
Bhishma overwhelms Yudhishthira and the twins, the Pandava allies gather around Bhishma, and the battle spreads across the field, with Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki and the Avanti princes in combat.
A section heading marking the start of the next section.

The Kauravas advance in an array with Bhishma in front, and Yudhishthira answers with the Sringataka array, then the armies engage in a fierce general battle in which Bhishma charges the Pandavas and Dhrishtadyumna's warriors rush to meet him.

A long section: Bhishma routs the Pandava forces, Bhima kills Bhishma's charioteer and then Sunabha and seven more of Duryodhana's brothers, the sons recall Vidura's warnings, and Duryodhana goes to Bhishma and laments that he is being left to suffer alone.
Bhishma, with tears in his eyes, replies that he and Drona will not survive, that Bhima will kill whomever he targets, and urges Duryodhana to fight on for heaven.
Dhritarashtra asks how Bhishma, Drona and Kripa could have allowed his sons to be slain one by one, and blames fate and his son Duryodhana's refusal to heed warnings.

Sanjaya says Vidura's warnings have now come true, then describes the midday battle: the Pandavas split into three bodies, Drona kills the Srinjayas, Bhima destroys the Kaurava elephants, the twins attack the cavalry, and the field is strewn with dead animals and men.

A long section: Sakuni and Kritavarma advance, Iravat, Arjuna's son by a Naga princess, brings his horses into the field and crashes into the Kaurava cavalry, the six sons of Suvala charge and are killed one by one, and Duryodhana sends the Rakshasa Alamvusha, who fights Iravat with illusions until Iravat is beheaded.
Arjuna, not yet aware of his son's death, kills Bhishma's guards, Bhishma and Drona terrify the Pandava army, and the battle is so fierce that no side shows mercy.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him what the Pandavas did when they heard of Iravat's death.

Sanjaya describes Ghatotkacha's roar that shakes the earth and the Kaurava troops, the Rakshasas attacking the elephant division of the Vangas, Duryodhana's counterattack and the slaughter of the Rakshasa leaders, and Ghatotkacha's speech accusing Duryodhana of the cruelty of the dice match and of Draupadi's humiliation before he attacks him with arrows.

A long section: Duryodhana resists Ghatotkacha's arrows, Ghatotkacha kills Bhagadatta's elephant with a dart, Bhishma calls for a rescue, Ghatotkacha defeats the rescuers one by one, and Salya is left wounded.

A long section: Ghatotkacha is surrounded and flies up, Yudhishthira sends Bhima with his allies to rescue him, the armies fight in a chaotic and bloody melee, and the Dhritarashtra troops are driven back.

A long section: Duryodhana wounds Bhima, Ghatotkacha is enraged and Abhimanyu and the Pandava warriors rush at the king, Drona is wounded and sinks down on his chariot, Bhima on foot fights Duryodhana and Aswatthaman, Nila is wounded by Aswatthaman, and Ghatotkacha creates an illusion that routs the Kauravas. Sanjaya reports that Bhishma and he cry out to the fleeing troops, but they flee to their camp at sunset, and the Pandavas shout in triumph.

A long section: Duryodhana reports to Bhishma that Ghatotkacha has defeated him and asks to face the Rakshasa himself, Bhishma tells him to fight the Pandava leaders and sends Bhagadatta against Ghatotkacha, Bhagadatta's elephant battles the Pandava warriors, Bhagadatta wounds Bhima and breaks his chariot, Arjuna comes to the spot and fights, and Bhima tells Krishna and Arjuna how Iravat was killed.

A long section: Arjuna grieves for Iravat and rebukes the war for wealth, then Krishna drives him into the battle. Bhima kills Vyudoroska, Kundalin and seven other sons, Drona shoots at Bhima who holds firm, the armies clash, and the night ends the fighting.
Bhishma, Bhagadatta and Gautama face Arjuna, Abhimanyu unseats Amvashta, and the close fighting leaves the field strewn with weapons, dead men and animals, until night and both armies withdraw.

A long section: Duryodhana complains that his commanders do not resist the Pandavas, Karna advises that Bhishma lay down his weapons so Karna can fight, Duryodhana sends for his retinue, travels in procession to Bhishma's tent, and presses him to kill the Pandavas or let Karna fight. Bhishma stays silent.

Bhishma, wounded by Duryodhana's words, answers calmly, cites the Pandava victories and Krishna's protection, promises to fight the Somakas and Panchalas, and says he will not kill Sikhandin. He then sends Duryodhana away and prepares for battle the next morning.
Duryodhana, sensing Bhishma's resolve to face Arjuna, insists that Bhishma must be protected, reports Bhishma's vow not to kill Sikhandin, and orders his brothers and others to surround Bhishma.
Duryodhana's army surrounds Bhishma and places him in the front. Arjuna then tells Dhrishtadyumna to put Sikhandin in front of Bhishma and promises to protect him.
Bhishma marches out and forms the Sarvatobhadra array, names the commanders on each wing and in the rear, and places Duryodhana in the centre of the Kaurava line.
Yudhishthira forms the Pandava array with Bhima and the twins in front, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and Satyaki in support, and Sikhandin, Arjuna, Ghatotkacha and others in the centre and rear.
The two armies advance with loud drums and conches, the sun grows dim, birds and jackals gather, meteors fall, and the animals weep, while the battle begins in an evil hour.

A long section: Abhimanyu routs the Kaurava ranks and is praised by the kings, Duryodhana asks Alamvusha to stop him, Alamvusha defeats the five sons of Draupadi, and the duel between Alamvusha and Abhimanyu begins.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe in full how Alamvusha fought Abhimanyu and how the other Pandava warriors fought.

A long section: Abhimanyu and Alamvusha trade blows and illusions, Abhimanyu uses a solar weapon to dispel the darkness, Alamvusha flees, Abhimanyu grinds the Kaurava troops, Bhishma attacks him, Arjuna comes to his son's aid, Kripa, Satyaki and Drona's son clash, and Drona and Arjuna face each other at the end.
Dhritarashtra asks how Drona and Arjuna, who are both dear to each other, could come to fight.

A long section: Sanjaya explains that Kshatriyas fight kin without regard, Arjuna and Drona exchange shots, Duryodhana sends Susarman against Drona, Arjuna routs the Trigartas with the Vayavya weapon until Drona answers with the Saila weapon, the Kaurava allies attack Arjuna, and Bhima kills many elephants with his mace until the Kaurava elephant division flees.

A long section: Bhishma fights Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Drupada and Sikhandin, sparing Sikhandin, the Pandava warriors rush at him, the general battle breaks out with the horrible sights of dead men and animals, the river of blood is described, and Duryodhana urges his commanders to fight. Sanjaya ends by blaming the war on the king.

A long section: Arjuna routs Susarman's men, Duryodhana and Bhishma attack Arjuna, the Pandava warriors surround Bhishma to protect him, many duels follow, including Satyaki's attack on Kritavarman and Bhishma's duel with Satyaki, and both sides fight on fiercely at noon.
A section heading marking the start of the next section.

A long section: Duryodhana tells Dussasana to protect Bhishma, Sakuni's horsemen and the extra cavalry charge the Pandavas and are cut down, Duryodhana sends Salya against Yudhishthira, Salya wounds several Pandavas, and Bhima comes to Yudhishthira's side at sunset.
A long section: Bhishma's shafts cut down the Pandava army, the Chedis, Kasis and other allies are destroyed, the field is strewn with wreckage, and the Pandava army breaks into flight.

Krishna reminds Arjuna of his vow to fight Bhishma, Arjuna agrees and charges. The two heroes duel, Bhishma breaks Arjuna's bows, and Krishna jumps down and rushes at Bhishma with a whip. Arjuna catches him and pleads with him to stop, Bhishma welcomes Krishna's attack, and Krishna goes back to the chariot. Bhishma keeps shooting until the sun sets, and both armies withdraw.

A long section: the armies withdraw at dusk, Bhishma is praised by the Kauravas, and the Pandavas take counsel at night. Yudhishthira, despairing, offers to go into exile, and Krishna offers to fight Bhishma himself.
Yudhishthira declines to ask Krishna to break his pledge, recalls that Bhishma promised to advise but not fight for the Pandavas, and proposes that they go to Bhishma and ask how he can be defeated.
Krishna agrees that the Pandavas should ask Bhishma. The brothers lay down their armour and visit his tent, where Bhishma welcomes them and offers to help.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how he can be defeated and says the grandsire's skill is unmatched.

Bhishma explains that he will not fight those who have thrown down their weapons, women, or others he will not strike, and that Sikhandin, who was once a woman, can stand before Arjuna, who alone with Krishna can defeat him.
Arjuna, grieved, tells Krishna he cannot fight his grandfather, recalling how he once sat on Bhishma's lap as a child, and says he will not fight him even if his army is destroyed.
Krishna answers that Arjuna must slay Bhishma as a Kshatriya's duty requires, and cites the teaching of Vrihaspati that even an honoured elder who comes as an enemy may be killed.
Arjuna proposes to place Sikhandin before Bhishma, since Bhishma will not strike him, and says he himself will hold back the other great warriors.
The Pandavas return to their tents with Krishna after their talk with Bhishma, and the chapter ends with them going to rest.
Dhritarashtra asks how Sikhandin advanced against Bhishma and how Bhishma advanced against the Pandavas.

Sanjaya describes the Pandava array with Sikhandin in front, Bhima and Arjuna guarding his wheels, Yudhishthira and the others behind, and the Kaurava array with Bhishma at the head, Drona, Aswatthaman and others behind him. The two armies clash, and the Kaurava troops are beaten back.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe what Bhishma did when his army was struck by the Pandavas.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma's assault on the Pandavas, his showers of arrows, his destruction of the Pandava warriors, and on the tenth day his defeat of Sikhandin's division. Bhishma refuses to fight Sikhandin, who taunts him and wounds him.
Arjuna urges Sikhandin to attack Bhishma and promises to protect him and hold back the Kaurava warriors, including Drona, Kripa and Duryodhana.
Dhritarashtra asks how Sikhandin attacked Bhishma on the tenth day and whether Bhishma's bow or chariot was broken.
Sanjaya says that neither Bhishma's bow nor his chariot was harmed, that Bhishma was destroying the Pandava forces, and that the Pandavas could not defeat him.

Arjuna arrives and the Kaurava troops flee. Duryodhana, terrified, begs Bhishma to protect them. Bhishma reminds him of his vows, promises to slay the Pandavas or die, and destroys many Pandava troops, leaving the field to a fierce battle.

A long section: Arjuna urges Sikhandin to attack Bhishma and the Pandava commanders rush forward, the Kaurava warriors meet them in pairs, Dussasana holds back Arjuna, the two exchange wounds, and Arjuna wounds Duryodhana with many shafts until Duryodhana retreats to Bhishma's car.

A long section: Satyaki fights Alamvusha and Bhagadatta, Duryodhana gathers cars to trap Satyaki, Sikhandin rushes at Bhishma, and a series of duels breaks out among the Pandava and Kaurava warriors, ending with Bhurisravas wounding Bhima.

A long section: Drona lists the omens, including meteors, cries of birds and jackals, and trembling idols, predicts that Arjuna will attack Bhishma, notes Bhishma's vow not to slay Sikhandin, and tells his son to fight Sikhandin and Bhima while he himself goes against Yudhishthira.

A long section: the Kaurava warriors attack Bhima together, he wounds Salya, Kripa and Jayadratha, breaks their bows and kills their horses, Arjuna arrives with Sikhandin before him, and Duryodhana sends Susarman with the Trigartas against Arjuna and Bhima.

A long section: Arjuna and Bhima battle Salya, Susarman and the other Kaurava kings, destroying chariots and men, Drona and Jayatsena engage Bhima, Bhishma and Duryodhana advance, Sikhandin rushes at Bhishma, and Dhrishtadyumna urges the Pandavas to attack him.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe how Bhishma and the Kurus fought on the tenth day.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma's ten days of carnage, then his resolve to die, and his plea to Yudhishthira to strike him with Arjuna and Sikhandin in front. Yudhishthira vows to defeat Bhishma, the armies clash in a general battle, and the uproar and dust are described as a fight between hawks over meat.

A long section: Abhimanyu fights Duryodhana, Aswatthaman fights Satyaki, and Paurava and Dhrishtaketu wound each other until both fall. Paurava is carried off by Jayatsena and Dhrishtaketu by Sahadeva.
Chitrasena and Susarman exchange many arrows, each wounding the other.
Abhimanyu fights Vrihadvala, shooting down his bow and wounding him. The battle for Bhishma's sake is compared to the old fight between Vali and Vasava.
Bhima slaughters the elephant division, Yudhishthira fights Salya, and Jayadratha and Virata trade heavy wounds.
Drona and Dhrishtadyumna fight fiercely, Drona breaks Dhrishtadyumna's bow and deflects his mace and dart, and their duel is described as a fierce struggle for Bhishma's sake.

Arjuna charges toward Bhishma, scattering the Kaurava troops, and Sikhandin attacks Bhishma. Bhishma fights back with a blazing shower of arrows, slaughters the Somakas, and drives back the Pandava forces. Only Arjuna and Sikhandin dare to approach him.

Sikhandin strikes Bhishma with arrows, but Bhishma will not strike back, and Arjuna urges Sikhandin on. Dussasana fights Arjuna to protect Bhishma, Arjuna drives Dussasana back, and Sikhandin keeps shooting Bhishma, who accepts the arrows calmly while slaughtering the Pandavas.

Duryodhana calls on all his warriors to attack Arjuna, promising Bhishma's protection. The Kaurava allies rush at Arjuna, who scatters them, defeats Kripa, Salya, Dussasana, Vikarna and Vivinsati, and fills the field with dead men and animals. Bhishma then readies a celestial weapon against Arjuna, and Sikhandin rushes at Bhishma, forcing him to withdraw it.
The two armies fight in a disordered melee in which warriors of different kinds fight each other, and all distinctions between the fighters disappear.

Salya, Kripa, Dussasana and Vikarna push back the Pandava army, Bhishma cuts down its warriors, and Arjuna fells many of the Kaurava elephants, while the Kaurava princes press forward to fight for Bhishma.

Dhrishtadyumna orders the Somakas to attack Bhishma, who destroys many of their warriors, including Satanika. Krishna tells Arjuna to block Bhishma, and Arjuna and the Pandava warriors rush at him. Bhishma refuses to strike Sikhandin out of regard for his former sex, and Sikhandin and Arjuna keep attacking him.

A long section: the Pandavas and Srinjayas strike Bhishma from every side, and his body is pierced without pain. Arjuna and Sikhandin cut down his bows, and Bhishma decides to die at a favourable time, as the gods and sages approve. Duryodhana's allies attack Arjuna in his defence, Arjuna keeps shooting Bhishma's bows and armour, and at sunset falls from his chariot onto his bed of arrows. Swans appear, and Bhishma, who can choose his time of death, resolves to wait until the sun turns north.

The Kauravas grieve and are stunned, the Pandavas blow their conches and Bhima shouts in triumph, the soldiers on both sides lay down their arms, and the sages praise Bhishma while he sits in meditation, waiting.
A section heading marking the start of the next section.
Dhritarashtra laments that Bhishma, who was not slain even by Parashurama, has been killed by Sikhandin, and asks Sanjaya for the details.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma falling at sunset without touching the ground, the grief and shame of the Kauravas, the Pandava celebrations, and Dussasana telling Drona, who faints. Both armies then stop fighting and gather at Bhishma's bedside. Bhishma asks for a pillow, rejects the soft cushions the kings offer, and asks Arjuna for one.

Arjuna, reverent and tearful, asks Bhishma what to do. Bhishma asks for a pillow, Arjuna supports his head with three arrows, and Bhishma praises him and says he will wait until the sun turns north before dying. He asks for a ditch to be dug around him and orders the kings to end their hostility.

Bhishma refuses the physicians and asks that they be dismissed with gifts. The kings admire his steadfastness, the armies gather around him, and then they return to their tents in the evening, grieving.
Krishna tells Yudhishthira that the victory is due to his good fortune and that Bhishma has been brought down, and Yudhishthira credits Krishna's protection, to which Krishna replies with a smile.

A long section: crowds of kings, women, children and spectators gather around Bhishma, and he asks for water but refuses it, saying he is no longer of the human world. He calls for Arjuna, who makes a spring rise from the earth with a special arrow. Bhishma praises Arjuna and urges Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, pleading that the bloodshed end with his death, and then he falls silent and turns to yoga.
Sanjaya says that Duryodhana does not accept this advice, like a dying man refusing medicine.
Karna, hearing of Bhishma's fall, comes to him, and Bhishma embraces him, reveals that he is Kunti's son, and asks him to join the Pandavas and end the feud.
Karna replies that he knows his birth, that he cannot abandon Duryodhana, and that he will fight the Pandavas, asking Bhishma to forgive his past harsh words.
Bhishma gives Karna leave to fight, urging him to act without anger and noting that he himself tried for a long time to make peace.
After Karna salutes Bhishma and is forgiven, he mounts his chariot and rides towards Duryodhana's quarters.
A closing line marking the end of the Bhishma Parva.
