Section heading naming the Dronabhisheka Parva.
An opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati.
Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra did after Bhishma, slain by Sikhandin, had fallen.
Vaisampayana says that Dhritarashtra, grieving, asks Sanjaya, who has come back from the camp, to report what happened.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him what the Kauravas did after Bhishma fell.
Sanjaya describes Bhishma's bed of arrows, the renewed fighting, the leaderless Kaurava army, and the kings calling for Karna.
Vaisampayana says Dhritarashtra answers Sanjaya's repeated praise of Karna with a sigh.
Dhritarashtra asks whether Karna can fill the gap left by Bhishma and fulfil his sons' hopes of victory.
Sanjaya says Karna hurries to help the Kaurava army once he learns that Bhishma has fallen.
Karna speaks to the soldiers, mourning Bhishma's virtues and saying that without him he sees the other heroes as already lost.
Karna consoles the Kauravas, vows to slay the Pandavas, and asks for his armour, chariot and weapons to be brought.
Karna rides out to battle in a splendid chariot, and Sanjaya compares him to Indra.
Sanjaya describes Bhishma lying on his arrow-bed and Karna dismounting in grief to address him, promising to avenge him against Arjuna and the Pandavas.
Bhishma blesses Karna, recalls his past conquests, and orders him to lead the Kauravas in battle.
Karna takes leave of Bhishma, goes to the Kaurava warriors, and is greeted with loud shouts and noise.
Duryodhana, pleased to see Karna mounted, says the army now has a proper leader and suggests settling the matter.
Karna asks Duryodhana to speak first, since he is the wisest of the kings.
Duryodhana recalls Bhishma's leadership and asks Karna whom to appoint next, stressing that an army needs a leader.
Karna says the warriors are all worthy but Drona, their teacher and a master of arms, should be made leader.
Sanjaya says that Duryodhana, having heard Karna, turns to Drona in the midst of the troops.
Duryodhana praises Drona's birth, learning and skill, compares him to the greatest figures, and asks him to lead the army against the Pandavas.
The Kaurava kings cry victory to Drona and shout in approval, and Drona prepares to speak.
Drona says he knows the Vedas and many weapons and will fight, but he cannot slay Dhrishtadyumna, who was made for his death.
Duryodhana installs Drona as commander with proper rites, and the Kaurava army celebrates, already thinking the Pandavas beaten.
The Kaurava divisions take up their positions with Karna at the head of the bowmen, and Sanjaya describes the Pandava formation led by Arjuna and Krishna.
Sanjaya describes ill omens, the start of the battle, and Drona's fierce assault that breaks the Pandava and Panchala ranks.
Section heading marking the start of Section VIII.
Sanjaya describes Yudhishthira ordering the Pandavas to surround Drona, Drona's rampage, his death at Dhrishtadyumna's hand, and the Pandavas' shouts of victory.
Dhritarashtra mourns Drona, asks how he could be slain and who guarded him, and then stops to regain his senses before asking more.
Vaisampayana says Dhritarashtra, overcome by grief, faints, is revived by his attendants and the royal women, and then asks Sanjaya to tell him about the battle.
Dhritarashtra asks, one by one, who in his army resisted each Pandava and their allies as they rushed at Drona, and then calls on Krishna to steady him.
Dhritarashtra recounts Krishna's feats since boyhood, the allies who will join the Pandavas, and his own guilt for the Kurus' ruin, and asks Sanjaya to describe the battle.
Sanjaya says he will describe Drona's fall, then reports Drona's offer of a boon, Duryodhana's request for Yudhishthira to be taken alive, and Drona's guarded reply.
Drona explains that Arjuna, his pupil, is too strong to oppose, so Arjuna must be drawn away before Yudhishthira can be seized.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana made Drona's promise known to all the troops, and that the sons regarded Yudhishthira as already taken.
Sanjaya reports the Kaurava shouts over the pledge, and Yudhishthira learning of it through spies and asking Arjuna to fight close by.
Arjuna vows to keep Yudhishthira from capture, though he will not kill his teacher, and says he has never broken a vow.
Sanjaya describes the battle beginning, the two sides held in a deadlock by Drona and Arjuna, and Drona then driving into Dhrishtadyumna's division.
Sanjaya describes Drona's assault as a terrible river of blood and dead, with the fallen warriors and their weapons making up its parts.
Many single combats follow, including Sakuni and Sahadeva, Bhima and Vivinsati, Nakula and Salya, and Abhimanyu's duels with Paurava, Jayadratha and Salya, before the Kauravas surround Abhimanyu.
Dhritarashtra says he envies those who can see such duels, and asks Sanjaya to tell him about Salya and Abhimanyu.
Sanjaya describes Salya and Bhima's mace duel, in which both fall, Kritavarman carries Salya away, and the Pandavas drive the Kaurava army in flight.
Sanjaya describes Vrishasena's lone stand, Drona's charge at Yudhishthira, Arjuna's arrival, and the withdrawal of both sides as the sun sets.
Drona tells Duryodhana that Arjuna must be drawn away before Yudhishthira can be seized, and that he will then take Yudhishthira himself.
The Trigarta ruler and his brothers vow to draw Arjuna away and kill him, and their allies swear the same oath by fire, and Arjuna accepts their challenge.
Yudhishthira warns Arjuna that Drona has resolved to seize him and asks Arjuna to thwart the plan.
Arjuna names Satyajit as Yudhishthira's protector, and says that if Satyajit falls Yudhishthira should leave the field.
Yudhishthira blesses Arjuna, who rides out against the Trigartas, and the two armies clash with great force.
Sanjaya describes the Samsaptakas' half-moon formation, Arjuna's conch blast that stuns them, his killing of Sudhanwan, and the Trigarta king rallying the fleeing warriors.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's charge against the Samsaptakas, the illusory images that confuse the enemy, Krishna's worry, the wind weapon, the slaughter that follows, and Drona's attack on Yudhishthira.
Drona arrays the Kaurava army in the shape of a Garuda with himself in its mouth, and Yudhishthira answers with a counter-array and asks Dhrishtadyumna to keep Drona from taking him.
Dhrishtadyumna vows that Drona will never seize Yudhishthira while he lives.
Dhrishtadyumna charges Drona, Durmukha blocks him, and the battle becomes a chaotic slaughter of men and elephants that ends with Drona pressing toward Yudhishthira.
Sanjaya describes Satyajit's duel with Drona, which ends with Satyajit beheaded, then Yudhishthira's flight, Satanika's death, and Drona's rampage through the Pandava ranks.
Many Pandava warriors attack Drona and fall one after another, Yudhishthira flees again, and Drona routs the Panchalas and Matsyas.
Dhritarashtra asks whether anyone dared to face Drona after the Pandavas were broken, praising Drona's fearless resolve.
Sanjaya says the Kauravas, seeing the enemy routed, assailed their fleeing forces from all sides, and Duryodhana laughed as he spoke to Karna.
Duryodhana boasts that the Panchalas are broken, that Bhima stands alone among his foes, and that the Pandavas have lost hope.
Karna replies that the Pandavas will not flee, recalls their grievances, and warns that Bhima and the others are coming to surround Drona.
Duryodhana rides to Drona's car with his brothers, while the Pandava warriors return to the fight, all determined to kill Drona.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe the distinguishing marks of the chariots of the warriors who attacked Drona under Bhima.
Sanjaya lists the Pandava allies advancing on Drona, each identified by the colour and breed of his horses, from Satyaki and Yudhishthira to the Panchala princes and their followers.
Sanjaya describes the standards and bows of the Pandava warriors, such as Bhima's silver lion and Yudhishthira's golden moon, and says the host looked like painted images.
Sanjaya reports many single combats across the field, including Drupada against Drona, Virata against Vinda and Anuvinda, and Ghatotkacha against Alambusha, with battle breaking out everywhere.
Section heading marking the start of Section XXIV.
Dhritarashtra asks how Arjuna fought, what he did to the Samsaptakas, and what the Samsaptakas did to him.
Bhima routs Duryodhana's elephant division, cuts Duryodhana's bow and standard, and kills the Anga king on his elephant, and the Kaurava division flees.

Bhagadatta's elephant Supratika fights Bhima, who escapes by getting under its belly; the Pandavas hear a false cry that Bhima is dead, and Bhagadatta's elephant then routs them, killing Ruchiparvan and driving off Yuyutsu.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's dilemma between Bhagadatta and the Samsaptakas, his slaughter of the Samsaptakas with the Brahma weapon, and Krishna's praise before Arjuna orders the advance on Bhagadatta.
Sanjaya describes Arjuna's turn against Susharman and his brothers, his sweep through the Kaurava host, and his clash with Bhagadatta, whom he refuses to strike from behind.
Dhritarashtra asks what Arjuna did to Bhagadatta and what Bhagadatta did to Arjuna.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna cutting down Bhagadatta's weapons, armour and elephant, Bhagadatta's Vaishnava weapon turning into a garland on Krishna's chest, Krishna's account of its history, and Arjuna's killing of Bhagadatta.
Sanjaya describes Arjuna circling Bhagadatta's body and killing Vrishaka and Achala with a single arrow after they attack him from both sides.
Sakuni's illusions are destroyed by Arjuna, Sakuni flees, Arjuna's arrows split the Kaurava army, and the battlefield is left in panic and carnage.
Dhritarashtra asks what the Kauravas felt when their divisions were routed and how they could rally from such flight.
Sanjaya describes the Kurus seizing an opening against Bhima's side, the two armies fighting over Drona's life, and Dhrishtadyumna finally checking Drona.
Nila attacks the Kaurava ranks, but Ashvatthama kills him, and the Pandavas fear that Arjuna is too far away to rescue them.
Sanjaya describes the long battle around Drona's car, from Bhima's attacks and the Pandava rally through Arjuna's arrival, his clash with Karna, and the withdrawal of both armies at sunset.
Heading naming the Abhimanyu-badha Parva, the section on the slaying of Abhimanyu.
Sanjaya says the Kauravas, beaten by Arjuna and disheartened, retire from the field with Drona's consent and pass a silent, cursed night.
Duryodhana rebukes Drona for failing to seize Yudhishthira, and Drona answers by promising to kill a great Pandava warrior and form an impenetrable array, if Arjuna can be drawn away.
The Samsaptakas challenge Arjuna again, Drona forms his circular array, and Abhimanyu, ordered by Yudhishthira, breaks into it before six warriors and Duhsasana's son kill him.
Dhritarashtra grieves that a boy was slain by so many grown warriors and asks Sanjaya to tell how it happened.
Sanjaya says he will describe in detail how Abhimanyu broke into the Kaurava ranks and how the warriors were struck down.
Sanjaya praises the Pandavas, Krishna and Yudhishthira, and says Abhimanyu had the qualities of all of them.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him in detail how the invincible Abhimanyu was slain.
Sanjaya tells the king to be still and bear his grief, and promises to describe the great slaughter of his kinsmen.
Sanjaya describes Drona's circular array, with the kings and princes at its heads and Duryodhana in its midst, and the armies begin to fight to the death.
Sanjaya describes the Pandava leaders attacking Drona's array, Drona driving them back, and Yudhishthira deciding to send Abhimanyu in to break it.
Abhimanyu says he has been taught how to break such an array, but he may not be able to come back out if he is trapped.
Yudhishthira tells Abhimanyu to break the array once so the Pandavas can follow him through.
Bhima promises to follow Abhimanyu with Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki and the others, and to enter the array again and again.
Abhimanyu vows to penetrate Drona's array and to slaughter the enemy single-handed, or not count himself Arjuna's son.
Yudhishthira blesses Abhimanyu and asks that his strength be increased.
Sanjaya says Abhimanyu orders his charioteer Sumitra to drive quickly toward Drona's army.
Sumitra warns Abhimanyu that Drona is a master of arms and that Abhimanyu, raised in luxury, is untested, but Abhimanyu urges him forward.
Abhimanyu boasts that he fears no one, breaks into Drona's array, and slaughters warriors, elephants and steeds, until the Kauravas lose heart and flee, leaving their wounded kin on the field.
Sanjaya describes the Kaurava warriors surrounding Abhimanyu, his wounding of Karna and Salya, his killing of the Asmaka ruler, and the rout that follows, with the gods praising him.
Dhritarashtra asks which warriors of his army tried to check Abhimanyu while he was grinding down the foremost bowmen.
Sanjaya says he will describe Abhimanyu's prowess as he broke the chariot ranks, protected by Drona himself.
Salya's younger brother attacks Abhimanyu and is killed, with his charioteer, car and all his gear, and the onlookers cheer.
The followers of Salya's brother rush at Abhimanyu, who fights them first gently and then fiercely until the Kaurava car-division turns and flees.
Dhritarashtra says he feels both shame and pride that one youth held off his son's army, and asks for the whole account of the encounter again.
Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's rampage through the Kaurava chiefs, Drona's praise of him to Kripa, Duryodhana's sneer, the order to attack, and Duhsasana's car duel with Abhimanyu.
Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu taunting Duhsasana, wounding him so he falls into a swoon and is carried off, Karna's counterattack, and Abhimanyu breaking Karna's bow and standard.
Sanjaya describes Karna's brother slain, Karna's flight, the rout of the Kaurava army, and Abhimanyu blazing through the field until the dead make it impassable.
Dhritarashtra asks whether any great warrior in Yudhishthira's army followed Abhimanyu into the Kaurava ranks.
Sanjaya says the Pandava leaders rushed after Abhimanyu, but Jayadratha rallied the fleeing Kauravas and checked the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra asks what austerities and gifts gave Jayadratha the strength to hold off the Pandavas alone.
Sanjaya tells how Jayadratha, humbled by Bhima, performed severe austerities, won Mahadeva's boon to check the four other Pandavas, and then held the Pandava host on his own.

Sanjaya describes Jayadratha's splendid chariot, his attacks on the Pandava leaders, the exchange in which Yudhishthira's arrow cuts his bow, and his blocking of every Pandava attempt to pass, thanks to the boon.

Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu disabling Vrishasena's chariot, killing Vasatiya, and then cutting down the warriors who surround him until the field is covered with dead and he seems to vanish in the dust.
Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu seizing Satyasravas, Rukmaratha's death, the Gandharva illusions that let him slay a hundred princes, and Duryodhana being driven back.
Dhritarashtra calls Abhimanyu's prowess almost incredible and asks what his army did next after Duryodhana was beaten back and a hundred princes slain.

Sanjaya describes the Kaurava flight, the attack by Drona and his allies, Abhimanyu's killing of Lakshmana, the six warriors who surround him, and his killing of Kratha's son, after which the Kauravas turn away.
Dhritarashtra asks which warriors of his army surrounded Abhimanyu while he rode his three-year-old steeds through the field.

Sanjaya describes the kings fleeing, the six great warriors attacking Abhimanyu, his shots at Drona, Kripa, Karna and Ashvatthama, his killing of Vrindaraka, and his slaying of the ruler of the Kosalas, which sends ten thousand kings in flight.

Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's duel with Karna, his killing of many warriors, Drona's advice to disarm him, the Kaurava warriors cutting away his bow, steeds and charioteers, and Abhimanyu, stripped of sword and shield, charging Drona with a wheel.
Section heading marking the start of Section XLVII.
Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's wheel being shattered, his mace fight with Ashvatthama, Kalikeya and Duhsasana's son, and his death from a blow to the head, while the Kauravas rejoice.
Sanjaya says the Pandava troops break, and Yudhishthira rallies them by saying the boy has gone to heaven and that they will still win.

Sanjaya describes the evening withdrawal, the field strewn with dead animals and men, the scavengers and Rakshasas feasting, the river of blood, and Abhimanyu lying like a fire no longer fed with butter.
Sanjaya describes the Pandava warriors laying down their arms and Yudhishthira lamenting Abhimanyu, blaming himself for sending him into Drona's array and predicting Arjuna's vengeance.
Sanjaya says the sage Vyasa comes to Yudhishthira, who laments that Abhimanyu, a child, was sent into an unequal battle and cannot regain his peace of mind.
Sanjaya says that Vyasa addresses the grieving Yudhishthira.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that wise men are not stunned by calamity, that the youth has gone to heaven, and that Death takes all beings.
Yudhishthira asks what Death is, whose child he is, and why he takes living creatures.
Sanjaya says that Vyasa, comforting Yudhishthira, prepares to answer.
Vyasa introduces the story of King Akampana, told by Narada, which is said to ease grief and is worth hearing every morning.
Narada's account: King Akampana, whose son Hari was slain in battle, asks Narada who Death is and what his power is.
Narada begins the tale of how Brahma, finding creation without decay, let his anger create a fire that threatened to consume the universe, and how Shiva came to him.
Shiva (Sthanu) tells Brahma that his creatures are being consumed by his fire and asks him to be gracious.
Brahma says he wanted only the good of the earth, but his wrath rose when the earth, burdened by creatures, pressed him to destroy them and he could find no means.
Shiva (Rudra) asks Brahma to restrain his wrath, since the fire is destroying rocks, rivers, trees and every living thing.
Narada says Brahma held in his wrath, a dark woman came out of his senses, and Brahma named her Death and ordered her to kill creatures; she wept, and Brahma caught her tears in his hands.
Narada tells how Death, unwilling to take life, pleads with Brahma and asks to be allowed to practise austerities instead.
Brahma tells Death to destroy creatures, saying the task is hers and no one will blame her for it.
Narada says that Death, frightened, turned away from Brahma and spent a vast span of time in austerities at sacred places until Brahma asked her why she was so severe.
Brahma tells Death that no sin will be hers, that her tears will become diseases, and that she must take the lives of creatures.
Narada says Death, fearing Brahma's curse, agreed, and he tells Akampana that death is ordained and that he should stop grieving for his son.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to cast off his grief, notes that Abhimanyu has won heaven by his heroism, and urges him to set out for battle with his brothers.
Sanjaya says Yudhishthira humbly asks Vyasa for more words of consolation.
Yudhishthira asks Vyasa to tell him of royal sages of old, their sacrifices and their gifts, to console him.
Vyasa tells how Srinjaya's gold-producing son was slain by robbers, and how Narada consoles the grieving king with the example of Marutta, who also died.
Narada recounts King Suhotra's wealth, his great sacrifices and his death, and tells Srinjaya not to mourn a son who made no sacrifices.
Narada recounts King Paurava's great gifts at his Horse-sacrifices and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve for a son who gave nothing.
Narada recounts King Sivi's vast gifts, Rudra's boon, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve for a son who made no sacrifices.
Narada recounts Rama's exile, his slaying of Ravana, his golden reign and his death, and urges Srinjaya again not to grieve.
Narada recounts Bhagiratha's gifts and the river Ganga's sitting on his lap, and urges Srinjaya again not to grieve for his son.
Narada recounts Dilipa's hundreds of sacrifices, his gift of the earth, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Mandhatri's unusual birth, his conquests and sacrifices, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Yayati's sacrifices, his lesson that desire is never satisfied, his retreat to the forest, and his death, and urges Srinjaya again not to grieve.
Narada recounts Amvarisha's single-handed victories over a thousand kings, his hundred sacrifices, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Sasavindu's many sons, his vast gifts at the Horse-sacrifice, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Gaya's hundred years of devotion, Agni's boons, his golden-altar sacrifice, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Rantideva's army of cooks, his gifts of gold, the river named after his sacrificial hides, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Bharata's childhood mastery over lions and elephants, his many Horse-sacrifices and gifts, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada describes Prithu's golden reign, his milking of the Earth by all classes of beings, his great gifts, and his death, and urges Srinjaya again not to grieve.
Narada recounts Rama's avenging of his father, his destruction of the Kshatriyas, his gift of the earth to Kasyapa, and his retreat, and urges Srinjaya not to grieve for his son.
Vyasa reports that Srinjaya, silent after the histories, tells Narada his grief is gone and asks what he should do now.
Narada tells Srinjaya that his grief is gone and that he may ask any boon.
Srinjaya replies that it is enough that Narada is pleased with him.
Narada promises to bring back Srinjaya's son, who was slain by robbers, from the terrible hell where he went.
Vyasa describes the restored son, sets Abhimanyu's brave death above him, bids Yudhishthira rise and not grieve, departs, and leaves Yudhishthira consoled but still troubled about facing Arjuna.
Sanjaya describes the close of the day, Arjuna's return from slaying the Samsaptakas, and his fear of omens as he asks Krishna whether his brother and friends are safe.
Krishna says the king and his friends are surely well and that Arjuna should not grieve over some minor misfortune elsewhere.
Arjuna finds the camp joyless, with no music or songs, and asks Krishna whether his brothers and allies are safe.
Arjuna sees his brothers grieving, asks for Abhimanyu, and laments his son's death at length, blaming the warriors and hearing Yuyutsu's rebuke of the Kaurava heroes.
Krishna consoles Arjuna by saying that death in battle is the way of heroes, and Arjuna sits in grief until Yudhishthira begins to speak.

Yudhishthira recounts Abhimanyu's breaking of the array, Jayadratha's boon checking the Pandavas, the six warriors' attack, and Abhimanyu's death at the hands of Duhsasana's son, and Arjuna falls in grief.
Arjuna swears to slay Jayadratha the next day, whatever allies may protect him, and calls down the fate of sinners on himself if he fails.
Arjuna's second oath: if Jayadratha is not slain by the next sunset he will enter the fire, and even if Jayadratha hides in the underworld or heaven, he will cut off his head.
Arjuna stretches the Gandiva, Krishna and Arjuna blow their conches, and the Pandava camp answers with loud shouts and music.
Jayadratha, stricken by fear of Arjuna's vow, asks leave to go home, and Duryodhana reassures him by naming the great warriors who will surround him.
That night Jayadratha goes to Drona and asks him to compare Jayadratha's own skill in archery with Arjuna's.
Drona says Arjuna is superior through discipline and hardship, promises to form an array Arjuna cannot pierce, and urges Jayadratha to act as a warrior should.
Krishna rebukes Arjuna's rash oath, spies report the Kaurava dismay, Jayadratha pleads for protection, and Drona arranges a cart-and-lotus array with six champions guarding Jayadratha.
Section heading marking the start of Section LXXVI.
Arjuna tells Krishna that his enemies together are weaker than him, and swears to kill Jayadratha even against Drona and all protecting gods.
Sanjaya says Arjuna then asks Krishna to have the chariot equipped before the night ends.
Sanjaya lists the omens of the night, from winds and thunder to a headless trunk seen on the sun, and says Arjuna sends Krishna to console the women.
Krishna tells Subhadra that Abhimanyu died honorably, that Jayadratha will fall by the next day, and that Arjuna's vow cannot fail.
Subhadra laments her son's beauty and courage, blames the warriors who failed to protect him, and wishes him the rewards of many virtuous acts.
Draupadi and Uttara join the mourning and faint. Krishna sprinkles water on them, consoles them, and then returns to Arjuna's tent.

Krishna readies a bed in Arjuna's tent, Arjuna makes the night offering to Shiva, and the camp stays awake worrying; at midnight Krishna tells Daruka to prepare the chariot, weapons and horses for the morning.
Daruka replies that the night will bring Arjuna's victory, and he will do as Krishna commanded.
In a dream Krishna scolds Arjuna for grieving, Arjuna voices his fear of failing his vow, and Krishna points him to Shiva. Arjuna then travels to Shiva's mountain and sings a long hymn of praise.
Sanjaya says that after the praise, Krishna and Arjuna go on to ask Shiva for the weapon.
Arjuna asks Shiva for the celestial weapon; Shiva sends him and Krishna to a lake, where the snakes become a bow and arrow, Arjuna learns the skill, and both return to camp delighted.
At dawn, music and singing from many instruments wake king Yudhishthira from his sleep.
Yudhishthira bathes, worships the fire, gives gifts to many Brahmanas, dresses in jewels, and sits on a golden seat; he then has Krishna brought in and welcomes him with honour.
Yudhishthira greets Krishna, the warriors take their seats, Yudhishthira begs Krishna to help the Pandavas and Arjuna's vow, and Krishna promises Jayadratha's death that day.

Yudhishthira embraces Arjuna and predicts victory, Arjuna recounts his vision of Shiva, the warriors ride out with omens of success, and Arjuna asks Satyaki to guard the king before Satyaki goes to Yudhishthira.
A heading that names the Jayadratha-Vadha section.

Dhritarashtra asks how the Kauravas reacted to Abhimanyu's death and Arjuna's advance, notes the silence in his sons' camps, and recalls his failed counsel for peace; he asks Sanjaya to report what Duryodhana decided.
Sanjaya tells the king that his lamentations are useless now, lists the times he could have prevented the disaster, and says he will now describe the fighting.
Drona blows his conch and sets out his divisions, then assures Jayadratha that the Pandavas cannot reach him behind Drona's guard, and Jayadratha moves to his station.
Durmarshana leads a large elephant force, Duhsasana and Vikarna take the front, and Drona forms his cart-shaped array with a lotus and needle, which pleases Duryodhana.
The armies are arrayed amid omens and noise, Durmarshana boasts he will face Arjuna alone, and the conches of Arjuna and Krishna terrify the Kaurava troops.
Arjuna asks Krishna to drive toward Durmarshana and break through the elephant division.
Arjuna cuts down the Kaurava warriors, their elephants and their horses, and the Kaurava army breaks and flees.
Dhritarashtra asks who advanced against Arjuna, or whether his warriors simply retreated behind Drona's array.
Sanjaya describes Duhsasana's elephant charge, Arjuna's slaughter of the elephants and their riders, and Duhsasana's flight to Drona.
Arjuna asks Drona for his blessing, saying he is like a father to him, and asks to pass through the array to kill Jayadratha.
Drona says Arjuna must first defeat him, and the two duel, with Drona cutting Arjuna's bowstring and burying him in arrows; Krishna then urges Arjuna to go around Drona and press on.
Drona asks where Arjuna is going, and Arjuna replies that Drona is his teacher and not his foe.
Arjuna plunges into the army, the Panchala princes follow him, and Jaya, Kritavarman and other allies rush to stop him.
Arjuna fights his way forward past Drona, then defeats Kritavarman, Srutayudha and Sudakshina, and Srutayudha dies when his mace turns back on him; Sudakshina then falls, and the troops flee.

Arjuna wipes out wave after wave of Kaurava allies, is knocked senseless by a spear and comforted by Krishna, kills the brothers Srutayus and Achyutayus, and continues the massacre of foreign troops until the field is a river of blood, ending with the death of Srutayus of the Amvashthas and Arjuna being surrounded.
Duryodhana rushes to Drona, says Arjuna has broken through the army, and blames Drona for not stopping him and for failing to save Jayadratha.
Drona says he does not blame Duryodhana, explains that Krishna's horses and Arjuna's arrows are too swift for him, and urges Duryodhana to fight Arjuna himself.
Duryodhana protests that he cannot resist Arjuna, who has already beaten Drona's best allies.
Drona promises that a golden armour will protect Duryodhana from any weapon and urges him to fight Arjuna in it.
Drona blesses Duryodhana by calling on many gods and sages, and tells how Shiva gave his armour to Indra to defeat Vritra.
Drona explains the armour's chain of owners, from Shiva through Angiras and Vrihaspati to himself, and says he uses its sacred words to protect Duryodhana.
Drona fastens the armour on Duryodhana with sacred cords and sends him out; the king advances with elephants, horses and chariots while the troops roar.

The Pandavas and Somakas charge Drona's array, Dhrishtadyumna splits the Kaurava host into three, and Drona fights back while many one-on-one duels break out, including Bhimasena and Yudhishthira against their Kaurava opponents.
Jayadratha stays at the rear, guarded on both wheels by Drona's son and Karna, with Kripa, Salya and others protecting his back.
A heading marking the start of Section XCV.

Sanjaya describes the battle's separate duels, including Vinda and Anuvinda against Virata, Valhika against Sikhandin, Duhsasana against Satyaki, the twins against Sakuni, Yudhishthira against Salya, and Vivinsati's group against Bhimasena.
The Pandavas split off to attack the three Kaurava groups, Drona and Dhrishtadyumna trade fierce arrow fire, and the field fills with the dead and with scavenging animals.
Dhrishtadyumna leaps onto Drona's chariot with a sword, Drona cuts down his shield and horses, Satyaki saves him with arrows, and the Panchalas withdraw him from the battle.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Drona did after Dhrishtadyumna was rescued by Satyaki.

Drona charges Satyaki, and the two fight a long duel in which Satyaki repeatedly cuts Drona's bows; Drona admires his skill, uses celestial weapons, and both weapons cancel out as the sun sets, drawing rescuers into the fight.
As evening falls, Arjuna and Krishna drive their chariot through the Kaurava ranks, guided by arrows that clear the way and by Krishna's skilful driving.
Vinda and Anuvinda attack Arjuna's tired horses, Arjuna kills both brothers and their followers, and the Kaurava forces surround him while he and Krishna discuss what to do next.
Arjuna tells Krishna that he will hold back the army while Krishna looks after the horses.

Arjuna stands alone on the ground against the Kshatriya host, Krishna notes the horses need water, Arjuna pierces the earth with a weapon to make a lake, and then builds an arrow hall, which pleases Krishna.
Arjuna fights on foot against the kings, Krishna tends the horses and makes them drink, then they remount and charge at Jayadratha while the Kauravas despair and Duryodhana hurries to block them.
Arjuna and Krishna pass through Drona's and the Bhojas' divisions, the Kaurava army despairs, Arjuna vows to kill Jayadratha even against Indra, and Duryodhana rides out to stop them.
Krishna urges Arjuna to attack Duryodhana, listing his wrongs against the Pandavas and arguing that his death will open the way forward.
Arjuna agrees and vows to avenge Draupadi's insult; the two heroes blow their conches, and Duryodhana taunts Arjuna to show his skill.
Duryodhana wounds Arjuna and Krishna, Arjuna's shots bounce off his armour, and Krishna questions Arjuna's strength.
Arjuna explains that the armour came down from Indra through a chain of teachers, that Drona fitted it on Duryodhana, and that he will still win.
Aswatthaman cuts down Arjuna's prepared arrows, Arjuna destroys Duryodhana's horses, charioteers, bow and car, the Kauravas rush to save him, and Krishna's conch and Arjuna's bow scatter them.
The Kaurava warriors rush forward, the eight protectors of Jayadratha surround Arjuna, the conches sound, and Arjuna cuts down Salya's bow and wounds his many attackers in turn.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe the battle standards of both sides.

Sanjaya lists the banners of the champions, from Arjuna's ape and Drona's son's lion tail to Jayadratha's silver boar and Duryodhana's gem-decked elephant, and then blames the king's policy for the slaughter as Arjuna faces his enemies alone.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what the Panchalas did against Drona's division after Arjuna saw Jayadratha.

The Panchalas and Pandavas strike at Drona's division and many duels break out, until Drona cuts down Yudhishthira's bow, horses and chariot, and the Pandava troops cry out that the king is dead before he escapes on Sahadeva's chariot.

Vrihatkshatra kills Kshemadhurti, Dhrishtaketu kills Viradhanwan, Sahadeva beats Durmukha and kills Niramitra, Satyaki defeats Vyaghradatta and his Magadha followers, and Drona furiously charges at Satyaki.

Somadatta's son wounds the five sons of Draupadi, then the Pandava princes unite against him, cut down his horses, bow and charioteer, and Sahadeva's son beheads him, which sends the Kaurava troops into flight.

Alamvusha fights Bhima with illusions, recalls that Bhima killed his brother Vaka, and rains down weapons that wreck the Pandava troops, until Bhima strikes back with the Tvashtri weapon and drives him off the field.

Ghatotkacha duels Alamvusha with illusions, the Pandavas surround Alamvusha with chariots, Ghatotkacha seizes and crushes him, the Pandavas celebrate, and the Kauravas cry out in grief as Ghatotkacha roars in triumph.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe how Satyaki fought Drona.

Drona and Satyaki trade arrows, Yudhishthira orders his men to rescue Satyaki, Drona routs the Pandava forces, and Yudhishthira, hearing the Krishna conch and fearing for Arjuna, begs Satyaki to go to Arjuna's side.
Satyaki pledges to fight the whole Kaurava army and to reach Arjuna, but first passes on Arjuna's request that he guard Yudhishthira against Drona.
Yudhishthira insists Satyaki must go to Arjuna, names the warriors who will protect him, and asserts that Dhrishtadyumna will hold back Drona.

Satyaki, fearing the charge of cowardice, agrees to follow Arjuna, lists the Kaurava forces he must face, including elephant divisions and warrior groups, and asks for his chariot to be equipped with weapons.
Yudhishthira provides arms, Satyaki's horses are fed and harnessed, the Brahmanas bless him, and after telling Bhima to guard the king, Satyaki charges into the Kaurava army.
Satyaki routs the Kaurava troops and fights Drona, who accuses him of abandoning Arjuna in cowardice and threatens him.
Satyaki answers that he will follow his teacher Arjuna's path and will not waste time fighting Drona.
Satyaki drives toward Karna's host, beheads Kritavarman's charioteer, and then is held up by the Kamboja division while Drona pursues him.
A heading that marks the start of Section CXIII.
Dhritarashtra laments that his well-paid army is being destroyed by Arjuna and Satyaki and asks Sanjaya what happened when they entered the host.
Sanjaya blames the king for ignoring Vidura's counsel, then describes how Kritavarman alone holds off the Pandavas, wounds Bhima and Sikhandin, and routs the Pandava and Panchala forces.
Satyaki returns to fight Kritavarman, routs his forces, then faces and scatters the Trigarta elephants, kills Jalasandha after a long duel, and the Kaurava troops flee as Drona comes to face Satyaki.
Satyaki is attacked by Drona and many Kaurava princes, wounds Duryodhana until he flees, then overcomes Kritavarman and presses on through the Kaurava ranks.
Drona and Satyaki trade arrows evenly, Drona's dart wounds Satyaki's charioteer, Satyaki drives himself, kills Drona's driver and scatters his horses, and Drona returns to hold the broken array.
Satyaki mocks his foes, cuts down King Sudarsana's horses and charioteer and then beheads him, and drives on along Arjuna's path while the warriors marvel at him.
Satyaki urges his charioteer across the blood-soaked ground toward the Kaurava ranks, saying Arjuna is near and Jayadratha will fall before sunset.
The charioteer says he is not afraid and reminds Satyaki that he has already beaten the Kambojas, Yavanas and Sakas.
Satyaki vows to kill these foreign troops and Duryodhana's allies, saying Duryodhana will grieve when he sees them slain.
Sanjaya narrates that the charioteer drives onward, Satyaki cuts down the Yavanas, Kambojas and Sakas in heaps, routs the survivors, and is praised by the heavenly musicians.

Satyaki, glittering in gold and fighting like a hunter, mows down the Kaurava troops, beats off Duryodhana and his brothers in a long duel, kills Duryodhana's charioteer, and routs the army on his way to Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how his sons could face Satyaki and says the Pandavas might as well lay down their arms, since Satyaki will surely destroy his sons.

Sanjaya blames the king's own evil counsel and describes the Samsaptakas, Duhsasana's stone-throwing hill tribesmen, and the Kaurava troops being slaughtered, and Drona hearing the uproar and turning to find Satyaki.

Drona rebukes Duhsasana for fleeing, recalls his insults to Draupadi and his reckless gambling, and urges him to make peace before the Pandavas destroy them all; Duhsasana ignores him and goes to fight Satyaki. Drona then kills Viraketu and other Panchala princes, fights a fierce duel with Dhrishtadyumna, cuts off his charioteer's head, and routs the Panchalas before returning to his array.
Duhsasana fights Satyaki and is driven off, the Trigartas are cut down, Satyaki strips Duhsasana of his bow and chariot, spares his life for Bhima's sake, and rides on toward Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra asks why no warrior in his army could stop Satyaki, who passed through the whole host alone.
Sanjaya describes the vast muster of both armies, and the Pandava princes urging their men to stop Satyaki and Arjuna before they reach Jayadratha.
Dhritarashtra worries that Duryodhana, fighting alone against many, might have turned back.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana drives into the Pandava host, wounds Bhima, the twins, Yudhishthira and others, and then Yudhishthira breaks his bow before Drona rescues him.
Drona fights Vrihatkshatra, the Kekaya prince, in a long duel, and kills him after a clash of Brahma weapons and an arrow through his chest.
Dhrishtaketu of the Chedis attacks Drona, loses his bow, horses and charioteer, and is killed when Drona's arrow pierces him, and his son is also slain by Drona.
Drona kills Jarasandha's son, then the Panchala princes flee in dread, Kshatradharman is killed, and Chekitana is driven back; Drupada rallies the Pandavas to charge Drona.
Yudhishthira, unable to see or hear Arjuna and Satyaki, fears for them both and decides to send Bhima to help Satyaki, so that the world cannot blame him for caring only for his brother.
Bhima tells Yudhishthira not to grieve and says he will go to Arjuna and Satyaki and send word back.
Bhima entrusts Yudhishthira to Dhrishtadyumna, saying he dares not disobey the king's order, and sets out in full armour, blessed with omens, while Yudhishthira blesses him.

Yudhishthira urges Bhima on again after hearing Krishna's conch, Bhima charges the Kaurava host, Drona warns him, Bhima answers with a challenge and hurls a mace that drives Drona's chariot into the ground, and Bhima kills Duhsasana's brothers and others while routing the Kaurava forces.
Bhima's great mace routs the kings who surround him, and he pushes on through the Kaurava ranks like Garuda.
Drona attacks Bhima, who leaps down, throws down Drona's chariot, crushes the Bhoja and Kamboja divisions, and then shouts for Arjuna; Arjuna and Krishna answer with their own roars.
Yudhishthira praises Arjuna's past feats, rejoices at Bhima's message, and worries whether Arjuna can slay Jayadratha before sunset and whether Duryodhana will make peace.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya who could stand against Bhima, saying he fears Bhima more than Arjuna, Krishna or Satyaki.
Karna challenges Bhima, the two trade arrows, Bhima cuts Karna's bow and kills his charioteer and horses, and Karna escapes to another chariot while Bhima's shout brings cheers from the Pandavas.
Duryodhana rides to Drona, complaining that Arjuna, Bhima and Satyaki have passed through his army and reached Jayadratha, and asks what should be done next.

Drona says the three Pandava heroes must be stopped, that Jayadratha is the real stake of this game of battle, and sends Duryodhana to guard him; Duryodhana then fights Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, disables their chariots and takes refuge on the Madra king's car while the two princes ride on toward Arjuna.
A heading marking the start of Section CXXX.
Sanjaya says Karna charges Bhima like an elephant against an elephant as the combatants watch in fear.
Dhritarashtra asks how Bhima could fight Karna, who once lost to Bhima and who is famed as the greatest bowman, and asks Sanjaya to tell him the outcome.

Karna mocks Bhima for trying to flee to Arjuna, Bhima takes up the challenge, and after a long duel Bhima cuts Karna's bow, slays his horses and charioteer, and wounds him so that he must mount another car.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Duryodhana said when Karna retreated, and how Bhima and Karna fought on.

Karna returns on a new chariot, and Bhima, remembering the wrongs done to the Pandavas, charges with reckless fury; their duel is evenly matched, the field is strewn with dead, and Krishna and Arjuna see that the burden may be too heavy for Bhima.
Dhritarashtra marvels at Bhima's skill against Karna, fears the Kauravas are already lost because of his son's arrogance and the Pandavas' repeated victories, and asks Sanjaya to describe the duel.

Sanjaya describes how Bhima cuts Karna's bow, kills his horses and charioteer, and shoots down Karna's dart; Durjaya rushes in to help Karna but is killed by Bhima, and Karna, weeping, is covered by Bhima's arrows.
Sanjaya describes Karna's chariot being broken, Durmukha's death, and Karna's wounded flight, all in one long report.
Dhritarashtra laments that fate rules, recalls Duryodhana's boasts about Karna, and fears Bhima's strength for his sons.
Sanjaya tells the king he is the root of the disaster, since he followed his sons' counsel, and asks him to hear the battle report.
Five more sons of Dhritarashtra rush at Bhima and are killed by his arrows, while Karna and Bhima turn their anger on each other.
Sanjaya gives a long account of the duel, the six brothers' deaths, and the king's sons losing heart.
Sanjaya's long report covers Karna's charge, Bhima's victory, Duryodhana's regret over Vidura's advice, and Sanjaya's blame of Dhritarashtra.
Dhritarashtra blames his own bad policy for the disaster and asks Sanjaya to report on the slaughter.
Sanjaya describes the arrow duel, the fleeing troops, the field covered with corpses and wreckage, and the closing comparison to fire in dry grass.
Sanjaya gives a very long account of the duel, ending with Arjuna scattering Karna and the Kaurava army.
Dhritarashtra laments his falling fame, Arjuna's entry into his army, and the likely death of the Sindhu ruler, then asks about Satyaki.
Sanjaya describes Satyaki's duel with Alamvusha, the death of Alamvusha, Satyaki's advance, and the closing joy of Arjuna and Krishna.
Sanjaya tells how Satyaki beats back the Trigarta and other divisions and reaches Arjuna, and how Krishna and Arjuna react.
Bhurisravas taunts Satyaki and the two fight with arrows, swords and wrestling until both are exhausted and bloody.
Krishna urges Arjuna to save Satyaki from Bhurisravas, and Arjuna's arrow cuts off the arm holding the sword.
Sanjaya describes Bhurisravas's arm, cut off by Arjuna, falling to the ground, and Bhurisravas turning to rebuke Arjuna.
Bhurisravas accuses Arjuna of breaking the rules of war and of disgracing the Kshatriya code, and Arjuna answers that he was protecting Satyaki.
Bhurisravas sits down to die by fast, while Arjuna asks him to go to the heavenly regions and the crowd murmurs against Arjuna.
Krishna blesses Bhurisravas and tells him to go to his heavenly realm.
Satyaki, freed from Bhurisravas, draws his sword and beheads him while the warriors protest, and the gods and Siddhas applaud Bhurisravas's end.
Satyaki defends himself, recalling how the Kauravas killed Abhimanyu when he was unarmed, and quotes an old verse.
Sanjaya says that no one spoke up for Satyaki's act, and closes by praising Bhurisravas's courage and his death.
Dhritarashtra asks how the unbeaten Satyaki could be thrown down by Bhurisravas.
Sanjaya traces the family lines of Satyaki and Bhurisravas, explains Somadatta's boon, praises the Vrishnis, and blames Dhritarashtra's policy.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how the battle went on after Bhurisravas's death.
Sanjaya describes Arjuna's push toward Jayadratha, the Kaurava leaders' efforts to stop him, Karna's disabling, and Ashwatthaman's rescue of the Sindhu king.
Sanjaya describes Arjuna's celestial weapons, his rampage through the army, Krishna's illusion of sunset, Jayadratha's beheading, and the death of Vriddhakshatra.
Sanjaya says the darkness was revealed as an illusion, the Pandavas blow their conches, Yudhishthira attacks Drona, and Arjuna keeps fighting after his vow is fulfilled.
A heading that marks the start of the next section, Section CXLVI.
Dhritarashtra asks what his warriors did after Jayadratha's death.
Kripa and Ashwatthaman shower Arjuna with arrows, Kripa swoons, and Arjuna grieves that he has struck his teacher, while Krishna says Satyaki can handle Karna.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Satyaki-Karna duel went and what car Satyaki rode after losing his own.
Sanjaya explains that Krishna had foreseen Satyaki's defeat by Bhurisravas and had readied his car, and that Satyaki and Karna then fought furiously until Karna was left carless.
Dhritarashtra asks whether Satyaki rode another car after his duel with Karna.
Sanjaya describes the new chariots brought for Satyaki and Karna and recounts the sons of Dhritarashtra killed by Bhima, Satyaki and Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra asks what Bhima did in the battle after the chariot duels.
Bhima reminds Arjuna of their vow and of Karna's insults, and Arjuna answers Karna, vows to kill Vrishasena, and receives Krishna's praise as the sun sets.
Krishna points out the battlefield to Arjuna, describing the dead kings, elephants, cars and riders strewn across the ground.
Krishna blows his conch, and he rides to Yudhishthira to tell him that Jayadratha is dead.
Sanjaya describes Krishna's report to Yudhishthira, the king's joy and praise, the Kauravas' coming ruin, and Arjuna's welcome to Bhima and Satyaki, with the Pandava army regaining its resolve.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's despair after Jayadratha's death and his speech to Drona, in which he blames himself and swears to fight on.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how the Kauravas took the deaths of Jayadratha and Bhurisravas and what Drona said to Duryodhana.
Sanjaya reports the wailing in the Kaurava ranks and Drona's grief at Duryodhana's words.
Drona answers Duryodhana with a long reproach, blaming him for ignoring Vidura and the dice game, vowing to fight on, and sending a message to Ashwatthaman.
Duryodhana tells Karna that Arjuna passed through Drona's formation and killed Jayadratha, blaming Drona and his own refusal to let Jayadratha go home.
Karna defends Drona, blames Fate for the defeat, and urges Duryodhana to fight on despite the losses.
Sanjaya says the Pandava divisions advance and the battle resumes, and blames Dhritarashtra's evil policy.
A heading that names the Ghatotkacha-badha Parva.
Sanjaya describes the fighting in the dusk, Duryodhana's assault on the Pandava host, Yudhishthira's wounding of him, the false cry of the king's death, and Drona's rescue.
Dhritarashtra asks who protected Drona and how such a great warrior could be brought down.
Sanjaya describes the Pandava divisions converging on Drona in the dark, the omens, the confused night battle, and Drona's slaughter of enemy troops.
Dhritarashtra asks a string of questions about Drona's fight and who was with him, and how the Pandavas and his own troops fared that night.
Sanjaya reports Drona's kills, Bhima's fist-fights with the Kalinga prince, Dhruva and others, the destruction of Durmada and Dushkarna, and the Pandavas' honor to Bhima as the Kaurava kings flee.

Sanjaya describes Somadatta's vow against Satyaki, their duel and Somadatta's collapse, Drona's rampage through the Pandava host, Arjuna and Bhima turning to face him, and Ashwatthaman's fight with Ghatotkacha, in which Anjanaparvan is killed.
Ghatotkacha challenges Ashwatthaman to fight him.
Ashwatthaman answers that a father and son should not fight, and that he bears no grudge against Ghatotkacha.
Ghatotkacha insists on the fight and conjures an illusion, which Ashwatthaman dispels with his own weapons; Ashwatthaman then warns Duryodhana to stand aside while he fights.
Duryodhana replies that Ashwatthaman's generosity is great.
Ashwatthaman orders Sakuni and a large force to attack the Pandavas, to be joined by Karna, Kripa, Salya and others.

Sanjaya describes Ashwatthaman's slaughter of the Rakshasa army, the battle with Ghatotkacha and Dhrishtadyumna, a river of blood, the killing of several Pandava princes, and the mortal wounding of Ghatotkacha, who is then carried off.
Sanjaya describes Somadatta's duel with Satyaki, Bhima's killing of Valhika and of many Kaurava princes and allies, and the wavering of the kings.
Yudhishthira destroys Kaurava divisions, Drona and Yudhishthira trade celestial weapons, and Arjuna and Bhima drive the routed Kaurava host back.
Duryodhana, facing the surging Pandava army, asks Karna to save his warriors.
Karna boasts that he will kill Arjuna with Indra's dart and give Duryodhana victory.
Kripa mocks Karna's boasting, reminding him of past defeats and saying his words are idle.
Kripa lists the allies of the Pandavas and warns that the Pandavas cannot be overcome.
Karna answers Kripa with scorn, threatens him, and insists that victory depends on Fate.
Ashwatthaman, seeing his uncle Kripa insulted, rushes at Karna in fury.
Ashwatthaman rebukes Karna, saying Arjuna's feats show how weak his boasts are, and vows to behead him.
Kripa and Duryodhana hold Ashwatthaman back, and Karna asks that he be let go.
Ashwatthaman forgives Karna for now, saying Arjuna will bring down his pride.
Duryodhana urges Ashwatthaman to calm down and forgive, pointing to the Pandava army coming against Karna.
Sanjaya says Ashwatthaman's anger is calmed, and Kripa, who is mild in temper, returns to speak.
Kripa forgives Karna in the same way, saying Arjuna will humble his pride.
Karna holds the Pandava host off with clouds of arrows, leaving the enemy kings dazed and their troops heaped with the dead, and Duryodhana asks Ashwatthaman to block Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra asks what Karna did when he met Arjuna, the foe he had always challenged.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's duel with Karna, in which Arjuna cuts Karna's bow, steeds and charioteer, and Karna flees on Kripa's chariot, after which Duryodhana tries to rally his men and go against Arjuna, and Ashwatthaman and Kripa move to stop him.
Duryodhana tells Ashwatthaman that Drona always shields the Pandavas and urges him to slay the Panchalas and Somakas.

Sanjaya describes Ashwatthaman's vow to fight recklessly for Duryodhana, his duel with Dhrishtadyumna, the destruction of Dhrishtadyumna's chariot, and his triumph over the Panchalas, as the Kauravas applaud him.
A heading that marks the start of Section CLX.
Sanjaya describes Yudhishthira and Bhima surrounding Ashwatthaman, Duryodhana and Drona joining the fight, the slaughter of many divisions, and the rout of the Kaurava host in the darkness.
Sanjaya describes Satyaki's duel with Somadatta, Somadatta's death, Yudhishthira's clash with Drona, and Krishna's advice to Yudhishthira to leave Drona and join Bhima.
Sanjaya describes how in the dark the warriors fight by name and voice, and many are killed or flee in confusion.
Dhritarashtra asks how the minds of the warriors fared in the darkness and how the armies became visible again.
Sanjaya describes the Kaurava army's reorganization, Duryodhana's order to light lamps, the lit host, and the Pandavas' answering lights, ending with Ashwatthaman scorching the Pandavas.
Sanjaya describes the lit field, the duels between heroes, and Arjuna's sweep through the Kaurava ranks.
Dhritarashtra asks what the Kaurava soldiers thought when Arjuna entered the army and who protected Drona.
Duryodhana orders his brothers and the Trigartas to shield Drona, names Dhrishtadyumna as the main threat, and the battle resumes with heavy losses on both sides.
Sanjaya describes Yudhishthira ordering the attack on Drona, the pairing of Kaurava and Pandava champions, and Kritavarman's defeat of Yudhishthira, who withdraws from battle.
Sanjaya describes Satyaki's duel with Bhuri and Bhuri's death, Ashwatthaman's attack on Satyaki, the duel between Ashwatthaman and Ghatotkacha, and Ghatotkacha's removal from the field.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana and Bhima fighting until Bhima's mace crushes Duryodhana's chariot, the Kauravas' panic at the news of his death, and the renewed battle around Drona.
Sanjaya describes Karna's defeat of Sahadeva, his mocking words and his decision to spare him, and Sahadeva's withdrawal.
Sanjaya describes Salya's duel with Virata and Satanika, the rout of the Pandava troops, the Rakshasa Alamvusha's challenge to Arjuna, and Arjuna's victory and advance toward Drona.
Sanjaya describes Satanika stripping Chitrasena of his armour, bow, chariot and steeds, and Chitrasena's retreat onto Hridika's son's chariot.
Sanjaya describes Vrishasena's duel with Drupada, Drupada's wounding and withdrawal, and the Panchalas fleeing from Karna's son.
Sanjaya describes Duhsasana's duel with Prativindhya, Prativindhya's loss of chariot and bow, his brothers' arrival, and the general melee at midnight.
Sanjaya describes Nakula's duel with Sakuni, Sakuni's wounding and downfall, Kripa's fight with Sikhandin, and the chaos of the night battle in which men kill their own side.

Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna's assault on Drona and the battle with Karna and his allies, Satyaki's duel with Karna and Vrishasena, Karna's warning about Arjuna, and Duryodhana's orders to Sakuni.
Sanjaya describes Satyaki's rout of the Kaurava kings, Duryodhana's loss of his chariot and bow, and his flight.
Sakuni and Uluka attack Arjuna, are beaten back, and Krishna and Arjuna blow their conches in victory.
Dhrishtadyumna cuts down Drona's bowstring and routs his men, and the Pandavas blow their conches in triumph.
Duryodhana rebukes Drona and Karna, they return to battle, Drona routs the Pandavas and Panchalas, and Krishna and Arjuna advance on Drona and Karna with Bhima's support.
Sanjaya describes the renewed night clash, in which warriors fight by names alone in the dark and the enemy's cries spread across the field.
Sanjaya describes Karna's duel with Dhrishtadyumna, Karna's rout of the Panchalas, and Yudhishthira's and Arjuna's dismay at the situation, with Arjuna resolving to face Karna.
Krishna tells Arjuna that Karna's dart is held for Arjuna, and calls on Ghatotkacha to face Karna, who comes forward ready to fight.
Krishna and Arjuna urge Ghatotkacha to fight Karna in single combat, with Satyaki guarding his rear.
Ghatotkacha promises to fight Karna and to spare no one that night.
Ghatotkacha rushes at Karna and their duel begins, which Sanjaya compares to Indra's fight with Prahlada.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's orders to Duhsasana and to Alamvusha, the Rakshasa duel with illusions, Ghatotkacha's killing of Alamvusha, his taunt to Duryodhana, and his advance on Karna.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe Ghatotkacha's appearance, car, steeds, weapons and armour, and the duel with Karna.

Sanjaya describes Ghatotkacha's appearance and chariot, the duel that follows with Karna's shafts, Ghatotkacha's illusions and weapons, Karna's countermeasures, the destruction of Ghatotkacha's steeds, and Ghatotkacha's threat before he vanishes.
Sanjaya describes the Rakshasa Alayudha arriving with a host to avenge Vaka, Kirmira and Hidimva and asking Duryodhana's leave to fight.
Duryodhana grants Alayudha's request and sends him out, and Sanjaya describes Alayudha's chariot and steeds and the Pandava kings readying themselves to meet him.

Sanjaya describes the Kauravas' delight at Alayudha's arrival, Duryodhana's order to him, Bhima's duel with Alayudha, Krishna's orders to the Pandava warriors, and the bloody mace and fist fight between Bhima and Alayudha.
Krishna asks Ghatotkacha to slay Alayudha, the two Rakshasas fight with illusions and weapons, Ghatotkacha kills Alayudha, and Duryodhana is dismayed at the death.
A heading that marks the start of Section CLXXIX.
Sanjaya describes Ghatotkacha's roar after Alayudha's death, Karna's assault on the Panchalas, and the fierce archery duel between Karna and Ghatotkacha.
Ghatotkacha uses a powerful weapon to kill Karna's steeds and driver and then vanishes.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his warriors thought when the Rakshasa vanished.

Sanjaya describes the Kauravas' terror at the Rakshasa's illusions, Karna's resolve, his use of Indra's dart on Ghatotkacha, Ghatotkacha's fall that crushes a full akshauhini of Kaurava troops, and Karna's triumphal return.
Sanjaya describes the Pandavas' grief at Ghatotkacha's death, Krishna's shouts of joy, and Arjuna's puzzled question about the reason for his delight.
Krishna explains that Karna's dart is spent, that Karna's armour and earrings are gone, and that Karna can be slain when his chariot wheels sink, while recalling the other enemies already slain.
Arjuna asks Krishna how Jarasandha and the other lords were slain for the Pandavas' good.

Krishna explains why these enemies were dangerous, how Jarasandha and Ekalavya were defeated, how the ruler of the Chedis and the Rakshasas were slain, and the state of the battle with Drona still raging.
Dhritarashtra asks why Karna did not hurl the dart at Arjuna, and suggests that Arjuna's death would have brought victory.
Sanjaya says Krishna sent Ghatotkacha to force Karna to waste the dart, blaming Dhritarashtra's evil policy for the result.
Dhritarashtra blames his son's foolishness and his advisers, and asks why Karna and Duryodhana did not use the dart against Arjuna.
Sanjaya recounts the Kaurava councils, which planned to kill Arjuna or failing him Krishna, and the Pandavas' dependence on Krishna.
Satyaki asks Krishna why Karna did not hurl the dart at Arjuna when he had resolved to do so.
Krishna explains that the Kauravas wanted the dart used on Arjuna, that Karna always intended it but he distracted Karna, and that the dart's loss brings him joy and relief.
Sanjaya notes that Krishna, devoted to Arjuna's good, spoke thus to Satyaki.
Dhritarashtra says Karna and Duryodhana acted against sound policy by not using the dart earlier on Krishna or Arjuna.
Sanjaya says the Kaurava warriors resolved each night to use the dart the next morning, but forgot the resolve each day, which he takes as a sign of destiny.
Dhritarashtra blames fate, Krishna and their own folly for the situation, notes the dart is spent on Ghatotkacha, and asks how the battle went on against Drona and the Pandava forces.

Sanjaya describes the Kaurava joy at Ghatotkacha's death and Yudhishthira's grief, which Krishna tries to lift. Yudhishthira answers by recalling Ghatotkacha's services and vows to take revenge on Karna.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that Arjuna's survival is a relief, that Ghatotkacha's death served a larger purpose, and that he should stay with virtue and fight the Kauravas. Then Vyasa vanishes.
Heading: a section title for the Drona-vadha Parva.

Yudhishthira orders his commanders to attack Drona with all their forces, and Duryodhana rushes to guard him. The fighting goes on until both armies are exhausted and many warriors drift into sleep. Arjuna calls for a rest, the Kauravas agree, and both sides stop fighting until the moon rises and the battle picks up again.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana, in anger, goes to Drona to stir both his wrath and his spirit.
Duryodhana complains that Drona spared the weary Pandavas, who have now grown stronger, and says Drona alone could destroy the three worlds with his weapons.
Drona, angered, answers that he will fight to the limit of his strength and swears to slay the Panchalas, then praises Arjuna's feats in several past battles.
Drona tells Duryodhana to go against Arjuna and mocks Karna, Sakuni, Duhsasana and Duryodhana's boasts. He urges them to fight the Pandavas now, and the battle starts.
Sanjaya describes the dawn restart of the battle, the Kaurava army divided into two, and Krishna directing Arjuna to keep Drona's division on his right. Bhima then speaks to Arjuna.
Bhima urges Arjuna to break Drona's division, saying a warrior must now prove his worth and repay his debt to truth and fame.

Arjuna pushes into the Kaurava front while Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni rain arrows on him. Drona moves north and kills Drupada, Virata and Drupada's grandsons, then defeats several other allied kingdoms. Dhrishtadyumna swears an oath to kill Drona or die trying, and Bhima turns on him.
Bhima rebukes Dhrishtadyumna for standing idle, then charges into Drona's army himself. The fight becomes very fierce as the morning sun rises.

Sanjaya says the battle restarts at sunrise and describes the uproar, the piles of weapons and bodies, a river of blood, and the dust that hides the whole field. The great warriors then pair off in fights, and the chapter closes on a scene of the dead, compared with a starry sky.
Duryodhana and Nakula meet in a fight. Nakula shoots at Duryodhana, who turns and drives him back, and Nakula calls out to him to wait, recalling the wrongs Duryodhana has done.

Sanjaya tells how Sahadeva cuts off Duhsasana's driver without being noticed, leaving Duhsasana to drive alone. Karna then fights Bhima with arrows and maces, destroying Bhima's car, standard and steeds, so Bhima leaps into Nakula's car.

Drona and Arjuna, teacher and pupil, fight a duel in which each matches the other's weapons. Gods, seers and celestial beings watch and praise them. Drona invokes the Brahma weapon, Arjuna answers with his own, and the duel turns into a general battle that darkens the sky with arrows.

Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna driving Duhsasana back, the warriors on both sides fighting fairly with no unfair weapons, and Duryodhana and Satyaki, boyhood friends, meeting in battle. They reproach each other for fighting, and Duryodhana laments the power of time and the lust for wealth.

Satyaki answers that a warrior must fight even his teachers and invites Duryodhana to kill him. The two duel, Satyaki wounds Duryodhana, and Karna and Bhima fight until both have lost their cars' wheels and weapons. Yudhishthira then urges the Pandava allies on, and Bhima and the twins ask Arjuna to clear the Kurus away from Drona.

Sanjaya describes Drona's massacre of the Panchalas and Srinjayas, the Pandavas' despair, and Krishna's suggestion that they claim Aswatthama is dead. Bhima kills an elephant of that name and tells Drona his son is dead. Drona doubts the news but, after being stung by it, fights on. Then sages ask him to lay down his arms, and he turns to Yudhishthira to ask whether the news is true.

Krishna urges Yudhishthira to tell a lie to save the army, and Bhima says that Drona will stop fighting if he hears the news from him. Yudhishthira says that Aswatthama is dead, muttering the word elephant. His chariot then touches the ground, and Drona, grief-stricken, can no longer fight Dhrishtadyumna as before.
Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna's duel with Drona, Drona's dwindling weapons and grief, Dhrishtadyumna's sword work, Satyaki's rescue of the prince, and the praise Arjuna and Krishna give him.

Sanjaya narrates the whole climax: Satyaki's fight with the Kuru leaders, Yudhishthira's order to attack Drona, the omens, Drona's Brahma weapon, Bhima's rebuke, Drona's death in meditation, and the Kaurava flight and Pandava joy. He says he saw this through Vyasa's grace.

Sanjaya describes the Kaurava army falling apart after Drona's death, with the leaders and their divisions fleeing, and soldiers abandoning their armour and chariots while calling on each other to stand.
Aswatthama alone charges the Pandava forces and fights them. Asked by him what has happened, Duryodhana is too ashamed and grief-stricken to speak, so he asks Kripa to explain.

Kripa tells how Drona used the Brahma weapon and how the Pandavas, urged on by Krishna, lied to him that Aswatthama had been slain. He then describes Yudhishthira's half-spoken word, Drona laying down his weapons, and Dhrishtadyumna beheading him despite Arjuna's pleas.
Sanjaya says that on hearing his father's death, Aswatthama burns with fury, grinds his teeth and breathes like an enraged snake, his eyes red as blood.
Dhritarashtra asks what Aswatthama said on hearing that Drona was killed unrighteously by Dhrishtadyumna, and praises Aswatthama's mastery of weapons and strength in battle.
Heading: marks the start of Section CXCVI.

Aswatthama, blazing with rage, vows to kill Dhrishtadyumna and Yudhishthira, boasts of his prowess, and tells the story of the Narayana weapon that the god gave his father. The Kuru army rallies to his words, and he invokes the weapon after washing with water.
Sanjaya describes the omens that come with the Narayana weapon, including storms, rivers running backward, darkness and carrion birds, which frighten gods and men alike.
Dhritarashtra asks what the Pandavas did to protect Dhrishtadyumna once the Kauravas came back to battle under Aswatthama.
Yudhishthira describes the Kaurava rout and asks Arjuna who has rallied the army, since the roaring sound seems like Indra himself has come.

Arjuna names Aswatthama and explains the omen of his birth. He then blames Yudhishthira's half-truth for Drona's fall, says Dhrishtadyumna's act was cruel, and declares that he now feels so guilty that death seems preferable to life.

Bhima angrily rebukes Arjuna for preaching virtue and praising Aswatthama, reminds him of the Pandavas' wrongs, and boasts that he alone will defeat Aswatthama. Dhrishtadyumna then defends the killing of Drona as just punishment and tells Arjuna not to reproach him, urging him to fight, which he says will bring victory.
Dhritarashtra laments that no Kshatriya avenged Drona's death and asks Sanjaya what the Pandavas said to Dhrishtadyumna.
Sanjaya says the assembly stays silent, Arjuna reproaches Dhrishtadyumna with a glance, and Satyaki angrily calls him a sinful murderer of his teacher, threatening him with his mace.
Dhrishtadyumna answers scornfully, saying he forgives Satyaki, then accuses him of killing the disarmed Bhurisravas, and lists the unfair acts of both sides in the war, urging Satyaki to fight.
Satyaki, trembling with rage, charges Dhrishtadyumna with his mace. Bhima seizes him and holds him back, while Sahadeva urges him to forgive and recalls the friendship between their peoples.
Dhrishtadyumna taunts Satyaki and demands to be let go so they can fight. Krishna and Yudhishthira then calm both men, and the Pandava army returns to battle.

Sanjaya describes Aswatthama's massacre, his vow to destroy the Pandavas and kill Dhrishtadyumna, the Kaurava rally, and the Narayana weapon's assault on the Pandava army. Yudhishthira then mourns Drona and orders retreat, Krishna tells the troops to lay down their arms, Bhima refuses and charges, Arjuna keeps his bow lowered, and Bhima is overwhelmed by the weapon's fire.
Sanjaya says Arjuna shields Bhima from the Narayana weapon, and Krishna persuades him to step down from his chariot and lay down his arms, after which the weapon is stilled.
The sky clears and the Pandavas re-form. Duryodhana urges Aswatthama to use the weapon again, but Aswatthama says it cannot be used twice and that defeat is worse than death.
Dhritarashtra asks what Aswatthama did next, now that the Pandavas were back in battle order.

Aswatthama, fighting on, wounds Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna, kills several Pandava champions, and fights a fierce duel with Bhima. Bhima's driver is knocked unconscious, and Bhima is carried off the field while the Panchalas flee.
Arjuna, roused by the losses of his allies, challenges Aswatthama to show his might and says he will crush his pride.
Dhritarashtra wonders why Arjuna would speak so harshly to Aswatthama, a man of great merit whom Arjuna loves.

Sanjaya explains that Arjuna's grief and anger at the losses and at Yudhishthira's rebuke drove him to insult Aswatthama. Aswatthama then invokes the Agneya weapon, which darkens the sky and burns the Pandava host.

The Kauravas cheer, and Arjuna answers with the Brahma weapon, which clears the darkness and shows that the Pandava forces are not destroyed. Aswatthama, dismayed, drops his bow and runs, and he meets Vyasa and asks why his weapon failed.
Vyasa begins his answer by telling how Narayana performed long austerities and then worshipped Rudra, praising him with a long hymn.
Vyasa continues that Rudra granted Narayana invincible power, that Arjuna is the sage Nara, that Aswatthama is a portion of Rudra, and that Krishna worships Siva.
Aswatthama bows to Vyasa, withdraws the Kuru army for the night, and the Pandavas also pull back. A closing line says Drona had fought for five days and gone to the realm of Brahma.
Dhritarashtra asks what his sons and the Pandavas did after Drona was slain by Dhrishtadyumna.

Sanjaya says Arjuna, after the Kuru rout, tells Vyasa that a blazing figure with a lance always ran ahead of his chariot, breaking the enemy so that Arjuna only finished off what it had already broken, and asks who it was.

Vyasa says Arjuna saw Siva, the first cause and lord of the universe, and urges him to take refuge in Siva. He lists many names and epithets of Siva and notes that no one can stand against a warrior with Siva going before him.

Vyasa retells Siva's deeds: his destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, his destruction of the triple city, and the incident of the child in Parvati's lap. He then explains that Siva is all the gods, lists many of his names and their meanings, and says Krishna showed Arjuna this god in a dream. He ends by telling Arjuna to go and fight, since Krishna is his protector.
Closing line: Sanjaya says Vyasa leaves Arjuna and goes back to where he came from.
Sanjaya's closing benediction says that reciting this Parva brings the fruit of Vedic study, freedom from sin, and blessings for each of the social classes.
Heading: marks the end of the Drona Parva.
Heading: the footnotes section begins.
Footnote 1 gives a literal rendering of a phrase describing the speech as an oration full of unrefined expressions.
Footnote 2 explains that the woman is stripped of robes and ornaments because she is a widow.
Footnote 3 says a Sarabha is a fabulous eight-legged animal supposed to be stronger than the lion.
Footnote 4 reads the verse as meaning that since such a hero is slain, nothing on earth is lasting, so grief over wealth and children is misplaced.
Footnote 5 notes a slight variant in the Bombay text and gives the sense: since all things die, there is no reason to fear doing one's duty.
