Duryodhana and the other Kaurava leaders grieve through the night, make Karna commander, fight two days, and see Karna killed by Arjuna. Sanjaya then reports to Dhritarashtra.
Janamejaya asks how Dhritarashtra could keep living after hearing of Karna's death and the earlier losses, and asks to hear the full account.
Sanjaya reaches the palace, bows to the grieving king, and asks whether Dhritarashtra regrets rejecting the counsel of Vidura, Krishna and others.
Dhritarashtra mourns Bhishma, Drona and Karna, asks what his own side did when the army broke, and asks how the Pandavas fought.
Sanjaya tells him not to grieve, since a wise man does not suffer over what fate brings and human plans may or may not succeed.
Dhritarashtra says he accepts that all this is fate and asks Sanjaya to tell him everything.

Sanjaya describes Drona's sons and the rest of the army as pale, silent and dejected, with weapons falling from their hands. Duryodhana then speaks to rouse them, praising Karna and boasting that Arjuna is a coward.
Duryodhana makes Karna commander. Karna fights hard, slaughters many enemies, and is at last killed by Arjuna.

Dhritarashtra falls senseless at the news, the women wail, and Sanjaya and Vidura revive the king and comfort the household. The king then sits silent, censures his sons and praises the Pandavas, and questions Sanjaya.
Dhritarashtra asks whether Duryodhana has already gone to Yama's abode, and asks Sanjaya to tell him the truth.
Sanjaya replies that Karna and his kinsmen have been slain, that Duhshasana was killed by a son of Pandu, and that Bhimasena drank his blood in anger.
Dhritarashtra, troubled by grief, asks Sanjaya to name who among the Kurus and Pandavas are still alive and who have died.

Sanjaya lists the fallen heroes one by one, including Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Duryodhana's brothers and allies, Bhagadatta, Jayadratha, and many kings and their troops. He compares Arjuna's killing of Karna to Indra slaying Vritra, and closes by blaming the disaster on Dhritarashtra's own evil policy and his sons.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to name the Pandava warriors killed by his own side, having already heard the list of his own dead.

Sanjaya lists the Pandava and allied dead, naming the killers in each case: Abhimanyu's death at the hands of many warriors, the kings Virata and Drupada killed by Drona, and many others. He ends by saying he has told all that was asked.
Dhritarashtra says he sees no hope for the rest of his army after the deaths of Bhishma, Drona and Karna, and asks who among his side is still alive.

Sanjaya lists the Kaurava warriors still on the field, including Ashvatthama, Kritavarma, Shalya, Gautama, the king of the Gandharas, the sons of Dhritarashtra and Karna, and Duryodhana himself, all ready to fight.
Dhritarashtra says that from these facts he can see plainly which side will win.
Vaishampayana says the king swoons when he learns how few of his army remain. He comes to, asks Sanjaya to wait, and then collapses to the ground.
Janamejaya asks what the king said after hearing of Karna's fall and the loss of his sons, and asks to hear all of it.
Vaishampayana describes the king's stunned lament, in which he praises Karna's strength and his conquests for Duryodhana, mourns his death at Arjuna's hands, and says he has no wish to live.
Sanjaya praises Dhritarashtra as wise and learned, and urges him to summon his courage and not give way to grief.

Dhritarashtra replies at great length. He blames destiny, calls Karna's death incredible, and wonders why he himself has not died of grief. He mourns Karna and Duhshasana, recalls Bhishma's and Yudhishthira's advice that Duryodhana ignored, and compares his own state to a bird with clipped wings. He then asks how Karna was killed, who stood by him, and how each of the Kaurava leaders reacted, ending by asking for a full account of the final fight.

Sanjaya describes the day's end: after Drona's death and the defeat of Ashvatthama's plans, Duryodhana rallies the retreating troops until dusk, then the Kauravas gather in their camp to take counsel.
Duryodhana asks his leaders for their opinions on what must be done.

Ashvatthama says the Kauravas should not despair and proposes Karna as commander. Duryodhana, pleased, appeals to Karna to take up the post, citing Karna's past service and the fall of Bhishma and Drona.
Karna accepts, saying he will vanquish the Pandavas and that Duryodhana should consider them already defeated.
The formal installation of Karna follows, with ritual vessels, blessings from Brahmanas, and praises. Karna sets out the army at sunrise, and Sanjaya compares him to a second sun.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Karna did after taking command and receiving the king's encouragement.

Sanjaya describes the noise of the Kaurava army preparing before dawn, Karna's splendid car and conch, and the crocodile-shaped formation, with Karna at its beak and named leaders at its eyes, head, neck, body, feet and tail.

Yudhishthira tells Arjuna that Karna is the only real threat left on the Kaurava side and urges him to kill Karna. Arjuna forms a half-moon array, both sides think the other already defeated, and the armies rush together.

Sanjaya describes the bloody general fighting, the Pandava forces advancing with their allies, and Bhima on his elephant. The duel between Bhima and Kshemadhurti on elephants goes back and forth until Bhima kills Kshemadhurti's elephant and then Kshemadhurti himself, and the Kaurava troops flee.

Karna cuts down Pandava ranks while the Pandavas attack the Kauravas. The leaders pair off in duels, among them Nakula against Karna, Bhima against Drona's son and Satyaki against the Kaikeya brothers. Satyaki kills Anuvinda, then fights Vinda and the other Kaikeya prince on foot with swords and kills the prince, and the Kaikeya army flees.

Srutakarman and Citrasena duel until Srutakarman cuts off Citrasena's head, and his troops flee. Prativindhya fights Citra, deflects Citra's dart and mace, and kills him with a lance. The Kaurava troops scatter, and Drona's son alone rushes at Bhima.

Sanjaya describes the evenly matched duel between Ashvatthama and Bhima, with each side countering the other's weapons and arrows, heavenly beings marvelling, and both warriors finally falling senseless to be carried off by their drivers.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe Arjuna's battle with the Samsaptakas and with Ashvatthama, and the battles of the other kings against the Pandavas.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna cutting down the Samsaptaka army, with chariots, elephants and men falling. Gods and heavenly beings praise him and Krishna, a voice names them as Nara and Narayana, and Ashvatthama calls Arjuna out to fight as a guest. Arjuna asks Krishna which duty to take up first, and Krishna drives him to Ashvatthama. Ashvatthama wounds both, and Arjuna cuts through all his arrows, then turns from the Samsaptakas to face Ashvatthama.

Sanjaya describes the duel between Arjuna and Ashvatthama, the wounds on both sides, and the slaughter of many Samsaptakas and other troops by Arjuna. Krishna tells Arjuna to stop sparing Ashvatthama. Arjuna then badly wounds him and cuts his horses' traces, so the horses carry Ashvatthama away. Ashvatthama retreats to Karna's army, and Arjuna and Krishna return to the Samsaptakas.

Sanjaya describes Krishna turning the chariot to the north to face Dandadhara, who rides an elephant and is slaughtering troops. Arjuna cuts off Dandadhara's arms and head, kills his elephant, then kills Danda and his elephant. The enemy elephants are destroyed, the army breaks, and Arjuna's allies praise him before he returns to the Samsaptakas.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna cutting down many warriors, cars, elephants and horses, while the samsaptakas and Kaurava allies press in on him. Krishna urges Arjuna to finish off the Samsaptakas and go after Karna. Krishna then shows Arjuna the battlefield, cataloguing the weapons, armour, ornaments and corpses. Returning to camp, they hear uproar from the Kaurava side and see Pandya attacking the army, cutting down many foes.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe in full the feats, spirit and pride of the Pandya hero he has mentioned before.

Sanjaya says Pandya thought himself greater than the foremost warriors, and describes him routing Karna's army and killing many allies. Ashvatthama challenges him, and their duel goes on with arrows, weapons and chariots, until Ashvatthama kills Pandya's elephant, cuts off his arms and head, and kills his followers. The Kaurava kings then honour Ashvatthama.
Dhritarashtra asks what Arjuna did after Pandya fell and Karna was routing the foe, saying Arjuna is his greatest fear.

Sanjaya reports that Krishna tells Arjuna the king and the other Pandavas have withdrawn, and that Karna is slaughtering the Srinjayas. Arjuna has Krishna drive on, and a fierce general battle breaks out. Karna kills many Pancala warriors and their chariots, and the bodies of men, horses and elephants pile up across the field.
Sanjaya describes the Kaurava elephant-warriors from many kingdoms attacking Dhrishtadyumna. Pandava allies rush to rescue him, and Satyaki kills the elephant of the Vanga king and then its rider.
Sahadeva kills the elephant of the Pundra king with three arrows, then advances on the Anga chief.

Nakula stops Sahadeva and kills the Anga chief and his elephant. The Anga and allied elephant-men attack, and a long fight follows in which Sahadeva and Nakula kill more elephants. The Kaurava force flees, and the Pandava leaders turn on Karna.

Sanjaya describes the duel: the brothers trade arrows, each cutting down the other's weapons, a sword is thrown and deflected, and at last Sahadeva's shaft pierces Duhshasana, who swoons and is driven from the field. Sahadeva then begins to destroy Duryodhana's division, as a man in anger crushes ants.

Long account of the duel and its aftermath. Nakula taunts Karna, and Karna answers with a rebuke about boasting. Their fight with bows and arrows fills the sky until Karna cuts Nakula's chariot and horses to pieces and leaves him on foot with a club. Karna disarms him, humiliates him, then lets him go, recalling Kunti's words. Nakula returns in shame to Yudhishthira, and Karna goes on to scatter the Pancalas, leaving the field strewn with broken chariots, elephants, horses and corpses, while the Pandava troops flee.

Sanjaya describes Uluka defeating Yuyutsu in a long duel, then Srutakarman and Satanika fighting until both lose their chariots. Shakuni fights Sutasoma, who battles on foot with a sword until Shakuni breaks it. Shakuni then routs the Pandava divisions, as Indra scattered the Daitya army.
Kripa checks Dhrishtadyumna and wounds him repeatedly until he is dazed. His charioteer turns the car away, and Kripa pursues him, blowing his conch. Warriors on both sides remark on Kripa's power.
Shikhandi fights Kritavarma. Both are wounded, and Kritavarma's arrow strikes Shikhandi down. Shikhandi's driver carries him off, and the Pandava army breaks and flees.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna scattering the Trigartas, Samsaptakas and their allies, and killing several kings in turn. Satyasena wounds Krishna's arm, and Arjuna beheads Satyasena and kills others. When the Samsaptakas surround him, Arjuna uses the Aindra weapon, and the field is covered with wreckage and corpses. The enemy force is almost wiped out, and Arjuna shines like a fire without smoke.

Yudhishthira fights Duryodhana, wounds him, destroys his chariot and weapons, and leaves him on foot in danger. Karna, Drona's son and Kripa hurry to his aid, and the Pandava brothers gather to fight them. The battle becomes a frenzy of elephants, horses and men, with many killed in every grim manner, and Karna, Arjuna and Bhima slaughter the Pancalas, Trigartas and Kuru elephant divisions respectively, as the sun passes its height.
Dhritarashtra says the Kauravas are as good as dead, and asks how Yudhishthira and Duryodhana fought in the afternoon battle.

Sanjaya describes the duel: Duryodhana cuts Yudhishthira's bow, the two trade arrows and a dart and a mace is raised, and Yudhishthira's dart fells Duryodhana. Bhima reminds Yudhishthira of his vow and stops him from finishing Duryodhana. Kritavarma comes up to help, and Bhima attacks him with a golden mace.

Sanjaya describes the bloody battle the Kauravas fight under Karna, the Pandava rout against Satyaki and Karna, Arjuna and Krishna charging in and scattering the Kaurava army, and Karna fighting on until his forces are nearly wiped out.
Sanjaya describes the sunset, the Kauravas withdrawing with their army in fear of a night battle, the Pandavas returning in triumph, and the Rakshasas and beasts gathering over the battlefield.
Dhritarashtra says Arjuna has defeated every warrior single-handed, praises the Kauravas for fighting such a man, and asks what Duryodhana did next.

Sanjaya describes the battered Kauravas returning to camp to take counsel. Karna, angry, says Arjuna was alert and had been helped by Krishna, and promises to defeat him next day. Duryodhana agrees, and the army rests and marshals a fresh array.
Dhritarashtra asks how Karna will fight next and laments that his trust in Karna and Shakuni has come to nothing, and that fate is supreme.

Sanjaya rebukes the king for the dice match and the other wrongs he allowed, and tells him not to dwell on the past. He says the king was warned and ignored counsel, so the slaughter has come, and he begins the account of the night's events.

Karna tells Duryodhana he will fight Arjuna next morning, and claims he has weapons equal to Arjuna's, as well as the bow Vijaya, which Rama gave him. He admits that Arjuna has the better charioteer in Krishna and the better bow Gandiva, and asks that Shalya be made his driver, with spare arrows and an escort of chariots. He says he will then be superior to Arjuna.
Duryodhana agrees with Karna's wishes and promises chariots, arrows and an escort, saying the kings will follow Karna into battle.
Duryodhana turns to address Shalya, the king of the Madras, as the scene closes.

Duryodhana humbly asks Shalya to drive Karna's chariot against Arjuna. He argues that Bhishma and Drona have fallen, that Karna is the army's remaining hope, and that Shalya should guard Karna as Krishna guards Arjuna.
Shalya, outraged, stands up in anger, with knitted brows and rolling eyes.

Shalya says Duryodhana insults him by asking him to drive. He refuses, saying he does not rank Karna as his equal, speaks of the castes and the proper duties of a Kshatriya, and asks leave to go home.
Duryodhana holds him back and flatters him, saying he never lies, that he is known as a barbed arrow to his foes, and that he is as good as Krishna.
Shalya is pleased and agrees to drive Karna's chariot in the battle with Arjuna, on condition he may say what he likes to Karna during the fight.
Duryodhana and Karna accept Shalya's terms and agree.

Duryodhana tells Shalya a story from the sage Markandeya about a battle between the gods and the Asuras. The three sons of Taraka win boons, Maya builds three cities for them, and Hari's lake revives slain Asuras. Indra cannot break the cities, so the gods seek help from the creator, who says only one arrow from a god can destroy them. The gods take refuge with Shiva, praise him with many names, and ask him what he will do for them.
Publisher's header line for the Gutenberg edition, not part of the narrative.
Duryodhana says that after the fears of the gods and sages were calmed, Brahma praised Shiva and asked him to destroy the Danavas.
Shiva replies that he will not fight alone, and that the gods should combine their forces with half his might.
The gods answer that the Danavas are twice as strong as they are.
Shiva says he will use half his energy against the enemies if the gods will do the same.
The gods reply that they cannot bear half of Shiva's energy, and ask him to use half of their combined strength instead.
Shiva agrees to fight with half of the gods' combined energy.
The gods accept, Shiva becomes greater than all beings, and is named Mahadeva. He asks for a chariot and bow for the battle.

The gods build a huge chariot from the parts of the universe, with the earth as its body, the mountains as axle and wheels, and the Vedas and sacred things as its guardians, bow and arrow and steeds all assembled.

Brahma agrees to drive the chariot. Shiva rides out, and when the chariot sinks Vishnu lifts it as a bull. Shiva shoots his arrow, the three cities burn and fall into the western ocean, and the gods go home. Duryodhana then urges Shalya to drive Karna as Brahma drove Rudra, and starts another story about Rama.
Duryodhana tells how Rama, son of Jamadagni, pleased Shiva with long penances and was given weapons. Rama later killed many Danavas for the gods and was given more weapons by Shiva in return.

Duryodhana says Rama taught all his weapons to Karna, and argues that Karna is probably a son of a god born into the Kshatriya order and abandoned as an infant, and could not have been born into the Suta caste.
Duryodhana says Brahma drove Rudra in the same way, and asks Shalya to hold the reins of Karna's horses in the same spirit.
Shalya recalls hearing the old story of Brahma and Rudra, notes that Krishna knows such things, and warns that Krishna will fight himself if Arjuna falls.
Duryodhana praises Karna as the best of warriors, lists his feats against the Pandavas, and urges Shalya to fight for him as Krishna serves the Pandavas.
Shalya agrees to drive for Karna, provided he may say what he likes to Karna during the battle.
Karna and Duryodhana accept, and Duryodhana embraces Karna. Karna asks Duryodhana to plead with Shalya once more, which Duryodhana does with a loud, persuasive appeal.
Shalya embraces Duryodhana, promises to do what he can, and asks Karna to forgive any blunt words he may say.
Karna tells Shalya to serve their cause as Brahma serves Ishana and Keshava serves Partha.
Karna's words continue with the same comparison to Keshava serving Partha.
Shalya says that self-praise is usually improper, but he will say that he is as skilled as Matali and can handle Karna's horses in battle, so Karna need not worry.
Duryodhana tells Karna that Shalya, who is greater than Krishna, will drive the chariot as Matali drives Indra's, and that they can surely beat the Parthas.

At morning Duryodhana again asks Shalya to guide Karna's horses. Shalya agrees, the chariot is prepared and blessed, and Karna and Shalya mount. Duryodhana then urges Karna to seize Yudhishthira or kill Arjuna and the Pandava brothers, and Karna boasts that Shalya's driving will help him defeat Partha.

Shalya answers Karna's boast by reminding him how formidable the Pandavas are, with Arjuna's Gandiva and Yudhishthira and the twins raining arrows like clouds, and warns Karna that he will not talk so proudly when he hears them.
Sanjaya says that Karna, ignoring Shalya's warning, speaks to him.
Karna begins a reply to Shalya, and the speech continues into the next scene.
Karna orders Shalya to proceed.

Sanjaya lists the omens as Karna sets out: earthquakes, meteors, storms, birds and beasts passing to the right, the horses falling, bones raining down, and weapons and banners trembling. The Kauravas, blind to the omens, cheer Karna, and Karna, recalling Bhishma and Drona, declares he will face Arjuna alone, regardless of his fate, and describes the chariot and weapons Rama gave him.
Sanjaya says that Shalya, mocking Karna's boasting, laughs aloud at him.

Shalya tells Karna to stop his bragging, and recalls Arjuna's old feats: his fights with Bhava, the rescue of Duryodhana, the defeat of the Gandharvas, and his victory over Karna in the cattle raid on Virata's kine.
Sanjaya says that Karna, angered by Shalya's praise of his enemy, answers him.
Karna says Shalya may praise Arjuna, but the praise is only deserved if Arjuna defeats him in the coming battle.
Shalya gives no answer. Karna tells him to proceed, and the chariot sets off against the enemy, and Karna looks for Arjuna among the Pandava army.

Karna tells every Pandava soldier he meets that whoever shows him Arjuna will be rewarded with wealth, cattle, villages, cars, elephants, horses, women and more. If that is not enough, he will kill Krishna and Arjuna and give their wealth to the finder. Karna blows his conch, the Kauravas rejoice, and Shalya laughs at his boasting.
Shalya tells Karna not to give away a golden chariot and its bulls, says the gift is foolish, and urges him to fight Arjuna with his army instead of boasting, since his time seems to be running out.
Karna replies that he seeks Arjuna relying on his own arms, and that Shalya, a foe in friend's clothing, cannot make him turn back, not even Indra with his thunder could do that.

Shalya mocks Karna's challenge at length, comparing him to a jackal, hare, frog, calf, dog and snake that foolishly takes on a lion, tiger, elephant or bird, and says Karna will be shown to be the lesser when Arjuna's bow sounds in battle.
Sanjaya says Karna, rebuked by Shalya, grows furious and answers him.

Karna says Shalya has no merit to judge Arjuna or Krishna, then boasts of a special shaft he has kept for Arjuna or Krishna alone, which he expects will kill them both. He calls Shalya a fool born in a sinful country, insults the Madrakas at length and their women and customs, says he is ready to die in battle, and threatens to crush Shalya's head with his mace if he speaks again. He ends by ordering Shalya to drive on.

Shalya introduces a fable about a crow fed on scraps by a merchant's children on the far side of the ocean. The crow becomes proud, and when swans arrive it challenges their leader to a flight contest, which the swans mock.

The swan and the crow take to the sky. The crow shows off many motions, while the swan flies in one steady manner. The crow seems to be winning, but then the swan flies far over the ocean, the crow tires and finds no island to rest on, and he begs for rescue.

The swan takes the exhausted crow on his back and carries him back to land, and the crow gives up his pride. Shalya applies it to Karna, pointing out Karna's past defeats at Virata's city and elsewhere, and urges him to seek the protection of Krishna and Arjuna, since they are far superior.

Karna, unmoved, answers Shalya at length. He says he will face Krishna and Arjuna anyway, recalls being cursed by Rama for hiding his caste, and vows to kill Arjuna with the brahmastra he will be able to use. He then recalls killing a Brahmana's calf by accident and being told that his wheel would sink in battle, rejects Shalya's rebukes, and ends by telling him to be silent and hear what he has to say.

Karna tells Shalya that words cannot scare him, that he was born to show valour and win glory, and that he spares Shalya for friendship, affection, alliance and the agreement he made. He says the task of serving Dhritarashtra depends on him, and that he would beat his foes without a thousand Shalyas.
Shalya tells Karna that his boasts are raving and that Shalya could defeat the enemy without a thousand Karnas.
Sanjaya says Karna answers Shalya with words even more bitter than before.

Karna quotes a Brahmana's account, heard at Dhritarashtra's court, of the Vahikas: their supposed customs, their drinking, their women's singing and dancing, and the lands they live in. He follows this with more quoted Brahmanas, who say the Arattas, Madrakas and others have no virtue, and then gives a list of peoples he considers impure and ends with a bitter verdict on the Madrakas.

Karna quotes more Brahmanas and legends about lawless peoples and their customs, the Vahikas and Arattas, and Kalmashapada's curse against the Madrakas, and calls Shalya their king, who shares in their sins. He ends by telling Shalya to keep quiet, and says he will kill Krishna and Arjuna after killing Shalya.
Shalya replies that every land has both good and bad people, that Karna's own Angas have faults, and that he should drop his anger.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana stops the argument, begging Shalya and calming Karna, and Karna, smiling, tells Shalya to proceed.

Sanjaya says that when Karna sees the Pandava array made by Dhrishtadyumna, he roars, makes his chariot rattle, and sets his troops in counter-array. He slaughters the Pandavas and strikes Yudhishthira with many arrows.
Dhritarashtra asks how Karna arrayed his forces against the Pandavas, who stood where, how the sons of Pandu arrayed theirs, and how Arjuna could be beaten in battle.

Sanjaya lists the Kaurava array: Kripa, the Magadhas and Kritavarma on the right, Shakuni and Uluka with Gandhara horsemen, the Samsaptakas on the left, the Kambojas, Sakas and Yavanas beyond them, Karna at the centre, then Duhshasana, Duryodhana with his brothers, Ashvatthama and the elephants. Yudhishthira then tells Arjuna to take measures against the array, and Arjuna promises to kill its foremost warriors.

Yudhishthira assigns his brothers and allies their targets: Arjuna against Karna, Bhima against Duryodhana, Nakula against Vrishasena, Sahadeva against Shakuni, Satanika against Duhshasana, Satyaki against Kritavarma, Pandya against Ashvatthama, and Yudhishthira himself against Kripa.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's chariot advancing with Krishna as driver. Shalya points out the omens, the dust, the banners and the weapons, and tells Karna that Arjuna will soon be there. Karna answers that Arjuna is surrounded by the Samsaptakas and will be lost among them.

Shalya scoffs at Karna's boast of killing Arjuna and names the Pandava heroes Karna will face, including Bhima, Yudhishthira, the twins, Draupadi's sons, Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki. The two armies then clash like the Ganga and Yamuna meeting.
Dhritarashtra asks how Arjuna attacked the Samsaptakas and how Karna fought the Pandavas, and asks for every detail, since he never tires of hearing of heroic deeds.

Sanjaya describes the Pandava army under Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi's sons. The Samsaptakas charge Arjuna, who cuts down their ranks, and the battle is compared to his old fight with the Nivatakavachas. Kripa, Kritavarma and Shakuni fight the Pancalas and their allies, while Duryodhana protects Karna. Karna wounds Yudhishthira and kills thousands of foes, and the battle is like the old war of gods and Asuras.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how Karna broke into the Pandava ranks and struck Yudhishthira, and who were the heroes Karna had to overcome before he could reach the king.

Sanjaya describes Karna's attack on the Pancalas and the din of the armies. Karna kills many Prabhadrakas, Cedis and Pancalas, while the Pandava heroes, led by Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki and the sons of Draupadi, close in on him. Karna's sons Sushena and Vrishasena fight fiercely around their father. Bhima kills Bhanusena, another son of Karna, and then fights Sushena. Vrishasena is disarmed by Satyaki, and Duhshasana rescues him. Karna then drives into Yudhishthira's division, destroying thirty chariots of the Cedis, and wounds the king with arrows while the armies fight on.

Long account in which Karna cuts through the Pandava host, Yudhishthira mocks him and shoots him down, Karna recovers and kills Yudhishthira's wheel-guards, then wounds and disarms the king, who flees. Karna pursues, reaches out to seize him, and is stopped by Shalya, who warns that Yudhishthira's power would burn them both. Karna mocks Yudhishthira and lets him go. Yudhishthira then rallies his men, and the battle becomes a vast, bloody carnage, with a river of blood flowing across the field, until the Kaurava army is driven back in flight.

Duryodhana tries to rally his fleeing army, and some Kaurava troops turn on Bhima. Karna orders Shalya to drive toward Bhima's chariot. Bhima asks Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna to guard Yudhishthira, and vows to kill Karna or die in the attempt.
Shalya warns Karna that Bhima is blazing with fury, like the fire at the end of an age, and could overwhelm the three worlds.

Karna laughs at Bhima, recalling how Bhima killed Kichaka in Virata's city, and says he has long wished to face Arjuna, but will fight Bhima first. Shalya urges him on, and Karna agrees to drive at Bhima.
Bhima and Karna duel. Karna cuts Bhima's bow and wounds him, Bhima answers with a huge shaft that knocks Karna senseless on his chariot, and Shalya carries him off as Bhima routs the Kaurava troops.
Dhritarashtra says that Bhima's defeat of Karna is an astonishing feat, reminds Sanjaya that Duryodhana always said Karna alone would destroy the Pandavas, and asks what Duryodhana did next.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana sending his brothers to protect Karna. Bhima kills many of them, including Vivitsu, Vikata, Saha and Kratha, and then Nanda and Upananda, and the survivors flee. Karna drives back to face Bhima, and their duel is fierce. Karna cuts Bhima's bow and standard, and Bhima hurls a mace that Karna destroys. Bhima's chariot and driver are destroyed, and he fights on foot, crushing hundreds of elephants, cars and horsemen. Karna pursues Yudhishthira, Satyaki aids Bhima, and the two armies crash together in a huge, confused fight at midday.
Sanjaya says the battle becomes so loud and mutual with insults that he believes the warriors' time is running out, and that the Pandavas and Kauravas are now mangling each other with sharp shafts.

Sanjaya describes the chaotic slaughter of cars, horses, elephants and foot soldiers, the field covered with blood, heads and limbs, the dust that hides friend from foe, and the blood rivers thick with corpses. Carrion creatures gather in glee, heroes shout out their names and lineage, and the Kaurava army weakens like a sinking ship.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna plunging into the Samsaptaka host and fighting Susharma, who wounds Krishna and cuts Arjuna's standard. The enemy then surrounds Arjuna's chariot, seizing Krishna and Arjuna, but Krishna throws them off. Arjuna blows his conch, Krishna answers, and Arjuna paralyses the Samsaptakas with the Naga weapon. Susharma calls up the Sauparna weapon, birds devour the snakes, and the enemy is freed. Susharma pierces Arjuna, who uses the Aindra weapon to slaughter thousands of warriors, and the Samsaptakas are finally outmatched.

Sanjaya says Kritavarma, Kripa, Drona's son, Karna, Uluka, Shakuni and Duryodhana try to rescue the army from Arjuna's onslaught, while Kripa's arrows cover the Srinjayas. Kripa fights Shikhandi, wounds him and kills his charioteer and horses, and Shikhandi attacks on foot with a sword before Suketu intervenes. Kripa kills Suketu, and Shikhandi withdraws. Meanwhile Dhrishtadyumna goes for Kripa, Kritavarma blocks him, Drona's son opposes Yudhishthira, and Duryodhana holds Nakula and Sahadeva while Karna confronts Bhima.

Kritavarma challenges Dhrishtadyumna, and the duel is as fierce as two hawks fighting over meat. Dhrishtadyumna wounds Kritavarma and covers him with arrows, but Kritavarma matches him. Dhrishtadyumna then kills Kritavarma's charioteer, and his Kaurava opponents surge forward for another round of fighting.
Sanjaya describes Ashvatthama's arrow barrage, which fills the sky and overwhelms Yudhishthira's protectors, and the Pandava warriors' attempt to hold their ground against it.
Sanjaya reports Duryodhana's duel with the twins and Dhrishtadyumna, the duel that leaves Duryodhana carless and carried off by his brothers, and the simultaneous slaughter by Karna and Bhima.
Karna scatters the Pancala leaders, and his ferocity is compared to a lion among deer and a fire among dry grass.

Yudhishthira and the Pandavas attack Karna, Arjuna clears the samsaptakas and the Kambojas, and Ashvatthama overwhelms Arjuna until Krishna rebukes Arjuna and Arjuna wounds Ashvatthama. Yudhishthira then retreats, wounded.

Duryodhana tells Karna and the kings that this battle is a chance for heroes to win either the earth or heaven, and the Kuru warriors cheer. Ashvatthama then swears to kill Dhrishtadyumna, and the armies charge into a bloody clash watched by gods and Apsaras.

Arjuna asks Krishna to find Yudhishthira, Krishna describes the dead, dying and grieving on the field, and then Krishna points out where the chief heroes are fighting before the fighting starts again.

Karna meets the Pandava leaders alone, fights Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki, and gains the upper hand, until Ashvatthama disarms Dhrishtadyumna and goes for him. Arjuna wounds Ashvatthama, who faints, Sahadeva carries Dhrishtadyumna away, and Krishna drives toward the samsaptakas.
A line from the Project Gutenberg edition header, not part of the narrative.
Krishna tells Arjuna that Yudhishthira is surrounded, that Karna is coming for him, and that Bhima is routing the Kaurava army, and urges Arjuna to take on Karna.
Sanjaya reports Arjuna's destruction of the remaining samsaptakas and his continued slaughter of the Kaurava army.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what the Kauravas did while Bhima and Yudhishthira were fighting.
Sanjaya describes the great mass of paired duels, including Karna against Shikhandi and Duhshasana against Dhrishtadyumna, and ends with the armies' clash described as the end of the age.
Nakula and Vrishasena trade arrows, and Karna scatters the Pandava troops while Nakula turns on the Kauravas.
Sahadeva kills Uluka's driver and horses, and Satyaki routs the Kaurava army while Shakuni is taken away.
Bhima leaves Duryodhana carless and then tears through the elephant divisions, while Kripa, Kritavarma and others clash with Yudhamanyu and Uttamauja.
Arjuna arrives on his chariot, Duryodhana surrounds Yudhishthira, and Karna checks the Pandava rescuers and drives Yudhishthira back until he retreats wounded.

Karna kills many Kaikayas, chases the wounded Yudhishthira, destroys the king's horses and the twins' chariots, and is urged by Shalya to turn to Arjuna or to Bhima's fight with Duryodhana, while Yudhishthira retreats to the camp.

Arjuna and Ashvatthama fight a long duel of divine weapons, Arjuna cuts Ashvatthama's horses and driver away, the Kaurava army breaks, and Karna's Bhargava weapon devastates the Pandava side until Arjuna seeks Yudhishthira.
Arjuna asks Bhima where Yudhishthira is, and Bhima says the king left the field badly wounded, and the two argue over who should go and who should hold the line against the samsaptakas.
Arjuna asks Krishna to drive him to the king.
Krishna tells Bhima to fight the samsaptakas and drives Arjuna to Yudhishthira, who is lying alone, and the king greets them with joy, believing Karna is dead.
Yudhishthira welcomes Krishna and Arjuna, recounts his defeat by Karna, and demands to hear how Karna was killed.
Arjuna recounts his duel with Ashvatthama, his escape from Karna's division, his request that others guard his chariot, and his vow to kill Karna that day.
Yudhishthira reproaches Arjuna for fleeing Karna and leaving Bhima, recalls the prophecy about Arjuna, and mocks his bow, car and banner.
Arjuna draws his sword against Yudhishthira, and Krishna asks why, noting that the Kauravas are already being beaten by Bhima and that the king is safe.
Krishna calls Arjuna's anger a sin and explains that killing is worse than untruth, and that truth and falsehood depend on the situation, with five cases where falsehood may be spoken.
Arjuna asks Krishna to tell him the stories of Valaka and Kausika.

Krishna tells the story of the hunter Valaka, who killed a blind beast and went to heaven, and of Kausika, who told robbers the truth and fell into hell, and then Arjuna asks for counsel on how to keep his vow without killing Yudhishthira.
Krishna explains that Yudhishthira spoke in anger to provoke Arjuna into killing Karna, and advises Arjuna to address his brother as 'thou' to inflict a kind of death without killing him.
Sanjaya says that Arjuna, approving of Krishna's counsel, now speaks harshly to Yudhishthira in a way he never had before.
Arjuna scolds Yudhishthira for sitting far from battle, praises Bhima's exploits, and blames the king's love of dice for the family's ruin.
Arjuna, ashamed, draws his sword to kill himself, Krishna rebukes him for thinking of suicide, and Arjuna boasts of his own feats and vows to kill Karna.
Yudhishthira, deeply hurt, offers to be killed or to go to the forest, Krishna and Arjuna beg his forgiveness, and the king accepts them both.
Krishna tells Arjuna his shame was misplaced and urges him to please Yudhishthira before fighting Karna, and Arjuna bows and asks his brother's forgiveness.
The brothers weep and embrace, Arjuna swears to kill Karna that day, and Krishna urges Yudhishthira to comfort and bless Arjuna.
Yudhishthira forgives Arjuna and tells him to go and slay Karna.
Arjuna bows to his brother, who embraces him and praises him.
Arjuna swears on Yudhishthira's feet to kill Karna and his followers that day, or not return from battle.
Yudhishthira blesses Arjuna with long life, victory and the destruction of his foes, and sends him off to kill Karna as Indra killed Vritra.
Arjuna orders his chariot readied, Daruka yokes the horses, Arjuna is blessed and sets out, and birds and omens gather around him as all creatures expect Karna to die.
Krishna praises Arjuna's skill and warns him not to underestimate Karna, describing the Suta's son as strong, proud and nearly his equal.
Krishna reviews the losses on both sides, the deeds of Bhishma, Drona and others, Karna's wrongs against the Pandavas, and urges Arjuna to kill Karna that day.
Arjuna, reassured by Krishna, vows in a long speech to slay Karna, answer his insults, and defeat the Kauravas, then rides off to rescue Bhima.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how the fight went when Arjuna set out, in a long opening question.
Dhritarashtra's question continues, asking what happened once Arjuna was in the battle.
Dhritarashtra ends his question by asking how the fight went.
Sanjaya describes the Pandava army's roar and the battle as a storm, with Uttamauja killing Sushena and Karna cutting down Uttamauja's horses, and Bhima scorching the Kaurava host.
Bhima orders his charioteer into the Kaurava host, scatters his enemies with arrows, and worries about Yudhishthira and Arjuna before asking how many arrows he still has.
Visoka lists Bhima's remaining arrows and other weapons, and assures him they will not run out.
Bhima vows to fight to the end, so that the Kauravas fall or all the world praises him, and he urges Arjuna to come quickly.
Visoka describes Arjuna's chariot, his banner and the signs of Krishna, and reports Arjuna's victories so far.
Bhima rewards Visoka with villages, slaves and chariots for the good news.
Arjuna drives into the Kaurava host and cuts down wave after wave of warriors, Bhima rejoices and renews his attack, and the Kaurava troops rally around Karna and go back to battle.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Duryodhana, Karna and the other Kaurava leaders did when Bhima had broken their army.
Karna orders Shalya to drive him into the Pancalas, and he cuts down the Pandava warriors, wounding Bhima, Satyaki and others, until the Pandava army breaks and flees and the Kauravas rejoice.
Arjuna creates a river of blood, orders Krishna to drive toward Karna, and Shalya urges Karna to face Arjuna, who is coming alone toward him.
Karna answers that he will fight Arjuna and Krishna, and that he will not return without killing two heroes or dying in the attempt.
Shalya asks who could defeat Arjuna when he is protected by Krishna.

Karna praises Arjuna's skill and the divine weapons he has gained, says Krishna's protection makes him invincible, and orders the Kaurava warriors to surround and wear out Arjuna. Arjuna cuts through the Kaurava attackers, and Drona's son, Kripa and others fall on him, and the whole field is darkened by arrows.
Arjuna drives off the Kaurava warriors who are attacking Bhima, rains arrows on the field, breaks the Kuru army, and meets Bhima to report that Yudhishthira is well.
Ten of Duryodhana's brothers attack Arjuna's chariot, and he cuts down their standards, horses, bows and heads with arrows and moves on.

Arjuna destroys ninety Samsaptaka chariots, the Kaurava force, and the Mleccha elephant riders, Bhima crushes the rest of the Kaurava army with his mace, and the Kauravas break and flee to Karna, who vows to protect them and attacks the Pancalas.

Karna kills many Pancala leaders and their horses and sons, Krishna urges Arjuna to go against Karna, Arjuna and Bhima drive toward Karna, and the sons of Draupadi rescue the Pandava commanders. Duhshasana and Bhima fight, Duhshasana wounds Bhima, and Bhima recovers and roars.
Duhshasana and Bhima fight, Bhima kills Duhshasana with his mace, drinks his blood as his vow requires, and boasts to the Kauravas that he will kill Duryodhana next.

Ten of Duryodhana's brothers attack Bhima, Arjuna destroys them, Shalya urges Karna to fight, and Vrishasena fights Nakula, cutting down his horses and car, until Nakula climbs onto Bhima's chariot and Arjuna turns to face Vrishasena.

The Pandava warriors rush to rescue Nakula, the Kaurava leaders engage them, Vrishasena wounds Arjuna and Krishna, Arjuna vows to kill Vrishasena, and then he shoots him down, and Karna rushes forward in grief and anger.
Seeing his son slain, Karna charges at Krishna and Arjuna in great fury.
Krishna points out Karna's chariot, with Shalya driving, and urges Arjuna to stay calm, recalling the divine favours he has won.
Arjuna vows that he will kill Karna that day and urges Krishna to drive quickly toward him.

The two heroes face each other across the field while armies cheer, gods and other beings take sides, Indra and Surya dispute the outcome, and Karna asks Shalya what he will do if Karna falls, and Shalya vows to kill Krishna and Arjuna.
A book heading: 'BOOK 9', marking the start of the next section of the text.
Krishna tells Arjuna that Karna cannot defeat him, and Arjuna promises to destroy Karna and Shalya that day and to comfort those who have grieved.

The sky fills with celestial beings as Arjuna and Karna clash, Arjuna beats back the five Kaurava leaders and is showered with flowers, Ashvatthama begs Duryodhana to make peace, and Duryodhana refuses and orders his men to attack.
Arjuna and Karna close with each other like two mighty elephants or mountains, each pouring arrows on the other.
The combat is compared to the battle of Indra and Vritra, and both heroes and their drivers are badly wounded.
The armies and spectators are frightened as the two warriors clash, and some cheer Arjuna forward.
The Somakas urge Arjuna to slay Karna, and the Kaurava warriors urge Karna to slay Arjuna.
Karna and Arjuna exchange opening volleys of ten arrows each and begin to wound each other.
Arjuna sends a storm of arrows at Karna, but Karna cuts them all away with his own.
Arjuna launches a fiery weapon, and Karna quenches it with the varuna weapon.
Karna then summons clouds that hide the sky and flood the field, and the fire is put out.

Arjuna clears the clouds with a wind weapon, and then drives back Karna with a volley of arrows. Karna responds with the Bhargava weapon and kills many Pancalas and Somakas. Bhima and Krishna urge Arjuna to act, and Arjuna sends the brahmastra and scatters the field with arrows, slaying many Kaurava warriors and wounding Karna. Karna keeps fighting, and Arjuna kills 2,000 Kaurava warriors, after which the Kauravas flee and Karna charges on alone.

The long duel: the two heroes fight with an endless storm of arrows, Karna fires the serpent-arrow Aswasena, Krishna sinks the chariot, and the arrow knocks off Arjuna's diadem; Karna's chariot wheel then sinks into the earth, and he pleads for a pause.

Arjuna answers with arrows that wound Karna, Karna is defeated and stunned, Arjuna holds back from killing him, Krishna urges him to finish the fight, and Karna begs for a pause as he frees his sunken wheel.
Krishna rebukes Karna for invoking virtue only now, listing his past wrongs against the Pandavas and Draupadi, and warns that he will not escape.
Karna's chariot wheel sinks as he wounds Arjuna, Arjuna cuts down his standard, and the Anjalika arrow takes off Karna's head, after which the Kauravas flee the field.
Shalya, who has lost his standard, goes to comfort Duryodhana, the Kauravas flee, Bhima and the Pandavas celebrate, and Shalya tells Duryodhana that Destiny has turned against them.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what the Kuru and Srinjaya armies looked like after Karna was killed and the Kauravas fled.

Sanjaya describes the rout: the Kauravas flee in panic, Duryodhana plans to fight from the rear, Bhima kills 25,000 foot soldiers, the Pandavas drive the remaining chariots, and Duryodhana tries in vain to rally his men with a speech on the duty of battle.
Sanjaya adds that the Kaurava warriors fled anyway, ignoring Duryodhana's appeal.
Sanjaya says that Shalya, seeing Duryodhana stunned by grief, speaks to him.
Shalya describes the battlefield piled with the dead, the wounded and the broken chariots, and urges Duryodhana to turn back to camp, saying Duryodhana himself is to blame.
Duryodhana weeps for Karna, the kings lead him back to camp, and the Kauravas go, looking back at Arjuna's banner, while Karna's body still shines.
Portents follow Karna's death, Arjuna and Krishna blow their conches, and the Kauravas flee the field, leaving Duryodhana behind.
After Karna's death the Kaurava army flees, Duryodhana withdraws the army on Shalya's advice, the leaders retreat to camp in grief, and Duryodhana orders his men to rest.
Krishna embraces Arjuna and tells him to report Karna's death to Yudhishthira, then goes with Arjuna to the king's tent and describes Karna's death to Yudhishthira, who is overjoyed.
Yudhishthira praises Krishna and Arjuna, saying that Krishna has made Arjuna's feats possible, and then goes out to see Karna's body.
The Pandava warriors welcome Yudhishthira and praise Krishna and Arjuna, and the army goes back to camp in joy.
Vaishampayana describes Dhritarashtra's grief at the news and says the reading of the Karna Parva brings merit to listeners.
A closing line: the end of the Karna Parva.
Edition title line: 'The Mahabharata'.
Edition title line: 'of'.
Edition title line: 'Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa'.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati, before the narration begins.
Janamejaya asks what the remaining Kauravas did after Karna was killed, and how Duryodhana behaved toward the Pandavas.
Vaishampayana narrates Shalya's command and death, Duryodhana's flight into a lake and death at Bhima's hands, and Sanjaya's report to the king listing the dead.
Dhritarashtra faints on hearing the news, Vidura and the others revive him, and Vidura gently comforts him.
Vaishampayana introduces Dhritarashtra's renewed lament after the women have been sent away.

Dhritarashtra mourns his sons, recalls their childhood, recounts Duryodhana's boasts about the allies he had, and concludes that all these losses must be destiny. He resolves to go into exile in the forest.
Vaishampayana says the king swoons again, then asks Sanjaya for the details of what happened.
Dhritarashtra asks who led the army after Drona and Karna fell, how Shalya and Duryodhana were killed, and asks Sanjaya to tell the whole account of the battle.
Sanjaya's full account of the rout: the panic after Karna's death, the Pandava attacks led by Bhima and Arjuna, and Duryodhana's speech urging his men to hold the field.
Sanjaya describes Kripa's appeal: he reminds Duryodhana of his dead allies, praises the Pandava warriors, and urges peace with Yudhishthira, then weeps and almost loses consciousness.
Duryodhana thanks Kripa but says the advice does not suit him. He lists the reasons the Pandavas will never forgive him, including the dice game, Draupadi's humiliation and Abhimanyu's death.

Duryodhana says he will not give up his pride or his kingdom. He prefers a warrior's death, honours his fallen allies, and says the Kauravas' noble dead have gone to heaven. The Kshatriyas applaud, and the army camps by the Sarasvati river, resolved to fight on.

Sanjaya describes the warriors camping in the hills, the Kaurava leaders' demand for a new commander, and Duryodhana approaching Ashvatthama, whom the text praises at length, to ask him to choose one.
Ashvatthama proposes Shalya as commander, citing his lineage, skill and loyalty, and the Kauravas cheer the choice.
Shalya accepts and promises to give everything he has to Duryodhana's service.
Duryodhana formally asks Shalya to take command and to fight as Kartikeya once did for the gods.
Shalya tells Duryodhana he will lead the army and will beat the Pandavas, and Duryodhana formally installs him with water poured over him as the troops cheer.
Shalya vows to fight the Pandavas, Krishna and their allies that day, whether he wins or dies.

The Kauravas feel relieved and sleep well that night. Yudhishthira, hearing the news, asks Krishna what to do, and Krishna praises Shalya but urges Arjuna to kill him without pity. The Pandavas then rest, feeling victorious after Karna's fall.
Duryodhana orders his men to arm. The Kaurava warriors gear up, the Kaurava leaders swear to fight together, and the Pandavas advance, with the field looking like a swelling sea.
Dhritarashtra says he has heard of the fall of Drona, Bhishma and Karna, and asks what happened next.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to tell him of the fall of Shalya and his son.
Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira slew Shalya.
Dhritarashtra asks how Bhima slew Duryodhana.

Sanjaya says he will describe the battle. He explains that the Kauravas hoped Shalya would destroy the Pandavas, and then describes Shalya's formation, the positions of the Kaurava commanders, and the Pandava divisions moving against them.
Dhritarashtra asks, after the fall of Bhishma, Drona and Karna, about the state of both sides.
Dhritarashtra's question continues, about the reduction of both armies.
Dhritarashtra's question continues, about the Pandavas' renewed anger in battle.
Dhritarashtra ends by asking Sanjaya about the strength of each army.
Dhritarashtra's question continues, asking for the strength of each army.

Sanjaya gives the numbers: about 11,000 cars, 10,700 elephants, 200,000 horses and three million foot-soldiers on the Kaurava side, and about 6,000 cars, 6,000 elephants, 10,000 horses and one million foot-soldiers left on the Pandava side. The two sides meet at dawn and the fighting becomes fierce.

Sanjaya describes the battle in grim detail: elephants, chariots and horsemen tear into one another, bodies and severed limbs cover the ground, and a river of blood carries the dead away. Bhima and Arjuna stun the Kaurava army, Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi turn on Shalya, and the Kaurava troops finally break and flee.
Sanjaya says Shalya drives straight at Yudhishthira and holds the Pandava army alone, so that the Kaurava troops return and a bloody battle breaks out.

Nakula duels Chitrasena and kills him, then fights Karna's sons Satyasena and Sushena, helped by Sutasoma. He kills Sushena and the Kaurava troops flee. Shalya rallies them, and the Pandava divisions turn on the Kaurava army and the battle becomes a general slaughter.
Sanjaya describes the carnage in general terms: the troops slaughter one another, elephants cry out and cowards flee while the brave are glad.
The battle is fought at sunrise. The Pandava heroes, protected by Yudhishthira, fight the Kaurava army, which grows weak and frightened, like deer before a forest fire.
Shalya comes to rescue the weakened Kaurava army, and the Pandavas attack him with arrows while he keeps firing back at their host in Yudhishthira's sight.

Omens appear as the armies clash. Shalya pours arrows on Yudhishthira and the Pandava commanders, and the Kaurava leaders protect him. Bhima's horses are killed, Shalya kills Sahadeva's horses, and Sahadeva kills Shalya's son. Bhima fights on foot with his mace, smashes Kritavarma's car, and attacks Shalya, whose lance wounds Bhima. Bhima pulls it out and kills Shalya's driver, and Shalya steps down from his chariot. The Pandavas cheer Bhima.

Sanjaya describes the mace duel between Shalya and Bhima, the praise of the onlookers, the fall of both fighters, and Kripa carrying Shalya from the field. The fighting resumes with Duryodhana wounding Chekitana with a lance, Yudhishthira cutting down Shalya's standard, and Shalya, enraged, raining arrows on the Pandavas until Yudhishthira is worn down.

Sanjaya describes the five Pandava warriors attacking Shalya together, Shalya's counterattacks, his destruction of their weapons, and the Pandava army's fear. Yudhishthira worries about Shalya's power, and the gods and Gandharvas are amazed as Shalya's arrows cover the field and the Pandavas press on.

Sanjaya describes Arjuna's attack on the Trigartas and Ashvatthama's army, his destruction of many cars, and his duel with Ashvatthama, in which neither can gain the upper hand. Ashvatthama kills Suratha and takes his chariot, and the fight at noon becomes fierce, with Arjuna alone against many.

Sanjaya describes the wide battle: Duryodhana fights Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi meets Kritavarma and Kripa, and Nakula wounds Shalya. Shalya breaks Nakula's bow and cars, then Yudhishthira, Bhima, Satyaki and Sahadeva all attack him. Satyaki's duel with Shalya ends in a mass of arrows across the field.

Sanjaya describes Shalya's push against the Pandavas, Yudhishthira's rage and vow to kill Shalya, and his plan for his chariot and protectors. The Pandavas and Pancalas attack. Bhima and Duryodhana fight, Duryodhana cuts Bhima's bow and standard, Bhima wounds Duryodhana and kills his driver. Yudhishthira destroys Shalya's steeds, drivers and standard, and Ashvatthama carries Shalya off the field.
A heading: Book 9.

Sanjaya describes the duel between Shalya and Yudhishthira, with Bhima, Satyaki, the twins and the Panchalas coming to Yudhishthira's aid. Shalya's arrows cut down bows, drivers, horses and armour. Yudhishthira, steedless and driverless, takes up a dart and hurls it, calling out that Shalya is slain.

Shalya tries to catch the dart but it pierces him, and he falls dead facing Yudhishthira. Shalya's younger brother attacks Yudhishthira and is killed. The Kauravas flee. Satyaki strips Kritavarma of his chariot and horses, Ashvatthama carries him off, and Duryodhana stands alone against the Pandavas. The Pandavas blow their conches and celebrate.

Sanjaya describes the Madraka warriors, numbering about 1,700 chariots, pressing into the Pandava host while Duryodhana, on an elephant, orders them to stop. Arjuna and the other Pandavas come to Yudhishthira's rescue, and the Madrakas are cut down.
Duryodhana tells Shakuni that the Madrakas ignored his orders and went in together.

Shakuni says that angry warriors do not obey, that the Kauravas must now stand together, and that all of them should go to save the Madrakas. The Kauravas move forward, but the Pandavas destroy the Madrakas, and the whole Kaurava army turns and flees.

Sanjaya describes the rout after Shalya's death, the Pandava celebrations, Duryodhana's order to his driver to fall back, and Duryodhana's speech urging his men to stand and die fighting. Bhima, on foot with his mace, kills the foot-soldiers who surround him, and the Kaurava kings rally to fight again.

Sanjaya describes Salwa on his great elephant routing the Pandava forces, Dhrishtadyumna's attack and his chariot being crushed, the Pandava heroes killing the elephant with mace and arrows, and Satyaki beheading Salwa as he falls with the elephant.

Sanjaya describes the rally after Salwa's death, Kritavarma's duel with Satyaki, Kritavarma's defeat and retreat with Kripa's help, and Duryodhana alone holding back the Pandava forces as the Kaurava army flees.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's arrows covering the Pandava army and his wounding of each of the Pandava leaders. The Kaurava warriors return to him, and a long series of single combats follows, including Ashvatthama and Bhima, Shakuni and Yudhishthira, Uluka and Nakula, Kritavarma and Satyaki, and Duryodhana and Dhrishtadyumna. Sanjaya ends by noting the dust and the blood that settles it, and the noon fighting.

Sanjaya describes the Kauravas rallying after their defeat. Yudhishthira kills Kritavarma's four horses and wounds Kripa, Ashvatthama carries Kritavarma away, and Duryodhana sends seven hundred cars against Yudhishthira, who is rescued by the Pandava heroes. Omens appear. Shakuni attacks the Pandava rear with Gandhara horsemen, and Yudhishthira sends Sahadeva and Draupadi's sons against him. When Shakuni's men are beaten, he retreats with a small remnant. The Pandava horsemen then withdraw, and Shakuni returns to attack Dhrishtadyumna's division, and the struggle goes on in disorder until the Pandavas encircle Shakuni and the combat ends in mutual slaughter.

Sanjaya describes Shakuni gathering seven hundred horsemen and telling Duryodhana to attack. Arjuna, seeing the Kauravas come on, tells Krishna the war should have ended after Bhishma, Drona and Karna fell, blames Duryodhana's folly and Vidura's warnings, and vows to kill the Kaurava warriors that day.
Sanjaya describes Krishna driving Arjuna into the Kaurava host, Arjuna's arrows striking men, horses and elephants, and his single-handed destruction of the Kaurava divisions.

Sanjaya describes the Kaurava army fleeing and regrouping, Dhrishtadyumna's attack on Duryodhana, the loss of Duryodhana's chariot, and the Kaurava elephants that surround the Pandavas. Arjuna and Bhima kill the elephants, and Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma search for Duryodhana. A Kuru warrior, speaking in the first person, recounts his defeat by Dhrishtadyumna and his capture by Satyaki.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's brothers, who unite against Bhima while Duryodhana is missing. Bhima kills them one by one. Srutarvan fights on, Bhima kills his driver and horses, and Srutarvan is beheaded after taking up a sword and shield. Bhima then slaughters hundreds of chariots, elephants, foot-soldiers and horses, and the Kaurava army is left very thin and cheerless.

Sanjaya describes Krishna urging Arjuna to strike at Duryodhana, who stands among his cavalry, and Arjuna answering that he will kill Duryodhana and the other remnants. Arjuna, Bhima and Sahadeva charge, Duryodhana lances Sahadeva, Arjuna slays the Trigarta leaders and their followers, and Bhima kills Sudarsana. The battle turns into a bloody general fight in which both sides fall, wailing for their kin.

Sanjaya describes the dreadful carnage as the Kaurava army shrinks to a remnant, and Duryodhana urges his fleeing troops back into the fight. Sahadeva kills Uluka, then breaks Shakuni's bow and his scimitar, mace and dart. Chasing Shakuni, Sahadeva cuts off his umbrella, standard, bow, arms and finally his head. The Kauravas flee in fear, and the Pandavas celebrate and praise Sahadeva.
A heading: the Hrada-pravesa Parva, the section title.
Sanjaya describes the last Kaurava rally, the Pandava assault that destroys it, and Duryodhana, the only survivor, fleeing on foot in grief and fear.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how many Pandava troops remained and what Duryodhana did when his army was destroyed.

Sanjaya gives the Pandava remnant's numbers, tells how Duryodhana fled into a lake, and recounts how Satyaki was about to kill him until Vyasa stopped him. He describes meeting Duryodhana, who hides in the lake by illusion and sends a message to Dhritarashtra. Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma find Sanjaya, and the women and camp-followers flee the camp in panic. Yuyutsu reaches Hastinapura with them, and Vidura praises him and tells him to rest before returning to Yudhishthira.
Dhritarashtra asks what the surviving Kaurava warriors, Kritavarma, Kripa and Ashvatthama, did after the army was destroyed, and what Duryodhana did.
Sanjaya describes the three warriors going to the lake, the Pandavas searching the field for Duryodhana, and the warriors urging the king from under the water to rise and fight.
Duryodhana says he is too tired and wounded to fight now, asks his friends to rest, and promises to fight the next morning.

Ashvatthama swears to slay every Panchala that night and the warriors insist on battle. Meanwhile, huntsmen who supplied Bhima with meat overhear the talk, find the Pandavas and tell them where Duryodhana is hidden. The Pandavas, Krishna and the others ride to the lake, and Duryodhana, hidden in the water, hears them coming. Kripa, Kritavarma and Ashvatthama leave and rest under a banyan tree.

Sanjaya describes the Pandavas arriving at the lake where Duryodhana is hiding by magic. Yudhishthira says Duryodhana has used illusion and that he will still be killed that day, even if Indra helps him.
Krishna tells Yudhishthira to answer illusion with his own cunning, and recalls many old victories won by stratagem, such as those of Indra, Vishnu and Rama.
Yudhishthira taunts Duryodhana: he calls him a boaster who hides in a lake instead of fighting, and tells him to rise and either win the earth or die fighting.
Sanjaya introduces Duryodhana's reply, which he gives from inside the water after hearing Yudhishthira's words.
The sentence continues: Duryodhana answers Yudhishthira from within the waters.
Duryodhana says he did not flee from fear but because his chariot, quivers and drivers were gone and he was alone, so he needed rest. He promises to rise and fight.
Yudhishthira says the Pandavas have rested and searched long enough, and tells Duryodhana to rise and fight, either to win the kingdom or to die a hero's death.
Duryodhana says his brothers and allies are dead, the earth is now like a widow, and he no longer wants it. He offers to give it to the Pandavas and retire to the forest in deerskin.

Yudhishthira refuses the gift, saying a Kshatriya cannot accept such a gift and that Duryodhana never gave them even a needle's point of land. He recalls the attempts to burn and poison the Pandavas and Draupadi's humiliation, and says Duryodhana must fight.
Sanjaya says the victorious Pandavas continue to rebuke and mock Duryodhana.
A heading: the Gada-yuddha Parva, the section title for the mace duel.
Dhritarashtra asks how his son, so proud and never before spoken to like this, could take such taunts, and asks Sanjaya to tell him exactly what was said.
Sanjaya says Duryodhana heard the taunts from within the water, grew miserable, sighed heavily, and answered the Pandavas from the lake.

Duryodhana says the Pandavas have their friends and chariots while he is alone and without a chariot, so he cannot fight them all at once. He asks them to fight him one at a time, and promises to rise and fight them all with his mace.
Yudhishthira praises Duryodhana's courage and agrees to a one-on-one fight with any weapon he chooses, promising him the kingship if he kills one of the brothers.
Duryodhana chooses the mace as his weapon and asks any one of the Pandavas to come forward and fight him on foot.
Yudhishthira tells Duryodhana to rise and fight them one at a time, to be a man, and that he will die that day even if Indra helps him.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana rising from the lake with his iron mace, in angry, blazing splendour, and warning the Pandavas that he will kill them all.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana standing on the bank, bloody and dripping, looking like the wrathful sun, as he summons the Pandavas to battle.
Duryodhana repeats that he will fight only one of them at a time, since fighting many at once would be improper for a man who is armourless and exhausted, and asks the gods to see the fight.
Yudhishthira rebukes Duryodhana for joining many warriors to kill Abhimanyu, says the Kshatriya code is cruel, and again offers the kingship to whichever brother he kills.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana arming himself in golden mail and a golden helmet, and challenging Sahadeva, Bhima, Nakula, Arjuna or Yudhishthira to a mace fight, promising to beat whoever accepts.

Krishna blames Yudhishthira's rash offer. He says Duryodhana has practised with the mace for thirteen years and, being so skilled, could beat any Pandava except Bhima. He calls the Pandavas' destiny one of exile.
Bhima tells Krishna not to grieve, promises to kill Duryodhana, and says his mace is heavier than Duryodhana's.

Krishna praises Bhima, lists the Kauravas killed in battle, and urges him to be careful. Bhima accepts the challenge, recalls the wrongs of Varanavata, the dice game and Draupadi's humiliation, and tells Duryodhana that he alone is left of his line.

Duryodhana answers that Bhima's words are empty and boasts that he has never lost a fair fight. He says he is the one who drove the Pandavas into the forest and into disguise. He warns that if the Pandavas beat him by trickery their shame will last. The Pandavas and Srinjayas cheer, and the weapons of the Pandavas begin to blaze.

Sanjaya describes Balarama's arrival at the field as the two pupils prepare to fight, his greeting by the Pandavas and Krishna, his remarks about his journey, and his seat among the kings for the duel.
Janamejaya asks why Balarama left the war, and Vaishampayana is asked to tell where he went and how he saw the battle.

Vaishampayana explains that Krishna failed to reconcile the sides and that Balarama, angry at Krishna's refusal to help the Kurus, set out on a pilgrimage along the Sarasvati. He gave away large gifts to Brahmanas and the needy at many sacred sites, and finally reached Kurukshetra.
Janamejaya asks for the origin, features and merits of the sacred sites on the Sarasvati, and the rules for visiting them.
Vaishampayana begins with Prabhasa, where the moon was cured of his phthisis, and explains that the place is named for the restoration of Soma's splendour.
Janamejaya asks why Soma was cursed and how he was cured at the place.

Vaishampayana tells how Daksha's twenty-seven daughters, wives of Soma, complained that he favoured Rohini. Daksha ordered Soma to treat them equally, but he did not, so Daksha cursed him with wasting. The herbs and creatures declined, and the gods pleaded with Daksha to lift the curse. Daksha agreed that Soma would wax and wane but would be restored if he bathed at Prabhasa. Soma bathed there and was restored. Balarama then visited Chamasodbheda and Udapana, where the Sarasvati seems to disappear underground.

Vaishampayana says Balarama goes on to Udapana, where the ascetic Trita once lived, and gives gifts and bathes there. The chapter gives the background: Trita drank Soma in a pit, and his brothers threw him down and cursed.
Janamejaya asks how Udapana came about, why Trita fell into a pit, why his brothers abandoned him, and how he performed his sacrifice.

Vaishampayana tells the story: three brothers, Ekata, Dwita and Trita, sons of Gautama, travel with cattle after a sacrifice. The two elder brothers decide to steal the cattle and leave Trita. A wolf frightens Trita into a dry well, and he performs a sacrifice in his mind. The gods come for their shares, the Sarasvati rises to lift him out, and Trita curses his brothers to become wolves, leopards, bears and apes. Balarama then bathes at Udapana and goes on to Vinasana.

Vaishampayana describes Balarama's visits to Vinasana, Subhumika, the Gandharva tirtha, Gargasrota, Sankha, the Dwaita lake and Nagadhanwana, and the gifts he gives at each. Past Nagadhanwana, he reaches the point where the Sarasvati turns east, and he is amazed.
Janamejaya asks why the Sarasvati bends eastward and why Balarama was astonished by it.

Vaishampayana explains that the Naimisha sages, after a twelve-year sacrifice, crowded the banks of the Sarasvati and had nowhere to hold their rites. The river made room for them by changing course, then returned westward. Balarama, wondering at this, visits Sapta-Saraswat, where the sage Mankanaka had performed penances.
Janamejaya asks why the tirtha is called Sapta-Saraswat, who Mankanaka was, and how he became successful, asking about his vows and learning.

Vaishampayana names the seven forms of the Sarasvati and tells how she appeared at sacrifices held by Brahma at Pushkara, by the sages at Naimisha, by Gaya, Auddalaka, Kuru, Daksha and Brahma, and how the seven joined at Sapta-Saraswat. He then tells how Mankanaka, a young ascetic, saw a woman bathing, and his seed fell into the river and was kept in a jar, where it became seven sages, fathers of the Maruts. Later a Kusha blade cut his hand, a juice flowed out, and he danced with joy until the gods went to Mahadeva.

Mahadeva asks why Mankanaka is dancing. The sage answers that he sees a juice from his wound, and Mahadeva shows him ash from his own thumb. Mankanaka recognises Rudra, praises him, and asks forgiveness. Mahadeva promises that anyone who worships at Sapta-Saraswat will reach the realm of the Sarasvati after death, and the chapter ends by noting that Mankanaka was a son of the wind god by Sukanya.
Vaishampayana says Balarama worships the dwellers of the tirtha and goes on to Usanas, also called Kapalamochana, where Sukra performed penances and where Rama once threw a Rakshasa's head.
Janamejaya asks why the place is called Kapalamochana and how the head came to stick to the sage.

Vaishampayana tells how Rama killed a Rakshasa in Dandaka and his severed head fell on the thigh of Mahodara, who was wandering. The head stuck to him, and he went all over the holy places in pain until he heard of this sacred spot and bathed in it. The head fell into the water and was lost, and the sage was freed. Balarama then gives gifts and goes on to Rushangu's asylum, where Arshtishena performed penance, and to other holy places like it.
Janamejaya asks how Arshtishena, Sindhudwipa, Devapi and Vishvamitra gained the status of Brahmanas, and asks for full details.

Vaishampayana tells how Arshtishena failed to master his lessons, did penance, won mastery of the Vedas, and gave the place three boons. He then tells how Vishvamitra, a king, left his throne to his son Vishvamitra, lost control of his kingdom, and attacked Vasishtha's hermitage. Vasishtha's cow created warriors who routed his army. Vishvamitra then did penance at this tirtha, won the boon of Brahmanhood from Brahma, and wandered the earth as a Brahmana. Balarama then gave gifts there and went on to Vaka's asylum.

Vaishampayana describes Balarama at Vaka's asylum, the sage Dalvya Vaka's sacrifice that poured Dhritarashtra's kingdom into the fire, and how the kingdom wasted away. Counsellors blamed the king's insult over the dead cattle, and the king begged Vaka's forgiveness at the riverbank, after which the kingdom was freed and Vaka returned to Naimisha.

Vaishampayana tells how Brihaspati made a sacrifice here with flesh to destroy the Asuras, and how Yayati's sacrifice at the Sarasvati produced milk and butter and gifts for the guests. Balarama then gives generous gifts and moves on to the sacred river site called Vasishthapavaha.
Janamejaya asks why the Vasishthapavaha current is so rapid, why the river carried off Vasishtha, and what caused the quarrel between Vasishtha and Vishvamitra.

Vaishampayana describes the rivalry of the two sages on opposite banks, the holy site called Sthanu-tirtha, and Vishvamitra's plan. He orders the Sarasvati to bring Vasishtha to him so that he can kill him, and the frightened river goes to Vasishtha to tell him.

Vasishtha tells the river to save herself. She washes away one bank and carries him to Vishvamitra's side, where he praises her. Vishvamitra, enraged, curses the Sarasvati to flow with blood. She flows that way for a year, and the place is named Vasishthapravaha. Later the river recovers its proper course.

Vaishampayana describes the Sarasvati flowing with blood, the Rakshasas drinking it and dancing, and the sages' decision to purify her. The Rakshasas beg for relief, and the sages teach them which foods are forbidden. The river takes the new form of Aruna, the Rakshasas are freed, and Indra bathes there to be cleansed of his sin.
A heading: Book 10.
Janamejaya asks why Indra was tainted by the sin of killing a Brahmana.
Janamejaya continues, asking how Indra was cleansed by bathing at the tirtha.

Vaishampayana tells how Indra made a covenant with Namuchi not to kill him by wet or dry means, day or night, then broke it by killing him with sea foam. Namuchi's head pursued Indra, who went to Brahma. Brahma told him to bathe at the Aruna confluence with the Sarasvati and offer gifts, and Indra was freed.

Vaishampayana describes Balarama's bathing at the Soma tirtha, where Soma once performed the Rajasuya sacrifice, Atri was the priest, Skanda defeated Taraka, and Kartikeya is said to dwell under a great asvattha tree.
Janamejaya asks for the time, place, manner and officiants of Skanda's investiture and wants to know how he defeated the Daityas.

Vaishampayana tells how Shiva's seed fell into fire, then into the Ganga and onto Himalaya, where the child grew. The six Krittikas claimed him and he took six faces to nurse from each. The gods, Brahma and the others gathered, and Shiva divided himself into four forms to meet Skanda's choice. Brahma made Skanda commander of the celestial army, and the gods gathered at the Sarasvati's bank on Himalaya for the rites.

Vaishampayana describes the rites of installation at Himalaya: Brihaspati makes the offerings, the gods and many others attend, Skanda is seated and anointed with water from the Sarasvati, and each god gives him companions. A long list follows of the many beings with odd faces and weapons who come to serve him, and they dance around him in joy.
Vaishampayana introduces the large bands of mothers, the slayers of foes who became Kumara's companions.
He says he will name them, and that they pervade the mobile and immobile universe.
He asks Janamejaya to listen to the names of these illustrious mothers.
He says the mothers are auspicious and fill the whole universe.
The first names of the mothers are given, beginning with Prabhavati and Vishalakshi.

The mothers, thousands in number, are described: long nails, large teeth, youthful and ornamented, able to change form, and of many complexions.
Their powers are described: they can grant boons, travel at will, and partake of the natures of many gods.
They are described as beautiful, strong and fearsome in battle, and as quick as the wind.
They live in trees, crossroads, caves, cremation grounds and mountains, and they speak many languages.

Indra gives Kartikeya a dart and a banner, Shiva gives him a great army, Vishnu a garland, Uma two cloths, and Ganga, Brihaspati, Garuda, Aruna, Varuna and Brahma other gifts, including victory in battle.
Skanda, now commander of the celestial forces, sets out with his companions and the mothers to destroy the Daityas, and his army is shown in splendour.
The gods' musicians play, and the gods praise Kartikeya while the Gandharvas sing and the Apsaras dance.
Skanda promises the gods that he will slay all who wish to slay them, and the gods regard their foes as already slain.
Skanda marches out with his army, and personified qualities such as success and courage lead the way.
The Daityas, Rakshasas and Danavas flee, and Skanda hurls his dart repeatedly, causing meteors and thunderbolts to fall, as at the end of the world.
Skanda kills Taraka with a hundred thousand Daityas around him, then kills Mahisha, Tripada and Hradodara with their followers.
Thousands of Daityas are burned by the dart, struck by banners, or fall at Skanda's roars. Skanda kills many foes.
Bali's son Vana attacks the gods from Mount Krauncha, and Skanda pierces the mountain with his dart, making the forests and creatures flee.
Skanda kills Bali's son and his brother, and the dart returns to his hand after each throw. The gods honour him.
The gods rejoice, and celestial women shower flowers. Different traditions name Skanda as a son of Sanat-kumara, Shiva, Agni, Uma, the Krittikas or Ganga.
Vaishampayana says the installation account is complete, that the tirtha became a second heaven, and that Balarama bathed at Taijasa, where Varuna was installed, and gave gifts.
Janamejaya says the story is wonderful, that he feels purified, and asks how Varuna was installed as lord of the waters at this tirtha.

Vaishampayana tells how the gods asked Varuna to rule all rivers and seas, and how he accepted and was installed. Balarama bathes at Agnitirtha, where Agni had hidden in a Sami tree, and the gods went to Brahma when the fire disappeared.
Janamejaya asks why Agni, creator of the worlds, disappeared and how the gods found him.

Vaishampayana says Agni hid in the Sami tree after a curse from Bhrigu, and the gods searched and found him. Agni was made to eat everything, as Bhrigu said. Balarama then visits Brahmayoni, the Kauvera tirtha, where Kuvera gained his powers, and Vadarapachana, where fruits are always abundant.

Vaishampayana tells how Sruvavati, a Brahmacharini, does severe penance to win Indra. Indra, disguised as Vasishtha, asks her to boil jujubes, and she burns her feet to keep the fire going. Pleased, Indra reveals himself and grants her boon. The place becomes a holy tirtha named Vadarapachana, and the chapter recalls how Arundhati and Shiva made the place sacred in an earlier drought.
Janamejaya asks who Sruvavati's mother was and how she was raised.

Vaishampayana says Sruvavati was born when Bharadwaja's seed fell on seeing the Apsara Ghritachi, kept in a leaf cup. Bharadwaja named her and raised her, and Balarama bathes and gives gifts before going on to the tirtha of Sakta.

Vaishampayana describes Balarama's visits to Indra's tirtha, where Indra gained the name Satakratu after a hundred sacrifices, to Rama's tirtha, where Parashurama gave the earth to Kasyapa, to the Yamuna, where Varuna held a Rajasuya, and finally to the Aditya tirtha, where Surya gained his power. Vishnu bathed there, and Vyasa and Asita-Devala gained yogic powers there.

Vaishampayana introduces Asita-Devala, an impartial householder who gives hospitality, and his guest Jaigishavya, a yogi. Devala is puzzled when Jaigishavya seems to bathe in the ocean before him and then be found in his hermitage. Devala flies to the heavens and watches Jaigishavya pass through many worlds, then asks the Siddhas where he has gone.
The Siddhas tell Devala that Jaigishavya has gone to the eternal realm of Brahman.
Devala tries to follow, falls back, and the Siddhas tell him he cannot reach Brahman.

Devala returns to his hermitage, finds Jaigishavya there, and asks to take up the life of liberation. Jaigishavya teaches him. Creatures and plants lament the loss of a provider, but Devala chooses liberation and attains the highest success. Narada disparages Jaigishavya, and the gods praise him. Balarama bathes at this tirtha and goes on to Soma's tirtha.

Vaishampayana says Balarama bathes at the place where the Lord of stars once performed the Rajasuya and a great battle with Taraka began, and then visits the tirtha of the sage Sarasvata, who taught the Vedas during a twelve-year drought.
Janamejaya asks why Sarasvata taught the Vedas during the drought.
Vaishampayana tells how the austere sage Dadhichi was tempted by Indra, who sent the Apsara Alambusa. Dadhichi's seed fell into the Sarasvati, which carried it until it became a child, Sarasvata.
The river gives the child to Dadhichi, saying she kept him through devotion, and Dadhichi blesses her waters for the gods and Apsaras.
Dadhichi praises the river and names the child Sarasvata. He says the boy will teach the Vedas in a drought and will make the river the foremost of holy rivers.
Indra, at war with the Danavas, finds no weapon able to kill them and is told that only Dadhichi's bones will do. He asks the gods to beg for them.
