Dadhichi gives up his life, and Indra uses his bones to make thunderbolts and other weapons. Indra kills many Daityas, and a later twelve-year drought forces the sages to scatter.
The Sarasvati tells Sarasvata to stay, promising to supply him with large fish, and he feeds the sages and the gods.
After the drought, the sages have forgotten the Vedas, and they ask Sarasvata to teach them. He says ability matters more than age, and he teaches them.
Sixty thousand sages become his disciples and bring grass for his seat. Balarama gives gifts there and moves on to an old woman's asylum.
Janamejaya asks why the maiden turned to penance, what her vow was, and asks for full details.

Vaishampayana describes Kuni-Garga, who created a daughter by his will and then died. She practised penance and worshipped the gods and ancestors for years, refusing marriage because she saw no suitable husband.
She continues her penance until she is too old to walk and resolves to depart for the other world.
Narada tells her she has no place in heaven because she did not marry, despite her great penance.
She offers half her penances to any sage who takes her hand, and Sringavat, son of Galava, accepts her on condition that she stays with him one night.
They marry according to rites, and she becomes a radiant young woman. Sringavat spends the night with her.
At morning she says the compact is fulfilled, promises a merit to those who spend a night at the tirtha, and departs for heaven.
Sringavat grieves for her and, accepting half her penances as agreed, follows her in death.
Balarama learns that Shalya has fallen, grieves for him, and asks the sages at Samantapanchaka for news of the battle, which they tell him in full.
The sages say Samantapanchaka is Brahman's northern altar and that the field is called Kurukshetra after King Kuru, who cultivated it for many years.
Balarama asks why Kuru ploughed the field and asks the sages to explain.

The sages tell how Indra asked Kuru why he ploughed, and Kuru said those who die there will go to heaven. Indra mocked him, but the gods agreed to grant the promise. The sages describe the sanctity of the land, its benefits, its boundaries, and the verse that Indra sang in its praise.
Balarama visits a hermitage linked to Vishnu and Sandilya's daughter, then proceeds up Himalaya through several tirthas. Narada arrives, and Balarama asks him for news of the battle and the field.

Narada reports the deaths of Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha, Karna, Bhurishrava and Shalya, and says only Kripa, Kritavarma and Ashvatthama survive. Duryodhana, pierced by the Pandavas' words, has risen from the lake and is about to fight Bhima. Narada urges Balarama to hurry and watch the duel.
Balarama dismisses his companions to Dwaraka, praises the Sarasvati in a verse, and rides in his chariot to see the duel between his two pupils.
Vaishampayana introduces Dhritarashtra's grief as he asks about the duel.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how his son fought Bhima when Balarama came to watch.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's joy at Balarama's arrival and Yudhishthira's honours to him. Balarama praises Kurukshetra as a sacred field where warriors who die go to heaven, and the Pandavas and Duryodhana move to the chosen spot on the southern bank of the Sarasvati. Both champions, in armour and with maces, are compared to gods and great beasts. Duryodhana, sure of his strength, calls on the assembled kings to watch, and they sit down to see the combat.
Dhritarashtra laments that his son, once lord of many armies and of the earth, now has to stand on foot with a mace, and says that this must be the work of fate.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's challenge, the omens of storm, thunder, eclipse and disturbed wells, and Bhima's long speech of vengeance listing the Kauravas' wrongs. Duryodhana answers with mockery that Bhima is a coward, and the kings cheer as the mace fighters advance.

Sanjaya describes the duel in detail. The two circle, strike and retreat, until both are exhausted and rest. They resume, with the gods and onlookers astonished. Duryodhana wins the right side, Bhima the left, and Duryodhana strikes Bhima's flank. Bhima's mace fails to reach him, and Duryodhana strikes Bhima on the head. Bhima stands firm, Duryodhana is knocked down by Bhima's blow, Duryodhana rises and knocks Bhima down, and the Pandavas then cheer. Duryodhana strikes Bhima again, Bhima rises, and the fight goes on.

Sanjaya says Duryodhana's mace has broken Bhima's coat of mail and left him struck. Gods shower flowers, the Pandavas and their allies fear the outcome, and Bhima stands up again, with rolling eyes, steadying himself and preparing to fight on.
Arjuna asks Krishna which of the two fighters is better and what each one's merits are.

Krishna says the two were taught equally. Bhima is stronger, Duryodhana more skilled, and only deception will let Bhima win. He recalls Bhima's vow to break Duryodhana's thighs and blames Yudhishthira for staking the outcome on one duel. Arjuna slaps his thigh as a signal. Bhima and Duryodhana fight on until Bhima strikes Duryodhana's thighs with his mace as Duryodhana leaps. Duryodhana falls, and the sky, earth and creatures react with terrible omens.

Sanjaya describes the Pandavas' joy and Bhima's taunts over the fallen Duryodhana, his foot on the king's head, and Yudhishthira's rebuke, which tells Bhima to stop crushing a king and kinsman, and then Yudhishthira's lament for Duryodhana and his own grief at the dead.
Dhritarashtra asks what the mighty Balarama did when Duryodhana was struck down unfairly.

Sanjaya describes Balarama condemning Bhima's blow below the navel as contrary to the rules of the mace fight, raising his plough and rushing at Bhima. Krishna holds him back, citing Bhima's vow and Maitreya's curse, and Balarama argues about morality, profit and pleasure. Krishna says the Kali age is near and asks him to be calm.

Balarama, unconvinced, declares that Yudhishthira has slain Duryodhana unfairly and that Duryodhana died a fair warrior. He ascends his chariot and leaves for Dwaraka. Krishna then goes to Yudhishthira, who sits downcast and sorrowful.
Krishna asks Yudhishthira why he allows Bhima to place his foot on the head of the fallen Duryodhana.
Yudhishthira says he does not like the act, but he has looked on in grief at the Kauravas' cruel acts and their exile of the Pandavas. He lets Bhima do as he wishes.
Krishna accepts Yudhishthira's words, and Bhima, glad of his victory, salutes Yudhishthira and says the earth is his, with its enemies all dead.
Yudhishthira says the hostilities are over, that Duryodhana is struck down, that the earth is won by following Krishna's counsel, and that the debts to their mother and their anger are paid.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what the Pandavas and Srinjayas did when Bhima struck down Duryodhana.
Dhritarashtra's question continues.

Sanjaya describes the Pandavas and Panchalas rejoicing and praising Bhima. Krishna tells them it is wrong to keep insulting a dead foe, since Duryodhana refused the Pandavas their share of the kingdom, and orders them to leave. Duryodhana, sitting up, glares at Krishna and begins to speak.

Krishna answers Duryodhana: he has been slain for his own sins, including refusing the Pandavas their share, poisoning Bhima, trying to burn them at the lacquer house, insulting Draupadi, cheating Yudhishthira at dice, and killing Abhimanyu. Duryodhana's own acts are the cause of his fall.

Duryodhana, in his last words, says he has studied, given gifts, ruled the earth and died in battle, a fortunate end for a Kshatriya. He will go to heaven with his brothers, while the Pandavas will be left in grief.

Flowers fall from heaven, the Gandharvas and Apsaras celebrate Duryodhana, and the Pandavas are ashamed. Krishna says the Kaurava warriors could not be beaten fairly, that he used illusion for their sake, and that when enemies are many, a foe must be defeated by any means, as the gods did.
Sanjaya describes the Kaurava warriors going to their tents, the Pandavas and their allies going to Duryodhana's tent, and its empty, ruined state.
Krishna asks Arjuna to put down his bow Gandiva and the quivers and to dismount first, and says he will follow.
Arjuna dismounts, Krishna follows, and the celestial ape on the chariot flag vanishes. The chariot, already scorched in battle by Drona and Karna, bursts into flames and burns to ashes.
Arjuna asks Krishna why the chariot burned and asks him to explain.
Krishna explains that the chariot had been burnt by many weapons and only held together because he rode on it. Once Arjuna had won, Krishna left it, and it burned.
Krishna embraces Yudhishthira, praises the victory and the survival of the Pandavas, and urges him to act now.
Krishna recalls that at Upaplavya Yudhishthira asked him to protect Arjuna, and he agreed.
Krishna says he has kept Arjuna safe, and that Arjuna and the others have survived. Yudhishthira, with his hair standing on end, thanks him.
Yudhishthira praises Krishna's grace, which let him defeat Drona's and Karna's weapons, the Samsaptakas and the Kaurava armies, and notes Vyasa's words that victory follows Krishna.
The Pandavas enter Duryodhana's camp, take its treasure, jewels, cattle and slaves, and cheer their victory before resting their animals.
Krishna suggests that the Pandavas camp outside the main camp that night for an auspicious rite, and they camp at the banks of the Oghavati.
Krishna, with Daruka at the reins, sets out for Hastinapura, and the Pandavas ask him to comfort Gandhari, who has lost her sons.
Janamejaya asks why Yudhishthira sent Krishna to Gandhari and why Krishna himself had to go, since the war was already won.

Vaishampayana says Yudhishthira feared Gandhari's wrath, and he sent Krishna to calm her. Krishna, arriving at Hastinapura, honours Vyasa, Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, and tells Dhritarashtra that the Pandavas were wronged, that the king's own folly caused the war, and that he must not blame them. He then comforts Gandhari, reminding her of her own earlier advice that victory follows righteousness. Krishna sees that Drona's son plans to kill the Pandavas by night, so he leaves quickly to protect them and returns to their camp to tell them what he has done.
Dhritarashtra asks what his son said after being kicked, with his thighs broken, lying on the ground in pride and anger.

Sanjaya describes Duryodhana, dusty and bleeding, gathering his hair and striking the ground, cursing Yudhishthira and Bhima for the unfair blow, and listing his past glories. He asks Sanjaya to tell his parents not to grieve and sends word to Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma. He then bids farewell to his friends and kinsmen and to the Kauravas who died before him, and asks Sanjaya to console his family. The messengers leave, weeping, and carry the news to Ashvatthama.

Sanjaya describes the three surviving Kaurava warriors reaching the field where Duryodhana lies broken and bloodied, surrounded by carrion beasts. They dismount and sit around him. Ashvatthama laments his fall and recalls his past splendour. Duryodhana replies that death is fated and that he dies in battle as a Kshatriya should, rejoicing in his fortune. He tells them they have done their duty and that fate cannot be overturned. Ashvatthama swears to kill every Panchala that night, and Duryodhana has Kripa install him as commander. Ashvatthama embraces the king and leaves, and Duryodhana lies alone through the night, with the warriors pondering what to do next.
Closing line: the Shalya Parva ends.
Heading: the title of the Mahabharata.
Heading: the word 'of' within the title.
Heading: the attribution to Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati, with the word Jaya.
Sanjaya reports that the three heroes head south, flee east after the Pandava uproar, and rest, tired and thirsty.
Dhritarashtra mourns Duryodhana, his own loss of status and his helplessness, and asks what Kritavarma, Kripa and Drona's son did next.
Sanjaya says the three enter a dense forest full of animals, birds, lakes and flowers, and rest there.
They reach a great banyan tree, perform their evening prayers, and the night falls with noisy creatures.
Kritavarma, Kripa and Ashvatthama sit under the banyan, grieving, and Kripa and Kritavarma fall asleep on the bare ground.
Ashvatthama stays awake and sees an owl attack the sleeping crows in the banyan, killing many of them.
Ashvatthama takes the owl's night attack as a lesson and resolves to strike his sleeping enemies by guile.
He recalls verses that justify attacking an enemy who is tired, asleep, leaderless or unaware.
He settles on a plan to kill the sleeping Pandavas and Panchalas, and wakes Kripa and Kritavarma, who say nothing in reply out of shame.
Ashvatthama, weeping, reports Duryodhana's death, Bhima's kick, and the enemy's celebrations, then asks his companions what to do.
Kripa says that destiny and exertion together govern all human acts, and neither works alone.
He says effort succeeds through destiny, and the wise combine skill with effort.
He says action is never wasted, idleness brings misery, and enjoying reward without effort invites ridicule.
He says effort fails without destiny, and a man should seek the counsel of the old before acting.
He blames Duryodhana for ignoring his well-wishers and fighting the Pandavas, and says the three are now ruined by following him.
Kripa suggests they ask Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura what to do, and says those whose efforts fail are under the sway of destiny.
Ashvatthama, grieving, answers Kripa by saying each man trusts his own understanding, which changes with time and fortune.
He compares intelligence to a physician's diagnosis and notes that a person's understanding shifts through youth, middle age and decline.
He says a chosen resolve should be carried out with effort, and he now reveals the resolve he has formed.
He recalls how the Creator gave each class its duty: learning to Brahmanas, energy to Kshatriyas, skill to Vaishyas, and service to Shudras.
Born a Brahmana but bound to Kshatriya duty, he says he will avenge his father as a warrior.
He describes his plan to attack the Panchalas while they sleep in camp, slay them including Dhrishtadyumna, and so find peace.
Kripa is pleased by Ashvatthama's vengeful resolve, urges him to rest for the night, and promises that he and Kritavarma will fight alongside him in the morning.
Kritavarma joins in: he and Kripa will not retreat without defeating the Pandavas, and they will help him in battle.
Ashvatthama, red-eyed with rage, says grief, anger, greed and lust keep him from sleep, and he cannot rest while his father's killer lives.
He says the Pandavas are protected by Krishna and Arjuna, his rage cannot be calmed, and he will kill the enemy in their sleep before he rests.
Kripa says that a person without understanding or self-control cannot grasp duty, while a wise man learns it by humble attention to elders.
Kripa says well-wishers should hold back a friend who is about to do wrong, and that the one who listens to them prospers.
Kripa argues that killing men who are asleep, unarmed or surrendering is against dharma, and the attack would bring Ashvatthama lasting shame.
Ashvatthama replies that the Pandavas have broken the rules before, citing the unfair deaths of his father, Karna, Bhishma, Bhurishrava and Duryodhana, and vows to kill the Panchalas in their sleep.
Sanjaya reports that Ashvatthama yokes his horses, and when Kritavarma and Kripa ask why, he explains that he will kill Dhrishtadyumna and asks them to arm and wait.
The three ride toward the sleeping Panchala camp, shining like sacrificial fires, and Ashvatthama halts at the gate.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Kripa and Kritavarma did when Drona's son stopped at the camp gate.
Sanjaya describes a gigantic, dazzling guardian dressed in tiger and deer skins, with snakes for ornaments, many eyes and a terrifying face.
Ashvatthama hurls a stream of celestial weapons, a blazing dart, a scimitar and a mace, but the being swallows each one.
With his weapons spent, Ashvatthama sees the sky full of images of Krishna, recalls Kripa's counsel, and admits he broke the rules of war by attacking the sleeping and unarmed.
He concludes that fate has turned against him, so his own effort will not succeed, and he resolves to seek the protection of Mahadeva, Shiva.
Ashvatthama steps down from his chariot, bows to Shiva, and asks for protection under his many names.
Heading: Book 11 begins.
Ashvatthama lists many of Shiva's titles and attributes, from his blue throat to his role as lord of ghostly beings, and asks for protection.
A golden altar and a blazing fire appear, along with many monstrous beings with animal faces and varied bodies.
Those beings carry many weapons, play instruments, dance and roar, and are described as drinkers of blood and fat.
Shiva's followers are described as all-powerful beings who serve the god and are fierce against the enemies of Brahma.
The beings gather around Ashvatthama, wanting to see the slaughter at the hour of sleep, but he feels no fear and offers his own self as a sacrifice.
Ashvatthama addresses the god and climbs onto the altar, offering his soul into the blazing fire.
Shiva appears and says he has been pleased by the devotion of Krishna, and that he protected the Pancalas at Krishna's word, though their lives have run out.
Shiva gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters his body, filling him with divine energy, and invisible beings and Rakshasas follow him toward the enemy camp.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya whether Kripa and Kritavarma fled in fear or fought on, and whether they achieved anything.
Sanjaya says Kripa and Kritavarma wait at the gate, and Ashvatthama urges them to make sure no one escapes, then he enters the camp like Yama.
Ashvatthama slips into the camp through an unguarded spot, finds Dhrishtadyumna asleep on a silk-covered bed, wakes him with a kick, and pins him down.
Dhrishtadyumna begs to be killed with a weapon, but Ashvatthama kicks him to death, and the guards, thinking a demon is attacking, make no outcry.
The women and guards wail, warriors come out, and Ashvatthama kills them with the rudrastra, then kills Uttamauja and Yudhamanyu in their beds.
Ashvatthama moves through the camp killing sleeping and unarmed warriors with his sword, until the terrified men flee or freeze, thinking him a demon.
Draupadi's sons, the Prabhadrakas and Shikhandi come against him, and he kills many of them, including Shikhandi, before attacking the remnants of Virata's army.
He kills the sons, grandsons and followers of Drupada one after another, and the Pandava warriors see the figure of Death-Night they had dreamed of.
Many Pandava archers wake and are cut down, and the rest run about, killing one another in panic, while Ashvatthama is likened to an elephant churning a lake.
The camp is in chaos: men cannot find weapons or recognise one another, animals break their ropes, and the fallen are trampled.
Rakshasas roar with joy as the camp turns into darkness and dust, guards abandon their posts, and men kill comrades they cannot recognise.
Kripa and Kritavarma kill the fugitives at the gate and then set fire to the Pandava camp in three places.
By the light of the fires Ashvatthama cuts down the warriors and leaves the ground strewn with mangled bodies.
The dying call for their kin, and some lament that Arjuna would never kill the sleeping or unarmed, so they blame Rakshasas, and many lie down in despair.
The noise of the dying fades, and before half the night is over Ashvatthama has sent the Pandava host to Yama's abode.
Rakshasas and Pishachas gather, gorging on flesh, drinking blood and dancing in delight.
Other flesh-eating creatures come in huge numbers to feast on the corpses and drink the fat that flows in streams.
At dawn Ashvatthama leaves the camp soaked in blood, his hand fused to his sword, and his grief for his father is said to have eased.
Ashvatthama meets Kripa and Kritavarma, tells them of his feat, and they report killing many Panchalas and Srinjayas at the gates.
Dhritarashtra asks why Ashvatthama, who had fought for Duryodhana, did not achieve this before, and why he did it only after Duryodhana's death.

Sanjaya says fear of the Pandavas and their protectors had held Ashvatthama back, and the feat succeeded only because the men were asleep. The three celebrate the slaughter and set out to tell the king.
Sanjaya describes how the three find Duryodhana still breathing, with broken thighs, bleeding, and surrounded by wolves and hyenas, and they weep over him.
Kripa laments that the mighty king lies on the ground beside his golden mace, and says that Time brings such reversals.
Ashvatthama laments the fall of Duryodhana, blames Bhima for an unfair blow, and blames Yudhishthira for allowing the king's head to be trampled.

Kripa praises Duryodhana's skill with the mace, says a warrior who dies facing the foe reaches heaven, and grieves for Gandhari and Dhritarashtra, while criticising Krishna and Arjuna for standing by.
The three lament that they cannot follow Duryodhana to heaven, and ask how they can live without the king who once protected and enriched them.
Ashvatthama asks the dying king to greet the fallen warriors who have gone before him, and to tell his teacher that Dhrishtadyumna has been slain.
Ashvatthama tells Duryodhana that only seven warriors survive on the Pandava side and only three on his, and reports the slaughter of the Pandava sons and Panchalas.
Duryodhana, revived by the news, says Ashvatthama has done what even Bhishma and Karna could not, and feels as great as Indra, and expects to meet them all in heaven.
Duryodhana falls silent and dies, and the three embrace his body; Sanjaya says he left at dawn and reports that both armies have been destroyed.
Vaishampayana says Dhritarashtra, on hearing of his son's death, sighs deeply and is plunged in anxiety.
Vaishampayana says that after the night, the charioteer of Dhrishtadyumna reports the night slaughter to Yudhishthira.
The charioteer says the sons of Draupadi and the children of Drupada were killed in their sleep, and that Kritavarma, Kripa and Ashvatthama destroyed the army; he is the only survivor.
Yudhishthira falls senseless, is held by Satyaki and his brothers, and laments that his victory has turned into defeat and prosperity into misery.
He mourns the warriors who had survived Karna and crossed the great ocean of battle, but were lost through heedlessness.
He says heedlessness is the surest cause of death, and compares the earlier fire of Bhishma's onslaught to the way the Pandava army has now been consumed.
He says heedless men gain neither knowledge nor fame, and blames the Pandavas' heedlessness for letting the enemy survivors kill so many princes.
He grieves for Draupadi, who will be overwhelmed when she learns that her brothers, sons and father have been killed.
He sends Nakula to bring Draupadi, then goes to the battlefield, sees his sons and friends mangled and dead, and collapses in grief.
Vaishampayana says Yudhishthira is overwhelmed by the slaughter of his sons, grandsons, brothers and allies, and his friends try to comfort him.
Nakula arrives with Draupadi, who has learned of the killing of her sons at Upaplavya, and she falls down in grief before Yudhishthira.
Bhima lifts her up and holds her, and Draupadi speaks bitterly, then vows to fast to death unless Drona's son is punished.
Yudhishthira tells her that her sons died nobly, and asks how she can be sure that Ashvatthama has fallen, since he has gone into a forest.
Draupadi says she has heard Ashvatthama wears a jewel on his head, and she will live only if she sees it brought to her and places it on Yudhishthira's head.
Draupadi asks Bhima to avenge her, recalling his past rescues at Varanavata, from Hidimba, and at Virata's city, and urges him to slay Drona's son.
Bhima takes up his bow, Nakula drives his chariot, and he sets out from the Pandava camp in pursuit of Ashvatthama's chariot.

Vaishampayana says Krishna urges Yudhishthira to help Bhima, who is grieving and alone, and warns that Ashvatthama holds the brahmashira, a weapon Drona taught him only with reluctance and an order never to use it against humans.
Krishna recalls that Ashvatthama came to him on the sea coast at Dvaraka and offered the brahmashira in exchange for the discus.
Krishna says he offered Ashvatthama his bow, dart, discus and mace instead, and told him to take whichever he could wield.
Ashvatthama tries to lift the discus with his left hand and then his right, fails to move it, and gives up exhausted.
Krishna rebukes him, saying that Arjuna, his closest friend, would never have asked such a thing, and that it is an unworthy request for a Brahmana.
Krishna says his son Pradyumna, born after long austerities, never asked for the discus either.
Krishna says Rama, Gada, Samba and the other Vrishni and Andhaka warriors never asked for it, and asks Ashvatthama whom he would fight with it.
Ashvatthama says he meant to fight Krishna with the discus, and that now that he has failed, he is leaving.
Ashvatthama leaves Dvaraka with horses, wealth and gems, and Krishna warns that he is wrathful and knows the brahmashira, so Bhima must be guarded.
Vaishampayana describes Krishna mounting his chariot, with its horses, standard and Garuda emblem.
Arjuna and Yudhishthira ride with Krishna, and the swift horses carry them off in pursuit.
They catch up with Bhima, who ignores them and charges on, and at the bank of the Ganga they see Vyasa and sages, and Ashvatthama in grass garments. Bhima calls out for him to wait.

Ashvatthama, seeing the Pandavas coming, turns a blade of grass into the brahmashira, says it is for the destruction of the Pandavas, and releases it, and a fire blazes out that threatens all three worlds.
Vaishampayana says Krishna reads Ashvatthama's intent and tells Arjuna to use the counter-weapon that Drona taught him to protect them all.
Arjuna dismounts, bows to the gods and his elders, wishes well to all, and releases his weapon to neutralise Ashvatthama's.
The two weapons blaze, thunder and meteors fall, and the earth trembles, until Narada and Vyasa come and stand between the two weapons to pacify the heroes.
The two sages ask why the heroes have used such weapons on men, since the fallen warriors, skilled as they were, never did so.
Arjuna sees the two sages blazing like fire, folds his hands, and asks them to find a way to save the Pandavas and the three worlds, since his weapon would otherwise destroy them.
Arjuna withdraws his weapon. The narrator explains that only a celibate, truthful and obedient warrior like Arjuna could do so.
Ashvatthama tells the sage that he released the weapon out of fear of Bhima, that he cannot withdraw it, and that it will destroy the Pandavas.
Vyasa says Arjuna used his weapon only to counter it, asks Ashvatthama to recall his weapon and give up his gem, and promises the Pandavas will spare his life in return.
Ashvatthama says the gem is precious and he is loath to part with it, but he offers it, and says he cannot recall the weapon, so he will send it against the Pandava women's wombs.
Vyasa tells Ashvatthama to do this, but to pursue no other purpose.
Ashvatthama throws the weapon into the wombs of the Pandava women.
Vaishampayana says that Krishna, seeing the weapon thrown, predicts that a child named Parikshit will be born to Virata's daughter, and Ashvatthama replies that Krishna's words will not come true.
Krishna answers that the child will die but be revived, calls Ashvatthama a coward and a killer of children, and curses him to wander alone for three thousand years.
Krishna says Parikshit will grow up, learn the Vedas and weapons, and rule the Kuru kingdom, and that he will revive the child himself.
Vyasa says that since Ashvatthama acted cruelly against the Pandavas, Krishna's words will come true in his case.
Ashvatthama accepts the sentence, saying he will live among men with the sage's words.
Ashvatthama says he accepts Krishna's and Vyasa's words, which he asks to come true.
Ashvatthama hands the gem to the Pandavas and leaves reluctantly for the forest, and the Pandavas take the gem to Draupadi, who is fasting, with Krishna, Vyasa and Narada.
The Pandavas return to camp, find Draupadi in grief, and sit around her.
Bhima gives her the gem and says her sons' slayer has been beaten, then reminds her of her bitter words to Krishna during the peace mission.
Bhima boasts that Duryodhana and Duhshasana have been slain, the debt is paid, and Ashvatthama has been stripped of his gem and weapons.

Draupadi says she only wanted repayment for the injury, respects Ashvatthama as a teacher's son, and asks Yudhishthira to wear the gem. He places it on his head, and she gives up her vow. Yudhishthira then asks Krishna a question.
Vaishampayana says Yudhishthira, grieving, asks Krishna how Ashvatthama could kill his sons, Drupada's children and Dhrishtadyumna single-handed.
The answer is that Ashvatthama had sought the aid of Mahadeva, who can grant great strength, and that Shiva is the beginning, middle and end of all creatures.
Brahma asks Rudra to create beings, and Rudra goes into the water to practise austerities, so Brahma creates another being to do the work.
The new beings turn on Brahma, wanting to devour him, so he assigns plants and weaker creatures as their food, and they multiply.
Rudra returns, sees the creatures multiplying without him, and in anger withdraws his generative organ into the earth, then goes to the Menjavat mountains to practise harsher austerities.
After the Krita age, the gods prepare a sacrifice and decide among themselves who will receive the offerings.
They leave out Rudra, who takes a bow made from parts of the sacrifice and sets out to destroy it.
Rudra arrives as a brahmacari with the bow, terrifying the earth, the wind and the gods, and wounds the sacrifice, which flees as a deer while he pursues it.
Rudra breaks the arms of Savitri, plucks the eyes of Bhaga and the teeth of Pushan, and paralyses the gods. Their plea for mercy makes the string of his bow break.

Rudra restores the limbs and the sacrifice, and the gods give him shares of the offerings. The answer concludes that Ashvatthama's deeds were done through Shiva's grace, and that Yudhishthira should now act.
Closing line: the Sauptika Parva ends.
Title line: The Mahabharata.
Connecting word: of.
Attribution line: Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Heading: the Jalapradanika parva begins.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati before the story begins.
Janamejaya asks what the old king and the surviving warriors did once they heard the news of the defeat.
Vaishampayana says Dhritarashtra was stricken after losing his hundred sons, and Sanjaya told him that grief serves no purpose and that the funeral rites must now be performed.
Dhritarashtra, bereft of his sons and advisers, falls to the ground like a felled tree.
Dhritarashtra mourns his losses, says he now wishes to die, and admits he ignored the advice he was given, including Krishna's proposal for peace.
Sanjaya tries to comfort him, blaming Duryodhana's pride and the king's own favouritism, and urges him to be steady; Vidura then speaks again to the king.
Vaishampayana introduces Vidura's comforting words to Dhritarashtra.
Vidura urges the king to stand up, says death takes everyone, argues that the fallen warriors have gone to a good end, and says that a life of actions bears its own fruit.
Dhritarashtra says Vidura's words have dispelled his grief and asks how the wise free themselves from mental suffering.

Vidura says that the wise overcome both grief and joy, that worldly concerns are fleeting, and that the body is like a house which is eventually destroyed, while the self endures and creatures reap the fruits of their actions.
Dhritarashtra asks how the wilderness of this world can be known and asks Vidura to explain it.

Vidura describes the stages of a creature's life from conception and birth, the calamities and diseases it meets, the greed and pride that blind it, and the death that comes unnoticed, ending with the advice to practise virtue and hold to truth.
Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to explain in detail the kind of understanding that lets one safely cross the wilderness of duties.

Vidura begins the parable of a Brahmana who wanders into a forest full of beasts, is hemmed in by a frightful woman and snakes, falls into a hidden pit, hangs from creepers, and is threatened by an elephant, rats, and bees while he sips honey and still clings to life.
Dhritarashtra expresses pity for the man in the parable and asks how he can be freed and where he lives.

Vidura says the parable is a figure for life: the forest is the world, the pit is the body, the beasts are diseases, the snake below is Time, the elephant is the year, the rats and snakes are days and nights, and the bees and honey are desires and their pleasures, and that knowing this lets one break free.
Dhritarashtra praises Vidura's parable and asks him to say more.

Vidura describes life as a long road and the world as a forest of diseases and dangers, uses the chariot image to explain how the senses and the mind pull a person into rebirth, and urges self-restraint, harmlessness and compassion as the way to reach the highest state.
Dhritarashtra faints after Vidura's words, is revived by his friends and attendants, and in his grief says he will end his life, until Vyasa begins to speak to him.

Vyasa tells Dhritarashtra that the king knows all things are impermanent, that the war was a fated consequence of Duryodhana's hostility, that Vidura tried hard for peace, and then recounts how Earth asked the gods for relief and Vishnu said Duryodhana would bring about the slaughter, and that the Pandavas were blameless and the king should live for their sake.
Dhritarashtra says he is overwhelmed but will not give up his life, and Vyasa vanishes.
Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra, Yudhishthira, and Kripa and the others did after Vyasa departed, and asks what Sanjaya said next.
Vaishampayana says that after Duryodhana and the army were slain, Sanjaya returned to Dhritarashtra, having lost his divine sight.
Sanjaya tells the king that the kings and his sons have all gone to death and that the funeral rites must now be performed.
Hearing this, the king falls to the ground, and Vidura tries to lift him up, repeating that death is the common end, grief cannot bring back the dead, and the fallen heroes have gone to heaven.

Dhritarashtra orders the royal ladies, Gandhari and Kunti among them, to be brought to him, and they gather and weep together while Vidura leads them out of the city toward the battlefield, with the citizens following and mourning loudly.

On the road, the three surviving warriors tell the blind king of Duryodhana's death, confess their night massacre of the Pandava camp, ask leave to flee, and then part from each other, with Ashvatthama heading for Vyasa's hermitage, and the text notes that the Pandavas later meet Ashvatthama and defeat him.

Yudhishthira and the Pandavas, with Krishna, Draupadi and others, set out to meet Dhritarashtra and find the grieving women of the Kuru household, who accuse Yudhishthira of cruelty; Dhritarashtra embraces him without much warmth, then seeks Bhima, and Krishna's iron figure of Bhima is crushed by the blind king, who is left bleeding; Krishna then explains that Bhima was not hurt and urges the king to accept the peace.
After the king is washed, Krishna reminds him of his learning and of the warnings given before the war, blames him for letting Duryodhana rule him, and urges him to restrain his anger toward Bhima.
Dhritarashtra agrees that Krishna is right, admits parental love led him astray, says he is now free of wrath, and embraces Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, weeping and blessing them.

The Pandavas visit Gandhari, who wishes to curse Yudhishthira, so Vyasa arrives and tells her to forgive, reminding her that she always said victory lies with righteousness, and Gandhari replies that she wishes no harm to the Pandavas, blames her own sons and Karna, and objects to Bhima striking Duryodhana below the navel.

Frightened, Bhima defends his foul acts as done out of fear and self-defence, citing Duryodhana's treachery, the insult to Draupadi and the years of exile; Gandhari rebukes him for drinking Duhshasana's blood, and Bhima replies that he only smeared his hands and was bound by his vow.
Gandhari laments that Bhima did not spare even one of her sons, leaving the blind couple without any support in their old age, though she would have grieved less had he kept to righteousness.

Gandhari asks where Yudhishthira is, and he presents himself to her curse; she says nothing, and her glance through the cloth over her eyes injures his toe. She then comforts the Pandavas, and Kunti embraces her sons and weeps with Draupadi.

Draupadi laments the loss of her children, and Kunti comforts her before they go to Gandhari together, and Gandhari answers that the destruction was caused by Time and was inevitable, so no one should grieve for it.
Closing line: the Jalapradanika parva of the Stri parva ends here.
Heading: the Stri-vilapa parva begins.

Gandhari sees the slaughter from afar with her spiritual eye, the king, the Pandavas, Krishna and the Kuru women go to the field, the women collapse at the sight of the bodies and the scavengers, Gandhari describes the carnage to Krishna, and her eyes fall on Duryodhana.

Gandhari faints when she sees Duryodhana lying dead, then revives, embraces him and mourns, recalling her words before the battle and her grief for the blind king, while describing the fallen prince, the mourning of his wife, and his reversal of fortune, before concluding that he has attained the heroes' regions.

Gandhari grieves for her hundred sons slain by Bhima, for the young widows wandering among the dead, and for the shame of the royal women, then recalls Duhshasana's insult to Draupadi, her own warnings to Duryodhana to cast off Shakuni and make peace, and Bhima's drinking of Duhshasana's blood.

Gandhari names her sons Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha one by one, describing each slain body, the wounds, the birds and beasts gathered there, and the grieving wives and women around them.

Gandhari praises Abhimanyu's courage and describes Uttara, the daughter of Virata, weeping over her dead husband, speaking to him and blaming the warriors who killed him, before the Matsya women drag Uttara away from the body of her father Virata and Gandhari names other fallen youths.

Gandhari mourns Karna, once a fierce fire, now slain by Arjuna and lying on the ground, with his women weeping, Yudhishthira's long sleeplessness, and the wives blaming the curse and the arrow that ended him, while the body is being torn by scavengers.

Gandhari mourns the lord of Avanti, Bahlika and Jayadratha as they lie among scavengers, describes Jayadratha's wives guarding his body, recalls how he was spared earlier out of regard for Duhshala, and grieves that her daughter is now a widow searching for her husband's head.

Gandhari mourns Shalya, Bhagadatta, Bhishma on his arrow bed, and Drona, describing their bodies, their great deeds and the grief of their women, then tells how Drona's disciples light his pyre while Kripi grieves, and how they go on toward the Ganga.

Gandhari describes Somadatta grieving over his son, and Bhurishrava's widows lying on the ground with his severed arm in their laps, and blaming Arjuna for the arm and Satyaki for killing Bhurishrava while he sat in a vow.

The widows speak over the arm, recalling the strength of the hand that once held many women and fought many foes, and they reproach Arjuna for striking it off, until the chief lady falls silent and the co-wives weep with her.

Gandhari mourns Shakuni, slain by Sahadeva and now being fanned by birds, recalls his deceit at dice that won Yudhishthira's kingdom, and fears that his trickery might divide her sons in the next world.

Gandhari mourns the Kamboja ruler and his queen, the Kalinga and Magadha rulers, Brihadbala of Kosala, the sons of Dhrishtadyumna, the Kekaya brothers, Drupada, Dhrishtaketu and his son, Lakshmana, and Vinda and Anuvinda, and she says Krishna and the Pandavas have escaped many great warriors while her sons did not, then complains that Krishna did nothing to stop the war.
Gandhari swoons with grief and anger and places all the blame for the war on Krishna.

Gandhari accuses Krishna of standing aside from the slaughter despite his power to stop it, and curses him to kill his own kin, to die in the wilderness thirty-six years later, and to see his women mourn as the Kuru women do.
Krishna calmly replies that only he can destroy the Vrishnis, that the curse helps him do this, and that the Yadavas will be killed by one another, and the Pandavas are left stunned and despairing.

The holy one tells Gandhari to stop grieving, says that Duryodhana's arrogance and cruelty caused the carnage, that grief only doubles itself, and he contrasts the purposes for which women of different classes bear children with the fate of a princess's sons, who are born to be slain.
Gandhari stays silent, and Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira how many fell and how many survived.
Yudhishthira gives the tally of the fallen and of the survivors.
Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira what destinations the warriors have reached.

Yudhishthira says warriors who fell bravely go to Indra's realm, those who died without courage go to the Gandharvas, those who fled or begged for mercy go to the Guhyakas, those who fell fighting unarmed go to Brahman, and the rest go to the Uttara Kurus.
Dhritarashtra asks by what knowledge Yudhishthira sees these things as if he were an ascetic with perfect insight.
Yudhishthira says that during his forest wanderings on pilgrimage he received spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa.
Dhritarashtra asks who will perform the last rites for the friendless dead and for those whose bodies lie unburied and torn by birds.

Yudhishthira orders Sudharma, Dhaumya, Sanjaya, Vidura, Yuyutsu and others to ensure the dead are cremated; they build pyres, burn the kings in order, including Duryodhana and his brothers and many other heroes, burn the friendless dead together, and then Yudhishthira leads Dhritarashtra to the Ganga.

At the Ganga, the Kuru women cast off their ornaments and offer water to their dead; Kunti reveals that Karna was her son by Surya and the Pandavas' eldest brother, and Yudhishthira laments the concealment and the grief it brought, makes the water offering for Karna, and rises from the river.
Closing line: the Stri Parva ends.
Colophon: the title of the Mahabharata.
Colophon: the word of.
Colophon: the author, Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Heading: the Rajadharmanusasana Parva section begins.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati.
Vaisampayana describes the month of mourning on the Ganga's banks, the sages who visit Yudhishthira, and Narada's praise of the victory with his question about whether the king is still grieving.
Yudhishthira replies that the victory feels like a defeat because of the kinsmen killed, then reveals that Karna was Kunti's hidden son and asks Narada to tell his story.
Vaisampayana says Narada, having been asked, begins to tell how Karna came to be cursed.
Karna, envious of Arjuna, is refused the Brahma weapon by Drona, learns it from Rama under a false Brahmin claim, and is cursed after accidentally killing a sacred cow.
Narada tells how Karna endures a worm's bite so as not to wake Rama, and how Rama, learning he is a Suta, curses the Brahma weapon to fail him against an equal.
Narada says Duryodhana carries off the maiden from the bride-choosing at Rajapura, and Karna drives back the kings who give chase.
Narada describes Karna's fight with Jarasandha, his rise to rule Champa, and the curses and schemes behind his death, then urges Yudhishthira not to grieve.
Narada falls silent and Yudhishthira grieves; Kunti says she and Surya failed to win Karna over, and Yudhishthira blames her and curses women to keep no secrets.
Yudhishthira grieves for Karna and the slain kinsmen, blames the war on Duryodhana, and announces he will renounce the kingdom and go to the woods.
Arjuna rebukes Yudhishthira's plan to renounce, argues that wealth is essential to virtue and that kings must hold and rule, and urges him to perform a great sacrifice.
Yudhishthira tells Arjuna he will live as a forest ascetic, begging for food, avoiding all injury, and detached from worldly life, which he sees as an illusion bound by death.
Bhimasena says Yudhishthira's understanding has gone astray, that renunciation is improper for a Kshatriya, and that one must act to gain success.
Arjuna begins an old story: Indra, as a golden bird, rebukes young Brahmin ascetics who left home for the forest and says they are not true eaters of sacrificial remnants.
The ascetics ask the bird what is good for them, saying his words inspire faith.
The bird says he will speak true and useful words if they do not turn against their better selves.
The ascetics agree to listen and ask him to instruct them.
The bird teaches that cows, gold, mantras and Brahmins are the highest of their kinds, that Vedic rites lead to success, and that the householder's life is the field of success.
Arjuna concludes that the ascetics gave up renunciation for household life, and urges Yudhishthira to rule the wide earth with that wisdom.
Vaisampayana says Nakula, having heard Arjuna, speaks to Yudhishthira with reasoned argument, aiming to change his brother's mind.
Nakula says the gods depend on action, the Pitris sustain life through action, and the learned who follow the Vedas reach the highest heaven.

Nakula argues that householder life is superior, that true renunciation means inner detachment, and that a false renouncer stays bound by desire; he warns that a king who fails to protect and give is an embodiment of Kali, and tells Yudhishthira not to grieve.

Sahadeva says giving up outward things is not enough without inner detachment, that the soul's eternity bears on the question of killing, and that a king must enjoy his earth; he then asks pardon for his words.
Vaisampayana says Draupadi, seated among the brothers, turns to Yudhishthira, who has stayed silent after his brothers' speeches.

Draupadi reproaches Yudhishthira for his retreat, reminds him of his vow to slay Duryodhana, argues that a king must use force, lists the continents he has conquered, and urges him to rule and perform sacrifices and gifts.
Vaisampayana says Arjuna speaks again after Draupadi's words, showing proper respect for his eldest brother.

Arjuna argues that the rod of chastisement is the basis of righteousness, that creatures live by devouring one another, that the gods are slayers too, and that Yudhishthira should take up the rod, rule and sacrifice.
Bhima says Yudhishthira's mind is clouded by grief, compares mental and bodily illness, recalls past humiliations, calls the present struggle one with his own mind, and urges a horse-sacrifice.
Yudhishthira answers that desire cannot be filled, urges Bhima to conquer his appetite, praises renunciation, quotes Janaka's verse, and concludes that understanding is supreme.
Arjuna tells the tale of King Janaka, who gave up his kingdom to beg, and of his queen's sharp rebuke that a giver of food is more honoured than a beggar.
Arjuna concludes that householders who practise charity, truth and worship can reach the regions of bliss.

Yudhishthira says Arjuna knows war but not the scriptures, ranks renunciation and knowledge of Brahma above wealth, describes the northern and southern paths, and concludes that Brahma is reached by asceticism and renunciation.
Vaisampayana says that after Yudhishthira stops, the eloquent ascetic Devasthana speaks to the king.
Devasthana argues that a king should perform great sacrifices rather than renounce, that wealth is made for sacrifice, and that Indra, Mahadeva, Marutta and Harischandra won glory through it.

Devasthana quotes Vrihaspati's teaching to Indra: contentment is the highest bliss, non-injury is the best religion, and a righteous king who passes on his crown and retires to the forest wins good fruit.

Arjuna argues that death in battle is a Kshatriya's proper end, that Yudhishthira should act and perform sacrifices as Indra did, and that the dead have gone to the highest end and fate cannot be resisted.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira remains silent after Arjuna's speech, and Vyasa, the island-born sage, speaks.
Vyasa says Arjuna is right: householder life is the highest duty, a king must support others, and wielding the rod of punishment is the chief Kshatriya duty.
Yudhishthira asks how King Sudyumna gained his highest success.
Vyasa tells how Likhita, eating fruit from his brother Sankha's hermitage without asking, goes to King Sudyumna and asks for punishment.
Vyasa continues: Sudyumna cuts off Likhita's hands, Sankha says the punishment has purified him, and Likhita's hands return through his penances.
Vyasa concludes that Sudyumna gained eminence by ruling, that punishing wrongdoers is the king's duty, and that shaving the head is not.

Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to enjoy his kingdom and sacrifice, lays out a king's duty to protect subjects and punish robbers, and tells how Hayagriva, slain in battle after righteous rule, now enjoys heaven.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira, seeing Arjuna angry, bows to Vyasa and prepares to answer.
Yudhishthira says the kingdom gives him no joy, and that the cries of widows and mothers keep him from peace.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa, skilled in yoga and the Vedas, now speaks to Yudhishthira.
Vyasa says Time governs all events, no one truly slays or is slain, grief grows when indulged, happiness and sorrow alternate, and a king's sacrifice is battle while his yoga is good government.

Yudhishthira argues to Arjuna that the poor can reach heaven, that sages gain bliss through study and contentment, that wealth brings injury and sin, and that it must go to sacrifice and worthy recipients.
Yudhishthira laments the fallen heroes, confesses his guilt over Bhishma, Drona and Karna, and resolves to fast to death.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa restrains Yudhishthira and tells him this cannot be.
Vyasa says all this is destiny, that union ends in dissolution, and that work and skill, not idleness, bring success, so Yudhishthira must act.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa eases the grief of Yudhishthira, who had resolved to end his own life.
Vyasa introduces the old story of Asma's discourse, in which King Janaka of Videha seeks counsel in his sorrow.
Janaka asks how a man should behave when kinsmen and wealth are gained or lost.

Asma replies that joy and grief come by destiny, that death is unavoidable, and that kin are like travellers at an inn, so one should study, sacrifice and rule righteously; Vyasa then urges Yudhishthira to cast off grief and enjoy the earth.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira remains silent, and Arjuna turns to Krishna.
Arjuna asks Madhava to comfort Yudhishthira, since the family has again fallen into great danger.
Vaisampayana says Krishna turns to Yudhishthira, takes his hand, and begins to speak.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira the fallen heroes are beyond recall and have won heaven, then recounts Narada's counsel to Srinjaya, listing ancient kings who died despite their great sacrifices and gifts.
Srinjaya says Narada's discourse has freed him from grief and asks Narada to restore his son through his grace.
Narada begins by promising to give Srinjaya back his son.
Narada names the son as Suvarnashthivin, given by Parvata and now dead.
Narada says the boy, golden in splendour, will live a thousand years.
Yudhishthira asks how Srinjaya's son came to be called Suvarnashthivin, why Parvata gave him, and why he died so young.
Krishna tells how the sages Narada and Parvata, guests of Srinjaya, quarrelled over Narada's love for the king's daughter, cursed each other, and later freed each other from the curses.
Vasudeva says Narada was himself involved and is present, and will tell Yudhishthira everything.
Yudhishthira asks Narada to tell of the child said to have produced gold waste, and Narada begins his account.

Narada tells how Srinjaya received a boon of a son, how Indra sent a tiger to kill him, how Narada restored him, and how the prince later ruled, closing with advice that Yudhishthira rise and perform great sacrifices.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa speaks again to Yudhishthira, who remains speechless and grieving.
Vyasa says a king must protect subjects and punish transgressors, and that the Kauravas were transgressors who were rightly slain.
Yudhishthira says he does not doubt Vyasa's teaching but still feels burning guilt for having caused so many deaths for the kingdom.
Vyasa asks whether man or the Supreme Being is the doer, argues by the axe example that the cutter is responsible, says acts bear fruit, and urges expiation while alive rather than self-destruction.
Yudhishthira laments that he alone caused the deaths of kin and kings, pictures the suffering of the widows and his own fall to hell, and asks what life he should take up.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa reflects for a while and then addresses Yudhishthira.

Vyasa says Time, not the Pandavas, took the lives of the fallen, that slaying to save a family or kingdom is no transgression, that the Horse-sacrifice expiates the guilt, and that Yudhishthira should comfort his brothers, seat the fallen men's kin on their thrones, and rule.
Yudhishthira asks what acts make a man liable to expiation and what acts free him from sin.
Vyasa lists lapses that need expiation, including killing a Brahmin and selling Vedic knowledge, then names acts done in self-defence, for a preceptor, or to save life that carry no sin.

Vyasa lists penances such as twelve years of mendicancy, gifts of cattle and wealth, fasts and the Horse-sacrifice, says all sins but the gravest can be expiated, and urges Yudhishthira to act rightly rather than give up his life.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira reflects briefly and then replies to the sage.
Heading: Section XXXVII begins.
Yudhishthira asks what food is clean, what gifts are praiseworthy, and who deserves them.
Vyasa recounts Manu's teaching to the Rishis on what food to eat, which foods and sources are forbidden to Brahmins, and that gifts to unlearned or unworthy persons are wasted or harmful.
Yudhishthira asks to hear the duties of kings and of all four orders, and how he can reconcile virtue with kingly duty.
Vaisampayana says Vyasa directs Yudhishthira to Bhishma, the old Kuru grandsire, and lists Bhishma's learning and teachers, and Yudhishthira replies to Vyasa.
Yudhishthira objects that he cannot approach Bhishma after having had him slain by deceit.
Vaisampayana says Krishna, moved to benefit all the four orders, addresses the king.
Krishna urges Yudhishthira to stop his grief, obey Vyasa, and heed the Brahmins, his brothers and the people.
Yudhishthira, persuaded by Krishna, Vyasa and others, sets out, and the procession enters the city in splendour, with the citizens cheering and the streets decked out.
The city welcomes the Pandavas and Draupadi with praise, Yudhishthira worships and gives gifts to Brahmins, and then the disguised Rakshasa Charvaka, a friend of Duryodhana, steps forward.
Charvaka tells Yudhishthira that the Brahmins call him a wicked slayer of kin and urges him to give up his life.
Yudhishthira begs the Brahmins not to scorn him and says he will soon give up his life.
The Brahmins say they said no such thing, and by their spiritual sight they expose the speaker as the Rakshasa Charvaka, friend of Duryodhana.
The enraged Brahmins utter a sacred sound that kills Charvaka, and they leave after blessing Yudhishthira.
Krishna tells Yudhishthira to honour Brahmins, explains that Charvaka's boon was undone by offending them, and urges him not to grieve and to rule well.

Yudhishthira takes his golden seat with his family and elders around him, the priests perform the coronation rites, Krishna and Dhritarashtra pour sanctified water over him, and Brahmins bless him in return for gifts.
Yudhishthira declares Dhritarashtra his father and god, asks his subjects to serve him, dismisses the citizens, and assigns offices to Bhima, Vidura, Sanjaya, Nakula, Arjuna, Dhaumya and Sahadeva.
Yudhishthira and Dhritarashtra perform funeral rites and charity for the fallen, the king founds food-halls and tanks in their names, and cares for widows, the blind and the destitute.
Yudhishthira thanks Krishna for regaining the kingdom and hymns him by many names and forms, and Krishna is pleased and begins to speak kindly to him.
Yudhishthira sends the people home and asks his brothers to rest, then gives each brother a former Kaurava palace, while Krishna and Satyaki take Arjuna's palace, and all feast and sleep.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what Yudhishthira did after regaining his kingdom and what Krishna did after that.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira gives gifts to Brahmins, servants and guests, honours his elders, and then approaches Krishna, who is seated in deep meditation and does not answer him.
Yudhishthira marvels at Krishna's stillness and asks its cause.
Krishna says Bhishma, on his bed of arrows, is thinking of him, recalls Bhishma's deeds and learning, and urges Yudhishthira to question him before he dies; Yudhishthira agrees.
Satyaki has Krishna's chariot yoked, and Daruka reports that it is ready.
Janamejaya asks how the Kuru grandsire, lying on his bed of arrows, gave up his body and what yoga he followed.
Vaisampayana says that at the sun's northward turn Bhishma drew his soul inward, surrounded by many sages including Vyasa and Narada, and then hymned Vasudeva with joined palms.
Bhishma hymns Krishna at great length, calling him the Supreme Being, the creator and dissolver of the universe, worshipped under countless forms and names.
Krishna grants Bhishma heavenly knowledge and departs; the sages praise both, and Krishna and the Pandavas ride away in their chariots, greeted by the people.

Vaisampayana says Krishna, Yudhishthira and the others ride to the battlefield, which is strewn with bones, and Krishna points out Rama's five lakes where Rama offered Kshatriya blood to his ancestors.
Yudhishthira doubts that Rama thrice exterminated the Kshatriyas and asks how the order could be destroyed and then regrow.
Vaisampayana says Krishna then gives Yudhishthira the full account of how the earth came to be filled with Kshatriyas again.
Krishna begins to tell how Rama, son of Jamadagni, destroyed the Kshatriyas, and traces the royal line through Kusika and Gadhi to the swap of sacred food meant for Satyavati and her mother.
Richika tells Satyavati that the swap has caused a fierce son to be conceived, and that her son will be a Brahmin.
Satyavati replies that Richika could create other worlds, and asks him to give her a righteous and peaceful son.
Richika says he has never lied, that the outcome was fixed by destiny, and that all of Satyavati's descendants will have Brahmanic virtues.
Satyavati asks that her grandson be such a man, but that she have a son of tranquil pursuits.
Richika says there is no real difference between a son and a grandson, and agrees to her wish.

Krishna recounts that Satyavati bore Jamadagni, whose son Rama took an axe from Mahadeva; the sons of Arjuna killed Jamadagni, Rama then slaughtered the Kshatriyas many times over, and Kasyapa took the earth.
The Earth speaks to Kasyapa, naming Kshatriyas hidden among women, bears, herders and others, and asks him to restore them as protectors.
Krishna says Kasyapa installed those hidden Kshatriyas as kings, and that the present Kshatriya families descend from them.
Vaisampayana says Krishna continues on his chariot after speaking with Yudhishthira, shining like the sun.
Yudhishthira marvels at Rama's feats, and Krishna and Yudhishthira go to Bhishma on the Oghavati banks, where sages sit around him.
Krishna asks Bhishma whether his mind is still clear, notes his mastery over death, praises his learning in every branch of duty, and asks him to comfort Yudhishthira.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma raises his head a little and speaks with joined hands.
Bhishma hymns Krishna as the origin and dissolution of all the worlds, and asks for what is good for him.
Krishna says he showed his form because of Bhishma's devotion, tells him fifty-six days of life remain before he departs at the sun's northward turn, and urges him to instruct Yudhishthira.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma replies to Krishna's words.
Bhishma, weakened by pain, says he cannot speak in Krishna's presence and asks Krishna to instruct Yudhishthira.
Krishna grants Bhishma a boon that pain, confusion and hunger will not overcome him, that his memory and understanding will stay clear, and that he will have celestial sight.
The sages worship Krishna, heavenly flowers fall, and at sunset the sages and the Pandavas take their leave for the city.
Krishna wakes before dawn, performs his rites and gifts, and sends Satyaki to ask Yudhishthira whether he is ready to go to Bhishma.
Yudhishthira asks for his chariot, says no soldiers should come, and notes that Bhishma will soon speak of great mysteries and should not be crowded.
Vaisampayana says the Pandavas join Krishna, and with Satyaki they drive to Bhishma, greet the sages, and approach the bed of arrows.
Janamejaya asks what was discussed when Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows with the Pandavas around him.
Vaisampayana says Narada and others gather, Narada urges the Pandavas to ask Bhishma before he dies, and Yudhishthira asks Krishna to speak first.
Krishna asks Bhishma whether he passed the night well and whether his pain and confusion have eased.
Bhishma says his pain has left him, that through Krishna's grace he knows past, present and future and the branches of duty, and asks why Krishna does not teach Yudhishthira himself.
Krishna says he will enhance Bhishma's fame, that Bhishma's words will carry the weight of the Vedas, and urges him to teach Yudhishthira as a father teaches his sons.
Bhishma agrees to discourse, says his speech and mind are steady, and asks Yudhishthira to question him, praising the king's virtues.
Krishna says Yudhishthira is too ashamed to approach Bhishma, having caused a great slaughter of those he should have honoured.
Bhishma says a Kshatriya's duty is to fight, even to slay kin and teachers in an unjust battle, and that a righteous battle brings heaven and fame.
Yudhishthira bows at Bhishma's feet, is welcomed with affection, and Bhishma tells him to ask without fear.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira, after bowing to Krishna and taking leave of the elders, begins his questions to Bhishma.
Yudhishthira calls kingly duties the highest science and the reins of the world, and asks Bhishma to speak on them first.
Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to honour gods and Brahmins, to act with prompt exertion, to keep to truth, and to be neither too mild nor too fierce.

Bhishma says Brahmins should be banished rather than physically punished, that a king should treat subjects as a mother her child, and that servants who grow too familiar with the king will disrespect him.

Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that a king must be ready for action, gives examples of severe discipline, advises secrecy and trusted servants, and describes the best king as one whose subjects live without fear.
Bhishma says protecting subjects is the essence of kingly duty, lists its means from spies and fair taxes to honest officers and fortifications, and says exertion is the root of kingly duty.
Vyasa and the others praise Bhishma, Yudhishthira promises to ask more the next day, and the company bathes, makes evening offerings and returns to the city.
Vaisampayana says the Pandavas and Yadavas ride out the next morning to Bhishma, greet the sages, and Yudhishthira worships Bhishma and asks his question.
Yudhishthira asks why one man should rule the whole world, what the word king means, and why the whole world bows to one man.

Bhishma recounts how disorder spread in the first age until the gods sought Brahma, who composed the treatise on punishment, which was abridged by later sages and passed to Vena, whose tyranny ended with the birth of the first true king, Prithu, who levelled the earth and was honoured by the gods.
Bhishma says the treatise covered every subject, that since then the learned have held a king no different from a god, and asks which subject Yudhishthira wants to hear next.
Yudhishthira asks the general and special duties of each order, which modes of life suit each, the duties of kings, the means by which kingdoms grow, and what a king should avoid.
Bhishma lists nine common duties, then the duties of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras, and concludes that sacrifice and devotion belong to every order, with the Brahmin foremost.

Bhishma names the four modes of life, Brahmacharya, Garhasthya, Vanaprastha and Bhaikshya, and sets out the duties of each, from study and service to a teacher through household duty to the mendicant's detachment.
Yudhishthira asks for duties suited to men like the Pandavas, which are auspicious, beneficial and approved by all.
Bhishma says the four modes of life are for Brahmins, that a Brahmin who adopts the callings of other orders is disgraced, and that men act under the influence of Time and their propensities.
Bhishma lists callings improper for a Brahmin, says a Brahmin who falls from duty becomes like a Sudra, and says gifts to such men bring no merit.
Bhishma describes the duties of the other orders and the modes of life open to Kshatriyas and Vaisyas, and concludes that the Kshatriya's duties underlie all the others.
Bhishma says all duties, including those of the four modes of life, fall under kingly duty, and tells how Mandhatri performed a sacrifice to see Narayana and Narayana appeared to him as Indra.
Indra asks Mandhatri what he seeks by seeing Narayana, and offers to grant him any other boon.
Mandhatri asks to see the first of gods and to learn how to perform the duties of a Kshatriya.
Indra explains that kingly duties came first from the Supreme, contain all other duties, and revived the eternal duties after Vishnu destroyed the Asuras, so Kshatriya duty is foremost.

Indra says Kshatriya duties are foremost, that kings must reclaim land, perform great sacrifices, avoid begging and protect subjects, and that Brahmins who neglect their duties should be treated like Sudras.
Mandhatri asks what duties the foreign and robber tribes should observe, and which duties kings should enforce on them.
Indra says robber tribes should honour parents, teachers and kings, follow the Vedas, dig wells, give water and gifts, and perform the sacrificial offerings.
Mandhatri says wicked men live disguised among all four orders and modes of life.
Indra warns that when kingly duty fails, false sects will multiply and men will go astray, and that he honours the king who watches over men's duties.
Bhishma says Narayana departed, and tells Yudhishthira to keep to the path the ancient kings followed.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the four modes of human life in detail.
Bhishma says that a just king earns the merit of each mode of life through his conduct, and that protecting the righteous is worth more than the asceticism of forest hermits.
Bhishma closes by telling Yudhishthira that if he keeps to the king's duty of protection, he will gain the merit of all four modes of life and all four orders.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what the principal duties of a kingdom are, after hearing about the four modes and orders.
Bhishma says that crowning a king is the first duty, because a kingdom without rule grows weak, is overrun by robbers, and its people devour one another.
Manu, asked to rule, declines because he fears the sins that come with governing a deceitful people.
The people promise Manu a share of their livestock, metals and grain, and a portion of the merit from his protection, and he accepts and sets out to restore order.
Bhishma advises that people should first choose a king, that he should be honoured and well provided for, and that he should speak and act with courtesy.
A heading marks the start of the next section, LXVIII.
Yudhishthira asks why the Brahmanas say the king is a god.
Bhishma introduces an old story of the sage Vrihaspati teaching King Vasumanas of Kosala, who approaches him with proper humility.
Vasumanas asks what makes creatures grow or perish, and by what worship they can gain lasting happiness.

Vrihaspati says all duties rest on the king: without his protection the strong would prey on the weak and religion, marriage, learning and trade would collapse, and he names the five forms the king takes and urges loyalty to him, after which Vasumanas begins to protect his subjects.
Yudhishthira asks what further duties a king has, how he should defend his kingdom and beat his enemies, how to use spies, and how to win the confidence of all his people.

Bhishma says a king must first conquer himself, then gives long advice on spies, peace and war, taxes, justice, fortifications and the seven limbs of a state, and closes with two verses of Vrihaspati.
Yudhishthira asks what benefit the science of chastisement, the king and the subjects each derive from the others.

Bhishma says the science of chastisement keeps each order to its duty, and that the king decides the age: full reliance on it brings the Krita age, while neglect brings the decline into Treta, Dwapara and Kali.
Yudhishthira asks whether a king who follows such conduct can easily gain lasting happiness here and hereafter.

Bhishma lists thirty-six virtues a king should practise, among them restraint, kindness, fair taxation, care in punishment and humility towards seniors, and says a king who keeps them gains great merit.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira, eager to learn, honoured his grandsire and began to rule by this teaching.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should protect his subjects so as to avoid grief and stay within righteousness.

Bhishma briefly lists the king's duties: honour learned Brahmanas, avoid lust and anger, collect a fair sixth of the produce as tax, and treat protecting subjects as the highest duty, whose reward only a king can earn.
Bhishma says a king should appoint as his priest someone who protects the good and punishes the wicked, and introduces the tale of Pururavas and the wind god Matariswan.
Pururavas asks where the Brahmana and the other three orders came from, and why the Brahmana is foremost.

Matariswan explains that the four orders sprang from Brahman's mouth, arms, thighs and feet, with the Brahmana to study the Vedas, the Kshatriya to rule, the Vaisya to farm and trade, and the Sudra to serve.
Pururavas asks whether the earth belongs to the Brahmana or to the Kshatriya.

The wind god says everything belongs to the Brahmana by birth, though in times of distress a king may give conquered land to a worthy one, and that the priest shares the king's merit, that sacrifice depends on a king, and that a king is like Indra, Yama and Dharma.
Bhishma urges a king to appoint a learned priest, says king and priest should be friends for the subjects' happiness, and introduces the talk of Aila and Kasyapa.
Aila asks which of the Brahmana and the Kshatriya is superior when they part ways, and on whom the other orders depend.
Kasyapa says that when the two quarrel the kingdom falls into disorder, with robbers, failed crops and lost learning.
Aila asks where Rudra comes from and what form he takes.
Kasyapa says Rudra dwells in human hearts and destroys the bodies he inhabits and others too, like a violent wind.
Aila observes that wind and rain do not visibly destroy men, but that men are ruined through lust and malice.
Kasyapa compares Rudra's stupefying force to a fire that spreads from one house across a village, striking honest and wicked alike.
Aila asks why men would act well if punishment falls on everyone regardless.
Kasyapa answers that the sinless are caught up when mixed with the sinful, as dry wood burns with wet, so they should keep apart.
Aila points out that the earth, sun, wind and water treat the honest and the wicked alike.
Kasyapa says the world treats the two groups alike but the next world does not, and that a king should install a learned priest and honour Brahmanas.

Bhishma says a kingdom's safety rests on the king and the king's on his priest, and recounts how Muchukunda conquered the earth, then fought Vaisravana's Rakshasas, which Vasishtha halted through penance.
Vaisravana rebukes Muchukunda for relying on Brahmana power, and Muchukunda replies that Brahmanas and Kshatriyas share one origin and each has its own power to protect the people.
Muchukunda declines sovereignty given as a gift and insists on ruling by his own arms, which surprises Vaisravana, and Bhishma concludes that a king who yields precedence to Brahmanas wins fame.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which conduct helps a king raise his subjects and win regions of felicity in the next world.
Bhishma says the king should be generous, sacrificial, devoted to protecting his people, honour the righteous, be deadly to foes, and takes a fourth share of the merit and sin of his subjects.
Yudhishthira says he values sovereignty only for the merit it brings, and resolves to leave the throne for a life of asceticism in the forest.
Bhishma says Yudhishthira's gentleness and compassion will not suffice for a king, and urges him to follow his father and grandfather and not shrink from duty.
Yudhishthira asks what acts lead to heaven, and what felicity and prosperity follow from them.
Bhishma says the man who gives relief from fear for even a moment is most worthy of heaven, and urges Yudhishthira to rule cheerfully, protect the good and punish the wicked.
Yudhishthira asks how Brahmanas who keep to their duties differ from those who do not.

Bhishma says learned, even-minded Brahmanas match Brahma and the gods, the unworthy are like Sudras, some callings rank as outcasts while others match Kshatriyas or Vaisyas, and the king may tax or discipline the unworthy and banish a learned thief who ignores support.
Yudhishthira asks whose wealth the king may claim and what conduct he should adopt.
Bhishma says the king may take wealth from all but worthy Brahmanas, should not spare unworthy ones, should keep Brahmanas provided for, and introduces the Kaikeya king seized by a Rakshasa.
The Kaikeya king answers the Rakshasa by listing how his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards, how each order keeps its duties, and how the helpless and ascetics are cared for.
The Rakshasa lets the king go, saying that a king who protects cows and Brahmanas has nothing to fear and wins heaven.
Bhishma advises kings to protect Brahmanas, who will bless them in return, and to discipline unworthy Brahmanas and separate them from the rest.
Yudhishthira asks whether a Brahmana in distress may follow the duties of a Vaisya.
Bhishma says a Brahmana who cannot manage Kshatriya duties may farm or keep cattle to make his living.
Yudhishthira asks which goods a Brahmana may sell without losing his hope of heaven.

Bhishma lists goods a Brahmana must never sell, such as wine, salt, honey, meat and cooked food, says that selling animals or Soma brings specific sins, and holds that fair exchange by agreement is lawful while force is sinful.
Yudhishthira asks how a king can remain the protector and refuge of his people if all the orders take up arms against him.
Bhishma says that when the king is weakened, all the orders should seek their good through gifts, penance and peace, and that Brahmanas should help strengthen him.
Yudhishthira asks who will protect the Brahmanas and the Vedas if the Kshatriyas turn hostile to them, and what the Brahmanas should do then.
Bhishma says Kshatriya power is defeated when it is turned against Brahmanas, that those who fight for them win heaven, and that a Brahmana may take up arms in three cases.
Yudhishthira asks whether a strong man of any order may suppress robbers and protect the people when the Kshatriyas have failed.
Bhishma says anyone who shields the helpless, of whatever order, deserves respect and rule, and that a king who cannot protect is as useless as a barren cow.
Yudhishthira asks what conduct and character suit the priests who perform his sacrifices.
Bhishma lists the qualities of a fit priest, including Vedic learning, loyalty, equal regard for all, honesty, freedom from usury, modesty, self-control and harmlessness.
Yudhishthira asks why the dakshina gift is not fixed by ordinance and whether devotion can help a sacrificer who is stained by falsehood.
Bhishma says dakshina is a required part of sacrifice, that a sacrifice must rest on good character, and that true penance lies in harmlessness, truth and compassion rather than bodily hardship.
Yudhishthira asks how a king's minister should behave and whom the king should trust or avoid.

Bhishma sorts friends into four kinds plus a righteous fifth, warns that trust must be balanced with watchfulness, advises one capable, honest person per task, and urges outward trust but inner caution toward kinsmen.
Yudhishthira asks how a man can win the hearts of both friends and foes when his kinsmen have turned against him.
Bhishma introduces a talk between Vasudeva and Narada, in which Vasudeva says his kinsmen wound him with cruel words and that he cannot side with either Ahuka or Akrura.
Narada says Vasudeva's trouble is internal and of his own making, since he gave away wealth that cannot be taken back, and warns that trying to recover it would bring bloodshed.
Vasudeva asks what weapon, not made of steel, could soften the hearts and tongues of his kinsmen.
Narada answers that generous feeding, forgiveness, sincerity, gentleness and honour are such a weapon, and urges Vasudeva to lead his people so that the Bhojas and Vrishnis are not ruined.

Bhishma gives a second means: protect the one who reports embezzlement by ministers, and tells how the sage Kalakavrikshiya, touring the kingdom with a crow in a cage, named the thieving officers of King Kshemadarsin and then came to the king after they killed his crow.
The sage warns the king of the perils of royal service, says the officials are plotting against him and the people, and says he will leave the kingdom because of their hostility.
King Kshemadarsin asks the sage to stay, promising him honour, and asks him to see that the rod of chastisement is used properly.

The sage advises the king to weaken the guilty men one by one, reminds him that he was once his father's friend, and the king then makes a Kshatriya minister and the sage his priest, after which he conquers the whole earth.
Yudhishthira asks what qualities a king's legislators, war ministers, courtiers, generals and counsellors should have.

Bhishma says the king should appoint men of good birth, loyalty, learning and self-control, avoid the greedy and unreliable, never confide in one who is not devoted to him, hold secret consultations in a quiet place, and keep at least three ministers.
Bhishma says he will cite an old conversation between Vrihaspati and Sakra.
Sakra asks Vrihaspati which single act wins the regard of all creatures and brings great fame.

Vrihaspati answers that agreeable speech does this: smiling, sweet words win love, frowns and silence breed hatred, gifts without kind words please no one, and a king who must punish should still speak sweetly.
