Bhishma says Sakra followed this advice and urges Yudhishthira to practise the same virtue.
Yudhishthira asks by what method a king ruling his subjects can gain great blessedness and eternal fame.
Bhishma says a king of cleansed soul who protects his subjects earns merit and fame here and hereafter by conducting himself righteously.
Yudhishthira observes that the virtues described so far are rarely found together in any one person, and asks how the king should deal with people.

Bhishma agrees such perfection is rare, names the mix of Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, Sudras and a Suta who should serve as ministers, and gives rules for fair judgement, graded punishment, the protection of envoys, and the advice that a king should trust no one fully, not even his son.
Yudhishthira asks what sort of city a king should dwell in, and whether he should use an existing one or have one built.
Bhishma names six kinds of citadels and describes the ideal well-defended, well-stocked and righteous city, along with the stores, craftsmen, spies and ascetics the king should keep close.
Yudhishthira asks how a kingdom can be consolidated and how it should be protected.
Bhishma describes a layered administration with headmen over ten, twenty, a hundred and a thousand villages, moderate taxes that leave the people able to work, and kindness toward the Vaisyas.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave if, though wealthy, he still desires more.

Bhishma advises taking revenue gently and gradually like a bee or a leech, restraining drinking, gambling and other vices, keeping beggars off the streets, and honouring the wealthy as partners in the people's welfare.
Bhishma closes by urging the king to love all creatures, practise truth and sincerity, and use his power to strengthen his treasury, friends and kingdom.
Bhishma forbids felling fruit-bearing trees, says a Brahmana in want should be supported rather than lost, and advises the king to keep spies and to examine his own conduct and reputation.
Yudhishthira asks how one man among equals in strength and skill rises above the rest and comes to rule them.

Bhishma says the strong prey on the weak in nature and among men, so the king must watch both subjects and foes, spare traders and farmers from heavy taxes, and remember that gifts sustain all beings.
Bhishma introduces the sage Utathya's teaching to King Mandhatri, son of Yuvanaswa.

Utathya says a king is made by righteousness and must uphold it, that neglecting it brings ruin, that Brahmanas must be honoured, and that pride and vice must be avoided, while the lack of restraint brings drought, floods, disorder and collapse of worship and property.

Utathya teaches that the king's conduct decides the state of the world and the four ages, compares a righteous king to a washerman who cleans the orders, and lists the king's duties of protecting the weak, punishing wrongdoers, honouring priests and avoiding pride.
Bhishma says Mandhatri followed this counsel, became lord of the whole earth, and urges Yudhishthira to act the same way.
Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king should behave, and wants Bhishma's answer.
Bhishma tells how King Vasumanas, a man of knowledge and purity, asks the sage Vamadeva to teach him the conduct that keeps a king within his duties.

Vamadeva says righteousness is the surest guide, that kings who follow it conquer the earth, while force, wicked ministers and caprice lead to ruin, and he recommends generosity, honour to the worthy and seeking the counsel of teachers.

Vamadeva continues that the king's conduct is copied by others, so he should be honest and kind, choose capable and loyal officers, watch rival kings through agents, attack only weaker neighbours, share state duties with trusted ministers, and never trust those who harbour ill will.
Vamadeva says a king should win without battle where possible, first secure his own power, and keep contented soldiers, a loyal people and a temper under control.
Bhishma says King Vasumana followed these counsels, and that Yudhishthira would also conquer both worlds by doing the same.
Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya should act in victory when he seeks to subdue another Kshatriya in battle.
Bhishma says the invader should call on the people to accept him and pay tribute, and that fighting is needed only if they resist.
Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya king should conduct himself in battle against another king.

Bhishma sets rules of fair combat: match mail with mail and army with army, answer deceit with deceit, do not strike the fallen, wounded or unarmed, avoid poisoned arrows, and keep to righteousness, since a sinful victory brings ruin.

Bhishma says a king should never conquer by unrighteous means, and lays out how to treat the vanquished: spare the disarmed, keep a defeated king in the palace for a year, return captured women, give cattle to Brahmanas, and win conquered subjects over with kindness and gifts.
Yudhishthira says Kshatriya practice seems very sinful, and asks by what acts a king wins regions of felicity.

Bhishma says kings are cleansed by punishing the wicked, supporting the good, and offering sacrifices and gifts, and that heroes who defend others and die in battle win heaven, while cowards and those who die at home without honour do not.
Yudhishthira asks what regions are won by heroes who die in battle without turning back.
Bhishma tells how King Amvarisha, son of Nabhaga, sees in heaven his former general Sudeva rising higher than himself.
Amvarisha recounts his own virtues, sacrifices and victories, and asks Indra why Sudeva has risen above him.
Indra answers that Sudeva often spread out the great sacrifice of battle, and that any warrior who advances in battle array takes part in it.
Amvarisha asks what the libations, offerings, fees and priests of that battle-sacrifice are.

Indra describes the battle as a sacrifice in full detail, with elephants as priests, weapons as ladles, blood as the final libation, and says brave heroes who die fighting win the highest regions while cowards sink to hell.
Bhishma says Amvarisha approved of Indra's words and understood how warriors win heaven through battle.

Bhishma tells how King Janaka of Mithila, before his battle with Pratardana, showed his warriors the heaven of brave men and the hell of deserters, then set out the battle order, advised against over-pursuit, and praised heroism.
Yudhishthira asks how kings seeking victory should lead their troops into battle even if this means slightly offending against righteousness.

Bhishma says a king may use crooked policy only to counter enemies, then covers preparations: stocking arms, choosing the season and safe roads, camp sites, troop positions, sparing the helpless, rewarding brave men, and battle formations.
A heading marks the start of Section CI.
Yudhishthira asks what temperament, appearance, dress and arms make combatants fit for battle.

Bhishma says troops should fight with the weapons they know, notes the styles of different peoples, lists the bodily and temperamental marks of brave fighters, and says the fiercest outlying tribes make the best vanguard, though they turn wrathful if treated mildly.
Yudhishthira asks what well-known signs predict the success of an army.

Bhishma lists omens of success such as cheerful troops, favourable winds, auspicious animals and birds and bright sacrificial fires, advises trying conciliation, division and gifts before fighting, and urges a mix of mildness and severity toward the defeated, with sorrow for the slain and honour for one's own brave men.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should treat a mild foe, a fierce foe and a foe with many allies and a large force.
Bhishma introduces an old discourse between Vrihaspati and Indra, in which Indra approaches the sage with joined palms.
Indra asks how he can subdue his foes through policy without exterminating them, and how to keep his newly won prosperity.

Vrihaspati advises concealing one's feelings, speaking sweetly to foes while planning, waiting for the right moment, corrupting the enemy's forces by division, gifts and poison, and never sleeping at ease after victory.
Indra asks how he can recognise a wicked person.
Vrihaspati says a wicked person speaks ill of others behind their backs, envies their success, avoids praising them, breaks promises when unobserved, eats apart and sorrows at others' joys.
Bhishma says Indra acted on these instructions and reduced all his enemies to subjection.
Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, treasury, army and wealth can seek happiness.
Bhishma tells of Kshemadarsin, who fell into great distress and approached the sage Kalakavrikshiya.
Kshemadarsin asks the sage what a ruined man can do, short of suicide, theft or begging, and asks for guidance toward happiness.

The sage says all things are impermanent and grief is pointless, and asks why the king should be unhappy with his lot, while the king replies that Time swept his kingdom away and he now lives on charity.
The sage advises him to stop craving, enjoy what he has, avoid envying others, and perhaps retire to the forest and live simply.
The sage says that if the king still has spirit he can recover his kingdom, and offers to set out a policy for doing so.
Kshemadarsin says he is willing to hear and act on the counsel, hoping the meeting will bear fruit.

The sage advises him to humble himself before his foes, serve Janaka of Mithila until he is trusted, then weaken his enemies through division, luxury, drained treasuries and misdirected sacrifices, even by poison and fraud.
Kshemadarsin says he will not live by deceit or win wealth by unrighteous means, and that the sage's advice does not suit him.
The sage praises his righteous disposition, promises a lasting union with Janaka, and says a loyal, learned minister of noble birth is a rare prize.

The sage presents Kshemadarsin to Janaka as a man of pure heart and royal birth, Janaka welcomes him as an equal, and the two kings make peace, with Janaka giving his daughter and jewels, reasoning that peace is the king's high duty.
Yudhishthira recaps the earlier topics and asks how a king should treat the many brave men around him, keeping them loyal and undivided.

Bhishma says enmity between king and nobility arises from greed in the king and wrath in the nobles, that united nobles prosper while disunion and oppression drive them to the enemy, and that the king should consult their leaders and settle quarrels early.
Yudhishthira asks which duties are most important for earning merit and fame here and hereafter.

Bhishma says honouring mother, father and preceptor is the chief duty, that they should be obeyed and served humbly, that the preceptor is worthy of the greatest reverence, and that injuring or neglecting them is a grave sin.
Yudhishthira asks how a person who holds to virtue should decide between truth and falsehood, and what eternal virtue is.

Bhishma says truth is generally right but must be withheld when it serves evil, that a falsehood may save life or others' wealth, that righteousness is what upholds creatures and prevents their injury, and that the deceitful should be met with deceit and the honest with honesty.
Yudhishthira asks how creatures, who are constantly afflicted in many ways, can overcome their difficulties.

Bhishma lists those who overcome difficulties, such as the upright, the truthful, the generous, the hospitable and the harmless, and says Krishna is Narayana, whose refuge protects those who seek it, and that reciting these verses also helps.
Yudhishthira asks how to tell people who are truly tranquil from those who only look tranquil.

Bhishma tells of King Paurika of Purika, cruel in life, who is reborn as a jackal, refuses meat, lives on fallen fruit, and speaks gently of virtue, so that a tiger takes him for a learned and righteous sage.
The tiger offers the jackal the post of minister and warns him of his own fierce nature.
The jackal accepts on conditions: he wants to be left free to live as he likes, to advise the tiger in private, and to be spared punishment for others' faults.

Envious old servants hide the tiger's meat in the jackal's den to frame him, the tiger's mother pleads for him, and a loyal agent exposes the plot, but the jackal, hurt by the insult, leaves the court and warns that such treatment breeds enemies and mistrust.
The jackal retires to the forest, rejects the tiger's entreaties, fasts to death and goes to heaven as a reward for his good deeds.
Yudhishthira asks what a king should do to become happy, and asks for a full answer.
Bhishma warns a king against the example of a camel of the Krita age who, after great austerities, won a boon from Brahman for a very long neck.

The camel grew idle, and when a storm drove him into a cave, a jackal and his wife ate his stretched neck and killed him, which Bhishma uses to urge intelligence, careful action and wise counsel over idleness.
Yudhishthira asks how a king without the usual aids should behave toward a powerful foe after winning a precious kingdom.
Bhishma introduces an old discourse between the Ocean, lord of rivers, and the rivers themselves.
The Ocean asks why the rivers sweep away great trees but never the canes on their banks.
Ganga explains that rigid trees resist the current and are uprooted, while the cane bends, knows the value of time and yielding, and rises again after the flood.
Bhishma says a man who resists a stronger foe able to destroy him will be ruined, and that a wise man who has weighed his strength against his foe's should act like the cane.
Yudhishthira asks how a learned, modest man should behave when an ignorant, conceited person heaps harsh insults on him in an assembly.

Bhishma advises patience: an abuser's merit passes to the patient man, the boasts and slanders of fools are empty, back-biters should be avoided, and one who endures such reproaches feels no pain from speech.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should keep his people content, which servants to choose, and how a king who keeps wicked companions loses the loyalty of good servants.

Bhishma says a king cannot rule alone, and that wise, loyal, honest and well-born ministers, supervisors of revenue and granaries, and fair judges bring a king prosperity, while the subjects should be won over by kindness.
Bhishma introduces the tale of a sage living in a forest, whose animals treat him as a master, and of a devoted dog who is threatened by a leopard and asks the sage for protection.
The sage transforms the dog into a golden leopard, then, when a hungry tiger approaches, into a tiger, and the transformed animal lives among the beasts as their king.
The transformed tiger is threatened by an elephant, which the sage changes it into, then by a lion, then by a Sarabha, and the creature finally grows ungrateful and plans to kill the sage.
The sage recounts how he transformed the dog from leopard to tiger, elephant, lion and Sarabha, reproves its ingratitude, and returns it to dog form.

Bhishma says the dog, returned to its own form, is driven from the hermitage, and urges kings to examine servants for truth, learning, birth and self-control, to choose ministers of noble birth with many virtues, to cultivate kingly virtues and a loyal army, and to win every man's love so that he may conquer the earth.

Bhishma says a king should give each servant the office he is fit for, choose honest, learned and well-born ministers, guard the treasury and granaries, care for kinsmen and the city, and asks what further Yudhishthira wishes to hear.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to speak of the duties of kingship in a way that can be easily remembered.

Bhishma says protecting all creatures is the highest duty, and that a king should act like a peacock, varying his conduct to suit his aims, keeping counsel secret, watching for danger, taxing gently like a bee, appointing honest officers, avoiding waste and flattery, and protecting his people.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain what Chastisement is, what form and origin it has, and how it stays watchful over the world.

Bhishma explains that Chastisement upholds righteousness and is called Vyavahara, describes its fearsome form, many names and power over all things, traces its roots in the Vedas, and ends with the rule that no one is exempt from the king's justice, not even parents, brothers, wives or priests.
Bhishma introduces King Vasuhoma of the Angas, a penitent king of great piety, and his visit from the king Mandhatri, whom he receives with hospitality.
Mandhatri asks Vasuhoma where Chastisement came from, what was awake before it, what its end is, and how it came to depend on the Kshatriya.

Vasuhoma explains that Chastisement vanished during Brahman's sacrifice and disorder followed, until Vishnu created it anew, and that the rod was passed from the gods and sages down to Manu and his sons, to be used with discrimination.
Bhishma says whoever listens to Vasuhoma's teaching and acts on it will gain the fulfilment of his wishes.
Yudhishthira asks how Virtue, Wealth and Pleasure relate, what their roots and fruits are, and why they sometimes mingle and sometimes stand apart.

Bhishma explains that Wealth rests on Virtue and Pleasure is its fruit, that all three rest on will and aim at liberation, that their impurities are greed for reward and hoarding, and introduces King Angaristha's question to the sage Kamandaka on how to undo sins.

Kamandaka says a king who pursues only pleasure loses his wisdom and virtue, and prescribes Vedic study, respect for Brahmanas, banishing wicked men, seeking the company of the good, and speaking kindly to all.
Yudhishthira asks how virtuous behaviour is acquired and what its characteristics are.
Bhishma says that Duryodhana, grieved at Yudhishthira's splendour at Indraprastha and mocked for his own errors, asked his father Dhritarashtra the same question.
Dhritarashtra asks Duryodhana why he is pale and emaciated when he has wealth, obedient brothers, fine robes and fine food.
Duryodhana replies that thousands of Brahmanas eat daily from gold plates at Yudhishthira's palace, and that his enemy's splendour burns him.
Dhritarashtra says that good conduct can win any prosperity, and cites Mandhatri, Janamejaya and Nabhaga, who won the earth by virtue.
Duryodhana asks how that conduct, which won the earth so quickly, can be acquired.
Dhritarashtra tells how Prahlada took Indra's sovereignty through his conduct, and how Indra first asked Vrihaspati for the source of happiness.
Vrihaspati sends Indra to Usanas, who sends him to Prahlada, and Indra comes to Prahlada disguised as a Brahmana disciple.
Prahlada says he rules by following the counsel of Brahmanas and Sukra, serving elders, controlling wrath and bearing no malice, and that this is the best good for a man.
The disguised Brahmana asks Prahlada for his conduct as a boon, and Prahlada's Behaviour, Righteousness, Truth, Good deeds, Might and Prosperity leave him one by one.
The goddess Prosperity explains that the Brahmana was Indra, who took Prahlada's sovereignty by taking his conduct, and that all virtues rest on conduct.
Bhishma says the goddess and the others departed, and that Duryodhana then asked his father how conduct is acquired.
Dhritarashtra says conduct is built by abstaining from injury in act, thought and word, by compassion and giving, and that wicked men who prosper do not keep their fortune long.
Dhritarashtra urges Duryodhana to be of good conduct if he wants greater prosperity than Yudhishthira's.
Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that Dhritarashtra spoke these words, and that he should act on them.
Yudhishthira asks what Hope is, where it arises, and laments that Duryodhana's obstinacy destroyed the hope he had cherished of peace.
Bhishma introduces the discourse between Sumitra and Rishabha, and tells how King Sumitra of the Haihayas chases a wounded deer through forests and across rivers, never giving up.
Sumitra arrives at a hermitage weary and hungry, is honoured by the ascetics, and tells them of his family, his hunt, his lost deer and his disappointed hope, asking which is vaster, hope or the sky.

Rishabha recounts how, on pilgrimage, he met the emaciated sage Tanu near the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, and how King Viradyumna, searching for his lost son Bhuridyumna, asked Tanu what is greater than hope.
Tanu says Bhuridyumna insulted a holy sage by refusing him a golden jar and vegetable bark, and the king honours Tanu, after which the sages gather around him and ask why he has come.
Viradyumna explains that he is a king whose only young son, Bhuridyumna, is lost, and that he is searching the forest for him.
Rishabha explains that Tanu, once slighted by the king, had resolved to drive hope from his mind, and so he remains silent.
Viradyumna asks what is the measure of hope's slenderness, and what is most difficult to acquire.
Rishabha says Tanu, recalling the king's past disregard, now speaks to him.
Tanu says nothing is as slender as hope, and that the images hope places before the mind are the hardest of all to win.
The king says he understands, and asks what is more slender than Tanu's own body.

Tanu names hopes more slender than his body, such as hope placed in a giver who never gives, in an ungrateful or cruel man, in a father longing for a lost son, in an old woman hoping for children, and in a maiden hoping for marriage.
The king asks for Tanu's grace, says his words are true, and wishes to be reunited with his child.
Tanu brings the prince to the spot, rebukes the king, reveals himself as the god of righteousness, and tells the king to drive off even the slenderest hope.
Bhishma says that Sumitra then gave up his hope, and urges Yudhishthira to be calm and collected like Himavat.
Yudhishthira says he is never satiated with Bhishma's teaching on morality and asks him to discourse further.
Bhishma tells of the sage Gotama, who lived for sixty thousand years in austerity on the Paripatra hills, and of Yama's visit to him.
Gotama asks how one can free oneself from the debt owed to mother and father, and how to win pure and difficult regions of bliss.
Yama says one should devote oneself to truth, purity and penance, worship one's mother and father without ceasing, and perform horse-sacrifices with generous gifts to Brahmanas.

Yudhishthira asks what a king should do when he has few friends, many enemies, an empty treasury, no troops and treacherous ministers, and whether he should seek wealth by evil means or die without it.

Bhishma says the question is subtle, that a king in extreme distress may take wealth from anyone but ascetics and Brahmanas, that treasury, army and people depend on one another, and that the treasury should be filled by righteous means, not by oppression.
Heading naming the Apaddharmanusasana Parva.
Yudhishthira asks what a weak king should do when his lands are taken, his wealth is gone and his allies cannot be supported.
Bhishma says an honest invader should be met with peace and the lost land restored, while a treacherous one may be bought off with land or even the capital.
Yudhishthira asks what a king should do when his own people turn against him, his treasury is empty and his counsels are leaked.
Bhishma advises peace with a righteous enemy and bold fighting against a wicked one, and says even a small loyal army can win or die honourably.
Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana should support his family when righteous rule has broken down and robbers hold the means of living.

Bhishma says the Brahmana should live by knowledge, and that a king may seize wealth from the wicked for the good without provoking revolt, though he must never oppress Brahmanas, must not believe slander, and should bear his burdens steadily.
Bhishma says a king must keep his treasury full, since a king without wealth loses respect, and he must deal firmly with robbers by bringing them under his rule rather than destroying them.
Bhishma says a Kshatriya should pursue merit and wealth and seek power, since power sustains righteousness, and he lists the penances that cleanse a sinner.
Bhishma introduces Kayavya, a skilled and devout robber who honours Brahmanas and his blind parents, and whom many robbers then wish to make their leader.
The robbers ask Kayavya to lead them and protect them the way a father or mother would.
Kayavya lays down rules: never kill women or non-combatants, spare Brahmanas, keep truth, and tax only those who refuse their dues.
Bhishma says the robbers obeyed Kayavya, prospered by giving up sin, and that hearing his story brings freedom from fear.
Heading: Section CXXXVI begins.

Bhishma quotes verses of Brahman that allow a king to take wealth from those who neglect sacrifice but protect the wealth of sacrificers and temples, and says that moral questions grow finer the more they are discussed.
Bhishma tells how three fish face draining water: the far-sighted one leaves early, the quick-witted one escapes by feigning capture, and the slow one is caught and dies.
Bhishma draws the lesson that procrastinators are destroyed, that foresight and presence of mind bring happiness, and that acting with regard to time and place wins the best results.
Yudhishthira asks how a weak king under attack from many powerful foes can choose friends and enemies and decide when to fight or make peace.
Bhishma replies that friends can turn into foes and back, so a king should sometimes make peace with enemies, and he introduces the tale of a cat and a mouse under a banyan tree.

The mouse Palita lives beneath a banyan where the cat Lomasa hunts birds, and the cat is caught in a hunter's net; seeing a mongoose and an owl waiting for himself, the mouse decides to strike a deal with the cat.
The grateful cat agrees to serve the mouse and accept the alliance, and the mouse says he will cut the net if the cat spares his life.
The mouse cuts the net slowly, then flees when the hunter arrives, and when the cat later asks for friendship the mouse refuses, arguing that all bonds rest on self-interest.
The cat, rebuked, is ashamed and speaks up.
The cat protests his loyalty and asks the mouse to renew their friendship, but the mouse refuses, advises constant mistrust, and slips into another hole.
Bhishma draws the morals: appear fearless while distrusting others, make peace with foes when it suits, and honour Brahmanas, and he urges Yudhishthira to act with the same wisdom.
Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule and fight his foes if he may trust no one.
Bhishma introduces the bird Pujani, who lived at King Brahmadatta's palace and fed her chick and the prince on fruit, until the prince killed her chick and she blinded him in revenge.
Brahmadatta says the injury has been repaid and the account is squared, and he asks Pujani to stay.
Pujani says that a wrongdoer should leave the wronged party, that soothing words should not be trusted, and that enmity passes down to descendants.
Brahmadatta insists that avenging an injury is no offence and again asks her to stay.
Pujani says that friendship cannot be rebuilt once one side has injured the other and the other has struck back.
Brahmadatta argues that injurer and avenger should unite, since mutual hatred has been seen to cool that way.
Pujani replies that enmity never dies, and that insincere conciliation can subdue even the strong.
Brahmadatta says that living together softens hostility, citing the Chandala and the dog, and that animosity fades quickly.
Pujani lists five causes of hostility, says the fire of enmity burns until one party is destroyed, and says she cannot trust him again.
Brahmadatta says Time causes all acts and deaths, so no one is truly to blame, and he asks her to forgive and stay.

Pujani challenges his view by asking why people avenge, why physicians treat the sick and why rites matter if Time rules all, then describes the miseries of life and warns against trusting a wronged foe.
Brahmadatta replies that withholding trust wins no object and that fear makes a man as good as dead.

Pujani argues that exertion matters more than fate, lists the marks of wisdom, and says she will leave a bad king's realm; she then describes a just king who protects his subjects and a tyrant who brings ruin on himself.
Bhishma closes that Pujani has taken her leave and gone away, and asks Yudhishthira what else he would like to hear.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave when righteousness and people decay and robbers overrun the land.
Bhishma says he will teach the policy for hard times, and introduces King Satrunjaya of the Sauviras, who asks the sage Bharadwaja how wealth is gained, increased, guarded and used.

Bharadwaja advises the king to keep the rod of punishment raised, to cut out his enemies' roots, to act humbly only in speech, to make and break alliances as needed, and to match sternness or mildness to the occasion.
Bhishma says the king followed this advice gladly and won prosperity for himself and his kin.
Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana and a king should live when righteousness has collapsed and famine, robbery and lawlessness prevail.
Bhishma says the king's conduct shapes the age, and tells how Viswamitra, starving after a twelve-year drought, wandered until he reached a Chandala hamlet and found a dog's haunch in a hut.
The Chandala challenges the intruder, Viswamitra admits he came to steal the meat out of hunger, and the Chandala warns that the theft and the unclean food are sinful.
The Chandala says the meat would cost the sage his long life and strength, and tells him to seek other food.
Viswamitra replies that no other meat can be had in famine, he has no money, and the dog's haunch seems to him to contain all six tastes.
The Chandala says that only certain five-clawed animals are clean food for the twice-born, and warns the sage away from unclean food.
Viswamitra cites Agastya, who ate the demon Vatapi while hungry, as a precedent for eating the haunch.
The Chandala says the act is wrong, asks him to seek other alms, and grudgingly allows him to take the meat if he insists.
Viswamitra says the good set the standard for duty, and that he now judges the dog's haunch better than any pure food.
The Chandala replies that an unrighteous act cannot become a lasting custom, and urges him not to sin by deceit.
Viswamitra says a Rishi cannot do wrong and that deer and dog are alike as animals, so he will eat the haunch.
The Chandala argues that Agastya acted at the request of Brahmanas, that righteousness is what is free of sin, and that Brahmanas should be kept alive.
Viswamitra says his body is dear to him and must be sustained, and that his hunger makes him fearless of the Chandala and his kin.
The Chandala says men give up their lives rather than eat unclean food, and that conquering hunger brings the highest rewards.
Viswamitra says he has kept strict vows and will eat the meat to protect the root of merit, and that the act is clean for a pure soul even if it is wrong.
The Chandala says he must restrain the sage, since a Brahmana who does wrong falls from his high state.
Viswamitra replies that cows drink no matter what frogs croak, and tells the Chandala not to claim authority over what is right.
The Chandala says he speaks only as a friend and asks the sage to do what is good and avoid temptation.
Viswamitra asks the Chandala, as a friend, to rescue him by giving up the haunch, so that he might be saved by righteousness rather than sin.
The Chandala refuses either to give or to let him take the meat, since both of them would sink to hell if a Brahmana ate it.
Viswamitra says he will sin now to save his sacred life and then cleanse himself, and asks which is better: death without food, or the unclean meal.
The Chandala says each person must judge his own duty, and that anyone who calls dog meat clean would abstain from nothing.
Viswamitra says eating unclean food is sinful in general, but in mortal danger, without killing or deceit, it matters little.
The Chandala says the sage's reasoning disregards the Veda and Arya morality and dissolves the difference between clean and unclean food.
Viswamitra argues that forbidden food does not cause a grave fall, that the warnings against drink are only words, and that no sin destroys one's merit.
The Chandala says that a learned man who takes meat from such a wretch as himself acts against the good and will feel remorse.

Viswamitra takes the haunch, offers it to the gods and ancestors, eats it, and later wins great ascetic success; Bhishma concludes that a wise person may save his life in distress and then regain his merit.
Yudhishthira says that if such cruelty can count as duty, nothing is forbidden and robbers would deserve respect, so he is bewildered and cannot follow the advice.
Bhishma replies that true duty comes from wisdom drawn from many sources, not from one-sided scripture, and that a king must be severe when needed and mild otherwise.
Yudhishthira asks whether any rule of kingship must never be broken.
Bhishma says Brahmanas must always be honoured, since they bring blessing when pleased and harm when angered.
Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from sheltering a suppliant who seeks protection.
Bhishma says the merit is great, and cites King Sivi and a pigeon who fed a foe seeking refuge with its own flesh.
Yudhishthira asks how the pigeon did this and what it gained.
Bhishma says he will tell the story that Rama, son of Bhrigu, once told King Muchukunda, which cleanses the hearer of sin.
Rama describes a cruel fowler who kills birds for their meat and has been cast off by everyone, and who is caught in a violent storm while hunting in the forest; at night he rests under a great tree.
The pigeon waits in the tree for his wife, grieves that she has not returned, and praises a faithful wife as the true center of a home.
Bhishma says the she-pigeon, captured by the fowler, hears her husband's lament and begins to reflect.
She reflects that a husband is a wife's highest deity, and urges her husband to rescue the suffering fowler by offering him hospitality, even telling him to remarry if she dies.
The pigeon welcomes the fowler, lights a fire to warm him, has no food to offer, and throws himself into the flames as a meal for his guest, while the fowler is overcome with remorse.
The fowler reproaches himself, vows to abandon hunting and live by severe penance, throws away his weapons and cages, and frees the captive she-pigeon.
The she-pigeon laments her husband, throws herself into the fire, finds him in heaven on a celestial car, and ascends with him.

The fowler, inspired by the pigeon couple, gives up food and runs into a forest fire, is cleansed by it and ascends to heaven, and Bhishma closes by praising the protection of suppliants and the cleansing power of the tale.
Yudhishthira asks how a person who sins out of ignorance can be cleansed.
Bhishma tells how Janamejaya, shunned by his priests and subjects after killing a Brahmana, wandered in penance until the sage Indrota, son of Sunaka, harshly rebuked him.
Janamejaya, burning with remorse, begs Saunaka to instruct and protect him and promises to honour Brahmanas again.
Saunaka says a fool's offences are no wonder, that a wise man pities rather than rages, and that the king should take refuge with Brahmanas.
Janamejaya says he repents his sins and will never again try to extinguish virtue.
Saunaka asks the king to lay down his pride, serve all creatures, and pledge not to injure Brahmanas, warning that his own kin and friends may mock him for speaking out.
Janamejaya swears, touching Saunaka's feet, that he will never again injure Brahmanas in thought, word or deed.

Saunaka teaches that a wise king combines sternness with kindness, lists purifying acts and sacred bathing places, gives graded remedies for repeated sin, and recounts how the gods asked Vrihaspati how sin is cleansed.
Vrihaspati replies that righteous acts done with understanding wash away sin as a dirty cloth is cleaned, and that one should not boast of wrongdoing.
The sage helps Janamejaya perform the horse-sacrifice, and the cleansed king returns to his kingdom shining like fire.
Yudhishthira asks whether Bhishma has ever known anyone restored to life after death.
Bhishma tells how a Brahmana's only son dies, his kin carry the body to the cremation ground, a vulture urges them to go home, and a jackal then urges them to stay.
The vulture scolds the kin for listening to a jackal and urges them to leave the body and attend to their own conduct.
The jackal laments the kin's coldness, says they should show grief, and urges them to wait until the sun sets.
The vulture replies that no dead creature has ever come back to life, that every life span is fixed, and that grief grows at the sight of the body.
The jackal says they should not abandon the child, cites precedents of revival, and the kin return and weep over the body in their laps.
The vulture says the child cannot be revived except by a god's boon, and that all mortals travel the same road and should live righteously.
The jackal laments the miseries of the world and insists the child could still live, so the kin should not go away.
Bhishma explains that the jackal's soothing falsehoods kept the kin at the cremation ground.
The vulture warns that the place is dangerous at night and that the funeral rites must be finished before dark.
The jackal says the wilderness is safe while the sun still shines, and that the kin should wait in hope.

Bhishma tells how the vulture and jackal keep arguing until Sankara, moved by the kin's prayer, restores the child to life for a hundred years and satisfies both animals' hunger, and the family returns home in joy.
Yudhishthira asks how a weak, boastful man who has provoked a powerful foe should act when that foe attacks him in anger.
Bhishma introduces the tale of the Salmali tree on the Himalaya, which shelters many creatures, and tells how Narada praises it and asks whether the wind god Pavana is its friend.
Narada remarks that the wind must be a friend of the Salmali tree, since no tree or mountain can resist the wind.
The Salmali boasts that the wind is neither its friend nor its master, that its own might far exceeds the wind's, and that it has repeatedly beaten him.
Narada rebukes the tree for arrogance and folly, says the wind is the mightiest of beings, and promises to report the insults to the wind-god.
Bhishma says Narada reported the Salmali's words to the wind-god.
Narada tells the wind that the tree scorned him with many abusive words, and praises the wind as the mightiest of beings.
Bhishma says the wind-god, enraged, goes to the Salmali.
The wind-god warns the Salmali that he will show his power, and says the tree stands only because the Grandsire once rested beneath it.

The Salmali laughs, says that strength of understanding matters more than brute force, and the wind promises a test the next day; the tree then decides to rely on its wit and prepare against the wind.
The Salmali cuts off its branches and leaves, and the wind comes towards it in rage, but is delighted to find the tree stripped bare.
The wind tells the tree that he would have done the same to it in anger, and that its own evil counsel has delivered it into his power.

Ashamed and remembering Narada's warning, the Salmali repents, and Bhishma draws the moral that a foolish person should not provoke the powerful, and that the wise overcome them by patience, citing Arjuna's victory over Duryodhana's armies.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the source and foundation of sin.

Bhishma says covetousness is the root of sin and of a long list of vices, can never be satisfied, and is overcome only by people who are free of greed, who are content, fearless and devoted to the good of others.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain covetousness and then ignorance in detail.
Bhishma says the ignorant man sins, earns infamy and sinks into hell, and that ignorance is the source of misery.
Yudhishthira asks for a full account of the origin, growth and effects of ignorance.
Bhishma says the faults he names are all ignorance, that ignorance and covetousness grow and fade together, and that kings such as Janaka gained heaven by restraining greed.
Yudhishthira asks which duties, among the many, bring the highest merit, both here and hereafter.

Bhishma says self-restraint is the highest duty, lists its marks such as forgiveness, truthfulness and mildness, describes the freedom and bliss of the restrained life, and notes that its only drawback is being mistaken for weakness.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira is delighted by the teaching and asks Bhishma to continue.
Bhishma teaches that penance underlies all creation, knowledge and success, that it cleanses even grave wrongs, and that abstaining from food is its highest form.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain truth, its signs, how it is gained and what it brings.
Bhishma calls truth the eternal duty and foundation of righteousness, lists its thirteen forms with a short account of each, and says truth outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices in the balance.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the origin and cure of wrath, lust, envy, pride, malice and related vices.
Bhishma calls these thirteen vices fierce foes, traces each to its source and remedy, such as compassion, knowledge and tranquillity, and says Yudhishthira has already conquered them.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the acts of malevolent people, whom he says he has not known well.

Bhishma describes the malevolent man as boastful, deceitful, covetous and slanderous, and says that the generous man who feeds Brahmanas and kin first is the opposite and should be sought out, while the malevolent should be avoided.
Bhishma sets out rules for giving to Brahmanas, the king's duty to support them, and the expiations prescribed for each sin, from drinking liquor to killing a Brahmana.
A heading marks the start of Section CLXXIV.
Vaisampayana says Nakula, skilled with the sword, questions Bhishma as he lies on his bed of arrows.
Nakula asks whether the bow or the sword is the foremost weapon in battle, and who first created the sword and taught its use.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma, master of the bow, answers Nakula in fine words.

Bhishma recounts the creation of the world, the wicked Danavas, and how Rudra, using the sword Asi created by Brahman, destroyed them, before the sword passed through a line of kings down to Kripa and the Pandavas, while Prithu first made the bow.
After Bhishma falls silent, Yudhishthira asks his brothers and Vidura which of Virtue, Wealth and Desire is greatest and which the mind should serve.
Vidura says Virtue is supreme, Wealth middling and Desire lowest, and that one should live self-restrained and treat all creatures as oneself.
Vaisampayana says Arjuna speaks next, urged on by the drift of the king's question.
Arjuna argues that action brings Wealth, that Virtue and Desire cannot be won without it, and that even ascetics and believers seek it.
Vaisampayana says the twin sons of Madri, Nakula and Sahadeva, speak next.
Nakula and Sahadeva say that Wealth should be sought by vigorous means, that Virtue should come first, then Wealth, and then Desire.
Vaisampayana says the twins fall silent and Bhimasena begins to speak.
Bhima argues that Desire is the foremost of the three, since Virtue and Wealth both spring from it, and that the best man attends to all three.
Yudhishthira, after reflecting, judges their speeches mistaken, says that liberation is the highest good, and says that all things follow the Ordainer's will.
The brothers bow and praise Yudhishthira, who then turns again to the son of the foremost of rivers to ask about duties.
Yudhishthira asks what kinds of men make gentle and worthy friends, and who can help in good times and bad.
Bhishma lists the kinds of men to avoid as friends, including the covetous, the cruel and the deceitful, and then the kinds to befriend, such as the well-born, the grateful and the steady.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to say who are the injurers of friends and the ungrateful.
Bhishma begins the tale of Gautama, a poor Brahmana without Vedic learning who settles in a robbers' village, learns to kill cranes, and is visited by an old friend who urges him to change his ways.

Gautama sets out for the sea, is separated from a merchant caravan by an elephant attack, and comes to a beautiful forest and a great banyan, where he rests and then sees the crane Rajadharman arrive, eyeing him first as prey.
Rajadharman welcomes Gautama as a dear guest and offers him worship according to the rites.
Gautama is amazed at the crane's sweet welcome and cannot stop staring at him.
Rajadharman introduces himself as a son of Kasyapa and welcomes his guest.
Rajadharman feeds Gautama, gives him a bed, learns he is poor, promises help, and sends him to his friend Virupaksha, a Rakshasa king who will give him wealth.
Virupaksha receives Gautama with honours and asks about his birth, practices and Vedic study, but Gautama gives only his name and race.
The king asks where Gautama lives and about his wife.
Gautama says he is a Middle-country Brahmana who lives among hunters and has married a Sudra widow.

The king, bound by his friend's request, holds a great feast for a thousand Brahmanas and gives Gautama gold; Gautama returns to the banyan, where the crane welcomes him, and Gautama, ungrateful, plots to kill the crane for food.

Gautama kills the crane while it sleeps, flees with the gold, is found out by the Rakshasa king's son, and is cast aside by the Rakshasas and robbers, who will not eat an ungrateful man because ingratitude has no expiation.

Virupaksha cremates the crane, Surabhi's milk revives him, Indra restores Gautama at the crane's request, and Bhishma closes with a long moral on gratitude to friends, ending with a question to Yudhishthira about what else he wishes to hear.
Vaisampayana begins to report Yudhishthira's reaction to Bhishma's words.
The sentence ends with Yudhishthira highly gratified by the teaching.
Heading: the Mokshadharma Parva begins.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the duties of those in each of the four modes of life.
Bhishma says religion has many paths, and that the inner penance which frees the soul brings its fruit in this world, so every wise person should seek liberation.
Yudhishthira asks how a person can kill grief at the loss of wealth, a wife, a son or a father.
Bhishma tells how a Brahmana, seeing King Senajit grieve for his dead son, reminds him that everyone will one day leave this world and that grief is folly.
Senajit asks what wisdom and penance could keep a man from grief.
The Brahmana argues that all creatures are bound by sorrow, that nothing is truly one's own, that joy and sorrow follow each other, and that destiny and freedom from desire bring peace.
The Brahmana tells how the courtesan Pingala, whose lover failed to come, found peace by casting off hope and desire.
Bhishma says that Senajit is persuaded by these words, sets aside his grief and grows happy.
Yudhishthira asks what good thing should be sought while time carries every creature toward death.
Bhishma introduces the story of Medhavin, a clever son of a Vedic Brahmana, who asks his father how to live when life is so brief.
The son asks his father to set out the duties and their rewards so that he can follow them.
The father lays out the stages of life: study the Vedas, have sons to honour the ancestors, perform the sacrifices, and then retire to the forest to meditate.
The son asks how his father can speak so calmly while the world is under attack from death and decay.
The father asks what he means by the world being assailed and what the irresistible dangers are.

The son replies that death and decay surround every creature, that each night shortens life, and that the wise should pursue truth and renounce ties to village life rather than perform elaborate animal sacrifices.
Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to act as the father did after hearing the son's words, devoted to truth.
Yudhishthira asks whence happiness and misery come to rich and poor alike, when they follow different practices.

Bhishma gives verses of Sampaka, sung by a miserable Brahmana, saying that happiness and sorrow come from destiny, that poverty freed from desire is peaceful, that wealth brings anxiety and pride, and that renunciation is the highest good.
Yudhishthira asks what a man should do for happiness when he craves wealth and cannot find it.

Bhishma says the happy man is even-minded and truthful and free from attachment, and tells how Manki, after a camel drags off his two bulls, reasons that destiny governs wealth and then renounces desire for good.

Bhishma cites King Janaka, who says his wealth is unlimited yet he owns nothing that a fire could take from him, and tells how the royal son of Nahusha, Yayati, asks the sage Vodhya for the secret of tranquillity.
Vodhya replies that he follows others' teaching without instructing, and names six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the shaft-maker and the maiden.

Bhishma explains that hope is the great agitator, and that each teacher shows a lesson, such as the osprey finding peace when it gives up its meat, the snake living in another's home, and the maiden wandering alone like a lone anklet.
Yudhishthira asks by what conduct a person can live free of grief and reach an excellent end.
Bhishma tells how King Prahlada questions a wise and serene wandering Brahmana.
Prahlada praises the Brahmana's freedom from desire and calm, and asks what learning and conduct have brought it about.
The Brahmana replies that all creatures meet death and change without a clear cause, so he takes whatever food and rest come, and keeps the Ajagara vow, which is free of fear and desire.
Bhishma says that one who casts off attachment, fear and desire and follows this vow passes his days in great delight.
Yudhishthira asks whether kinsmen, action, wealth or wisdom should be a person's refuge.

Bhishma says wisdom is the highest refuge and recounts how Indra, disguised as a jackal, talks the despairing Brahmana Kasyapa out of suicide, reminds him of the value of his human birth, and names his past pride as the cause of his fall.
Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penances and service to teachers bring wisdom and high felicity.
Bhishma says that desire and anger lead to sin and suffering, that deeds bear fruit in later lives as a shadow follows its owner, and that repentance and penance can cleanse the past.
Yudhishthira asks who created the universe, how creatures and castes came about, and where the dead go.
Bhishma introduces the teaching that the sage Bhrigu gave to Bharadwaja, who found him seated on Mount Kailasa.
Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu who created the universe and its creatures, where castes and the moral order come from, and where the dead go.
Bhrigu describes a primeval being, Manasa, who creates the elements, a lotus and Brahman, and whose body is the universe itself.
Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu how far the sky, the horizons, the earth and the wind extend.
Bhrigu says the sky is infinite and has many regions, with layers of water and fire beyond the reach of the sun and moon, and that even the gods cannot measure it.
Bharadwaja asks why Brahman is called the first-born if he came from the lotus.
Bhrigu says the earth is the lotus, and that Mount Sumeru forms its centre, where Brahman created the worlds.
Bharadwaja asks how the creator, dwelling in Meru, made the diverse objects of the world.
Bhrigu says the creator first made water to sustain life, and that earth, mountains and clouds are all forms of solidified water.
Bharadwaja asks how water, fire, wind and earth first arose.
Bhrigu tells how seers who fasted for a thousand years heard a celestial voice describe how space, water, wind, fire and earth came into being in turn.
Bharadwaja asks why only the five primal elements are called creatures, when Brahman made thousands.

Bhrigu says the five elements are called great because they pervade all things, with wind as activity, space as sound, fire as heat, water as liquid and earth as solid matter, and the senses partake of them.
Bharadwaja objects that trees show none of the elements' signs of hearing, seeing, heat, motion or sense, so they cannot be made of the five elements.

Bhrigu answers that trees have space, heat, feeling, hearing, sight, scent and taste, so they live, and describes how the elements, the senses, the breaths and the properties of scent, taste, form, touch and sound appear in living bodies.
Bharadwaja asks how bodily heat dwells in the body and how wind enables it to move and act.
Bhrigu explains that heat lies in the head, that the five breaths govern life, the senses, excretion, the joints and digestion, and that yogins reach Brahma by holding the soul in the brain.

Bharadwaja objects that life, if it were only wind or inner heat, would merge back into outer air or fire at death, that gifts to Brahmanas could not help the dead, and that everything comes from seeds and perishes.
Bhrigu says the living creature is not destroyed with the body, but passes into another form, as fire cannot be seen once its fuel is consumed.
Bharadwaja objects that fire is simply extinguished when its fuel runs out, so that what has no action or trace has truly perished.
Bhrigu replies that fire merges into space, that the vital heat sustaining the breaths leaves the body, and that the body falls back to earth while the elements take form only in living creatures.
Bharadwaja asks what the living agent is, if the body is only five elements, since the agent seems not to hear or see when the mind is elsewhere and feels nothing in sleep.
Bhrigu says the mind too is made of the elements, that an inner Soul witnesses the senses and migrates from body to body after death, and that the Supreme Soul creates the worlds.
Bhrigu says Brahman first made the Prajapatis, then Truth, Duty, Penance and the Vedas, and then all beings, with white for Brahmanas, red for Kshatriyas, yellow for Vaisyas and black for Sudras.
Bharadwaja objects that colour cannot tell men apart, since all share the same passions and bodily functions, and that the creatures are too many to sort into classes.

Bhrigu says all men were once Brahmanas, that conduct turned some into Kshatriyas, Vaisyas or Sudras, that those who lost knowledge became Pisachas, Rakshasas and other beings, and that the Rishis made a lasting creation by their penance and yoga.
Bharadwaja asks by what acts one becomes a Brahmana, a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or a Sudra.
Bhrigu describes each class by its conduct, from the Brahmana's rites, study and truthfulness to the Sudra's uncleanness, then urges control of greed and anger and renunciation as the way to Brahma.
Bhrigu says truth is Brahma and the root of penance and creation, that untruth leads to darkness, and that happiness is the aim toward which all action tends.
Bharadwaja doubts that happiness is the highest aim, since Brahma and Shiva, who conquered desire, do not pursue it.
Bhrigu replies that those ruled by anger and greed suffer disease, death and loss, while heaven has no hunger, thirst or sin, so happiness is the highest goal.
Bharadwaja asks what gifts, righteousness, conduct, penance, Vedic study and fire offerings each bring.
Bhrigu says offerings burn sin, study brings peace, gifts bring pleasure and penance heaven, and gifts to the good follow the giver after death.
Bharadwaja asks which duties belong to whom, what marks duty, and how many kinds there are.
Bhrigu says the wise who perform their duties win heaven, while those who neglect them are led into folly.
Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu to set out the four modes of life that Brahman laid down, with the practices for each.
Bhrigu describes the student's discipline under his teacher, the householder's family life and enjoyments, and the forest dweller's simple life, and praises the householder who lives modestly.
Bhrigu describes forest hermits who bathe, perform daily rites, live on wild roots and fruit, sleep on the bare ground and endure heat and cold until their bodies waste away.
Bhrigu describes wandering renouncers who give up fire, wealth, family and comforts, harm no creature, stay only briefly in any place, and take alms only in their bowls.
Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu to describe a region beyond this world that he has heard of but never seen.

Bhrigu describes a sacred northern land beyond the Himalaya where people are righteous, free from disease and sin, and where the fruits of deeds are visible, while this world is the field of action where good and evil are both found.
Bhishma says Bhrigu finished his teaching, Bharadwaja worshipped him, and Bhishma asks Yudhishthira what more he wishes to hear.
Yudhishthira asks his grandsire Bhishma to teach him the rules of conduct, since Bhishma knows all duties.

Bhishma separates good from wicked men, then lists practices such as morning worship, eating customs, honouring Brahmanas and elders, and the value of concealing no sin, ending with the claim that righteousness brings happiness after death.
Yudhishthira asks what the Adhyatma is, how the universe came to be, and where it goes at dissolution.

Bhishma gives a long discourse: the five elements and their senses, the mind and understanding, the three qualities and what each produces, the soul as an unacting witness compared to a fish in water and a lamp in a vessel, the doubt about whether the qualities survive liberation, and a closing call to detachment and self-knowledge.

Bhishma says he will teach the four kinds of yoga meditation, which sages used to reach liberation, and describes how the yogin withdraws the senses, keeps the mind steady, deals with its restlessness through patience, and reaches a happiness that brings him to Nirvana.
Yudhishthira asks what fruit silent reciters gain, where they go after death, and whether their path belongs to Sankhya, yoga or work.

Bhishma tells an old story of Yama, Time and a Brahmana, explains that Sankhya and yoga both involve recitation, and then describes the reciter's withdrawal with kusa grass, the Gayatri, meditation and release into Brahma.
Yudhishthira asks whether the high end gained by reciters is their only destination.
Bhishma lists the ways a reciter falls into hell, including unfinished practice, lack of faith, pride, contempt for others, and recitation driven by desire, attachment or delusion.
Yudhishthira asks why reciters who attain the supreme essence, identified with the syllable Om, must still be reborn.
Bhishma answers that reciters without true knowledge and wisdom meet various hells, and that the discipline itself is excellent but has these faults.
Yudhishthira asks what kind of hell a reciter may enter and asks Bhishma to explain.

Bhishma praises Yudhishthira's righteousness, describes the splendid heavens of the gods, and says these look like hell beside the supreme region that is free from time, pain and the three qualities, which a reciter reaches by merging with his Soul.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to narrate the full story of the dispute between Time, Mrityu, Yama, Ikshvaku and a Brahmana.
Bhishma introduces Ikshvaku, son of Surya, and a learned Brahmana of the Kusika line who lived at the foot of the Himalayas and recited the Gayatri for a thousand years.
Savitri appears, is pleased, and grants the Brahmana's wish to delight in his recitation, and says that Dharma, Time, Yama and Mrityu will come and dispute with him.
After the thousand years of observance, Dharma shows himself and says the Brahmana has earned the regions of felicity and can give up his body to reach them.
Dharma tells the Brahmana he has won rewards among gods and men and may cast off his breaths and go wherever he likes.
The Brahmana replies that he does not want those rewards and will not give up his body, which is subject to both joy and sorrow.
Dharma insists that the body should be cast off, and asks him to go to heaven or name some other wish.
The Brahmana says he does not want heaven without his body and asks Dharma to leave him.
Dharma urges him to drop his attachment to the body and go to regions free from passion, where he will suffer no more.
The Brahmana says his delight is in recitation and he does not wish for even the eternal regions with his body.
Dharma warns that Time, Mrityu and Yama are now coming to him if he will not give up his body.
Bhishma says the three figures that take away all creatures approach the Brahmana and speak to him.
Yama tells him that a high reward awaits him for his penances and pious conduct.
Time says the reward matches his completed recitation and that the time has come for him to ascend to heaven.
Mrityu introduces herself in her true form and says she has come, urged by Time, to bear him away.
The Brahmana welcomes Surya's son, Time, Mrityu and Dharma and asks what he can do for them.
Bhishma says the Brahmana offers them water and the usual honours, and king Ikshvaku arrives on pilgrimage, greets them and asks what the Brahmana can give him.
Ikshvaku offers the Brahmana some wealth, asking how much he should give.
The Brahmana says there are two kinds of Brahmanas and that he has given up accepting gifts, so he asks instead what he can give the king.
Ikshvaku answers that a Kshatriya cannot say give, and that a Kshatriya's request is for battle.
The Brahmana says each of them keeps to the duties of his own order, so there is little difference between them.
The king says the Brahmana first offered according to his might, so he asks him for the fruit of his recitations.
The Brahmana teases the king for talking about battle and asks why he does not challenge him to one.
The king explains that Brahmanas have the thunder of speech and Kshatriyas the might of arms, so this exchange of words is their fight.
The Brahmana resolves to give what he can and asks the king to name it without delay.
The king says that if he is to be given anything, it should be the fruit of the thousand years of recitation.
The Brahmana offers the king the highest fruit, half of it, or all of it without hesitation.
The king says he does not need the fruit and asks what it actually is.
The Brahmana admits he does not know what the fruit is, and points to Dharma, Time, Yama and Mrityu as witnesses to the gift.
The king says he will not want fruits he cannot even name, and that the Brahmana may keep them.
The Brahmana insists that he has given his fruits and that the king must keep his word, and he gives a long speech on the supremacy of truth over all penances, sacrifices and vows.
The king replies that a Kshatriya's duties are to fight and protect, and asks how he can accept a gift.
The Brahmana says he never sought the king and that the king came to him asking, so he should accept.
Dharma declares himself and says the Brahmana should receive the reward of giving, and the king should gain the merit of truth.
Heaven, in embodied form, says that both men are equal in the merit they have earned and that the dispute should end.
The king says he has no use for Heaven, and offers the Brahmana his own rewards if the Brahmana wants them.
The Brahmana says he once accepted gifts in ignorance, but now keeps to abstention, and he declines the king's rewards because he wants only penance and Vedic study.
The king offers to share his reward with the Brahmana, or to let the Brahmana take all of his merit.
Two ill-dressed figures arrive, each claiming the other owes him a debt, and both ask the king to judge.
Virupa says he owes Vikrita the merit of a cow gift and is ready to repay it, but Vikrita refuses.
Vikrita says Virupa owes him nothing and calls his claim false.
The king asks Virupa to explain the debt so that he can judge fairly.
Virupa explains that Vikrita once gave a cow to a Brahmana and passed on the merit, and that Virupa later gave two cows to a poor Brahmana and now wants to repay the merit twice over.
The king tells Vikrita to accept the payment that is due to him.
Vikrita replies that what he gave away is gone, so Virupa owes him nothing and may leave.
The king says Vikrita's refusal seems improper and that he may deserve punishment.
Vikrita says a gift once made cannot be taken back, and asks the king to punish him if he is guilty.
Virupa warns that the king will punish Vikrita for refusing a repayment that is offered.
Vikrita says he gave what was his own freely, will not take it back, and tells Virupa he may go.
The Brahmana says the king has heard both sides and should accept the gift he has pledged.
The king calls the matter as deep as a bottomless pit, says that refusing the Brahmana's gift would be a great sin, and sends the two men away with their gains.
The Brahmana says he has pledged the gift and will curse the king if he refuses it.
The king says he will accept the gift only to keep the two duties in balance, and asks the Brahmana to give what is owed.
The Brahmana offers the king all the fruits he has won by reciting the Gayatri.
The king says he will return a gift so that they stand equal.
Virupa reveals that he and Vikrita are Desire and Wrath, who provoked the exchange, and tells the king to go to the regions he has earned.

Bhishma explains that a Gayatri reciter goes to Brahman, Agni, Surya, Soma, Vayu or Earth, and takes on the nature of that region if still attached, but a reciter free of attachment enters the Supreme.
Heading: Section CC begins.
Yudhishthira asks what the Brahmana and the king said to Virupa, what end they gained, and what they did afterwards.
Bhishma says the Brahmana honours the gods and tells the king to rise to eminence, since Savitri had granted him a boon of endless devotion to recitation, and he wishes to resume his recitation.
The king offers to split the reward with the Brahmana if his recitation has lost its fruit through the gift and he wishes to practise again.

The Brahmana proposes that they become equal in the next life, and a large gathering of gods, sages and spirits appears; Heaven praises both men, and the two withdraw their senses, fix their breath, and are absorbed into the Creator.
Brahman says that those who study the Vedas, other sacred traditions, or practise yoga will reach his region after death, and then departs.
Bhishma says the gods return to their homes and the assembly follows Dharma, and he ends his account of how reciters are rewarded.
Yudhishthira begins to ask what the fruits of yoga are.
His question continues, asking about knowledge of all the Vedas and of the observances and vows.
He asks how the creature-soul may be known and asks Bhishma to tell him.
Bhishma tells the old story of Manu and his disciple Vrihaspati, who asks about the cause of the universe, the fruits of knowledge and sacrifice, and how a soul leaves one body and takes another.
Manu replies that acts spring from a wish for happiness and to avoid misery, that knowledge comes from wanting to escape both, and that a person who acts out of desire goes to hell.
Vrihaspati replies that human aims are the pursuit of what is agreeable and the avoidance of what is disagreeable, and that acts are the means to both.

Manu says liberation from acts leads to Brahma, that acts are shaped by the three qualities, that knowledge sees dangers, and that the fruits of acts are enjoyed in body, speech and mind; he then describes the supreme being as beyond the senses, sexless and without direction.

Manu describes the elements returning to space, the Self beyond all sensory qualities, the lamp and ministers images of knowledge governing the senses, the Soul passing through bodies while remaining unseen, and the acts it carries with it.

Manu describes the Soul as the witness that cannot be seen by the senses, compares its knowability to hidden things such as the moon and Rahu, and concludes that it keeps the fruits of its acts after leaving the body.

Manu compares sleep and death to a dream, explains that the Soul is seen only in a calm mind, and describes the layers from senses to mind to understanding to Soul to the Supreme, ending with the claim that the senses cannot grasp the Soul but it sees all.

Manu advises against dwelling on sorrow, explains how to meet mental and physical suffering, describes how the understanding must be withdrawn into contemplation to reach the qualityless Brahma, and ends by saying that rebirth follows attachment while Knowledge follows freedom from it.

Manu describes how the soul moves between bodies according to past acts, traces the chain from knowledge to fruit, identifies Vishnu as the Supreme Brahma beyond Time, and says Brahma, which has no beginning or end, is reached through detachment, self-restraint and abstention from acts.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to tell him in detail about Vishnu, the indestructible creator, known as Narayana, Hrishikesa, Govinda and Kesava.

Bhishma says he learned this from Rama, Narada and Vyasa, and describes how Vishnu created the elements, Consciousness and the lotus-born Brahman, slew the demon Madhu, and then brought forth the sages, Daksha's daughters, the gods and the demons, with Vishnu later appearing as a dwarf among the Adityas.

Vishnu creates days, nights, seasons, clouds and creatures, makes the four orders of men from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, appoints Brahma, Virupaksha, Yama, Kubera, Varuna and Indra as rulers, and describes how sexual union arose only in the Dwapara age.
Bhishma describes the sinful peoples of the southern and northern regions, who arose in the Treta age and whose wars with the Kshatriyas followed.
Bhishma says Narada proclaims Krishna as the eternal Supreme God, and that Kesava is invincible and more than an ordinary man.
Yudhishthira asks who the first Prajapatis were and which holy Rishis live in each direction.

Bhishma names the seven sons of the self-born Brahman and the later Prajapatis, lists the Adityas, Aswins, Vasus and Maruts with their social orders, places the great Rishis in the East, South, West and North, and says that remembering their names and visiting these quarters purifies a person.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe Krishna's power, his great feats, and why he took the form of an animal.

Bhishma tells how the Danavas oppressed the gods and the earth, how Brahman says Vishnu will take the form of a boar to destroy them, how the boar overpowers the demons as they seize it, and how its roars shake the universe and earn Vishnu the names Sanatana and Padmanabha.
Brahman explains to the gods that the sound comes from the Supreme God Krishna, who has slain the chief Danavas and returned to his own nature, so they need not fear.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the yoga by which he may obtain emancipation.

Bhishma tells of a disciple who asks his preceptor where he and the teacher come from, what the final cause is, why beings with one material cause have different beginnings and ends, and how the Vedas and Smritis treat rites for different classes.

The preceptor calls the question Adhyatma, names Vasudeva as the supreme cause, describes creation and the recovery of lost Vedas after each dissolution, lists the elements of primordial matter and their sixteen modifications, and explains that the Soul is the doer, is seen only through yoga, and passes from body to body by its acts.

Bhishma explains that beings come from the unmanifest, the Soul is eternal and not stained by the qualities or the dust of existence, the cosmos turns like a wheel, and true knowledge frees the Soul from rebirth, as fire prevents seeds from sprouting.
Bhishma says the wise prefer abstention from acts, that attachment to the senses dulls knowledge like iron dulling gold, and that the body is made of elements and its faults must be examined.

Bhishma compares the body to a house plastered with earth, advises eating like a patient taking medicine, urges self-restraint and virtues, and lists the states that the qualities of goodness, passion and darkness produce.
Yudhishthira asks which faults the seeker should abandon, which should be weakened, which keep recurring, and which the stupefied may treat as tolerable.

Bhishma says the pure soul uproots every fault, goodness is the means of freedom, and that rites performed with mantras are not cruel but purify, while passion and darkness drive unrighteous acts, sleep, procrastination and cruelty.

Bhishma traces the chain from passion and darkness through desire, acts and birth in the womb, presents women, desire and children as bonds that the wise should avoid, explains that the senses take shape according to past acts, and concludes that the Soul is freed when thirst is gone and the senses are made weak.
Bhishma says he will explain the means of conquering the senses according to scripture, and that man is the foremost of living creatures.

Bhishma says the learned twice-born are the best of men, that virtues such as purity, truth and forgiveness are not enough for liberation, that Brahmacharya leads to Brahma, and that the practitioner must avoid women, perform expiations for desire, and control the passions and the body's ducts.

Bhishma urges the seeker to see the sorrows of the world, avoid attachment and pride, practise truth, non-injury and forgiveness, live simply by alms, control the understanding, mind and senses, and so reach eternal Brahma and freedom from ignorance.

Bhishma tells the yogin to avoid sleep and dreams, explains that dreams arise from fatigue and past impressions while the mind stays active, describes deep sleep and the Soul, and says Brahma is reached by crossing darkness and withdrawing the senses and mind.

Bhishma says no one knows Brahma without understanding the four topics, the body and the Soul; describes the paths of activity and renunciation; explains that Prakriti and Purusha are both eternal but differ; uses the turban image for the Soul and the qualities; urges yoga and detachment; and describes the different ways of worshipping Brahma.

Bhishma says that those who follow this path gain the highest end, that desire weaves the universe like a loom weaves cloth, that knowing Prakriti and Purusha frees one from desire, and that Narayana taught these means out of compassion.
Yudhishthira asks how Janaka of Mithila, who was devoted to emancipation, reached it after giving up worldly enjoyments.

Bhishma recounts how King Janadeva, dissatisfied with his hundred preceptors, is taught by the sage Panchasikha, who argues that the Soul is distinct from the body and survives death, refutes the sceptics, the view that rebirth comes from ignorance and desire, and the idea that the Soul is extinguished, and leaves the king wondering.
Bhishma says Janadeva, instructed by Panchasikha, asks again whether there is existence or non-existence after death.
Janadeva asks what the difference is between ignorance and knowledge, and what is gained or lost by each, if nothing is retained after death, since rites and action would then seem pointless.

Panchasikha calms the king by describing the body as a union of elements, senses and mind, explaining the five senses and five organs of action and the three qualities of experience, urging renunciation of all things, and using images of the silkworm, the lotus leaf and Janaka's burning city to show the Soul is untouched, after which Janadeva finds peace and the teaching frees its reader from sorrow.
Yudhishthira asks what conduct brings happiness, what brings woe, and what frees a person from fear and brings success.

Bhishma praises self-restraint as the basis of rites, penance and truth, describes the calm, fearless and virtuous character of the self-restrained, and urges Brahmanas to master lust and wrath while living calmly.
Yudhishthira asks whether the twice-born who eat the leftovers of sacrifices, including meat and wine, for children and heaven commit a wrong.
Bhishma says those who eat forbidden food without observing the Vedic rites are fallen, and those who do so under ritual observance rise to heaven but fall again when their merit is used up.
Yudhishthira notes that common people regard fasting as penance.
Yudhishthira asks whether fasting really is penance or something else.

Bhishma says fasting, measured in months, fortnights or days, is not true penance to the good and may even hinder knowledge of the Soul, while renunciation of acts and humility toward all creatures are the highest penance and make a person a fasting, celibate, vegetarian and hospitable figure.
Yudhishthira asks how such a person comes to be regarded as always fasting, celibate, living on sacrificial remnants, or devoted to guests.

Bhishma explains that such a person eats at fixed times, speaks the truth, approaches his wife only in her season, eats no meat not offered in sacrifice, gives generously, stays awake by day, and eats only after feeding servants, guests and the gods.
Yudhishthira asks whether man is really the doer of his acts, which bear fruit for enjoyment or suffering.
Bhishma introduces Prahlada, a detached and self-controlled Daitya who is sitting alone when Indra approaches to test his calm after his fall and asks about the best path to knowledge of the Soul.

Prahlada says that ignorance causes stupefaction, that beings arise by their own nature without effort, that the person does not truly act, and that even emancipation and self-knowledge come from Nature.

Prahlada compares acts to a crow's cawing that merely announces food, says he feels no affection, aversion or grief, and explains that the Soul, separated from everything, cannot enjoy felicity, so he desires nothing.
Indra asks Prahlada what means lead to this wisdom and tranquillity.
Prahlada says that simplicity, heedfulness, purifying the Soul, mastering the passions and serving elders lead to emancipation, and that wisdom and tranquillity come from Nature.
Indra, filled with wonder, praises Prahlada and returns to his own abode.
Yudhishthira asks how a king who has lost his prosperity and been crushed by Time can still live on the earth.
Bhishma introduces Vasava, who asks Brahma where Vali, the generous son of Virochana, has gone, since he no longer sees Vali's splendour.
Brahma says Indra should not ask this, but tells him that Vali may have been reborn as a beast such as a camel, bull, ass or horse and may now be staying in an empty room.
Indra asks whether he should kill Vali or spare him if he finds him.
Brahma tells Indra not to harm Vali, who does not deserve death, and to seek moral instruction from him.
Bhishma says Indra travels the earth on Airavata and finds Vali living as an ass in an empty room, as Brahma foretold.
Indra mocks Vali's fall, recalls his golden umbrella, fans, dancers, sacrifices and garland, and asks whether he grieves.
Vali answers that his treasures are hidden and will return when his time comes, that Indra's taunts do not suit him, and that the wise are not moved by fortune.
Bhishma says that Indra, laughing at the sighing Vali, asks a sharper question than before.
Indra asks whether Vali grieves now that his power and kinsmen are gone and all the worlds are no longer his.

Vali says he does not grieve, since all things are transitory and governed by Time, the body and life arise and pass together, the wise are not stupefied, and no one is truly the slayer, and he adds that Time sweeps away all, including Indra.

Vali says that fortune and misfortune are ordained, that Indra's power also depends on Time, that Brahma is Time and every creature is bound to it, and that Indra will also pass away, so he should be calm and not boast.
Bhishma says Indra sees the goddess of prosperity emerge from Vali's body, blazing with radiance, and looks at her with wonder.
