Indra asks Vali who the radiant, plumed, bejewelled woman is, emitting glory from his body.
Vali says he does not know whether she is an Asura, celestial or human, and tells Indra to ask her himself.
Indra asks her name and why she has left the Daitya lord to stand as a radiant form.
Sree says Vali did not know her, gives her names Duhshaha, Vidhitsa, Bhuti, Lakshmi and Sree, and says neither Indra nor the gods know her.
Indra asks Sree why she deserts Vali after living in him for a long time, and whether it is his own act or Vali's.
Sree says neither the Creator nor the Ordainer governs her, that Time moves her from place to place, and that Indra should not disregard Vali.
Indra asks again why she leaves Vali and why she comes to him.

Sree says she lives in truth, gifts, vows, penance, valour and virtue, and that Vali has fallen from these by turning against the Brahmanas, touching ghee with unclean hands, and boasting of his devotion.
Indra says there is no one among gods or men who can bear her forever.
Sree says that none of the gods, Gandharvas, Asuras or Rakshasas can bear her forever.
Sree completes the point that no being can bear her for all time.
Indra asks how he should conduct himself so that Sree will remain with him always, and promises to obey her.
Sree tells Indra to divide her into four parts, as the Vedas direct.
Indra says he will assign the places according to each being's power to bear her, and that the earth, mother of all, can bear a fourth part.
Sree yields up a quarter of herself to be set in the earth and asks Indra to place the second quarter.
Indra says the waters serve human beings in many ways and can bear a fourth part.
Sree gives a second quarter to the waters and asks Indra to place the third.
Indra says the Vedas, sacrifices and deities are established in fire, which can bear the third part.
Sree gives her third quarter to fire and asks Indra to assign the last quarter.
Indra says the good among men, devoted to the Brahmanas and truthful in speech, can bear the last quarter.
Sree gives the fourth quarter to the good and asks Indra to continue protecting her in her parts.
Indra says he has distributed her among creatures and will punish anyone who offends her, and Vali, deserted by Sree, speaks.
Vali predicts that when the sun shines only on Brahma's region at Sumeru, the gods and Asuras will fight again, and that he will conquer them all.
Indra says Brahma commanded him never to kill Vali, so he spares him, and then explains the sun's six-month northern and southern courses that make the seasons.
Bhishma says Vali goes south and Indra goes north, and Indra ascends to the sky after hearing Vali's humble speech.
Bhishma says Indra asks the fallen Namuchi, calm as the still ocean, whether he grieves over his fall or lives cheerfully.

Namuchi says grief only wastes the body and pleases foes, that one cannot lift another's sorrow, that the one Ordainer governs all beings and events, that the wise accept pleasure and pain as ordained, and that whoever knows this is the foremost of his kind.
Yudhishthira asks what is good for a man sunk in dire distress after losing friends or his kingdom, and asks Bhishma to answer him.

Bhishma says fortitude is the highest good in distress, that it keeps the body and health, and that it leads back to prosperity; he then tells how Vali, after his defeat, was deceived by Vishnu and lost his sway, and how Indra on Airavata found him unmoved in a sea-shore cave and asked how he could be so calm.

Vali replies that Indra's power and his own fall both come from Time, that good deeds cannot save anyone from Time, that many Indras and kings have fallen before, and that he does not grieve because grief only wastes the body and weakens one's power.
Indra, hearing these words, restrains his wrath.

Indra admits that all things are subject to Time and says he will leave Vali in peace, predicting that his bonds will loosen as the world falls into disorder, before returning to his heaven and sovereignty.
Heading: Section CCXXVIII begins.
Yudhishthira asks for the signs that show a person's future greatness and future fall.
Bhishma says the mind itself shows these signs, and tells how Narada and Indra, bathing by the Ganga, see the goddess Sree descend in splendour to greet them.
Indra asks Sree who she is, why she has come, and where she is going.

Sree names herself Padma, Lakshmi, Bhuti and Sree, lists the qualities she embodies, says she dwells with valiant, virtuous and Brahma-devoted people, and says she left the Asuras because they had become wicked.
Indra asks what conduct of the Asuras led her to leave them.

Sree recalls the virtues the Danavas once had, then lists their decline into disorder, disrespect for elders, neglect of rites and wrong eating, and says she has come to Indra for those who keep to duty.
Narada and Indra welcome Sree, the gods gather, and the world is renewed with rain, good crops and virtue, and Bhishma says that those who hear this story gain prosperity.
Yudhishthira asks by what disposition, duties, knowledge and energy one reaches the immutable Brahma that lies beyond primordial nature.
Bhishma says that one who practises renunciation, eats moderately and controls the senses can reach Brahma, and introduces the discourse between Jaigishavya and Asita-Devala.
Devala asks Jaigishavya why he is not pleased by praise nor angered by blame, and what his wisdom is and where it comes from.
Bhishma says Jaigishavya answers in words of high meaning and full faith.

Jaigishavya describes the wise as even toward praise and blame, not given to recrimination, not grieving over past or future, free from envy and wrath, indifferent to gain and loss, and says only such a person reaches Brahma beyond primordial nature.
Yudhishthira asks which man is dear to all, gladdens everyone, and has every merit and accomplishment.
Bhishma says he will recite words that Kesava once spoke on an earlier occasion.
The passage introduces Kesava's answer to Ugrasena's question.
Ugrasena says that everyone speaks highly of the sage Narada and asks Kesava to name his merits.

Kesava (Vasudeva) lists Narada's learning, humility, self-control, courage, truthfulness, purity, freedom from envy and anger, equal regard for all, and his refusal to disparage others, and concludes that everyone who has these merits is loved.

Yudhishthira asks for the origin and end of creatures, their meditation and acts, the divisions of time, the lengths of the ages, and the truth about the world's genesis, and asks Bhishma to discourse further, since he has been drawn to yoga by an earlier teaching.
Bhishma says he will recite an old narrative of Vyasa's teaching to his son Suka, who, after studying the Vedas, asked his father about the Creator and the duties of a Brahmana.
Suka asks Vyasa who is the Creator of all beings, as known through time, and what duties a Brahmana should perform.
Bhishma says Vyasa, who knows past and future and all duties, replied to his son.

Vyasa says that before creation only Brahma exists, unborn and beyond knowledge; he measures time from winks of the eye through days, months and years, and then the day and night of the Pitris and gods; he gives the lengths of the four yugas and their morning and evening periods, says that duty declines through them, names Penance, Knowledge, Sacrifice and Gift as the chief duty of each, and says that a thousand such yugas make one day of Brahman, who sleeps in dissolution and wakes to create.

Vyasa describes how Brahma creates the universe from Mind and the elements in layers, how the Creator enters the body to make all beings, how creation repeats with the same attributes and is shaped by rival views of effort, fate and nature, how penance and the Vedas underlie all names and acts, how sacrifices vary by age, and how Time creates and swallows creatures, before he sums up his teaching to Suka.

Vyasa describes how at dissolution fire consumes the universe, the elements fold into one another until only Space remains, Mind and then Time and energy are absorbed into Iswara and the unmanifest Brahma, and this cycle repeats through Brahman's days and nights of a thousand yugas each.

Vyasa lists the Brahmana's duties: study under a preceptor, the four modes of life with householder life as the root, paying the three debts, teaching, sacrifice and gift; he then names many kings and sages who won heaven through giving away wealth, land, limbs and even their children or lives.

Vyasa urges study of the Vedas, a life of faith, restraint and duty, and the crossing of the river of Time, which carries all beings toward Yama, on the raft of wisdom, warning that fools sink and that acting without clear vision keeps a person in rebirth.

Vyasa says knowledge is the raft across the stream of Time, lists the requirements of yoga, compares the body to a chariot whose parts are virtues, knowledge and the soul, describes the stages of concentration in which the yogin sees the soul through fog, water, fire, wind and ether and gains power over the elements, and concludes that the Sankhya and yoga paths both lead to emancipation.
Vyasa says the meditative person, carried up and down by life's ocean, should grasp the raft of knowledge and rely on it alone for emancipation.
Suka asks what this knowledge is: learning that dispels error, action that reaches the goal, or abstention from action that extends the soul, and asks how birth and death may be avoided.

Vyasa says those who hold that all things exist by nature alone gain no truth, that wisdom in using means leads to success, that creatures are ranked by their attributes, and that Brahmanas who know the Vedas and the Soul are the highest, and gods among men.

Vyasa says the Brahmana's prescribed duties are obligatory if they lead to knowledge, reviews the rival views on whether effort, necessity, nature or time causes action, notes that the people of the Krita age practised penance and that the sacrifices differ by order, says the Vedas decline through the later ages, and concludes that Time creates, sustains and destroys all creatures, who rest upon it.
Bhishma says that Suka applauds his father's instruction and sets out to ask about the duties that lead to emancipation.

Suka asks by what means a wise and learned man attains Brahma, which can be known neither by perception, inference nor the Vedas, and whether penance, celibacy, renunciation, Sankhya or yoga is the way, and how the mind and senses can be made single-minded.

Vyasa says that only knowledge, penance, sense-control and renunciation lead to success, describes the elements, senses, mind and knowledge that make up the body, says the Soul is beyond body and nature, seen only by the inner light, present in every creature, and that one who sees all beings in the Soul and the Soul in all reaches Brahma and immortality.

Vyasa says he has answered Suka by the Sankhya doctrine and now gives the yoga method, covering the five impediments, restraint of the senses and mind, the six-month vision of Brahma as a smokeless flame, the disregard of supernatural powers, the equal regard for gain and loss, praise and blame, and earth and gold, and the fact that even a woman or a person of lower birth reaches the highest end by it.
Bhishma says that wise people who learn these words from their teachers and reflect on them attain equality with Brahman until the universal dissolution.
Suka says the Vedas both command action and forbid it, and asks where knowledge and action each lead.

Bhishma says Vyasa answers with two paths, the destructible one of action and the indestructible one of knowledge, saying that action brings rebirth while knowledge leads to eternal Brahma beyond pleasure and pain, that the man of knowledge remains subtly existent like the moon at the close of the dark fortnight while the man of action is like the new moon, and that the soul is above mind and knowledge.

Suka says there are two kinds of creation and asks which course of righteousness good people should follow under Time, given the Vedas' contradictory commands to act and to abstain, so that he may reach the indestructible Soul.

Vyasa says that the path established by Brahma and kept by the great Rishis leads through Brahmacharya, forest austerity, benevolence and mendicancy, and urges Suka to shun flattery and live alone in the forest.
Suka says the Vedic commands look contradictory and asks how both can be authoritative, and how release can be won without breaking the duty of action.
Bhishma says that Vyasa, pleased by his son's words, replied.

Vyasa says that the four stages of life lead to the same end when they are duly observed, that one who passes through all four without desire or aversion is fit to know Brahma, and then describes the student's duty of serving and studying under his preceptor, before he returns to householder life.

Vyasa describes the householder's four ways of storing grain, his duties of hospitality, restraint and avoiding quarrels, the merit that each duty brings, and the higher merit of the forest and renunciation stages.
Bhishma says Yudhishthira has heard the duties of the householder and now asks him to listen to the duties of the forest life and the sacred spot dwellers who adopt it.

Vyasa says that when wrinkles, white hair and grandchildren appear, the householder should go to the forest, keep his fires and cattle, eat once a day, live on wild grains, perform the five sacrifices, endure hardships, and name ancient sages who won heaven this way, then, weakened by age, adopt full renunciation, perform a one-day self-sacrifice, give up all attachments, eat sparingly, shave, and move through the world without harming any creature.
Suka asks how one who seeks the highest knowledge should set the soul on yoga while living the highest stage of life.

Vyasa says that after the first stages of life purify him, the renouncer should practise yoga alone, beg food, speak little, live on little and sleep in solitude, regard abstention from injury as the duty that contains all others, recognise the Soul within the body, and be like the free and unattached sky, honoured by the gods as a true Brahmana.

Vyasa describes the hierarchy from the senses through mind, understanding and Mahat to Prakriti and Brahma, explains how the Yogin withdraws the senses into the Soul, purifies his heart and reaches immortality, says the teaching is the essence of the Vedas to be given only to the worthy, and invites Suka to ask about anything else he doubts.
Suka asks Vyasa to discourse again on Adhyatma, what it is and where it comes from.

Vyasa says earth, water, light, wind and space are the great entities that make up all creatures, differ in proportion according to the Creator's purpose, and undergo creation and destruction like a tortoise stretching and withdrawing its limbs.
Suka asks how this unequal distribution may be understood, and which elements are the senses and which the attributes.

Vyasa explains which element gives rise to sound, touch, form, taste and scent, the roles of mind, understanding and Soul, and the three qualities of goodness, passion and darkness together with the signs by which each is recognised.

Vyasa explains that the mind forms ideas and the understanding discriminates, that the understanding becomes the senses through its modifications, that the three qualities bind it while the Soul above witnesses them, that the Soul is seen once darkness is removed, that the Soul and understanding are distinct yet always united like fish and water, gnat and fig, and blade and grass, and that a Yogin who acts without attachment is never soiled.

Vyasa says the understanding creates the objects, the Soul presides over them without mingling, the qualities may or may not be destroyed by knowledge, one should act without anger, joy or envy and cut the knot of the heart through knowledge, the wise who know the Soul are free of distress and reach liberation, and acts done without desire do not bind the doer in this life or the next.
Suka asks his father Vyasa to name the foremost of all duties.

Vyasa answers at length: restrain the senses, know the Soul within, cross the river of life, and pass this knowledge only to a worthy disciple. He ends by telling the teacher to give it with a glad heart.
Vyasa describes the conduct of a true Brahmana, the escape from desire, the aims of the Vedas, and the yogin who gains freedom from rebirth.

Vyasa tells the teacher to repeat the earlier teaching, then links the five elements and time to living beings, assigns each sense to an element, names the mind, understanding and Soul, and ends by saying the one who sees all beings as unstained avoids errors in action.

Vyasa describes the subtle Soul, compares it to sunlight and its reflection in water, notes that rajas and tamas blind people to it, names Sandilya's yoga duties, and ends by saying that understanding the seven subtle entities and the Supreme cause leads to high Brahma.

Vyasa describes desire as a tree in the heart, with error as its seed and ignorance as its root, says yoga can cut it down, and then compares the body to a city whose understanding and mind are corrupted by rajas, which then seizes the Soul.
Bhishma repeats Vyasa's teaching to his son and lists the properties of earth, water, fire, wind and space, along with those of the mind and the understanding.
Yudhishthira asks how the understanding can have five properties, and how the senses can count as properties of the elements, and asks Bhishma to explain.
Bhishma answers that the understanding has sixty properties in all, that these entities are created and not eternal like the Soul, and that one should seek tranquillity through knowing Brahma.
Yudhishthira grieves over the dead kings lying on the battlefield and asks what animation and death are, and what it is that dies.
Bhishma tells of King Anukampaka, who lost his son Hari and his kingdom in battle, and how the king met the sage Narada and told him his grief.

Narada begins his tale: the Grandsire's creatures multiplied until the worlds were overcrowded, and the Grandsire, unable to find a way to destroy them, grew wrathful and sent out a fire that threatened all things, until Shiva came to plead for them.
Shiva pleads on behalf of creatures burned by the Grandsire's fire and asks him not to be angry.
The Grandsire says he is not angry for its own sake, that the earth was sinking under the weight of creatures, and that his wrath came because he could find no other remedy.
Shiva begs him to calm the fire, saying that the plants, waters and living things are being consumed and cannot be restored once destroyed, and asks that beings be reborn again and again.

The Grandsire calms his fire and sets birth and death in order. A lady in black and red comes out of his body, and he tells her to slay the creatures without favour. She sheds tears and holds them in her joined palms as she begins to plead.

Death, humbled, asks the Grandsire how she, sprung from him, can do such a terrible deed, and says she cannot kill the young and the old, the innocent, or her own loved ones, and asks for leave to undertake austerities.

The Grandsire insists that she carry out his order without reflection. Death keeps refusing and undertakes long austerities at many sacred places. The Grandsire finally answers that no demerit will fall on her, gives her Desire and Wrath as her agents, and says her tears will become diseases. He says wind is the life of all beings and tells the king not to grieve for his son, who has gone to heaven.
Yudhishthira says people doubt what righteousness is, where it comes from, and whether it serves this world, the next, or both, and asks Bhishma to explain.

Bhishma answers: the practice of the good, the Smritis and the Vedas are the sources of righteousness, with purpose as a fourth. He gives examples on truth, honest conduct, charity, and not wronging others, and ends by urging Yudhishthira never to set his mind on wrongdoing.

Yudhishthira says he can judge right from wrong by inner reasoning, but still doubts that duty can be settled by the scriptures, the conduct of the good, or the ages, and concludes that only what the learned of old called righteousness is righteousness.
Bhishma introduces the old story of Jajali, a Brahmana forest-dweller whose severe penances took him to the sea, and who boasted to the Pisachas that no one could equal him.
Yudhishthira asks what hard feats Jajali performed to win such success.

Bhishma describes Jajali's austerities, and how he stood still while birds nested and raised young on his head, then felt pride when they left, until a voice rebuked him and he set out to find Tuladhara.
Tuladhara greets Jajali and explains that Jajali's pride came when the birds flew off, and that the voice in the sky was what angered him.
Heading for the next section, CCLXII.
Bhishma says Jajali replies to Tuladhara's greeting with a question.
Jajali asks how a seller of scents and herbs has gained such firm understanding and where his knowledge came from.
Bhishma introduces Tuladhara, a Vaisya, who explains the ways of morality to the ascetic Jajali.

Tuladhara explains that morality is universal friendliness and harmlessness, describes his honest trade and even-minded way of living, argues that harmlessness is the highest duty, criticizes cruel treatment of animals and people, retells how Nahusha's sin was spread among creatures, and says he treats his praisers and his injurers alike.
Jajali objects that Tuladhara's doctrine would close heaven, end farming and food, and bring sacrifice to an end.

Tuladhara replies that he does not reject sacrifice, only greedy and violent ritual, and says sacrifices made with faith and without desire of fruit lead to Brahma. He allows that a man of cleansed soul may even offer a cow, but tells others to offer plants and herbs.
Jajali says he has never heard these teachings of the mental sacrifice before and asks Tuladhara to explain them.

Tuladhara says faithless sacrifices are not true sacrifices, names clarified butter and a rice-ball as proper offerings, and says the Soul is a sacred place, so there is no need to wander to holy sites.
Bhishma says Tuladhara's duties were applauded because they agree with reason and are kept by the good and wise.
Tuladhara asks Jajali to watch the birds that once nested on his head, now flying home, and to call them to show who truly follows the path of duty.

The birds answer that harmless acts bring benefit both here and hereafter, that acts that hurt others destroy faith, and that faith and self-restraint make sacrifice fruitful. They end by praising faith and urging Jajali to follow his own path with faith.
Bhishma says Tuladhara and Jajali both went to heaven, and that Jajali, having heard these teachings, grew calm. He asks Yudhishthira what other truths he wants to hear.

Bhishma tells of King Vichakhy, who saw a bull mangled and heard the cries of kine at a cow-slaughter sacrifice, and blessed all kine, condemning animal sacrifice and calling harmlessness the highest duty.
Yudhishthira asks how a man who wants to do no harm can keep his body alive when the body and dangers are always at odds.
Bhishma says one should gain merit where one can, so the body does not languish and death does not come early.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how a person should judge hard acts he is bound to do or to refrain from, and whether such judgment should be quick or slow.

Bhishma tells the story of Chirakarin, nicknamed for his long reflection, who was ordered by his father to kill his mother and deliberated for a long time, then concluded that she was innocent and that the father should be obeyed as well. When Gautama returned, he repented, told how Indra had come in disguise, and praised his son for his delay. The chapter closes with verses praising long reflection before acting on anger or violence.
Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect his subjects without harming anyone.
Bhishma recounts the case of Dyumatsena and his son Satyavat, where prisoners were led out for execution, and Satyavat declared that killing can never be a righteous act.
Dyumatsena argues that sparing the guilty would blur right and wrong and bring about a breakdown of the world, and asks Satyavat to explain how society could go on without punishment.

Satyavat proposes that Brahmanas guide the other orders and that offenders be corrected gently and not killed, and Dyumatsena answers that punishment has grown harsher as men have declined from the earlier ages.
Satyavat advises that sacrifice and a king's good example can restrain wrongdoers, and recounts that Manu and the Creator set out how punishment should change as righteousness fades from age to age.
Yudhishthira asks which is superior, the duties of the householder or the duties of yoga, since both lead to enjoyment and liberation.
Bhishma says both paths are good, and tells how King Nahusha was about to slaughter a cow for a guest, and how the sage Kapila cried out in dismay at the sight.
Kapila says he does not blame the Vedas, that all four stages of life lead to the same end, and asks whether there is a higher duty than harmlessness.

The cow, speaking through the sage Syumarasmi, defends sacrifice as the root of the world. It names the animals and offerings used, says sacrifice must be done without desire for reward, and states that those who do not sacrifice have neither this world nor the next.
Kapila says the Yatis gain Brahma through knowledge and self-restraint, so the householder's duties are not needed by those who have reached that end.
Syumarasmi argues that the householder life supports all the other stages, and that Vedic rites and mantras are needed for births, deaths, and offerings to the Pitris.
Kapila says that the sacrifices are difficult and their fruits are temporary, and he describes the four doors of the body and how self-control should guard speech, food, sexual conduct and anger.
Syumarasmi asks how the Vedas can both enjoin and forbid acts, and why renunciation is praised if acts are necessary.
Kapila asks what visible results come from the acts that men of action pursue, compared with the yogi's path.
Syumarasmi introduces himself as a seeker of knowledge, says he knows the Vedas and the logic that explains them, and asks what visible fruit yoga gives, as no one is free from grief or desire.
Kapila says that knowledge helps people cross the river of life and death, and warns that proud men who lack understanding fall into the darkness of tamas and its vices.
Syumarasmi agrees the scriptures teach that equity is right and grief follows unrighteousness, says that few can renounce action, and asks Kapila to teach him about Emancipation without delay.
Kapila says the Vedas are authoritative, rites cleanse the body so the twice-born can receive knowledge of Brahma, and men of old who lived by duty and self-discipline never needed expiation.
Syumarasmi asks which people, among those who give gifts, study, or renounce after enjoying wealth, reach the highest place in heaven.
Kapila says householders are auspicious and gain many blessings, but cannot enjoy the happiness that comes with renunciation.
Syumarasmi says both paths depend on a means, knowledge for renunciation and acts for householders, but both aim at Emancipation, so he asks for the truth about their relative worth.
Kapila says acts only cleanse the body, knowledge is the highest end, and he lists the qualities such as forgiveness, truthfulness and renunciation that lead to Brahma.
Yudhishthira asks which of religion, profit, and pleasure is the highest aim.
Bhishma begins the story of a poor Brahmana who wanted wealth for sacrifice, and who prayed to the cloud Kundadhara after his penances failed.
Kundadhara grants the Brahmana his prayer for virtue rather than wealth, and the gods agree, while the Brahmana cares nothing for costly cloth.
The Brahmana resolves that if no one values good deeds, he will go to the forest and live righteously.
The Brahmana does great penances, gains spiritual vision, and boasts that his word can bestow sovereignty, so Kundadhara shows him kings sunk in hell.
Kundadhara rebukes the Brahmana for his greed and asks him to look at the carnal desires that shut men out of heaven.
Bhishma says the Brahmana then sees many men enslaved by lust, wrath, greed, fear, pride, sleep, procrastination and idleness.
Kundadhara explains that these vices enchain men, that no one becomes virtuous without the gods' leave, and that the Brahmana's power comes from virtue.
The Brahmana bows and repents, Kundadhara forgives him and disappears, and Bhishma concludes that virtue, not wealth, brings the greater happiness.
Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is ordained for virtue alone, not for heaven or wealth.
Bhishma says he will relate the story Narada once told of a Brahmana who lived on gleanings and performed sacrifices.

Narada tells of the Brahmana Satya and his wife Pushkaradharini, who disapproves of his cruel rites. A deer asks to be sacrificed, the goddess Savitri urges Satya to do what the deer asks, but he refuses, and when the deer presses him Satya is tempted to slay the deer until Dharma, who had taken the deer's form, stops him, saying killing is no part of sacrifice. Narada closes by saying that abstaining from injury is the religion with the fullest reward.
Yudhishthira asks by what means a man becomes sinful or virtuous, and how he attains renunciation and liberation.

Bhishma says desire follows the senses, then attachment and greed lead to hypocrisy and sin, while the righteous man turns to knowledge, gives up even the rewards of virtue, and reaches liberation, and he ends by urging Yudhishthira to hold to virtue.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the means by which liberation is won.

Bhishma praises the question and gives the single path to liberation, with remedies for each fault: forgiveness against anger, patience against desire, knowledge against ignorance, contentment against greed, and self-control against sleep and fear, ending with the restraint of speech, body and mind without desire.
Bhishma introduces the talk between Narada and the sage Asita-Devala, who sat at ease, when Narada asked him about the origin and dissolution of creatures.
Narada asks where the universe came from and where it all goes at the great dissolution.

Asita names the five essences, adds Time, Ignorance and past acts as causes, and describes how the senses, mind and understanding work, how sleep and dreams arise, and how the Jiva migrates until knowledge frees it to reach Brahma.
Yudhishthira laments that he and his people have killed brothers, kin, friends and sons in their thirst for wealth, and asks how that thirst can be ended.

Bhishma tells of the king of Videha, who says he has nothing yet lives happily, that desire grows as wealth grows, and that giving up desire brings the highest happiness, and Mandavya, pleased, turns to liberation.
Yudhishthira asks what good he should seek, since time is running swiftly and brings terror to all creatures.
Bhishma introduces the story of Medhavin, a learned son of a Vedic father, who asks his father how to use his short life.
Medhavin asks what a wise man should do while life runs quickly, so that he may pursue virtue under his father's guidance.
The father advises study of the Vedas, household life with offspring to rescue his ancestors, sacrifice, and then life in the forest as a sage.
The son asks how his father can speak so calmly when the world is under siege by such bolts of time.
The father asks what besieges the world and what the falling bolts are, and whether his son is trying to frighten him.

The son answers that Death and decrepitude beset the world, that day and night wear away life, and that Death takes everyone without warning, so virtue should be practised now. He urges truth, a sacrifice of the self in place of ritual killing, and renunciation, and asks how his father can rest at ease.
Bhishma says the father acted as his son advised, and urges Yudhishthira to do the same, devoted to truth.
Yudhishthira asks what conduct, knowledge and devotion lead to the unchanging place of Brahma beyond Prakriti.

Bhishma describes the renouncer's life of frugality, self-control, harmlessness, and detachment, from begging and dwelling to food, praise and blame, and ends by saying the sage Harita taught this path to lasting bright regions.
Yudhishthira says that he and his brothers, though born of the gods, have endured much sorrow, and asks when he can give up sovereignty for renunciation.

Bhishma says everything has an end, even rebirth, that the soul is clouded by ignorance and desire, and introduces Vritra, who after his defeat was unmoved by grief, and whom his preceptor Usanas questions.
Vritra says he understands the coming and going of creatures, who sink into hell or rise to heaven and are reborn according to their acts, and Usanas calls his words foolish.
Vritra recalls his old penances and his battle with Indra, where he saw Narayana, and asks Usanas how high prosperity arises, how it falls away, and how a creature can attain eternal Brahma.
Bhishma tells Yudhishthira and his brothers to listen as he recounts what the sage Usanas said in reply to the Danava prince.
Usanas bows to the Lord who holds the earth and sky, and promises to speak of the greatness of Vishnu, whose head is the place of final liberation.
Sanatkumara arrives, is honoured, and at Usanas's request begins to teach Vritra about Vishnu's greatness.

Sanatkumara says the universe rests on Vishnu, who creates and withdraws all things, and that he is reached through restraint of the senses. He describes purification through many lives, the cycles of creation, the six colours that come from the three qualities, and the stages by which a soul rises and falls until it reaches Brahma.
Vritra says the teaching agrees with the truth, that his sorrow and sin are gone, and that Vishnu, who is the Supreme Soul, holds the universe.
Bhishma says Vritra then gave up his breath, joining his soul to the Supreme Soul in yoga, and so reached the highest state.
Yudhishthira asks whether Janardana (Krishna) is the illustrious Lord that Sanatkumara spoke of to Vritra.
Bhishma says the highest Deity creates all things, and that Kesava is a portion of that Supreme Lord, who is the Creator of pure soul and rests in the waters at universal dissolution.
Yudhishthira says Vritra must have foreseen his end and so was not grieved, and he asks whether he and his brothers will reach a white, pure state or a lower one.
Bhishma tells the Pandavas that they are born of a pure race and will rise to the gods' regions, then be numbered among the Siddhas, and urges them to have no fear.
Yudhishthira asks how the devoted and learned Vritra could be overcome by Indra, and asks for an account of the battle.
Bhishma describes Vritra's huge size and fearsome look, the terror of Indra's army, and the battle, in which Vritra's rocks and illusions stupefy Indra until Vasishtha restores him.
Vasishtha urges Indra not to yield to weakness, reminding him that the gods, Vishnu, and Siva are watching, and to slay his foe.
Indra is strengthened and uses yoga to dispel Vritra's illusions. Mahadeva's energy becomes a fever in Vritra's body, and Vishnu enters Indra's thunderbolt at the urging of the sages.
Mahesvara tells Indra that Vritra is hard to defeat, that Brahman granted him great powers after long penances, and that he should now slay him with the thunderbolt.
Indra vows to slay the son of Diti with his thunderbolt before the eyes of the god who gave him strength.
Bhishma says the Asuras lose their memory and their illusions vanish, the gods and sages rejoice, and Indra's form on his car is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.

Bhishma describes Vritra's symptoms under the fever, then Indra's thunderbolt kills him, and the sin of Brahmanicide, a fierce woman, comes out of his body and seizes Indra, who then hides in a lotus stalk.
Brahmanicide, seeing Brahma pleased, asks only for a dwelling place once she leaves Indra.
Brahma agrees, and calls on Agni, who appears and asks what he should do.
Brahma says he will divide the sin and asks Agni to take a fourth part of it to free Indra.
Agni asks how he himself will be freed from the sin.
Brahma tells Agni that the sin will pass to any man who, in a dull mood, refuses to make offerings to him.
Agni accepts, and Brahma summons the trees, herbs and grasses, who ask how they can be freed from the sin.
Brahma tells the trees that the sin will pass to any man who cuts or tears them on Parva days.
Brahma summons the Apsaras and asks them to take a portion of the sin for Indra's sake.
The Apsaras agree but ask how they will be freed from the bargain.
Brahma says the sin will leave them and pass to any man who has intercourse with women during their menstrual time.
The Waters come to Brahma at his summons and ask what he wants.
Brahma gives the Waters a fourth part of the sin, which came upon Indra after he slew Vritra.
The Waters ask how they may be freed, and say that Brahma is their only refuge.
Brahma says the sin will pass to any man who fouls the waters with phlegm, urine and dung.

Bhishma says Brahmanicide left Indra, who performed a horse sacrifice and was cleansed, that the cocks born of Vritra's blood are unclean food for the twice-born, and that reciting this tale on Parva days removes sin.
Yudhishthira asks how Fever arose, since Vritra was first stupefied by Fever and then slain by Indra's thunderbolt.
Bhishma describes Mount Savitri on Meru and Mahadeva seated there with Uma, attended by the gods, sages, Ganga, and the followers of Nandi.
Daksha begins a sacrifice, the gods set out for it, and Uma asks Mahadeva why they are going.
Mahadeva says that Daksha is holding a horse sacrifice and that the gods are going to it.
Uma asks why Mahadeva does not go to the sacrifice himself.
Uma repeats her question and asks what stops him from going to that place.
Mahadeva explains that the gods had agreed that he would receive no share of any sacrifice, and so they give him none.
Uma tells him he is the greatest of beings yet is denied a share, and she is filled with grief.

Mahadeva sends his followers, who destroy the sacrifice, and he chases the sacrifice in the form of a deer, and from the sweat on his brow a fierce being rises who burns it, and Brahma appears to make peace.

Brahma tells Mahadeva that he will receive a share, and that Fever should be spread among many creatures, and Mahadeva agrees and distributes Fever, and Bhishma closes by saying Vritra was first struck by it and that reading this story brings freedom from disease.
Janamejaya asks how Daksha's horse sacrifice was destroyed in the age of Vaivaswata Manu, and how Daksha reunited the divided parts of the sacrifice after Uma's grief and Mahadeva's wrath.

Vaisampayana describes Daksha's sacrifice on the breast of Himavat, to which gods, demons, spirits and sages come, and Dadhichi warns that the sacrifice is ruined because Rudra is not worshipped in it.
Daksha says he knows the eleven Rudras but does not know who this Maheswara is.
Dadhichi says that since no god is greater than Maheswara, the sacrifice will surely be ruined.
Daksha says he will offer the sacrifice to Vishnu, the Lord of all sacrifices, rather than Rudra.
Vaisampayana says that Uma, seated with her lord, then spoke.
Uma asks what gifts or penances might win Shiva a share of the offerings, and Shiva replies that she does not know him and that all sacrifices are dedicated to him.
Uma says even ordinary men praise themselves in front of their wives.
Shiva says he does not praise himself, and that he will create a being to destroy the sacrifice that has displeased her.
Shiva creates Virabhadra, who sets out with Mahakali and a host of spirits, and they wreck the sacrifice with fire, destruction and uproar, until the gods ask who he is.

Virabhadra says he is not Rudra and came only to destroy the sacrifice, sent by Rudra, with his companion who sprang from Uma's wrath. Daksha bows to Maheswara and sings his praises, and Shiva appears from the sacrificial pit and asks Daksha what he wants. The text notes that the five and a half verses of the hymn appear to be later interpolations.
Daksha asks that the wrecked and polluted offerings be made useful to him, and Shiva grants his wish, and Daksha praises him by his thousand and eight names.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to recite the names by which Daksha praised the great god.
Bhishma says he will recite the names, both secret and open, of the god of gods.

Daksha's long hymn praises Shiva in many names and forms, calling him the lord of all, the destroyer of Andhaka, the three-eyed, the source of all gods, and the one who destroyed the sacrifice in the form of a deer, and it ends with Daksha asking forgiveness for not inviting him.
A heading marks the start of the next section, CCCII.
Shiva, pleased with the praise, tells Daksha he needs no more praise, and promises him the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred Vajapeyas for this incomplete sacrifice.

Shiva consoles Daksha, says this is not the first time he has destroyed Daksha's sacrifice, and teaches him the Pasupata religion, which leads to liberation and is open to all who practise self-control. He then disappears with Uma and his followers, and Bhishma explains that the hymn brings success, long life, protection from spirits, freedom from fear, and a place among Shiva's attendants.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain what Adhyatma is with respect to man and where it arises.

Bhishma says Adhyatma explains everything, names the five great essences that create and dissolve all creatures, and explains how the senses, mind, understanding, and the three qualities arise from them, with the understanding creating the attributes while the Soul only watches. He ends by saying knowledge carries one across the flood of delusion and ends sorrow and wrongdoing.
Yudhishthira asks how sorrow and death can be prevented for living creatures.
Bhishma says he will tell the old discourse between Narada and Samanga.
Narada sees Samanga bow low to his superiors, always cheerful and untroubled, and asks how he is so free of anxiety.

Samanga says he knows the past, present and future, that all creatures live by the fruits of past acts, that wisdom comes from freedom of the senses from error, and that by long penance he has overcome desire, so grief cannot afflict him.
Yudhishthira asks what is beneficial for a man who does not know the scriptures, is always in doubt, and lacks self-restraint.

Bhishma says that serving the teacher, honouring the elders, and listening to the scriptures are of supreme benefit, and tells how Galava asks Narada which course is beneficial, since the scriptures differ.

Narada says the four stages of life each have their own duties, that true excellence lies in friendship, truth, mildness, and study, that boasting and idleness are faults, and that a man should live among righteous people, under a just king, and away from places of sin, and that the highest good is hard to state.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave, keeping the highest aim in view, and what qualities keep him free from attachment.
Bhishma says he will recite the old teaching that Arishtanemi gave to Sagara when Sagara asked for his counsel.
Sagara asks what good will bring happiness here and how one can avoid grief and agitation.

Arishtanemi says liberation is true happiness, which ignorant men who cling to children, animals and wealth cannot see. He advises raising children, enjoying the senses in measure, and letting go of attachments, since each creature lives and suffers by its own acts. He then lists the marks of the freed man: contentment, equal regard for all, awareness of death and disease, and detachment from pleasure and pain. Sagara follows this teaching and rules well.
Yudhishthira asks why Usanas sided with the Asuras against the gods, how he got the name Sukra, and why he cannot reach the middle of the sky.

Bhishma says Usanas robbed Kubera of his wealth by entering him through yoga, and that when Kubera complained to Shiva, Shiva raised his lance, Usanas sat on its tip, Shiva bent the lance into his bow Pinaka, and swallowed Usanas.
Yudhishthira asks how Usanas could move about inside Shiva's stomach, and what Shiva did while he was there.

Bhishma says Shiva sat in meditation in the waters for ages, then Brahma came to ask after him. Inside, Usanas kept praying for a way out, and Shiva told him to leave by the urethra, and he came out shining and was named Sukra.
Uma tells Shiva that the Brahmana has become her son and that one who comes out of his stomach should not be slain.
Shiva, calmed by Uma, lets Usanas go, and Bhishma says he has told the story of the Bhargava as Yudhishthira asked.
Yudhishthira asks what good acts a man should do to gain benefit in this world and the next, saying he never tires of Bhishma's words.
Bhishma says King Janaka asked the sage Parasara what is beneficial for all creatures, and Parasara answered to please the king.

Parasara says that righteousness through right action is the highest good, that the four classes each have their duties, and that every creature takes its fate from its own past acts. He answers the sceptic who denies this, says the acts of eye, mind, tongue and limbs bear fruit, and lists the virtues that bring happiness. He ends by saying that a man must not do what he would censure in others, and that those who fail in their duties deserve pity.

Parasara says the wise man steers his body and senses with the reins of knowledge, that sins done knowingly bring sorrow while those done in ignorance can be expiated, that deliberate acts increase merit, and that kings should protect their subjects, while those in later life should retire to the forest and treat all creatures as themselves.

Parasara says that people mostly act for themselves, that gifts and fair wealth bring merit, that a man owes debts to the Rishis, gods, Pitris, fellow men, servants and himself, and that parents, the sacred fire and the teacher must be honoured.

Parasara explains that the Sudra should serve the higher classes and keep company with good people, that the Vaishya farms and tends cattle, the Kshatriya protects, the Brahmana studies, and each class gains respect by keeping to its duty, and he explains that gifts made with respect bring the greatest merit.

Parasara explains the lawful livelihoods of each class, warns against trades that are censured, tells how men's pride, wrath and desire grew until Shiva destroyed the three Asura chiefs, and then how the seven Rishis appointed Indra and kings, and urges avoiding harm and seeking knowledge of the Soul.

Parasara explains that householders grow attached to wealth and kin, that despair leads to awakening, study and penance, that penance is open to all, that penance done for fruit brings misery, and that householders should do their duties with effort, since they are the refuge of all other orders.
Janaka asks why men of different classes differ in colour, since the Srutis say all offspring are the father himself and all men sprang from Brahmanas.
Parasara says the classes arose when penance declined, that the Lord created the four classes from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, and that mixed castes arose from their intermixture.
Janaka asks how men of mixed birth came to be Brahmanas, if all were of one origin.
Parasara says sages born of mixed wombs became Rishis through penance, names several such sages, and says the Gotras were founded by the penances of their founders.
Janaka asks Parasara to tell him the special duties of each class and their common duties.

Parasara lists the special duties: Brahmanas accept gifts, sacrifice and teach, Kshatriyas protect, Vaishyas farm, rear cattle and trade, and Sudras serve the higher classes. He then lists common duties such as compassion, truthfulness, hospitality and self-restraint, and says even a virtuous Sudra is to be honoured.
Janaka asks whether a man is stained by his acts or by the class in which he is born.
Parasara says both can stain a man, but acts stain him more than birth does.
Janaka asks which acts are righteous and do no harm to other creatures.
Parasara says that those who give up domestic fire and attachment, and climb the path of yoga, reach liberation, and that all classes gain heaven by truthful and righteous conduct.

Parasara speaks at length on devotion to elders, the rules of battle for Kshatriyas, the dissolution of the body and the roving soul's rebirth, the righteous and sinful deaths, ignorance as the chief foe, the four stages of life, the value of human birth, kindness to all creatures, sacred places, cremation rites, and the Vedas being for the stainless.
Bhishma says the high-souled sage spoke all this to the ruler of the Videhas in days of old for his benefit.
Bhishma says Janaka, king of Mithila, again questioned the sage Parasara about all duties.
Janaka asks what is good, what is the best path for living creatures, what is never destroyed, and where one need not return.

Parasara answers that detachment and knowledge are the highest good, that harmlessness is the greatest gift, that sin clings only to the attached, that family and wealth cannot help after death, and that each creature bears the fruit of its past acts.
Bhishma says Janaka received the sage's teaching in the way the sage gave it.
Janaka, the foremost of the righteous, hears everything the Rishi says.
Janaka hears the sage's words and gains great happiness from them.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what he thinks of truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and wisdom, which learned men praise.
Bhishma says Brahma, the unborn Lord, took the form of a golden swan and wandered the three worlds until he came upon the Sadhyas.
The Sadhyas call themselves deities, say they have heard that the swan is learned, and ask what is the highest object and the one act that frees one from bonds.

The swan says one should practise austerity, self-restraint, truth and mental control, avoid wounding others with cruel words, meet insults with forgiveness, hold forgiveness and truth as the highest virtues, and treat truth as the only way to heaven.
The Sadhyas ask what covers the world, why people fail to shine, why they cast off friends, and why they fail to reach heaven.
The swan says ignorance covers the world, malice keeps men from shining, covetousness makes them abandon friends, and attachment keeps them from heaven.
The Sadhyas ask who among Brahmanas is always happy, who keeps silence amid many, who is strong though weak, and who avoids quarrels.
The swan answers that the wise man among Brahmanas is each of these.
The Sadhyas ask where the divinity, purity, impurity and humanity of Brahmanas lie.
The swan answers that divinity lies in Vedic study, purity in vows and observances, impurity in reproach, and humanity in death.
Bhishma ends the discourse by saying that the body is the seat of acts and that the Jiva is truth.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the difference between the Sankhya and Yoga systems of philosophy.

Bhishma says each school praises its own view and gives reasons for it, that the Yogins hold that one who denies God cannot be freed, and that both systems are approved, both require purity, compassion and vows, and they differ mainly in the scriptures they follow.
Yudhishthira asks why, if the vows, purity and fruits are the same, the scriptures of the two systems differ.

Bhishma says that the Yogin who casts off five faults breaks free, that the strong Yogin escapes the world's nets as a large fish or bird does while the weak are caught, that a strong Yogin can create many bodies, and that meditation like a bowman's aim, a boatman's steady hand, or a charioteer's control brings liberation, with the Jiva joined to the subtle Soul at parts of the body.
Yudhishthira asks what diet and what conquests give a Yogin his power.

Bhishma lists diets, from broken rice and barley to water and milk taken at longer and longer intervals and abstention from meat, and the mastery of desire, anger, fear and sleep that Yoga needs. He describes the Yoga path as a dangerous road that few can walk, and says its highest fruit is union with Brahma, through which the Yogin can enter the gods, the elements and all creatures.
Closing line: the second part of the Santi Parva ends here.
Yudhishthira praises the account of Yoga he has heard and asks Bhishma to now explain the Sankhya principles.

Bhishma calls the Sankhya doctrine faultless and lists the wise who hold it, then describes their knowledge of the world's faults, the three qualities and the chain of elements leading up to Narayana.
Yudhishthira asks what faults Bhishma sees in the body and asks for a full and true answer.
Bhishma names five bodily faults, explains how each is overcome, and describes the ocean of life that the wise cross to reach the Supreme Soul.
Yudhishthira asks whether the liberated keep memory and consciousness, noting that the answer bears on the two ways of life and on what deep sleep is.
Bhishma calls the question proper but hard, explains that the senses serve the soul and rest in sleep, and says a freed soul merges into Brahma and does not return.

Bhishma says Sankhya knowledge feeds all other learning, that its adherents rise to godly status or to Brahma, and that the wise man who masters it becomes like Narayana, who creates and reabsorbs the universe in cycles.
Yudhishthira asks what the Undeteriorating and the Deteriorating are, and says he wants to hear it all from Bhishma while Bhishma still has time to teach.
Bhishma tells the old story of Vasishtha and king Karala, who asks Vasishtha about the supreme Brahma and what the universe returns to at its destruction.
Vasishtha describes the measure of the cosmic days, the creation of Hiranyagarbha, and the elements and senses that make up every living body, all of which he calls destructible.
Vasishtha names Vishnu as the twenty-fifth principle beyond the twenty-four, and explains how the soul, joined to Prakriti, takes on the three qualities and so falls into different destinies.
Vasishtha describes the forgetful soul's endless births and sufferings, the many ascetic and worldly roles it takes on, and the cycle of acts driven by Prakriti.
Vasishtha compares Jiva to the moon's sixteen portions, fifteen subject to change and one pure, and says emancipation means release from union with Prakriti.
Janaka compares the union of male and female to that of Purusha and Prakriti, asks how Emancipation can then exist, and asks for direct evidence of it.

Vasishtha says memorized texts without understanding are of no use, then argues that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same truth, that the Supreme Soul is beyond attributes, and that unity and multiplicity mark the two kinds of being.
Janaka admits he has not grasped unity and multiplicity and asks Vasishtha to explain again the knower, Jiva, knowledge, ignorance, and the Sankhya and Yoga systems in detail.
Vasishtha describes Yoga as contemplation through concentration and breath control, the stillness it demands, and the Supreme Soul that the Yogin sees shining in the heart.

Vasishtha sets out the Sankhya principles from Prakriti down to the senses, their dissolution in reverse order, and the distinction between Kshetra, Kshetrajna and Purusha, and says that one who knows the Soul does not return to the world.

Vasishtha defines knowledge and ignorance through the principles, explains why both Prakriti and the Jiva are called indestructible and destructible, and gives the Jiva's lament at its bondage to Prakriti.
Vasishtha says Sankhya and Yoga teach the same knowledge, that it can awaken any listener, and that Yoga speaks of Brahma and the Jiva as two only because of ignorance.

Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, explains how the Jiva is freed by recognizing itself as distinct from Prakriti, and says that a soul takes on the qualities of whatever it unites with.
Vasishtha lists the kinds of people who may and may not receive this knowledge, calls on Karala to be fearless, and says he received the teaching from Hiranyagarbha.
Bhishma closes by tracing the teaching from Hiranyagarbha through Vasishtha and Narada to himself, and tells the king that knowledge of Kshara and Akshara frees him from ignorance.
King Vasuman, of Janaka's race, meets a Rishi of Bhrigu's line in the forest and asks what benefits a man with an unstable body and strong desires.
The Rishi advises restraint, righteous conduct, honest gifts, purity, patience and firmness, and keeping company with the virtuous.
Vasuman accepts the counsel and sets his mind on righteousness.
A section heading marking the start of Section CCCXI.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach him about what is beyond duty, doubt, birth and death, and is eternal and free from effort.
Bhishma introduces an old dialogue between Yajnavalkya and king Daivarati of Janaka's race, who asks the Rishi a question.
The king asks how many kinds of senses and Prakriti there are, what the Unmanifest and highest Brahma are, and what birth, death and the limits of age mean.
Yajnavalkya names the eight Prakriti principles and sixteen modifications, then gives the stages of creation that make up the twenty-four principles.

Yajnavalkya gives the length of Brahma's day and night, describes his emergence from a golden egg, the creation of the elements and the qualities of sound and touch, and says the mind directs the senses.
Yajnavalkya describes the dissolution of creation, from Maharudra's fire through the absorption of each element into Sambhu, and then announces the three frames of teaching.

Yajnavalkya pairs each sense and faculty with its inner organ, outer object and presiding deity, then describes how Prakriti multiplies the three qualities and lists the traits of Sattwa, Rajas and Tamas.
Yajnavalkya explains how the three qualities mix to decide where a being is reborn, and that Prakriti acts only when presided over by Purusha, who remains unchanged.
Janaka asks how Prakriti can be inanimate while Purusha is intelligent, and asks for teaching on Emancipation, Sankhya, Yoga, and the signs of approaching death.

Yajnavalkya explains that Purusha seems to take on attributes but is in truth beyond them, that Prakriti seems alive only through union with him, and that the two are distinct, as shown by images like the worm in the fig and the fish in water.

Yajnavalkya presents Yoga as one with Sankhya, describes breath and sense control, the eight powers and the two kinds of practice, and portrays the calm of one absorbed in Samadhi who beholds the Supreme Soul.

Yajnavalkya links each exit point of the soul at death to a heavenly region, then lists the signs that foretell death within a year, six months, a week or a day, and advises the wise to unite with the Supreme Soul.
Yajnavalkya tells how Surya granted him the Yajush texts, how Saraswati entered him, and how he received the Satapatha Brahmana and taught it to his disciples.
Yajnavalkya says he taught fifty branches of learning, then recounts the Gandharva Viswavasu's long list of questions on the universe, Vedic lore and Vidya.
Viswavasu asks Yajnavalkya to discourse again on the Jiva and the Supreme Soul, naming many earlier teachers whose views he has heard.
Yajnavalkya explains that Prakriti is known by Jiva, that Purusha is unchanging and distinct from Prakriti, and that Vedic study without this knowledge is a useless burden.
Viswavasu praises Yajnavalkya's answers and blesses him.
Viswavasu departs and spreads the teaching, and Yajnavalkya says liberation comes from knowledge, which is open to every order of people.
Bhishma describes king Daivarati's gifts, his handing of the kingdom to his son, his life as a renunciant, and his teaching that the Supreme must be known and the Soul is its own possession.
Yudhishthira asks whether penance, ritual, knowledge of the Srutis or medicine can prevent decrepitude and death, after great power and wealth.
Bhishma tells of Janaka's question to the sage Panchasikha, who answers that time sweeps all creatures on, and that only the path of renunciation escapes birth and death.
Yudhishthira asks how one can gain Emancipation without leaving the householder's life, and how the gross and subtle bodies are cast off.
Bhishma tells of king Dharmadhyaja, devoted to renunciation, whose fame leads the mendicant Sulabha to take a beautiful form by Yoga, visit his court and bind his mind to hers.
Janaka asks who Sulabha is, says he is a disciple of Panchasikha, argues that kingship does not bar freedom, and rebukes her conduct and her motive.
Bhishma says Sulabha is not abashed by the rebuke.
Sulabha replies with a long argument on the rules of debate, the limits of kingship, the separateness of souls, and her own birth and purpose in coming to the king.
Bhishma says that Janaka, hearing these words, could not reply.
Yudhishthira asks how Suka, son of Vyasa, was won over to renunciation, and asks for teaching on the Unmanifest, the Manifest and Brahma.
Vyasa, seeing his son careless, urges him to master the senses, practise truth and righteousness, honour the wise, and prepare for death, which will take him alone with only his deeds.
Suka, moved by his father's words, leaves to seek a teacher who can teach the path to liberation.
Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penances and service to elders have real efficacy, and asks Bhishma to speak of it.
Bhishma says evil conduct brings poverty and fear, while faith, self-restraint and generosity bring joy, and that every deed follows its doer and ripens at its proper time.
Yudhishthira asks how Suka was born, how he came to be drawn to Brahma as a boy, and how he reached his goal.
Bhishma says merit lies in restraining the senses, and tells how Vyasa, meditating on Mahadeva on Mount Meru, asks for a son and is granted one.

Bhishma tells how Vyasa's desire for the apsara Ghritachi leads to Suka's birth from the fire-sticks, how the gods celebrate, and how Suka masters the Vedas under Vrihaspati before turning toward liberation.
Vyasa sends Suka to king Janaka, Suka walks to Mithila, is tested by palace women, and spends the night absorbed in Yoga.
Janaka receives Suka with honour, offering a costly seat, water, and kine, and asks the purpose of his visit.
Suka says his father sent him to learn the duties of a Brahmana and the path to Emancipation, and asks whether knowledge or penance leads there.
Janaka describes the stages of a Brahmana's life, from study and household life to forest life and renunciation.
Suka asks whether a man with a purified understanding must still pass through the stages of life.

Janaka says understanding and true knowledge are required, that a teacher is the helmsman and knowledge the boat, and that Suka already has the knowledge and has passed beyond the objects of the senses.
Suka goes north to the Himalayas, passing scenes of Skanda's dart and Mahadeva's penance, and reports his conversation with Janaka to his father Vyasa, who is teaching disciples there.
The disciples ask Vyasa for a boon that no sixth disciple should share the Vedas, and Vyasa sets out rules on who may receive Vedic teaching and how it should be given.
Vyasa's disciples leave to teach and perform sacrifices among people, and Vyasa is left alone with Suka, troubled, until Narada arrives.
Narada says the silence of Vedic recitation has robbed the mountain of its beauty, and Vyasa asks what he should do.
Narada says the stain of the Vedas is the halting of their recitation, and urges Vyasa to recite with his son and drive away the fears caused by Rakshasas.
A violent wind interrupts their recitation, and Vyasa treats it as an omen, then explains the winds and the two paths of the gods and the fathers after death.
When the wind has passed, Vyasa tells Suka to resume reciting and goes off to bathe in the Ganges.
Narada visits Suka, who honours him and asks what will help him most.

Narada, recalling Sanatkumara, urges Suka to restrain desire and wrath, drop attachment, meet all creatures with friendship, and cross the river of life by the boat of the body, casting off even the understanding through knowledge of the Supreme Soul.
Narada advises that wisdom lets a person avoid grieving over the past, that grief doubles sorrow, and that contentment, guarding the senses and finding peace in the self bring happiness.
Narada describes the uncertainty of fortune, the sufferings of birth and disease, and the soul's passage from one body to the next, and says that the deities were once men taught to leave the Earth.
Suka weighs this teaching, decides to reach an eternal state through Yoga, resolves to enter the sun, and departs for Kailasa after taking leave of his father, who asked him to stay.
Suka sits in Yoga on a mountain peak, sees his own soul freed from attachment, and begins his Yoga practice.
Suka tells Narada that he has seen the path to Emancipation and asks for his blessing.
Suka rises through the sky, passes the Apsaras and Urvasi, and asks the world to answer his father's calls once he is gone, and they agree.

Bhishma describes Suka's passing into Brahma with cosmic omens, Vyasa's grief at a son who answers only as an echo, and Mahadeva's consolation that the son's fame will last and his shadow will remain with Vyasa.
Yudhishthira asks who is the highest deity and Pitri, what rites should be performed, and how one attains heaven and Emancipation.
Bhishma says the question is a deep mystery and recounts how Narada visited Narayana and Nara at their hermitage, after Narayana took fourfold form as the sons of Dharma.
Narada praises Narayana as unborn, eternal and the source of the universe, and asks whom Narayana worships.
Narayana explains that the inner soul, Kshetrajna, beyond the three qualities is the highest object of worship, that unmanifest Prakriti is its companion, and that the Prajapatis obeyed this law.
A section heading marking the start of Section CCCXXXVI.
Bhishma says that Narada, after Narayana's teaching, addresses Narayana for the good of the world.
Narada asks Narayana's leave to see his original nature, then goes to the White Island and describes its inhabitants, who have no senses, do not eat, and have winkless eyes.
Yudhishthira asks how the White Island people were born, what end they reach, and whether emancipated men share their marks.
Bhishma tells of King Uparichara, a devotee of Narayana, and how the seven seers, at Narayana's command, compose a treatise on duties that is to be passed down through Vrihaspati.
Bhishma tells how Vrihaspati became the priest of king Uparichara's Horse-sacrifice, where no animals were slain, and how Hari took his share unseen, angering Vrihaspati.
Yudhishthira asks why Hari alone took his share invisibly when the other deities appeared openly.

The Sadasyas calm Vrihaspati, and the sons of Brahman describe their penance, their journey to the White Island and the voice that told them that only the favour of its people brings the sight of Narayana, and the chapter ends with Vasu's fall and rise.
Yudhishthira asks why king Vasu, so devoted to Narayana, fell from heaven and was sunk into the earth.
Bhishma recounts an old debate in which the gods urge that goats be sacrificed, since the word aja is understood to mean a goat.
The Rishis reply that the Vedas call for seed offerings and that slaughter cannot be the religion of the Krita age.
Vasu comes through the sky, and the gods and Rishis ask him to judge which kind of offering is right.
The Rishis say sacrifices should use grain, while the gods say animals, and both sides ask Vasu to decide.
Vasu sides with the gods and is cursed to fall from heaven; the gods then provide for him, and Narayana sends Garuda to lift him back to the sky.
Bhishma says he has told the origin of the spiritual sons of Brahman and now turns to Narada's journey to the White Island.
Narada reaches the White Island, is honoured by its people, and begins silent recitation and Yoga there with his arms raised.
Narada's long hymn praises Narayana through a litany of names and forms, as the soul beyond attributes, the source of the Vedas, sacrifices and the gods, and ends with his wish to behold him.
Narayana appears to Narada in a wondrous universal form with a thousand eyes, many heads and arms, and holding the emblems of sacrifice.
Narayana tells Narada that he has been devoted and that the sages Ekata, Dwita and Trita could not see him, then promises him a boon.
Narada says that seeing Narayana is the highest boon, and calls him the Lord whose eye is the universe.
Narayana explains his nature as the Purusha beyond the attributes, the source and dissolution of the universe, his fourfold form, and his descents as boar, man-lion, Rama, Krishna and Kalki.
Narayana vanishes, and Narada goes to Vadari and later repeats the teaching in Brahman's abode.
Yudhishthira asks why Brahman, the Creator, was unaware of Narayana's greatness, which Narada had made known.
Bhishma explains that Brahman honours Narayana as supreme, traces how the narrative passed through Surya, the sages, Asita and Santanu, and says hearing it with devotion leads to the highest end.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira and his brothers became devoted to Narayana, and that Vyasa chanted Narayana's name and returned to his hermitage.
Bhishma closes by saying he has repeated the narrative he heard from his father.
Suta closes the frame, saying that Janamejaya was guided by the recitation and that the listeners at Saunaka's sacrifice in Naimisha should worship Narayana.
Saunaka asks why Narayana, who ordains abstention, also makes the deities takers of shares in sacrifice.
Sauti says he will recite what Vaisampayana told king Janamejaya when the king asked the same question.
Janamejaya asks why the gods, who take shares in sacrifice, have not turned to the path of liberation, and asks for the reason.
Vaisampayana says that Vyasa answered this doubt by describing creation from the Supreme Soul through Aniruddha, the eight Prakritis and the Rudras, and the gods' request to Brahman for their roles.
Brahman tells the gods to seek guidance from the unmanifest Being, and they go to the Ocean of Milk and perform severe penance for a thousand years.
Narayana speaks to the assembled gods, promising to increase their strength and granting them shares in sacrifice.
Vaisampayana says the gods and Brahman hold a sacrifice to Vishnu, who accepts the offerings unseen and promises that human sacrifices will give the gods their shares.
The gods ask where they should go when righteousness declines in the coming ages.
Narayana answers that the gods should seek places where the Vedas, sacrifices, penance and truth still flourish, and that sin will not touch them there.
Vyasa says that Brahman, left alone, sees Narayana appear with a horse's head, and Narayana embraces him.
Narayana charges Brahman with the ordering of creation, promises to appear in incarnate forms when needed, and vanishes, and Brahman returns to his own region.
Vaisampayana closes by saying that whoever hears or recites this discourse with devotion gains health, wealth, sons and fulfilment of desires.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to explain the meanings of the names by which Vyasa and his disciples hymned Hari.
Vaisampayana says that Arjuna once asked Krishna about the meaning of some of his names.
Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the names found in the Vedas and Puranas, since none but Krishna can do so.

Krishna explains that his names come from his nature and deeds, names Narayana, Vasudeva, Vishnu, Damodara and Kesava, and says that he and Rudra are one, and that the best worshippers seek him alone.
Arjuna asks how Agni and Soma came to share one original nature.
Krishna recounts the origin of Agni and Soma from Brahman, the honour of Brahmanas, and the stories of Indra's sins, Viswarupa's death, Nahusha's fall and Indra's restoration.
Krishna tells more stories, including Soma's curse and the marks on the moon, and explains many of his own names, such as Hari, Govinda, Krishna and Kapila.
Arjuna asks who won the battle between Rudra and Narayana.
Krishna describes the omens of the battle, Brahma's plea to stop it, and the peace in which Narayana and Rudra mark each other's bodies.
Krishna says that Rudra is his wrath-born form, that the two are one, and that Arjuna should bow to Rudra, who first slew the foes Arjuna has defeated.
Saunaka praises the story, says that talk of Narayana outweighs pilgrimages, and asks why Narada went back to Vadari after seeing Aniruddha.
Sauti says that Janamejaya, during his snake sacrifice, asked Vyasa the question that Saunaka has raised.
Janamejaya's question itself: what Narada did after White Island, how long he stayed at Vadari, and what the two sages said to him. He praises the Narayana teaching as drawn from the Bharata.
Vaisampayana begins the tale. Narada travels from White Island to Meru and Gandhamadana, reaches Vadari, and finds the two sages with their marks and penances. They welcome and honour him.
Nara and Narayana ask Narada whether he has seen the Supreme Soul on White Island.

Narada says he saw the immutable Being on White Island and sees the same marks in Nara and Narayana. He describes the devotion of the White Island folk, and says he came back under the Lord's orders to stay with them.

Nara and Narayana praise Narada for seeing Narayana and explain that the elements arise from the Lord, with each linked to a sense or quality. They describe the stages by which the liberated enter Vasudeva, and say they were born in Dharma's house to serve the Lord's future manifestations.
Vaisampayana says Narada joined his hands, devoted himself to Narayana, recited mantras, and stayed at Vadari for a thousand celestial years.
Vaisampayana says that Narada, having finished the rites for the deities, begins the rites for the Pitris. Nara asks what he is worshipping and what he hopes to gain.

Narada replies that worship of the deities is the highest sacrifice and equal to worshipping the eternal Supreme Soul. He explains that Narayana is father, mother, and grandfather of all, and recalls how sons and sires once exchanged their knowledge of the Srutis and offered each other Pindas. He asks why the Pitris are called Pindas.

Nara and Narayana explain that the Earth was submerged and that Govinda, as a boar, raised her up. Afterwards Vishnu shook three balls of mud from his tusk, set them on grass, and offered them with sesame.

The god Vrishakapi, the same Vishnu in the story, declares that the three balls are the Pitris, and that he is their father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. He offers them with rites and then vanishes, which is why the Pitris are called Pindas. The passage closes by saying Narayana is the soul of all things.
Narada returns to his own retreat, and Vaisampayana tells Janamejaya that hating Narayana brings ruin, that Vyasa is Narayana on earth, and that the horse sacrifice should go on.

Sauti says the king carried out the sacrificial rites, notes that Narada first recited this teaching before a large audience including the Pandavas, Krishna, and Bhishma, and then praises Narayana at length.
Janamejaya recalls what he has heard about Narayana's births and the boar, and asks why the horse-headed form appeared in the northeastern ocean and what Brahma did after seeing it.
Sauti says he will tell the same old story that Vaisampayana once told at the snake sacrifice, since Janamejaya had asked the same question then.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana directly why Hari took the horse-headed form that Brahma saw on the northern shore.
Vaisampayana describes the world dissolving into primal Darkness, Brahma arising from Aniruddha to create, and two demons born from drops in the lotus seizing the Vedas and diving into the ocean.
Brahma laments that the Vedas are gone, asks who will restore them, and begins to praise Hari with joined hands.
Brahma praises Narayana, who then takes a horse-headed form, recovers the Vedas, and kills the demons Madhu and Kaitabha, earning the name Madhusudana.

Vaisampayana closes by calling this horse-headed form the oldest of Narayana's forms, says that reciting its story preserves learning, and presents Narayana as the source and refuge of the Vedas, Yoga, Sankhya, and all qualities.
Janamejaya says that Hari favours those devoted to him, that devotion may be superior to knowledge, and asks who first taught it, what its practices are, and when they began.

Vaisampayana says the teaching is hard to grasp, came from Narayana in the Krita age, and passed through Brahma's many births and a long line of Rishis and kings to Ikshaku, reaching the speaker through Narada and Vyasa.
Janamejaya asks why many learned Brahmins follow other vows and rites instead of this path.
Vaisampayana says people have three dispositions, that the Sattwa type is nearest to liberation, that liberation depends on Narayana, and that those of mixed or dull nature do not receive his favour.
Janamejaya asks how a being subject to change can reach the Supreme Purusha, and asks for the path of Pravritti to be explained in order.

Vaisampayana says the highest goal lies in giving up action, that the Sankhya, Aranyaka, and Pancharatra teachings form one whole, and that the teaching was passed to Yudhishthira through Narada and Vyasa. He ends by calling it hard to practise and naming Krishna as protector and destroyer of the universe.
Janamejaya asks whether the Sankhya, Pancharatra, and Aranyaka systems preach the same duties or different ones, and asks for an account of Pravritti.
Vaisampayana bows to Vyasa, son of Satyavati and Parasara, and calls him a portion of Narayana and the inexhaustible source of the Vedas.
Janamejaya asks how Vyasa, whose lineage he has already heard, could be a son of Narayana, and asks for the story of that birth.
Vaisampayana says that Vyasa, weary after composing the Mahabharata, was attended by his disciples on the Himalayas, and that they asked him to explain the Vedas and his own birth.

Vyasa tells his disciples that in the Krita age Narayana created Brahma, then took many forms to lighten the Earth, and appointed the sage Apantaratamas to arrange the Vedas, foretelling that he would be reborn as Vyasa. Vyasa adds that he is that same sage.
Vaisampayana names the founders of the Sankhya, Yoga, Pancharatra, Vedic, and Pasupata cults, and says that all of them treat Narayana as the one object of worship.
