Janamejaya asks whether there are many Purushas or one, who is the foremost of them, and what is the source of all things.

Vaisampayana says the Sankhya and Yoga schools speak of many Purushas that share one origin in the Supreme Purusha. He then begins the tale of Brahma's discourse with Mahadeva on the mountain Vaijayanta.
Brahma welcomes his son Mahadeva after a long absence and asks about his penances and his study of the Vedas.
Mahadeva says all is well and asks why Brahma has withdrawn to a lonely mountain away from his heavenly home.
Brahma says that he has made Vaijayanta his home and meditates there on the one universal Purusha.
Mahadeva notes that many Purushas have been created and asks which Purusha Brahma is meditating on.
Brahma answers that the many Purushas rest on one Purusha, who is beyond all attributes, and that those who shed their attributes can enter into him.

Brahma describes the one Purusha as eternal, unseen by the undisciplined, present in all bodies, and known as Kshetrajna, then explains that he is Narayana, the Supreme Soul, in the fourfold form, and that Brahma himself and all the Vedas come from him.
Sauti says Vaisampayana, after praising Narayana to Janamejaya, now recounts Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma in the presence of the Pandavas, the Rishis, and Krishna.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to say which duties are foremost for persons in each mode of life, having already heard about the religion of liberation.
Bhishma says every duty can lead to heaven if performed well, then says this question was once discussed by Narada and Indra, and that he will repeat that story.

Bhishma describes a learned, virtuous Brahmin of Atri's line in the city of Mahapadma, with a large family, who is troubled about which of three kinds of duty to follow, and who then receives a guest.
The host tells the guest he wants to give his household to his son and seek liberation, but is held back by attachment, and he asks what path he should take.
Bhishma says the guest, a wise Brahmin, answered the host in a gentle voice.

The guest says he is equally confused and lists many routes to heaven, including renunciation, sacrifice, study, truth, and battle, concluding that his own understanding has been clouded by the question.

The guest says he will still try to instruct the host, names the Naga Padmanabha in a city of Nagas in the Naimisha forest by the Gomati, and lists his many virtues as a guide who is generous, learned, and fair.
The host says he feels as relieved as a weary traveller or a thirsty man who finds water, promises to act on the guest's advice, and invites him to rest for the night.
Bhishma says the two talk through the night about renunciation, and in the morning the host sends his guest off and sets out for the Naga's home with his mind fixed on it.
The Brahmin travels through forests and holy waters, asks an ascetic about the Naga, and arrives at the Naga's house, where the Naga's chaste wife greets him as a guest.
The Brahmin says he is well received and has come only to see her husband.
The wife explains that her husband is pulling the Sun's car for a month and will be back in fifteen days, and offers to help in other ways.
The Brahmin says he will wait on the bank of the Gomati, living on simple food, and asks her to tell the Naga he has come, which he repeats.

Bhishma says the Naga's relatives, including his brother, children, and wife, come to the Brahmin on the Gomati, see him fasting and reciting mantras, and beg him to eat, saying his fast reflects badly on them.
The Brahmin says he will break his fast after eight more days, if the Naga is still away, and asks the relatives to go home and not to disturb his vow.
Bhishma says the Naga comes home after finishing his work for the Sun, and asks his wife whether she has kept up the worship of gods and guests and remained virtuous in his absence.

The wife says she has kept her duties, lists the duties of disciples, Brahmins, servants, kings, Kshatriyas, Sudras, and householders, and reports that the Brahmin is waiting by the Gomati, urging the Naga to go to him.
The Naga asks his wife whether the Brahmin could be a god in disguise, since humans seldom seek out the Nagas, and says Nagas are hard for humans to see.

The wife says the guest is not a god who lives on air, that he sincerely reveres her husband, and that a man must not turn a guest away. She lists the merits of generosity, truth, and duty, and urges him to see the Brahmin.
The Naga says her words have calmed his wrath, cites Ravana, the sons of Kartavirya, and Kartavirya himself as examples of wrath's downfall, and resolves to go and speak with the Brahmin.
Bhishma says the Naga goes to the waiting Brahmin, wondering what business brought him, and greets him kindly, asking whom he worships in this quiet spot.
The Brahmin, named Dharmaranya, says he came to see the Naga Padmanabha on some business, and has been reciting the Vedas and practising yoga while he waits.
The Naga says he is the Naga the Brahmin seeks, praises his conduct, and offers to do whatever is asked of him, since the Brahmin's merit has bound them to him.
The Brahmin says he seeks to reach the Supreme Soul through the individual soul, and asks the Naga first to answer a question about the wonders he has seen before he states his request.
The Brahmin asks the Naga, who pulls the Sun's car in turn, to describe any wonder he has seen on his journeys.

The Naga describes the Sun's wonders, including the wind, the rains, and the Soul said to dwell in the solar disc, then tells of a shining being that approached the Sun at noon and merged into him, leaving the Nagas unable to say which was which.

Surya explains that the being is neither a god, an Asura, nor a Naga, but a Brahmin who reached the Sun's disc through the Unccha vow and devotion to Mahadeva, and who still circles the Earth from there.
Editor's note: there was no section CCLXIV in the source edition.
The Brahmin thanks the Naga for his teaching, says he is satisfied, and asks to be remembered and sent for now and then.
The Naga asks what business brought the Brahmin, says he should stay, since he and the Brahmin are now friends.
The Brahmin agrees that the Naga is equal to the gods in wisdom, says his doubt is resolved through the Unccha vow, and takes his leave.
Bhishma says the Brahmin went to the sage Chyavana to be initiated into the Unccha life, and traces the story through Janaka, Narada, Indra, and the Vasus to himself.
Closing line: the end of the Santi Parva.

Note 820: the note explains na in the verse as the nominative of nri, meaning the dreamer, and praises Nilakantha's ingenuity.
Note 821: dreamless sleep is a temporary dissociation of soul from mind and senses caused by Tamas, and differs from the eternal felicity of liberation.
Note 822: liberation is untouched by darkness, though it may seem like dreamless sleep, and the verse says no trace of sorrow is seen in it.
Note 823: in both sleep and liberation the qualities are discarded, and swakarmapratyayah refers to rebirth from past acts.
Note 824: creatures exist through Avidya, desire, and acts, and the note asks how the eternal soul could be called destructible, which it treats as an unanswerable question.
Note 825: the gross body dissolves into the subtle, the subtle into the potential form, and that into the Supreme Soul.
Note 826: merit and sin are destroyed when one is unattached and practises abstention, and the phrase refers to Saguna Brahma.
Note 827: urnanabha means a worm that spins thread, here a silk-worm, which completes the analogy.
Note 828: the Burdwan rendering of nipatyasaktah is wrong, and K.P. Singha gives the sense but changes another word.
Note 829: samudayah is explained as hetu, cause.
Note 830: the verse refers to giving food and clothes to the poor and needy in times of scarcity.
Note 831: the reading vrataluvdhah is preferred, and the Bengal reading would mean that men are deceived by their vows.
Note 832: Bhishma's two answers show that giving pain to others, such as sacrificing animals, and giving pain to oneself are both censurable.
Note 833: existence and non-existence both come into being and cease, meaning all phenomena appear and disappear.
Note 834: this refers to the theory that the soul is really inactive amid its seeming activity.
Note 835: the Burdwan rendering of the second line is wrong, since it has Gandharvas dance before thee.
Note 836: both vernacular translators misread the verse; Vali circled the earth hurling a wooden samya, marking out sacrificial spaces.
Note 837: pravyaharaya is explained as meaning at a great distance.
Note 838: he who regards himself as the slayer is steeped in ignorance, as the soul never acts, which the note compares with the Gita.
Note 839: the note compares this with the saying usually credited to Napoleon that St Helena was written in the book of Fate.
Note 840: a literal rendering would be that Time cooks everything.
Note 841: bhujyante is explained as meaning are consumed or gathered in.
Note 842: Brahma is indestructible as the living soul, and destructible as it appears in the form of the not-Self.
Note 843: the translator expands verse 50, since a literal version would be unintelligible.
Note 844: a thing that is borne with great difficulty.
Note 845: literally a desire for action, meaning abundance produced by labour.
Note 846: all the names given imply plenty and prosperity.
Note 847: a person whose hands are not washed after rising from or during his meals.
Note 848: the Puranic view is that the world stands around Meru, and that in the Savarnika Manwantara darkness will surround all but the top of Meru.
Note 849: all things are destructible instead of being eternal.
Note 850: hridyam means the true nature, and kalyanam means liberation.
Note 851: one who strives for liberation through yoga gains wonderful powers, and his objects follow without his seeking them.
Note 852: a wise man never regards himself as the actor and so feels no sorrow, while a fool who thinks himself the actor cannot bear sorrow calmly.
Note 853: the verse says right conclusions about duties are very rare.
Note 854: the speaker is said to resemble Gautama, who was calm after Indra violated Ahalya, not the passion-ruled Indra, and so Namuchi was master of his senses.
Note 855: the we is a pronoun of dignity that refers to the speaker alone.
Note 856: the sentence is a question, and K.P. Singha is right where the Burdwan translator is wrong.
Note 857: the Asuras had long stopped sacrifices, and with Indra's victory the sacrifices and universal peace returned.
Note 858: dhruvadwarabhavam is probably a Himalayan pass, though the vernacular translators took it as the Pole-star region, and the Puranic river from Vishnu's foot is mentioned.
Note 859: the note recalls the discourse between Mejnour and a neophyte in Lord Lytton's Zanoni on the Apennine ridges.
Note 860: K.P. Singha translates this verse wrongly.
Note 861: explains uchchhishta, meaning the hand or leftover food made unclean by eating, which is a particular Hindu notion.
Note 862: yavasa is pasture grass.
Note 863: explains payasa as rice in sugared milk, krisara as milk, sesame, and rice, and sashkuli as a pie of rice or barley.
Note 864: no merit attaches to feeding an unlettered person.
Note 865: the correct reading is vyabhajat, since the Bengal reading would repeat the first line.
Note 866: everything except the Supreme Soul can be affected by Prakriti, which is why Brahma is said to be above Prakriti.
Note 867: the verb nihnuvanti means conceal, that is, do not brag of, and both vernacular translators misrender this verse.
Note 868: K.P. Singha mistranslates this verse.
Note 869: the Burdwan translator misunderstands anavajnata, and K.P. Singha skips it.
Note 870: a householder who is truly unattached to wife, children, and possessions is compared to a lotus leaf that water does not soak, which is more meritorious than fleeing from desire.
Note 871: the words kalajnanena nishthitam set limits to the periods of creation and dissolution, as the days and nights of Brahman.
Note 872: agre is explained as before creation.
Note 873: the Krita age lasts 4,800 years, the Treta 3,600, the Dwapara 2,400, and the Kali 1,200, in years of the deities, and verses 15 to 17 and 20 to 21 occur in Manusmriti.
Note 874: this verse occurs in Manusmriti with a slightly different reading, and the translator follows Medhatithi's gloss.
Note 875: the total of 12,000 years makes a Devayuga, and a thousand Devayugas make a day of Brahman.
Note 876: the external world is nothing but Mind transformed, which is why Mind is called Vyaktatmaka, and the note records a difference in how some texts divide the section.
Note 877: tejomayam is explained as having the principle of desire within it, without which creation could not happen.
Note 878: Mahat means pure or subtle intelligence, from which the manifest world starts.
Note 879: the seven great entities are Mahat, Mind, and the five elemental entities of space and the rest.
Note 880: verses 4 to 7 occur in Manusmriti, corresponding to its verses 75 to 78.
Note 881: the living soul is called Purusha, the resident of the body, because Avidya covers it and it takes a case of primordial matter shaped by acts.
Note 882: the seven entities combine into the limbs, then into the full body with its parts, and the subtle body receives the residue of acts, so creation runs in a series.
Note 883: the six and ten parts are the five gross elements and the eleven senses, the gross body forms first, then the subtle body, and then the Soul enters to witness.
Note 884: this refers to the variety of beings and of the relations between them.
Note 885: anubhe is explained as beyond both, and the Sattwasthas are those who regard Brahma as the sole cause.
Note 886: the Vedas are speech, so the Creator uttered words before creating, and the note notes a close resemblance to the first chapter of Genesis.
Note 887: all things were made well by Brahma, and the note again compares the words of Genesis, where God saw that things were good.

Note 888: nama means the Rigveda, bheda means the wife, tapah means penance, karma means daily rites, yama means sacrifice, akhya means good works, aloka means three kinds of meditation, and siddhi means liberation in this life.
Note 889: gahanam means the inconceivable Brahma, and vedavadeshu means the words of the Vedas.
Note 890: in the other ages people perform Vedic acts from low motives, and even in the Kali age such rites are known but done for sordid gain.
Note 891: the construction of this verse is set out, following the commentator.
Note 892: mind is the essence of all the manifest, and the swallowing up is the dissolution of the outer universe, but the section seems to describe the yogin's withdrawal of the senses.
Note 893: verses 16 and 17 are a yoga mystery, and the translator compares them to a proposition of the Principia that a reader must study first.
Note 894: jatakarma is a rite with Vedic mantras after a child's birth, and many such rites follow until the end of pupilage.
Note 895: no fee is charged for tuition, though the pupil may give a final fee after studies, set by the teacher.
Note 896: by children one pays the debt to ancestors, by study the debt to the Rishis, and by sacrifice the debt to the gods.
Note 897: taking anything from a daughter's father-in-law or relatives is a deadly sin, and those who sell their daughters in marriage are counted fallen.
Note 898: a householder must honour the gods and the Pitris, and a Brahmin has no means for this but accepting gifts, so such acceptance is not sinful.
Note 899: kritadapi is explained as cooked food.
Note 900: no gift is too valuable for such persons.
Note 901: the first and fourth verses are triplets in the Bengal texts.
Note 902: these are religious acts.
Note 903: the note praises the image of the trees of benevolence that creatures carried down the river of Time may catch hold of, and says the Burdwan translator misunderstands the image.
Note 904: K.P. Singha misunderstands this verse, and the Burdwan translator is also inaccurate.

Note 905: sets out the conditions of yoga: a clean solitary place, abstention from food and amusements, faith in the scriptures, pure food, control of the senses, and reflection on birth, death, and sorrow.
Note 906: explains the parts of the chariot as images of virtues, naming the seat, fence, pole, axle, yoke, wheel, rim, hub, and goad.
Note 907: following Hamilton's faculties, dharana is the representative faculty by which the mind is held on one image, and yogins train it first.
Note 908: the seven kinds of dharana belong to earth, wind, space, water, fire, consciousness, and understanding.
Note 909: these are explained further below.
Note 910: the construction of these lines is difficult, and the note says yogatah means according to rules, and vikrama means the order of conceptions.
Note 911: pasyatah means of that which sees, namely the Atman or Soul.
Note 912: the Understanding is called the soul of the five elements and of individuality because these rest on it.
Note 913: all that is manifest springs from the Unmanifest Supreme Soul, which the yogin sees in everything.
Note 914: na kritina means kriti eva, and nirakriti means regardless of dress, and K.P. Singha misrenders both.
Note 915: the man who has neither friend nor foe regards all creatures with equal benevolence, and takes praise and blame alike.
Note 916: extraordinary powers come to yogins, and one who is led by them falls into hell, while one who transcends them gains liberation.
Note 917: dhirah means one who meditates, and santi means liberation, and the note says the speaker prefers Sankhya here.
Note 918: compare the Gita, chapter 5, verses 4 and 5.
Note 919: brahmanam is an Arsha form of brahmam.
Note 920: vidya is the teaching that dispels error, like seeing a cord as a snake, and nivritti is the doctrine of the Sunyavadins and Lokayatikas, who seek annihilation.
Note 921: the construction is set out, and the commentator takes the speaker to be attacking the Sunyavadins, who say the world appears by its own nature.
Note 922: the Bombay text reads putwatrinamishikamva.
Note 923: enam is singular, and the speaker rejects both the Sunyavadin and Lokayatika views of Nature as the cause, since both are false.
Note 924: both vernacular translators skip paribhava, which means the existence of the others, and the two terms refer to the Nihilists and the Lokayatikas.
Note 925: wisdom achieves ends by applying means, and nature does not build palaces, so exertion answers both Nihilists and Lokayatikas.
Note 926: para means the Chit or Soul, avara means all else, and prajna, jnana, and vidya are equivalent.
Note 927: cheshta means intelligent energy, both mental and physical, that distinguishes things.
Note 928: the itarani are birds of the air, khechara, not Pisachas, though Pisachas may belong to that class.
Note 929: the foremost are foremost, and the middling are observers of caste duties, so popular opinion is taken first before the higher view.
Note 930: the Vedas were not yet written down, so their contents rested in the memory of those who knew them.
Note 931: knowledge of the Soul means understanding birth and death, and avoiding rebirth, while the ignorant keep going round in rebirths.
Note 932: the phrase means the power that comes of yoga.
Note 933: para means high, often Brahma or the Soul, and the Burdwan rendering as other scriptures is wrong.
Note 934: one should see everything as one's own, and yoga leads to this, and the true Brahmana who realises it is a god on earth; adhiyajna and adhidaivata mean the Soul.
Note 935: the difference between anta and nidhan is not clear, and K.P. Singha's rendering is correct while the Burdwan version is nonsense.
Note 936: the question is whether karma is obligatory or optional, and since knowledge is needed for liberation, acts may be needed as means to it.
Note 937: the note sets out the construction of the difficult first line, and admires Nilakantha's patience.
Note 938: daiva is explained as fate or time, which the translator renders as necessity, while vritti means conduct and avivekam means a combination of the three.
Note 939: inspired with doubt refers to doubts about the Srutis, and tranquil souls are those free of doubt.
Note 940: in the Treta and later ages people devoted themselves to one Veda only, while the men of the Krita age treated all the Vedas as one.
Note 941: by penance the living soul gains the power to create and reaches Brahma and universal power.
Note 942: this verse answers the question of which knowledge is meant, since in the Vedanta knowledge leads to Brahma, which is hidden even from those who study the rites.
Note 943: the second line corresponds to verse 87 of Chapter 2 of the Manusmriti.
Note 944: they are seen and not seen is an idiom meaning becoming invisible.
Note 945: kine give no sweet milk, the soil ceases to be fertile, water loses its sweetness, and herbs lose their healing power.
Note 946: the commentator links swadharmasthah with asramah, but the translator prefers the more obvious construction.
Note 947: varshati means nourishes, and angani are the observances of yoga and of rites and vows, which the Vedas cause to grow.
Note 948: prabhava is origin and sthanam is support, which the translators wrongly ran together, and swabhavena means by Brahma's own nature.
Note 949: yatha in the first line means yat prakarakam, of that kind.
Note 950: the four words indicate the four modes of life.
Note 951: the ignorant take the great non-self entities for the self or its possessions.
Note 952: the Yoga view of the soul as the enjoyer but not the actor is wrong, and the Sankhya view that the soul neither acts nor enjoys is true, since the deities in the senses act and enjoy.
Note 953: bhutatma is rendered as knowledge, following the commentator's phrase the living being with the intellect as its vehicle.
Note 954: niyama and visarga are explained as destruction and creation, though the translator prefers restraining and employing.
Note 955: the objects of the senses exist in the heart as concepts, and swabhava means attributes such as heat and cold.
Note 956: a very difficult verse on the body, knowledge, and the three attributes, which the note says is the body's image in a dream, with Prakriti as the true refuge of knowledge.
Note 957: such men behold Brahma in all things, and abhijanah means disciples or a family of disciples.
Note 958: the word tatam means pervaded, not spread, as the Gita uses it.
Note 959: the Vedas teach that all is one's soul, and the degree of realising this is the degree of attaining Brahma.
Note 960: the track of such a person is as invisible as the sky, and even the gods are stupefied about the object he seeks.
Note 961: the thing in which Time is cooked is Brahma.
Note 962: Brahma is not found in any particular spot, however holy.
Note 963: Brahma is infinite.
Note 964: niyatah means unwavering and vasi means without the fault of an adjunct, while hansa means moving, hence gatimati.
Note 965: the Soul residing in the body is identical with the Supreme Soul, which only men of wisdom know.
Note 966: the construction shows there is no difference between the individual and the Supreme Soul.
Note 967: sattwena is explained as by intelligence or knowledge.
Note 968: the brilliant seed is Brahma, and the essence of all this is Brahma's juice.
Note 969: Brahma opened his eyes to become many, and by his glance he became the Soul of all things mobile and immobile.
Note 970: the commentator reads Brahmanah padam as Prakriti, but the translator keeps the obvious sense.
Note 971: parimitam kalam is explained as six months, as the Srutis say.

Note 972: these verses set out the yoga ideal and its powers, but a yogin who is led away by these powers falls into hell; pramoha, brahma, and avarta are technical terms, and equality with the wind means speed and power to move through the sky.
Note 973: a chaitya is a sacred tree standing on its roots with a raised platform around it, and vrikshagra means in front of a tree.
Note 974: the commentator says one should imitate the wind by being unattached, and aniketah means without a house or fixed abode.
Note 975: savda-brahma is the mystic syllable Om, and K.P. Singha takes it as a sign that such a man transcends Vedic rites.
Note 976: the Sudra order is meant as inferior, and Vyasa says all classes may take up the path of yoga, though only the three higher orders study Sankhya.
Note 977: fixed senses means senses fixed on the mind and the mind on the understanding, while ajaram means unchanging and subtlety means incapable of being grasped.
Note 978: anu anudrisya is taken as following the teacher's words, and abhutagatim means until the destruction of all beings.
Note 979: the Vedas proclaim both acts and knowledge, and acts are not laid down for one who has knowledge.
Note 980: the highest duty, explained by the commentator, is to see the self through yoga.
Note 981: na vartate does not mean annihilated but refers to one who does not know himself as I am.
Note 982: by mind and by act is explained as by resolve.
Note 983: the man of acts is like the new moon, which grows and decays.
Note 984: this has been explained in an earlier section.
Note 985: the soul in the body is untouched by its attributes, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf that does not soak it, and the phrase means a soul whose mind is restrained by yoga.
Note 986: the three attributes have the nature of Jiva, which is an accident of the Soul, and the Soul comes from the Supreme Soul.
Note 987: two creations are named: the twenty-four entities from Prakriti, and a derivative creation of senses and objects that binds the individual.
Note 988: the course of righteousness is regulated by the character of the Yuga that sets in.
Note 989: Suka asks how two apparently conflicting declarations are one, and wants his father to explain more clearly.
Note 990: the course of conduct of human beings means the distinction between right and wrong, and the phrase vimuktatma is taken to mean one who has cast off the body.
Note 991: the translator does not follow the commentator on this line.
Note 992: when the huts are smokeless and the husking rod is silent, the mendicant is unlikely to receive much alms.
Note 993: if two declarations conflict, both cannot be scriptural, so the question is how the authority of both can be kept.
Note 994: the Burdwan translator blunders in rendering jaghanyasayi, since jaghanya means later in time.
Note 995: the disciple should not clamour for lessons but approach the preceptor only when summoned, and both vernacular translators misread this.
Note 996: the disciple should cast humble glances and not stare boldly.
Note 997: learning was never sold, and the final fee is a token of gratitude, with the story of Galava as a warning about pressing the fee.
Note 998: the fourth kind of conduct, kapoti or unchha, is gathering the seeds of grain fallen from the ears and left by the reapers.
Note 999: each of the four kinds of gathering is more meritorious than the one before, so the fourth is first in merit.
Note 1000: a householder who cooks must share the food with a student, a wanderer, or a guest, and eating all of it is a grave sin.
Note 1001: the commentator says relatives are named because disputes over inheritance are likely with them.
Note 1002: those named, if duly honoured, can send the householder to the places indicated or make him comfortable there.
Note 1003: the three forms of domesticity are the kumbhadhanya, the aswastana or unchhasila, and the kapoti, and the Burdwan version misnames them.
Note 1004: the Burdwan version of this verse is incorrect.
Note 1005: a cow is sacred, and forest recluses kept cows for merit and for the ghee used in sacrifice, with the story of Vasishtha's cow.
Note 1006: the five sacrifices are the Agnihotra, Darsapurnamasi, Chaturmasya, Pasu, and Soma.
Note 1007: the Burdwan translator misunderstands abhravakasah, which Wilson explains correctly.
Note 1008: the grain eaten is not cleaned with a regular husking or cleaning apparatus.
Note 1009: only a very small portion of the grain comes out for drink or mixes with the water.
Note 1010: yathavasah and akritacramah are adjectives of Sudivatandi, not names of Rishis, as the Burdwan translator took them.
Note 1011: the sage's wishes were immediately fulfilled, whether they were blessings or curses.
Note 1012: niranandah is explained as free from the troubles of lunar penance and similar rites.
Note 1013: anakstrah means luminous, different from the stars, and anadhrishyah means fearless.
Note 1014: atmayaji performs his own funeral rites, atmakrida takes pleasure in the self, and atmasraya takes refuge in the self.
Note 1015: examples of such sacrifices are the Brahma-yajna and similar rites.
Note 1016: once ordinary sacrifice has purified the mind, the sacrificer offers into the self, meaning yoga, and no longer needs visible fires.
Note 1017: orthodox twice-born men still offer five small mouthfuls to the five vital breaths before eating.
Note 1018: vapya means causing a shave, which a renouncer must have, and the Burdwan translator wrongly reads parivyapta.
Note 1019: abhaya means giving freedom from fear, that is a life of total harmlessness, which is the great duty of the fourth stage.

Note 1020: yama includes universal benevolence, truth, faith, celibacy, and detachment, and niyama includes purity, contentment, study, and meditation, and the renouncer should seek the Soul and drop caste marks.
Note 1021: the commentator says the first line answers the son's question, and the speaker then gives the straight path to Brahma.
Note 1022: bhava-samahitah means one whose mind is composed.
Note 1023: the skull is to be used as a drinking vessel, and kuchela means faded, reddish-brown rags.
Note 1024: as elephants in a well cannot get out, so a man whose hard words do not stir him is fit for mendicancy.
Note 1025: the yogin withdraws his senses and mind by pratyahara so that a crowded place looks empty to him.
Note 1026: the mendicant should never eat to full satiety, but leave his hunger only partly satisfied.
Note 1027: the commentator reads kaunjara as a yogin in samadhi, and the fruits of yoga absorb every other fruit, even Indra's rank.
Note 1028: the single duty of harmlessness, the fourth stage, gives the merit that all the other duties give together.
Note 1029: haryartham means for the sake of Hari, meaning a disciple or attendant who takes away merit, and another reading gives for the happiness of others.
Note 1030: all acts, whether general or religious, involve injury to others.
Note 1031: tikshnam tanum means the religion of sacrifices and acts, and the line means that he attains liberation, from which creatures are free from fear.
Note 1032: a tentative version is offered that follows the words of the original.
Note 1033: the images apply to the Supreme Soul: vaster than the firmament, golden as pure knowledge, born of the egg, with many feathers for its limbs, and luminous with rays.
Note 1034: a man who understands the wheel of Time deserves universal regard, and its joints are the sacred lunar days.
Note 1035: unconsciousness, the sleep of dreamless slumber, is the origin of the universe, and jiva feeds the deities and senses, which in turn are swallowed by that open mouth.
Note 1036: smriti is memory, so one whose smriti is lost has confounded right and wrong, and atmanah sampradanena means surrender to one's passions.
Note 1037: chittam is the gross understanding, sattwa is the subtle one that thinks of Brahma, and kalanjara means one who subdues Time.
Note 1038: purification is transcending the sense of duality, righteousness is inferior to liberation, and atmani sthitwa means living in one's true nature.
Note 1039: atmanam here means the Jiva-soul and atmani means the Supreme Soul, and the second line keeps the same distinction.
Note 1040: Brahmanas who have finished their Vedic study and entered the householder stage, with faith and pure conduct, are meant.
Note 1041: adhyatma here means the twenty-seven usual topics of philosophy, including the organs, the breaths, the elements, desire, acts, and avidya.
Note 1042: the second clause means what one sees in the desire that is the cause.
Note 1043: mind, understanding, and nature come from their previous states, and in their functions they seize particular attributes such as scent and form.
Note 1044: the senses and mind are the understanding in a particular shape, the mind cherishes and discards impressions, and the understanding reaches certainty.
Note 1045: the phrase from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head means the whole person, the self that says I.
Note 1046: the verse establishes that the attributes of form, and the senses and mind that apprehend them, are the understanding itself.
Note 1047: the three attributes come from their counterparts in a previous life, and so affect the objects of the senses.
Note 1048: the last word in the first line is aprabodhita, not prabodhita.
Note 1049: the word atman is used in several senses, and the place decides which.
Note 1050: vela means tide or current, and the understanding can transcend the three attributes by yoga.
Note 1051: the Bengal texts give this as a single line, while the Bombay text makes verse 9 a triplet, and medhyani means knowledge of forms.
Note 1052: the note reads the theory as a kind of idealism, in which the tree is only an image formed in the mind by vision.
Note 1053: the speaker opposes the view that qualities inhere in objects, and the wife's limbs simile shows they follow the mind, like the spokes of a wheel.
Note 1054: the version is offered tentatively, and compares verse 42 of section 194.
Note 1055: once the darkness of the understanding is dispelled, the soul becomes visible.
Note 1056: this is one who adopts Sannyasa, the last stage, after passing through the earlier ones.
Note 1057: gunan means objects, Sattivadin means one who is good, and vikriyatah means undergoing change.
Note 1058: the commentator says the gunas are not destroyed by knowledge in the way a pot is broken, but bind as a rope or snake does, so they can return.
Note 1059: the two opinions make little practical difference, and conduct is not much changed by either.
Note 1060: janmasamartham is competence by birth or by the duties of one's order, and parayanam means what leads to liberation.
Note 1061: the Bengal reading buddhah is preferred over the Bombay reading suddhah.
Note 1062: lokam means objects of enjoyment, such as a wife, aturam means afflicted with faults, and ubhayam kritakritam means grief and no grief.
Note 1063: many verses match section 194 with verbal changes, some slight and some making a material difference.
Note 1064: pastures means all external and inner objects that the senses and mind attend to, whose home is Brahma.
Note 1065: the word atma in the first line is indefinite, and the translator takes the inner Soul to be the Chit unmodified by birth and attributes.
Note 1066: abhavapratipattyartham is explained as for attaining the unborn, meaning the soul.
Note 1067: the commentator explains the first line as meaning that the speaker has truly treated the subject.
Note 1068: tasya tasya refers to the senses, pracharah means conduct, and pasyatah means the wise man.
Note 1069: one who only knows the Vedas and keeps celibacy is not a superior Brahmin, since more is needed.
Note 1070: sarvavit is taken as Brahmavit, the contented man is one satisfied with self-knowledge, and K.P. Singha is right on the two negatives.
Note 1071: avidhanat is explained as not following either kindness or its opposite.
Note 1072: kamakantah is explained as lovely through desires.
Note 1073: heaven is Brahma with attributes, tranquillity is Brahma without them, and the Vedas and truth matter only as far as they lead to tranquillity.
Note 1074: both vernacular translators misrender this verse, and the note explains ichchasi, santoshat, sattwam, and manas.
Note 1075: samagrah means fully satisfied with knowledge, and contentment from verse 13 makes up six attributes.
Note 1076: the six must be free of Rajas and Tamas, the three are hearing, reflection, and contemplation, and knowing the Soul within the body brings freedom.
Note 1077: anweti is explained as grows.
Note 1078: the reading saviseshani is preferred, and the note explains vishesha and avishesha in yoga terms.
Note 1079: one who has transcended the gunas disregards the power that their destruction is said to bring.
Note 1080: karyyatam is Prakriti, the active principle, while Purusha is inactive, and the supreme cause is Brahma without attributes.
Note 1081: dwandwani is governed by anushthitah, and the speaker has discussed the subject at length and now treats it briefly.
Note 1082: panchasu means among the five elements, and the commentator shows that bhava, abhava, and time fall within the elements.

An opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and the goddess Saraswati.
Yudhishthira says he finds no peace of mind, since he feels he caused the war's deaths and Bhishma's suffering, and asks how he can be cleansed of sin.
Bhishma asks why Yudhishthira blames his own soul, then begins an old tale about Gautami, whose son died of a snakebite, and the fowler Arjunaka, who binds the serpent.
Gautami asks the fowler to free the serpent, since killing it is sinful and would not bring her son back.
The fowler insists on killing the serpent, arguing that revenge is how practical people ease their grief.
Gautami replies that the boy's death was predestined, so the serpent should not be destroyed, and asks the fowler to forgive it.
The fowler argues that killing an enemy earns great merit, as a sacrifice does.
Gautami asks what good comes from tormenting an enemy, and suggests they earn merit by releasing it.
The fowler argues that protecting many from one wicked creature matters more, and tells Gautami to let him kill it.
Gautami repeats that killing the serpent will not restore her son and asks the fowler to release it.
The fowler cites Indra's killing of Vritra and Mahadeva's share of a destroyed sacrifice to urge the serpent's immediate death.
Bhishma says Gautami does not give in, and that the bound serpent, struggling to stay calm, speaks in a human voice.
The serpent says it bit the child only because Mrityu sent it, so any sin lies with Mrityu.
The fowler replies that the serpent, as the instrument of the act, is still guilty and deserves death.
The serpent argues that it is no independent cause, like the potter's wheel and rod, so any fault lies in the whole set of causes.
The fowler says that even a non-prime cause deserves death, and that a doer cannot escape implication in an evil act.
The serpent says no effect comes without an intervening act, so its role should be weighed alone, and any guilt rests on whoever incited it.
The fowler calls the serpent undeserving of life and says it committed an atrocious act by killing the infant.
The serpent replies with the analogy of priests who pour butter into a fire and do not take the sacrifice's merit, so it should not be judged that way.
Bhishma says the serpent has finished speaking as Mrityu directed it to.
Mrityu appears in person and addresses the serpent.
Mrityu says Kala guides both of them, that Kala drives all beings and all things, and so neither is the cause of the child's death.
The serpent says it does not blame Mrityu or fully excuse him, since it only acts under his direction.
Bhishma continues: the serpent asks the fowler to stop binding it, since it has heard Mrityu and is blameless.
The fowler says neither of their words clears them, calls Mrityu cruel, and vows to kill the serpent as well.
Mrityu says he and the serpent are not free agents but depend on Kala and carry out their appointed work.
The fowler asks how pleasure and anger, which come from good and bad deeds, can arise if both of them are dependent on Kala.
Mrityu says everything is done under Kala's influence, so he and the serpent deserve no censure.
Bhishma says that Kala arrives at the scene of this dispute over morality and speaks to all three.
Kala says none of the three is guilty, that the child's own karma was the true cause, and that all beings are bound by their karma.
Gautami accepts that her own past deeds caused her son's death, asks Kala and Mrityu to leave, and asks the fowler to release the serpent.

Bhishma says Kala, Mrityu and the serpent return to their places and Gautami and the fowler are calmed, then tells Yudhishthira to put aside grief, since men go to heaven or hell by their karma and the kings were slain through Kala's acts.
Vaisampayana begins the frame narration, saying Yudhishthira was consoled after hearing all this.
Yudhishthira, now consoled, speaks again and asks Bhishma a further question.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whether any householder has ever conquered Mrityu through virtue, and asks for the story.

Bhishma traces the royal line to Duryodhana, whose daughter Agni marries; their son Sudarsana vows to honor every guest, Mrityu tests him through a Brahmana and Oghavati, and Dharma appears to praise him as having conquered Death.
Indra approaches the Brahmana in a chariot, and Bhishma concludes that honoring a guest is the householder's highest duty and that the story brings glory to those who hear it.
Yudhishthira asks how the Kshatriya Viswamitra became a Brahmana, citing his feats and the failure of Matanga, and asks Bhishma to explain how it happened without a new body.
Bhishma begins the account of how Viswamitra became a Brahmana, tracing the royal line down to King Gadhi and his daughter Satyavati, whom the sage Richika seeks.
Gadhi asks Richika for a dowry of a thousand horses, each with one black ear, before he will give his daughter.

Varuna supplies the horses, Gadhi gives Satyavati in marriage, the mother and daughter swap their sacred food and trees, Richika warns the swap will reverse their sons' destinies, Satyavati pleads, and Viswamitra and Jamadagni are born, with Viswamitra's many sons listed and Bhishma concluding the story.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the merits of compassion and the characteristics of devout men.
Bhishma tells how a fowler's poisoned arrow withers a tree, how the parrot in its hollow refuses to leave it, and how Indra comes in disguise to ask why.
The parrot refuses to desert the tree that raised him, so Indra grants a boon, the tree revives under nectar, and the parrot later joins Indra, a lesson about companionship with the pious.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which is more powerful, Exertion or Destiny.
Bhishma says the question was once put by Vasishtha to Brahma, whether a life is shaped by present acts or by acts from earlier lives, called destiny.
Brahma answers with the image of seed and soil: destiny is useless without personal effort, idleness brings loss, and even the gods rose through their own deeds.

Brahma gives examples of kings and sages who fell or were restored by their own deeds, notes the Pandavas regained their kingdom by valour, and concludes that destiny joined with exertion is what works.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the fruits of good deeds.

Bhishma explains that deeds bear fruit in similar states of later lives, lists rewards for hospitality, austerity, diet, vows and sacrifice, and says past deeds follow a person as a calf finds its mother.
Vaisampayana reports that the Kuru princes were amazed and delighted, and compares falsehood in speech to rites performed wrongly, which bring evil results.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whom he honors and likes, what he thinks of in times of affliction, and what helps in this life and after death.

Bhishma says he most cherishes learned Brahmanas and generous givers, values Brahmanas above his own kin, explains why they must be served with reverence, and says Kshatriyas must protect the Brahmanas and the Vedas.
Yudhishthira asks what becomes of people who promise a gift to Brahmanas and do not give it.
Bhishma says such a person's hopes and good deeds come to nothing, and tells of a jackal, reborn for failing to give a promised gift, eating carrion while his former friend, now an ape, asks why.
The jackal asks the ape what sin made him an ape.
The ape says he once took fruits that belonged to Brahmanas, so one should never take their property and should keep one's promises to them.

Bhishma says he learned this from his preceptor and from Krishna, and that Brahmanas must not be disregarded, since their raised expectations burn like fire and gifts to them bring the highest heaven.
Yudhishthira asks whether teaching someone of low birth brings fault on the teacher.
Bhishma describes a Himalayan asylum full of sages and a Sudra, moved by its holiness, who asks the head ascetic to accept him as a disciple.
The head ascetic says a Sudra cannot take the vows of renunciation, but he may stay and serve the community.

The Sudra builds a hut, lives austerely, and welcomes guests, and a visiting Rishi teaches him the ancestor rites; both are later reborn, the Sudra as a prince who becomes king, and the Rishi as a priest who serves him, and the king laughs at him repeatedly, so the priest asks for a single boon.
The king replies that he will grant the boon and would grant a hundred if asked.
The king says that a single boon is a small request, given how fond he is of the priest.
The king says his affection and respect for the priest mean he refuses him nothing.
The king repeats that there is nothing he cannot give.
The priest asks for only one boon, that the king swear to tell the truth, and not any falsehood.
Bhishma says the king agrees to answer truthfully if he knows the answer, and to say nothing if he does not.
The priest asks why the king laughs at him on every occasion, says it shames him, and demands a true answer.

The king reveals that he was once a Sudra who did penance, that the priest taught him the rites, that the teaching cost the priest his penances, and that this is why he laughs at the reversal of their fortunes; he urges the priest to seek a better birth.

Dismissed from office, the priest gives gifts, does penance, and attains success at the old asylum, and Bhishma concludes that Brahmanas should not instruct the low-born, that teaching for pay pollutes the teacher, and that one should teach only what is right and meritorious.
Yudhishthira asks in what kind of man or woman the goddess of prosperity always resides.
The question continues, asking Bhishma, chief of the Bharatas, where prosperity always stays.
Bhishma says Rukmini, mother of Pradyumna, once asked Sree in Krishna's presence which people she favors and which she shuns.

Sree says she stays with the diligent, eloquent, self-controlled, grateful and devout, and avoids the idle, unbelieving, ungrateful, thieving and quarrelsome; she names the good and bad women of a household, the auspicious places and creatures she favors, and says she dwells in Narayana, in whom righteousness is complete.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which of man or woman gets greater pleasure from union, and asks for a truthful answer.

Bhishma tells how king Bhangaswana, who performed a sacrifice Indra dislikes, is stupefied by Indra on a hunt and turned into a woman after bathing in a lake, and how Indra later sets her sons against each other, before Indra reveals himself and offers a boon.
The lady says a woman's affection is greater than a man's, so she asks that the sons she bore as a woman be restored to life.
Indra is pleased and offers her a choice of remaining a woman or returning to manhood.
The lady chooses to remain a woman because women take greater pleasure in union, Indra grants her wish and returns to heaven, and Bhishma concludes that woman enjoys greater pleasure than man.
Yudhishthira asks how a man should conduct himself and what practices help him pass well in this world and the next.

Bhishma says to avoid ten wrong actions, naming killing, theft and adultery of the body, harsh and idle talk, exposing others' faults and lying of speech, and greed, malice and disbelief in the Vedas of the mind, and that good and bad acts bring sure results.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to recite Mahadeva's names and tell of his power.
Bhishma says he cannot fully describe Mahadeva, and that only Krishna, who won Mahadeva's favour through penance at Vadari, can do so.
Vaisampayana says that Bhishma then addressed Vasudeva on the subject.
Bhishma asks Vasudeva to recite the names of Mahadeva as Tandi once did before Brahma, so that the assembled sages may hear them.
Vasudeva replies that even the gods cannot fully know Mahadeva, but he will recite some of his attributes.
Vaisampayana resumes the narration after Vasudeva's words.
Vasudeva begins his discourse on the attributes of Mahadeva.
The discourse concerns Mahadeva, who is endued with the highest intelligence.
Vasudeva purifies himself by touching water before he speaks.

Vasudeva recounts how he went on Garuda to Himavat to win a son for Jambavati, found the asylum of Upamanyu, heard Upamanyu's list of Shiva's past favours to demons and sages, and learned how Upamanyu as a boy longed for milk and was told by his mother to seek Mahadeva.
Upamanyu's mother says Mahadeva is hard to know and promises to describe his many forms.
The mother lists Mahadeva's forms, and Upamanyu then undertakes long austerities until Indra comes and offers him boons, which he refuses in favour of Mahadeva alone.
Indra asks what reason Upamanyu has for his belief.
Indra's question continues, asking why a Supreme Being should be the cause of all causes.

Upamanyu answers with a long argument that Mahadeva is the supreme cause, source of Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, and then describes seeing Mahadeva on his white bull with Uma, surrounded by gods and his weapons.
Upamanyu hymns Mahadeva under many names, bows, and offers water, and the gods praise him while Mahadeva speaks with a smile.
Mahadeva says he is pleased with Upamanyu, who in turn praises him and asks for knowledge, milk-based food for his kin, and Mahadeva's presence at the asylum.
Mahadeva grants Upamanyu freedom from suffering, youth, fame, an ocean of milk, and companionship after a kalpa, and the asylum is blessed.
Vasudeva says he is amazed and asks Upamanyu whether Mahadeva will show him favour too.
Upamanyu promises that Vasudeva will see Mahadeva within six months and gives him mantras to recite.
Vasudeva describes his initiation and months of austerity, then his vision of Mahadeva with Uma in a cloud, surrounded by Rudras and gods, and Mahadeva's words that Vasudeva is dear to him.
Vasudeva hymns Mahadeva as the source of all things, and Mahadeva says he is pleased and tells Vasudeva to ask for eight boons.

Vasudeva bows to Mahadeva and asks for virtue, victory, fame, might, Yoga and many children, and Mahadeva agrees; Uma then says Vasudeva will have a son named Samva and offers him eight further boons.
Vasudeva names his requests to Uma, and she grants them, promising him many wives, great affection, beauty, and daily guests at his palace.
Vasudeva says that the god and goddess vanished after granting him boons, and that he told all this to Upamanyu, who bowed to Mahadeva and spoke to him.
Upamanyu declares that there is no deity like Sarva, no greater refuge, no giver of such boons, and no equal in battle.
Upamanyu begins the story of Tandi, who worshipped Mahadeva for ten thousand years, and then beheld him and fell into wonder at his unknowable nature.
Tandi's long hymn calls Mahadeva the holiest of holies, the source and end of everything, the forms of the gods and the elements, and the one sought by Vedas, sacrifice and Yoga.
Upamanyu says Mahadeva, with Uma beside him, is gratified by Tandi's praise, and Tandi has said that not even Brahma or Vishnu can know him.
Mahadeva grants Tandi indestructibility, fame, knowledge, and a son who will write Sutras, and Tandi asks only that his devotion remain steady.
Upamanyu says that Mahadeva then vanished, that Tandi came to his asylum, and that Tandi passed on the thousand names of Mahadeva, first recited by Brahma, which Upamanyu now offers to Krishna.
Vasudeva says that Upamanyu, joining his hands in reverence and concentrating, began to recite the abstract of Mahadeva's names from the beginning.

Upamanyu presents the hymn as an essence of Brahma's ten thousand names, which cleanses sin like the four Vedas, calls Mahadeva Eternal Brahman, and starts a long list of his names as a series of 'thou art' phrases.
A section heading, 'Section XVIII,' appears in the text at this point.
The list of names continues, describing Mahadeva as the source of the Vedas, the bearer of Ganga, the husband of Uma, a boar and horse-headed incarnation, and the maker of many forms.

Upamanyu says the hymn has been praised by Tandi and brings Emancipation and heaven, then traces its line of transmission from Brahma through Sakra, Mrityu, the Rudras, Tandi, Sukra, Gautama, Manu, Narayana, Yama, Nachiketa and Markandeya, and gives it to Krishna.
Krishna says that one who recites the hymn for a year with a pure heart, self-control and chastity gains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and is safe from demons, spirits and snakes.

The Island-born Krishna urges Yudhishthira to recite the hymn, and then Kapila, Charusirsha, Valmiki, Jamadagni's son, Viswamitra, Asita-Devala, Gritsamada and Vasudeva each describe the favours Mahadeva gave them for devotion, such as knowledge, a hundred sons, cleansing from sin, weapons, Brahmanhood, restored merit, release from a curse, and boons.
Jaigishavya says that Mahadeva gave him the eight attributes of sovereignty at Varanasi.
Garga says that Mahadeva gave him knowledge of Time and a thousand learned sons, and extended his life to ten million years.
Parasara says that Mahadeva promised him a son named Krishna, who would arrange the Vedas and be reckoned among the seven Rishis.
Mandavya says that, though wrongly impaled for theft, Mahadeva freed him, promised him long life and heaven, and then vanished with his attendants.

Galava says that, when his mother lamented that his father would never see him again, Mahadeva promised that father, mother and son would be spared death, and Galava found his father alive and embraced him.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira was amazed at these accounts, and that Krishna spoke again to him.
Krishna quotes Upamanyu, who says that sinners cannot reach Isana while devotees, even worms and birds, are freed from rebirth through devotion to Mahadeva.

Krishna recites a long list of the powers and beings that arose from the Creator and says that reciting the hymn for a month earns the merit of a horse-sacrifice, and brings benefit to each of the four classes and a heavenly reward.
Yudhishthira asks what the saying about performing all duties together in marriage means, given that spouses die at different times and women are called false in the scriptures.
Bhishma tells how Ashtavakra asks the sage Vadanya for his daughter Suprabha, and Vadanya agrees on condition that Ashtavakra first travels to the sacred north.
Ashtavakra asks what he will see there and says he will obey.
Vadanya describes the route past Kuvera's realm to the Himavat plateau of Rudra, where Uma once practised austerities, and tells him to honour a female ascetic in a blue forest on his way back.
Ashtavakra agrees to the journey and asks Vadanya to keep his own word.

Ashtavakra bathes in the sacred Vahuda, reaches Kuvera's realm, and is entertained with dance and music until a year has passed unnoticed; he then moves north to a golden mansion, where seven maidens appear and an aged woman embraces him and urges him to lie with her.
Ashtavakra refuses to approach another man's wife and says he seeks marriage only for offspring, asking her to desist.
The lady argues that women are driven by desire and seldom devoted to their husbands, and that they wreck families as rivers break their banks.
Ashtavakra asks her to stop, agrees to stay a while, and wonders whether her ugliness is the result of a curse; then he asks her for water for his evening rites.

Bhishma says the old woman rubs Ashtavakra with fragrant oil and washes him with her soft hands, the night passes unnoticed, he worships the sun at dawn and is served delicious food, and at midnight she leaves her own bed for his.
Ashtavakra says his mind turns from congress with another's wife, and asks her to leave his bed and desist of her own accord.
Bhishma says the lady answers that she is her own mistress and that accepting her would bring him no sin.
Ashtavakra replies that women can never be their own mistresses, as the Creator himself decreed.
The lady says she is tormented by desire and that Ashtavakra will incur sin by refusing her.
Ashtavakra says that many faults drag down the man who follows his desires, that he can control his own inclinations, and asks her to return to her bed.
The lady bows, submits to him, and offers to be his wife, declaring again that she is her own mistress and that any sin will be hers alone.
Ashtavakra asks how she can be her own mistress, since a woman is protected by her father, husband and sons in turn.
The lady says she has kept the vow of celibacy since maidenhood and begs him not to destroy her devotion by refusing to marry her.
Ashtavakra says he is inclined to her but asks whether taking her would go against Vadanya's wishes, wonders why her beauty was hidden by age, and resolves to keep to his restraint and truth.
Yudhishthira asks why the lady had no fear of Ashtavakra's curse, and how he came back safely from that place.
Ashtavakra asks the lady how she alters her form, and insists she speak truly before a Brahmana.

The lady says the trial was devised to test him, that she is the embodiment of the northern quarter, that Vadanya sent him so she could instruct him, and that he will return safely, win a chosen bride and have a son.
Ashtavakra returns to Vadanya, rests at home, and reports what he saw in the north, and Vadanya gives him his daughter in marriage.
Ashtavakra takes Suprabha as his wife and lives on at his hermitage, free from mental fever.
Yudhishthira asks which Brahmanas the wise call proper objects of gifts, and whether those who bear the marks of their order are the ones meant.
Bhishma says gifts are proper for any Brahmana who keeps the duties of his own order, whether or not he bears the marks of a student.
Yudhishthira asks what fault an unpurified person incurs when he gives butter or food with devotion to the twice-born.
Bhishma says devotion cleanses even a person who lacks self-restraint, and does so for all acts, not just giving.
Yudhishthira says Brahmanas hired for rites to the gods need not be examined, but those hired for rites to the ancestors should be checked for conduct and skill.
Bhishma says that the merit of rites for the gods comes through the gods' grace, and recalls Markandeya's teaching that Brahmanas are always devoted to Brahman.
Yudhishthira asks why five kinds of people, a stranger, one learned in his duties, a relative by marriage, an ascetic and a sacrificer, are regarded as proper.

Bhishma says the first three must have purity of birth, devotion, learning, compassion, modesty, sincerity and truthfulness, that the other two need five of these, and introduces the views of four great beings.
The Earth says that every sin dissolves as a clod in the ocean through the three duties of officiating at sacrifice, teaching and receiving gifts.
Kasyapa says that the Vedas, the Sankhya philosophy, the Puranas and high birth cannot save a twice-born man who falls from good conduct.
Agni says that a learned Brahmana who uses his learning to destroy others' reputation falls from righteousness and cannot reach the regions of felicity.
Markandeya says he does not know whether a thousand horse-sacrifices would weigh even half as much as Truth on a scale.
Bhishma says the four great beings then departed.
Yudhishthira asks whether a Sraddha offering is well performed when it is given to celibate Brahmanas who solicit it.
Bhishma says a celibate Brahmana who solicits and eats a Sraddha offering falls from his vow, though the Sraddha itself is not stained.
Yudhishthira says the wise call Righteousness many-ended and many-doored, and asks for the settled conclusions.

Bhishma lists the marks of Righteousness, such as non-injury, truth, forgiveness, compassion, self-restraint and candour, and warns that giving to hypocrites who preach virtue while sinning brings suffering in hell.
Yudhishthira asks what is superior to celibacy, and what the highest mark and purity of virtue is.
Bhishma says abstaining from honey and meat is superior to celibacy, and that self-restraint and renunciation are the best marks and purity.
Yudhishthira asks when one should practise Righteousness, when one should seek wealth, and when one should enjoy pleasure.

Bhishma says to earn wealth first, then practise Righteousness, then enjoy pleasure without clinging to any of them, and lists lying in court, deceiving the king and wronging teachers as equal to Brahmanicide, and harming the king or a cow as equal to foeticide.
Yudhishthira asks which Brahmanas are good, which gifts earn great merit, and which Brahmanas should be fed.

Bhishma says Brahmanas free from anger, devoted to righteousness, truthful and self-restrained are good, that one who knows the four Vedas and six duties is worthy, that one such Brahmana can rescue a whole family, and that a worthy Brahmana should be invited and honoured even from afar.
Yudhishthira asks what rules govern the acts performed for the gods and ancestors at Sraddhas.

Bhishma says the rites for the gods are done in the forenoon and those for the ancestors in the afternoon, and lists offerings that become the Rakshasas' portion, such as untimely gifts, food touched by dogs or impure women, and food given without proper rites.

Bhishma lists the Brahmanas who should not be invited to Sraddhas, including outcasts, the diseased, physicians, paid performers, sellers of Soma and of Vedic lore, lenders of money, and those who serve Sudras.

Bhishma lists the Brahmanas who may be invited, such as those who keep the rites and the Gayatri or live by farming, and a well-born Brahmana who takes up arms, while those who turn to trade are excluded, and he gives the words to be spoken by each class.
Yudhishthira asks to whom the offerings to gods and ancestors should be given to earn the greatest reward.

Bhishma says that gifts to needy, ascetic and ruined Brahmanas earn great merit, and then lists deeds that send people to hell, such as lying, adultery, robbery, cheating women, spoiling water and buildings, and eating without sharing.

Bhishma names deeds that lead to heaven, such as honouring Brahmanas, truthfulness, serving parents, founding retreats and towns, feeding and charity, and protecting others, and then ends his teaching on rites and gifts.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the circumstances in which a person becomes guilty of Brahmanicide without killing a Brahmana.

Bhishma says he once asked Vyasa the same question, and Vyasa listed acts that count as Brahmanicide: refusing food to an invited Brahmana on a false pretext, ruining a learned Brahmana's means of living, obstructing thirsty cattle, condemning the Srutis, withholding a daughter from a worthy groom, causing grief to Brahmanas, robbing the blind, lame or simple, and burning hermitages or towns.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to speak of the merit of pilgrimage, bathing and hearing about the sacred waters on earth, and to name them.
Bhishma says that Angiras made the list, and that Gautama asked him what merit a bath in these waters brings toward the next world.

Angiras lists the sacred waters across the land and the rewards of fasting and bathing at each, including heaven, the merit of horse-sacrifices, cleansing from sin, beauty and power, and says the teaching, recited or heard, brings a good birth and memory of past lives.
Vaisampayana describes Bhishma, felled by Arjuna, lying on his bed of arrows and visited by many great Rishis, who converse with him and then vanish while the Pandavas bow to them.
After the Rishis leave, Yudhishthira bows at Bhishma's feet and resumes his questions on righteousness.
Yudhishthira asks which countries, provinces, retreats, mountains and rivers are foremost in sanctity.
Bhishma recounts an old tale of a Brahmana who keeps the Sila and Unccha vows, who hosts a Rishi crowned with success and then talks with him on the Vedas and Upanishads.
The poor Brahmana puts Yudhishthira's question to the Rishi, asking which countries, rivers and mountains are most sacred.

The Rishi answers that the places along the Bhagirathi Ganga are holiest, and praises her at great length: her waters cleanse sin, rescue ancestors, lead to heaven and surpass sacrifices, and even her sight and name bring merit.
Bhishma says the Rishi then rose into the sky, the Brahmana worshipped Ganga and gained success, and he urges Yudhishthira to seek her with devotion.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira and his brothers were delighted, and that reciting or hearing this praise of Ganga cleanses every sin.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whether a Kshatriya, Vaisya or Sudra can attain Brahmanahood by penance, by rites or by learning.

Bhishma says Brahmanahood cannot be won directly from the other three orders, but is reached only after many births, and tells of Matanga, a boy raised with Brahmana rites, who beats a she-ass for running to its mother and asks her why he has been rebuked.
The she-ass says Matanga was begotten by a Sudra barber upon a Brahmana woman, so he is a Chandala by birth and not a Brahmana.
Matanga returns home, and his father asks why he came back without gathering the sacrificial requisites.
Matanga says that a person with a stained birth cannot be happy, resolves on the austerest penance, and is approached by Indra, who offers him any boon.
Matanga asks, as his boon, that he may attain the status of a Brahmana by means of his penance.
Indra warns Matanga that the status of a Brahmana cannot be won by one of impure birth, and urges him to abandon the pursuit before he is destroyed.

Matanga, undeterred by Indra, stands on one foot for a hundred years; Indra returns and explains that a person must pass through the Pukkasa, Sudra, Vaisya and Kshatriya orders and through several grades of Brahmana over immense spans of time before reaching Brahmanahood, and asks Matanga to choose some other boon.
Matanga refuses Indra's advice and spends a thousand years in penance, standing on one foot.
After another thousand years, Matanga asks Indra why he still has not won Brahmana status.
Indra says a Chandala can never become a Brahmana; Matanga goes to Prayaga and Gaya and penances until he collapses, and Indra catches him.
Indra explains that Brahmana status is out of Matanga's reach, describes its honour and dangers, and asks him to choose another boon.
Matanga protests that Indra is wounding a man already dead, blames his mother for his birth, and asks for some other boon.
Bhishma says Indra again urges Matanga to name a boon.
Matanga asks for the power to change shape, fly, enjoy pleasures, be honoured by Brahmanas and Kshatriyas, and win lasting fame.

Indra grants him fame as the deity of a verse measure and worship from women, then leaves; Matanga dies and goes to a high place, and Bhishma concludes that Brahmana status is high and comes only by birth.
Yudhishthira asks how Vitahavya gained Brahmana status, since Viswamitra did too, and whether it came by a boon or by penance.
Bhishma begins the story: Haihaya's hundred sons take Kasi from Haryyaswa and later defeat Sudeva, and Divodasa rebuilds Benares and fights them for a thousand days.
Divodasa loses his army and treasury, flees his capital, and seeks refuge with the sage Bharadwaja.

Divodasa pleads for protection; Bharadwaja arranges a sacrifice that brings a son, Pratarddana, who quickly masters the Vedas and arms and defeats the Vitahavya sons; Vitahavya flees to Bhrigu, and Pratarddana follows him there.

Pratarddana asks for Vitahavya, but Bhrigu says no Kshatriya is in his hermitage; Pratarddana leaves, and Vitahavya becomes a Brahmana by Bhrigu's word. The text then gives the line from Gritsamada through Ruru and Pramadvara to Saunaka.
Yudhishthira asks which men in the three worlds deserve reverence and says he never tires of hearing such talk.
Bhishma introduces an old dialogue in which Narada worships many Brahmanas, and Krishna asks whom he is honouring.
Narada names the Brahmanas he honours and lists their virtues, such as penance, Vedic study, self-restraint, charity and hospitality, and says those who keep them cross every calamity.
Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to honour the deities, the ancestors, the Brahmanas and guests, and says this brings a good end.
Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from protecting creatures that beg for shelter.
Bhishma tells of a pigeon chased by a hawk that takes shelter in King Vrishadarbha's lap, and the king comforts it.
The hawk argues that the pigeon is its rightful food and that the king's authority does not extend to birds of the sky.
The king is struck with wonder but does not dismiss the hawk's words, and he turns to answer.
The king offers the hawk other meats such as beef, boar, deer or buffalo, and says he will not abandon a creature that sought his protection.
The hawk refuses other meat, says hawks eat pigeons by natural law, and asks for the king's own flesh equal in weight to the pigeon.

The king cuts his own flesh to weigh against the pigeon; the palace grieves, the earth trembles, and the king finally climbs onto the scale. The gods arrive, showers of nectar and flowers fall, and the king rises to heaven. The text then draws its moral and says reciting the story cleanses sin.
Yudhishthira asks which act a king should put first, and which one brings happiness in both worlds.

Bhishma says that worshipping Brahmanas is the king's foremost duty, describes the varied kinds of Brahmanas and their powers, notes that insulting them brings downfall, and ends by saying no one can overcome them.

Bhishma says Brahmanas must be revered and supported, that the kingdom's peace depends on it, and that the Kshatriyas who fought them were defeated; he then introduces a talk between Vasudeva and the Earth.
Vasudeva asks the Earth by what conduct a householder can cleanse all his sins.
The Earth replies that serving Brahmanas cleanses and brings prosperity, fame and self-knowledge, and that speaking against them brings ruin.
Bhishma says Krishna praised the Earth's words and urges Yudhishthira to always worship the superior Brahmanas.
Bhishma says Brahmanas deserve worship by birth and recites Brahma's verses on their duties, their study and sacrifice, their power, and the need for kings to serve them.
A note says the Anusasana Parva continues in Volume XI.
A heading marks the start of Section XXXVI.
Bhishma introduces the story: Sakra, disguised as a matted-haired ascetic, visits the Asura Samvara in a plain car.
Sakra asks Samvara how he won leadership over his people.
Samvara says he respects Brahmanas, learns from them, serves them and takes their teaching to heart; he compares them to bees filling honeycomb.
Samvara repeats Soma's teaching to his father: Brahmanas gain success through penance and speech, should study the Vedas, and should not stay idle at home.
Bhishma says Sakra was moved by these words, began to honour Brahmanas, and gained the chiefdom of the gods.
Yudhishthira asks which kind of person is the best recipient of a gift: a stranger, a long-known companion, or a visitor from far away.
Bhishma says all three are equal in claim, that gifts should not harm one's dependants, and that a newcomer, a familiar person and a distant traveller all deserve gifts.
Yudhishthira agrees that gifts must not break the scriptures, and says the giver must first judge whether the gift will benefit the recipient.
Bhishma lists the qualities of a worthy recipient, condemns quarrelsome and proud Brahmanas, and sets out the householder's duties to the gods, sages, ancestors, Brahmanas and guests.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to speak about the nature of women, whom he calls the root of evil and very frail.
Bhishma introduces an old story in which Narada meets the Apsara Panchachuda in Brahma's realm and asks her a question.
Panchachuda says she will answer if the subject is within her knowledge.
Narada asks her to explain the disposition of women.
Panchachuda says she cannot speak ill of her own sex, Narada says that speaking the truth is no fault, and she agrees to answer.
Panchachuda lists the faults she attributes to women: they break their restraints, favour any man who courts them, are never satisfied, and were created with these faults.
Yudhishthira asks why men are drawn to women despite their faults, how women are said to deceive men, whether women can be restrained, and whether anyone has ever succeeded in restraining them.
Bhishma says women are sinful and recounts how Brahma created them after the gods feared human righteousness; then he introduces the story of Vipula guarding the wife of his teacher, Devasarman.
Devasarman says he is leaving for a sacrifice, warns that Indra covets his wife Ruchi, and asks Vipula to guard her closely.
Vipula agrees to do so, but as his teacher is about to leave he asks one more question.
Vipula asks what forms Indra takes and what his body and power are like.
Bhishma says the sage Devasarman truly described all of Indra's illusions to Vipula.
Devasarman describes Indra's many shapes; Vipula weighs the options and decides to enter Ruchi's body by yoga power, staying unseen to guard her until his teacher returns.

Indra takes a beautiful form and enters the hermitage; Vipula sits motionless inside Ruchi, who cannot rise to welcome him, and Indra speaks to her while Vipula controls her words; Indra is shamed, sees Vipula, and fears his curse.
Vipula comes out of Ruchi's body and rebukes Indra, recalls Gautama's curse that gave him his sex-marks, and warns him to respect the Brahmanas and leave.
Indra slips away in shame; Devasarman returns, hears Vipula's account, praises him, and grants him a boon that he will never fall from righteousness.

Vipula, proud of his penance, is sent by his teacher to fetch the same flowers that Ruchi's sister wants; he finds them, passes two quarrelling couples and a group of dice players who each swear oaths naming his fate, and at last recalls that he never told his teacher about entering Ruchi's body; he delivers the flowers and honours his teacher.
Bhishma says Devasarman addressed his disciple Vipula on his return from the errand.
Devasarman says he knows how Vipula protected Ruchi, and asks what Vipula saw on his journey.
Vipula asks who the two couples and six men were, since they seemed to know him.

Devasarman explains that they were Day and Night and the six Seasons, who witness every deed; he says Vipula's concealment was a fault, but his protection of Ruchi was proper, so he sends him to heaven. Bhishma adds that he heard this from Markandeya, and that women should be guarded, virtuous women are blessed, men should not be over-attached, and only Vipula protected women.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whom a father should choose as a husband for his daughter, calling marriage the foremost duty.
Bhishma says the father should judge the groom's conduct, learning and birth before giving his daughter, and describes the Brahma and Gandharva forms of marriage and the Asura form of purchase.

Bhishma describes the Rakshasa form, calls three of the five forms righteous and two not, gives the number of wives each caste may take, and sets rules on marriage ages, unmarried girls, and whom one may not wed.
Yudhishthira asks whose wife the girl becomes when a dower is paid, promised, or simply displayed, or when a suitor takes her hand with rites.

Bhishma says the girl's hand must be given with proper rites and the kinsmen's consent, that a marriage forced on an unwilling girl brings sin, and that a girl promised to another does not make a later marriage wrong.
Yudhishthira asks how a father should act when a more eligible suitor appears after a dower has been accepted from another.
Bhishma says a dower does not make a girl a wife, that such a payment is a price rather than a marriage, and that a promise or a father's declaration is not marriage either.

Bhishma recounts how he seized two maidens for Vichitravirya, and how king Valhika ruled that a wife is made by the proper giving and taking of her hand, not by a sale. Prince Satyavat then answers questions on a dower-giver who dies, a widow's remarriage to a brother-in-law, and the wedding rites that end at the seventh step, concluding with the gift of a maiden with water and the circling of the fire.
Yudhishthira asks what the father or kinsmen should do when a man who gave a dowry walks away from the marriage.

Bhishma says the girl should be maintained by her father, and that the dowry-giver may claim her, but may not marry her by proper rites; he cites Savitri's choice of a husband and an opinion of a king of Videha's line that women are never free.
Yudhishthira asks on what authority a man's wealth passes to others when he has only daughters.

Bhishma says a daughter is like a son, and explains inheritance rules for daughters and daughters' sons, including the case where a sold daughter's sons belong to the buyer. He cites Yama's verse on the hell awaiting those who sell children, condemns the Arsha and forced marriages as sale or sin, and says no wealth gained by sin can buy merit.

Bhishma recites Daksha's view that a maiden for whom no dowry is taken is not sold, then urges respect and kindness towards wives, warns that a family whose women suffer will decline, and cites Manu's charge to men to protect women.
Yudhishthira asks how the property of a Brahmana with wives from four classes should pass to his sons.

Bhishma says a Brahmana should marry within the three higher classes, and that a Sudra wife brings sin and expiation; he then divides the Brahmana's property into ten parts, four to the Brahmana wife's son, three to the Kshatriya's, two to the Vaisya's and one to the Sudra's, only if the father gives it; he adds rules on a wife's own allowance and the daughter's share.
Yudhishthira asks why the Sudra-born son should get any share at all, since all the sons are Brahmanas by birth.

Bhishma says all wives are called Data, but the Brahmana wife ranks highest; he explains that Brahmanas and Kshatriyas each have a proper rank, and that the Kshatriya's son takes a larger share than the Vaisya's because Kshatriyas protect society.
Yudhishthira says Bhishma has explained the rules for Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira asks what rules apply to the other classes.

Bhishma gives the rules for Kshatriyas (two wives, eight shares) and Vaisyas (one wife, five shares), says the Sudra may have only one wife, and states that the eldest son takes one extra share, a rule Kasyapa declared.
Yudhishthira asks what duties fall to those born of mixed classes, through lust, greed or ignorance of birth.

Bhishma says the four orders were set up for sacrifice, explains the status and duties of the offspring of each mixed pairing, such as the Parasara, Ugra, Suta, Vaidehaka, Chandala, Magadha and Nishada, and their multiplication into many lower castes; he warns that lust and women's pull lead men astray, so wise men avoid excessive attachment.
