Yudhishthira asks whether there are signs by which a person of impure birth, who looks respectable, can be recognised.

Bhishma says birth shows in conduct, that a son takes after his sire or his mother, and that goodness of understanding only counts when it matches the person's order; he advises avoiding women with whom offspring would be improper.
Yudhishthira asks for teaching on the orders, the sons of different wives, and the disputes that arise over sons.

Bhishma lists the kinds of sons: a son of one's loins, a son begotten by an invited man, a son begotten without consent, a son of a fallen man, the given, the made, the Adhyudha, and the Kanina, as well as the six Apadhwansajas and six Apasadas.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the Apadhwansajas and the Apasadas.
Bhishma explains the Apadhwansajas (sons of a Brahmana, Kshatriya or Vaisya by lower wives) and the Apasadas (Chandala, Vratya, Vaidya, Magadha, Vamaka and Suta), and says all six are sons.
Yudhishthira asks whether the son belongs to the one who owns the soil or to the one who gave the seed, and whether both are equal.
Bhishma says a son belongs to the seed-giver, unless the seed-giver abandons him, in which case he belongs to his mother's husband; the same goes for the Adhyudha.
Yudhishthira asks how the mother's husband can own a son when the seed-giver made the child.

Bhishma says the seed alone does not make a son, that a child born in the soil of a man who married a pregnant woman belongs to the soil-owner, and that the made son is the one who has been adopted and brought up.
Yudhishthira asks what kind of son the made son is, whose sonship rests on rearing rather than seed or soil.
Bhishma says a child abandoned by his parents and raised by a finder, who cannot trace the parents, becomes the rearer's made son and takes the rearer's order.
Yudhishthira asks what purification rites apply to such a son and whom he should marry.

Bhishma says the purification rites follow the rearer's custom and kin, and that children of unwed or pre-marriage birth receive the same rites as other sons; he ends by asking whether Yudhishthira wants more.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about compassion at another's suffering, the bonds that come from living together, and the blessedness of cows.
Bhishma introduces the story of Nahusha and the sage Chyavana, who takes a twelve-year vow and stands in the river like a post while the current rushes past him.
A group of fishermen cast a large net, drag Chyavana up with the fish, and bow to him; the fish die, and Chyavana is moved to pity. The fishermen apologise and offer to do whatever he wishes.
Chyavana says he will either die with the fish or be sold with them, and does not want to abandon them; the fishermen go in fear to report to king Nahusha.
Bhishma says Nahusha hears of Chyavana's plight, goes to the spot with his ministers and priest, and honours the sage.
Nahusha asks Chyavana what he should do, promising to accomplish anything.
Chyavana asks Nahusha to pay the fishermen the price of himself and the fish.
Nahusha orders his priest to give the fishermen a thousand coins for the sage.
Chyavana says a thousand coins cannot be his price and asks Nahusha to set a fair value.
Nahusha offers a hundred thousand coins and asks if that is enough.
Chyavana refuses that sum and asks Nahusha to consult his ministers about a fair price.
Nahusha orders his priest to give the fishermen a crore of coins.
Nahusha adds that more should be paid if a crore is not enough.
Chyavana refuses even a crore and asks Nahusha to consult the Brahmanas.
Nahusha offers half of his kingdom, or all of it, as the price.
Chyavana refuses the kingdom and asks Nahusha to consult the sages.
Nahusha is grieved and deliberates with his advisers; a sage born of a cow arrives and promises to satisfy both the king and Chyavana.
Nahusha begs the cow-born sage to name the price, since Chyavana's anger could destroy the three worlds.
The cow-born sage says Brahmanas have no price and cows are priceless, so a cow should be the price; Nahusha is glad.
Nahusha tells Chyavana that he has been bought for a cow, which is his proper price.
Chyavana accepts and praises cows at length as the source of sacrifice, prosperity and heaven.
Bhishma says he can only describe part of the glory of cows.
The fishermen beg Chyavana's grace and offer to take back the cow.
Chyavana accepts the cow back and tells the fishermen to go to heaven with their catch.

The fishermen and fish ascend to heaven; Nahusha is amazed; the two sages grant him boons, and Chyavana returns to his hermitage. Bhishma closes by listing the topics of compassion, companionship, the blessings of cows, and true righteousness, and asks Yudhishthira what else he wants to know.

Yudhishthira asks how Rama, born into a Brahmana family, came to follow Kshatriya ways, and how a Kshatriya son of Kusika became a Brahmana; he also asks why the grandsons, rather than the sons, of Richika and Kusika took opposite paths.
Bhishma tells of Chyavana, who sees that his own race will be stained by a Kusika descendant's Kshatriya ways, and decides to bring ruin on the Kusika line; he asks King Kusika to let him stay.
Kusika says living with a guest is not an ordained custom, but he agrees to do whatever the sage asks.
Kusika and his queen honour Chyavana with water, food and every courtesy, and offer their wealth, kingdom and throne.

Chyavana declines the riches and asks the king and queen to serve him during a vow; they wait on him through twenty-one days and nights without food while he sleeps, then he leaves unseen and the stricken king searches for him.
Yudhishthira asks what Kusika and his queen did after Chyavana disappeared.

Kusika returns home in grief, then finds Chyavana asleep on his bed again; the couple resume serving him, bathe him in oil, and prepare a lavish feast, which Chyavana sets on fire; the sage then sets the king and queen to yoke themselves to a battle-car and drives them through the city, goading them until they bleed, while they show no anger.

Chyavana gives away the royal treasure, then heals the couple with a touch, and tells Kusika he has passed the test and may return to the city; Kusika and his queen go home youthful and beautiful, and Chyavana turns the riverbank into a splendid retreat.

Kusika goes to the wood and sees a golden palace, wondrous trees, birds and musicians; the scene vanishes when Chyavana is approached, and the king reflects on the power of penance and the status of Brahmanas. Chyavana tells the king he has passed the fiery test and offers a boon.
Kusika says that surviving the ordeal and pleasing the sage are boon enough, and asks the sage to answer some doubts he has.
Chyavana offers Kusika a boon and asks him to name his doubt.
Kusika asks why Chyavana slept, went out in silence, vanished, burned the food, drove the car, gave away wealth, and showed the golden wonders, and why they vanished.

Chyavana says the Creator foretold a clash of Brahmana and Kshatriya energy, so he came to destroy Kusika's race; finding the king blameless, he tested him to show the rewards of penance, and he promises that a grandson will become a Brahmana and an ascetic of great fire, and that a descendant in the third generation will gain Brahmana status.
Kusika says this is a high boon, asks that his race attain Brahmanahood, and asks how this will come about and who will be his kin and friends.

Chyavana foretells the Kshatriya-Bhargava conflict, the rise of Urva and Richika, Jamadagni's marriage to Gadhi's daughter, the birth of Viswamitra as a Kshatriya, and the exchange of sons that makes Kusika's third descendant a Brahmana.
Kusika accepts the promise and asks for his race to attain Brahmana status; Chyavana grants it and leaves, and Bhishma says the births of Rama and Viswamitra happened as foretold.
Yudhishthira grieves over the millions slain in the war and the widows left behind, believing the Kurus he killed will send him to hell, and asks Bhishma for instruction in penance.
The narrator Vaisampayana says Bhishma reflected on Yudhishthira's words and prepared to answer.

Bhishma lists the rewards that various acts bring after death, such as heaven, fame and wealth from penances and vows, and especially from gifts of cows, land, houses, food, lamps, garments, and other goods to Brahmanas.

Vaisampayana reports that Yudhishthira is moved to seek the end reserved for heroes and no longer despises the householder's life; he asks the brothers to accept the grandsire's words, and they all agree.
Yudhishthira asks what rewards come from planting trees and digging tanks.

Bhishma says a tank earns honour, that its water counts as sacrifices by season, that gifts of water are the foremost gifts, and that planting trees brings fame and rescues ancestors; he ends by urging tanks, trees, sacrifice and truth.
Yudhishthira asks which gift is most distinguished and which one follows the giver into the next world.

Bhishma calls kindness, relief for the distressed, and gifts given without vanity the highest gifts; he praises gifts of gold, cows and land, urges generosity to the poor and worthy, and says that kings must honour Brahmanas, whose disciplined lives make giving to them a sacrifice; he closes by declaring that the Brahmanas are dearer to him than anyone.
Yudhishthira asks which of two equally qualified Brahmanas deserves a gift more, the one who begs or the one who does not.

Bhishma says a gift to one who does not ask earns greater merit, that a Brahmana's firmness lies in not begging, that begging is a reproach, and that kings should seek out and honour such Brahmanas with houses, food and other gifts, as a kind of sacrifice.
Yudhishthira asks where the rewards of gifts and sacrifices are earned, which is greater, to whom gifts should go, and how and when they should be made.

Bhishma says a Kshatriya's sacrifices and gifts purify him, that kings should support worthy Brahmanas with cattle, food, homes and goods, and that such giving outweighs royal sacrifices; he warns that wealth extorted from subjects spoils a sacrifice, that a king must protect the weak and the hungry, that the king bears a share of his subjects' sins if he fails to do so, and that subjects may rise against a king who plunders them.
Yudhishthira asks which gift is the best or foremost of all, since kings make many gifts to many men.

Bhishma says the gift of earth is the first and highest, since land lasts and yields wealth to its owner; he explains that giving land cleanses sinners, that a king should give land to learned Brahmanas, that taking land from the righteous is a grave sin, and recites the verse by which Rama gave the whole earth to Kasyapa.
Indra asks the teacher Vrihaspati which gift leads to heaven and to lasting merit.

Vrihaspati replies that a gift of earth to the worthy brings merit beyond great sacrifices, that taking back a gift of earth is punished, that giving land to Brahmanas rescues one's ancestors, and that earth-gifts bring heavenly rewards.

Bhishma says Indra then gave the whole earth to Vrihaspati, and advises reciting these verses at funeral rites, so that the offerings are not seized by demons; he closes by asking whether Yudhishthira wants to hear more.
Yudhishthira asks which gifts a king should make to accomplished Brahmanas, which gifts gratify them at once, and which rewards both here and hereafter.
Bhishma says he once put the same questions to the sage Narada and is about to recite Narada's answer.

Narada says food is the foremost gift, that all life and every rite rests on food, and that gifts of food to Brahmanas, guests, the poor, and even dogs or outcastes bring merit; he describes the cycle of rain and crops that feeds creatures, and the rewards of a feast-giver.

Bhishma says he has always given food on Narada's advice and urges Yudhishthira to do the same, then describes the shining heavenly mansions with their food, rivers of milk and abundant goods that await those who give food.
A heading marks the start of Section LXIV.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to discuss gifts in relation to the conjunctions of the planets and stars.
Bhishma introduces a discourse in which Narada, visiting Dwaraka, answers Devaki's question about gifts.

Narada lists the gifts for each lunar constellation in turn, from Krittika through Bharani, such as ghee-rich Payasa, venison, cows, gold, cars and cloths, along with the heavenly rewards each brings.
Bhishma says Devaki herself repeated this teaching to her daughters-in-law, the wives of Krishna.

Bhishma cites Atri on the value of gold gifts, Harischandra on gold's cleansing and life-lengthening power, and Manu on drink as the best gift; he praises digging wells and tanks, gifts of ghee and firewood, and umbrellas, and ends by citing Sandilya's view that a car is the best gift.
Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from giving sandals to a Brahmana whose feet are scorched by hot sand.
Bhishma says sandals protect the feet, overcome enemies, and bring the merit of gifting a fine vehicle.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to repeat the merits of gifts of sesame, land, cows and food.

Bhishma says sesame was made by Brahma as food for the Pitris and that gifts of sesame purify the giver; he gives examples of sages who reached heaven by such gifts, and prepares to tell of the gods' request for earth.
The gods ask Brahma for a piece of earth to hold their sacrifice, saying that a sacrifice performed on land not lawfully obtained brings no merit.
Brahma grants the gods a piece of earth on which to hold their sacrifice.

The gods hold their sacrifice on the Himavat mountain with famous sages present, and attach a sixth part of its merit to the gift of earth; Bhishma then praises gifts of a house, shelter, land, mineral-rich land, and kine, and says that Brahma's cows should not be given to butchers, farmers, atheists or herdsmen; he ends by praising the gift of food and the merit of gifts of sesame, earth, and kine.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the great merits of giving drink, now that he has heard about food.

Bhishma says food and drink together are unmatched as gifts, that all life depends on food, and that everything, including food and nectar, arises from water; he says the gift of water brings long life, fame and victory, and cites Manu's promise of endless heaven.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to speak again about gifts of sesame, lamps, food and robes.

Bhishma tells the story of Yama sending a messenger to fetch the learned Brahmana Sarmin of Agastya's line from the town of Parnasala; the messenger instead brings another Brahmana, whom Yama honours and wants returned.
Yama says he cannot fix a man's allotted time, so he cannot let the Brahmana stay; he tells him to go home and say what he needs from Yama.
The Brahmana asks Yama what acts bring the greatest merit.

Yama teaches that gifts of sesame are supremely meritorious, that they should be made on certain days and at Sraddhas, that water-gifts and water stations are rare and praiseworthy, and that wells and tanks should be dug.

Bhishma says the messenger returned the Brahmana home and then fetched the rightful Sarmin, whom Yama honoured and sent back with the same instructions; Bhishma adds that lamps for dark places please the Pitris and the gods, that gems and robes bring merit when rightly given, and that a son is the greatest acquisition.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma again about the rules of gifts, especially the gift of earth, which classes may make gifts, and what the Vedas say.

Bhishma names kine, earth and knowledge as three gifts of equal worth, says that teaching sound lessons to a disciple matches giving earth and kine, and praises cows as mothers of all creatures who must not be kicked or harmed.
Yudhishthira asks which cows are fit to give, which should be passed over, and who should and should not receive them.

Bhishma says cows should not go to the unrighteous, the greedy, liars or those who neglect the Pitris and gods; he praises gifts of ten cows to a learned, poor Brahmana, lists those worthy of support, and warns that robbing a Brahmana is as sinful as giving a cow is meritorious.

Bhishma tells how king Nriga was punished for taking a Brahmana's cow: Yadava youths find a huge lizard in a well and bring Krishna, who draws it out and learns it is the soul of Nriga; Nriga confesses that he gave away a cow that another Brahmana had lost, that both Brahmanas refused his offers of many cows, gold and horses; Yama then judged that his sin of breaking his oath and taking a Brahmana's property must be paid for; Nriga fell into the well as a lizard, and Yama had promised that Krishna would rescue him, which he now does, and Krishna then recites the verse that a Brahmana's property destroys the taker and that goodness brings rescue, so one must not harm kine.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for more on the merits of giving cows, saying he is never tired of his words.

Bhishma tells of the sage Uddalaki, who sends his son Nachiketa for firewood, Kusa grass, flowers, water and potherbs; the son finds that the current has swept them away, the father curses him to meet Yama, the boy dies, and the father's grief restores him; Nachiketa then describes Yama's realm, its mansions and rivers of milk and ghee, and Yama's rules for gifts of cows.

Nachiketa says Yama taught him substitutes for cows, such as cows made of ghee, sesame or water, and urged him to give cows regularly; Nachiketa says the curse was a blessing that let him see the rewards of giving.
Yudhishthira asks about the regions reserved for those who give cows, since he has heard of Nachiketa's teaching and of Nriga's fate.
Bhishma introduces a discourse between Brahma and the sacrificer Indra.

Indra says the residents of the cow-givers' regions outshine the gods of heaven and asks what those regions are, what they yield, how long the rewards last, and how gifts of many cows compare with gifts of few.

Brahma tells Indra that the cow-givers' regions are beyond even Indra's sight and describes their qualities, the virtues and vows that lead there, the sins that bar the way, the merit of gifts of cows by class and means, and the rules for choosing recipients and performing the gift; he closes by praising the reverence for cows, and the rewards for a rescuer of cows and Brahmanas.
Indra asks what becomes of a man who knowingly steals a cow or sells one for greed.

Brahma says that killers, eaters and sellers of cows, and those who let them be slaughtered for profit, will rot in hell for as many years as the cow has hairs; a stolen cow given away still brings the punishment for theft; gold is the best Dakshina for cow-gifts, and it rescues the giver's ancestors and descendants.

Bhishma says Brahma taught this to Indra, who taught Dasaratha, who taught Rama, who taught Lakshmana; the sages and righteous kings kept it, and Bhishma's own teacher passed it on to him; whoever recites it at assemblies, sacrifices and gifts of cows gains lasting heaven.
Yudhishthira asks about the rewards of vows, study, gifts, the refusal of gifts, teaching, heroism in battle, purity, celibacy, service to parents and teachers, and compassion.

Bhishma says those who keep vows to the end, study the Vedas, and practise self-restraint win lasting honour and happiness; self-restraint outweighs gifts because a giver may be spoiled by anger; he describes the rewards of teachers, students, warriors and gift-givers, names many kinds of heroes, says truth outweighs a thousand horse-sacrifices, and ends by praising lifelong celibacy and service to parents, which spare a man from hell.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out in detail the rules that govern gifts of cows, since they lead to lasting heaven.

Bhishma says a lawfully acquired cow given away rescues the giver's family; he recounts how Mandhatri asked Vrihaspati about the rite, which requires honouring Brahmanas, choosing cows of the Rohini class, spending the night in the cow-pen with mantras, giving the cow with a calf and a bull at sunrise, and using substitutes such as the value of a cow, cloth or gold; he gives the rewards for each, and names kings who won heaven by this rite.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira followed Bhishma's teaching: he gave cows often, lived on barley and dung, slept on bare earth, revered cows, and stopped yoking cattle to his vehicles.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira again asks Bhishma for the details of cow-gifts.
Yudhishthira says he has not tired of Bhishma's words and asks for more on the merit of giving cows.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma goes on to describe the merit of cow-gifts.

Bhishma says a cow with a calf, gentle and young, wrapped in cloth, cleanses a giver's sins; a sick, dry, weak or unpaid cow should never be given; only strong, well-behaved, fragrant cows are worthy, and the Kapila is the best, as the Ganga is the best river.
Yudhishthira asks why the Kapila cow is especially praised, when all good cows should count alike.

Bhishma tells how Daksha, asked by Brahma to create living things, made food first, and how his breath made the cow Surabhi, whose golden Kapila daughters sustained creatures; froth from their milk fell on Mahadeva, who angered at the milk and glared at the cows; Daksha said the milk stays pure, gave Mahadeva a bull, and Mahadeva became the bull-bannered lord of cattle; Bhishma closes by praising Kapila cow-gifts and their rewards.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira and his brothers gave bulls and cows of many colours to the Brahmanas, and gave hundreds of thousands of cows in sacrifices.
Bhishma says that king Saudasa of Ikshvaku's line asked his priest Vasishtha, a great and long-lived sage, what sacred thing brings merit if recited.
Saudasa asks Vasishtha which sacred thing in the three worlds brings great merit when recited at all times.
Vasishtha bows to the cows, purifies himself, and begins to teach the mystery of cows.

Vasishtha praises cows as the refuge of all creatures, the source of sacrifice and prosperity, and the proper food for the gods; he says that gifts to cows and the honour shown to them bring prosperity, and gives rules: never eat their flesh, never soil their dung, bow to them morning and evening, say their names at night and morning, and end every rite and every fear with their names.

Vasishtha tells how the cows of old performed penance, asked Brahma that they become the best gifts and that their dung purify people, received the boon, and became the refuge of the world; he then lists the regions gained by giving cows of various colours and calves, and bulls, to the gods and their realms, and describes the giver's welcome in heaven and his return to a noble family.

Vasishtha recites a mantra calling cows the source of ghee and milk and asking them to stay near him, says it cleanses daily sins when recited after washing; he describes the rivers of milk and curds that await those who give a thousand cows, calls cows the refuge of the universe, says a Kapila cow given with a calf and brass vessel carries the giver safely past Yama's palace, and says no gift or refuge is higher than the cow.
Bhishma says Saudasa took Vasishtha's words to heart, gave many cows to Brahmanas with restrained senses, and won many regions of felicity.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the most sacred of all sacred things.

Bhishma says cows are the foremost of sacred things, that they sustain all creatures with their milk and clarified butter, and that kings like Mandhatri, Yayati and Nahusha gave cows by the thousand; he introduces Suka asking his father Vyasa, called the Island-born Krishna in the text, which sacrifice and act is greatest.

Vyasa says cows are the stay and refuge of creatures; that they were once hornless until they worshipped Brahma, who gave them horns and their wishes; he describes the splendid region of the cow-givers, with its flowers, gems, streams and lakes; he gives mantras, cow-product fasts and the reward of Gomati chants, and says cows can grant any wish when served with reverence.
Bhishma says Suka took his father's words to heart and worshipped cows every day, and urges Yudhishthira to do the same.
Yudhishthira asks how cow dung came to hold Sree, the goddess of fortune, and asks Bhishma to explain.
Bhishma introduces a conversation between the cows and Sree, who enters a herd in beautiful form, and the cows are amazed.
The cows ask Sree who she is, where she comes from and where she goes.
Sree says she is dear to all creatures, that she brings success to gods and sages and that she wants to dwell in each cow.
The cows say she is fickle and passed around, so they do not want her, and bid her go elsewhere.
Sree asks why the cows reject her, saying that no one turns her away and that she is hard to win.
The cows say they do not slight her, but she is restless, so they let her go wherever she chooses.
Sree pleads that she will be shunned by all the world if the cows reject her, and offers to dwell even in the most unclean parts of their bodies.
Bhishma says the kind cows took counsel together and then spoke to Sree.
The cows say she should live in their urine and dung, since both are sacred.
Sree thanks the cows, accepts their offer, and agrees to the compact.
Bhishma says Sree vanished before the cows, and that he will now tell more of the glory of cows.

Bhishma says the givers of cows and those who eat the remnants of offerings always sacrifice, since ghee is the root of sacrifice; he tells how the gods and sages honoured Brahma, and how Indra asked why the cows' realm is higher than the gods'; Brahma explains that cows are the limbs of sacrifice, that calves help with tilling, and that Surabhi, daughter of Daksha, won the boon of an eternal realm called Goloka through long austerities; Brahma then tells Indra that the path to that realm is through chastity, penance, truth and gifts.

Bhishma says Indra took up daily worship of cows after hearing Brahma, and that the devoted, men and women alike, gain sons, wealth, learning and happiness; he closes the account of the sanctity of cows.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma why gold is the best sacrificial gift, and what gold is, where it came from, and what it stands for.
Bhishma tells how, while performing his father's rites, a hand rose from the ground through the grass. He offered the cake on the grass instead, and in a dream his ancestors urged him to give gold.

The sages tell Parashurama that gold, born from Agni's seed, is a cleanser. Vasishtha explains that each kind of gift stands for a deity or world, and that gold holds them all, so giving it is the highest gift.
Vasishtha begins a tale of Rudra and Uma, whose seed the gods asked him to hold back; a fallen drop grew into a blazing power, and the Asura Taraka then harried the gods.
The gods ask Brahma to rescue them from the Asura Taraka, who has been troubling them and the sages.
Brahma says he cannot approve of wrong and orders Taraka destroyed, promising the gods that their fear will be eased.
The gods point out that Taraka cannot be killed by gods, Asuras or Rakshasas, and that Uma's curse has left them without offspring.
Brahma explains that Agni, who was absent when the curse fell, will beget a son to destroy Taraka, and he sends the gods to search for Agni.

Agni hides in the waters; a frog betrays him and is cursed, and the gods bless the frogs. Next an elephant reveals Agni in an Aswattha tree, and Agni curses the elephants before moving to a Sami tree.
The gods bless the elephants, and a parrot reveals Agni in the Sami tree; Agni curses the parrots, and the gods bless them and make Sami wood the fire-producing fuel for rites.
Agni asks why the gods have come, and he offers to do whatever they require.
The gods ask Agni to beget a heroic son who can destroy Taraka, and Agni agrees and goes to Ganga, who becomes distressed by his seed.
Ganga describes the golden fetus she has cast out, and Agni asks about it; the child is reared as Kartikeya, and gold is named Agni's offspring and held sacred.
Vasishtha tells of a sacrifice of Rudra in the form of Varuna, from which the sacrificial elements, Brahma's seed and the sages were born.
Rudra, in his Varuna form, claims the sacrificial offspring as his own, since he is the sacrificer and the offspring came from the fire.

Agni and Brahma also claim the offspring, and Brahma says the fruit belongs to whoever supplied the seed. The gods ask him to bless all sides, and he agrees; the text then teaches gold as a fire substitute, lists gold gifts at sunrise, midday and twilight, and tells of Kartikeya's victory over Taraka.
Bhishma concludes that Parashurama gave gold gifts after hearing this, and urges Yudhishthira to give gold to the Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira asks how Taraka met his end, since he had become unslayable to the gods.
Bhishma tells how the six Krittikas bore and reared the child, how the gods gave him gifts, and how he grew up to slay Taraka. He ends by urging gifts of gold.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach the ordinances for the Sraddha, as Bhishma has done for the four orders.
Vaisampayana says that Bhishma then sets out the Sraddha ritual.

Bhishma says the Pitris must always be honored first, and that the rite is best done on the afternoon of the new moon. He lists the benefits of each lunar day and says the dark fortnight and afternoon are better.
Yudhishthira asks which offering to the Pitris becomes inexhaustible, and which Havi lasts for all time.

Bhishma lists the foods and how long each keeps the Pitris satisfied, from sesame and rice to several meats, including beef. He names offerings that never run out, quotes verses on offering on certain days and constellations, and ends with the merit of a son going to Gaya and of water offered on death anniversaries.
Bhishma lists the constellations for optional Sraddhas, the benefits each brings, and how Sasavindu followed them to rule the whole earth.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which kinds of Brahmanas should receive the offerings made at Sraddhas.

Bhishma says Brahmanas must be vetted before a Sraddha, and gives a long list of kinds who pollute the line, from criminals and certain tradesmen to people with some defects. Their share is said to feed Rakshasas.
Bhishma lists the learned and disciplined Brahmanas who sanctify the line and should be invited, and warns that feeding friends or unworthy people wastes the offerings and yields no merit.
Heading: the next section, Section XCI, begins.
Yudhishthira asks who first conceived the Sraddha, when, what its essence is, and which foods and grains must not be offered.

Bhishma tells how Nimi, grieving for his dead son, held the first Sraddha; Atri then says Brahma himself ordained it, names the deities to be honored, lists the foods to avoid, and bars outcastes from the rite.
After Nimi's rite the sages hold Sraddhas, but the Pitris and gods fall ill from the heavy offerings, and they go to Soma for relief, who sends them to Brahma.
The gods ask Brahma for relief, and he points them to Agni, who sits beside him.

Agni offers to share the offerings with the Pitris so they can digest them, which is why a share goes to fire first. Bhishma then sets out the order of cakes and water offerings, names the Pitris, says the rite frees the dead from misery, and says he will turn to gifts again.
Yudhishthira asks whether Brahmanas under a fast may eat a Sraddha offering at another's invitation without breaking their vow.
Bhishma says those whose vows the Vedas do not prescribe may eat, but those whose vows are Vedic break them by eating.
Yudhishthira asks whether fasting is truly a penance.
Bhishma says a month-long fast does not make one an ascetic, that renunciation is the best penance, and lists a Brahmana's duties, from celibacy to truthfulness and hospitality.
Yudhishthira asks how one becomes always fasting, keeps vows, eats leftovers, and becomes a welcome guest.
Bhishma defines fasting, celibacy, truthfulness, abstaining from meat and eating leftovers, and says these bring heavenly rewards.
Yudhishthira asks what difference there is between the giver and the receiver of gifts to Brahmanas.
Bhishma says a receiver is little harmed by a righteous giver but sinks to hell with an unrighteous one, and begins an old tale of sages starving in a drought.
King Saivya, son of Vrishadarbha, meets the starving sages, who are cooking a dead prince's body, and offers them cattle, mules, bulls, and villages.
The sages refuse the king's offers, leaving the flesh uncooked. The king's men then bring figs stuffed with gold, and Atri refuses them as a trap.
Vasishtha says that even one gold coin is counted as a hundred or a thousand in the fault of accepting it.
Kasyapa says all the grain, gold, animals and women in the world cannot satisfy one person, so one should seek calm.
Bharadwaja compares human greed to a Ruru's horns, which keep growing without measure.
Gautama says a man is like the ocean, which no amount of river water can fill.
Viswamitra says every desire satisfied is followed at once by another that pierces like a shaft.
Jamadagni says abstaining from gifts supports penance, while accepting them destroys its merit.
Arundhati says the pursuit of righteousness is better than the pursuit of worldly wealth.
Ganda says that if such great sages fear this, a weak person like her fears it even more.
Pasusakha says the wealth of righteousness is the highest, and he serves the Brahmanas to learn to value it.
The sages wish the king joy of his gifts, and note that the figs they refused held gold inside.
Bhishma says the sages leave the gold-filled figs and go wherever they wish.
The ministers report to the king that the sages have found the gold and gone.
Vrishadarbhi, enraged, offers libations in his chamber and conjures the terrible Rakshasi Yatudhani from the fire, who asks what he wants.
The king orders Yatudhani to follow the seven sages, Arundhati, and the maidservant and her husband, learn what their names mean, and slay them.
The sages wander in the forest, and Arundhati admires a well-fed mendicant with a dog.
Vasishtha says the mendicant keeps up his fire worship morning and evening, which the sages cannot, so he is well-fed.
Atri says the mendicant feels no hunger and has kept his Vedas, unlike the sages.
Viswamitra says the mendicant still keeps his duties, while the sages have grown idle and lost their learning.
Jamadagni says the mendicant has no need to store a year's grain and fuel, as the sages must.
Kasyapa says the mendicant lacks the four full brothers who beg from house to house, as the sages' families do.
Bharadwaja says the mendicant has no regret for cursing his spouse, unlike the sages.
Gautama says the mendicant lacks the sages' three Kusa-grass coverings and single worn deerskin.
The mendicant greets the sages, and they wander together until they reach a lotus lake guarded by Yatudhani, whom they question.
Yatudhani refuses to say who she is and says she is the lake's guard.
The sages say they are hungry and ask to gather lotus-stalks.
The sages finish their request, asking leave to gather some lotus-stalks.
Yatudhani agrees, on condition that each sage first gives his name.
Bhishma says Atri, understanding that she means to slay them, speaks to her.
Atri explains his name, saying he cleanses the world of sin and studies the Vedas through his nights.
Yatudhani says she cannot understand the explanation and orders him into the lake.
Vasishtha explains his name by his Yoga wealth and his life as the foremost householder.
Yatudhani says she cannot follow the explanation and tells him to plunge in.
Kasyapa explains that he guards his body and gains brightness through penance, which gives him his name.
Yatudhani again calls the explanation incomprehensible and orders him into the lake.
Bharadwaja explains that he supports his sons, pupils, deities, Brahmanas and wife, which gives him his name.
Yatudhani calls Bharadwaja's explanation incomprehensible and sends him into the lake.
Gotama says he conquered heaven and earth by self-restraint, treats all creatures alike, and was born with a light that dispelled darkness.
Yatudhani says that explanation too is incomprehensible.
Viswamitra says the gods are his friends and he is a friend to the whole universe, which is why he has that name.
Yatudhani rejects Viswamitra's explanation and orders him into the lake.
Jamadagni says he sprang from the sacrificial fire of the gods.
Jamadagni concludes that this is why he bears his name.
Yatudhani rejects this explanation and orders him into the lake.
Arundhati says she stays at her husband's side, holds the earth with him, and keeps his heart turned to her, which gives her name.
Yatudhani rejects Arundhati's explanation as well.
Ganda says her name means part of the cheek, and that she has that part a little raised.
Yatudhani rejects this explanation as incomprehensible.
Pasusakha says he protects and tends all animals and is their friend, which is why he has his name.
Yatudhani rejects this explanation and orders him into the lake.
Sunahsakha says he cannot explain his name the way the others did, and gives it to her plainly.
Yatudhani says Sunahsakha has named himself only once and she did not catch it, so he must repeat it.
Sunahsakha says that since she did not catch it, he will strike her with his triple stick and burn her to ashes.
The stick reduces the Rakshasi to ashes. The sages return from the lake to find their gathered lotus-stalks gone.
The sages ask who has stolen the stalks they gathered to eat.
The sages suspect one another and agree that each must swear to his innocence.
Atri's oath calls down penalties on the thief, such as touching cattle with his foot and studying the Vedas on forbidden days.
Vasishtha's oath lists penalties such as abandoning study, becoming an unrestrained mendicant, or selling one's daughter.
Kasyapa's oath calls down penalties such as false testimony, eating unsacrificed flesh, and sex by day.
Bharadwaja's oath lists penalties such as cruelty to women, relatives and cattle, and disrespect to one's teacher.
Jamadagni's oath lists penalties such as fouling water, having no friends, and living off a wife's earnings.
Gotama's oath calls down penalties such as throwing away the Vedas, abandoning the sacred fires, and selling Soma.
Viswamitra's oath lists penalties such as seeing his teachers supported by others, being always impure, and serving impure priests.
Arundhati's oath, phrased for a woman, calls down penalties such as humbling her mother-in-law, eating alone, and bearing a heroic son.
Ganda's oath, also phrased for a woman, lists penalties such as lying, selling her daughter, and living in slavery.
Pasusakha's oath calls down penalties such as being born of a slave-mother and having worthless children.
Sunahsakha's oath gives the thief the merit of giving his daughter to a learned Brahmana.
The sages say the oaths are no oaths at all, since all the acts listed are desirable for Brahmanas, and accuse Sunahsakha of taking their stalks.
Sunahsakha confesses that he took the stalks to test them, says he slew Yatudhani to save them, and reveals that he is Vasava, Indra.
Bhishma says the sages praise Indra and ascend to heaven with him for resisting temptation, and closes with a lesson against greed and the merit of reciting this tale.
Bhishma tells how the sages, touring the holy waters, find Agastya's stalks gone. Agastya laments that righteousness is failing, and the sages begin their oaths of innocence.
Bhrigu's oath calls down penalties such as censuring and assailing others and eating the flesh along the backbone of sacrificed animals.
Vasishtha's oath calls down penalties such as neglecting Vedic study, leashing hounds, and living in towns as a mendicant.
Kasyapa's oath calls down penalties such as selling everything everywhere, misusing deposits, and giving false evidence.
Gautama's oath calls down penalties such as pride, subjection to desire and wrath, and farming driven by malice.
Angiras's oath calls down penalties such as impurity, Brahmanicide, and refusing expiation.
Dhundhumara's oath calls down penalties such as ingratitude to friends, birth from a Sudra woman, and eating good food alone.
Dilipa's oath calls down the misery of a Brahmana who lives in a one-well village and has sex with a Sudra woman.
Puru's oath calls down penalties such as practising medicine for money and living off his wife's and father-in-law's earnings.
Sukra's oath calls down penalties such as eating unsacrificed flesh, sex by day, and serving a king.
Jamadagni's oath calls down penalties such as studying the Vedas on forbidden days, feeding friends at Sraddhas, and eating at a Sudra's Sraddha.
Sivi's oath calls down penalties such as dying without a sacred fire, obstructing other sacrifices, and quarrelling with ascetics.
Yayati's oath calls down penalties such as sex with his wife out of season and disregard for the Vedas.
Nahusha's oath calls down penalties such as living at home after taking up mendicancy, and taking payment for teaching.
Amvarisha's oath calls down penalties such as cruelty to women, kinsmen and cattle, and Brahmanicide.
Narada's oath calls down penalties such as identifying body with soul, studying under a bad teacher, and disrespect for elders.
Nabhaga's oath calls down penalties such as lying, quarrelling with the righteous, and selling his daughter for a price.
Kavi's oath calls down penalties such as kicking a cow, urinating facing the sun, and abandoning one who seeks shelter.
Viswamitra's oath calls down penalties such as deceitful service, becoming a king's priest, and assisting at unfit sacrifices.
Parvata's oath calls down penalties such as becoming a village chief, travelling on asses, and leashing hounds for a living.
Bharadwaja's oath calls down the faults of a cruel and untruthful person.
Ashtaka's oath calls down a foolish, capricious and unrighteous rule for the thief as king.
Galava's oath calls down penalties such as being more infamous than a sinner, wronging kin, and boasting of gifts.
Arundhati's oath, phrased for a woman, calls down penalties such as speaking ill of her mother-in-law, disgust for her husband, and eating alone.
The Valakhilyas' oath calls down penalties such as begging on one foot at a village entrance and every breach of duty.
Sunahsakha's oath calls down penalties such as sleeping comfortably after neglecting the daily rite, and unrestrained conduct as a mendicant.
Surabhi's oath, phrased for a cow, calls down milking with her legs bound with human hair, by a calf not her own, into a white brass vessel.
Bhishma says that after the oaths, Indra, pleased, turns his gaze on the angry Agastya and speaks.
Indra blesses the thief instead of cursing him, granting the merit of giving a daughter to a learned Brahmana and the region of Brahman.
Agastya says Indra has uttered a blessing rather than a curse, admits that he took the stalks, and demands their return.
Indra says he took the stalks not from greed but to hear the sages discuss duty, and asks Agastya to forgive him and take them back.
Agastya takes back his stalks, the sages visit other holy waters, and Bhishma says reciting this tale on Parva days brings merit, learning and heaven.
Yudhishthira asks who introduced the custom of giving umbrellas and sandals at rites, why it was introduced, and what it means.
Bhishma introduces the tale of Jamadagni, who practises archery while his wife Renuka fetches his arrows, and she is delayed one noon by the sun's heat.
Renuka explains that the heat scorched her head and feet and she rested under a tree, and asks her husband not to be angry.
Jamadagni vows to destroy the sun with his weapons that very day.
Surya comes to him as a Brahmana and argues that he draws up water and makes rain, and so sustains food, life and every rite, asking Jamadagni to calm his anger.
Yudhishthira asks how Jamadagni responded to Surya's plea.
Bhishma says Jamadagni's anger does not ease, and Surya, as a Brahmana, asks how he can pierce the sun, which is always moving.
Jamadagni says he sees the sun both moving and still, and will shoot it at midday when it seems to pause.
Surya admits the offense and asks Jamadagni for protection.
Jamadagni, smiling, agrees to protect the suppliant and asks Surya to find a remedy for the heat, saying a man who slays a suppliant can commit any crime.
Jamadagni falls silent, and Surya gives him an umbrella and a pair of sandals.
Surya says the umbrella shields the head and the sandals protect the feet, and that giving them at rites will be an inflexible custom.
Bhishma says Surya began the custom, urges Yudhishthira to give umbrellas and sandals to Brahmanas, and lists the heavenly rewards for doing so.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for all the duties of the householder and what he must do to prosper in this world.
Bhishma recounts the old tale of Vasudeva, who praises the goddess Earth and then asks her the same question.
Vasudeva asks what a householder should do, and how those acts bear good fruit.

The goddess Earth lists the duties: worship of the Rishis, deities, Pitris and men, daily fire rites, offerings to the directions, hospitality to guests, and food for dogs, outcasts and birds, all leading to heaven.
Bhishma says Vasudeva acted on this teaching, and urges Yudhishthira to do the same to gain fame and heaven.
Yudhishthira asks what the gift of light is, how it began, and what merit it brings.
Bhishma introduces the tale of Suvarna, a learned gold-complexioned Brahmana, who meets Manu and asks why flowers are offered to the deities.
Manu introduces Sukra's discourse to the Asura Vali on the merit of flowers, incense and lamps.
Vali asks Sukra what merit flowers, incense and lamps bring.

Sukra explains the origin of herbs, sorts flowers and incenses by the beings they suit, and says lamps bring energy and are best when made with ghee; he urges Vali offerings to the deities and the household gods. He then passes the teaching down to Narada, who recounted it to Bhishma.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to repeat the merits of incense and lamps, and why householders offer Valis on the ground.
Bhishma tells how Nahusha, who won heaven by merit, kept up his rites until pride made him stop and have the Rishis carry him, and Bhrigu asks Agastya why they should endure this.
Agastya says Brahma granted Nahusha a boon that drains the power of any Rishi who sees him, so none can curse him, and he asks Bhrigu what to do.
Bhrigu says he acts at the Grandsire's command, and promises to hurl Nahusha down and curse him to become a snake, with Agastya as witness.
Yudhishthira asks how Nahusha came into distress, how he was hurled down, and how he lost the sovereignty of the gods.

Bhishma recounts Nahusha's earlier piety, his later neglect of rites, and his yoking of Agastya. Bhrigu hides in Agastya's hair, and after Nahusha kicks Agastya's head, Bhrigu curses him to become a snake, which he does; Nahusha keeps his memory and asks for the curse to end.

Bhrigu promises that a king named Yudhishthira will free Nahusha from the curse. Brahma then restores Indra to heaven, and Bhishma closes by urging householders to give lamps at evening for beauty and celestial sight.
Yudhishthira asks where wretched men go who steal or misappropriate articles belonging to Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira's question continues, naming those who steal such articles.
Yudhishthira's question ends.
Bhishma says he will recount a conversation between a Chandala and a low Kshatriya.
The Kshatriya notices the old Chandala, dust-covered and anxious about a few drops of milk on his body, and asks why he bothers to wash them off.

The Chandala tells how stolen kine's milk fell on Soma plants, sending the thieving king, his Brahmanas and all milk-drinkers to hell, and how his own pride and forbidden meat turned him from a learned Brahmana into an outcast. He asks how he may be freed.
The Kshatriya replies that only by giving up his life in battle for a Brahmana's sake will the Chandala be freed.
The Chandala gives up his life in battle to guard a Brahmana's wealth and wins a good end, and Bhishma says one should always protect Brahmanas' property.
Yudhishthira asks whether all pious men reach the same region, or differ in status.
Bhishma says people reach different regions by their deeds, and tells how Gautama nursed an orphan elephant calf until it grew, and how Indra, disguised as King Dhritarashtra, seized it.
King Dhritarashtra offers Gautama a thousand kine, a hundred maidservants, gold and other wealth, asking what Brahmanas want with elephants.
Gautama refuses the wealth, saying Brahmanas have no use for it.
The king says elephants belong to kings, that taking this one for his vehicle is no sin, and tells Gautama to stop obstructing him.
Gautama vows to follow the king to Yama's realm and take the elephant back from him there.
The king says only the faithless and sinful go to Yama's realm, and he will go to a higher one.
Gautama says Yama's realm is where truth prevails and the weak can challenge the strong, and he will force the king there.
The king says only those who treat their own parents and eldest sister as enemies go to Yama's realm, and he will not go there.
Gautama names Kuvera's Mandakini region, where Gandharvas, Yakshas and Apsaras dwell, as the next place he will follow the king.
The king says the hospitable, the shelter-givers and those who eat what is left after feeding dependants go to Kuvera's Mandakini, and he will go higher.
Gautama names the flower-decked woods on the summit of Meru as the next place he will follow.
The king says learned, truthful and compassionate Brahmanas who make honey gifts go to such regions, and asks Gautama to name another if he knows one.
Gautama names the woods owned by Narada, filled with song, as the place he will follow the king.
The king says those who never beg and who love music and dancing go to those regions, and he will go higher.
The king says those who take delight in music and dancing and roam in joy go to such regions.
The king repeats that he will go to a higher region.
The king declares that he will not go to that region.
Gautama names the Uttara-Kuru land, where Sakra grants every wish and women live freely, as the next place he will follow.
The king says those free from desire, who abstain from meat and violence and are free from attachment, go to such regions, and he will go higher.
Gautama names the fragrant, sorrowless abode of Soma as the next place he will follow.
The king says givers who take nothing back, who are hospitable and forgiving, go to such regions, and he will go higher.
Gautama names the eternal regions at the foot of the Sun god as the next place he will follow.
The king says those devoted to the Vedas and to their teachers go to such regions, and he will go higher.
Gautama names the abode of Varuna as the next place he will follow.
The king says those who keep the Chaturmasya vow and perform a hundred and ten sacrifices go to such regions, and he will go higher.
Gautama says that above them are the regions of Indra, which are hard to reach.
Gautama says these regions are free from passion and sorrow and coveted by all men.
Gautama adds that he will follow the king even to Indra's own abode.
Gautama repeats his vow to force the king to give up the elephant.
The king says those who live a hundred years, study the Vedas and sacrifice with devotion go to Sakra's region, and he will go higher.
Gautama names the superior regions of the Prajapatis above the heavens as the place he will follow.
The king says kings who bathed after the Rajasuya and horse sacrifices go to such regions, and he will not go there.
Gautama names the eternal regions of kine, free from oppression, as the next place he will follow.
The king says those who give kine, keep celibacy and make pilgrimages to a long list of sacred waters go to the regions of kine, and he will not go there.
Gautama names the region without cold, hunger, joy or sorrow, the abode of the self-born Brahma, as the next place he will follow.
The king says those free from attachment who are devoted to Yoga and Sattwa reach Brahma's region, and Gautama will not find him there.
Gautama says he will follow the king where the Rathantara is sung and the Pundarika rite is held, and recognizes him as Indra, asking pardon for any slight.
Indra admits he is Maghavat, says he came to seize the elephant, and bows to Gautama, asking for his command.
Gautama asks Indra for the white ten-year-old elephant that he has raised as his own child.
Indra says the elephant has come to Gautama, sniffing his feet, and asks him to pray for Indra's welfare.
Gautama says he always thinks of Indra's good and asks for Indra's blessing, and he accepts the elephant as a gift.
Indra says Gautama alone among the truthful Rishis recognized him, and invites him and his elephant to heaven without delay.
Bhishma says Indra took Gautama and the elephant to heaven, and that whoever recites this tale daily reaches Brahma's region as Gautama did.
Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest, since Bhishma has already taught him about gifts, tranquillity, truth and compassion.
Bhishma says a person reaches the region matching his penance, and that fasting is the highest penance. He introduces Bhagiratha, who reached a region few can enter, and Brahma asks how he got there.
Bhagiratha lists his many gifts and sacrifices, saying none of them won this region, and that the fast revealed by Usanas did, which he calls the highest penance.
Bhishma says Brahma honored Bhagiratha, and urges Yudhishthira to keep the fast, honor Brahmanas with gifts, and free himself from greed.
Yudhishthira asks why people die young, and what brings long life, fame and wealth: penance, celibacy, recitation, medicine, deeds or speech.

Bhishma says conduct decides long life, wealth and fame, and lists a long series of daily rules: rising before dawn, prayers, cleanliness, eating, speech, sleep, sexual conduct, marriage, respect for elders and avoiding harm. He ends by saying conduct brings long life, fame and heaven.
Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should behave toward his younger brothers, and how they should behave toward him.

Bhishma tells the eldest brother to treat younger brothers as a good teacher treats his pupils, correcting faults gently and not dividing the family. He ranks the teacher, father and mother in reverence, and says the eldest brother takes the father's place after his death.
Yudhishthira asks why people of all classes observe fasts, what merit and heaven the fasts bring, and what to give after a fast.
Vaisampayana says that Bhishma, versed in duty, answers Yudhishthira.
Bhishma says he once asked the sage Angiras the same questions about fasting, and that Angiras answered him.

Angiras sets out the rules: Brahmanas and Kshatriyas may fast up to three nights and Vaisyas and Sudras one, and monthly fasts bring wealth, progeny and long life. Yearly and longer fasts are said to earn the merit of great sacrifices and a long stay in heaven, no fast beyond a month is prescribed, and the sages reached heaven by fasting.
Yudhishthira points out that sacrifices need wealth, and asks what rites can give poor people the same merit.

Bhishma says Angiras taught fasts that equal sacrifices, and goes through them by length and pattern, from a day or two up to a month. Each is matched to a sacrifice such as the Agnishtoma, Vajapeya or Horse-sacrifice, and to a heavenly stay, ending with Brahma's region.
Bhishma says a poor man may gain the fruit of sacrifices by fasting while also worshipping the deities and Brahmanas, and urges Yudhishthira to trust those who keep such vows.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to name the foremost Tirtha, the one that brings the greatest purity.

Bhishma says the best is the inner Tirtha of Manasa, whose waters are truth and whose lake is understanding. Its fruits are freedom from greed and the virtues of truth, mildness, compassion and self-restraint, and inner purity is better than washing in water. Sacred places on earth add to this, and purity from both sources is the best.
Heading: Section CIX begins.
Yudhishthira asks which fasts bring the highest, most beneficial and surest fruit.

Bhishma recites a fast on the twelfth day of each month, with worship of Krishna under a different name, from Kesava in Margasirsha, which earns the Horse-sacrifice, to Damodara in Kartika, which earns the merit of all sacrifices. A year of worship as Pundarikaksha brings recall of past lives, and the vow ends with gifts to Brahmanas, a fast that Vishnu declared unsurpassed.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira approaches Bhishma, who lies on a bed of arrows, and puts a question to him.
Yudhishthira asks how one gains beauty, prosperity, a pleasing disposition, merit, wealth, pleasure and happiness.

Bhishma says the Chandravrata vow begins in Margasirsha, when the moon stands in a sequence of constellations matched to the parts of the body, and it ends with gifts of ghee to Vedic Brahmanas. Its fruit is knowledge and a fullness like the full moon.
Yudhishthira asks what conduct leads to heaven or hell, and what follows a person's body into the next world.
Bhishma says Vrihaspati is coming and should be asked, since no one else can explain this mystery.
Vaisampayana says Vrihaspati arrives from the sky, is honored by all, including Dhritarashtra, and Yudhishthira puts his question to him.
Yudhishthira asks whether father, mother, son, teacher, kinsmen or friends follow the dead body, which lies like wood or clay.

Vrihaspati says each person is born, suffers and dies alone, and relatives turn away after a moment of mourning, so only righteousness follows. He urges the pursuit of righteousness and wealth won by lawful means.
Yudhishthira asks how piety can follow a body that becomes subtle and invisible.
Vrihaspati says the five elements, mind, Yama, the soul, day and night witness every deed. At death the vital breaths leave the body, and the soul takes another body.
Yudhishthira asks how the vital seed comes into being.
Vrihaspati says the elements are fed and gratified, which generates the vital seed; in union it flows and causes conception.
Yudhishthira asks how the soul grows once it enters a body.
Vrihaspati says the soul, once it enters the seed, takes a body formed from the elements, and the deities of the elements witness its deeds.
Yudhishthira asks where the soul resides, once the body and elements are gone, to feel joy and pain.

Vrihaspati explains that the soul is reborn according to its acts, that righteousness brings lasting joy, and that sinners go to Yama's realm and take lower births. He lists animal rebirths for many sins, from theft of grain, cloth, milk and oil to betrayal of trust, injury to teachers and parents, and adultery, and says the sins are exhausted in time, then urges Yudhishthira to hold to righteousness.
Yudhishthira asks what good end sinners can reach in this world and in heaven.

Vrihaspati says repentance and confession before learned Brahmanas cleanse sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food are the best merit, which each class may give according to its means. He stresses that food is life and that feeding deserving Brahmanas frees a person from hell.
Yudhishthira asks which of non-injury, Vedic rites, meditation, self-control, penance and service to teachers brings a person the most merit.

Vrihaspati says all six are doors to piety, and that the highest good comes from universal compassion, from treating all creatures as oneself and never doing what one would not wish done to oneself. Such a person leaves no trace for others to follow, and what one does to others returns to one.
Vaisampayana says that Vrihaspati, having spoken, rose into heaven before their eyes.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira addresses his grandsire, who lies on the bed of arrows.
Yudhishthira says that the Rishis and deities praise compassion, and asks how someone who has harmed others in word, thought and deed can cleanse himself from misery.

Bhishma says compassion has four parts, and all must be kept, as an animal cannot stand on three legs. Injury comes through thought, word and deed, so one should first give up thought, then word, and argues against eating meat, whose taste enslaves the mind, and recalls righteous men who gave their own flesh to protect others.
Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings at Sraddhas square with the rule against harm, and what merit and sin attach to killing, buying and eating meat, as well as to long life and strength.

Bhishma says abstaining from meat and harm brings long life and goodwill, and cites the views of Manu, Narada and Vrihaspati. He says all who kill, buy, cook, approve or eat meat share the sin, allows only meat sanctified by mantras in the Pitri rites, and tells of Vasu's fall for saying meat is edible. He praises abstaining in Karttika, lists the righteous kings who did so, and says hearing this teaching cleanses sin.
Yudhishthira is dismayed that people crave flesh above all other foods, and asks Bhishma about the merit of abstaining and what is edible.

Bhishma agrees that meat is tasty and strengthening, but says abstaining brings great merit, that flesh is for sacrifice, and that one who kills is in turn killed. He calls abstention from cruelty the highest religion, gift, penance, truth and friendship.
Yudhishthira asks why many die in battle, whether desiring death or life, and what end they reach, since giving up life is hard.
Bhishma says all creatures live by their own nature, and tells the old tale of the sage Vyasa, who saw a worm moving fast on a road where carts passed.
Vyasa asks the worm why it is in such haste and what it is fleeing.
The worm says the rumble of a large cart and the bulls' breathing terrify it, and that death is painful and life hard to win, so it flees from happiness into woe.
Vyasa tells the worm that, as a lowly creature without the pleasures of the senses, death might be a benefit to it.

The worm says every creature clings to the state it is in, so it wants to live. It recalls that it was a cruel Sudra usurer who neglected guests and the gods, but that it once honored a Brahmana guest, which kept its memory, and it asks Vyasa for guidance.

Vyasa says the worm's memory survives through a past merit, and that it may rise again; the worm stays on the road, is crushed by the cart, and after many animal forms is reborn a Kshatriya, coming back to thank Vyasa.
The reborn Kshatriya describes his princely fortune, thanks Vyasa, and asks what he should now do.

Vyasa praises the Kshatriya's gratitude, notes his old sin, and says he may rise to a Brahmana by dying bravely in battle for kine or Brahmanas, since lower births rise by steps through Sudra, Vaisya and Kshatriya.
The reborn Kshatriya, remembering his previous births, begins severe austerities, and Vyasa comes to see him.
Vyasa says a Kshatriya's penance is the protection of all creatures, and that by keeping to it he will become a Brahmana.
The Kshatriya, though living in the woods, rules his subjects righteously and, after casting off his Kshatriya body, becomes a Brahmana. Vyasa comes to him again.
Vyasa tells him not to fear death, since righteous acts bring good births, and that only the loss of righteousness should be feared.
The former worm, now a Brahmana, thanks Vyasa for lifting him from happiness to greater happiness through righteousness.

The former worm sets up a thousand sacrificial stakes and reaches Brahma's realm. Bhishma says the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra also attained good ends, and urges Yudhishthira not to mourn them.
Yudhishthira asks which is superior among knowledge, penance and gifts.
Bhishma tells how Vyasa, in disguise, was fed by the sage Maitreya at Varanasi and laughed aloud in delight, and how Maitreya asked why.

Vyasa explains that gifts surpass ablutions and Vedic vows, names non-injury, truth and giving as the three tracks of the best vow, and notes that people are righteous, sinful or neither. He urges Yudhishthira to give, sacrifice and rejoice.
Bhishma says Maitreya, a learned sage of a prosperous line who valued righteous acts, answers Vyasa's words.
Maitreya says Vyasa is right, and asks permission to speak.
Vyasa invites Maitreya to say whatever he wishes.

Maitreya praises Vyasa's teaching and purity, and argues that Brahmanas who have penance, Vedic learning and pure birth are the field of gifts, and that gifts to unworthy receivers are wasted and harm both sides. Gifts to the worthy bring merit to giver and receiver alike, and such Brahmanas deserve worship.

Vyasa praises Maitreya's knowledge and says penance surpasses gifts, since it cleanses sins and wins the Vedas and heaven, while gifts also bring happiness and honour, and the worthy deserve respect. He advises Maitreya on householder duties, blesses him, and departs; Maitreya returns the blessing.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the conduct of good and chaste women.

Bhishma tells how Sumana asks Sandili how she reached heaven. Sandili answers that outward signs are not what won it, but her devotion to her husband, in-laws, guests and gods, her discretion, honesty, and careful household conduct.
Bhishma says Sandili departs after speaking, and that anyone who reads this story at full and new moon gains heaven and great joy.
Yudhishthira asks which is more effective, conciliation or gifts.
Bhishma says people are moved by conciliation or gifts according to their nature, and tells how a calm Brahmana, seized by a Rakshasa, asked why the Rakshasa was so pale and lean.
The Brahmana gives a long list of flattering reasons for the Rakshasa's paleness, each sympathetic to his troubles. The Rakshasa, pleased, makes him a friend, gives him wealth and lets him go.
Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should behave, which gift is best, and when each should be given.
Vaisampayana says that Bhishma, thus questioned by the king, begins to explain these mysteries of duty.

Bhishma says these mysteries come from Vyasa and from Yama's penance, and lists the beings they please and the people to whom gifts should not be made. A heavenly messenger then asks the Pitris why sex and feasting are barred on Sraddha days, and about the three rice-balls.

The Pitris say that a man who has sex or eats at a Sraddha on that day lies in his seed for a month. They direct that the first rice-ball go into water, the second be given to the wife, and the third be cast into fire.
The messenger asks what each of the three rice-balls reaches, and how each one gratifies the deities and rescues the Pitris.

The Pitris praise the question and say only Markandeya fully knows these rites. The first ball gratifies the moon, the wife's ball brings children, the fire ball grants wishes, and the officiating Brahmana must keep purity that day.
Bhishma says the sage Vidyutprabha asks Indra how men can atone for killing worms, ants, snakes and birds.

Indra prescribes bathing at holy places for three days and touching a cow's back. Vidyutprabha adds a rite of eating Shashtika rice with milk, and standing on one foot on a mountain facing a fire, which cleanses sins.

Vrihaspati names sins such as urinating facing the sun, disrespect for the wind, neglect of the fire and milking cows whose calves are very young, and lists their harms. The gods then ask the Pitris which acts please them and how to repay the debt owed to them.

The Pitris answer that freeing blue bulls, giving sesame and water on the new moon, and lighting lamps in the rains clear that debt, and that begetting children rescues ancestors from hell. Gargya asks what merits these gifts bring.

The Pitris say that a freed blue bull's water and mud satisfy the ancestors for long ages, lamps in the rains bring radiance, and sesame-and-water gifts at the new moon bring healthy children. Bhishma closes by saying he has explained everything in order.
Bhishma says Indra asks Vishnu what acts gratify him, and how men can please him.
Vishnu says that detracting Brahmanas displeases him, and that worshipping Brahmanas, honoring guests, and worshipping the cow, the Aswattha and cow-dung whirl all count as worship of him.
Indra asks why Vishnu praises such small things, since Vishnu creates and destroys all things.
Vishnu smiles, recalls his victories as the boar, the dwarf and the disc, and says that feeding Brahmanas and dawn worship bring the merit of purity and the blessing of Amrita.
Baladeva says that touching a cow, ghee, curds, mustard and Priyangu at dawn cleanses sin, and that the Rishis avoid impurity during Sraddhas.
The deities say that using a copper vessel with water for vows and offerings makes a devotee's wishes succeed, while the same acts done otherwise bring little merit.
Dharma says Sraddha offerings must not go to Brahmanas who serve kings, keep cattle, trade, act, quarrel or marry Sudra women, and that a guest sent away hungry brings loss on the host.
Agni says the man who kicks a cow, a Brahmana or a blazing fire faces infamy, lasting hell, and rejection of his offerings, so one should never touch them with the feet.
Viswamitra says that offering rice boiled in sugared milk at noon in Bhadrapada under Magha, facing south in an elephant's shade, earns Sraddha merit for thirteen years.
The cow gives a prayer to be said while adoring her, which cleanses sins and wins the region of Indra.
Vasishtha and the seven Rishis circle Brahma and ask how men of good conduct, without worldly means, can gain the merit of sacrifices.
Brahma says that on the Pausha full moon under Rohini, bathing and lying under the open sky, then drinking the moon's rays, earns the merit of great sacrifices.
Vibhavasu (Surya) describes two offerings to the sun on full-moon days and warns that cutting trees or using a tooth-stick on new-moon days brings sin and angers the ancestors.
Sree says a house with scattered vessels and beaten women drives the gods and ancestors away, so they refuse its offerings.
Angiras says a man's offspring multiply if he stands under a Karanja tree every night for a year with a lamp and Suvarchala roots in his hand.
Gargya lists duties such as hospitality, lamps at sacrifice halls, no daytime sleep, no meat, and no harm to cows and Brahmanas, and says the gods reject Sraddha offerings when impure women are near.
Dhaumya says broken pots and beds, roosters, dogs and trees growing inside the house are inauspicious, so no tree should be planted at home.
Jamadagni says a man with an impure heart goes to hell even after grand sacrifices, and a poor Brahmana's small gift of barley with a pure heart earned him Brahman's realm.

Vayu lists rainy-season offerings to the ancestors and Brahmanas, names sins such as letting a Sudra light the fire or letting unfit women assist, gives a three-day expiation, and promises heaven to those who avoid or cleanse these faults.
Lomasa warns against adultery, sex with barren women and taking Brahmana property, then praises gifts of ghee, sesame, water, lamps and Krisara food and says what merit each brings.
Bhishma says the sages ask Arundhati, wife of Vasishtha, to disclose a high mystery of duty.
Arundhati says the teaching should reach only faithful or pure-hearted listeners and describes the cow-horn rite; the gods and sages applaud her.
Brahman praises her teaching and grants that her penances will keep growing.
Yama relays Chitragupta's teachings on water, lamps, sandals, umbrellas and Kapila cows, and Surya then names five kinds of sinners to avoid.
Bhishma says the gods, ancestors and sages ask the Pramathas why they afflict some men and what acts protect against them.
The Pramathas name the unclean acts that make men easy prey and then list the protective marks, offerings, fires and household objects that keep them out.
Bhishma says the Grandsire Brahman names the naga Renuka and sends him to the mighty elephants that hold up the world.
Renuka asks the elephants to teach him the mysteries of religion and duty.
The elephants prescribe Vali offerings at an ant-hill with mantras, flowers, sugar, rice and cloth, describe their rewards, and the gods and sages applaud Renuka.
Maheswara says a month of daily feeding of cows, with one meal a day for oneself, brings great merit, and mentions the bull on his standard as a sign of his favour for cows.
Skanda teaches two rites: smearing the body with earth from a blue bull's horns and bathing after three days, and offering honeyed food in a copper vessel to the full moon.
Vishnu says that daily hearing, reading or reciting these teachings keeps a person from evil and fear and brings merit.
Bhishma calls this knowledge more precious than the whole earth and says it must not be taught to the faithless, atheists, the unkind, and others he names.
Yudhishthira asks from whom a Brahmana may accept food.
He adds the same question for a Kshatriya, a Vaisya and a Sudra.
He completes the question about the Vaisya and the Sudra.
Bhishma sets out which givers each class may take food from, and says that food from Sudras, physicians, harlots and others is defiling, while the duties of each class are briefly described.
Yudhishthira asks what expiation a Brahmana must perform after accepting different foods, especially those offered to the gods and ancestors.
Bhishma lists expiations for accepting many foods and gifts and for eating in a dead person's house or with other classes, and ends with a rite for food partly eaten by another class.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which is better in this world, charity or devotion.

Bhishma names kings and sages, from Atreya and Sivi to Bhagiratha, who reached heaven through gifts, teaching or sacrifice, says their fame lasts, and promises to answer more questions in the morning.
Yudhishthira asks how many kinds of gift there are, what fruits each brings, and to whom each should be made.
Bhishma names five motives for giving, illustrates each with a short example, and says gifts increase merit and fame.
Yudhishthira praises Bhishma's learning and asks him to teach on religion and profit, since no one else can now serve as their teacher.
The narrator, Vaisampayana, says Bhishma, moved by affection for the king, prepares to answer.

Bhishma promises tales of Vishnu's power and of a doubt that troubled Rudra and his spouse, and describes Krishna's long vow, when sages came and a fire from his mouth burned a mountain and was then restored.
The sages praise Krishna as creator and destroyer and ask him to explain the fire.
Krishna says the fire is his own energy from a penance for a son equal to him, and asks the sages to tell him something wonderful they have heard.
The sages ask Narada to relate the wonder they saw on the Himavat mountains, and he begins his story.
Bhishma introduces Narada's account of a discourse between Sankara and his spouse Uma.
Narada describes Shiva seated on the Himavat among gods, ghosts and sages, then Uma covering his eyes, the third eye opening and burning the mountain, and Shiva restoring it at her plea.
Uma asks why the third eye appeared, why he burned the mountain, and why he then restored it.
Shiva answers that her covering of his eyes plunged the world into darkness, so he made the third eye to protect creatures, and he later restored Himavat to please her.
Uma asks why his faces differ, why his hair and throat are as they are, why he always holds the Pinaka, and why he is a Brahmacharin, and says she wishes to share his duties.
Narada says Shiva, pleased with Uma, agrees to explain the reasons for his forms.
Shiva explains that Tilottama's beauty made him grow four faces to watch her, that each face has its own role, and that Indra's thunderbolt scorched his throat blue.
Uma asks why he has chosen a bull as his mount when many other fine vehicles exist.
Shiva says the bull arose from Surabhi's kine, where a calf's froth angered him, and Brahma gave him the bull as mount and banner device.
Uma asks why he lives in a crematorium, full of bones and carrion, rather than in his heavenly mansions.
Shiva says he finds no spot more sacred than the crematorium, where his ghostly companions gather, and calls it a kind of heaven.
Uma asks what marks religion and how people come to know its details well enough to observe them.
Narada says the sages worshipped the goddess with hymns in reply.
Shiva names the foremost householder virtues, then five chief duties, including avoiding others' spouses, not taking what is not given, and avoiding honey and meat.
Uma asks what the meritorious duties of the four orders are.
Shiva says Brahmanas are gods on earth, that fasting and self-restraint are their duty, and that Vedic study is the source of all piety.
Uma says her doubts are not settled and asks for the duties of each of the four orders in detail.
Shiva sets out the duties of Brahmanas, householders, kings, Vaisyas and Sudras, covering study, household rites, royal justice, trade and service.
Uma asks what duties are common to all the orders.

Shiva describes the three religions of Vedas, Smritis and righteous custom, the six duties of Brahmanas, the marks of a good householder, the path of Pravritti, and the path of Nivritti with its four kinds of mendicants.
Uma asks about the high religion of the Rishis, and says she is drawn to those who live in ascetic retreats.

Shiva describes the Phenapas who live on froth, the Valkhilyas in the sun's disc, the Chakracharas near Soma, other ascetic groups, and the austere practices of the Munis, ending with a call to be friendly to all creatures.
A heading marks the start of Section CXLII.
Uma asks about the sacred rules followed by forest recluses who depend on themselves alone for protection.
Shiva describes the daily rites, diet, hardships and postures of forest recluses, and says those who follow them reach Brahma's region or Soma's.
Uma asks how the rules differ for recluses who roam freely and for those who keep wives.
Shiva says free and married recluses have different marks, but both should perform rites and avoid harm, and that sincerity is the core of righteousness.
Uma asks which duties bring splendour to ascetics, reward kings and poor men, and lead forest dwellers to an eternal place.
Shiva lists the rewards for fasting, ascetic vows, self-denial and heroic death, which range from heavenly realms to kingship and other regions.
Uma asks how a Vaisya can become a Sudra, how Kshatriyas and Brahmanas can fall in caste, and how such falls can be prevented.

Shiva says birth gives the first order but conduct keeps it, lists the faults that cost a Brahmana his status, sets out the duties by which Sudras and Vaisyas can rise, and says conduct alone makes a Brahmana.
Uma asks what conduct and acts take men to heaven, given that thought, word and deed bind them.
Shiva lists conduct that leads to heaven: living righteously, earning wealth honestly, avoiding harm and others' spouses, and restraint in sex.
Uma asks which words bind men and which free them.
Shiva lists speech that leads to heaven, such as avoiding lies, harsh and cruel words, and quarrels, and speaking gently and truthfully.
Uma asks which mental acts or thoughts bind a person.
Shiva describes good thoughts that lead to heaven, such as not coveting others' goods or spouses, friendliness to all, compassion, faith and justice.
Uma asks what acts make a life long or short, and why people differ in fortune, birth, looks, wisdom and suffering.
Shiva says cruelty brings hell and a short life, while those who spare all creatures gain long life and divine status.
Uma asks by what disposition, conduct, acts and gifts a man reaches heaven.
