Shiva describes the generous giver who gains heaven and a rich birth, the stingy and arrogant who sink to hell and humble birth, the gentle who gain heaven, and the violent who sink to hell.
Uma asks why some people are wise and others foolish, and why some are born blind, diseased or impotent.
Shiva says learners who seek what is good gain wisdom and heaven, while those who lust after others' wives or harm others suffer blindness, disease or impotence.
Uma asks which acts are faulty and which lead to the highest good.
Shiva says a man who asks Brahmanas about righteousness and follows what is good gains heaven and is born intelligent.
Uma asks why some men hate righteousness, while others keep vows, perform sacrifices or act like Rakshasas.
Shiva says men who follow the Vedas keep their vows, while those led by folly reject them and become the lowest of men, the Brahmarakshasas.
Narada says that after speaking, Mahadeva wanted to listen, so he asked his wife to speak.
Shiva praises Uma's knowledge and virtue, names several goddesses who revered their husbands, and asks her to explain women's duties.
Uma says she will first consult the sacred rivers, and calls them, with Ganga foremost, to her.
Uma says she wants the rivers' opinions first, and Ganga, chosen to answer, praises Uma's learning and encourages her to speak.

Uma describes the wife's duties: devotion to her husband as a god, cheerful service, household rites, care for kin and guests, and sharing in his merit, even when he asks something improper in distress.
Narada says Mahadeva praised Uma and dismissed the assembly, and the spirits, rivers, Gandharvas and Apsaras departed.
The Rishis ask Shiva to tell them the glory of Vasudeva.

Shiva praises Hari as the eternal supreme being and source of the gods, then traces his future birth through Manu and Yadu, foretells his victory over Jarasandha and his rule from Dwaraka, and urges all to worship him.
Narada describes the storm and the vanishing of the ghostly host, recalls the burning of Himavat, and says the Rishis took Krishna for the eternal Brahma and recited Shiva's glory to him.
The Rishis praise Krishna, say nothing is hidden from him, take their leave, and wish him a son like himself.

Bhishma says Krishna returned to Dwaraka where Rukmini bore a son, praises him at length as the eternal source who guided the Pandavas, and tells Yudhishthira not to grieve, since Time, which is Krishna, slew the fallen; he also urges worship of Mahadeva and blames Duryodhana and his companions for the ruin of the Kurus.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira stays silent while Bhishma speaks, the kings and Rishis applaud, and Yudhishthira later asks Bhishma another question.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira, having heard the duties and sacred acts, asks Bhishma another question.
Yudhishthira asks who is the one god and sole refuge, which religion is foremost, and which mantras free a being from the bonds of birth and life.
Bhishma says Vasudeva, the infinite lord, should be praised by reciting his thousand names, and then gives the names in sets with explanatory notes, ending with a salutation.
Bhishma says the reciter gains success by caste, freedom from fear and disease, prosperity, and final liberation, and calls the hymn composed by Vyasa.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for a silent recitation that brings daily merit and success on journeys, at new buildings and at sacrifices, and that is consistent with the Vedas.

Bhishma gives the Savitri mantra, with salutations to Vasishtha, Parasara, Ananta and many gods, and lists the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Aswins and Rishis to be named, along with the protections the recitation brings and the kings who used it.
Yudhishthira asks who deserves worship, whom to bow to, and what conduct is faultless toward different classes.

Bhishma says Brahmanas deserve worship and are the upholders of the world, lists their virtues, and says even an ignorant or wicked Brahmana remains a god, as fire and ghee remain sacred wherever they are.
Yudhishthira asks what reward and success come from worshipping Brahmanas.

Bhishma tells of King Arjuna, who ruled from Mahishmati and won boons from Dattatreya, including a thousand arms in battle, two at home, and the power to rule righteously; a voice then tells him Brahmanas are superior to Kshatriyas.
Arjuna boasts that he can subdue the Brahmanas, who depend on Kshatriyas, and the wind god warns him to bow to them, or they will strip him of his kingdom.
Arjuna asks the wind god what a Brahmana is like and whether he resembles the wind, water, fire, the sun or the sky.

The wind god cites the power of Brahmanas, from Kasyapa and Angiras to Gautama, Kapila and Aurva, tells Arjuna to honour Agni and Brahmanas, says Brahman was not born from an egg, and Arjuna falls silent.

The wind god tells how the Anga king's gift of the earth led Kasyapa to save her, then tells how Varuna took Utathya's wife, how Angiras dried the waters and Utathya made the land barren until she was returned, and asks whether any Kshatriya is greater than Utathya.

The wind god tells how Agastya burned the Danavas who had driven the gods from their sacrifices and refused to destroy the Asuras underground, since that would cost him penance, and asks whether any Kshatriya is greater.
Bhishma says Arjuna stays silent, and the wind god tells how Vasishtha burned the Khalins, brought the Ganga to the lake, and saved the gods, and asks whether any Kshatriya surpasses him.
Bhishma says Arjuna remains silent, and the wind god tells how Rahu struck the sun and moon with arrows in the gods' battle with the Danavas, and how the gods came to Atri for help.
Atri takes the forms of the sun and moon, drives off the darkness, defeats the Asuras, and the wind god asks whether any Kshatriya is greater than this Brahmana.
The wind god tells of Chyavana, who had promised the Aswins that the gods would let them drink Soma, and who asked Indra to do so.
Indra says the Aswins have been cast out and are not counted among the gods, so he will not drink Soma with them.
Chyavana insists the Aswins are gods, being sons of Surya, and warns that disobedience will bring evil on the gods.
Indra says again that he will not drink Soma with the Aswins.
Chyavana vows that Indra will drink Soma with the Aswins that very day, by his compulsion.

The wind god says Chyavana began the rite, Indra attacked with a mountain and thunderbolt, and Chyavana paralysed him, created the monster Mada from his libations, and forced Indra to bow; Mada was then given his roles in dice, hunting, drink and women, and the wind god asks whether Arjuna knows a Kshatriya higher than Chyavana.
Bhishma says Arjuna stays silent, and the wind god tells how Chyavana took the earth from the gods, who had already lost heaven, so they turned to Brahman for protection.
The gods tell Brahman that Chyavana took the earth and the Kapas took heaven.
Brahman sends the gods to the Brahmanas, who agree to subdue the Kapas, even after the messenger Dhanin describes the Kapas' many virtues and urges them to stop.

The Brahmanas refuse, the Kapas attack, and the Brahmanas burn them with sacred fires; Narada tells the gods that the Brahmanas were the victors, and the gods regain strength, and Arjuna worships the wind god.
Arjuna says he lives for the Brahmanas, and that his might comes from Dattatreya's grace.
The wind god urges Arjuna to protect the Brahmanas as a Kshatriya should and warns of future danger from the race of Bhrigu.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what fruit and prosperity come from worshipping Brahmanas.

Bhishma says his faculties are failing and that Krishna should answer, then praises Krishna at length as the creator of all, who appears in every age, lifted Govardhana, and is the many-named Vishwaksena in whom the cosmos is contained.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna to explain the prosperity that comes from honouring Brahmanas.

Krishna tells how Pradyumna asked him the same question, then recounts how the sage Durvasa stayed in his house, wrecked his goods, yoked Rukmini to a car, and then blessed Krishna and Rukmini and restored everything, after which Krishna always honoured Brahmanas.
A heading marks the start of Section CLX.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna to explain the knowledge he gained through Durvasa's grace and the names of that high-souled one.

Krishna says he recites the Sata-rudriya each morning, praises Mahadeva as supreme, recounts his fierce deeds at Daksha's sacrifice and against the Asuras' three cities, and says Durvasa was Mahadeva himself.
Krishna names Mahadeva and his forms, explains the sense of names such as Maheswara, Rudra, Mahadeva, Sthanu, Pasupati and Iswara, and says Brahmanas recite the Sata-rudriya in his honour.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which is the authority for a conclusion, direct perception or scripture.
Bhishma says doubts are easy to raise and hard to settle, and calls it foolish to say that only perception is authoritative, since Brahman is understood only through long study and yoga.
Yudhishthira asks which of four sources is most authoritative: perception, inference, scripture, or the practice of the good.
Bhishma says Righteousness is attacked by wicked men and can be obscured, so doubts attach to perception, inference and good conduct, and the wise should be consulted.
Yudhishthira says his understanding is confused, since if the three are authorities then Righteousness seems to be of three kinds.

Bhishma says Righteousness is one though seen from three points, tells Yudhishthira to follow the rules without wrangling, and names harmlessness, truth, forgiveness and liberality as its foundations, along with honour to Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira asks what becomes of those who hate Righteousness and of those who uphold it.
Bhishma says haters of Righteousness go to hell, while those who honour it reach heaven, and he calls Brahmanas, the eldest sons of Brahman, its embodiment.
Yudhishthira asks how the wicked and the good can be recognised.
Bhishma lists the marks of the good: courteous conduct, honour to elders and Brahmanas, rules on food, speech and sex, and confession of sins, which is said to be needed before sin can be destroyed.
Yudhishthira asks why wealth and success seem to fall to the fortunate and not to the hardworking or learned, since some fools prosper and some learned men fail.

Bhishma says that if effort fails, one should practise austerity, make gifts, avoid cruelty and be gentle, and that all creatures' fates follow their acts and nature, so Yudhishthira should be tranquil.

Bhishma says Time moves creatures toward good or evil, Righteousness keeps the soul pure and cannot be overcome by sin, the four orders share one substance but different duties, heavenly rewards pass but Righteousness does not, and inequalities among men come from past acts.
Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira asks Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, a question about sin.
Yudhishthira asks what helps a person in this world, what brings happiness, and what destroys sin.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma recites the names of the deities to Yudhishthira, who wants to hear them.
Bhishma says naming the gods, Rishis, sacred rivers and mountains, and kings morning, noon and evening cleanses sins, and closes with a prayer for growth, long life and victory.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what Yudhishthira did after hearing Bhishma's teachings and having his doubts resolved.

Vaisampayana says Vyasa tells Bhishma that Yudhishthira is ready to leave, and Bhishma sends him back to the city with advice to rule well and a summons to return when the sun turns north, and Yudhishthira agrees and goes to the city named after the elephant.

Yudhishthira consoles the widows, recovers his kingdom, is installed on the throne, and after fifty nights sets out with funeral materials to find Bhishma still on his bed, surrounded by sages and kings.
Bhishma greets Yudhishthira, says the sun has begun its northward course and Magha has come, and says he has lain on the arrows for fifty-eight nights.
Bhishma tells Dhritarashtra not to grieve, since what was fated has happened, and asks him to cherish the Pandavas, whom he calls his sons in moral terms.
Vaisampayana says Bhishma then turns to Vasudeva.
Bhishma praises Krishna as the supreme soul and asks leave to depart, recalling that he urged Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas and that Duryodhana refused.
Vasudeva grants Bhishma leave and says he will attain the status of the Vasus, comparing him to Markandeya.
Bhishma bids his friends and kin farewell, urges them to seek truth and keep company with righteous Brahmanas, and asks Yudhishthira to honour Brahmanas, priests and preceptors.
Bhishma's life-breaths rise through his head and leave for heaven, the Pandavas and Vidura prepare and light his funeral pyre, and Ganga laments her son while Krishna consoles her.
Consoled by Krishna and Vyasa, Ganga regains her composure and the kings take their leave of her banks.
A line marks the end of the Anusasana Parva.

Footnote 2 says the wind kindles dry twigs, in the commentator's words.
Footnote 3 glosses a term as the releaser from bonds.

Yudhishthira, overcome, falls by the Ganga; Krishna and Bhima lift him, and the brothers sit around him. Dhritarashtra urges him to rise and rule, and recalls Vidura's advice he rejected, ending with his own regret.

Vaisampayana reports that Dhritarashtra's words have calmed Yudhishthira, and that Krishna then advises him: excessive grief harms the dead, so he should perform sacrifices, feed the gods, the ancestors and guests, and give to the needy, since his duty is done.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that sins are removed by penance, sacrifice and gifts, and urges him to hold the Rajasuya and the horse sacrifice as earlier kings did.
Yudhishthira asks Vyasa to recount the history of the royal sage Marutta.
Vyasa lists the ancestors from Manu down to Marutta, including the sons of Vinsa and Karandhama, and describes Marutta's sacrifice on Mount Meru with golden vessels.
Yudhishthira asks how Marutta gained his power and gold, where that wealth is now, and how it could be recovered.
Vyasa tells of the quarrel between Vrihaspati and his brother Samvarta, Vrihaspati's rise as Indra's priest, Marutta's power, Indra's demand that Vrihaspati abandon Marutta, and Vrihaspati's refusal.
Vaisampayana reports that Indra's envy ends after Vrihaspati's reply, and that Indra praises him and returns home.
Vyasa introduces the old legend of Vrihaspati and Marutta, and says Marutta prepared a sacrifice after Vrihaspati's earlier agreement with Indra and asks him to officiate.
Vrihaspati says he cannot serve Marutta because he has promised Indra to serve him.
Marutta reminds Vrihaspati that he is the family priest and should officiate at his sacrifice.
Vrihaspati replies that he has served only the Immortals and will not serve mortal men, so Marutta must find another priest.
Vyasa describes Marutta returning home in despair, meeting Narada, who greets him and asks what troubles him.
Vaisampayana says Marutta told Narada about the rebuff from Vrihaspati.
Marutta says he no longer wishes to live, since Vrihaspati's refusal has left him stained with sin.
Vyasa says Narada's reply revives Marutta.
Narada tells Marutta that Samvarta, Angira's son, wanders the earth naked, and that Samvarta could perform the sacrifice if he is pleased with him.
Marutta feels restored and asks where Samvarta can be found and how he can win his protection.

Narada explains that Samvarta wanders near Varanasi as a madman, and tells Marutta to place a corpse at the city gate, follow the man who turns away, and seek his protection; if Samvarta asks who sent him, he should name Narada, and if asked to follow Narada, say Narada has entered the fire.
Marutta follows Narada's instructions, leaves a corpse at the gate, and follows Samvarta, who covers him with filth and spittle. Marutta persists until Samvarta, tired, sits to rest under a fig tree.
Samvarta asks how Marutta came to know him and warns that a lie will split his head.
Marutta says Narada told him that Samvarta is the son of their family priest.
Samvarta confirms the message and asks where Narada is now.
Marutta says Narada has entered the fire after commending him to Samvarta.
Vyasa describes Samvarta pleased but raving, claiming his brother has gone over to Indra and taken his goods, and telling Marutta to seek Vrihaspati's permission first.
Marutta explains that Vrihaspati refused because Indra forbade him to serve Marutta, and that he now wants Samvarta's help and will spend his wealth on it.
Samvarta agrees on condition that Marutta stays steadfast, fearing the anger of Vrihaspati and Indra.
Marutta swears that he will never abandon Samvarta.
Samvarta accepts, promising to make the sacrifice's rewards lasting and to raise Marutta nearly to Indra's level.

Samvarta describes Munjaban, Shiva's mountain with its gold mines and guardians, and tells Marutta to worship Shiva by his many names to obtain the gold; Marutta does so and prepares the sacrifice, and Vrihaspati, distressed by the rival's prosperity, grows pale and sick, and Indra comes to him.
Indra asks Vrihaspati whether he sleeps well, whether his servants are pleasing, and whether the gods protect him.
Vrihaspati says all is well in his own household and that the gods care for him.
Indra asks why Vrihaspati looks pale and in pain, and offers to kill whoever is harming him.
Vrihaspati says Marutta's great sacrifice, with Samvarta as priest, is what troubles him, and asks that Samvarta not officiate.
Indra says Vrihaspati already has all he could want as the gods' priest and asks what Samvarta could do to him now.
Vrihaspati says a rival's prosperity pains him, and asks Indra to restrain Samvarta and Marutta.
Indra tells Agni to take Vrihaspati to Marutta and promise that Vrihaspati will officiate and make him immortal.
Agni agrees to act as the messenger and sets out.
Vyasa describes Agni racing through the forests like a strong wind.
Marutta sees Agni arrive and asks the sage to offer him a seat, water and a cow.
Agni accepts the hospitality and identifies himself as Indra's messenger.
Marutta asks whether Indra is happy, pleased with him, and whether the other gods remain loyal.
Agni says Indra is content and wants to free Marutta from old age, then delivers the offer that Vrihaspati will serve as priest and grant immortality.
Marutta refuses, saying Samvarta will be his priest, since Vrihaspati has served Indra and should not serve mortals.
Agni promises that with Vrihaspati as priest Marutta would win the highest heavens and every realm.
Samvarta tells Agni never to bring Vrihaspati again, threatening to burn him with his fierce eyes.
Vyasa says Agni, trembling, returns to the gods, where Indra sees him with Vrihaspati and asks what happened.
Indra asks Agni whether Marutta accepted the message.
Agni reports that Marutta refused, clung to Vrihaspati, and insisted on Samvarta as priest.
Indra tells Agni to go back and threaten Marutta with a thunderbolt if he still refuses.
Agni refuses to go and suggests that Indra send a Gandharva, recalling Samvarta's furious threat.
Indra says no one can match Agni's power and that his words carry no weight.
Agni says that Indra, for all his power, could not prevent Vritra from taking his sovereignty.
Indra boasts of defeating his foes and says no one can live in peace after provoking him.

Agni recalls how the sage Chyavana, at the sacrifice of Saryati, fought Indra, and how Indra had to seek the sage's protection; Agni concludes that Brahmanas are stronger and he will not oppose Samvarta.
Indra tells Dhritarashtra to deliver to Marutta the demand that he accept Vrihaspati, or be struck with the thunderbolt.
Vyasa says Dhritarashtra goes to Marutta's court and delivers Indra's message.
Dhritarashtra, a Gandharva, introduces himself and repeats Indra's threat to strike Marutta with the thunderbolt unless he takes Vrihaspati as priest.
Marutta refuses, saying that breaking faith with a friend is as grave as killing a Brahmana, and that Vrihaspati should serve Indra while Samvarta serves him.
The Gandharva warns that Indra's war cry can be heard in the sky and that Indra will strike openly, so Marutta should think of his safety.
Vyasa says that after hearing the threat, Marutta tells Samvarta about it.
Marutta says that the thunder clouds mean Indra is near, asks Samvarta to protect him, and says his assistants are frightened.
Samvarta promises to calm the danger with his incantations and says Agni will protect Marutta.
Marutta says the crashing thunder and winds terrify him and have disturbed his peace of mind.
Samvarta promises to still the thunder with the winds and offers Marutta any boon he desires.
Marutta asks that Indra come to the sacrifice in person and accept his offerings, along with the other gods.
Samvarta says that, by his incantations, he has drawn Indra to the sacrifice, and the gods are hastening there.
Indra arrives in his chariot, drinks the Soma offered by Marutta, and is welcomed with honour.
Samvarta welcomes Indra, says the sacrifice has been made grand, and asks him to drink the Soma again.
Marutta thanks Indra for coming and says that Samvarta, Vrihaspati's younger brother, performs his sacrifice.
Indra says he knows Samvarta, whom he invited, and that his resentment against Marutta is gone.
Samvarta asks Indra to give the directions for the sacrifice and assign the shares of the gods, so the world knows it was done by Indra.

Vyasa says Indra orders the gods to build the hall and the rooms, and to prepare the sacrifice; the gods carry out the work, and Samvarta offers the oblations, after which the gods drink Soma and return home. Marutta gives gold to the Brahmanas and fills his treasury, and Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to gather the same gold and perform the sacrifice.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira is delighted by Vyasa's words and begins to consult his ministers about his sacrifice.
Vaisampayana says that after Vyasa's speech, Krishna sees the grieving Yudhishthira and addresses him.

Krishna tells the story of Indra's war with Vritra, in which Vritra drains one quality after another from the elements and finally from Indra, until Indra is saved and kills Vritra with an unseen thunderbolt.

Krishna explains physical and mental ailments and the balance of humours and qualities, reminds Yudhishthira of his past sufferings, and says he must now overcome his own mind alone before governing his kingdom.

Krishna teaches that salvation depends on giving up attachment to bodily pleasures, explains death and the eternal spirit, recites the Kamagita with Desire's boast of its disguises, and urges Yudhishthira to offer the horse sacrifice and stop grieving.

Vaisampayana reports that Yudhishthira is consoled by the sages and his family, performs the funeral rites and gifts, asks for guidance to the Himalayas for the sacrifice, and returns to Hastinapura with Dhritarashtra to rule with his brothers.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what Vasudeva and Dhananjaya did once the Pandavas had regained and pacified their kingdom.
Vaisampayana describes the two travelling in pleasure, recalling the war at Indraprastha, and Krishna comforting Arjuna, who finds relief.
Krishna says the kingdom is now secure under Yudhishthira and asks Arjuna to tell the king he is leaving for Dwaravati; Arjuna sorrowfully agrees.
Heading: the Anugita Parva begins.
Janamejaya asks what Krishna and Arjuna talked about once they returned to the assembly rooms after their victory.
Vaisampayana describes Arjuna enjoying his recovered kingdom with Krishna in a palace, and Arjuna saying he has forgotten Krishna's teaching from the battle and asks to hear it again.
Vaisampayana says Krishna embraces Arjuna and prepares to reply.
Krishna says that he cannot fully repeat the earlier teaching, and offers instead an old story of a Brahmana visitor from the heavenly regions to set out the same truths.
The Brahmana introduces the story: the sage Kasyapa, seeking merit, comes to an accomplished Brahmana who has mastered the mysteries of religion and serves him as a disciple.
The accomplished Brahmana says that worldly rewards are temporary, describes his own many births and sorrows, and tells how he took refuge in the Formless and found his release.
Vasudeva says that a Brahmana visitor asks the sage hard questions, and the sage answers them one by one.
Kasyapa asks how the body dissolves, how another is acquired, how the soul is freed from rebirth, and where a bodiless soul's deeds remain.
The Brahmana says that the emancipated sage answered Kasyapa's questions one after another, and he now recites them.
The sage explains how harmful habits and excess heat and wind force the soul out of the body in pain, how it carries its deeds with it, and what heavens and hells await it.

The sage explains that deeds bear fruit in each new body and that the soul enters the womb carrying them, lists virtues such as gifts, restraint and compassion, describes Brahma's creation and Pradhana, and says the wise who see the world as impermanent cross the ocean of rebirth.
The sage lists the marks of the liberated person, describes the soul seen in deep meditation as a fibre is drawn from a reed, and gives instructions on Yoga and meditation on the body.
The sage recalls the disciple's questions about digestion and breath and his own answers, then says the disciple left after the teaching.
Vasudeva says the teaching is a mystery among the gods that the confused cannot grasp, that liberation is open even to women, Vaisyas and Sudras, and that Yoga practised for six months brings it.

Vasudeva tells of a Brahmana who has mastered knowledge, whose wife asks where she will go with him, since he has given up rites; he answers that action cannot be avoided and describes the soul's seat, the breaths, the inner seven-flamed fire, and the sevenfold creation.
The Brahmana describes an inner sacrifice with ten priests, ten libations, ten fires, the mind as ladle, and the knower living in the body, and says that Word arose from the Veda and then Mind.
The wife asks why Word arose after Mind, whether Prana takes refuge in Mind, and what restrains Prana in dreamless sleep.
The Brahmana explains that Apana controls Prana, that the mind depends on Prana, and tells of Word and Mind asking the Soul which is superior, with Mind judged superior and Word yielding.
The Brahmana says he has two minds, one unmoving and one moving, and describes how Word can flow with or without utterance, and how Word, once sinking into Apana, returned to Prana.
The wife asks what Word said long ago when speech could not come out.
The Brahmana explains how Word moves through the breaths from Prana to Apana, Udana, Vyana and Samana, so Mind is the fixed one and Word the moving one.
The Brahmana names seven inner priests, the nose, eye, tongue, skin, ear, mind and understanding, which dwell in subtle space and do not perceive one another.
The wife asks how these priests fail to perceive one another and what their natures are.
The Brahmana explains that each sense perceives only its own object, and introduces an old story of a debate between the senses and the mind.
The Mind claims that the senses cannot work without it, since it is the eternal and foremost element.
The Senses reply that the Mind depends on them, that enjoyment requires their objects, and that rules bind only the weak.
The Brahmana names Prana, Apana, Udana, Samana and Vyana as the five inner priests.
The wife says she had believed there are seven priests and asks how there can be five.
The Brahmana explains that the breaths arise from one another, and that the good beings asked the Grandsire which of them is foremost.
The Grandsire says the foremost is the one on whose extinction and movement all the breaths depend.
Prana claims to be foremost, since all breaths stop when he stops and start when he moves.
Samana and Udana tell Prana that he is not foremost, since Apana is under his control, and Prana moves on.
Apana makes the same claim to be foremost, based on the same reasoning.
Vyana, disputing Apana, claims the same supremacy.
The others reject Vyana's claim, Samana makes his own claim, and Udana claims the same.
Brahma tells the breaths that none is superior, that each has its own attributes and sphere, and asks them to uphold one another.
The Brahmana introduces the old discourse between Narada and the Rishi Devamata.
Devamata asks which life-breath comes first in a newborn creature.
Narada says what comes first is what is separate from the creature, and that the breaths work in pairs moving across, upward and downward.
Devamata asks which breath produces a creature and asks for the pairs.
Narada traces the breaths to wish, sensation, seed and blood, links them to fire, the pairs of opposites, and calm, which is Brahman.

The Brahmana describes a four-part sacrifice of agent, instrument, action and release, lists the senses and their objects as causes, and says the breaths and renunciation serve as the inner rites and fee, closing with the praise of Narayana.

The Brahmana teaches that one inner ruler, preceptor, kinsman, dispeller and enemy dwell in the heart, tells how the Lord of creatures answers all beings with Om and each group takes a different disposition, and describes the brahmacharin who lives in Brahman.
The Brahmana says he has crossed the dangerous worldly forest and entered the wider forest of Brahman.
His wife asks where that forest is and what its trees, rivers and hills are like.

The Brahmana describes the forest's sevenfold trees, fruits, guests and hermitages, its inner fire of the senses, intelligence as its tree and liberation as its fruit, and the streams that lead the sages to Brahman.
The Brahmana says he is free of desire and aversion, and begins the tale of the Yati who objects to the goat sacrifice and the Adhwaryu who defends it.
The Yati says the goat's life-breaths should be returned, asks for the consent of its kin, and says that non-violence is the foremost duty.
The Adhwaryu says that all things have life and that living is impossible without some slaughter.
The Yati says the soul has an indestructible part, that the body is not the soul, and that the freed person has no fear.
The Adhwaryu thanks the Yati, says he will follow the wise, and claims that he is not at fault in performing the rite with mantras.
The Brahmana says that the Yati fell silent, the priest finished the sacrifice without delusion, and the wise live by this understanding.
The Brahmana introduces Kartaviryarjuna, the thousand-armed king who conquers the earth, and tells how he shoots hundreds of arrows at the ocean, which begs him to stop.
Arjuna asks the ocean to name any archer equal to him in battle.

The ocean points him to Rama, the son of Jamadagni, whom Arjuna attacks and who kills him with an axe; Rama then slaughters Kshatriyas, a heavenly voice and his ancestors tell him to stop, and he refuses until they tell him a Brahmana should not slay kings.
The Pitris tell of the royal sage Alarka, who conquered the earth and then turned his mind to the subtle inner life.
Alarka says he has conquered his mind and resolves to aim arrows at it.
The mind replies that the arrows will only pierce Alarka's own vital parts and tells him to find other weapons.
Alarka says the nose craves perfumes and resolves to aim arrows at it.
The nose replies that the arrows will only harm Alarka himself.
Alarka says the tongue craves savoury tastes and resolves to shoot at it.
The tongue replies that the arrows will only pierce Alarka.
Alarka says the skin craves touch and resolves to tear it with feathered arrows.
The skin replies that the arrows would only pierce Alarka's vital parts.
Alarka says the ear craves sounds and resolves to shoot at it.
The ear replies that the arrows would only harm Alarka.
Alarka says the eye craves colours.
Alarka resolves to destroy the eye with sharp arrows.
The eye replies that the arrows would only pierce Alarka's own vital parts.
Alarka says the understanding forms many judgements and resolves to shoot at it.
The understanding replies that the arrows would only pierce Alarka's vital parts.

Alarka, unable to find weapons against the senses, turns to concentrated Yoga, slays the senses with one arrow, and sings that Yoga is the highest happiness; the grandsires tell Rama to stop killing Kshatriyas and take up penance, which he does and succeeds.

The Brahmana names the three sets of three qualities as inner foes, then quotes King Amvarisha, who says craving remains the greatest foe he failed to conquer and that the soul alone is the true king.
The Brahmana recounts how King Janaka orders a guilty Brahmana banished, and how the Brahmana, asking where he may go, leaves the king stunned into silence.
Janaka says he cannot find any part of his kingdom, not on earth, in Mithila or among his children, and that he regards everything as both his and not his.
The Brahmana asks what understanding has freed Janaka from the idea of mine.

Janaka says all things are impermanent, that he does not crave the pleasures of the senses, and that his acts serve the gods and ancestors; the Brahmana then reveals he is Dharma and praises the king.
The Brahmana describes his liberated life and his knowledge of the universe, explains that there is one path for all Brahmanas, and tells his wife she need not fear the world to come.
The wife asks why this knowledge is hard to grasp, and asks how it can be gained.
The Brahmana describes devotion to Brahman as the lower fire-stick, the teacher as the upper, and study and austerity as the friction that produces the fire of knowledge.
The wife asks how the Kshetrajna, which is called a symbol of Brahman, can be grasped.
The Brahmana says the Kshetrajna has no qualities, can be perceived by a cleansed understanding as bees find flowers, and that practice leads to what lies above it.
The holy one continues the frame of the story: once the Kshetrajna is destroyed in her understanding, the wife becomes beyond the Kshetrajna through her knowledge.
Arjuna asks where the Brahmana and his wife are, by whom such success was won.
Krishna says that his mind is the Brahmana, his understanding is the Brahmana's wife, and he himself is the Kshetrajna.
Heading: Section XXXV begins.
Arjuna asks Krishna to expound Brahma, the highest object of knowledge.
Krishna introduces an old dialogue in which a devoted disciple asks his preceptor what the highest good is.
The disciple asks a series of questions about where he is, the origin of creatures, what truth is, what sin and happiness are, and asks for release from worldly life.
Krishna says the preceptor, pleased with the disciple's service and humility, answered all his questions.

The preceptor says the teaching is from Brahma, that knowledge is the highest object and renunciation the best penance, and tells how the great sages asked Brahma about the highest good, starting with the question of how a good man should act.

Brahma answers that all creatures arise from Truth, that the four stages of life form a path, that the twenty-four elements, with one more, must be understood, and that whoever understands them is freed from sin.

Brahma describes the body as a city ruled by the three qualities, lists the faults of Darkness, shows the lower births it leads to, explains how such beings may rise, and urges that Darkness be understood and left behind.

Brahma lists the qualities of Passion, from desire and pride to trade and ritual, describes the people it drives toward pleasure and reward, and says that understanding these qualities frees one from them.
Brahma describes the qualities of Goodness, such as joy, truth, forgiveness and freedom from ego, the rising path of the good, and their enjoyment of what they desire without attachment.

Brahma explains that the three qualities always act together, that one dominates in each creature, that they are linked to castes and to many things in the world, and that understanding them frees one from the body.
Brahma says that the Great Soul, Mahat, arose first from the unmanifest, lists its names, describes the Being in every heart, and says the one who knows it is freed from delusion.
Brahma says that Egoism arises from the Great Soul as the second creation, is the source of all creatures, and that the sages who are content with knowledge of the self reach the eternal world.

Brahma describes the five elements arising from Egoism, the dissolution of creation in reverse order, the breaths and organs with their deities, the four kinds of birth, the withdrawal of the senses, and the Highest seen in all creatures.

Brahma names the foremost of each class of beings and things, urges kings to protect the Brahmanas and good men, sets out non-injury as the highest duty, gives the marks of each sense and element and their governing powers, and describes the Kshetrajna as pure knowledge that is not seized by symbols.

Brahma lists the first of many things, from day and the sun to the householder's life and the Ganga, says that all things created end in destruction while knowledge has no end, and concludes that pure knowledge frees one from sin.

Brahma describes the wheel of life, says that understanding its motion frees one from delusion, lays out the householder's duties and six acts, and says that faithful observance of these duties wins heaven.

Brahma describes the duties of the student, the forest dweller and the wandering renunciant in detail, including diet, dress, vows, begging, freedom from possessions, and the inner self that brings release at death.

Brahma calls renunciation the best penance, describes Brahman as beyond the opposites and the qualities, uses the tree and two birds as images, and says that one who understands the field and transcends the qualities is freed from sin.

Brahma describes Brahman as a tree, a forest, the unmanifest and beyond distress, says that inner peace and breath control lead to immortality, ties the self to Goodness, and says that the self and Nature are distinct, though they are joined like a fish in water.
The preceptor says that the Brahmanas were still in doubt and once more questioned the Grandsire.

The Rishis say that teachings on duty contradict one another, list the many rival views, and ask Brahma which duty is most worthy and how the knower of the field is linked to Nature; the Creator then prepares to answer.

Brahma teaches that harmlessness is the highest duty and knowledge the highest happiness, explains the knower and Nature, gives their order and the qualities of the elements, and places the soul above all of them.
Brahma says that the mind rules the elements and that the body is a chariot driven by the mind, with penance achieving all things, attachment as death, and the immortal self as the goal.
The preceptor says the sages who followed Brahma's teaching attained many regions of happiness, and urges the hearer to do likewise.
Vasudeva says that the pupil followed the teaching and attained emancipation, having done what he should.
Arjuna asks who the Brahmana and the pupil were.
Vasudeva says that he is the preceptor and Arjuna's mind the pupil, urges Arjuna to practise the teaching, and asks leave to visit his father.
Vaisampayana reports that Arjuna answers Krishna, saying they will go to the elephant-named city, meet Yudhishthira and tell him of Krishna's intention to leave.

Krishna orders his car yoked, the party sets out for the elephant-named city, and Arjuna praises Krishna as the soul of the universe who won the war, and the two arrive at the palace, meet Dhritarashtra and the family, and spend the night.
Yudhishthira asks the two heroes what they want to say to him.
Arjuna asks Yudhishthira to let Krishna visit his father in the city of the Anarttas, since he has been away a long time.
Yudhishthira grants leave, asks Krishna to see his uncles and the family in Dvaraka, to return for the horse sacrifice, and to take gems and wealth.
Krishna is about to respond to Yudhishthira.
Krishna says all the wealth is Yudhishthira's, takes leave of Kunti and the family, and sets out with his sister Subhadra, Satyaki, Bhima and others, toward the city of the Anarttas.

Krishna rides home, marks of divine favour attend him, and in a desert he meets the ascetic Utanka, who asks whether he has made peace between the Kurus and Pandavas and whether the kin will live in harmony.
Krishna says he tried hard to make peace, but the Kauravas refused advice and were destroyed, leaving only the five Pandavas alive.
Utanka, angered, says that Krishna should have forced the Kauravas to keep the peace and threatens him with a curse.
Krishna asks Utanka to hear his teaching on the self before cursing him, and says he does not want the ascetic's penance destroyed.
Utanka asks Krishna to teach him the faultless Adhyatma, so that he can decide whether to bless or curse Krishna.

Krishna declares that all the qualities, beings, Vedas, sacrifices and Dharma come from him, that he takes birth in many forms to uphold righteousness, and that the Kauravas were destroyed for their unrighteousness while the Pandavas gained fame.
Utanka says that his anger is gone, that he now knows Krishna as creator of the universe, and asks to see Krishna's sovereign form.
Vaisampayana describes Krishna showing Utanka the vast form of Vishnu, with many faces and arms, blazing like a thousand suns, filling all space.
Utanka praises the cosmic form, which covers the earth, sky and quarters, and asks to see the human form again.
Vaisampayana reports that Krishna invites Utanka to ask for a boon, and Utanka asks for water whenever he needs it in the desert, and Krishna agrees to grant it.

Utanka, thirsty, calls on Krishna in the desert, meets a hunter who offers water; Utanka refuses in anger. Krishna explains that the hunter was Indra, that Indra had been asked to give nectar, and promises the clouds that will bring water to the desert.
Janamejaya asks what penances made Utanka willing to curse Vishnu.

Vaisampayana describes Utanka's devotion to his teacher Gautama, who would not let him leave, and his old age, which Utanka did not notice until he dropped his load of wood and wept at the sight of a white lock of hair.
Utanka tells Gautama he has served him for a hundred years without rest and asks to be allowed to go.
Gautama says he did not notice the years passing and gives Utanka leave to go.
Utanka asks what fee he should bring his teacher before leaving.
Gautama says that pleasing the teacher is the fee, and offers his daughter in marriage if Utanka becomes a youth; Utanka is made young and marries her, then asks Ahalya what gift he may bring.
Ahalya says she is satisfied and tells him to go.
Utanka asks again for a command he can fulfil for her.
Ahalya asks him to bring the celestial ear-rings of Saudasa's queen; Utanka sets out, and Gautama warns that the cursed king may kill him.
Ahalya says she did not know the danger and asks that Utanka be spared; Gautama agrees, and Utanka meets Saudasa in a deserted forest.
Vaisampayana describes Utanka undisturbed by the sight of the frightful king, and Saudasa greeting him as a meal at the sixth hour.
Utanka says he is on his teacher's business and that one should not harm a person engaged in such a task.
Saudasa says he is hungry and cannot let Utanka go.
Utanka proposes a compact: he will go do his errand and return to be eaten; he asks for what he seeks, since Saudasa is a generous giver.
Saudasa asks Utanka to name the object he seeks.
Utanka asks Saudasa for the jewelled ear-rings worn by his queen.
Saudasa says the ear-rings belong to his wife and asks Utanka to ask for something else.
Utanka says Saudasa should not use this pretext and should give the ear-rings truthfully.
Saudasa tells Utanka to go to the queen and ask for them in his name.
Utanka asks why Saudasa will not go himself.
Saudasa says Utanka will find the queen near a fountain, since he himself cannot leave at the sixth hour.
Utanka asks Madayanti for the ear-rings; she demands a sign from her husband and describes the ear-rings' powers to produce gold, protect the wearer and fit any size.
Utanka asks Saudasa for a sign to convince Madayanti, and the king gives him one.
Saudasa says he has no refuge and asks Utanka to take the ear-rings; Madayanti gives them, and Utanka asks Saudasa what his words meant.
Saudasa explains that a king hostile to Brahmanas cannot prosper, and that he gave the ear-rings because he sees no refuge; he asks Utanka to keep the promise.
Utanka promises to return, but asks a question first.
Saudasa says he will answer whatever Utanka asks.
Utanka asks whether he should return to the cannibal king, since the two are now friends.
Saudasa advises him not to return, since he will die if he comes back.

Utanka takes the ear-rings and sets out; he hangs them in his deer-skin in a tree, and fruit falls and loosens the knot, so a Naga of Airavata's race steals them into an anthill, and Utanka digs with his staff for thirty-five days.
Indra, disguised as a Brahmana, tells Utanka that his purpose cannot be achieved with a staff, since the Naga world is far away.
Utanka says he will give up his life before Indra's eyes if he does not recover the ear-rings.
Indra fuses his thunderbolt with Utanka's staff, the earth opens, and Utanka enters the Naga world, which he finds rich and splendid.
Utanka asks how he knew the steed who appears to him at the gate of the Naga world.

The steed, who is the fire-god and his old teacher's teacher, asks Utanka to blow into its body; smoke fills the Naga world, the Nagas bow to Utanka and return the ear-rings, and Utanka brings them to Ahalya and tells Gautama what happened.
Janamejaya asks what Govinda did after granting the boon to Utanka.

Vaisampayana describes Krishna's journey to Dvaraka with Satyaki, the festival on Raivataka hill with its lights, songs and gifts, the welcome of his kin, his embrace by his parents, and his account of the great battle to his father.
Vasudeva asks Krishna to describe the great battle, which Krishna witnessed, including the Kuru and Pandava leaders.
Vaisampayana says that Krishna described the slaughter of the Kaurava heroes before his father and mother.

Krishna describes the commanders in turn: Bhishma falls to Sikhandin, Drona is slain by Dhrishtadyumna, Karna falls to Arjuna, Salya to Yudhishthira, Sakuni to Sahadeva, Duryodhana to Bhima in a lake, and the Pandava camp is slain at night by Drona's son, leaving only the five Pandavas and a few allies alive.
Vaisampayana says that the Vrishnis, hearing the account, are filled with grief and sorrow.

Vaisampayana says that Krishna left out Abhimanyu's death to spare their father, that Subhadra asks to hear of it and faints, that Vasudeva falls senseless too, and that when he recovers he asks Krishna how his grandson died, whether he fought bravely, and whether he was killed by deceit, then Krishna describes the fall of Abhimanyu, Subhadra's grief with Draupadi and Uttara, and Kunti's comfort and arrangements for the rites.

Vaisampayana says that Vasudeva performs Abhimanyu's rites and feeds many Brahmanas, while the Pandavas and Uttara remain grieving; Vyasa then appears, promises Uttara a son who will rule after the Pandavas and tells Arjuna his grandson will be a high-souled prince, and urges Yudhishthira to hold the horse sacrifice, so the king sets his mind on the journey to bring wealth.
Janamejaya asks what steps Yudhishthira took to obtain the wealth Marutta buried.

Yudhishthira consults his brothers on how to bring the buried wealth; Bhima proposes worshipping Shiva to win over the Kinnaras guarding the treasure, and the brothers agree, make offerings, and set out under a favourable constellation, after taking leave of the elders.

The army marches cheerfully, crossing lakes, rivers, forests and mountains, and Yudhishthira reaches the spot where the wealth is buried, makes camp with Brahmanas in front, and the Brahmanas call for a fast of water alone while the brothers pass the night on kusa grass.

The Brahmanas advise offerings to Mahadeva; Dhaumya performs rites with cakes and flowers for Shiva, his attendants, Kubera and the Yakshas; Yudhishthira gives cattle to the Brahmanas, digs up the buried vessels and coins, loads them onto camels, elephants and other vehicles, and returns to the city, marching short stages and cheering the Kurus.

Vaisampayana describes Vasudeva returning to the Kuru capital for the horse sacrifice with his kin, and the birth of Parikshit, who lies lifeless after Ashvatthama's weapon; Kunti meets Krishna in tears, begs him to revive the child as he once promised, and falls to the ground; Krishna lifts her and comforts her.
Subhadra grieves over the dead child, blames Ashvatthama's weapon, recalls Krishna's earlier promise to save the child of Kiritin's son, and begs him to revive the child, or she will die.
Krishna agrees to revive the child, enters the prepared birth chamber, and Uttara, brought there by Draupadi, laments her dead child and begs Krishna to revive him, with her own life at stake.
Uttara faints, the palace is filled with mourning, Uttara revives and begs Krishna to save her child, and Krishna vows on his own truth to revive the child, which then begins to move.

After the weapon is withdrawn, the child revives, heavenly praise is heard, Krishna gives gifts and names the child Parikshit, and a month later the Pandavas return with their treasure to a city hung with garlands and banners.
Vasudeva goes out with his ministers to see the Pandavas.

The Pandavas enter Hastinapura with the treasure in their van, worship Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Yuyutsu, and hear of Parikshit's birth; after some days Vyasa comes, and Yudhishthira asks his leave to spend the treasure on the horse sacrifice.
Vyasa grants leave and urges Yudhishthira to perform the horse sacrifice, which cleanses all sins.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna to take up the rites of initiation and lead the sacrifice, calling him the goal of all creatures and the highest preceptor.
Krishna accepts, calls Yudhishthira the king and the senior, and pledges to do all he is asked, with the brothers taking part in the sacrifice.
Yudhishthira asks Vyasa to perform his initiation at the proper time, as the sacrifice depends on him.
Vyasa fixes the rite for the full moon of Chaitra and tells Yudhishthira to choose a horse, have it roam the earth, and have the necessaries prepared.
Yudhishthira agrees, gathers the articles, and tells Vyasa all is ready; Vyasa asks that the articles be made of gold and that the horse be released.
Yudhishthira asks Vyasa who will guard the horse as it roams the earth.
Krishna names Arjuna to guard the horse, and names Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva to their tasks; Yudhishthira carries out the instructions and appoints Arjuna.
Yudhishthira tells Arjuna to protect the horse, avoid battle where possible, and invite the kings to the sacrifice.
Vaisampayana says that Yudhishthira orders Bhima and Nakula to guard the city and sets Sahadeva to attend the guests.

The initiation is completed, Yudhishthira shines in his sacrificial garb, the horse is released by Vyasa, and Arjuna follows it on his chariot while the crowds bless him; the horse roams north and east, and Arjuna fights many kings in many lands.

The Trigartas surround Arjuna to seize the horse, Arjuna asks them to desist as Yudhishthira ordered, they refuse, Arjuna defeats Suryavarman and his brothers, Dhritavarman wounds him so that Gandiva falls, Arjuna recovers and routs the Trigartas, and they submit to him.

The horse enters Pragjyotisha, Vajradatta seizes it, Arjuna's arrows force him to flee, and he returns on an elephant; Arjuna cuts down his arrows, wounds Vajradatta, and pierces the elephant, which bleeds heavily.

On the fourth day Vajradatta taunts Arjuna over Bhagadatta's death and charges on his elephant, Arjuna brings the beast down, spares the king on Yudhishthira's order, and the defeated king agrees to attend the sacrifice on the full moon of Chaitra.
Heading: Section LXXVII begins.

The Saindhava warriors surround Arjuna with cars and arrows, omens appear in the sky, Arjuna falls senseless and drops Gandiva, the gods and sages pray for him, and when he recovers he draws Gandiva and scatters the Saindhavas, who flee in grief and fear.

Arjuna, recalling Yudhishthira's order, fights the Saindhavas, cuts down their arrows and weapons, spares those who yield, receives Dussala and her grandson, makes peace, and follows the horse toward Manipura.

Vabhruvahana comes out with gifts to greet his father Arjuna, who rebukes him for not fighting as a Kshatriya; Ulupi urges her son to fight; the two battle, Arjuna is wounded and falls, the prince is also struck down, and Chitrangada comes to the field and sees her husband dead.
Chitrangada, recovering, blames Ulupi for her husband's death, begs her to revive him, and threatens to starve herself on the battlefield.
Vabhruvahana, grieving, reproaches himself for killing his father, asks the Brahmanas for expiation, and vows to starve himself to death.

Ulupi brings a gem that revives the dead, reveals that the fight was an illusion to test her son and for his father's benefit; the prince places the gem on Arjuna's chest, and Arjuna revives to heavenly praise, and asks why the women are on the field.

Arjuna asks why Ulupi and Chitrangada have come; Ulupi explains that she arranged his defeat by his son to lift the Vasus' curse over his unfair victory against Bhishma; Arjuna thanks her, asks his son to come to the sacrifice, and, since his vow forbids him to enter a city while the horse wanders, leaves with the blessing of his son and wives.

The horse turns toward Hastinapura and then reaches Rajagriha, where Meghasandhi, king of Magadha, challenges Arjuna, is disarmed and spared, and submits; the horse then moves along the coast into Banga, Pundra and Kosala, where Arjuna defeats many Mlechchha armies.

The horse travels through the southern and western realms, Arjuna subdues kings and tribes along the way, he is honoured at Dwaravati by Ugrasena and Vasudeva, and the horse then moves toward Gandhara, where a fierce battle with the son of Sakuni is about to begin.

Sakuni's son leads a large Gandhara army against Arjuna, who defeats his warriors, spares their king at the request of his mother, and urges the king to end hostilities and attend Yudhishthira's sacrifice.

Yudhishthira learns that Arjuna is returning with the horse and that Arjuna is well; he sets the date of the sacrifice in the month of Magha, and Bhima builds the sacrificial grounds with golden halls and arches, invites great kings with their gifts, houses the guests and Brahmanas, and arranges food and stables; when all is ready, Yudhishthira rejoices with his brothers.
The sacrifice begins; eloquent debaters argue; the kings marvel at the golden grounds, the great abundance of animals and food, and feasting for Brahmanas and Vaisyas goes on from day to day.

Yudhishthira asks Bhima to honour the arriving kings; Krishna arrives with the Vrishnis and reports Arjuna's message, sent by an agent, that Arjuna is near and worn by battles, asking that the kings be honoured, that no slaughter like the one at the Rajasuya be allowed, and that Vabhruvahana be welcomed; Yudhishthira approves.

Yudhishthira asks why Arjuna always suffers, Krishna names only a small feature of his face as the cause, Draupadi is angered, Arjuna's envoy brings news of his return, Yudhishthira, Krishna and Dhritarashtra go out to meet Arjuna and the citizens praise him, and Vabhruvahana arrives with his mothers and goes to Kunti.

Vabhruvahana greets his kin and is honoured with gifts and a golden car; Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to begin the sacrifice and pay threefold Dakshina, which will cleanse him of the sin of slaying his kin; Yudhishthira takes the vow and performs the Horse-sacrifice with carefully ordered rites, golden stakes and a golden altar, and about three hundred animals bound to the stakes, while sages, Gandharvas and Apsaras attend.

The priests sacrifice the horse with Draupadi beside its body, its marrow is cooked and offered, Yudhishthira gives a thousand crores of gold and the whole earth to Vyasa, who returns the earth for a price, Krishna then gives it back to Yudhishthira, who pays millions of coins in place of the Dakshina; the priests divide the wealth, the kings and Vabhruvahana are sent home with gifts, Krishna and the Vrishnis leave for Dwaravati, and Yudhishthira, cleansed of sin, returns to his capital.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to tell of a wonderful incident at his ancestors' sacrifice.

At the end of the Horse-sacrifice, while gifts are praised and flowers fall on Yudhishthira, a blue-eyed mongoose, half of it golden, speaks in a voice like thunder, saying the sacrifice is not worth a prastha of barley given by a liberal Brahmana of Kurukshetra.

The mongoose says it will tell the Brahmanas of the Unccha Brahmana, who lived by gleaning with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, and who, in a famine, shared a single prastha of barley with a hungry guest.
The Brahmana, unable to feed the guest, accepts his wife's share and then his son's, and the father says he is old and feels little hunger, so he gives the barley away.
The son says he is his father's offspring, who rescues the father, and asks the father to save himself through him.
The father takes his son's share, gives it to the guest, and the daughter-in-law then offers her share for the sake of the grandchildren and the family's merit.
The father-in-law refuses to take the daughter-in-law's share, since she is weakened by hunger, and says it would be wrong.
The daughter-in-law insists that the father-in-law is the god of her god and that she is devoted to him, and asks him to take her share.

The Brahmana takes her share and gives it to the guest, who reveals himself as the god of righteousness, praises the gift, and invites the family to heaven, where they ascend; the mongoose then says the barley dust and the water left behind made half its body gold, and that the Horse-sacrifice has not made the rest golden, so the gift is greater than the sacrifice.
Vaisampayana closes the story by saying that sacrifice should not be overvalued, since penance, harmlessness, contentment, sincerity, self-restraint, truth and gifts equal it in merit.
Janamejaya asks why the mongoose belittled the great Horse-sacrifice, since kings and sages win heaven through sacrifices and Yudhishthira is a model of prosperity.

Vaisampayana recounts the sacrifice of Indra, where the sages objected to killing animals and asked for grain; the dispute was referred to King Vasu, who answered falsely and was cast into the nether world, and Vaisampayana concludes that unlawful wealth gives no merit while lawful and sincere gifts, of grain, fruit or water, bring heaven, as the example of ancient kings shows.
Janamejaya asks how heaven can come from lawfully earned wealth, and asks Vaisampayana to explain the surety of the highest end in sacrifice.
Vaisampayana begins the tale of Agastya's great sacrifice, which lasted twelve years, during which Indra withheld rain and the rishis worried about the food supply.
The rishis say that Agastya's sacrifice has been made with lawful gifts, but that Indra's withheld rain now threatens it, and they ask him to keep his power in check.
Janamejaya asks who the golden-headed mongoose was and how it spoke a human language.
Vaisampayana says that Anger, taking the form of Dharma, spoiled the milk of the sage Jamadagni, and that Anger was overcome by the sage's forgiveness and then cursed to be a mongoose.

Jamadagni tells Anger to go freely, since no harm was done; the Pitris tell Anger that disparaging Dharma will end its curse, and the mongoose disparaged the sacrifice of Yudhishthira, freeing it, since Yudhishthira is Dharma's self.
Heading: the Aswamedha Parva ends here.
