Note 131: Brahman is above the Prajapatis and Vishnu above Brahman; the translator thinks Telang misreads this.
Note 132: the spokes are the 'bandhanam', the nave is 'pariskandha', and home is the rim, since it limits affections and acts as the rim limits a wheel.
Note 133: the wheel phrase recurs; the translator reads 'asaktaprabhavapavyam' differently from Nilakantha and cannot find the source of Telang's 'never fatigued'.
Note 134: the student should go to his teacher's house, study and serve there, and then return to family life.
Note 135: the last three duties bring merit; the first three are the means of livelihood.
Note 136: Havishya is food cooked without meat in a single vessel, with milk or ghee allowed, and offered to the gods.
Note 137: Vilwa is Aegle marmelos, and Palasa is Butea frondosa.
Note 138: the forest dweller eats fruits, roots and leaves first, then drinks water, then breathes air; the sects differ, and the path is set at initiation.
Note 139: the renouncer begs only where cooking is finished and everyone has eaten, so he is not overfed by a householder who sees him.
Note 140: the ascetic should not bathe by plunging into a stream, lake or tank.
Note 141: 'kalakankhi' probably means letting time pass indifferently.
Note 142: the self has no qualities; those who seek it practise these duties, which form the path to it.
Note 143: 'that which has Brahman for its origin' means the Vedas.
Note 144: commentators differ on 'the ten or the twelve'; Nilakantha counts the limbs of Yoga and the four virtues of friendliness, compassion, gladness and equanimity.

Note 145: the Unmanifest is the state where the three qualities are combined; when goodness prevails, Purusha emerges, and their relation is both unity and difference, shown by the gnat and the udumbara, the fish and the water, and the drop and the lotus leaf.
Note 146: the doubts concern whether duties must be done and whether they bear fruit here and hereafter.
Note 147: the thinking or enjoying agent is the subject and what is thought or enjoyed is the object; the translator follows Telang in using these terms.
Note 148: 'sattva pradipa' means the light of Nature, which Nilakantha reads as knowledge; Arjuna Misra's reading is that knowledge of truth comes to the self through Nature.
Note 149: as a traveller needs provisions, so one on life's journey needs knowledge; action is not the proper means, since it may or may not bear fruit.
Note 150: one should not care for external things.
Note 151: once knowledge, the highest seat, is attained, the acts enjoined by scripture need not be done.
Note 152: a car is comfortable only on a car road; where the road fails, the car becomes a burden, so one leaves it.
Note 153: Arjuna Misra's stages are action with desire, action without desire, and then knowledge; Nilakantha lists action, Yoga, and the state of the Hansa or Paramahansa.
Note 154: 'katu' means pungent or sharp, as chili is.
Note 155: these are the notes of the Hindu musical scale.
Note 156: the understanding acts on what the mind presents to it, so it is the lord, served by the mind.
Note 157: 'sarvan srijati' means creating all things by becoming the universal cause, the unmanifest; there is no difference between such a one and the Supreme Soul.
Note 158: one who reads the book called the Veda does not truly know it; one who knows Kshetrajna truly knows the Veda.
Note 159: 'Mrityu' and 'mama' each have two syllables, and 'Brahman' and 'na-mama' have three, which gives the play that mineness is death and its absence is eternal.
Note 160: the sixteen are the five elements, the four organs of knowledge with the mind, and the four organs of action.
Note 161: Purusha here is the embodied self with consciousness of the body, which true knowledge destroys; 'eaters of Amrita' are those who offer food to the gods, ancestors and guests.
Note 162: Purusha here is the individual self freed from consciousness of the body.
Note 163: in a dream all that is seen is unreal; once tranquillity is reached the surroundings are equally unreal, and the Soul dwells in itself.
Note 164: the sages behold all worldly objects, past, present and future, which arise from earlier causes.
Note 165: the Supreme can be known only in the measure He chooses to be known.
Note 166: Vasudeva is Krishna's father and Yudhishthira's maternal uncle; Yudhishthira asks Krishna to convey his respect to Vasudeva and Valadeva.
Note 167: Hastinapura is also called Nagapura, both words meaning elephant; the 'city called after the elephant' is the usual name of the Kuru capital.
Note 168: 'mahyam' means 'for me', referring to Krishna's divine nature.
Note 169: a Brahmana loses penance by cursing another, rightly or wrongly, so forgiveness was the strength of ascetic Brahmanas.
Note 170: 'asat' is what does not exist, like a hare's horns; 'sadasat' is what exists and perishes; 'sadasat param' is the Unmanifest; all three come from Vasudeva.
Note 171: teachers in India taught without fee, and pupils gave a final Dakshina; Gautama is already satisfied with Utanka, so no gift is needed.
Note 172: the king's words are meant for his queen, who will understand: cursed by Vasishtha, he is a man-eater, and a gift of the ear-rings to a worthy Brahmana might bring merit to save him.
Note 173: another allusion to Vasishtha's curse; Madayanti is the king's only refuge, since her gift of the ear-rings to a worthy Brahmana may bring the merit he needs.
Note 174: a Brahmana is truthful, so Utanka will keep his word; acting falsely toward a friend is theft, which reminds the king not to harm him.
Note 175: Vilwa is Aegle marmelos.
Note 176: 'chamu' here means a division, standing for an Akshauhini.
Note 177: 'Kavi' or 'Kavya' is another name for Sukra, the preceptor of the Daityas.
Note 178: 'Krishna' here means Vyasa, who was called the island-born Krishna.
Note 179: the constellation Dhruba means Rohini and the three Uttaras; Sunday is called the Dhruva-day.
Note 180: Agnivesya was another name for Dhaumya.
Note 181: the six roads run in two sets of three, north-south and east-west, dividing the camp into nine squares.
Note 182: a karaputa is a pair of wooden chests joined by chains or cords, carried by camels or bullocks.
Note 183: the first line of verse 17 is terse; literally, each vessel was joined to another, and each half of the load balanced on a scale.
Note 184: 'Vilava' is Arjuna.
Note 185: before a grave rite Hindus touch water to the lips, nostrils, ears and eyes, a rite called achamana.
Note 186: Vaisravana's abode is called Alaka; Vaisravana is Kubera, lord of treasure, friend of Mahadeva and chief of the Yakshas.
Note 187: the last line is slightly expanded in the translation.
Note 188: Yudhishthira is the eldest brother, so if he sacrifices his brothers are regarded as sacrificing with him.
Note 189: the sphya is a wooden sword used to slay the sacrificial animal, and the kurcha a handful of kusa grass; Vyasa directs that both be of pure gold.
Note 190: the Samsaptakas who fought Arjuna at Kurukshetra were Trigarta warriors led by Susarman, named for their oath to conquer or die.
Note 191: the translator reads 'Parthadupadravat' for 'Parthamupadravat', since the printed reading seems wrong.
Note 192: Bhagadatta was Indra's friend, and Indra was Arjuna's father.
Note 193: the allusion is to Mahadeva pursuing Sacrifice, who fled from him in the form of a deer.
Note 194: the Brahmanas were to receive Arjuna duly, and the treasure was offered as a mark of respect.
Note 195: Ulupi was one of Arjuna's wives, and so stepmother to Vabhruvahana.
Note 196: 'yahubharyyata', meaning polygamy in the first line, should be read as polyandry in the second, where the reference is to many husbands.
Note 197: to sit in Praya is to remain in one spot, abstaining from food and drink until one's life-breath leaves.
Note 198: grief does not kill; one dies only when one's hour comes, otherwise Ulupi's rival's affliction would have killed her.
Note 199: the name of the city was Suktimati.
Note 200: the etymology of Gudakesa as lord of sleep is fanciful.
Note 201: Sakuni was Duryodhana's maternal uncle, and so Arjuna's too, making Sakuni's son Arjuna's cousin.
Note 202: 'chara' does not always mean a spy; the ancient kings had spies and an intelligence service, whose successors were the harkaras of the Mughal period.
Note 203: hetuvadins are dialecticians who dispute the reasons for things.
Note 204: Krishna always called Draupadi his 'sakhi', or friend, showing a chivalry toward women at a time when they were held inferior.
Note 205: the Dakshina for the horse-sacrifice is fixed by rule, and Vyasa advises tripling it, which triples the sacrificer's merit.
Note 206: the Diksha is the initiation, in which mantras declare the intention to perform the sacrifice.
Note 207: the procedure follows the scriptures, and where they are silent it follows reasonable inference.
Note 208: Pravargya is a special preliminary rite; Abhishava is the pressing of Soma juice after it is consecrated with mantras.
Note 209: the woods are Vilwa (Aegle marmelos), Khadira (Acacia catechu), Saravarnin (Butea frondosa), Devadaru (Pinus deodara), and Sleshmataka, a small tree; some other tree may be meant here.
Note 210: the translator is unsure what the constructions were; they were probably figures drawn in gold-dust on the altar.
Note 211: each animal is matched to a particular deity.
Note 212: 'suvibhaktan' means properly grouped, so there was no dispute over precedence.
Note 213: Khandavaraga was made of long pepper, dried ginger, mung-bean juice and sugar, and is perhaps today's mungka laddu.
Note 214: the unccha vow means eating grains picked up after the harvest, as a pigeon does.
Note 215: the twelve-hour day is divided into eight divisions.
Note 216: a prastha is four kudavas, and a kudava is about twelve double handfuls.
Note 217: the verse is obscure; the translator reads it as the son urging his father to keep himself alive by taking his share, since the thought of an unfed guest would kill him.
Note 218: a daughter-in-law should be well treated for the good results every family seeks, so the father cannot deprive her of food.
Note 219: Diksha is the initiatory rite before a sacrifice or vow, lasting until the sacrifice or vow is complete.
Note 220: the Bombay text reads the first line differently, so that the sage creates the materials by thought alone.
Note 221: if penance yields great results, part of it is spent, and the Rishis did not want Agastya's penance used up on his sacrifice.

Note 222: the translator suspects the mongoose passage is an interpolation, perhaps invented so that Yudhishthira's great sacrifice would not be criticised, while noting that a small gift of barley under hardship is the nobler lesson.
Title block: the Mahabharata.
Title block: 'of'.
Title block: attributed to Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Section heading naming the Asramavasa Parva.
Opening invocation, bowing to Narayana, Nara and Saraswati before the recital.
Janamejaya asks how the Pandavas behaved toward the old king and Gandhari after regaining the kingdom, and for how many years they ruled.

Vaisampayana says the Pandavas ruled under Dhritarashtra's guidance and waited on him and Gandhari with honour, supplied with comforts and gifts, while Vidura, Sanjaya, Yuyutsu, Kripa and Vyasa attended him; only Bhima could not let go of the dice match.
The Pandavas honour the old king, who lives contentedly; Yudhishthira makes gifts on his behalf, the brothers follow his orders, and Gandhari makes offerings for her slain sons.
Dhritarashtra sees no ill-will in Yudhishthira and is pleased; Yudhishthira forgives old wrongs and punishes anyone who speaks against the king, while Bhima obeys only outwardly and grows cheerless.

The Kurus see no change in Yudhishthira's warmth toward Dhritarashtra, but Bhima secretly defies him, then openly boasts before him and Gandhari that his arms killed the sons, which deeply saddens the old king; after fifteen years Dhritarashtra despairs, and he calls his friends to speak.

Dhritarashtra confesses he backed Duryodhana against the advice of Vasudeva, the wise men and Vyasa, regrets not giving the Pandavas their share, and describes his fasting, sleeping on grass and his and Gandhari's penances.
Dhritarashtra says the fallen sons have gone to a warrior's reward and asks leave to live in the forest with Gandhari, noting that a king shares in the merit and sin of his realm.
Yudhishthira says he cannot bear the old king's suffering, calls himself unworthy of the throne, offers it to Yuyutsu or anyone else, and vows to follow him if he goes to the forest.
Dhritarashtra says he has long been cared for and it is his family's custom to retire in old age, and asks Yudhishthira's permission.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya and Kripa to speak for him, then leans on Gandhari and seems to lose consciousness, and Yudhishthira is filled with grief.
Yudhishthira laments that the strong king now leans on a woman, blames himself, and says he will fast if the old king and Gandhari do.
Yudhishthira bathes the old king's chest and face with cold water and touches him with his hand, and Dhritarashtra regains his senses.
Dhritarashtra asks to be touched and embraced again, says he is weak from missing his meal, and credits Yudhishthira's touch with restoring him.

Yudhishthira embraces the old king, the others weep, and Dhritarashtra again asks leave. Yudhishthira agrees to do what pleases him and asks him to eat; the old king agrees to eat with permission, and then Vyasa comes in.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira not to obstruct the old king, who is nearing the end of life, since retirement to the woods is what royal sages do.
Yudhishthira calls Vyasa his preceptor, father and the refuge of the kingdom and says a son must obey his father.
Vyasa agrees, recalls that Pandu revered the old king, notes that the Pandavas have served him faithfully, and says the old king bears no anger against them.

Vyasa soothes the old king, Yudhishthira says he agrees, Vyasa leaves for the forest, and Yudhishthira asks his father to eat before he goes to the forest retreat, promising to carry out the advice of the others.
Section heading marking the start of Section V.

Dhritarashtra goes home with Gandhari and his attendants, eats with Kunti and the others, and then tells Yudhishthira to rule his kingdom by heeding the elders, choosing trusted ministers, keeping spies, guarding his city and person, punishing offenders fairly, and keeping a daily routine.

Dhritarashtra lists the circles of friends and foes, the six policies, the rules for making war or peace, the protection of the helpless, and the image of the cane, ending with advice that a hopeless defender should fall fighting.

Dhritarashtra advises Yudhishthira to weigh war and peace carefully, to fight only when his side is strong and his foe weak, to gather several kinds of power, to prepare his army well, and to rule his subjects righteously, which he says earns great merit.

Yudhishthira promises to follow the advice and asks for more teaching, noting that Bhishma has gone to heaven and the slayer of Madhu (Krishna) has left for Dwaraka, while Vidura and Sanjaya will go to the forest with the old king.
Dhritarashtra tells him to stop, since he has borne great toil, then goes to Gandhari's apartments, where she asks when he will leave with Yudhishthira's permission.

Dhritarashtra says he has the blessing of Vyasa, will leave once Yudhishthira agrees, and first wants to give away wealth in memory of his sons who were addicted to the dice, inviting the people to his house.

Yudhishthira brings what is needed, and Brahmins and people of all classes gather; Dhritarashtra tells them he has long lived with them, asks their leave to go to the forest, and they lament aloud in tears.

Dhritarashtra recalls the earlier kings, admits his own and Duryodhana's faults that led to the slaughter, asks the people to forgive him and Gandhari, commends Yudhishthira and his brothers to their care, and begs their pardon for his sons; the citizens weep and say nothing.
Dhritarashtra, seeing the citizens too grief-stricken to speak, asks their leave again, saying he has the consent of his father the island-born Krishna (Vyasa) and of Yudhishthira.
The citizens weep, then choose the learned Brahmin Samba to reply, and he tells the old king that his rule was good and that Duryodhana never wronged them, praising Yudhishthira as well.
Samba says the destruction of the Kurus was caused by fate and could not be stopped, names the chief warriors who fell, and asks the king to absolve his son and to trust the Pandavas to rule well.
The assembly approves, the old king thanks the people and sends them away, and he returns to his mansion with Gandhari.

Vidura reports Dhritarashtra's plan to leave on the Kartika full moon and asks for wealth for the funeral offerings; Yudhishthira and Arjuna agree, Bhima objects bitterly, Arjuna urges him to yield, and Yudhishthira tells him to be silent.

Arjuna tells his elder brother Bhima that they should honour Dhritarashtra and forget old wrongs, and Yudhishthira tells Vidura to say that the old king may take as much wealth from the treasury as he wants for the funeral gifts, and asks that Bhima not be made unhappy.
Yudhishthira praises Arjuna, Bhima glares at Arjuna, and Yudhishthira says Dhritarashtra may take what he likes from his and Arjuna's houses and that his own body is at the king's disposal.

Vidura reports to Dhritarashtra the brothers' offers of wealth and service, Bhima's reluctant consent, and the charitable gifts they suggest; Dhritarashtra is pleased and resolves to make large gifts on the Kartika full moon.

Dhritarashtra invites thousands of Brahmins and sages and gives away vast quantities of goods, animals and maidens, naming each dead kinsman in turn; Yudhishthira approves, the gifts are multiplied for the recipients, food and entertainment follow, and after ten days the old king feels freed from his debts to his sons and grandsons.

Dhritarashtra completes the rites on the Kartika full moon, dresses in deer-skin and bark, and leaves with Gandhari, Kunti and the others while Yudhishthira faints and the Pandavas, Vidura, Sanjaya, Kripa and Dhaumya follow, and the citizens lament.

The old king leaves the city through a crowded street, bids the people go home, keeps Vidura and Sanjaya with him, hands Kripa and Yuyutsu over to Yudhishthira, and Kunti refuses her son's request to return and keeps holding Gandhari as they go.

Kunti asks Yudhishthira to care for Sahadeva, Draupadi and the other brothers, confesses that she never revealed Karna's birth as the son of Surya, and says she will live in the forest with Gandhari, serving her in-laws.

Yudhishthira refuses to let her go and reminds her of Vidula's words and of the wisdom she once gave them through Vasudeva, Bhima pleads with her too, but Kunti ignores them; Draupadi and Subhadra follow weeping, and Kunti then speaks to her children.

Kunti says she urged her sons to courage after the dice loss to keep their fame and to avenge Draupadi's humiliation, that she has no wish for the kingdom they won, and that she will do penance, so they should stop following her and keep to righteousness.

The Pandavas, ashamed, stop following Kunti, who will not return despite Dhritarashtra's appeal through Gandhari; the Pandavas go back to a city in mourning, while Dhritarashtra's party camps on the banks of the Bhagirathi, performs its rites and sleeps, then sets out again the next morning.

Following Vidura's advice, Dhritarashtra makes his home on the Bhagirathi, meets visitors, bathes, moves to Kurukshetra and Satayupa's hermitage, is initiated into the forest life by Vyasa, and his household, including Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya, takes up barks, skins and severe austerities.
Narada, Parvata, Devala, Vyasa and the royal sage Satayupa come to see Dhritarashtra, Kunti serves them, and they speak to the old king on religion and righteousness until Narada speaks up.

Narada recounts several earlier kings, from Sahasrachitya to Sasaloman, who won heaven by penance in the forest, and says Dhritarashtra and Gandhari will do the same, Pandu watches over them, Vidura will enter Yudhishthira, and Sanjaya will rise to heaven through meditation.
The assembly praises Narada and honours him, and Satayupa asks him what final region Dhritarashtra will reach and when.
Narada says that in Indra's abode he heard that Dhritarashtra has three years of life left, after which he will go to Kuvera's realm, and that the question is a secret of the gods.
Dhritarashtra and the others are cheered by Narada's words, and the company leaves by the path of those who have attained success.

The Brahmins and citizens wonder how the old king, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya will fare in the forest, the Pandavas have no joy in rule, study or women, grieve for Abhimanyu, Karna and the other dead, and are only kept going by the survival of Parikshit.

The Pandavas, grieving and neglecting their duties, worry about Kunti and the old couple, Sahadeva and Draupadi urge a visit, Yudhishthira orders the army, carts, kitchens and pavilions readied, and after five days of waiting for citizens he sets out.

The army marches out with Kripa in command, Yudhishthira rides in state with Brahmins and bards, Bhima on an elephant, the twins on horses, Arjuna on a chariot, Draupadi and the women in litters, Yuyutsu and Dhaumya guard the city, and after crossing the Yamuna the whole crowd sees the hermitage and enters the forest in high spirits.

The Pandavas walk to the hermitage on foot, learn from ascetics that the old king is at the Yamuna, Sahadeva runs to Kunti, who hurries ahead of the old couple, the brothers fall to the ground in greeting, the king recognises them by voice and touch, and Yudhishthira presents the whole court to him.
The Pandavas sit with the old king in his hermitage, and visiting ascetics ask who each of them is, along with Draupadi and the other ladies of the household.

Sanjaya describes Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Kunti's daughters-in-law and the widows, pointing out Krishna (Draupadi), Subhadra, Ulupi, Chitrangada, the wives of Bhima and the twins, Virata's daughter who was Abhimanyu's wife, and the widows of Dhritarashtra's sons.
After the ascetics leave, the old king sits with the Pandavas and the women and children, and makes the usual polite enquiries.
Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira a long series of questions about his welfare, his household, his kingdom, the Brahmins, the women, and whether the Kuru race has kept its fame.
Yudhishthira is ready to answer and begins by asking after the old king in turn.

Yudhishthira asks whether the old king's penance is going well, whether Kunti can serve him without fatigue and whether she still grieves for her sons and blames the brothers, and asks where Vidura and Sanjaya are.

Dhritarashtra says Vidura lives on air and is seen in the forest, Vidura then appears emaciated and naked, runs from Yudhishthira, stops, and enters Yudhishthira's body by Yoga, leaving his own body dead; a voice tells Yudhishthira not to burn it, since Vidura was Dharma and goes to the Santanika regions, and Dhritarashtra then offers the brothers fruits and roots, which they eat before sleeping under a tree.

The Pandavas spend the night on the ground beside their mother, Yudhishthira tours the hermitages with his brothers and gives gifts to the ascetics, returns to Dhritarashtra, who welcomes the brothers and Kunti, and Satayupa and the others arrive, followed by Vyasa, who takes an honoured seat as the assembly sits down.

Vyasa asks Dhritarashtra about his penances and grief, asks after Gandhari, Kunti and the Pandavas, explains that Vidura was Dharma born by a curse and Vyasa's own power and that Yudhishthira is also Dharma's son, and offers to show a wonder or grant any wish.
Section heading naming the Putradarsana Parva, the Parva of the sight of sons.
Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what wonder Vyasa worked, how many days the Pandavas stayed in the forest, and what food they lived on.
The Pandavas live a month in the forest, sages come and talk with them, and Vyasa offers the old king any boon; Dhritarashtra, grieving for his sons and their ruin, says he has no peace of mind.
Gandhari, Kunti, Draupadi and Subhadra grieve afresh; Gandhari begs Vyasa to let the king see his children; Vyasa asks Kunti what is on her mind, and she prepares to tell him something from the past.

Kunti tells Vyasa that the sage Durvasas gave her a mantra, that she summoned the sun god, who fathered Karna and restored her virginity, and that she set the child in the water and never acknowledged him; she asks Vyasa to let her see her son and the king his wish. Vyasa tells her she is blameless, since gods can beget children by thought, sight or touch.

Vyasa promises Gandhari, Kunti and Draupadi that they will see their dead, explains that the heroes were portions of divine beings who came down to earth for a purpose, names several of them, and tells everyone to go to the Bhagirathi.
The whole company, including Dhritarashtra and the Pandavas, goes to the Bhagirathi, takes up camp on the bank, and waits out the day until night falls.

After the evening rites, the company gathers and Vyasa calls up the dead from the Bhagirathi, Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Duryodhana and the other warriors of both sides rise in celestial robes, Gandhari and Dhritarashtra receive divine sight, and the old king is full of joy.

Sons, wives, brothers and friends meet the dead, the Pandavas are reconciled with Karna, and everyone spends the night in happiness; then Vyasa dismisses the crowd, the dead return to their heavenly realms, the widows bathe in the river to join their husbands, and the text ends with rewards promised to those who hear or recite this narrative.
Sauti says Janamejaya was pleased with the story and asks Vaisampayana how dead bodies can return in their old forms.

Vaisampayana says deeds are never lost, the body is born from deeds, the soul is not harmed by pleasure or pain, grief over separation is foolish, and only knowing body from self frees a person from error.
Vaisampayana says Dhritarashtra, who had never seen his sons, now sees them through Vyasa's grace, and that Vidura and Dhritarashtra both attained success through their penances and Vyasa.
Janamejaya asks that Vyasa also show him his father as he was when he died, so that he may believe the story.

Sauti says Vyasa brings Parikshit back to life in his former form, along with Samika and Sringin, and Janamejaya bathes and pours water on his father, then speaks to Astika about the wonder of the sacrifice.
Astika says the sacrifice where Vyasa is present will conquer both worlds, recalls the destruction of the snakes and Takshaka's escape, and says the king has gained merit from seeing this history.
Sauti says Janamejaya honours Vaisampayana and asks him for the sequel to Dhritarashtra's life in the forest.
Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra and Yudhishthira did after seeing the dead.

Dhritarashtra is comforted, the crowd leaves, and Vyasa urges Dhritarashtra to send Yudhishthira back to rule, since more than a month has passed, and Dhritarashtra tells Yudhishthira he is content and has no need of him.
Yudhishthira says he has done nothing wrong and will serve the old couple, but Gandhari insists he return to the throne and obey his father.
Yudhishthira laments that the old king casts him off, names the ruined peoples, and says he wants only penance; Sahadeva says he will stay with his mothers, and Kunti sends all of them back home.
Yudhishthira agrees to go, Dhritarashtra blesses and dismisses the brothers, the women take their leave, and the party sets off for Hastinapura.
Section heading naming the Naradagamana Parva, the Parva of Narada's coming.
Two years after the return, Narada visits Yudhishthira, who welcomes him and asks about his health and the lands he has passed through.
Narada says he has not seen Yudhishthira for a long time and has come from his hermitage after visiting many sacred waters, including the Ganga.
Yudhishthira asks whether Narada has seen his father on the Ganga and asks after the health of the king, Gandhari, Kunti and Sanjaya.

Narada says the old king went to Gangadvara with his fire, Gandhari, Kunti and Sanjaya, lived on air and pebbles in severe penance, and finally sat in meditation as a forest fire burned him, Gandhari and Kunti; Sanjaya escaped to the Himalayas, and the ascetics did not mourn.
Hearing of the death, the Pandavas, the women of the palace and the citizens wail; Yudhishthira cries out in grief, then steadies himself and begins to speak.

Yudhishthira laments that fate is unpredictable, recalls his father's former splendour, grieves most for Kunti, blames the fire-god and Sahadeva, imagines her last cries, and the Pandavas and household weep as the cries fill the palace.

Narada says the old king was not burned by a profane fire, but by his own sacred fire, which the attending priests left in the forest and which spread into a blaze, and that Gandhari and Kunti have also attained a good end, so Yudhishthira should perform the water rites with his brothers.

The Pandavas, the household and the citizens go to the Ganga, make water offerings to the three, send men to Gangadvara for the cremation, and on the twelfth day give lavish gifts in memory of the old king and queens, after which Narada comforts Yudhishthira and departs, and Dhritarashtra's life is summed up as three years in the forest and fifteen in the city.
The closing benediction says that whoever listens to this Asramavasika Parva with attention and then feeds Brahmins with offerings will be rewarded.
Heading marking the end of the Asramavasika Parva.
Heading that introduces the translator's footnotes.
Note 1 explains the word Aralikas as cooks who prepared herbs cut with a blade, and describes the spiced preparation called Ragakhandava.
Note 2 recounts how the burdened earth asked the Grandsire for relief, and Vishnu incarnated as Krishna to lighten her load.

Title line naming the Mahabharata.
The connecting word of the title line.
Attribution line naming Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa as the author.
An opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati, and to the word Jaya.
Yudhishthira sees strange omens in the thirty-sixth year, hears of the Vrishni slaughter, and he and his brothers sink into despair.
Janamejaya asks how the Andhakas, Vrishnis and Bhojas came to be destroyed while Vasudeva was still alive.
Vaishampayana says a great calamity fell on the Vrishnis in the thirty-sixth year, and Time drove them to die through the iron bolt.
Janamejaya asks who cursed these heroes and asks for a full account.
Some Vrishni heroes, including Samva, disguise him as a pregnant woman and ask the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanwa and Narada about the child.
The sages see through the trick and curse that Samva will bear an iron bolt that destroys the clan, with only Rama and Janardana spared.
Krishna accepts that what is fated will happen. Samva bears the bolt, Ugrasena has it ground to powder and thrown into the sea, and a ban on making liquor is proclaimed under penalty of death.
Time appears in Vrishni homes, many unnatural omens follow, and Krishna recognizes the thirty-sixth year and orders the clan to the sea-coast for a pilgrimage.
Dreams and portents appear, the clan goes to Prabhasa with families and supplies, and the feasting begins there.
Uddhava leaves for his own journey, the men drink heavily at the revels, and Yuyudhana mocks Kritavarma, which Pradyumna applauds.
Kritavarma insults Satyaki by pointing at him and recalling how Satyaki had treated the armless Bhurishrava.
Krishna is angered, Satyaki recalls Kritavarma's wrong against Satrajit, and Satyaki swears to kill him as Draupadi's sons were killed.
Satyaki kills Kritavarma, a brawl spreads, Satyaki and Pradyumna die, and Krishna turns blades of grass into iron bolts that destroy the clan. Daruka and Vabhru then urge Krishna to go to Rama.
Krishna and Vabhru find Rama alone under a tree, and Krishna sends Daruka to tell Arjuna of the destruction.
Krishna tells Vabhru to protect the women, Vabhru is killed by a bolt, and Krishna asks Rama to wait for him.
Krishna tells his father to protect the women, says he will go to the forest with Rama, and comforts the grieving women with the promise that Arjuna will come.
In the forest Krishna sees Rama's soul leave his mouth as a white serpent, and the nagas and sacred rivers receive it at the ocean.
Krishna recalls Gandhari's words and Durvasas's earlier words, decides his own time to leave has come, and lies down in yoga.
The hunter Jara shoots Krishna in the heel, mistaking him for a deer. Krishna comforts him and rises to heaven, where the gods and sages welcome him.
Daruka tells the Pandavas of the Vrishni deaths, Arjuna goes to Dwaraka and sees the empty city and its grieving women, and he comforts them before going to his uncle.
Arjuna bows to his uncle, who is too overcome to greet him in the usual way and weeps for his dead sons and kin.

The uncle speaks of his grief, blames the sages' curse rather than any individual, and relays Krishna's last words: Arjuna should take charge of the women and the kingdom. He says he will starve himself.
Arjuna tells his uncle that the Earth is unbearable without the Vrishni heroes, orders the citizens to prepare, names Vajra as the new king, and sets a date for leaving.
Krishna dies through yoga, the women mourn in his house, and his body is carried out with ceremony. His wives burn on the pyre, and Arjuna lights it.
Arjuna performs the rites for the slain Vrishnis, cremates Rama and Vasudeva, and leads a large procession of widows and people out of the city.

The sea floods Dwaraka behind them. On the road, Abhira robbers attack, Arjuna's bow and weapons fail him, and many women are taken. He settles the remaining women and people in different places, and some widows burn themselves or go to the forest. Arjuna then goes to Vyasa's retreat.
Arjuna enters the hermitage of Vyasa and finds him sitting alone.
Arjuna introduces himself and waits. Vyasa welcomes him, asks him to sit, and questions him about possible impurities or defeats that might explain his dejection.
Arjuna recounts the Vrishni slaughter at Prabhasa, the robbery of the women, his failed strength and weapons, and Krishna's departure, and says he does not want to live.

Vyasa consoles him: the destruction was fated and Krishna allowed it, Krishna was the ancient sage who drove Arjuna's chariot, the Pandavas have done their divine work, and it is now time for them to depart.
Opening invocation that bows to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after hearing of the Vrishni and Andhaka fight and Krishna's ascent.
Vaishampayana reports that Yudhishthira, blaming Time, resolves to leave the world, and Arjuna and the twins agree.
The brothers hand the kingdom to Yuyutsu and install Parikshit, and Yudhishthira speaks to Subhadra about the rule of Parikshit and Vajra.
Yudhishthira offers water to the dead Yadavas and Krishna, honours sages with feasts and gifts, and places Parikshit under Kripa as his teacher.
Yudhishthira tells his subjects of his plan; they object but he persuades them. The brothers, Draupadi and the sacred fires are given up, and all put on bark garments.
The five brothers, Draupadi and a dog set out eastward while the citizens turn back, and Ulupi and Chitrangada go to their own places.
At the sea of red waters, the fire god appears and asks Arjuna to give up Gandiva and the quivers, and tells him the discus has vanished.
Arjuna throws the bow and quivers into the sea, the fire god departs, and the Pandavas turn south, west and north on their circuit of the earth.
The Pandavas cross Himavat and a sand desert and reach Meru; Draupadi falls, and Bhima asks Yudhishthira what she did wrong.
Yudhishthira says Draupadi favoured Arjuna above the others, and that she now bears the result.
Sahadeva falls, and Bhima asks why this humble brother has fallen.
Yudhishthira says Sahadeva thought no one equal to him in wisdom, and that this was his fault.
Nakula falls, and Bhima laments that this obedient brother, unmatched in beauty, has fallen too.
Yudhishthira says Nakula thought himself the most beautiful and that fate must be borne.
Arjuna falls in grief, and Bhima says Arjuna never spoke an untruth, so asks what evil brought him down.
Yudhishthira says Arjuna boasted he would defeat all foes in a single day and did not do it.
Yudhishthira walks on, and then Bhima falls.
Bhima, having fallen, begins to speak to Yudhishthira, calling himself the king's darling.
Bhima continues, asking the king why he has dropped down.
He asks the king to tell him the reason if he knows it.
Yudhishthira says Bhima ate greedily, boasted of strength, and never thought of others while eating.
Yudhishthira walks on without looking back, and only the dog follows him.
Shakra arrives in a chariot, filling the sky and earth with noise, and invites the son of Pritha to climb aboard; Yudhishthira says he will not go without his brothers and Draupadi.
Shakra replies that the brothers have gone to heaven before him and that Yudhishthira alone will go there in his own body.
Yudhishthira asks that the dog, devoted to him, be allowed to come along.
Shakra offers immortality and heaven's rewards if Yudhishthira casts off the dog, which he says is not cruel.
Yudhishthira refuses, saying it is hard for a righteous man to commit an unrighteous act, and he will not give up one devoted to him.
Shakra says there is no place in heaven for those with dogs, and that the Krodhavasas take away their merit, so he should abandon the dog.
Yudhishthira says abandoning a devoted follower is as sinful as killing a Brahmana, and lists the people he vows never to forsake.
Shakra says a dog's sight of offerings takes them away, and Yudhishthira answers that he could not revive his dead brothers and lists four acts equal to abandoning a devoted one.
The dog changes into Dharma, the god of righteousness, who speaks to Yudhishthira with praise.
Dharma recalls the test at the Dwaita woods, where Yudhishthira asked for Nakula's revival, and says he gave up heaven's chariot rather than the dog, so his reward is secure.
Dharma, Shakra, the Maruts, the Ashvinis and others lift Yudhishthira onto a car to heaven, and Narada praises him as the only man to reach heaven in his own body.
Yudhishthira greets the gods and sages and says he will go wherever his brothers have gone, whether happy or miserable.
Shakra urges him to stay in the heaven he has earned and asks why human affections still hold him.
Yudhishthira says he will not stay apart from his brothers and Draupadi, and wants to go where they have gone.
A line marking the end of the Mahaprasthanika section.
Title line: The Mahabharata.
Connecting word: of.
Author line naming Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Opening invocation to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati.
Janamejaya asks what regions his ancestors reached in heaven, and asks Vaishampayana to tell him.
Yudhishthira sees Duryodhana seated in splendor among the gods and is filled with rage, and turns away.
Yudhishthira tells his companions he will not share heaven with Duryodhana, recalling the wrongs done to his family.
Narada smiles and says enmities end in heaven. He notes Duryodhana's honor there for dying as a warrior.
Narada tells Yudhishthira to put aside the old sufferings and greet Duryodhana as heaven's customs require.
Yudhishthira asks where his brothers and allies are, and names a long list of fallen heroes he does not see.
Yudhishthira says heaven is empty without his brothers and allies, and asks to see the great warriors who died for him.
The gods tell him that if he longs to be with them, he may go, and they will do as he wishes.
The messenger leads Yudhishthira along a foul, dark road to where his fallen comrades are.
The road is described in detail: boiling rivers, razor-leaved trees, iron jars of boiling oil, and tortured sinners.
Yudhishthira asks how much farther they must go, where his brothers are, and what region this is.
The messenger says this is as far as he may go and offers to take Yudhishthira back if he is tired.
Overcome by the stench, Yudhishthira turns to go back, then hears pleas from all sides to stay a moment longer.
Yudhishthira cries out in pity. The voices sound familiar to him, though he cannot place them.
Yudhishthira asks the voices who they are.
Yudhishthira asks the voices who they are and why they remain in this place.
One voice answers, I am Karna.
Other voices claim the names Bhimasena, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva.
More voices name Dhrishtadyumna, Draupadi and the sons of Draupadi.
The narrator notes that the voices spoke in this way.
Yudhishthira wonders what sin these righteous people could have committed, while Duryodhana prospers, and asks whether he is dreaming.
Yudhishthira grows furious, rebukes the gods and Dharma, and tells the messenger to report back that he will stay with his suffering brothers. The messenger reports to Indra.
The gods, led by Indra, and Dharma arrive, the darkness lifts, the hellish sights vanish, and a pleasant breeze blows.

Indra welcomes Yudhishthira, says the illusions have ended, and explains that Yudhishthira was shown hell because of his earlier deception of Drona. He says the sinners, including Yudhishthira's brothers and allies, have all been cleansed.

Indra says Karna has gained success, urges Yudhishthira to let go of grief, and invites him to enjoy the heavenly regions he earned, including those won by the Rajasuya sacrifice. He names royal sages who dwell there and points to the Ganga as the way to cleanse his human nature.
Dharma praises his son for devotion, truthfulness and self-control, and says this was the third test, recalling the earlier tests at the lake and in the form of a dog.
Dharma says his brothers did not deserve hell and that the whole affair was an illusion made by Indra. He says Draupadi did not deserve it either, and urges Yudhishthira to bathe in the Ganga.

Yudhishthira bathes in the Ganga, casts off his human body, and is freed of enmity and grief. Surrounded by the gods, he proceeds to the heroes, the Pandavas and Dhartarashtras, who are at peace in their places.
Yudhishthira, praised by gods and sages, goes to where the Kuru heroes are. He sees Govinda in his Brahma-form, and Phalguna adoring him, and they greet him with honor.
He sees Karna shining like many suns, Bhima sitting among the Maruts beside the wind god, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva in the place of the Ashvinis.

He sees Draupadi, wearing lotus garlands and shining with sunlike splendor. Yudhishthira wants to question her, but Indra speaks first, explaining that she was born for Yudhishthira's sake and that the five sons were his and hers.

Indra identifies more of the dead: Dhritarashtra as a Gandharva king, Karna as Yudhishthira's eldest brother, Abhimanyu with Soma, Pandu with Kunti and Madri, Bhishma among the Vasus, and Drona beside Brihaspati. Other kings who fought for Duryodhana now move among the Gandharvas and Yakshas, having earned heaven by their merit.
Janamejaya asks how long Bhishma, Drona, Dhritarashtra, Karna, Ghatotkaca and many others remained in heaven, and whether their place there is lasting.
Sauti says the Rishi, with Vyasa's permission, begins to answer the king's question.
Vaishampayana says not everyone returns to his own nature when his deeds end, and that Vyasa, who knows the end of every act, taught him this mystery.

A long catalogue follows. Bhishma joins the Vasus, Drona enters Brihaspati, Abhimanyu enters Soma, Karna enters Surya, Yudhishthira joins the god of Righteousness, and Vasudeva enters Narayana. The 16,000 wives of Vasudeva rise to heaven as Apsaras after plunging into the Sarasvati. The fallen warriors become gods or Yakshas, and Duryodhana's side become Rakshasas.
Sauti says Janamejaya was amazed. The priests finish the rites, Astika is glad, Janamejaya gives gifts to the Brahmanas, and he returns to the city named after the elephant.

Sauti says he has told everything that Vaishampayana recited at the snake sacrifice, at Vyasa's command. He describes the composer, Krishna, as a truthful and all-knowing sage, and says the work aims to spread the fame of the Pandavas and other Kshatriyas.
Those who recite or hear the work are promised cleansing of sins, a place in heaven, and food for the ancestors at rites.
The name is explained. The work's topic is the Bharata family, so it is called Bharata, and its great weight makes it Mahabharata. Those who understand it are cleansed and may reach liberation.

The work is said to hold everything found elsewhere. It is called Jaya, and Krishna made a shorter version and a longer one of sixty lakhs of verses, divided among the worlds of the gods, Pitris, Yakshas and humans.
Narada recited it to the gods, Asita-Devala to the Pitris, Suka to the Rakshasas and Yakshas, and Vaishampayana to human beings. Listening with devotion brings fame and cleansing.
Vyasa had his son Suka recite the work along with four verses on life's transience, the fleeting nature of joy and fear, righteousness as the lasting good, and the eternal soul.
Reciting the work at dawn brings reward and high success. The work is compared to the ocean and the Himalayas as a mine of gems, and is praised as nectar and sacred.
Janamejaya asks what rites should be followed in hearing the Bharata, what rewards follow, which deities to worship, which gifts to give at each parva, and what qualities the reciter should have.
Vaishampayana says he will explain briefly. The work contains the births of gods and Rishis and the whole universe, including the Rudras, Adityas, Gandharvas, mountains and seasons.

Hearing the work cleanses even terrible sins. The listener should make offerings to the honored figures and give Brahmanas cattle, gems, maidens, land, cloth, conveyances and other goods, even one's own self.
The listener should hear the work without doubt, with cheer and joy, and give gifts according to his means as he listens.
The listener must be truthful, self-controlled and faithful. The reciter must be pure, learned, white-clad, free of malice and generous.
The reciter should recite calmly, clearly and sweetly, with proper emphasis, and begin with a salute to Narayana, Nara and Sarasvati and the word Jaya.
At the first Parana, gifts to Brahmanas earn the reward of the Agnishtoma sacrifice and a heavenly car with Apsaras in attendance.
At the second Parana, the listener earns the reward of the Atiratra vow and rides a car made of precious gems, receiving high honor in heaven.
At the third Parana, the listener earns the reward of the Dwadasaha vow and lives in heaven for countless years like a god.
At the fourth Parana, the listener earns the reward of the Vajapeya sacrifice.
At the fifth Parana, the fruits are doubled. The listener rides a car like the rising sun and enjoys bliss with Indra for many years.
The sixth Parana doubles the fruits and the seventh triples them, with a car like the Kailasa peak and Apsaras to wait on him.
The eighth Parana brings the reward of the Rajasuya sacrifice. The listener rides a moon-bright car, served by beautiful women, and rests in their laps.
The ninth Parana brings the reward of the Horse-sacrifice. The listener rides a golden-pillared car with Apsaras and Gandharvas around him.
The tenth Parana brings a bell-hung car, crowned and gleaming, from which he roams the heavenly regions.

The listener is honored in heaven for 21,000 years, visiting the regions of the Sun, Moon, Siva and Vishnu. The reciter should be given animals, cars, gold, cloth and perfume, and worshipped as a god.
Gifts should be given to Brahmanas and Kshatriyas after checking their birth, character and devotion. Blessings are said before the reading, and the reciter is first fed honey and frumenty.
During the Astika-parva, Brahmanas are fed fruit, roots, frumenty, honey, clarified butter and sweet rice.
During the Sabha-parva, Brahmanas are fed havisya along with cakes and sweets.
During the Aranyaka-parva, the superior Brahmanas are fed fruit and roots.
During the Arani-parva, water pots and many kinds of fine food, rice and fruit are given to Brahmanas.
During the Virata-parva, robes are given. During the Udyoga-parva, Brahmanas receive perfume, garlands and fine food.
During the Bhishma-parva, cars and conveyances are given, along with pure, well-cooked food.
During the Drona-parva, Brahmanas receive superior food, beds, bows and swords.
During the Karna-parva, the householder feeds Brahmanas the finest pure, well-cooked food with a focused mind.
During the Shalya-parva, sweets, sweet rice, wheat cakes, and nourishing food and drink are given.
During the Gada-parva, Brahmanas are fed food mixed with mudga.
During the Stri-parva, Brahmanas receive gems and precious stones. During the Aishika-parva, ghee-rice comes first, then fine food.
During the Shanti-parva, Brahmanas are fed havisya.
During the Asvamedhika-parva, agreeable food is given. During the Asramvasika-parva, Brahmanas are fed havisya.
During the Mausala-parva, scents and pleasing garlands are given.
During the Mahaprasthanika-parva, similar agreeable presents are given.
During the Svarga-parva, Brahmanas are fed havisya.
When the Harivansa ends, a thousand Brahmanas are fed, each receives a cow with a gold piece, and the poor receive half of that.

When all the parvas are done, the householder gives the reciter a copy of the Mahabharata with gold. The book is worshipped with rites, gifts and feasts for Brahmanas, and the reciter must be learned and clear of voice.
Vaishampayana says he has given the rules as asked, urges the king to follow them with faith, and praises the Bharata as sacred, the highest scripture, and a path to liberation.

The Bharata praises Hari in the Vedas, Ramayana and itself. Listening destroys sin like sunrise dispels darkness. Women seeking children are urged to hear it, and gifts such as a gold-horned cow, ornaments and land are recommended, along with a homa after the reading.
Anyone who listens devotedly is cleansed of every sin, even grave ones, and reaches the realm of Vishnu.
Heading: the end of the Svargarohanika-parva.
Closing line: the Eighteen parvas of the Mahabharata are now complete.
